Notable amendments: 42nd (the mini-Constitution), 44th (restored the property right as a legal right), 52nd (anti-defection), 73rd and 74th (Panchayats and Municipalities), 86th (education), 101st (GST), 103rd (EWS quota), 104th (extended SC/ST reservation, ended Anglo-Indian nomination), 106th (women's reservation, 2023). The procedure was borrowed partly from the South African constitution.

question: Consider the following statements : Attorney General of India can 1. take part in the proceedings of the Lok Sabha 2. be amember of a committee of the Lok Sabha 3. speak in the Lok Sabha 4. vote in the Lok Sabha B-BRO-M-HTA/46A Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Attorney General (AG) of India is the first law officer of the Government of India, appointed by the President under Article 76 and holding office during the pleasure of the President. He must be a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. His duties include advising the Government on legal matters and appearing for it in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Article 88 gives the AG (and every Minister) the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting, and any parliamentary committee of which he is named a member, but expressly says he shall have no right to vote. This explains the elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 3 flow directly from Article 88, while statement 4 contradicts its last clause. Hence any option containing 4 (option b) is out. Option (a) and (d) are incomplete because they omit committee membership. The AG is not a member of Parliament, not a member of the Cabinet, and does not get a fixed term or a constitutionally fixed remuneration; it is determined by the President. He is also not debarred from private practice, though he cannot advise against the Government.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it recognises only participation in proceedings and ignores the rights to speak and to sit on committees under Article 88.
(b) is wrong: it includes voting (4), which Article 88 expressly denies the Attorney General.
(c) is correct: the AG can take part in proceedings, be a committee member and speak, but cannot vote.
(d) is wrong: it omits committee membership (2), which Article 88 permits.
keyfact: Article 88: Attorney General can speak, take part and sit on committees of Parliament, but cannot vote.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: the AG can indeed take part in proceedings, but this is only one of the rights. Article 88 gives the AG, like a Minister, the right to speak and take part in either House, joint sittings and committees of which he is a named member. He has no vote. The AG is appointed by the President under Article 76, must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, and holds office during the President's pleasure. There is no fixed tenure in the Constitution.

Option (b) 2 and 4: it correctly includes committee membership but wrongly includes voting. Under Article 88 the AG has no vote in either House or in committees. Voting is a right of members only. Ministers who are not members of a House also cannot vote there. The AG is not removed by impeachment but by the President, in practice on resignation when the Government changes. His fee is decided by the President.

Option (c) 1, 2 and 3: the correct answer. Article 88 grants the AG rights to speak, take part in proceedings, and be a committee member in either House, without voting. Article 76 governs his appointment and Article 76(2) his duties. Article 105 privileges apply to him as to MPs. The first AG was M. C. Setalvad (1950-63). The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitor Generals assist him but are not mentioned in the Constitution.

Option (d) 1 and 3 only: it is partially right but leaves out committee membership. The AG may be named a member of a parliamentary committee under Article 88 and then takes part without a vote. The Advocate General of a State is the corresponding State office under Article 165, appointed by the Governor, qualified to be a High Court judge, with parallel rights in the State Legislature under Article 177.
related: Article 76: Attorney General of India; Article 165: Advocate General of a State.
Article 88: AG and Ministers can speak and take part in Parliament but cannot vote unless they are members.
AG holds office during the pleasure of the President; no fixed tenure in the Constitution.
Qualification: eligible to be appointed a Supreme Court judge.
M. C. Setalvad was the first Attorney General of India.
Article 105 privileges are available to the AG as to MPs.
Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are not mentioned in the Constitution.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 88 lets the AG take part in the proceedings of either House of Parliament. The AG is the Union's chief legal adviser under Article 76, appointed by the President from persons qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. He has the right of audience in all courts in India. Though not a member of Parliament, this participation right exists so he can assist on legal questions. He is not a full-time government servant and may do private practice, subject to restrictions.

2 — Correct: Article 88 extends the AG's right to take part in proceedings to any parliamentary committee of which he is named a member. This is a right to be a member if named, without voting rights. Similar rights apply to Ministers. The AG is assisted by Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General, who are statutory or administrative appointments not mentioned in the Constitution's Article 76. The AG's remuneration is decided by the President, not fixed by the Constitution.

3 — Correct: Article 88 expressly gives the AG the right to speak in the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and joint sittings. The AG enjoys the privileges and immunities available to a Member of Parliament under Article 105 as extended by Article 105(4). The AG must give legal advice to the Government on matters referred by the President, and perform other legal duties assigned. He cannot advise against the Union or take briefs where he is required to advise.

4 — Incorrect: Article 88 explicitly states that the AG has no right to vote in the Houses. Voting is limited to members of the House. The AG is not an elected or nominated member of Parliament. The same rule applies to Ministers who are not members of a particular House. The AG also does not belong to the Council of Ministers; he is a constitutional office-holder, not a political executive, and holds office at the President's pleasure.
summary: The answer is (c): 1, 2 and 3. Under Article 88 read with Article 76(3), the Attorney General has the right to speak in, take part in the proceedings of, and be a member of any committee of either House of Parliament (or any joint sitting) of which he is named a member, but he has no right to vote.
topic_notes: The Attorney General of India is a constitutional office under Article 76. He is appointed by the President and must be qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court judge, meaning a citizen who has been a High Court judge for five years, or a High Court advocate for ten years, or in the President's opinion a distinguished jurist. The Constitution does not fix his tenure, and he holds office during the pleasure of the President; his remuneration is also decided by the President. By convention, he resigns when the Government resigns or is replaced. His duties are to advise the Government on legal matters referred to him, to perform other legal duties assigned by the President, and to discharge functions conferred by the Constitution or any other law. He has the right of audience in all courts of India. Under Article 88 he may speak in and take part in the proceedings of both Houses, joint sittings and committees of which he is named a member, but cannot vote. He enjoys the privileges of an MP under Article 105. Restrictions: he should not advise against the Government of India, should not defend accused persons in criminal cases without permission, should not accept directorship in a company without permission, and should not hold advice or brief in cases where he is called upon to advise or appear for the Government. He is not a government servant barred from private practice. Related offices: the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General help him. The Advocate General of a State (Article 165) is the State equivalent. The Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148) is a separate office with security of tenure. UPSC could next ask about Article 76 qualifications, comparison with Advocate General, removal procedure, and privileges.

question:
With reference to the usefulness of the by-products of sugar industry, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Bagasse can be used as biomass fuel for the generation of energy.
2. Molasses can be used as one of the feedstocks for the production of synthetic chemical fertilizers.
3. Molasses can be used for the production of ethanol. Select the correct answer using the codes given below
subject: Economy
detail: Sugar mills yield three main by-products: bagasse (fibrous residue after juice extraction), molasses (dark viscous liquid left after sugar crystallisation) and press mud (filter cake). Bagasse has a calorific value of about 2,200-2,500 kcal/kg and is burnt in boilers for process steam and electricity. Surplus power is exported to the grid under bagasse cogeneration policies, and bagasse is also used for paper and pulp and for compressed biogas. Molasses is rich in fermentable sugars (about 45-50 percent), so yeast converts it into ethanol. This is the basis of India's Ethanol Blending Programme, and molasses also feeds distilleries making rectified spirit and potable liquor. Molasses is also used as cattle feed additive. Synthetic chemical fertilizers such as urea, DAP and ammonium sulphate come from ammonia, made from natural gas or naphtha via the Haber-Bosch process, plus phosphate rock and potash. Molasses is therefore not a feedstock for them. Press mud, not molasses, is used as an organic manure and in bio-compost. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong, so options (b) and (d) go. Statement 1 is certainly right, which eliminates nothing further, but (a) fails because statement 3 is also right. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, which is also correct, since molasses is fermented to ethanol.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is incorrect because molasses is not a feedstock for synthetic chemical fertilizers.
Right: statements 1 (bagasse as biomass fuel) and 3 (molasses for ethanol) are correct, and statement 2 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because synthetic fertilizers are made from ammonia, natural gas or naphtha and rock phosphate.
keyfact: Bagasse gives energy (cogeneration) and molasses gives ethanol, but synthetic fertilizers do not come from molasses.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: it recognises bagasse as biomass fuel. Bagasse is the fibrous cane residue (about 30 percent of cane crushed) burnt in mill boilers for steam and power, and surplus electricity is sold to the grid through cogeneration. It is also a raw material for paper, pulp and board. It is incomplete here because molasses to ethanol is also true.

Option (b) 2 and 3 only: it pairs a false claim with a true one. Molasses is the syrup left after sugar crystallisation, with about 45-50 percent sugars. It is used for ethanol, rum and other alcohol, cattle feed, yeast and citric acid. It is not a feedstock for synthetic fertilizers, so this option is wrong.

Option (c) 1 and 3 only: the correct answer. Bagasse is used as biomass fuel for energy and molasses for ethanol. India's cogeneration capacity from sugar mills runs to several thousand MW, and molasses-based distilleries supply ethanol for blending in petrol under the Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme, which reached 20 percent blending in 2025.

Option (d) 1, 2 and 3: it wrongly accepts all three statements. Synthetic chemical fertilizers such as urea, DAP and MOP derive from ammonia (natural gas or naphtha), phosphate rock and potash, not molasses. Sugar by-products do support organic manure through press mud and treated spent wash, but that is not synthetic fertilizer production.
related: Bagasse is the fibrous residue after sugarcane crushing and a major source of biomass cogeneration power.
Molasses is the main feedstock for ethanol in India through the Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme.
Press mud (filter cake) is used as organic manure and for bio-compost.
India reached 20 percent ethanol blending (E20) in 2025, ahead of the National Policy on Biofuels 2018 target date of 2030, later advanced to 2025-26.
The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane is fixed by the Centre on CACP's recommendation.
Synthetic urea is made from ammonia produced via the Haber-Bosch process, using natural gas or naphtha.
Spent wash from molasses distilleries is a major water pollutant and is treated by biomethanation.
statements: 1 — Correct: Bagasse is widely used as a biomass fuel in sugar mill boilers and cogeneration plants. Bagasse is the fibrous residue left after crushing sugarcane, making up about 28-30 percent of cane by weight. Mills burn it in high-pressure boilers to produce steam and electricity for their own use, making them energy self-sufficient, and sell surplus power to the grid. India's MNRE supports bagasse cogeneration. Bagasse is also used to make paper, pulp, particle board and biodegradable tableware, and it can yield compressed biogas.

2 — Incorrect: Molasses is not a feedstock for synthetic chemical fertilizers. Synthetic nitrogen fertilizers such as urea are made from ammonia, produced by the Haber-Bosch process from hydrogen (from natural gas, naphtha or coal) and atmospheric nitrogen. Phosphatic fertilizers come from rock phosphate and potassic ones from potash. Molasses has only a limited use in organic and biofertilizer preparations, and spent wash from molasses distilleries is used as potash-rich manure after treatment. Press mud is the better-known sugar by-product used as organic manure.

3 — Correct: Molasses is a key feedstock for ethanol production. Molasses is the thick, dark syrup left after sugar crystallisation and contains roughly 45-50 percent fermentable sugars. Yeast ferments it into ethanol, which is distilled and dehydrated to fuel-grade ethanol. This underpins India's Ethanol Blending Programme under the National Policy on Biofuels 2018, which aimed at 20 percent blending (E20) by 2025-26; E20 was reached in 2025. Ethanol can also be made directly from cane juice and B-heavy molasses.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct. Bagasse is burnt in cogeneration plants to produce steam and power, and molasses is fermented to make ethanol. Molasses is not a feedstock for synthetic chemical fertilizers, which are made from natural gas, naphtha, ammonia and rock phosphate.
topic_notes: Sugar industry by-products are a recurring theme in UPSC prelims. Sugarcane crushing gives about 10 percent sugar, 28-30 percent bagasse, 4 percent molasses and 3-4 percent press mud (filter cake) by weight of cane. Bagasse: burnt for steam and power (cogeneration), with mills becoming net power exporters; also used for paper, pulp, packaging, particle board and compressed biogas. Molasses: grades A, B and C, with C-molasses (final molasses) being the usual distillery feedstock. Uses are ethanol, rectified spirit, potable alcohol, rum, cattle feed, yeast, acetic and citric acid. Press mud: rich in organic matter and phosphorus, used for bio-compost and to make wax. Spent wash from distilleries is a pollutant and is treated by biomethanation and used for fertigation. Policy angles: the National Policy on Biofuels 2018 allows ethanol from cane juice, B-heavy molasses, sugar-containing materials and damaged grain, and advanced the E20 target to 2025-26. The Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme is run by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, and the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of cane is fixed by the Centre on the recommendation of CACP, while states announce State Advised Prices. Sugar is under the Essential Commodities Act. The Sugar Development Fund supports mills, and the Cane (Control) Order 1966 governs payments. India is among the top two sugar producers with Brazil, and Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka are the leading producing states. Brazil's flex-fuel vehicle experience is a common comparison. Other biomass examples: rice husk, coconut shells and agricultural residue used for power and biochar.

question: Variations in the length of daytime and nighttime from season to season are due to
options: the earth’s rotation on its axis
the earth’s revolution round the sun in an elliptical manner
revolution of the earth on a tilted axis
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Seasonal variation in day and night length needs two things together: revolution (orbital motion around the sun) and the tilted, parallel axis. The axis is inclined at 23.5° from the perpendicular to the orbital plane, and it points toward the Pole Star (Polaris) throughout the year. Hence, in June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, so the circle of illumination divides latitudes unequally, giving longer days there; in December the situation reverses. Around 21 March and 23 September (equinoxes) the sun is overhead at the equator and day equals night everywhere. The solstices are 21 June (summer in the north, the Tropic of Cancer receives vertical rays, the longest day in the north) and 22 December (the Tropic of Capricorn gets vertical rays). Elimination: rotation alone gives day and night cycle, not their changing length. Elliptical orbit changes earth-sun distance (perihelion about 3 January, aphelion about 4 July) but does not cause seasons. Latitude determines the extent of variation but is not the cause. Without the tilt, days would be 12 hours throughout the year.
explanations: Incorrect: rotation on its axis (about 24 hours, west to east) causes the alternation of day and night, not seasonal changes in their length.

Incorrect: the elliptical orbit causes changes in earth-sun distance (perihelion and aphelion) and the unequal lengths of seasons, but it does not cause varying day length. If the axis were not tilted, the orbit's shape alone would not alter day length.
Incorrect: latitude governs how large the variation is at a given place (none at the equator, extreme at the poles), but it is an effect modifier, not the cause of seasonal variation.

Correct: the axial tilt of 23.5°, together with revolution around the sun and the axis's constant orientation, makes the sun's vertical rays shift between the tropics and changes the illumination of each hemisphere, which produces seasonal variation in day and night length.
keyfact: Seasons and changing day length are caused by the earth's 23.5° axial tilt together with its revolution around the sun, not by rotation or by distance from the sun.
option_notes: Rotation is the earth's spinning on its axis from west to east, one turn in about 23 hours 56 minutes (sidereal day), with a solar day of 24 hours. It causes day and night, the apparent east-to-west movement of the sun, the Coriolis effect, tides' daily timing and time differences between longitudes (15° per hour). It does not by itself cause seasons.

Revolution is the earth's orbital motion around the sun in an elliptical path, taking about 365¼ days (hence leap years). Perihelion is about 3 January (about 147 million km) and aphelion about 4 July (about 152 million km). The orbit's shape affects the speed of the earth and the lengths of the seasons, but the seasons themselves arise from the axial tilt.

Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equator (0° to 90°). Key parallels are the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N), the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S), the Arctic Circle (66.5°N) and the Antarctic Circle (66.5°S). Latitude determines the climate zones (torrid, temperate, frigid) and the amount of seasonal variation in day length, with polar regions experiencing midnight sun and polar night.

The axial tilt of 23.5° from the vertical to the orbital plane (66.5° to the ecliptic plane) stays parallel to itself during revolution, which is called parallelism of the axis. It causes the four seasons, the solstices (21 June, 22 December), the equinoxes (21 March, 23 September), the shifting of the vertical rays between the tropics, the midnight sun and the polar day and night.
related: Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) passes through 8 Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
Equinoxes fall on about 21 March and 23 September, with equal day and night everywhere.
Perihelion is about 3 January and aphelion about 4 July.
The earth's axis is tilted 23.5° from the vertical, and makes 66.5° with its orbital plane.
The earth rotates west to east, one rotation in about 24 hours, and the sun appears to rise in the east.
At the poles there is about six months of daylight followed by about six months of night.
Uranus has an axial tilt of about 98° and rotates almost on its side.
Time changes by 4 minutes per degree of longitude, and the Prime Meridian is at 0° (Greenwich).
summary: The answer is (d): revolution of the earth on a tilted axis. The earth's axis is inclined at 23.5° to the orbital plane (66.5° to the plane of the ecliptic) and keeps pointing in a fixed direction, so as the earth revolves around the sun, each hemisphere receives varying durations of sunlight through the year.
topic_notes: Seasons and day length result from the tilt of the earth's axis combined with revolution. The axis is inclined at 23.5° from the normal to the orbital plane, making 66.5° with the ecliptic plane, and it keeps pointing towards Polaris, so it stays parallel to itself. The circle of illumination (the boundary between day and night) is always perpendicular to the sun's rays, but it does not coincide with the axis, so it divides each parallel unequally except at the equator. Key dates: summer solstice 21 June (the sun is vertically overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere, with 24-hour daylight at the Arctic Circle); winter solstice 22 December (the sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn; the shortest day in the north); equinoxes about 21 March and 23 September (12-hour days and nights everywhere, sun overhead at the equator). At the equator the day is about 12 hours all year. Beyond the polar circles there are periods of continuous daylight (midnight sun) and continuous darkness, lasting about six months at the poles. The earth is at perihelion about 3 January and at aphelion about 4 July. Thus the Northern Hemisphere has summer when the earth is farthest from the sun, which proves that distance isn't the cause of seasons. Other angles: the Indian Standard Time meridian is 82.5°E; time changes by 4 minutes per degree of longitude; the International Date Line is near 180°; the Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states; Mercury has almost no tilt and Uranus is tilted about 98°, giving extreme seasons. Leap year: an extra day in February is added to compensate for the 6 hours of surplus in a year.

question:
The Narmada river flows to the west, while most other large peninsular rivers flow to the east. Why?
1. It occupies a linear rift valley.
2. It flows between the Vindhyas and the Satpuras.
3. The land slopes to the west from Central India. Select the correct answer using the codes given below
subject: Geography
detail: Most large Peninsular rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) flow east because the Deccan Plateau tilts eastward, a slope inherited from the uplift of the Western Ghats during the Cenozoic breakup of Gondwana. The Narmada and Tapi are exceptions: they flow in E-W rift (graben) valleys formed by faulting along the Narmada-Son lineament. The rivers follow these troughs westward and drain into the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay). Because they run in troughs rather than carving V-shaped valleys, they have no true delta and form estuaries. Elimination: statement 2 describes the geographic position (Vindhyas to the north, Satpuras to the south), which is true as a fact but is not the cause of the direction. The ranges are themselves the flanks of the rift, so the rift is the explanation. Statement 3 is false because Central India slopes broadly east, not west, which is why most rivers go east. Any option containing 2 or 3 is therefore eliminated, leaving (a). The Narmada rises at Amarkantak (Maikal range), is about 1,312 km long, and has the Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur and the Sardar Sarovar Dam in Gujarat.
explanations: Correct. The Narmada occupies a rift valley, a structural trough formed by faulting, and this is why it flows west against the general eastward tilt of the Peninsula.
Wrong. Statement 3 is false and statement 2 is only a locational description, not the cause. Together they cannot form the correct answer.
Wrong. Statement 3 is false because Central India slopes east. Statement 1 is true, but pairing it with 3 makes the option incorrect.
Wrong. Statement 1 is correct, so 'None' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: The Narmada flows west because it follows a linear rift valley (the Narmada-Son lineament), not because of a westward slope.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: This is the correct key. It states that the Narmada flows in a linear rift valley (graben) along the Narmada-Son lineament. Rift valley rivers follow fault-bounded troughs and often form estuaries rather than deltas. The Narmada and Tapi are the two major west-flowing rivers of the Peninsula, and both drain into the Arabian Sea through the Gulf of Khambhat.

Option (b), 2 and 3: This combines the position of the river between the Vindhyas and Satpuras with a westward slope. The Narmada does lie between those ranges (Vindhyas to the north, Satpuras to the south), but position is not causation. A westward slope from Central India is false, because the Peninsula tilts east. The Satpuras extend from Rajpipla in Gujarat to Maikal in Chhattisgarh.

Option (c), 1 and 3: This pairs the true rift valley statement with the false claim of a westward slope. The regional slope of the Deccan is eastward, as shown by the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi draining to the Bay of Bengal. Statement 3 contradicts this, so the option is wrong even though statement 1 is right.

Option (d), None: This would mean that none of the three statements explains the Narmada's flow. It is wrong because the rift valley (statement 1) is the accepted geological reason. The Narmada rises at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh and flows about 1,312 km, with Omkareshwar and the Sardar Sarovar Dam among its notable features.
related: The Narmada and Tapi flow in rift valleys and form estuaries, not deltas.
The Narmada rises at Amarkantak and is about 1,312 km long.
The Tapi (Tapti) rises near Multai in Betul district and is about 724 km long.
The Damodar flows in a rift valley but drains east; it is known as the 'Sorrow of Bengal'.
The Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal was set up in 1969 and gave its award in 1979.
Sardar Sarovar Dam is on the Narmada in Gujarat; Omkareshwar and Indira Sagar are in Madhya Pradesh.
Dhuandhar Falls is near Jabalpur on the Narmada.
The Peninsular plateau tilts east, so Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi and Kaveri flow to the Bay of Bengal.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Narmada flows in a rift valley, which is the real reason for its westward course. The Narmada rift (graben) lies along the Narmada-Son lineament, a fault zone of ancient Precambrian origin that was reactivated during the Gondwana breakup and Deccan volcanism. The river runs between fault-bounded blocks, so it is structurally controlled and follows the trough westward over about 1,312 km through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat. It enters the Arabian Sea through the Gulf of Khambhat in an estuary. The Tapi and the Damodar (in the east) also flow in rift valleys.

2 — Incorrect: This is a true location fact but not the cause. The Narmada does flow between the Vindhya range (north) and the Satpura range (south). However, these ranges are the uplifted flanks of the same rift (horsts) and do not themselves force the river westward. Many rivers flow between ranges in other directions, for example the Son, which flows east along the Kaimur and Vindhya ranges. The Vindhyas are a block-and-escarpment range, and the Satpuras are a horst range running from Rajpipla to Maikal, with Dhupgarh (1,350 m) as the highest peak. UPSC treats this statement as a distractor because it describes position, not cause.

3 — Incorrect: The land of Central India does not slope west; the Peninsular plateau tilts generally eastward. That tilt explains why the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri drain into the Bay of Bengal. The Western Ghats are a high watershed close to the western coast, which leaves little room for long west-flowing rivers. West-flowing rivers like the Narmada, Tapi, Sabarmati and Mahi are exceptions with short or structurally controlled courses. The slope is westward only locally inside the rift trough, which is not the same as a regional slope from Central India.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. The Narmada flows west because it occupies a linear rift valley (a fault-controlled trough), so the valley's alignment, not the general slope of the Peninsula, directs its course to the Arabian Sea.
topic_notes: Peninsular drainage is mostly east-flowing because the Western Ghats lie close to the west coast and the plateau tilts east. The main east-flowing rivers are the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. They form deltas and drain into the Bay of Bengal. The main west-flowing rivers are the Narmada and Tapi, which flow in rift valleys, and the shorter Sabarmati, Mahi, and the rivers of the Konkan and Malabar coasts. The Narmada-Tapi pair is distinctive because both flow in faulted troughs, so they have straight courses, little tributary development, and estuaries. The Narmada is about 1,312 km long, rises at Amarkantak (about 1,057 m), and passes through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat. Its features include the Kapildhara falls, the Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur, the Marble Rocks gorge, and the Omkareshwar and Sardar Sarovar projects. The Tapi rises near Multai in the Betul district of Madhya Pradesh and is about 724 km long. The Narmada is the largest west-flowing river of the Peninsula. The Damodar in eastern India also flows in a rift valley (a Gondwana graben) and is called the 'Sorrow of Bengal', although it flows east. Peninsular rivers are older, have reached graded profiles, and are seasonal and rain-fed, unlike the Himalayan rivers. The Western Ghats act as the major water divide. Other angles UPSC could ask are: river capture, drainage patterns (dendritic, trellis, radial, rectangular), inter-state river disputes (Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal 1969, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri), and the Interlinking of Rivers programme, such as Ken-Betwa.

question: On the planet earth, most of the freshwater exists as ice caps and glaciers. Out of the remaining freshwater, the largest proportion
options: is found in atmosphere as moisture and clouds
is found in freshwater lakes and rivers
subject: Geography
detail: Earth's water is about 97% saline (oceans) and only about 2.5-3% fresh. Of this freshwater, roughly 68.7% is locked in glaciers, ice caps and permanent snow (Antarctica, Greenland, mountain glaciers). Groundwater is next at about 30.1% (USGS figures), so it is the largest share of the freshwater that remains once ice is excluded. Surface and other freshwater make up only about 1.2%, and within that category ground ice and permafrost are the largest part (about 69%), followed by lakes (about 20%), soil moisture (about 3%), atmospheric water vapour (about 3%), wetlands (about 2.6%), rivers (about 0.5%) and living organisms (about 0.3%). Elimination logic: atmosphere, rivers and lakes, and soil moisture are all tiny fractions of one percent of total freshwater, so none can compete with groundwater. Remember that in terms of readily accessible and usable freshwater, groundwater and surface lakes and rivers matter most, and groundwater is by far the larger store. India is the world's largest extractor of groundwater.
explanations: Incorrect: atmospheric moisture and clouds hold only about 0.001% of total water, roughly 3% of the non-ice surface freshwater, which is negligible compared with groundwater.
Incorrect: rivers hold about 0.0002% of total water and lakes only a small fraction of freshwater; together they are far smaller than groundwater.
Correct: groundwater is about 30% of all freshwater and is the largest share after ice caps and glaciers.
Incorrect: soil moisture is only about 0.05% of freshwater, tiny next to groundwater.
keyfact: Freshwater: about 69% ice and glaciers, about 30% groundwater, and about 1% everything else (lakes, rivers, soil, atmosphere).
option_notes: Atmospheric water is water vapour, clouds and precipitation in transit, totalling about 12,900 cubic km, about 0.001% of all water. Its residence time is only about 9 days. It drives the hydrological cycle through evaporation, condensation and precipitation. Humidity, dew point and cloud formation are linked concepts. Despite its small volume it is vital for weather, rainfall distribution and monsoon dynamics.

Lakes and rivers are the main visible surface freshwater. Freshwater lakes hold about 91,000 cubic km, and rivers only about 2,100 cubic km, or about 0.0002% of total water. Yet they supply most human water use. Lake Baikal holds about 20% of unfrozen surface freshwater. Rivers have a short residence time of about 2-6 months. Many saline lakes, like the Caspian Sea, are not counted as freshwater.

Groundwater is water stored in soil pores and rock aquifers below the water table. It is about 30% of global freshwater and about 1.7% of all water. Aquifers may be unconfined or confined (artesian). Recharge occurs by infiltration. India is the largest user of groundwater, extracting about a quarter of the global total. The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) monitors it, and the Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) targets sustainable management. Overextraction causes depletion and contamination by arsenic, fluoride and nitrate.

Soil moisture is water held in the unsaturated zone of the soil. It is only about 0.05% of freshwater, yet it is critical for agriculture, plant growth, and runoff and infiltration processes. It is measured by satellites such as SMAP and SMOS. Concepts include field capacity, wilting point and available water capacity. Soil moisture drought is the 'agricultural drought' indicator.
related: About 97% of Earth's water is saline; only about 2.5-3% is fresh.
Glaciers and ice caps hold about 68.7% of freshwater; groundwater about 30%.
Antarctica contains about 90% of the world's ice.
Lake Baikal is the deepest lake and holds about 20% of unfrozen surface freshwater.
India is the world's largest groundwater user; the CGWB is the apex body for groundwater assessment.
Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) promotes community-led groundwater management in water-stressed states.
World Water Day is observed on 22 March.
Residence time of atmospheric water is about 9 days.
summary: The answer is (c) groundwater. After ice caps and glaciers (about 68-69% of freshwater), groundwater holds roughly 30% of the world's freshwater, far more than lakes, rivers, soil moisture or atmospheric vapour.
topic_notes: Distribution of Earth's water: about 97.5% is saline (oceans, saline lakes and groundwater) and about 2.5% is fresh. Of freshwater, about 68.7% is in glaciers and ice caps, about 30.1% is groundwater, and about 1.2% is surface and other freshwater. In that last 1.2%, ground ice and permafrost make up about 69%, lakes about 20%, soil moisture about 3.8%, atmosphere about 3%, wetlands about 2.6%, rivers about 0.5% and biota about 0.26%. Oceans hold about 96.5% of total water. Antarctica holds about 90% of the world's ice. If all glaciers melted, sea level would rise about 60-70 m. Hydrological cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and percolation. Residence times: atmosphere about 9 days, rivers weeks to months, lakes years to decades, groundwater from hundreds to thousands of years, ice sheets up to hundreds of thousands of years, oceans about 3,000-4,000 years. India: about 4% of world freshwater resources for about 18% of the population. Groundwater is the source of about 60% of irrigation and 85% of rural drinking water. The CGWB assesses blocks as safe, semi-critical, critical or over-exploited. Related schemes: Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Jal Jeevan Mission, Atal Bhujal Yojana, National Water Policy 2012, and Aquifer Mapping (NAQUIM). Related days: World Water Day on 22 March. Other angles UPSC may ask: water stress and scarcity indices, the Falkenmark indicator, virtual water, desalination and the Ramsar wetlands.

question:
Consider the following pairs :
1. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve : Garo Hills
2. Logtak (Loktak) Lake : Barail Range
3. Namdapha National Park : Dafla Hills Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests the location of protected areas in North-East India. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve (designated 1988, UNESCO MAB network 2009) lies in the West Garo Hills of Meghalaya. It is known for the Nokrek ridge, the citrus gene sanctuary (Citrus indica, the Memang Narang) and the red panda. Pair 1 is therefore correct. Loktak is the largest freshwater lake in North-East India, in Bishnupur district of Manipur. It is famous for its phumdis, which form Keibul Lamjao National Park, the only floating national park and the home of the sangai (Brow-antlered deer). It is a Ramsar site (1990) and is on the Montreux Record. The Barail Range lies in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur, near the Cachar and Dima Hasao areas, so pair 2 is wrong. Namdapha, in Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh, is a Tiger Reserve and Project Elephant area. It lies in the Eastern Himalayan foothills and the Patkai range near the Myanmar border, and it is the only park with four big cats. The Dafla Hills lie in central Arunachal Pradesh, so pair 3 is wrong. With only pair 1 correct, (a) is the answer.
explanations: Correct: only pair 1 is matched correctly, because Nokrek is in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya.
Wrong: pair 2 is incorrect, so '2 and 3 only' fails. Loktak is in Manipur's Imphal valley, not the Barail Range, and pair 3 is also wrong.
Wrong: pairs 2 and 3 are both mismatched, so all three cannot be correct.
Wrong: pair 1 is correct, so 'None' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: Nokrek = Garo Hills (Meghalaya); Loktak = Manipur valley; Namdapha = Patkai range, Arunachal Pradesh.
option_notes: Option (a) is 1 only, the correct answer. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve is in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya, and it is a UNESCO MAB site since 2009. It is known for citrus gene diversity and the red panda. Garo Hills also host Balpakram National Park, in South Garo Hills, which is known for its wildlife and its canyon-like landscape. The Garo-Khasi-Jaintia hills form the Meghalaya plateau, an extension of the Peninsular block.

Option (b) is 2 and 3 only, which is wrong. Loktak is a Ramsar lake in Manipur, known for its phumdis, and Namdapha is a Tiger Reserve in Arunachal Pradesh. Both are real and important sites, but they are not located in the Barail Range or the Dafla Hills. Keibul Lamjao hosts the sangai. Namdapha is known for having four big cat species and for its range of altitudes from about 200 m to 4,500 m.

Option (c) is 1, 2 and 3, which is wrong. It would require Loktak in the Barail and Namdapha in the Dafla Hills. The Barail Range separates the Barak valley from the Brahmaputra valley and the Dima Hasao area, and it extends into Nagaland and Manipur. The Dafla Hills are in Arunachal Pradesh, home to the Nyishi tribe, also called Dafla. Neither contains these two sites.

Option (d) is None, which is wrong. It would mean Nokrek is not in the Garo Hills, but Nokrek is in the West Garo Hills. Nokrek is Meghalaya's only UNESCO biosphere reserve. Other Indian biosphere reserves in the North-East include Dibru-Saikhowa (Assam), Dihang-Dibang (Arunachal Pradesh), Manas (Assam) and Khangchendzonga (Sikkim).
related: Loktak Lake is the largest freshwater lake in North-East India and is on the Montreux Record.
Keibul Lamjao is the world's only floating national park, protecting the sangai.
Nokrek Biosphere Reserve was added to UNESCO's MAB network in 2009.
Namdapha is in Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh, and has four big cat species.
Barail Range lies in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur.
Dafla Hills are in Arunachal Pradesh, home to the Nyishi tribe.
Balpakram National Park is in the South Garo Hills, Meghalaya.
Manas in Assam is a World Heritage Site, a Tiger Reserve and a biosphere reserve.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nokrek lies in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve was notified in 1988 and joined the UNESCO MAB network in 2009. Its core is Nokrek National Park, with Tura Peak nearby, in West Garo Hills. It holds wild relatives of citrus (Citrus indica) and is home to the red panda, elephants, hoolock gibbons and tigers. The Simsang river rises here. It is a key site for Project Elephant and gene-pool conservation.

2 — Incorrect: Loktak Lake is in Manipur's Imphal valley, in Bishnupur district, not in the Barail Range. It is the largest freshwater lake in the North-East and is fed by the Manipur river. It is known for phumdis (floating masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter). Keibul Lamjao National Park, the world's only floating national park, protects the endangered sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii). It became a Ramsar site in 1990 and is on the Montreux Record. The Ithai barrage on the Manipur river has affected its hydrology.

3 — Incorrect: Namdapha National Park is in Changlang district of Arunachal Pradesh, on the Myanmar border, in the Patkai range. It is the largest protected area in the Eastern Himalayas. It was declared a national park in 1983 and a Tiger Reserve under Project Tiger. It has the tiger, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard. The Noa-Dihing river flows through it. It has tropical to alpine vegetation and the Namdapha flying squirrel. The Dafla Hills are elsewhere, near the Subansiri and Kameng areas.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Nokrek Biosphere Reserve is in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya, but Loktak Lake lies in Manipur's Imphal valley, not the Barail Range, and Namdapha National Park is in the Patkai range of Arunachal Pradesh, not the Dafla Hills.
topic_notes: North-East India has a high concentration of biodiversity hotspots, and UPSC often asks about the locations of protected areas there. Meghalaya has Nokrek Biosphere Reserve and Balpakram National Park in the Garo Hills, and Siju Wildlife Sanctuary. Assam has Kaziranga, Manas, Nameri, Orang, Dibru-Saikhowa and Raimona National Parks. Kaziranga is famous for the one-horned rhinoceros, Manas is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Tiger Reserve, and Dibru-Saikhowa is a biosphere reserve known for feral horses and white-winged wood ducks. Arunachal Pradesh has Namdapha, Mouling, Pakke Tiger Reserve and Dihang-Dibang Biosphere Reserve. Manipur has Loktak Lake, Keibul Lamjao National Park, Sirohi National Park and Yangoupokpi-Lokchao Sanctuary. Sikkim has Khangchendzonga, a mixed World Heritage Site. Mizoram has Dampa Tiger Reserve and Murlen National Park. Nagaland has Intanki and Fakim, and Tripura has Sepahijala and Clouded Leopard National Park. The Ramsar sites in the region include Loktak, Deepor Beel and Rudrasagar Lake. The hill ranges are also commonly asked: Patkai, Naga, Barail, Mizo (Lushai), Garo-Khasi-Jaintia, Mishmi, Dafla, Abor, Miri and Apatani hills. For revision, pair each park or lake with its state, river, flagship species and conservation status (Tiger Reserve, Biosphere Reserve, Ramsar or World Heritage).

question:
Consider the following :
1. Electromagnetic radiation Geothermal energy AnkwD Gravitational force Plate movements Rotation of the earth . Revolution of the earth Which of the above are responsible for bringing dynamic changes on the surface of the earth?
subject: Geography
detail: Earth's surface is shaped by exogenic (external) and endogenic (internal) forces. Exogenic processes (weathering, erosion, deposition) are powered mainly by solar electromagnetic radiation, which heats the atmosphere and oceans, creates winds, the water cycle, glaciers and rivers. Gravity is the directional force behind mass wasting, river flow, glacial movement and tides, and it also holds the atmosphere in place. Endogenic forces come from Earth's interior: geothermal energy, from primordial heat and radioactive decay, drives mantle convection, volcanism and earthquakes. Plate movements (plate tectonics) cause mountain building, rift valleys, ocean-basin changes and continental drift. Rotation causes day and night, the Coriolis deflection of winds and ocean currents, and tidal bulges. Revolution, together with the 23.5° axial tilt, causes seasons and varying insolation, which affect weathering and erosion. Because each of the six influences surface change either directly or by modifying other processes, no item can be dropped. This makes options (a), (b) and (c) incomplete, and the all-inclusive option (d) is correct. Elimination tip: when every item is a recognised physical driver, suspect 'all of the above'.
explanations: Wrong: 1, 2, 3 and 4 omit rotation and revolution, which also influence tides, winds, currents and seasons that alter the surface.
Wrong: this leaves out geothermal energy and plate movements, the key endogenic drivers of volcanism, earthquakes and mountain building.
Wrong: this omits solar electromagnetic radiation, the main driver of exogenic processes, and gravity.
Correct: all six factors, solar radiation, geothermal energy, gravity, plate movements, rotation and revolution, bring dynamic surface change.
keyfact: Solar radiation and gravity drive exogenic processes, geothermal heat and plate movements drive endogenic ones, and rotation and revolution modulate both, so all six change Earth's surface.
option_notes: Option (a) lists radiation, geothermal energy, gravity and plate movements. These are the main energy sources and forces, both exogenic and endogenic, behind landform change. Alone they are incomplete here because the astronomical motions of rotation and revolution also modulate winds, tides, seasons and the intensity of surface processes.

Option (b) lists radiation, gravity, rotation and revolution, which are mostly external or astronomical influences. Solar energy and gravity drive weathering, erosion and deposition, while rotation and revolution control day-night cycles, Coriolis effects and seasons. It ignores internal forces like geothermal heat and tectonics, which create relief such as mountains and rifts.

Option (c) lists geothermal energy, gravity, plate movements, rotation and revolution as the sources of change. Geothermal heat and plate tectonics are endogenic forces that build mountains, volcanoes and ocean basins. Omitting solar electromagnetic radiation makes it wrong, since the Sun powers the weather, water cycle and erosion that sculpt landscapes.

Option (d) combines every factor: solar radiation and gravity (exogenic), geothermal energy and plate movements (endogenic), and rotation and revolution (astronomical modulators). Together they explain the creation of relief by internal forces and its levelling by external forces. It is the official answer and reflects the integrated view of geomorphic processes.
related: Endogenic forces build relief, while exogenic forces wear it down (gradation).
Sources of Earth's internal heat: radioactive decay and primordial heat from formation.
Moho discontinuity separates crust and mantle; Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle and core.
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912; Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading.
Earth's axial tilt is 23.5°, which causes seasons together with revolution.
Spring tides occur at new and full moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are aligned.
Epeirogenic movements raise or lower continents, while orogenic movements build mountains.
The Coriolis force deflects winds right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.
statements: 1 — Correct: Electromagnetic radiation, chiefly solar, drives weathering, winds, rainfall and erosion. Solar radiation supplies about 99.9% of Earth's surface energy, with the Sun's output peaking in visible light. Insolation differences between equator and poles drive atmospheric and ocean circulation. Freeze-thaw, thermal expansion of rocks and the hydrological cycle are all solar-powered. Exogenic processes are largely solar-driven, and they level landscapes (gradation) while endogenic forces build relief.

2 — Correct: Geothermal energy is Earth's internal heat, from primordial accretion heat and radioactive decay of uranium, thorium and potassium-40. It drives mantle convection, magma generation, volcanoes, geysers and hot springs. The geothermal gradient is about 25–30°C per km in the crust. Core temperature is estimated at about 5,000–6,000°C. Endogenic processes such as volcanism and diastrophism arise from this heat. India's geothermal sites include Puga (Ladakh) and Manikaran.

3 — Correct: Gravitational force pulls materials downslope, causing landslides, rockfalls, soil creep and mass movements. It drives river flow, glacier motion and rainfall, and also gives rise to tides through lunar and solar attraction. Gravity retains the atmosphere and is essential for isostasy, the balance of crustal blocks. It is described as the 'directional force' behind gradational processes. Newton's law of gravitation explains its dependence on mass and distance.

4 — Correct: Plate movements, explained by plate tectonics (developed in the 1960s from Wegener's continental drift of 1912 and Harry Hess's sea-floor spreading), cause mountains, trenches, earthquakes and volcanoes. There are 7 major plates, including Pacific, Eurasian and Indian. Boundaries are divergent, convergent or transform. The Himalayas formed from the Indian–Eurasian collision, and the Pacific Ring of Fire is the most seismically active belt.

5 — Correct: Earth's rotation, on its axis from west to east once in about 24 hours, produces day and night and the Coriolis force. It deflects winds and ocean currents (right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern) and shapes the timing of tides. It also causes the equatorial bulge and flattening at the poles. These effects influence climate and erosion patterns, and thus surface landforms.

6 — Correct: Revolution is Earth's orbit around the Sun, taking about 365.25 days, at an average distance of about 150 million km. Combined with the 23.5° axial tilt it gives seasons, solstices (21 June, 22 December) and equinoxes (21 March, 23 September). Seasonal changes in insolation influence weathering, river discharge, glaciation and vegetation. Perihelion occurs about 3 January and aphelion about 4 July. Milankovitch cycles link orbital variations with ice ages.
summary: The answer is (d): all six factors bring dynamic changes to the Earth's surface. Electromagnetic radiation (solar energy) drives weather and exogenic processes, while geothermal energy and plate movements drive endogenic processes. Gravity, rotation and revolution shape the processes and patterns that act on the surface.
topic_notes: Geomorphic processes are the physical and chemical forces that change Earth's surface. They are divided into endogenic (internal) and exogenic (external) processes. Endogenic forces originate in the interior, powered by geothermal heat from radioactive decay and residual formation heat. They include diastrophism (orogenic movements building mountains, epeirogenic movements raising or lowering continents, earthquakes, plate tectonics) and volcanism. They create relief and are described as land-building forces. Exogenic forces act on the surface and are driven mainly by solar energy and gravity. They include weathering (physical, chemical, biological), mass wasting, erosion and deposition, carried out by running water, wind, glaciers, waves and groundwater. They are described as land-wearing or gradational forces, and they tend to level the landscape. Temperature, rainfall, vegetation and slope control their intensity. Plate tectonics: Wegener's continental drift (1912), Hess's sea-floor spreading (1960s), and the modern theory (McKenzie, Parker, Morgan, 1967-68). There are 7 major plates, and the Indian plate moves northward at roughly 5 cm per year. Boundary types are divergent (mid-ocean ridges, rifts), convergent (subduction, collision zones, trenches) and transform (San Andreas fault). Astronomical factors: rotation causes day and night, Coriolis force and tidal timing; revolution plus axial tilt of 23.5° causes seasons. Tides are caused by gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun, with spring tides at new and full moon and neap tides at quarter phases. Earth's interior layers are crust, mantle and core; the Moho and Gutenberg discontinuities separate them. Likely UPSC angles: endogenic versus exogenic classification, sources of earth's heat, plate boundaries and associated landforms, and the role of solar energy in the climate system.

question:
Which of the following bodies does not/do not find mention in the Constitution?
1. National Development Council
2. Planning Commission
3. Zonal Councils Select the correct answer using the codes given below
subject: Polity
detail: The question asks which bodies find no mention in the Constitution, so each body must be checked against the constitutional text. The Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet, with the Prime Minister as chairman. It was an extra-constitutional, non-statutory body. It was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015, also by a Cabinet resolution. The National Development Council was set up on 6 August 1952 by an executive resolution to give states a say in planning. It was likewise extra-constitutional and non-statutory. The Zonal Councils (five of them: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern) were created under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. They are therefore statutory, not constitutional. The North Eastern Council was created separately by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971. The Inter-State Council, by contrast, is constitutional under Article 263, which is a common trap. Elimination: because all three are absent from the Constitution, only option (d) is correct. Options (a), (b) and (c) each wrongly treat one or more of them as constitutional.
explanations: Wrong: this option is incomplete. The NDC and the Planning Commission are indeed not in the Constitution, but it leaves out the Zonal Councils, which are also absent from it.
Wrong: this treats only the Planning Commission as absent from the Constitution. The NDC and the Zonal Councils are also non-constitutional, so it understates the answer.
Wrong: this correctly includes the NDC and the Zonal Councils but omits the Planning Commission, which is also extra-constitutional.

Correct: the NDC and the Planning Commission were created by executive resolutions and the Zonal Councils by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. None of them is mentioned in the Constitution, so all three qualify.
keyfact: NDC and Planning Commission: Cabinet resolutions (extra-constitutional); Zonal Councils: States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (statutory); none is in the Constitution.
option_notes: Option (a) names the NDC and the Planning Commission. Both were created by Union Cabinet resolutions (the Planning Commission on 15 March 1950, the NDC on 6 August 1952). Neither was a constitutional or statutory body. The Planning Commission drew up the Five-Year Plans and the NDC, chaired by the Prime Minister, approved them. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015, and the NDC fell into disuse after that.

Option (b) names only the Planning Commission. It was an extra-constitutional, non-statutory advisory and planning body created in 1950. The Prime Minister was chairman and a Deputy Chairman was its working head. It was based on the Cabinet's decision and the recommendations of the Advisory Planning Board. Its legal footing rested on Entry 20 of the Concurrent List, which covers economic and social planning. NITI Aayog replaced it in 2015.

Option (c) names the NDC and the Zonal Councils. The NDC was formed in 1952 by executive resolution. The Zonal Councils were formed under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, so they are statutory. The five Zonal Councils each have the Union Home Minister as chairman and the Chief Ministers as vice-chairmen by rotation. Each is an advisory forum for inter-state and Centre-state cooperation.

Option (d) covers all three bodies: the NDC, the Planning Commission and the Zonal Councils. None has a basis in the constitutional text. The first two rest on executive resolutions, and the Zonal Councils on a parliamentary statute (the States Reorganisation Act, 1956). This is the official answer. By contrast, the Finance Commission (Art. 280), the Inter-State Council (Art. 263) and the UPSC (Art. 315) are constitutional bodies.
related: The Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 and replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
The NDC was set up on 6 August 1952 by executive resolution.
The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body under Article 263.
The Zonal Councils were set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; there are five.
The Union Home Minister is the common chairman of the Zonal Councils.
The Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 every five years.
The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
NITI Aayog is non-constitutional and non-statutory; the Prime Minister is its chairperson.
statements: 1 — Correct: The NDC is not mentioned in the Constitution. It was created by a Cabinet resolution, so it is extra-constitutional. The National Development Council was set up on 6 August 1952. Its members were the Prime Minister (chairman), all Union Cabinet ministers, the Chief Ministers of all states, the administrators of Union Territories and the members of the Planning Commission. Its role was to secure cooperation between the states and the Planning Commission, review the working of the Plan and recommend measures to achieve Plan targets. It approved the Five-Year Plans before they were placed before Parliament. Its functions were advisory only. After the Planning Commission was abolished in 2015, the NDC was also effectively discontinued.

2 — Correct: The Planning Commission is not mentioned in the Constitution. It was set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution, on the Union Cabinet's decision, which makes it a non-constitutional and non-statutory body. The Prime Minister was its chairman, and a Deputy Chairman held full-time executive charge. It prepared the Five-Year Plans, the first of which began in 1951. Its legal basis comes from Entry 20 of the Concurrent List (economic and social planning), not from any article creating it. NITI Aayog replaced it on 1 January 2015. The 12th Five-Year Plan (2012-17) was the last.

3 — Correct: The Zonal Councils are not mentioned in the Constitution. They are statutory bodies established by Parliament under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. There are five: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern. The Union Home Minister is the common chairman of all of them. The Chief Minister of each state in the zone serves as vice-chairman by rotation for one year. Their purpose is to promote cooperation and coordination among states, Union Territories and the Centre. They are advisory bodies and discuss matters such as economic and social planning, border disputes and linguistic minorities. The North Eastern Council was constituted separately by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971.
summary: The answer is (d): none of the National Development Council, the Planning Commission or the Zonal Councils is mentioned in the Constitution. The NDC and Planning Commission were created by executive resolutions of the Union Cabinet, and the Zonal Councils by an Act of Parliament, the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
topic_notes: The question tests the difference between constitutional, statutory and extra-constitutional bodies. Constitutional bodies are created directly by the Constitution. Examples are the Election Commission (Art. 324), the UPSC (Art. 315), the State PSCs (Art. 315), the Finance Commission (Art. 280), the CAG (Art. 148), the Attorney General (Art. 76), the Advocate General (Art. 165), the National Commission for SCs (Art. 338), the National Commission for STs (Art. 338A) and the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Art. 350B). Statutory bodies are created by Acts of Parliament. Examples are the NHRC (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993), the CVC (originally set up by a 1964 resolution, given statutory status in 2003), the Zonal Councils, the Lokpal, the National Green Tribunal (2010), SEBI (1992) and the Competition Commission. Extra-constitutional and non-statutory bodies are created by executive resolutions. These were the Planning Commission and the NDC. NITI Aayog (1 January 2015) is also set up by a Cabinet resolution, so it is non-constitutional and non-statutory. NITI Aayog is chaired by the Prime Minister and has a Vice-Chairperson and a CEO. Its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories. It follows a bottom-up approach and acts as a think tank. The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 under Art. 263, on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. The Zonal Councils were conceived by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1956 and are advisory. The North Eastern Council was constituted in 1971 and amended in 2002. The Eastern Zonal Council includes Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal. The Southern Zonal Council includes Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. UPSC often asks which body falls into which category.

question: The demand for the Tebhaga Peasant Movement in Bengal was for
options: the reduction of the share of the landlords from one-half of the crop to one-third
the grant of ownership of land to peasants as they were the actual cultivators of the land
the uprooting of Zamindari system and the end of serfdom
subject: Polity
detail: Tebhaga was a movement of bargadars (sharecroppers/bataidars) in Bengal in 1946-47, led by the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha, the peasant front of the Communist Party of India. The Floud Commission (1940) had recommended that the sharecropper keep two-thirds of the crop, but this was never implemented. In September 1946 the Kisan Sabha gave the call to retain two-thirds of the harvest and to stock paddy on their own threshing floors (nij khamar) instead of the jotedar's. The movement was strongest in North Bengal districts such as Dinajpur, Rangpur, Jalpaiguri and Malda, and also in parts of 24 Parganas and Mymensingh. Women (Nari Bahini) took part prominently. Famous names include Ila Mitra, Charu Majumdar, Kamrup Sen and Bhabani Sen. The Muslim League ministry (Suhrawardy) drafted the Bengal Bargadars' Temporary Regulation Bill in 1947, which was only partly acted upon, and the West Bengal Bargadars Act followed in 1950. Elimination logic: (b) land ownership, (c) abolition of zamindari and (d) debt cancellation were broader agrarian demands that were not the specific Tebhaga slogan. Tebhaga was about the crop share, not ownership.
explanations: Correct: the core demand was to reduce the landlord's share from one-half to one-third, so the bargadar would get two-thirds.
Incorrect: Tebhaga did not demand transfer of ownership to the cultivators. It sought better crop-sharing terms for tenants who stayed sharecroppers.
Incorrect: abolition of the zamindari system was not the slogan of Tebhaga. It was a later policy outcome (West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act 1953), not the movement's demand.
Incorrect: debt cancellation was a demand in other agitations (for example the Deccan Riots of 1875 and Kisan Sabha campaigns), not the defining demand of Tebhaga.
keyfact: Tebhaga (1946-47, Bengal Kisan Sabha) demanded two-thirds of the crop for the sharecropper and one-third for the jotedar, instead of the 50:50 split.
option_notes: The one-half to one-third share cut is the actual Tebhaga demand. Bargadars traditionally gave half of the crop (adhi or bhag system) to the jotedar and sought to keep two-thirds. The call was given by the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1946, with the Floud Commission recommendation as background. It was most intense in North Bengal and led to the 1950 West Bengal Bargadars Act.

Ownership of land to cultivators was the broader slogan of 'land to the tiller'. It was raised by the Communists in Telangana (1946-51) and in later land reform debates. It was not the Tebhaga demand, which assumed the sharecropper would continue to cultivate the jotedar's land on revised terms.

Abolition of zamindari was a demand of the Kisan Sabha and the Congress agrarian programme before 1947. It was carried out after independence through state laws, such as the UP Zamindari Abolition Act 1950 and the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act 1953. Serfdom, as in bonded labour, was abolished later by the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976.

Writing off peasant debts was the aim of measures like the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879 and the debt conciliation boards of the 1930s. It also featured in the Kisan Sabha's demands and in the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act 1935. Moneylender oppression was central to the Deccan Riots 1875 and the Moplah rebellion, not to Tebhaga.
related: Tebhaga means 'three shares': the peasant keeps 2/3 of the crop and the landlord gets 1/3.
Tebhaga was led by the Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha, linked to the CPI, in 1946-47.
The Floud Commission (1940) recommended two-thirds of the crop for sharecroppers.
The All India Kisan Sabha was founded in 1936 at Lucknow, with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as president.
Ila Mitra was a woman leader of Tebhaga in Nachole, Rajshahi.
The Telangana peasant armed struggle (1946-51) was against the Nizam's jagirdars and deshmukhs.
The West Bengal Bargadars Act 1950 recorded the rights of sharecroppers.
Operation Barga (1978) in West Bengal registered sharecroppers under the Left Front government.
summary: The answer is (a). The Tebhaga movement (1946-47) was a sharecroppers' (bargadars') agitation in Bengal demanding that the jotedars/landlords' share be cut from one-half to one-third of the produce, with two-thirds going to the cultivator (tebhaga means 'three shares').
topic_notes: Tebhaga (1946-47) is the best-known peasant movement in Bengal in the last years of British rule. Bargadars cultivated land owned by jotedars, who were often wealthy rich peasants or small landlords, and paid half the crop plus various illegal cesses (abwabs). The Floud Land Revenue Commission (1938-40) had recommended giving two-thirds to the sharecropper. The Bengal Provincial Kisan Sabha, with its CPI cadres, started the movement after the 1943 famine, and it spread across North Bengal and the Sundarbans fringes. Slogan: 'Nij khamare dhan tolo' (take the paddy to your own threshing floor) and 'Tebhaga chai' (we want two-thirds). Police firing killed many peasants, including at Khanpur in Dinajpur, and Ila Mitra became a legend in Nachole, Rajshahi. The Suhrawardy ministry's Bargadari Bill was not passed before Partition, and the movement faded. Other peasant movements to revise: the Indigo Revolt 1859-60 in Bengal, the Pabna Agrarian League 1873, the Deccan Riots 1875, the Champaran Satyagraha 1917, the Kheda Satyagraha 1918, the Bardoli Satyagraha 1928, the Moplah Rebellion 1921, the Eka Movement in Awadh 1921-22, the Telangana movement 1946-51, and the Warli revolt in Maharashtra 1945-47. Organisations: the All India Kisan Sabha was formed in Lucknow in April 1936 with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as the first president and N.G. Ranga as general secretary. Sahajanand also founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929.

question: The Parliament can make any law for whole or any part of India for implementing international treaties
options: with the consent of all the States
with the consent of the majority of States
with the consent of the States concerned
without the consent of any State
subject: Polity
detail: Article 253 of the Constitution says that, despite anything in the preceding provisions of Chapter I (Part XI), Parliament has power to make any law for the whole or any part of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with another country, or any decision made at an international conference, association or other body. This means that even a subject in the State List (List II) can be legislated upon by Parliament if needed to implement an international obligation. No State consent, no resolution by State legislatures and no ratification by States is required, which marks the unitary bias of Indian federalism. Contrast this with Article 252, where Parliament legislates for two or more States only if their legislatures pass resolutions, and with Article 249, where Rajya Sabha passes a two-thirds resolution in the national interest. Elimination: options (a), (b) and (c) all assume a consent requirement, which Article 253 does not impose. Examples of laws under Article 253 are the United Nations (Privileges and Immunities) Act 1947, the Geneva Convention Act 1960, the Anti-Hijacking Act 1982, the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993. Judicial support comes from cases like Maganbhai Patel v. Union of India (1970).
explanations: Wrong: Article 253 does not require the consent of all States; treaties are a Union matter and Parliament acts on its own.

Wrong: No majority-of-States consent is needed either; this resembles the ratification requirement for constitutional amendments under Article 368(2) affecting federal features, which is a different matter.
Wrong: Even States directly concerned need not consent. Consent through resolution is required only under Article 252 (legislation for two or more States by consent), not for treaty implementation.

Correct: Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate on any subject, including State List subjects, to implement treaties, agreements, conventions or decisions of international bodies without State consent.
keyfact: Article 253: Parliament can legislate on any subject, even in the State List, to implement international treaties, without any State's consent.
option_notes: Consent of all States: this is not a constitutional requirement for any ordinary Union legislation. Close analogues are absent; even constitutional amendments under Article 368(2) need ratification by only half of the State legislatures, and only for federal provisions such as representation of States in Parliament, the Seventh Schedule and the Union and State executive power.

Consent of the majority of States: this is not the rule for treaty laws. The nearest idea is ratification by not less than one-half of State legislatures for certain amendments under Article 368(2). Treaty implementation under Article 253 and the Union's treaty-making power under Entry 14 of the Union List do not involve State majorities.

Consent of the States concerned: this reflects Article 252, under which Parliament may legislate for two or more States on a State List matter if their legislatures pass resolutions, with other States able to adopt the law later. Examples are the Prize Competitions Act 1955 and the Water Act 1974. It is distinct from Article 253.

Without the consent of any State: this is Article 253, giving Parliament overriding legislative power to implement international treaties, agreements, conventions and decisions of international conferences. It extends to State List subjects and expresses the Constitution's unitary bias. Entry 14 of the Union List covers entering into treaties and implementing them.
related: Article 253: Parliament legislates to implement treaties, agreements or conventions, even on State List subjects.
Article 252: Parliament legislates for two or more States by their consent, and other States can adopt the law later.
Article 249: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject in the national interest.
Article 250: Parliament can legislate on State List subjects during a National Emergency.
Article 254: Repugnancy in the Concurrent List, with Union law prevailing unless State law has Presidential assent.
Entry 14 of the Union List: entering into treaties and agreements with foreign countries and implementing them.
Article 246A: special provision on GST, giving concurrent powers to Parliament and State legislatures.
42nd Amendment 1976 transferred five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List.
summary: The answer is (d): Parliament can legislate for the whole or any part of India to implement international treaties without the consent of any State. Article 253 gives Parliament this power notwithstanding the distribution of legislative powers in Articles 245-252 and the Seventh Schedule.
topic_notes: Centre-State legislative relations are in Part XI (Articles 245-255). Article 245 gives territorial extent: Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and State legislatures for their State. Article 246 distributes subjects among the Union List (originally 97, now 98 entries), State List (66, now 59 entries) and Concurrent List (47, now 52 entries). Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List and residuary powers (Article 248, Entry 97). Parliament can legislate on State List subjects in five situations: (1) Article 249, when Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting that it is necessary in the national interest, valid for one year and renewable, with the law lapsing six months after the resolution ceases; (2) Article 250, during a National Emergency; (3) Article 252, by consent of two or more States through resolutions; (4) Article 253, to implement international treaties and agreements; (5) Article 356, during President's Rule in a State, when Parliament can confer on the President the power to legislate. Article 254 deals with repugnancy between Union and State law on Concurrent List subjects, where the Union law prevails unless the State law has received Presidential assent. Article 255 deals with the requirement of recommendations and previous sanctions being treated as a matter of procedure only. Article 251 provides that if there is inconsistency between Union laws under 249/250 and State laws, the State law is inoperative to the extent of the repugnancy. Under Article 246A, Parliament and State legislatures have concurrent powers on GST. Related UPSC angles include the Sarkaria Commission, the Punchhi Commission, Inter-State Council (Article 263), and Seventh Schedule shifts via the 42nd Amendment, which moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice to the Concurrent List.

question: In the grasslands, trees do not replace the grasses as a part of an ecological succession because of
options: limited sunlight and paucity of nutrients
subject: Environment
detail: Ecological succession normally proceeds from pioneer species to a stable climax community, whose type is set by climate, chiefly rainfall and temperature. Grasslands are typically found in regions with moderate to low, seasonal rainfall (roughly 25-75 cm), too dry for continuous forest but too wet for desert. Limited soil moisture, prolonged dry seasons and periodic drought prevent tree seedlings from establishing deep roots. Fire is the second key factor: grasses have basal meristems and extensive underground rhizomes or roots, so they resprout quickly after burning, while tree seedlings and saplings are killed. Grazing and browsing by herbivores also suppress woody growth. Such communities are sometimes called disclimax or fire climax or edaphic/climatic climax, where disturbance maintains the vegetation. Elimination logic: (a) insects and fungi are not the dominant controlling factors; (b) grasslands are generally open and sunlit, and nutrient-poor soil is not the main reason; shade limitation does not apply since there are few trees. (d) is wrong because (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: insects and fungi may affect individual plants but are not the primary factors that arrest succession in grasslands.
Wrong: grasslands are open with abundant sunlight, so sunlight is not limiting, and nutrient poverty is not the main determinant of the absence of trees.
Correct: low or erratic rainfall (water limits) and recurrent fires prevent trees from establishing, while grasses regenerate quickly, keeping the community as grassland.
Wrong: since option (c) is correct, 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: Grasslands persist because limited and erratic water plus recurrent fire (and grazing) stop tree seedlings from establishing, arresting succession.
option_notes: Insects and fungi act as herbivores, pests, decomposers and pathogens. Fungi (including mycorrhizae) help in nutrient uptake and decomposition, and termites and other insects recycle nutrients. They can influence plant health locally, but they do not decide the vegetation type of a biome. Climate, soil and disturbance (fire, grazing) are the broad determinants of whether an area becomes forest or grassland.

Limited sunlight is typical of the forest floor, where canopy shading restricts understorey growth, not of open grasslands. Paucity of nutrients is characteristic of some tropical rainforest soils (leached laterites) and of nutrient-poor ecosystems like bogs, yet forests thrive in them through rapid nutrient cycling. Light and nutrient limits therefore do not explain the absence of trees in grasslands.

Water limits and fire are the key controls in grasslands such as the savannas of Africa, the prairies of North America, the pampas of Argentina, the steppes of Eurasia and the veldt of South Africa. Seasonal drought restricts deep-rooted trees, while fire kills seedlings. Grasses, with underground buds and rapid regrowth, are adapted to both, so they persist as a fire or climatic climax.

'None of the above' would be correct only if all listed factors were irrelevant. Here, water limits and fire are the accepted ecological explanation for the maintenance of grasslands, so this option is incorrect. In UPSC, such an option is usually a distractor in factual questions with a clearly identifiable correct choice.
related: Succession ending in a stable community in equilibrium with climate is called the climax community.
Primary succession on bare rock starts with lichens (pioneer species).
Secondary succession is faster because soil is already present.
Savannas: Africa; Prairies: North America; Pampas: Argentina; Veldt: South Africa; Steppes: Eurasia.
Hydrarch succession starts in water; xerarch succession starts on dry areas.
Banni grassland is in Kutch, Gujarat, and is one of the largest grasslands in India.
Invasive Prosopis juliflora has spread across many Indian grasslands.
