Fire-maintained community that blocks succession is a disclimax or fire climax.
summary: The answer is (c) water limits and fire. Grasslands occur where rainfall is too low or too erratic to support forests, and recurrent fires (along with grazing) destroy tree seedlings while grasses regenerate from protected underground growing points, so succession is arrested at the grassland stage.
topic_notes: Ecological succession is the orderly, directional change in community structure over time. Primary succession begins on bare areas with no soil (rock, lava, glacial deposits), starting with pioneers such as lichens (hydrarch succession begins in water, xerarch on dry rock). Secondary succession starts where soil exists, after disturbances such as fire, flood or abandoned farmland, and is faster. The final stable stage is the climax community, determined mainly by climate. Where recurrent disturbance holds a community back, it is called a disclimax, fire climax or plagioclimax. Grasslands are such cases. Major grassland types: tropical savanna (Africa, with acacia and scattered trees; Indian examples include the Terai and parts of the Deccan), temperate grasslands (prairies, steppes, pampas, veldt, Canterbury downs, with fertile chernozem soils), and montane or alpine meadows. India has the Terai-Duar savannas, the Banni grasslands in Kutch, semi-arid Deccan grasslands and the Shola-grassland mosaic in the Western Ghats. Features of grasses: basal growth, fibrous roots, drought tolerance, silica in leaves, and fire and grazing tolerance. Important principles: pioneer species, seral stages, autogenic and allogenic succession, net primary productivity increases and then stabilises as a climax is approached, species diversity rises during succession, and biomass and nutrient conservation increase. Related UPSC angles: tropical rainforest vs savanna, effects of fire suppression (woody encroachment), the role of grazers like blackbuck and rhinoceros, invasive species such as Prosopis juliflora and Lantana, and the Biome map.

ocr: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of ecosystems in the order of decreasing productivity? (a) Oceans, lakes, grasslands, mangroves (b) Mangroves, oceans, grasslands, lakes (c) Mangroves, grasslands, lakes, oceans (ad) Oceans, mangroves, lakes, grasslands B-BRO-M-HTA/46A
subject: Environment
detail: Primary productivity is the rate at which producers fix solar energy into organic matter, measured as net primary productivity (NPP) in g/m²/year or kcal/m²/year. It depends on light, nutrients, water, temperature and the type of producers. Per unit area, estuaries, mangroves, swamps, marshes, coral reefs and tropical rainforests rank highest. These systems receive nutrient-rich runoff and detritus, trap sediments, and have dense vegetation. Temperate and tropical grasslands have moderate NPP, as water limits their growth. Lakes are lower still, limited by nutrients (oligotrophic lakes) and by light penetration in deeper water, although eutrophic lakes can be quite productive. The open ocean covers about 70% of the Earth's surface, so it contributes the most total global productivity, but per square metre it is very low because nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus and iron are scarce in the sunlit zone and phytoplankton are the only producers. The question asks about decreasing productivity, so the ranking is by productivity per unit area. Elimination: oceans cannot come first, since they are the lowest per unit area. That removes (a) and (d). Between (b) and (c), (b) puts oceans above lakes and grasslands, which is wrong. Only (c) puts oceans last.
explanations: Incorrect: it places oceans first and mangroves last, which is the reverse of the real trend. Open oceans have the lowest productivity per unit area.
Incorrect: it puts oceans second, above grasslands and lakes. Oceans are less productive per unit area than both, so this ordering fails.

Correct: mangroves (very high, nutrient-rich, shallow, sunlit) > grasslands (moderate) > lakes (lower, nutrient and light limited) > open oceans (lowest per unit area). This matches the official answer.
Incorrect: it begins with oceans, which are the least productive per unit area. It also puts lakes above grasslands, which is wrong.
keyfact: Per unit area: mangroves/estuaries > grasslands > lakes > open ocean, the lowest, although oceans give the largest total productivity because of their area.
option_notes: Oceans cover about 71% of the Earth and hold most of its biosphere volume. Phytoplankton such as diatoms and dinoflagellates are the main producers. Productivity per unit area in the open ocean is very low, about 125 g/m²/year, because nutrients and iron are scarce. Because of the huge area, oceans still contribute about half of global NPP. Coastal upwelling zones such as Peru and Somalia are far more productive than the open sea.

Lakes are standing freshwater ecosystems with zones: littoral, limnetic and profundal. They are classed as oligotrophic (nutrient-poor, clear), mesotrophic or eutrophic (nutrient-rich, algal blooms). Productivity is moderate, about 250 g/m²/year on average. Eutrophication from nitrogen and phosphorus runoff reduces dissolved oxygen. Examples include Chilika (a brackish lagoon, Ramsar site), Wular, Dal and Loktak.

Grasslands are dominated by grasses, with few trees, and occur where rainfall is moderate (about 250-900 mm). Types include tropical savannas, temperate prairies, steppes, pampas and veld. Their productivity is moderate, about 600 g/m²/year, and is limited by water and by fire and grazing. They have deep, fertile soils, which is why many have been turned into farmland. Indian examples are the Terai, Banni and Shola grasslands.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant forests of tropical and subtropical intertidal coasts. They have pneumatophores (breathing roots), stilt roots and viviparous germination. Their productivity is very high, often over 2000 g/m²/year. They protect coasts from storms and tsunamis, serve as fish nurseries and store blue carbon. The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world, and India's mangrove cover is about 4,990 sq km (ISFR 2021). Key species include Rhizophora, Avicennia and Heritiera fomes (sundari).
related: Net primary productivity = Gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses.
Estuaries, swamps and marshes, and mangroves rank among the highest in productivity per unit area.
Open oceans have the lowest productivity per unit area but the largest total contribution among aquatic systems.
Lindeman's 10 percent law explains energy transfer between trophic levels.
Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world; Bhitarkanika is in Odisha.
MISHTI was launched in 2023 for mangrove plantation along India's coast and on salt pans.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies that causes algal blooms and oxygen depletion.
Pyramids of energy are always upright; the pyramid of biomass in oceans can be inverted.
summary: The correct answer is (c): Mangroves > Grasslands > Lakes > Oceans. Mangroves, like estuaries and wetlands, are among the most productive ecosystems because of abundant nutrients, shallow water, and strong sunlight. The open ocean has very low productivity per unit area because nutrients and light are limited.
topic_notes:
Productivity terms: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total organic matter produced by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP minus respiration losses. Secondary productivity is the rate at which consumers form new organic matter. Net ecosystem productivity is also used. Biomass is the standing crop, measured as mass per unit area.

Global pattern: The whole biosphere produces about 170 billion tonnes (dry weight) of organic matter a year. Oceans, because of their area, account for roughly 55 billion tonnes, a share lower than their area would suggest (the remainder is land). Per unit area, ecosystems rank roughly as follows: swamps, marshes, estuaries and mangroves, then coral reefs and tropical rainforests, then temperate forests, then savannas and grasslands, then agricultural land, then lakes and streams, then tundra, then desert, and lastly the open ocean. Deserts and the open ocean are the lowest.

Limiting factors: On land these are water and temperature. In oceans they are nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, iron) and light. Iron fertilisation has been proposed as a geoengineering approach to boost ocean carbon uptake.

Ecological principles: Lindeman's 10 percent law means only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level. Pyramids of energy are always upright, while pyramids of biomass and numbers can be inverted. In a pond, the biomass pyramid is inverted. Ecotones and edge effects raise productivity at habitat boundaries, which is why estuaries and mangroves, as ecotones, are so rich.

Indian context: Ramsar sites such as Chilika, Keoladeo and Sundarbans; Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes (MISHTI, 2023); the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) rules classify mangroves as CRZ-I; the Wetland Rules (2017) govern wetland conservation.

question: Contour bunding is a method of soil conservation used in
options: desert margins, liable to strong wind action
low flat plains, close to stream courses, liable to flooding scrublands, liable to spread of
None of the above Government enacted the
subject: Geography
detail: Contour bunding is a mechanical soil conservation method in which small embankments (bunds) of earth, stone or vegetation are built along contour lines, that is, across the slope at the same elevation. The bunds slow down surface runoff, let water infiltrate, trap eroded sediment and reduce rill and gully formation. It suits gentle to moderate slopes (roughly 2-6 percent, up to about 10 percent) in semi-arid and sub-humid regions with moderate rainfall and permeable soils. Related methods include contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, graded bunding, check dams and gully plugging. Elimination logic: (a) desert margins face wind erosion, which is controlled by shelterbelts, windbreaks and sand-dune stabilisation, not by contour bunds that act against water flow. (b) Low flat plains near streams face flooding, which needs embankments, levees and drainage, and there is no slope to contour. (c) Weed-infested scrublands need clearing, weeding or herbicides, which are unrelated to bunding. None of these three fits a method meant for sloping land with water erosion, so (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: desert margins suffer wind erosion, controlled by shelterbelts, windbreaks, mulching and dune stabilisation. Contour bunds work against water runoff on slopes.
Incorrect: low flat plains near streams are flood-prone and need levees, embankments and drainage. Contour bunding needs a slope and does not stop river flooding.
Incorrect: weed or scrub spread is a vegetation-management problem handled by clearing, weeding or herbicides, not by contour bunds.
Correct: contour bunding is for sloping, rain-fed lands with water erosion, which none of (a)-(c) describes, so none of the above applies.
keyfact: Contour bunding checks water erosion on sloping, moderate-rainfall land, so none of the given options (a)-(c) fits; answer (d).
option_notes: Desert margins: areas at the edge of arid zones such as the Thar fringes in Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat. They face wind erosion, sand drift and desertification. Controls include shelterbelts, windbreaks, afforestation with species like khejri and Prosopis, sand-dune fixation and the Desert Development Programme, started in 1977-78. The Great Green Wall in Africa is a global example.

Low flat plains close to streams: floodplains such as the Ganga-Brahmaputra basin, regularly inundated in the monsoon. They get fertile alluvium but face flood damage. Management uses embankments, levees, flood forecasting, drainage, river training, floodplain zoning and reservoirs. Bihar's Kosi, the 'sorrow of Bihar', is a famous flood-prone river. Soil conservation is not primarily by contour bunds.

Weed-infested scrublands: degraded lands where unwanted vegetation such as Lantana camara, Prosopis juliflora or Parthenium spreads. Management includes mechanical removal, biological control, herbicides and reclamation through afforestation or pasture development. Such lands are often classed as wastelands, and the National Wastelands Development Board and Integrated Wastelands Development Programme dealt with them.

None of the above: the correct choice. Contour bunding is used on sloping farmland, typically 2-6 percent slope, in semi-arid regions with moderate rainfall of about 600-800 mm. It is common on the Deccan plateau, Maharashtra and Karnataka. The bunds hold moisture, reduce runoff velocity and trap silt, and are often supported by grass or trees on the bunds.
related: Contour bunding suits gently sloping, semi-arid land with moderate rainfall.
Shelterbelts and windbreaks control wind erosion in desert margins.
Terrace farming is used on steep hill slopes to reduce runoff.
Gully erosion creates ravines, notably in the Chambal region.
CSWCRTI is in Dehradun and was established in 1954.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015.
Desert Development Programme began in 1977-78.
Strip cropping and contour ploughing are agronomic erosion-control methods.
summary: The official answer is (d), None of the above. Contour bunding is used on sloping or hilly land with moderate rainfall to check runoff and soil erosion, not on desert margins, flood-prone flat plains or weed-infested scrublands.
topic_notes: Soil erosion is the detachment and transport of topsoil by water, wind, ice or gravity. Water erosion appears as sheet, rill, gully and splash erosion. Ravines in the Chambal region show severe gully erosion. Wind erosion is dominant in arid and semi-arid zones. Soil conservation methods fall into agronomic (biological) and mechanical groups. Agronomic methods include contour ploughing, strip cropping, crop rotation, mulching, cover crops, agroforestry and intercropping. Mechanical methods include contour bunding, graded bunds, terracing, check dams, gully plugging, trenching and bench terracing. Terracing suits steeper hill slopes, as in the Himalayan and Western Ghats regions. Shelterbelts and windbreaks protect against wind. Contour bunding is best on slopes below about 6 percent, where bunds follow equal-elevation lines and hold water to improve infiltration and soil moisture. Graded bunds are used in higher-rainfall areas to carry excess water safely off the field. Institutions and programmes: Central Soil and Water Conservation Research and Training Institute (CSWCRTI), Dehradun, set up in 1954; the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning, Nagpur; the Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP), now part of PMKSY's watershed component; the Soil Health Card scheme launched in 2015; and the Desert Development Programme and Drought Prone Areas Programme. India loses large amounts of topsoil each year, and roughly 30 percent of land is degraded by some estimates. Future questions could ask which method suits which terrain: windbreaks for deserts, terracing for steep hills, embankments for floods, and contour bunding for moderate slopes.

question: The Panchayat Extension to Scheduled Areas (PESA) Act in 1996. Which one of the following is not identified as its objective? To provide self-governance
options: in tribal areas To free tribal people from
subject: Polity
detail: The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 extends Part IX of the Constitution (Articles 243-243ZG) to Fifth Schedule areas, which Article 243M had initially excluded. It followed the Bhuria Committee (1995) recommendations. Its stated objectives include enabling tribal self-rule through gram sabhas, recognising and preserving traditional customs, community resources and cultural identity, safeguarding tribal rights over minor forest produce, land and water, preventing land alienation, regulating money-lending and intoxicants, and freeing tribals from exploitation. The Gram Sabha is central: it must be consulted on land acquisition, approves development plans and identifies beneficiaries. Autonomous districts and regions with district and regional councils are created under the Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2) and 275(1)) for Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. PESA works inside the ordinary Panchayat structure and creates no autonomous regions. Elimination: the three options on self-governance, traditional rights and freedom from exploitation are all PESA goals, leaving autonomous regions as the odd one out. Note the question's options are scrambled by OCR, but the logic is the same.
explanations: Option (a), recognising traditional rights, is a genuine PESA objective: the Act safeguards customs, cultural identity and community resources, so it is not the exception.
Option (b), providing self-governance in tribal areas, is a core PESA objective through empowered gram sabhas, so it is not the exception.
Option (c), creating autonomous regions, is not a PESA objective. Autonomous districts and regions come under the Sixth Schedule. Hence this is the correct answer.

Option (d), freeing tribal people from exploitation, is a stated aim of PESA, through controls on land alienation, money-lending and liquor and ownership of minor forest produce, so it is not the exception.
keyfact: PESA 1996 extends Panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas for tribal self-rule; autonomous regions belong to the Sixth Schedule.
option_notes: Recognition of traditional rights: PESA requires state laws to be consistent with customary law, social and religious practices and traditional management of community resources. The Gram Sabha is competent to safeguard and preserve the traditions and customs of the people, their cultural identity and community resources, and to settle disputes in the customary manner. The Forest Rights Act 2006 later complements this for forest dwellers.

Self-governance in tribal areas: PESA aims to enable tribal communities to govern themselves through their own systems of self-government. The Gram Sabha or Panchayat at the appropriate level must be consulted before land acquisition and resettlement, approves plans and programmes, and controls local institutions, markets and processes. This realises the slogan 'our government in our villages' (mava nate mava raj).

Creation of autonomous regions: this belongs to the Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2)), covering tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils have legislative, judicial and executive powers over land, forests, village administration and so on. PESA does not create them; it applies to Fifth Schedule areas in ten states.

Freedom from exploitation: PESA seeks to protect tribals from exploitation by moneylenders, traders and contractors. Gram Sabhas have powers to prevent alienation of tribal land and restore unlawfully alienated land, to exercise control over money-lending and to regulate sale and consumption of intoxicants. They also have ownership of minor forest produce and control over village markets.
related: PESA was enacted in 1996 following the Bhuria Committee report.
PESA extends Part IX (Panchayats) to Fifth Schedule areas.
Article 243M(4)(b) originally excluded Scheduled Areas from Part IX.
Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
Ten states have Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas.
The Gram Sabha is the central institution under PESA.
Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights.
Governor, not the President, makes regulations for Fifth Schedule areas.
summary: The answer is (c): creating autonomous regions is not an objective of the PESA Act, 1996. PESA extends Part IX (Panchayats) to Fifth Schedule areas to provide self-governance, recognise traditional rights and free tribals from exploitation. Autonomous regions/districts belong to the Sixth Schedule, a different constitutional mechanism.
topic_notes: PESA, 1996 was enacted on 24 December 1996 to extend Part IX Panchayats to Fifth Schedule Areas, which were excluded by Article 243M(4)(b). It followed the Dileep Singh Bhuria Committee (1994-95). Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) governs administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; the Governor has wide powers, including regulating land transfer and money-lending, and a Tribes Advisory Council operates. Ten states have Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan. The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2), 275(1)) covers tribal areas in the four north-eastern states, with Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils. The President declares Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule. Key PESA features: the Gram Sabha is the central body, a state legislation cannot be inconsistent with customary law, the reservation for Scheduled Tribes in Panchayats is proportional to population, and the Chairperson at all levels must be a ST for the Panchayats at the village level, with at least half of seats for ST at all tiers. Gram Sabha powers include approval of plans, identifying beneficiaries, mandatory consultation on land acquisition, planning and managing minor water bodies, controlling minor minerals leasing, and ownership of minor forest produce. The Ministry of Panchayati Raj is the nodal ministry; the Ministry of Tribal Affairs is also relevant. Related laws: Forest Rights Act 2006, Samatha judgment (1997), Niyamgiri case (2013). Other angles: Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects), 73rd Amendment 1992, Article 243D reservation, Article 243G.

question: Under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, who shall be the authority to initiate the process for determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights or both?
subject: Economy
detail: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (in force from 31 December 2007; Rules notified 1 January 2008) recognises and vests forest rights in forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers who have occupied forest land before 13 December 2005. Section 6 lays down a three-tier process. The Gram Sabha initiates the process, receives claims, verifies them, passes a resolution and forwards it to the Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC). The SDLC examines the resolution and prepares the record of forest rights, which goes to the District Level Committee (DLC). The DLC, chaired by the District Collector, gives the final decision. State Level Monitoring Committee monitors the process. The Forest Rights Committee, elected by the Gram Sabha (10-15 members, at least one-third women), assists in verification. Elimination: the Forest Department, Collector and Tahsildar/BDO are officials who take part in committees at higher levels, but the Act deliberately places initiation with the Gram Sabha to ensure democratic, community-led recognition. Hence only (d) fits.
explanations: Wrong: the State Forest Department has representation in the SDLC and DLC but does not initiate the process; the Act was meant to correct the historical injustice done by forest bureaucracy.
Wrong: the District Collector chairs the District Level Committee, which gives the final decision on claims, but does not initiate determination of rights.
Wrong: revenue officials such as the Tahsildar/BDO may sit on the Sub-Divisional Level Committee or help in records, but they do not start the process.
Correct: Section 6(1) of the FRA 2006 states that the Gram Sabha shall be the authority to initiate the process for determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights or both.
keyfact: Under FRA 2006 Section 6, the Gram Sabha initiates determination of rights; the SDLC examines and the Collector-led DLC finally approves.
option_notes: The State Forest Department manages reserved and protected forests under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. Its officials (such as the Divisional Forest Officer) are members of the Sub-Divisional and District Level Committees under FRA. Historically, its control over forests led to the denial of customary rights, which FRA 2006 sought to correct.

The District Collector or Deputy Commissioner is the head of district revenue and general administration. Under FRA Rules, the Collector chairs the District Level Committee, which hears petitions against SDLC decisions and gives the final approval of forest rights records. The DLC also includes the DFO and the Tribal Welfare Department officer, along with three elected Panchayati Raj members.

The Tahsildar, Block Development Officer or Mandal Revenue Officer is a sub-district revenue or development official, with different names in different states. They maintain land records and implement rural schemes. Under FRA they typically serve on the Sub-Divisional Level Committee, helping verify claims, but have no power to initiate the determination process.

The Gram Sabha is the body of all adult members of a village on the electoral roll, recognised under Article 243(b) of the Constitution. Under FRA Section 6 it initiates determination of rights, passes resolutions, and elects the Forest Rights Committee. Under Section 5 it also protects wildlife, forests and biodiversity. The Gram Sabha is the cornerstone of the Act.
related: FRA 2006 was notified for operation on 31 December 2007; the Rules came on 1 January 2008.
The nodal ministry for FRA is the Ministry of Tribal Affairs.
The cut-off date for recognising forest rights is 13 December 2005.
Individual forest land rights are limited to a maximum of 4 hectares.
Other Traditional Forest Dwellers must have lived in the area for at least 75 years (three generations).
The District Level Committee, chaired by the Collector, finally approves forest rights claims.
PESA 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas and empowers Gram Sabhas.
The Niyamgiri case (2013) upheld the Gram Sabha's role regarding bauxite mining and forest rights.
summary: The answer is (d) Gram Sabha. Section 6(1) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 makes the Gram Sabha the authority to initiate the process of determining the nature and extent of individual or community forest rights (or both) that may be given to eligible forest dwellers.
topic_notes: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (also called the Tribal Rights Act or Tribal Bill) was enacted to undo the historical injustice to forest dwellers whose rights were not recorded when state forests were consolidated during colonial and post-independence periods. It is administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, not the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The cut-off date is 13 December 2005 for occupation. Other traditional forest dwellers must have resided in the area for at least three generations (75 years). Individual rights are capped at 4 hectares of land under occupation for habitation or self-cultivation. Community rights include nistar, minor forest produce ownership, grazing, fishing, access to water bodies, rights of pastoralists and rights for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), including habitat rights. Section 3(1)(i) recognises the right to protect, regenerate, conserve or manage Community Forest Resources. Section 4(2) allows relocation from critical wildlife habitats only with free informed consent of the Gram Sabha and settlement of rights. Section 5 gives duties to holders of rights. The process runs from the Gram Sabha to SDLC to DLC, with the State Level Monitoring Committee overseeing it. Rights recognised are heritable but not alienable or transferable. The 2013 Supreme Court Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (Niyamgiri) judgment affirmed the Gram Sabha's power to decide on mining affecting forest rights and religious practices of the Dongria Kondh. Related legislation includes PESA 1996, which empowers Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas (Fifth Schedule), and Article 244. Future questions may ask about the nodal ministry, the cut-off date, the ceiling on land, Community Forest Resource rights, and Gram Sabha powers.

question: Improper handling and storage of cereal grains and oilseeds result in the production of toxins known as aflatoxins which are not generally destroyed by normal _ cooking process. Aflatoxins are produced by
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Aflatoxins are toxic, carcinogenic secondary metabolites of filamentous fungi (moulds) of the genus Aspergillus, mainly A. flavus (hence 'A-fla-toxin') and A. parasiticus, with A. nomius also implicated. They contaminate maize, groundnut (peanut), cottonseed, tree nuts, rice, wheat, spices and dried fruits, especially when grain moisture is high (above about 14%) and storage is warm and humid (25-35 degrees C). The main types are B1, B2, G1 and G2; B1 is the most potent natural liver carcinogen known, and IARC places it in Group 1. Aflatoxin M1 appears in the milk of animals that eat contaminated feed. The toxins are heat-stable (they break down only above roughly 250 degrees C), so normal cooking does not destroy them. Effects include aflatoxicosis, liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma), immune suppression and stunting in children. Prevention relies on proper drying, clean and dry storage, aeration and good crop practices. Elimination logic: aflatoxins are produced by fungi. Bacteria, protozoa and viruses do not make them, so (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out. Only moulds fit.
explanations: Incorrect: bacteria produce other toxins (for example botulinum toxin from Clostridium botulinum), but not aflatoxins, which are fungal metabolites.
Incorrect: protozoa are single-celled eukaryotic parasites (Plasmodium, Entamoeba, Giardia). They do not produce aflatoxins and do not grow on stored grain to make toxins.
Correct: aflatoxins are produced by moulds, chiefly Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus, growing on poorly stored cereals and oilseeds.
Incorrect: viruses are non-cellular obligate parasites with no metabolism of their own, so they cannot synthesise toxins like aflatoxin.
keyfact: Aflatoxins are heat-stable carcinogenic toxins made by the mould Aspergillus flavus (and A. parasiticus) on poorly stored grains and oilseeds.
option_notes: Bacteria are prokaryotic microorganisms. Some cause food poisoning through toxins, such as Clostridium botulinum (botulism), Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Salmonella, E. coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus. They are unrelated to aflatoxins. Many are useful too: Lactobacillus in curd, Rhizobium in nitrogen fixation, Streptomyces for antibiotics. Their cell walls contain peptidoglycan, and they reproduce by binary fission.

Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotic organisms, mostly heterotrophic. Disease-causing examples are Plasmodium (malaria), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery), Giardia (giardiasis), Trypanosoma (sleeping sickness) and Leishmania (kala-azar). They move by pseudopodia, cilia or flagella. They are not sources of aflatoxin or of grain-storage toxins.

Moulds are multicellular filamentous fungi that grow as hyphae forming a mycelium. Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus produce aflatoxins, which are heat-stable and are potent liver carcinogens (B1 is IARC Group 1). Other mycotoxin producers include Penicillium (ochratoxin), Fusarium (fumonisin, zearalenone) and Claviceps purpurea (ergot, ergotism). Moulds thrive in warm, humid, damp storage conditions.

Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites made of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat (capsid). They multiply only inside host cells. Examples include HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, hepatitis viruses and the tobacco mosaic virus (the first virus discovered, by Ivanovsky and Beijerinck). They produce no metabolic toxins such as aflatoxin.
related: Aflatoxins are produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus.
Aflatoxin B1 is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen and mainly damages the liver.
Aflatoxin M1 is found in milk of animals fed contaminated feed.
Aflatoxins are heat-stable and survive normal cooking.
Ergotism is caused by Claviceps purpurea, a fungus that infects rye.
Turkey X disease (1960, UK) led to the discovery of aflatoxins.
FSSAI is the statutory body under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Aflasafe is a biocontrol product using atoxigenic Aspergillus strains.
summary: The answer is (c) moulds. Aflatoxins are secondary metabolites produced by fungi, chiefly Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, which grow on improperly stored cereals, oilseeds and nuts in warm, humid conditions.
topic_notes: Mycotoxins are toxic secondary metabolites of fungi that contaminate food and feed. Aflatoxins are the best known. They were identified after the 1960 'Turkey X disease' outbreak in England, which killed over 100,000 turkey poults fed on contaminated Brazilian groundnut meal. Producers are Aspergillus flavus (B1 and B2) and A. parasiticus (B1, B2, G1, G2). Aflatoxin B1 is the most toxic and is metabolised in the liver to a reactive epoxide that damages DNA (the p53 gene mutation is linked to it). Chronic exposure causes hepatocellular carcinoma, especially with hepatitis B; acute exposure causes aflatoxicosis. M1 and M2 are hydroxylated metabolites that appear in milk. Contamination is favoured by drought stress and insect damage before harvest, and by high moisture and temperature in storage. Crops at greatest risk are maize, groundnut, cottonseed, chillies, tree nuts and dried fruits. Controls include drying grain to under 12-13% moisture, hermetic storage, good aeration, biocontrol with atoxigenic strains (Aflasafe, developed in Nigeria by IITA), and sorting. In India, FSSAI sets a limit of 30 ppb total aflatoxin in most foods and 0.5 ppb of M1 in milk. Other mycotoxins: ochratoxin A (Aspergillus ochraceus, Penicillium), fumonisins and trichothecenes (Fusarium), patulin (Penicillium expansum in apples), and ergot alkaloids (Claviceps). Related ideas are the ban on groundnut exports rejected by the EU for aflatoxin, and food safety under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

question: Economic Justice’ as one of the objectives of the Indian Constitution has been provided in
options: the Preamble and the Fundamental Rights
the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy
the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of State Policy
subject: Polity
detail: Economic justice means the absence of exploitation and a fair distribution of wealth, income and opportunity, so that social position does not depend on economic status. The Constitution states it in two places. First, the Preamble, which secures to all citizens 'JUSTICE, social, economic and political'. The words come from the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru in 1946 and were adopted on 26 November 1949. Second, Part IV (Articles 36-51), the DPSP, which is not justiciable (Art. 37) but is fundamental to governance. Article 38 directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. Article 39 covers an adequate means of livelihood, equitable distribution of material resources, prevention of concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work, and protection of workers and children. Article 39A provides equal justice and free legal aid. Articles 41-43 deal with the right to work, just and humane conditions, and a living wage. Elimination logic: Fundamental Rights (Part III) chiefly secure civil and political liberties and equality before law, so any option containing them (a, c) is out. Since (b) is correct, (d) is also wrong.
explanations: Wrong: the Preamble does contain economic justice, but Fundamental Rights are mainly civil and political rights and do not set economic justice as an objective.
Correct: the Preamble names economic justice, and the DPSP (Arts. 38, 39, 41-43) set out the socio-economic directions to achieve it.
Wrong: Fundamental Rights do not embody economic justice as such, so this pairing is incorrect even though DPSP does.
Wrong: economic justice is clearly provided for in the Preamble and the DPSP.
keyfact: Economic justice appears in the Preamble ('Justice, social, economic and political') and in the DPSP (Arts. 38-39, 41-43), not in the Fundamental Rights.
option_notes: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution. It declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, and secures justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. 'Socialist' and 'secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Arts. 12-35), are justiciable, and are enforceable through Art. 32 and Art. 226. They largely protect individual civil and political liberties.

The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946) and was held part of the Constitution in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), after Berubari (1960) had held otherwise. DPSP are in Part IV (Arts. 36-51), were borrowed from the Irish Constitution, and are non-justiciable. They aim at a welfare state and socio-economic democracy. Gandhian, socialist and liberal-intellectual principles are included.

Fundamental Rights (Part III) and DPSP (Part IV) are together called the 'conscience of the Constitution'. Minerva Mills (1980) held that harmony and balance between them is a basic feature. Fundamental Rights are negative limits on the State and ensure political democracy. DPSP are positive obligations that ensure socio-economic democracy. The 25th Amendment (Art. 31C) gave priority to Arts. 39(b) and (c).

'None of the above' would be right only if economic justice appeared nowhere in the Constitution. It does appear, in the Preamble and in Part IV. The three kinds of justice, social, economic and political, are the first Preambular ideal. The other ideals are liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, equality of status and opportunity, and fraternity assuring dignity and the unity and integrity of the nation.
related: Art. 38 directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
Art. 39(b) and (c) deal with distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
Art. 39A (42nd Amendment) provides equal justice and free legal aid.
DPSP were borrowed from the Irish Constitution and are non-justiciable under Art. 37.
The words 'socialist' and 'secular' were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Berubari Union (1960) said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) reversed this.
Art. 43B on promotion of cooperative societies was added by the 97th Amendment, 2011.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that harmony between FRs and DPSP is a basic feature.
summary: The answer is (b): the Preamble and the Directive Principles of State Policy. The Preamble promises 'JUSTICE, social, economic and political', and Part IV (DPSP), especially Articles 38 and 39, gives concrete content to economic justice.
topic_notes: The Preamble, Fundamental Rights and DPSP together express the philosophy of the Constitution. The Preamble opens with 'We, the people of India' and declares the source of authority and the objectives. It was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, which added socialist, secular and integrity. Justice in the Preamble has three forms. Social justice means no discrimination on grounds of caste, creed, sex, and so on. Economic justice means no discrimination on the basis of wealth, income and economic status. Political justice means equal political rights, such as universal adult franchise (Art. 326) and equal access to political office. This triad was taken from the Russian Revolution ideal, while liberty, equality and fraternity came from the French Revolution. DPSP in Part IV are classified as socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Arts. 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) and liberal-intellectual (Arts. 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). Key amendments: 42nd (1976) added Arts. 39A, 43A and 48A; 44th (1978) added Art. 38(2) on minimising inequalities in income; 86th (2002) added Art. 21A and changed Art. 45; 97th (2011) added Art. 43B on cooperative societies. Judicial landmarks: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) held that DPSP are subordinate to FRs; Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Minerva Mills (1980) held that balance between Parts III and IV is basic structure; Unni Krishnan (1993) on education. Related angles UPSC may ask: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art. 51A, from the Swaran Singh Committee, 42nd Amendment), sources of the Constitution, differences between FR and DPSP, and the Preamble as part of the basic structure.

question:
Due to improper/indiscriminate disposal of old and used computers or their parts, which of the following are released into the environment as e-waste?
1. Beryllium Cadmium Se he Chromium Heptachlor Mercury Lead Plutonium Select the correct answer using the codes given below
subject: Environment
detail: E-waste from discarded computers contains toxic metals that contaminate soil, water and air when it is dumped in landfills or burned in the open. The standard UPSC list is: lead (CRT monitors, solder, circuit boards), cadmium (batteries, chips, semiconductors), mercury (LCD backlights, switches, flat-screen lamps), chromium (hexavalent chromium for corrosion protection of steel casings), and beryllium (motherboards and connectors, as beryllium-copper alloy). Other items include brominated flame retardants (PBDEs, PBBs), PVC, and arsenic and barium. Heptachlor is an organochlorine pesticide listed under the Stockholm Convention on POPs, so it is linked to agriculture, not electronics. Plutonium is a radioactive element used in nuclear weapons and reactors, with no role in computers. The question's OCR text lost the numbering, but the order is evidently 1 Beryllium, 2 Cadmium, 3 Chromium, 4 Heptachlor, 5 Mercury, 6 Lead, 7 Plutonium. Elimination: any option containing 4 or 7 is wrong, which leaves only (b). India regulates e-waste under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, with amendments in 2018 and the 2022 rules.
explanations: Wrong: it includes heptachlor (4) and plutonium (7) and omits cadmium and chromium, which are in fact e-waste constituents.
Correct: it lists exactly beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead, all of which are used in computers and released as e-waste.
Wrong: it leaves out the key metals beryllium, cadmium and chromium and adds heptachlor and plutonium, which do not come from computers.
Wrong: it includes all seven items, but heptachlor (a pesticide) and plutonium (a nuclear material) are not part of computer e-waste.
keyfact: Computer e-waste toxins: lead, cadmium, mercury, chromium, beryllium (plus BFRs); heptachlor is a pesticide and plutonium is nuclear, so neither is e-waste.
option_notes: Option (a) combines items 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7: beryllium, chromium, heptachlor, lead and plutonium. Heptachlor is an organochlorine pesticide and a POP listed under the Stockholm Convention. Plutonium is a radioactive element used in nuclear weapons and reactors. This option wrongly leaves out cadmium and mercury, both well-known e-waste toxins.

Option (b) is the official answer, containing beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead. These are the heavy metals and toxic elements typically found in computer parts. Beryllium sits in motherboards, cadmium in batteries and chips, chromium in casings, mercury in LCD backlights and lead in solder and CRT glass. All are hazardous to health and the environment when e-waste is improperly dumped or burned.

Option (c) combines cadmium, heptachlor, mercury and plutonium (2, 4, 5 and 7 in the numbering used here). It mixes two genuine e-waste metals with a pesticide and a radioactive element. It omits lead, chromium and beryllium, which makes it incorrect.

Option (d) claims all seven items are e-waste. This would require heptachlor (an agricultural POP pesticide) and plutonium (a nuclear fuel and weapon material) to be computer components, which they are not. UPSC uses this type of 'all of the above' option as a trap for students who recognise only that the items are all 'toxic'.
related: Basel Convention (1989) regulates transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, including e-waste.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 introduced EPR, PROs and a deposit refund scheme.
The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 came into effect from 1 April 2023 with EPR certificates.
Minamata Convention deals with mercury; Itai-itai disease is linked to cadmium.
Heptachlor is a POP listed under the Stockholm Convention.
CPCB is the nodal authority monitoring e-waste rules in India.
Moradabad and Seelampur are known e-waste recycling hubs in India.
EU RoHS restricts lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB and PBDE in electronics.
statements: 1 — Correct: Beryllium is used in computer motherboards and connectors and is released as e-waste. Beryllium is a lightweight, strong metal, often used as a beryllium-copper alloy for springs and contacts. Its dust and fumes are carcinogenic and cause chronic beryllium disease (berylliosis), a lung condition. It is an atomic number 4 alkaline earth metal. Improper recycling by burning or acid leaching exposes workers and local communities.

2 — Correct: Cadmium is found in rechargeable Ni-Cd batteries, chip resistors, semiconductors and older CRT screens. It is a toxic heavy metal that accumulates in the kidneys and bones. Chronic exposure caused Itai-itai disease in Japan, from contaminated river water and rice. It is a carcinogen and is restricted under the EU RoHS directive. Its release in e-waste contaminates soil and groundwater.

3 — Correct: Chromium, especially hexavalent chromium (Cr VI), is used as a corrosion protector on steel plates and casings, and for data tapes and floppy disks. Hexavalent chromium is highly toxic and carcinogenic, damaging DNA, the lungs and the liver. It is restricted under RoHS. Burning or dumping e-waste releases it into soil and water, and it is well known from the Erin Brockovich case.

4 — Incorrect: Heptachlor is an organochlorine insecticide used on crops and termites, not a computer component. It is a Persistent Organic Pollutant, listed in Annex A (elimination) of the Stockholm Convention (2001, in force 2004). It bioaccumulates and is a probable human carcinogen. It is not an e-waste constituent.

5 — Correct: Mercury is used in LCD backlights (CFL lamps), switches, relays, thermostats and some batteries. It is a neurotoxin; methylmercury bioaccumulates in fish. Minamata disease in Japan resulted from mercury poisoning. The Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013, in force 2017) regulates it. Burning or crushing e-waste releases mercury vapour.

6 — Correct: Lead is used in CRT glass (to shield radiation), solder on circuit boards, and batteries. A CRT monitor may contain several kilograms of lead. It damages the nervous system, kidneys and blood, and especially impairs children's intellectual development. It is a major component of toxic e-waste and is restricted under RoHS.

7 — Incorrect: Plutonium is a radioactive transuranic element (atomic number 94) produced in nuclear reactors and used in nuclear weapons and as fuel in fast breeder reactors. It is not used in computers. Radioactive americium-241 appears in smoke detectors, but not plutonium in computers. So it is not part of computer e-waste.
summary: The answer is (b): 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 only, meaning beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead. These are the heavy metals and toxic elements used in computer components, and they leach out when e-waste is dumped or burned. Heptachlor (a pesticide) and plutonium (a nuclear material) are not components of computers.
topic_notes:
E-waste means discarded electrical and electronic equipment, including computers, phones, TVs and batteries. India is among the top e-waste generators in the world, after China and the USA. Most of it is handled by the informal sector, in places such as Moradabad, Seelampur (Delhi) and Bengaluru. Informal recycling uses open burning and acid baths, which release dioxins, furans and heavy metals.

Key toxic constituents: lead (CRT, solder), cadmium (batteries, semiconductors), mercury (LCD lamps, switches), hexavalent chromium (casings), beryllium (connectors), brominated flame retardants (PBDEs), PVC, arsenic and barium. Health effects include neurological damage, kidney damage, cancers and developmental disorders.

Legal framework in India: E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, in force from 2012, introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 added producer responsibility organisations (PROs), a deposit refund scheme, dismantlers and refurbishers, and collection targets. Amendments came in 2018. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022, effective April 2023, introduced EPR certificates, a central online portal for trading, and a floor price. They are administered by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) with State Pollution Control Boards.

International angle: the Basel Convention (1989, in force 1992) controls transboundary movement of hazardous waste, and the Basel Ban Amendment prohibits exports from OECD to non-OECD countries. The Stockholm Convention covers POPs such as heptachlor. The Minamata Convention covers mercury. The Rotterdam Convention covers prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals. The EU RoHS directive restricts hazardous substances in electronics, and WEEE is the EU's e-waste directive. The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the UN and ITU. Related ideas include urban mining, the circular economy and green computing, and the BIS and the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) also work on e-waste.

question: Acid rain is caused by the pollution of environment by
subject: Environment
detail: Acid rain (acid deposition) is rainfall, snow, fog or dry particles with pH below about 5.6. Natural rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6) because atmospheric CO2 dissolves to form weak carbonic acid, so CO2 alone is not the cause of acid rain. The term was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872 in Manchester, England. The main culprits are SO2, released by burning coal and oil in thermal power plants and by smelters, and nitrogen oxides (NO, NO2, N2O), released from vehicles and industry. In the atmosphere they are oxidised and react with water vapour to form H2SO4 and HNO3. Effects include damage to marble monuments (the Taj Mahal's 'marble cancer', Mathura refinery concern), acidification of lakes and soils, leaching of nutrients such as calcium and magnesium, forest dieback, and corrosion of buildings and metals. Elimination: (a) pairs CO2 with nitrogen gas, which is inert; (b) CO is a toxic gas that is not acid-forming; (c) ozone is a pollutant and greenhouse gas, and CO2 gives only normal rain acidity. Only (d) names both acid-forming oxides.
explanations: Wrong: CO2 only makes natural rain mildly acidic, and molecular nitrogen (N2) is inert and does not form acids. The nitrogen oxides are the problem, not nitrogen itself.
Wrong: carbon monoxide is a poisonous product of incomplete combustion and is largely insoluble in water. It does not produce strong acids, and CO2 is not the cause.
Wrong: ozone is a secondary pollutant (smog) and a greenhouse gas, and tropospheric ozone harms the lungs and crops. It is not the main cause of acid rain, and CO2 does not make rain acidic enough.
Correct: nitrogen oxides (including nitrous oxide in the question's wording) and sulphur dioxide are oxidised to nitric and sulphuric acids, which cause acid rain. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: Acid rain = SO2 + NOx converted to sulphuric and nitric acids; normal rain pH is about 5.6, and acid rain is below that.
option_notes: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas (about 0.04% of air) from fossil fuel burning, deforestation and respiration. It dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, giving natural rain a pH of about 5.6. Nitrogen makes up 78% of air and is chemically inert; it is fixed by lightning and by bacteria such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter.

Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas from incomplete combustion of carbon fuels, mostly from vehicles. It binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which reduces oxygen transport, and it can be fatal in closed spaces. It is a criterion pollutant under India's NAAQS. CO2 is the fully oxidised product of combustion and a major greenhouse gas.

Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere shields against UV-B, and the Montreal Protocol (1987) controls ozone-depleting substances. In the troposphere it is a harmful secondary pollutant formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight, and it is a component of photochemical smog. It is measured in Dobson Units. Carbon dioxide is the key greenhouse gas behind global warming.

Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a long-lived greenhouse gas (about 265-300 times the warming potential of CO2) from fertilisers, soil bacteria and combustion, and it also depletes ozone. Sulphur dioxide comes from coal and oil burning, smelting and volcanoes. Together with NO and NO2 they are the precursors of sulphuric and nitric acid in acid rain.
related: Normal unpolluted rain has a pH of about 5.6 because of dissolved CO2 (carbonic acid).
The term 'acid rain' was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872.
Main acid rain precursors: SO2 and NOx, giving H2SO4 and HNO3.
Taj Mahal marble damage (marble cancer) is linked to SO2 pollution; the Taj Trapezium Zone was created to curb it.
Flue gas desulphurisation (scrubbers) reduces SO2 emissions from thermal power plants.
CLRTAP (Geneva, 1979) is the main treaty on transboundary air pollution and acid rain.
Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential about 265-300 times that of CO2.
BS-VI fuel norms in India were implemented nationwide from 1 April 2020 to cut sulphur and NOx emissions.
summary: The answer is (d) nitrous oxide and sulphur dioxide. Acid rain forms when sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) are oxidised in the atmosphere and dissolve in water, forming sulphuric and nitric acids that fall as acidic precipitation.
topic_notes: Acid rain is part of acid deposition, which has wet forms (rain, snow, fog) and dry forms (acidic gases and particles settling). Normal rain has pH about 5.6; rain below this is called acid rain. Main precursors are SO2 (mainly from coal-fired power plants, smelters and refineries) and NOx (vehicles, industry). Reactions: SO2 + OH/O2 and water gives H2SO4; NO2 + water gives HNO3. Sulphuric acid usually contributes the larger share of acidity. The term was coined by Robert Angus Smith (1872). Pollutants can travel hundreds of kilometres, so acid rain is often transboundary. In Europe and North America, it damaged Scandinavian lakes, the Black Forest and the Adirondacks. The 1979 Geneva Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP) addresses it. In the USA, the Clean Air Act amendments of 1990 set up a cap-and-trade scheme for SO2. Effects: acidified lakes and fish death, aluminium leaching from soil, loss of soil nutrients, forest damage, corrosion of limestone and marble (stone leprosy), and human respiratory problems. In India, the Taj Mahal's yellowing led to the Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ) of about 10,400 sq km and a Supreme Court case (M.C. Mehta). Mitigation measures include flue gas desulphurisation (scrubbers), low-sulphur fuels, catalytic converters, BS-VI norms (April 2020), shifting to renewables, and liming of lakes. Related topics for UPSC: photochemical smog, ozone depletion, greenhouse gases and their GWP, eutrophication, and the Montreal, Kyoto and Paris agreements.

question:
With reference to food chains in ecosystems, consider the following statements :
1. A food chain illustrates the order in which a chain of organisms feed upon each other.
2. Food chains are found within the populations of a species.
3. A food chain illustrates the numbers of each organism which are eaten by others. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Environment
detail: A food chain is a linear sequence showing who eats whom and how energy and nutrients pass from one trophic level to the next: producers (autotrophs) to primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), tertiary consumers and top carnivores, with decomposers acting at every level. Statement 1 is the textbook definition. Statement 2 is wrong because a food chain links different species, such as grass, grasshopper, frog, snake and eagle, across a community. A population is the group of one species in an area, so feeding relations between species cannot lie within it. Cannibalism within a species is an exception and does not define a food chain. Statement 3 is wrong because a food chain does not quantify how many organisms are eaten. Numbers are shown by ecological pyramids (pyramid of numbers, biomass and energy). Energy flow follows Lindeman's 10 per cent law, with only about 10 per cent of energy passing to the next level. Grazing food chains begin with living plants, and detritus food chains begin with dead organic matter. Interlinked chains form a food web. Elimination: statements 2 and 3 are false, so only (a) survives.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is true because a food chain shows the order of feeding. Statements 2 and 3 are false, so only statement 1 is correct.
Wrong. It includes statement 2, which is false. Food chains connect different species in a community, not members of a single species population.
Wrong. It includes statements 2 and 3, both false. Numbers eaten are shown by ecological pyramids, not by a food chain.
Wrong. Statement 1 is a correct, textbook definition of a food chain, so 'None' cannot be right.
keyfact: A food chain shows the order of feeding between different species; numbers and biomass are shown by ecological pyramids, not by food chains.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this is the correct choice. It reflects the accepted definition of a food chain as a sequence of feeding relationships among organisms. Producers form the first trophic level, then herbivores, carnivores and top carnivores. Energy flows one way through the chain, and only about 10 per cent is passed on at each level, so chains are short, usually 4 to 5 levels.

Option (b), 1 and 2 only: this adds the claim that food chains occur within populations of a species. A population is a group of one species, while chains cross species lines. Related concepts include the community (all populations in an area), the ecosystem (community plus abiotic factors) and the niche (the role of a species). Interspecific feeding links create chains, and chains interlink into webs.

Option (c), 1, 2 and 3: this accepts all statements. Statement 3 confuses a food chain with an ecological pyramid. Pyramids show numbers, biomass or energy at each trophic level. The pyramid of energy is always upright, while pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted. Elton introduced pyramids in 1927. Pyramids are a quantitative tool, whereas food chains are qualitative.

Option (d), None: this says no statement is correct. It is wrong because statement 1 is the standard definition. A food chain depicts who eats whom in order. Types are grazing and detritus chains. Also note that a parasitic food chain exists, where parasites feed on hosts, and decomposers can link to every level.
related: Lindeman's 10 per cent law: about 10 per cent of energy passes to the next trophic level.
Pyramid of energy is always upright; pyramid of biomass in oceans is often inverted.
Arthur Tansley coined the term 'ecosystem' in 1935.
Detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter and is carried on by decomposers.
Biomagnification: DDT and mercury concentrate at higher trophic levels, such as in Minamata disease.
Food web is a network of interlinked food chains and increases ecosystem stability.
Net primary productivity equals GPP minus respiration losses.
Producers occupy the first trophic level in every food chain.
statements: 1 — Correct: This is the standard definition of a food chain. A food chain is the linear sequence of organisms through which food energy passes, from producers to herbivores to carnivores. Each step is a trophic level. The two main types are the grazing food chain, which starts with green plants and is the main route in terrestrial and shallow-water ecosystems, and the detritus food chain, which starts with dead organic matter and dominates in forest floors and deep ocean. Chains usually have 4 to 5 links because energy is lost as heat at each transfer, following Lindeman's 10 per cent law. Food webs are networks of many interlinked chains.

2 — Incorrect: Food chains link different species within a community, not individuals of the same species within a population. A population is a group of one species in an area. Examples of chains are grass to deer to tiger, or phytoplankton to zooplankton to fish to bird. Each organism occupies a trophic level based on what it eats. A community is made of many populations, and feeding relationships connect them. Intraspecific interactions such as competition, cannibalism and parental care are separate ecological concepts. Interspecific interactions include predation, competition, commensalism, mutualism and parasitism, and food chains arise from predation and herbivory between species.

3 — Incorrect: A food chain shows the order of feeding, not the quantity eaten. Numbers of organisms at each trophic level are shown by the pyramid of numbers, which can be upright (grassland) or inverted (a single tree supporting many insects and parasites). Biomass is shown by the pyramid of biomass, which is inverted in oceans because phytoplankton have a small standing crop but a rapid turnover. Energy is shown by the pyramid of energy, which is always upright because energy is lost at each level. Charles Elton introduced the pyramid of numbers in 1927, and Raymond Lindeman formulated the trophic-dynamic concept and the 10 per cent law in 1942.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. A food chain shows the sequence in which organisms feed on one another, from producers to top consumers. It does not operate within a single species' population, and it does not show numbers eaten.
topic_notes: A food chain is the linear transfer of food energy from producers through a series of consumers. Trophic levels: T1 producers (autotrophs), T2 primary consumers (herbivores), T3 secondary consumers (carnivores), T4 tertiary consumers and top carnivores. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and recycle nutrients. Types: grazing food chain (starts with green plants, uses solar energy), detritus food chain (starts with dead organic matter, dominant in many ecosystems and in energy terms in forests), and parasitic chain. A food web is the network of interconnected chains and gives ecosystem stability. Energy flow is unidirectional. Lindeman's 10 per cent law (1942) states that roughly 10 per cent of energy is transferred to the next trophic level, and the rest is lost as heat in respiration and metabolism. This limits chain length to about 4 or 5 levels. Ecological pyramids: pyramid of energy is always upright; pyramid of numbers can be upright (grassland) or inverted (tree ecosystem); pyramid of biomass is upright on land and often inverted in aquatic ecosystems. Gross primary productivity (GPP) minus respiration gives net primary productivity (NPP). Biomagnification means that toxins such as DDT and mercury become more concentrated at higher trophic levels, as seen in Minamata disease. Key related terms: standing crop, standing state, keystone species, ecological niche, and ecotone. Charles Elton introduced food chain and pyramid ideas, and Arthur Tansley coined the term ecosystem in 1935. Likely UPSC angles include the difference between food chain and food web, inverted pyramids, the 10 per cent law, biomagnification, and which ecosystem has the highest productivity (tropical rainforests on land, estuaries and coral reefs in water).

question:
Consider the following pairs : National Park River flowing through the Park
1. Corbett National Park : Ganga
2. Kaziranga National Park : Manas
3. Silent Valley National Park : Kaveri Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests the river-park associations that UPSC likes to set as traps, where the river named is a plausible but wrong neighbour. Jim Corbett National Park (Uttarakhand, est. 1936 as Hailey National Park, India's oldest national park and the first Project Tiger reserve in 1973) is drained by the Ramganga. The Ramganga is a tributary of the Ganga, but it is not the Ganga itself, and the Ganga does not flow through the park. Kaziranga (Assam, UNESCO World Heritage Site 1985, famous for the one-horned rhino) lies on the southern floodplain of the Brahmaputra. The Manas is a separate park and river, a Brahmaputra tributary, on the Bhutan border. Silent Valley (Kerala, Palakkad district, declared a national park in 1984) is drained by the Kunthipuzha, which feeds the Bharathapuzha. The Kaveri does not flow through Kerala's Silent Valley. Since every pair fails, (a), (b) and (c) are eliminated and (d) is correct. The lesson: for each park, remember the specific river and not just the major river system.
explanations: Wrong: pair 1 is incorrect since Corbett has the Ramganga, and pair 2 is also incorrect since Kaziranga has the Brahmaputra, not the Manas.
Wrong: pair 3 is incorrect since Silent Valley is on the Kunthipuzha, not the Kaveri, so '3 only' cannot hold.
Wrong: both pairs 1 and 3 name the wrong river (Ganga instead of Ramganga; Kaveri instead of Kunthipuzha).
Correct: all three pairs are mismatched, so none is correct.
keyfact: Corbett = Ramganga, Kaziranga = Brahmaputra, Silent Valley = Kunthipuzha, so all three pairs are wrong and the answer is (d).
option_notes: Options 1 and 2 together: Corbett (Uttarakhand, Ramganga, 1936, oldest national park, Project Tiger 1973) and Kaziranga (Assam, Brahmaputra floodplain, one-horned rhino, UNESCO 1985, Tiger Reserve 2006). Each is a famous park, but neither pairing is right here, so this combination is wrong.

Pair 3 alone: Silent Valley in Palakkad, Kerala, Western Ghats and Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, declared a national park in 1984. The river is the Kunthipuzha, a tributary of the Bharathapuzha, not the Kaveri. It is known for lion-tailed macaques and the Save Silent Valley movement.

Pairs 1 and 3: the Ganga is the major river of north India, rising as the Bhagirathi at Gangotri, but it does not flow through Corbett. The Kaveri rises at Talakaveri in Karnataka and flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to the Bay of Bengal, not through Silent Valley.
None: this is the correct choice. UPSC sometimes makes 'none' the answer when all pairs are plausible but subtly wrong. Always check each pair independently, and know the exact river of each park.
related: Corbett is India's oldest national park (1936), originally Hailey National Park.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973, with Corbett as one of the first nine reserves.
Kaziranga holds about two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinos.
Manas is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Tiger Reserve and Elephant Reserve on the Bhutan border.
Silent Valley is on the Kunthipuzha and was saved by a movement against a hydroelectric project.
Keibul Lamjao on Loktak Lake is the world's only floating national park.
Ramganga is a Ganga tributary that rises in Uttarakhand and joins the Ganga near Kannauj.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Corbett is drained by the Ramganga, not the Ganga. Jim Corbett National Park lies in Nainital and Pauri Garhwal districts of Uttarakhand. It was established in 1936 as Hailey National Park, making it India's oldest national park, and was renamed in 1956 after the naturalist and hunter Jim Corbett. It was the site of the launch of Project Tiger in 1973. The Ramganga flows through the Patli Dun valley and the Ramganga reservoir at Kalagarh. The park is known for Bengal tigers, elephants and the Dhikala zone.

2 — Incorrect: Kaziranga lies along the Brahmaputra, whereas Manas is a distinct park and river. Kaziranga National Park, in Golaghat, Nagaon and Sonitpur districts of Assam, became a national park in 1974 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. It holds about two-thirds of the world's greater one-horned rhinoceros. It is also a Tiger Reserve (2006) and an Important Bird Area. The Manas River is a Brahmaputra tributary flowing through Manas National Park (Assam, bordering Bhutan), a World Heritage Site (1985), Project Tiger reserve and Elephant Reserve.

3 — Incorrect: Silent Valley is drained by the Kunthipuzha, not the Kaveri. Silent Valley National Park is in Palakkad district, Kerala, in the Nilgiri hills and Western Ghats. It was declared a national park in 1984 and inaugurated in 1985 by Rajiv Gandhi. The Save Silent Valley movement in the 1970s opposed a hydroelectric project on the Kunthipuzha. It protects tropical evergreen forest and is a core of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. It is home to the lion-tailed macaque. The Kunthipuzha is a tributary of the Bharathapuzha.
summary: The answer is (d): none of the three pairs is correctly matched. Corbett is on the Ramganga, Kaziranga on the Brahmaputra, and Silent Valley on the Kunthipuzha (a Bharathapuzha/Ponnani tributary).
topic_notes: National parks and their rivers are a recurring prelims theme. Corbett (Uttarakhand): Ramganga. Kaziranga (Assam): Brahmaputra, with Diphlu and Mora Diphlu rivers inside it. Manas (Assam): Manas River. Silent Valley (Kerala): Kunthipuzha. Other pairs worth knowing: Periyar (Kerala) with the Periyar river and the Mullaperiyar dam; Bandipur with the Kabini and Nugu; Nagarhole with the Kabini; Ranthambore with the Chambal tributaries (Banas); Kanha (Madhya Pradesh) with the Banjar; Bandhavgarh with the Johilla; Panna (Madhya Pradesh) with the Ken; Sundarbans (West Bengal) in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta; Keibul Lamjao (Manipur) on Loktak Lake, the only floating national park; Dachigam (J&K) with the Dagwan; Gir (Gujarat) with the Hiran and others; Tadoba with the Andhari; Satpura with the Denwa; Pench with the Pench river; Simlipal (Odisha) with the Budhabalanga. Key background: India has over 100 national parks, which are protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Project Tiger was launched in 1973. The Western Ghats were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2012. India has several UNESCO natural World Heritage Sites: Kaziranga, Manas, Keoladeo, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats, and the Great Himalayan National Park. UPSC may ask which river flows through which park, which park holds a specific species, or which parks are in which state or biosphere reserve.

question:
Consider the following organisms :
1. Agaricus
2. Nostoc
3. Spirogyra Which of the above is/are used as biofertilizer/biofertilizers?
subject: Environment
detail: A biofertilizer is a preparation containing living microorganisms that enrich soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, solubilising phosphate or mobilising nutrients. The main groups are: (i) nitrogen fixers, including symbiotic Rhizobium (legumes), Frankia (actinorhizal plants such as Casuarina), Azolla with the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae, free-living Azotobacter and Azospirillum, and cyanobacteria such as Nostoc, Anabaena, Aulosira and Tolypothrix; (ii) phosphate solubilisers such as Bacillus and Pseudomonas; and (iii) mycorrhizae (VAM fungi), which improve phosphorus uptake. Nostoc has specialised cells called heterocysts that contain the enzyme nitrogenase and fix nitrogen. Blue-green algal (BGA) biofertilizer is widely used in rice fields and can supply roughly 20-30 kg N per hectare. Agaricus bisporus is the button mushroom, a saprophytic food fungus, not a soil inoculant. Spirogyra is a filamentous freshwater green alga, common in ponds, and is a primary producer with no nitrogenase. Elimination: once Agaricus is ruled out, options (a) and (c) fall; once Spirogyra is ruled out, (d) falls.
explanations: Wrong: it includes Agaricus, which is a mushroom grown for food and not a biofertilizer.
Correct: Nostoc is the only organism in the list that fixes atmospheric nitrogen and is used as a biofertilizer.
Wrong: it includes Spirogyra, a green alga that cannot fix nitrogen.
Wrong: it names only Spirogyra and leaves out Nostoc, the real biofertilizer.
keyfact: Nostoc, a heterocyst-bearing cyanobacterium, fixes nitrogen and is a biofertilizer; Agaricus (mushroom) and Spirogyra (green alga) are not.
option_notes: Agaricus and Nostoc together: Agaricus is a genus of basidiomycete fungi, and Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom) is the most widely cultivated edible mushroom. It is saprophytic and lives on compost. Nostoc is a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium. The pairing mixes a food fungus with a true biofertilizer, so it is wrong because Agaricus does not qualify.

Nostoc only: Nostoc is a filamentous cyanobacterium with heterocysts that fix nitrogen through nitrogenase. It is found in soil, water and rocks, and is a symbiont in lichens, cycad roots and hornworts. It is a major component of blue-green algal biofertilizer for rice. Related biofertilizers are Anabaena, Aulosira, Tolypothrix, and Azolla with Anabaena azollae. This is the correct option.

Nostoc and Spirogyra: Nostoc is a valid nitrogen-fixing biofertilizer. Spirogyra is a filamentous freshwater green alga, with spiral chloroplasts and reproduction by conjugation. It is a primary producer in ponds but has no nitrogen-fixing ability. The pair is therefore wrong because Spirogyra is included.

Spirogyra only: Spirogyra is a green alga in Chlorophyta, called pond scum. Its cells have ribbon-like spiral chloroplasts with pyrenoids. It reproduces by fragmentation and conjugation. It does not fix nitrogen and is not used as a biofertilizer. It is used mainly as a model organism in botany teaching and as food for aquatic life.
related: Azolla with Anabaena azollae is a biofertilizer for paddy and also a cattle feed.
Rhizobium forms root nodules on legumes and uses leghaemoglobin to protect nitrogenase.
Heterocysts are the specialised nitrogen-fixing cells of cyanobacteria.
Frankia is a symbiotic nitrogen fixer in Casuarina and Alnus.
Mycorrhizae (VAM) improve phosphorus uptake and are fungal biofertilizers.
Azotobacter is a free-living aerobic nitrogen fixer.
Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) are not biofertilizers.
Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Agaricus is an edible mushroom, not a biofertilizer. Agaricus is a genus of basidiomycete fungi. Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom) is the most widely cultivated mushroom in the world. It is saprophytic, growing on composted manure and straw, and is grown for food. It cannot fix nitrogen. Fungi that do act as biofertilizers are mycorrhizae such as VAM (Glomus), which improve phosphorus uptake. Spent mushroom compost can be used as a soil conditioner, but the organism itself is not classed as a biofertilizer.

2 — Correct: Nostoc is a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium. Nostoc is a filamentous cyanobacterium (blue-green alga) that forms gelatinous colonies in soil, freshwater and on rocks. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen in heterocysts using nitrogenase. It also lives symbiotically in lichens, in cycad coralloid roots, in the hornwort Anthoceros and in the water fern Azolla (Anabaena is the usual partner). In India, BGA biofertilizers of Nostoc, Anabaena, Aulosira and others are applied to paddy, where they also add organic matter and improve soil structure.

3 — Incorrect: Spirogyra is a green alga that does not fix nitrogen. Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga (Chlorophyta) found in freshwater ponds and slow streams, and is known as pond scum or water silk. It has spiral ribbon-shaped chloroplasts. It reproduces vegetatively by fragmentation and sexually by conjugation (scalariform or lateral). It lacks heterocysts and nitrogenase, so it cannot enrich soil nitrogen. It is used in teaching as a model for algal structure and is a food source for aquatic animals.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Nostoc is a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium (blue-green alga) used as a biofertilizer, especially in paddy fields. Agaricus is an edible mushroom (a fungus) and Spirogyra is a green alga with no nitrogen-fixing ability, so neither is a biofertilizer.
topic_notes: Biofertilizers are living microbial inoculants that improve soil fertility and plant nutrition without chemical inputs. They are cheaper and eco-friendly, and they reduce dependence on urea and other chemical fertilizers. Main categories: (1) Nitrogen fixers. Symbiotic: Rhizobium in legume root nodules, Frankia in Casuarina and Alnus, Anabaena azollae in Azolla. Free-living: Azotobacter (aerobic, used for wheat, maize, cotton), Azospirillum (associative, used for cereals and millets), Clostridium (anaerobic) and cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena, Aulosira, Tolypothrix, Scytonema). (2) Phosphate solubilisers: Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Aspergillus and Penicillium. (3) Phosphate mobilisers: mycorrhizae, such as VAM or Glomus, and ectomycorrhizae. (4) Potash mobilisers: Frateuria aurantia. (5) Plant growth promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR). Biological nitrogen fixation is carried out by prokaryotes only, using the enzyme nitrogenase, which is oxygen-sensitive. Leghaemoglobin in legume nodules protects it, and heterocysts do so in cyanobacteria. Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) and denitrifying bacteria (Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus) are part of the nitrogen cycle but are not used as biofertilizers. In India, the National Project on Development and Use of Biofertilizers (NPDB) is based at Ghaziabad, with regional centres. Biofertilizers are regulated under the Fertiliser (Control) Order, 1985, and promoted through the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana and the National Mission on Sustainable Agriculture. Azolla is also used as green manure and cattle feed. Other angles UPSC may take: lichens as symbiosis, the difference between biofertilizers, biopesticides and green manures, and organic farming in Sikkim.

question:
Which of the following adds/add nitrogen to the soil?
1. Excretion of urea by animals
2. Burning of coal by man
3. Death of vegetation Select the correct answer using the codes given below
subject: Environment
detail: The nitrogen cycle has five main steps: fixation, ammonification (mineralisation), nitrification, assimilation and denitrification. Soil gains nitrogen mainly by biological fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Anabaena, Nostoc), by atmospheric fixation (lightning forms oxides that are washed down by rain), by industrial fixation (the Haber-Bosch process for fertiliser), and by recycling of organic matter. Animal wastes such as urea, uric acid and dung, and dead plants and animals, contain organic nitrogen. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) convert it into ammonia (ammonification). Nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, then Nitrobacter) turn ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate, which plants absorb. Urea is also hydrolysed by the enzyme urease to ammonium carbonate and ammonia. Statements 1 and 3 are therefore correct. Burning coal oxidises the small nitrogen content of the fuel and some atmospheric nitrogen into NOx. These gases go into the atmosphere and cause smog and acid rain, and they are not a deliberate or main input to soil. Any deposition is indirect and incidental.
