Statement 3 is incorrect because the aim is monetary control, not capping profits. Statement 4 is incorrect because CRR is held with the RBI and is not vault cash. Banks hold vault cash separately for daily needs. Since only statement 1 holds, option (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct. CRR and SLR limit the funds banks can lend, so the RBI uses them to control credit creation. This is the main purpose of statutory reserves.
Wrong. Statement 1 is right but statement 2 is not. Deposit safety comes from prudential norms and DICGC insurance, not from statutory reserves.
Wrong. Statement 3 is false because reserve ratios are not meant to curb bank profits. Statement 2 is also false.
Wrong. Statement 4 is false because CRR is held with the RBI, not in vaults. Statements 2 and 3 are false too.
keyfact: CRR and SLR are credit-control tools of the RBI, not guarantees of deposit safety, profit limits or vault cash rules.
option_notes: Statement 1 alone. Statutory reserves (CRR and SLR) are monetary tools used to control credit and liquidity. CRR is set by the RBI under Section 42 of the RBI Act, and SLR under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act. In inflationary periods the RBI raises them to draw out liquidity, and in downturns it lowers them. Together with the repo rate, reverse repo and OMOs, they make up the RBI's quantitative instruments of monetary policy.

Statements 1 and 2 only. This option wrongly adds the idea that reserves make deposits safe and liquid. Deposit safety comes from DICGC insurance (Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank), capital adequacy under Basel norms and RBI supervision. SLR assets do offer some liquidity, but that is incidental. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is the main law for bank regulation in India.

Statements 2 and 3 only. This option misses the main purpose, credit control, and adds a false claim about limiting profits. Bank profitability is shaped by net interest margin, NPAs and provisioning norms. CRR earns no interest, which does reduce profits, but that is a cost and not an aim. Priority sector lending and interest rate benchmarks are separate regulatory tools.

Statements 1, 2, 3 and 4. This option accepts all the statements, including the false ones. Vault cash is the physical currency banks keep in branches and ATMs. It is separate from CRR, which sits with the RBI as a balance. Banks decide their cash holdings from operational needs. Cash in hand can count toward SLR but not toward CRR.
related: CRR is maintained as cash with the RBI and earns no interest.
SLR can be held in cash, gold or approved securities, and its statutory ceiling is 40% of NDTL.
CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934, and SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
Raising CRR reduces the money supply and is a contractionary measure.
DICGC insures deposits up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank.
The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to banks.
The MPC has six members and targets CPI inflation of 4% (±2%).
The standing deposit facility (SDF) was introduced in 2022.
statements: 1 — Correct: CRR and SLR cut or expand lendable resources, so the RBI can control credit creation. CRR is the share of NDTL held as cash with the RBI, and banks earn no interest on it. SLR is held in cash, gold or approved securities with the bank itself. Raising the ratios is a contractionary tool and lowering them is expansionary. CRR has no statutory floor or ceiling after the 2006 amendment to the RBI Act, and SLR is capped at 40% of NDTL. SLR is currently 18% and CRR is 4% (verify the latest figures).

2 — Incorrect: Statutory reserves are not designed to make deposits safe. They are a monetary policy tool, even though SLR assets add some liquidity cushion. Depositor protection rests on capital adequacy norms (Basel III), RBI supervision and DICGC deposit insurance. DICGC was set up in 1978, and its cover was raised from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 5 lakh in February 2020. Banks must pay the insurance premium themselves. CRR funds cannot be freely used to meet depositors' demands.

3 — Incorrect: No reserve requirement aims to limit bank profits. Higher CRR can reduce bank profitability since no interest is paid on it, but that is a side effect, not the purpose. Profit-related regulation works differently, through the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, prudential norms and priority sector lending. Banks' margins are influenced by the repo rate and the marginal cost of funds based lending rate (MCLR), and now by external benchmark lending rates (EBLR).

4 — Incorrect: Statutory reserves are not meant to force banks to hold vault cash. CRR is held with the RBI, not in the bank's vault. Banks keep cash in their vaults and ATMs on their own, according to day-to-day operational needs. Cash in hand may count toward SLR, but SLR is not aimed at vault cash. CRR balances are also not available for daily use, apart from a minimum daily maintenance requirement. Liquidity management tools include the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) and the marginal standing facility (MSF).
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Statutory reserve requirements (CRR and SLR) are mainly tools that let the RBI control credit creation and liquidity in the banking system. They do not exist to guarantee deposit safety, limit bank profits or ensure vault cash.
topic_notes:
Statutory reserve requirements are the legal minimum reserves that banks must keep against their deposit liabilities. They have two parts. CRR is held in cash with the RBI, earns no interest, and is calculated on NDTL. The 2006 amendment to the RBI Act removed the statutory floor and ceiling, so the RBI can set it freely. SLR is held in cash, gold or approved securities (such as G-secs and state development loans). The statutory maximum is 40% of NDTL, and the rate has been 18% in recent years (verify the latest figure). CRR has been around 4% (verify the latest figure). Purposes: control credit creation and the money multiplier, manage liquidity, ensure banks invest in government securities (SLR gives the government a captive market for borrowing), and give a basic liquidity buffer.

Other RBI instruments:
- Repo: the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities.
- Reverse repo: the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks.
- Standing deposit facility (SDF): introduced in 2022 as the floor of the LAF corridor.
- MSF: the rate for emergency borrowing, set above the repo rate.
- Bank rate: a longer-term rate, aligned with the MSF rate.
- OMOs: outright purchase or sale of government securities.
- Market stabilisation scheme (MSS): used to absorb surplus liquidity.

The Monetary Policy Committee (six members, set up in 2016 under an amended RBI Act) sets the repo rate with a CPI inflation target of 4% (±2%).

UPSC angles: the effect of raising CRR or SLR on money supply, the difference between CRR and SLR, who sets which ratio, deposit insurance (DICGC), Basel III norms, and liquidity versus capital requirements. Remember that CRR is a cash balance with the RBI, while SLR is held by the bank itself in liquid assets.

question: Recently, a series of uprisings of people referred to as ‘Arab Spring’ originally started from
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Arab Spring was a wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings across the Arab world from late 2010 onwards. Its trigger was the self-immolation of Mohamed Bouazizi, a fruit seller in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, on 17 December 2010, in protest against police harassment and corruption. The protests, driven by unemployment, corruption, authoritarian rule and rising food prices, forced President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali to flee to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011. This is called the Jasmine Revolution. The example spread quickly. Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011 after protests in Tahrir Square. Libya's Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown and killed in October 2011 after a civil war with NATO intervention. Yemen's Ali Abdullah Saleh stepped down under a Gulf Cooperation Council deal. Syria's uprising became a prolonged civil war. Bahrain's protests were suppressed. Elimination logic: Egypt is the most famous event and so the most tempting wrong answer, but it came after Tunisia. Syria's protests began in March 2011. Lebanon had no comparable uprising at that time. Tunisia is the only country whose transition remained broadly democratic.
explanations: Incorrect: Egypt's uprising began on 25 January 2011, after Tunisia's. It was inspired by Tunisia's success and led to Mubarak's resignation.
Incorrect: Lebanon was not the origin of the Arab Spring. It had no regime-toppling uprising in 2010-11, and its major protests came later (2005 Cedar Revolution, 2019).
Incorrect: Syria's protests began in March 2011 in Daraa and turned into a civil war. They came months after the Tunisian revolt.
Correct: Tunisia was the birthplace. The Bouazizi self-immolation of December 2010 sparked the Jasmine Revolution, and Ben Ali fled on 14 January 2011.
keyfact: The Arab Spring began in Tunisia (Sidi Bouzid, 17 Dec 2010, Bouazizi's self-immolation), not Egypt.
option_notes: Egypt: the most populous Arab country. The 2011 revolution (18 days of protests centred on Tahrir Square) ended Hosni Mubarak's 30-year rule. Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood was elected in 2012 and was removed by the military under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in July 2013. Sisi has been president since 2014. Egypt controls the Suez Canal.

Lebanon: a Levant country with a confessional power-sharing system (president Maronite Christian, PM Sunni, speaker Shia). It had the 2005 Cedar Revolution, which ended Syrian military presence, and the 2019-20 protests over corruption and economic collapse. Hezbollah is a powerful armed group. The Beirut port explosion happened in August 2020.

Syria: protests began in March 2011 in Daraa against Bashar al-Assad, whose family had ruled since 1971. They escalated into a civil war involving ISIS, Kurdish forces, Russia, Iran, Turkey and the US, and created millions of refugees. Assad's government fell in December 2024 after a rebel offensive led by HTS.

Tunisia: a North African country, capital Tunis, which gained independence from France in 1956. Ben Ali ruled from 1987 to 2011. After the Jasmine Revolution it adopted a democratic constitution in 2014. The National Dialogue Quartet won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize. President Kais Saied's 2021 power grab has reversed some of the democratic gains.
related: The Arab Spring began on 17 December 2010 with Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia.
Tunisia's uprising is called the Jasmine Revolution; Ben Ali fled on 14 January 2011.
Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011 after protests in Tahrir Square, Cairo.
Gaddafi was killed in October 2011; UNSC Resolution 1973 authorised the no-fly zone over Libya.
The Tunisian National Dialogue Quartet won the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize.
Operation Safe Homecoming (2011) was India's evacuation of its nationals from Libya.
Syria's Assad government fell in December 2024.
Tunisia is the only Arab Spring country widely seen as having made a democratic transition, though it has regressed since 2021.
summary: The answer is (d) Tunisia. The Arab Spring began in Tunisia in December 2010 after the self-immolation of street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi, and it then spread to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain and Syria.
topic_notes: The Arab Spring (2010-12 and after) was a series of anti-government protests, uprisings and armed rebellions across the Middle East and North Africa. Its causes included authoritarian rule, corruption, youth unemployment, inequality, rising food prices and the spread of social media and satellite TV (Al Jazeera, Facebook, Twitter). The spark was Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation in Sidi Bouzid on 17 December 2010. Outcomes by country: Tunisia saw Ben Ali flee (January 2011) and a democratic transition. Egypt saw Mubarak resign (February 2011), then Morsi's election and the 2013 coup. Libya saw Gaddafi killed (October 2011), NATO action under UN Security Council Resolution 1973, and continuing fragmentation. Yemen saw Saleh hand over power to Hadi, followed by civil war with the Houthis. Syria descended into civil war. Bahrain's protests were crushed with Saudi-led GCC help. Morocco, Jordan and Oman made limited reforms. Algeria and Sudan had later protests (2019) that are sometimes called the second wave of the Arab Spring. Key terms are the Jasmine Revolution (Tunisia), Tahrir Square (Egypt), the Muslim Brotherhood and the Arab League. Related geopolitics UPSC may ask about include the Syrian refugee crisis, ISIS, the Gulf Cooperation Council, India's evacuation operations (Operation Safe Homecoming in Libya, 2011), and the effect on oil prices and Indian diaspora remittances.

ocr: Consider the following countries : 1. Denmark Japan ar wn Russian Federation United Kingdom United States of America Which of the above are the members of the ‘Arctic Council’? (a) 1,2 and 3 (b) 2,3 and 4 fo} 1,4 and 5 (dq) 1, 3 and 5
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Arctic Council is a high-level intergovernmental forum set up by the Ottawa Declaration of 1996. It promotes cooperation, coordination and interaction among Arctic States, Arctic indigenous communities and other Arctic inhabitants on common Arctic issues, especially sustainable development and environmental protection. It has eight members: Canada, Denmark (with Greenland and the Faroe Islands), Finland, Iceland, Norway, the Russian Federation, Sweden and the United States. These are the states with territory within the Arctic Circle. Six organisations of indigenous peoples hold the status of Permanent Participants. Non-Arctic states, intergovernmental bodies and NGOs can be Observers; they may attend meetings but have no vote. Observer states include the UK, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Italy, Japan, China, India, South Korea and Singapore. India became an Observer in 2013, along with China, Japan, South Korea, Italy and Singapore. The chairmanship rotates every two years. The Council is not a treaty body and cannot make legally binding decisions. Elimination logic: Japan is an Observer, so it is not a member. This removes (a). The UK is also an Observer, so (b) and (c) are removed. Only (d) contains only genuine members.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes Japan, which is only an Observer in the Arctic Council and not a member.
(b) is wrong because it includes Japan and the United Kingdom, both Observers, and it leaves out Denmark and the USA, who are members.
(c) is wrong because the UK is an Observer, and it leaves out the Russian Federation, which is a member.
(d) is correct because Denmark, the Russian Federation and the USA are all full members of the Arctic Council. This is the official answer.
keyfact: Arctic Council members are the 8 Arctic states (Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, USA); Japan, the UK and India are only Observers.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 3, combines Denmark, Japan and Russia. Denmark and Russia are members, but Japan is an Observer admitted in 2013. Japan's Arctic involvement is scientific and economic, including polar research, the Northern Sea Route and energy. It runs research stations such as the one at Ny-Ålesund. Japan's Arctic policy was formulated in 2015. Observer status does not give the right to vote in the Council.

Option (b), 2, 3 and 4, combines Japan, Russia and the UK. Russia is a member, while Japan and the UK are Observers. The UK has Observer status in the Council and is a party to the 1920 Svalbard Treaty. The Council has eight members in all and several dozen Observers, including states, intergovernmental bodies and NGOs. Observers are approved at the biennial Ministerial meetings by consensus.

Option (c), 1, 4 and 5, combines Denmark, the UK and the USA. Denmark and the USA are members, while the UK is an Observer. The US is a member because of Alaska and Denmark because of Greenland and the Faroe Islands. The UK's Arctic engagement includes funding research through NERC, and it is geographically close but not an Arctic state. A common mistake is to treat the UK as a member because of its involvement in northern waters.

Option (d), 1, 3 and 5, combines Denmark, Russia and the USA, all of whom are full Arctic Council members. Together with Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden they make up the eight members. Denmark, Russia and the USA, plus Canada and Norway, are the five Arctic Ocean coastal states. The Council was formed by the Ottawa Declaration in 1996, and its secretariat is in Tromsø, Norway.
related: Arctic Council was set up by the Ottawa Declaration, 1996.
It has 8 members: Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, USA.
India got Observer status in the Arctic Council in 2013.
India's Arctic station is Himadri at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, set up in 2008.
The Arctic Council Secretariat is in Tromsø, Norway.
India's Arctic Policy was released in March 2022.
The 1920 Svalbard Treaty gave sovereignty over Svalbard to Norway.
The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and came into force in 1961.
statements: 1 — Correct: Denmark is a member through Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Denmark is an Arctic state because Greenland, an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, lies within the Arctic Circle. The Kingdom of Denmark is represented in the Council jointly with Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Greenland has self-rule, and its capital is Nuuk. Denmark was a founding signatory of the 1996 Ottawa Declaration. It is also one of the five Arctic Ocean coastal states, the 'Arctic Five', which signed the 2008 Ilulissat Declaration on Arctic Ocean governance under UNCLOS. Copenhagen has often been involved in Arctic continental shelf claims.

2 — Incorrect: Japan is not a member. Japan has been an Observer in the Arctic Council since 2013, when the Kiruna Ministerial meeting in Sweden admitted six new Observer states. Japan has no Arctic territory. Its interests in the region are scientific research, shipping routes along the Northern Sea Route, and energy and fisheries. It runs polar research programmes, including the Arctic Challenge for Sustainability project, and operates a research station at Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard. Observers cannot vote but may take part in working groups and projects.

3 — Correct: The Russian Federation is a member and has the longest Arctic coastline. Russia has the longest Arctic coastline and the largest Arctic population, with cities such as Murmansk and Norilsk. It is one of the Arctic Five coastal states. It controls the Northern Sea Route and has large oil and gas reserves in the Yamal and Barents regions. It has filed claims to extend its continental shelf under UNCLOS, including the Lomonosov Ridge. It chaired the Council in 2021-23. In 2022, other members paused cooperation with Russia after the invasion of Ukraine, and work resumed later in a limited way.

4 — Incorrect: The United Kingdom is not a member. The UK is an Observer, having been a member of the Council's Observer group since 1998. It is a non-Arctic state, although it is geographically close to the region. The UK conducts Arctic research through the British Antarctic Survey and the Natural Environment Research Council, and its research station at Ny-Ålesund is called Arctic Research Station. It is a party to the 1920 Svalbard Treaty. It cannot vote in the Council but may take part in working groups.

5 — Correct: The United States is a member through Alaska. The US became an Arctic state through Alaska, purchased from Russia in 1867. It is one of the Arctic Five and a founding member of the Council. Its Arctic region includes Utqiagvik (formerly Barrow) on the North Slope, with oil fields such as Prudhoe Bay. The US has signed but not ratified UNCLOS. It chaired the Council in 2015-17 and has often emphasised climate research and indigenous participation.
summary: The answer is (d) 1, 3 and 5. Denmark (through Greenland and the Faroe Islands), the Russian Federation and the United States of America (through Alaska) are Arctic Council members, whereas Japan and the United Kingdom are only Observers.
topic_notes: The Arctic Council was established on 19 September 1996 by the Ottawa Declaration. It is a high-level intergovernmental forum rather than a treaty organisation, so its decisions and recommendations are not legally binding. It works by consensus among its members. Its members are Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the USA. Six Permanent Participants represent indigenous peoples: the Aleut International Association, Arctic Athabaskan Council, Gwich'in Council International, Inuit Circumpolar Council, Russian Association of Indigenous Peoples of the North (RAIPON) and the Saami Council. Observers include non-Arctic states, intergovernmental and inter-parliamentary organisations, and NGOs. In 2013, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Italy were admitted as Observers. India's Arctic research station Himadri is at Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard, set up in 2008, and India released its Arctic Policy in March 2022. The Council has working groups such as AMAP (Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme), CAFF (Conservation of Arctic Flora and Fauna), PAME (Protection of the Arctic Marine Environment), EPPR, SDWG and ACAP. The chair rotates every two years among the members. The Secretariat has been in Tromsø, Norway, since 2013. It has facilitated three legally binding agreements among members: on search and rescue (2011), marine oil pollution preparedness and response (2013), and enhancing scientific cooperation (2017). Related issues include Arctic ice melt and climate change, the opening of the Northern Sea Route and Northwest Passage, the Svalbard Treaty of 1920, the Ilulissat Declaration of 2008 and UNCLOS claims to the continental shelf. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 is the contrasting regime in the south. Arctic warming is happening about two to four times faster than the global average.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Region often Country in news
1. Chechnya : Russian Federation
2. Darfur : Mali
3. Swat Valley : Iraq Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a 'regions in the news' geography question, a staple of UPSC prelims. Chechnya lies in the North Caucasus and is a constituent republic of Russia, with Grozny as its capital. It was the site of the First (1994-96) and Second (1999-2009) Chechen Wars, and is headed by Ramzan Kadyrov. Darfur is the western region of Sudan, where conflict began in 2003 between the government-backed Janjaweed militia and rebel groups (SLM/A and JEM). The ICC issued an arrest warrant for President Omar al-Bashir. Mali's troubled region is the north (Azawad, Timbuktu, Gao, Kidal), where the Tuareg rebellion and Islamist insurgency erupted in 2012. The Swat Valley is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, where the Taliban rose to prominence around 2007-09 and Malala Yousafzai was shot in 2012. Elimination logic: once you know Darfur is Sudan or Swat is Pakistan, options (b), (c) and (d) all fall away, leaving (a). Only pair 1 is correct.
explanations: Correct: only pair 1 is rightly matched, since Chechnya is in the Russian Federation, while Darfur is in Sudan and Swat is in Pakistan.
Incorrect: it includes pair 2 (Darfur-Mali) and pair 3 (Swat-Iraq), and both are wrong.
Incorrect: pair 3 is wrong because Swat Valley is in Pakistan, not Iraq, so pairing it with pair 1 fails.
Incorrect: pairs 2 and 3 are both mismatched, so not all three can be right.
keyfact: Chechnya is in Russia, Darfur in Sudan, Swat Valley in Pakistan.
option_notes: 1 only: This is the correct answer. Only the Chechnya-Russia pairing holds. Chechnya is a North Caucasus republic of Russia, scene of two post-Soviet wars and ongoing Islamist insurgency. Its capital is Grozny, and it has been led by Ramzan Kadyrov since 2007. The other pairs mismatch Darfur (Sudan) and Swat (Pakistan).

2 and 3 only: Wrong, since both pairs are mismatched. Darfur is in Sudan, where conflict started in 2003 with Janjaweed violence and a humanitarian crisis, and the ICC indicted al-Bashir. Swat is a valley in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, linked to the Taliban and to Malala Yousafzai. The option also excludes the correct pair 1, Chechnya-Russia.

1 and 3 only: Wrong because pair 3 fails. Swat Valley is in northwest Pakistan, a former princely state merged in 1969. It saw Taliban control from 2007-09 and the army's Operation Rah-e-Rast in 2009. Malala was shot there in 2012. Iraq's hotspots are Mosul, Anbar, Fallujah and Kurdistan, not Swat. Pair 1 is correct but pair 3 is not.

1, 2 and 3: Wrong, as it asserts that all pairs are correct. Pair 2 fails because Darfur is in Sudan, not Mali. Mali's crisis zone is the north (Azawad: Timbuktu, Gao, Kidal), which saw a Tuareg rebellion and Islamist takeover in 2012 and French intervention (Operation Serval, 2013). Pair 3 also fails, since Swat is in Pakistan.
related: Darfur is in western Sudan; the conflict began in 2003.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Omar al-Bashir for Darfur crimes.
Malala Yousafzai, from Swat, won the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize.
Azawad is the northern Mali region claimed by Tuareg separatists in 2012.
Grozny is the capital of Chechnya.
Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fight the Sudanese army in the war that began in April 2023.
Nagorno-Karabakh is an Armenian-populated enclave in Azerbaijan.
Crimea was annexed by Russia in 2014.
statements: 1 — Correct: Chechnya is a republic of the Russian Federation. It lies in the North Caucasus, borders Georgia, and has Grozny as its capital. Russia fought two wars there: 1994-96, which ended in de facto independence, and from 1999, after which Russian control was restored. Chechen separatism has been linked to Islamist militancy, and Ramzan Kadyrov has led the republic since 2007. The population is mainly Muslim Chechens. Attacks such as the 2002 Moscow theatre siege and the 2004 Beslan school siege were linked to Chechen militants.

2 — Incorrect: Darfur is in western Sudan, not Mali. The conflict began in 2003, when rebels such as the SLM/A and JEM rose up against Khartoum over marginalisation. The government-backed Janjaweed militia carried out mass atrocities, and the UN called it a humanitarian catastrophe. The AU-UN hybrid mission UNAMID was deployed in 2007 and ended in 2020. The ICC indicted Omar al-Bashir for genocide and war crimes. South Sudan became independent in 2011. Mali's crisis is in the north, around Azawad and Timbuktu.

3 — Incorrect: The Swat Valley is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, Pakistan, not Iraq. It was a princely state that merged with Pakistan in 1969. Under Maulana Fazlullah the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) took control around 2007-09, imposing sharia and shutting girls' schools. The army's Operation Rah-e-Rast in 2009 retook the valley. Malala Yousafzai, a Swat schoolgirl, was shot in 2012 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014. Iraq's regions in the news include Mosul, Anbar and Kurdistan.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Chechnya is a republic within the Russian Federation, whereas Darfur is in Sudan (not Mali) and the Swat Valley is in Pakistan (not Iraq).
topic_notes: UPSC regularly asks 'region-country' matching to test current-affairs geography. Key hotspots to know. Russia: Chechnya, Dagestan, Crimea (annexed 2014), Donbas. Sudan: Darfur (since 2003), Kordofan, Blue Nile, Abyei (disputed with South Sudan). Since April 2023 there has been a war between the Sudanese Army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF, descended from the Janjaweed). Mali and the Sahel: Azawad, Timbuktu, Gao, Kidal; Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have had coups and left ECOWAS, forming the Alliance of Sahel States. Pakistan: Swat, Waziristan (North and South), Balochistan, Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Iraq: Mosul, Anbar, Kirkuk, Kurdistan (Erbil), Sinjar (Yazidis). Syria: Aleppo, Idlib, Golan (Israeli-held). Myanmar: Rakhine (Rohingya), Kachin, Shan. Ethiopia: Tigray. Yemen: Houthis, Aden. Others: Nagorno-Karabakh (Azerbaijan, taken back in 2023), Xinjiang (China), Donetsk and Luhansk (Ukraine), Gaza and West Bank (Palestine), Kashmir. Study method: make a table of region, country, neighbours, capital, and the cause of conflict. Note related organisations and missions such as UNAMID, MINUSMA (ended 2023), AU, ECOWAS and ICC. Also learn the rivers, resources and ethnic groups involved, such as Tuareg in Mali, Fur and Zaghawa in Darfur, Pashtuns in Swat, and Kurds in Iraq.

ocr: With reference to Agni-IV Missile, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Itis a surface-to-surface missile. 2, It is fuelled by liquid propellant only. 3. It can deliver one-tonne nuclear warheads about 7500 km away. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa} 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Agni-IV is a DRDO-developed, two-stage, solid-fuelled, road-mobile surface-to-surface ballistic missile. It was first tested in November 2011 from Wheeler Island (now Abdul Kalam Island), Odisha, and has since been user-tested by the Strategic Forces Command. Its range is about 4,000 km, and it carries a payload of roughly 1 tonne, which can be a nuclear warhead. It uses a ring laser gyro-based inertial navigation system backed by a micro-navigation system, and it has a composite rocket motor and a re-entry heat shield. Statement 1 is correct because it is a surface-to-surface missile. Statement 2 is wrong on two counts: Agni missiles use solid propellant, and the 'only liquid' claim is false. Liquid propellant is the hallmark of the early Prithvi and some Scud-derived designs, not the Agni series. Statement 3 is wrong because 7,500 km is not Agni-IV's range. That figure is closer to the 5,000 km-plus Agni-V class, and Agni-V is officially cited at over 5,000 km (about 5,000 to 8,000 km in some estimates), so the figure is a deliberate distractor. Elimination: since statement 2 is clearly false, options (b) and (d) go out. Since statement 3 is also false, option (c) goes out. That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is true, while statements 2 (liquid only) and 3 (7,500 km) are false, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong. It includes statement 2, which is false because Agni-IV is solid-fuelled, and statement 3, which is false because its range is about 4,000 km.
Wrong. Statement 3 is false, since the range is about 4,000 km and not 7,500 km, even though statement 1 is true.
Wrong. It includes both false statements, 2 and 3, so it cannot be correct.
keyfact: Agni-IV: surface-to-surface, two-stage SOLID-fuel IRBM, range about 4,000 km (not liquid-fuelled, not 7,500 km).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only': Agni-IV is a surface-to-surface missile and no other statement holds. It is a two-stage, solid-fuelled, road-mobile IRBM developed by DRDO, with a range of about 4,000 km. It was first tested successfully in 2011 from Wheeler Island, Odisha, and it carries a payload of about 1 tonne. The Strategic Forces Command operates it as part of India's nuclear deterrent, and it has been repeatedly user-tested since 2014.
related: Agni-IV range is about 4,000 km, and it is solid-fuelled with two stages.
Agni-V is an ICBM-class missile with a range of over 5,000 km, and it was tested with MIRV in March 2024 (Mission Divyastra).
The IGMDP was launched in 1983 under Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
The Strategic Forces Command, created in 2003, manages India's nuclear weapons.
Agni tests are usually held at Abdul Kalam Island (formerly Wheeler Island), Odisha.
India joined the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) in 2016.
India follows a 'No First Use' policy and credible minimum deterrence.
Prithvi was India's first IGMDP missile and was initially liquid-fuelled.
statements: 1 — Correct: Agni-IV is a surface-to-surface ballistic missile. It belongs to India's Agni series, developed by DRDO's Advanced Systems Laboratory under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme legacy. It is a road-mobile, two-stage, solid-propellant IRBM with a range of about 4,000 km. It was first flight-tested in 2011 (a failure in December 2010 for its earlier version, then success in November 2011). It has since been inducted for the Strategic Forces Command, which manages India's nuclear arsenal. It has a ring laser gyro-based INS and a composite rocket motor.

2 — Incorrect: Agni-IV is not fuelled by liquid propellant only. It uses solid propellant in both stages. Solid fuel gives quick launch readiness, easier storage and better mobility than liquid fuel, which must be loaded shortly before launch. Liquid propellants were used in the early Prithvi missiles (Prithvi-I and II) and in the second stage of the Agni-II variant's predecessor Agni-I technology demonstrator, which combined a solid first stage with a liquid second stage. The Agni-I to Agni-V series generally uses solid motors, giving canisterised, rapid-launch capability.

3 — Incorrect: Agni-IV cannot deliver a one-tonne warhead 7,500 km. Its range is about 4,000 km with a payload of roughly 1 tonne. Agni-V is the longer-range ICBM-class missile, with a three-stage solid design and a range of over 5,000 km, first tested in April 2012 and later tested with MIRV technology (Mission Divyastra, March 2024). Agni-III has about 3,000 km and Agni-II about 2,000 km. Agni-Prime (Agni-P) is a newer canisterised missile with a range of 1,000 to 2,000 km.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. Agni-IV is a surface-to-surface intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) with a range of about 4,000 km. It uses solid propellant in a two-stage design, and it is not a 7,500 km weapon.
topic_notes: The Agni series is India's family of nuclear-capable surface-to-surface ballistic missiles. It was developed by DRDO under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP), led by Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam and launched in 1983. The IGMDP produced Prithvi, Agni, Akash, Trishul and Nag. Agni-I (about 700-900 km, medium-range) is a single-stage solid missile. Agni-II (about 2,000-3,000 km) is a two-stage solid missile. Agni-III (about 3,000-5,000 km) is also a two-stage solid missile. Agni-IV (about 4,000 km) is a two-stage solid missile with an advanced avionics suite. Agni-V (over 5,000 km, ICBM-class) is a three-stage solid missile and was tested with MIRV capability in 2024. Agni-Prime is a canisterised, newer-generation missile that replaces older Agni-I and II types. Launch sites are at the Integrated Test Range, Chandipur and Abdul Kalam Island (formerly Wheeler Island) in Odisha. Classification by range: short-range under about 1,000 km, medium-range about 1,000-3,000 km, intermediate-range about 3,000-5,500 km, and ICBM above about 5,500 km. Other missile families to remember: Prithvi (surface-to-surface, early versions liquid-fuelled), Dhanush (ship-launched), Sagarika/K-15 and K-4 (submarine-launched), BrahMos (supersonic cruise missile, India-Russia), Nirbhay (subsonic cruise missile), Akash (surface-to-air), and Astra (air-to-air). India follows a 'No First Use' nuclear doctrine with credible minimum deterrence. It has been a member of the MTCR since 2016, though not of the NPT. Likely angles for future questions: the range ranking of the Agni missiles, solid versus liquid fuel, MIRV technology, and the SFC's role under the Nuclear Command Authority.

question:
With reference to two nonconventional energy sources called ‘coalbed methane’ and ‘shale gas’, consider the following statements :
1. Coalbed methane is the pure methane gas extracted from coal seams, while shale gas is a mixture of propane and butane only that can be extracted from fine-grained sedimentary ” rocks.
2. In India, abundant coalbed methane sources exist, but so far no shale gas sources have been found. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Environment
detail: Coalbed methane (CBM) is methane adsorbed in coal seams, extracted by dewatering the seam to lower pressure. It is not perfectly pure, because it usually contains small amounts of CO2, nitrogen and heavier hydrocarbons. Shale gas is natural gas, predominantly methane, trapped in fine-grained, low-permeability shale. It is extracted by horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing (fracking). Propane and butane are components of LPG and natural gas liquids, and they are not the main constituents of shale gas, so the word 'only' in Statement 1 makes it wrong. Statement 2 is also wrong. India has CBM blocks awarded under the CBM policy of 1997 (Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Sohagpur and others). India also has shale formations in the Cambay, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery, Damodar and Assam-Arakan basins. ONGC drilled the first shale gas exploratory well in the Damodar valley (West Bengal) in 2011, and the Shale Gas and Oil Policy followed in 2013. Elimination: Statement 1 fails on its factual claim about shale gas composition, and Statement 2 fails on its claim that no shale gas has been found. Both are false, so the answer is (d).
explanations: Wrong. Statement 1 mischaracterises shale gas as 'propane and butane only', and Statement 2 is also false, so 1 alone cannot be correct.
Wrong. Statement 2 says that no shale gas has been found in India. Shale gas has in fact been identified, and exploration has begun.
Wrong. Both statements contain factual errors, so they cannot both be correct.
Correct. Shale gas is mainly methane, not propane and butane only, and India has both CBM and shale gas resources, so neither statement holds.
keyfact: Shale gas is mostly methane, not propane-butane, and India has both CBM and shale gas resources.
option_notes: Option (a) refers to Statement 1 alone. Its claim about shale gas composition is wrong, because shale gas is predominantly methane (typically 70-90 percent), with some ethane and smaller amounts of heavier gases. CBM is also described as 'pure', which is only loosely true. Propane and butane are the main constituents of LPG, which is produced from natural gas processing and from refining crude oil. The statement fails because of the word 'only'.

Option (b) refers to Statement 2 alone. It claims abundant CBM but no shale gas in India. The CBM part is broadly true, since India has large coal reserves and CBM blocks have been awarded across several rounds. The shale part is false: shale formations have been mapped and test wells drilled by ONGC and Oil India. Large-scale commercial shale production has not yet begun, which is a different matter from none being found.

Option (c) says both statements are correct. Each statement contains a factual error: Statement 1 on the composition of shale gas, and Statement 2 on the presence of shale gas in India. A student who recalls that CBM is methane and that India has coal might be lured to this option, but the shale claims in both statements contradict it.

Option (d) is the official answer. Shale gas is natural gas, mostly methane, locked in shale and extracted by fracking. India has CBM in coalfields and shale gas potential in several sedimentary basins. India's first CBM commercial production started in 2007 in West Bengal. Neither statement can be accepted as written, and both claims fail on the facts.
related: CBM is mainly methane adsorbed in coal seams and is recovered by dewatering.
Shale gas is mainly methane and is recovered by hydraulic fracturing (fracking).
India's first shale gas exploratory well was drilled by ONGC in 2011 near Durgapur, West Bengal.
The Shale Gas and Oil Policy was announced in 2013.
HELP (Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy) was launched in 2016 with Open Acreage Licensing.
Raniganj in West Bengal was the site of India's first commercial CBM production.
Propane and butane are the main constituents of LPG.
India targets raising natural gas to about 15 percent of its energy mix by 2030.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: CBM is mostly methane but not strictly pure, and shale gas is mainly methane, not a propane-butane-only mixture. CBM is methane adsorbed on the coal matrix and released when reservoir pressure is lowered by pumping out water. Shale gas is held in organic-rich, fine-grained sedimentary rock with very low permeability and is recovered by horizontal drilling with hydraulic fracturing. Propane and butane are natural gas liquids and the main components of LPG. The USA led the shale revolution from about 2008 onward, and shale gas has changed global gas markets.

2 — Incorrect: India has CBM resources, but shale gas has also been identified. India's CBM resources are estimated at about 92 trillion cubic feet (TCF), mainly in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Commercial CBM production began at Raniganj (South) in West Bengal, with Great Eastern Energy Corporation as an early producer. Shale gas potential exists in the Cambay, KG, Cauvery, Vindhyan and Damodar basins. ONGC drilled the first shale well at Durgapur in 2011. The Shale Gas and Oil Policy of 2013 allowed NOCs to explore shale gas in their nominated blocks, and HELP (2016) later replaced the older licensing regime.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Shale gas is chiefly methane, not a propane-butane-only mixture, and India has both coalbed methane and shale gas resources that have been identified.
topic_notes: Unconventional hydrocarbons are oil and gas resources that cannot be produced by conventional wells alone and need special stimulation. The main types are coalbed methane, shale gas, tight gas, shale (tight) oil and gas hydrates. CBM is methane adsorbed in coal; it is recovered by dewatering the seam, and it is a cleaner fuel than coal. India's CBM resources are estimated at about 92 TCF, and the main CBM-bearing states are Jharkhand, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Telangana and Rajasthan. The CBM policy was adopted in 1997, and the first CBM block bidding round was held in 2001. Shale gas is held in fine-grained, organic-rich shale with very low permeability. It is extracted by horizontal drilling plus hydraulic fracturing, in which water, sand and chemicals are injected at high pressure. Environmental concerns include heavy water use, groundwater contamination, induced seismicity, methane leakage and disposal of flowback water. The USA is the leading producer, followed by China, Canada and Argentina. India's shale basins include Cambay, KG, Cauvery, Assam-Arakan, the Vindhyan and the Damodar basin. Policies to know: the New Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP), the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP, 2016) with Open Acreage Licensing, and the Shale Gas and Oil Policy (2013). Other unconventional sources are gas hydrates (methane clathrates), found in the KG basin and the Andaman region under the National Gas Hydrate Programme. Other angles are the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH), which regulates upstream activity under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, and the National Gas Grid. Natural gas is also the transition fuel in India's plan to raise its share in the energy mix to 15 percent by 2030.

ocr: With reference to ‘Changpa’ community of India, consider the following statements : 1. They live mainly in the State of Uttarakhand. 2, They rear the Pashmina goats that yield a fine wool. 3. They are kept in the category of Scheduled Tribes. 7 Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b} 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only fd) 1,2 and 3
subject: Polity
detail: The Changpa (also Champa) are a semi-nomadic highland people of the Changthang region, the western extension of the Tibetan plateau, lying at about 4,500 m in eastern Ladakh (Leh district, including Rupshu, Kharnak, Hanle, Korzok around Tso Moriri). They are Tibetan Buddhists (largely Drukpa Kagyu), live in yak-hair tents called rebo, and move seasonally with herds of yaks, sheep, and especially Changthangi (Pashmina) goats whose undercoat gives the fine cashmere wool known as Pashmina, or 'Cashmere', woven mainly in Kashmir. Many Changpa were Tibetan refugees from the 1960s who settled at Kharnak and Sumdo. They are recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh; the Changpa were among the groups for which the Ladakh tribal list (Bodh/Boto, Balti, Brokpa, Changpa, Garra, Mon, Purigpa) was drawn. Elimination: Statement 1 is wrong because Uttarakhand's pastoral tribes are Bhotiyas, Van Gujjars, and Jaunsaris, not Changpa. Since 2 and 3 are right, only (b) fits. Remember the keyword pair: Changpa = Ladakh = Pashmina.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which is false because the Changpa live in Ladakh (Changthang), not Uttarakhand.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 are right — Changpa rear Pashmina goats and are classed as a Scheduled Tribe — and statement 1 is wrong.
Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, so 3 alone is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the community is from Ladakh, so 'all three' fails.
keyfact: Changpa = Ladakh's Changthang nomads, Pashmina goat herders and a Scheduled Tribe (not Uttarakhand).
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would mean the Changpa live in Uttarakhand. In fact Uttarakhand is home to the Bhotiya, Jaunsari, Tharu, Buksa and Raji tribes plus the pastoral Van Gujjars, who rear buffaloes and migrate between the Shivaliks and alpine meadows (bugyals). Uttarakhand became a state in 2000, and its tribal population is about 3%. Bhotiyas traditionally traded with Tibet through passes such as Lipulekh and Niti until the 1962 war.

Option (b) '2 and 3 only' is the official answer. It reflects that the Changpa are Pashmina-herding Scheduled Tribe nomads of Ladakh's Changthang plateau, whose Changthangi goats yield Pashmina. They are Tibetan Buddhists with roots in Tibet and live in rebo tents. The group is notified as an ST under Article 342 and is concentrated around Leh district. Their traditional economy is pastoralism and barter of wool, salt and dairy produce.

Option (c) '3 only' correctly says the Changpa are a Scheduled Tribe but leaves out their Pashmina goat-rearing. Scheduled Tribes are specified under Article 342, with the definition in Article 366(25). The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes was created by the 89th Amendment (2003) under Article 338A. Ladakh's tribes include Balti, Bodh, Brokpa, Changpa, Garra, Mon and Purigpa.

Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' would require the Changpa to live mainly in Uttarakhand, which is false. Their homeland is Changthang in Ladakh, extending to Tibet. The geographical error in statement 1 is a classic UPSC trap, mixing Himalayan communities of different states: Bhotiyas (Uttarakhand), Gaddis (Himachal), Bakarwals and Gujjars (J&K), Monpas (Arunachal), Lepchas (Sikkim).
related: Changpa: semi-nomadic Tibetan-origin herders of Changthang, Ladakh.
Changthangi goat gives Pashmina (cashmere) wool; combed, not sheared.
Shahtoosh comes from the endangered Tibetan antelope (chiru) and is banned.
Scheduled Tribes are notified under Article 342; defined in Article 366(25).
Ladakh became a Union Territory on 31 October 2019.
Van Gujjars are the pastoral nomads of Uttarakhand's Shivalik forests.
Bakarwals are goat-herding nomads of Jammu and Kashmir (Pir Panjal).
Hanle in Changthang hosts an Indian Astronomical Observatory and a Dark Sky Reserve.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Changpa live mainly in Ladakh (J&K, now UT of Ladakh), not Uttarakhand. Uttarakhand's Himalayan communities include the Bhotiyas (Johari, Jad, Marchha, Tolcha), Tharu, Buksa, Raji, Jaunsari and the pastoral Van Gujjars. The Changpa inhabit the Changthang plateau at about 4,000-4,500 m, mostly in Leh district, near Tso Moriri, Pangong and Hanle, and also across the border in Tibet. They are nomads who migrate to graze their herds across Rupshu, Kharnak and Korzok and dwell in yak-hair tents called rebo.

2 — Correct: The Changpa rear Changthangi goats (Capra hircus) whose soft undercoat gives Pashmina, also called cashmere, the finest commercial wool. Raw wool is combed, not sheared, in spring, and sold largely to Kashmir for spinning and weaving into shawls. The goat thrives at extreme altitude and cold, below -30°C. Pashmina has a GI tag (Kashmir Pashmina), and the Changthangi breed also gives some Ladakhi products. Pashmina fibre is 12-15 microns thick. The Changpa also keep yaks, sheep, horses and dogs (Tibetan mastiff).

3 — Correct: The Changpa are listed as a Scheduled Tribe (ST) in J&K/Ladakh. Scheduled Tribes are notified under Article 342 of the Constitution by the President; Article 366(25) defines them. The Changpa are among Ladakh's ST communities, alongside Balti, Beda, Bodh, Brokpa (Dard), Garra, Mon and Purigpa. They are also a Particularly Vulnerable group by occupation (not formally PVTG). Their nomadic life is threatened by climate change, grazing disputes and border tensions. Ladakh's tribal population is over 90%.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. The Changpa (Changpa/Champa) are a semi-nomadic pastoral Tibetan-origin community living mainly in the Changthang plateau of Ladakh (Jammu & Kashmir, now UT of Ladakh), not Uttarakhand. They rear Pashmina goats (Changthangi goats) and are notified as a Scheduled Tribe.
topic_notes: The Changpa (Champa) are semi-nomadic pastoralists of the Changthang ('northern plains') plateau, an extension of the Tibetan plateau spreading across eastern Ladakh and western Tibet. Altitude averages 4,000-4,500 m, with lakes such as Pangong Tso, Tso Moriri and Tso Kar, and the Changthang Cold Desert Wildlife Sanctuary and Hanle (Dark Sky Reserve, Indian Astronomical Observatory). Their livelihood centres on Changthangi goats producing Pashmina, plus sheep, yaks and horses. Raw Pashmina is mostly sold to Kashmir traders; the Ladakh Pashmina Growers Cooperative Marketing Society and the 'Looms of Ladakh' initiative aim at local value addition. Changpa live in yak-hair tents (rebo), are mostly Buddhist (Drukpa Kagyu) and celebrate the Losar festival. Some Changpa settled around Kharnak and Sumdo. Threats include climate change, rangeland degradation, wildlife predation (snow leopard, wolves), grazing disputes along the LAC and pressure to leave nomadism. Related pastoral communities: Bakarwals and Gujjars (J&K), Gaddis (Himachal), Van Gujjars (Uttarakhand), Bhotiyas (Uttarakhand), Raikas/Rabaris (Rajasthan/Gujarat), Maldharis (Gujarat Gir), Kuruba (Karnataka), Dhangars (Maharashtra), Toda (Nilgiris, buffalo herders). Ladakh became a Union Territory on 31 Oct 2019 following the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019. Scheduled Tribes are notified under Article 342; Fifth and Sixth Schedules govern their areas; Ladakh was included in the Sixth Schedule demand discussion, and Leh has the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (LAHDC) since 1995. Pashmina from Changthangi goat has a GI tag (Kashmir Pashmina). Shahtoosh, from the Tibetan antelope (chiru), is banned under CITES and the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, and must not be confused with Pashmina.

ocr: In India, cluster bean (Guar) is traditionally used as a vegetable or animal feed, but recently the cultivation of this has assumed significance. Which one of the following statements is correct in this context? {a} The oil extracted from seeds is used in the manufacture of biodegradable plastics {ob} The gum made from its seeds is used in the extraction of shale gas (c) The leaf extract of this plant has the properties of anti- histamines (da) It is a source of high quality biodiesel
subject: Environment
detail: Guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba) is a drought-tolerant kharif legume grown in arid and semi-arid north-western India. India produces about 80 percent of the world's guar, and Rajasthan alone contributes roughly 70 percent of India's output. The endosperm of the seed is processed into guar gum (guaran), a water-soluble galactomannan polysaccharide. It is a powerful thickener and gelling agent. In the food industry it is used in ice cream, sauces and bakery products, and it is also used in textiles, paper, cosmetics and explosives. Its biggest boost came from the shale gas and oil boom in the USA, where guar gum is used in hydraulic fracturing (fracking) fluid to increase viscosity and carry the proppant (sand) into fractures. Hence guar exports surged around 2011-2014. Elimination logic: guar seeds are not known as an oil source, so (a) fails. Guar has no recognised antihistamine leaf extract, so (c) fails. It is also not a notable biodiesel feedstock; Jatropha and Pongamia are the typical biodiesel crops, so (d) fails. Only (b) matches the real industrial use.
explanations: Incorrect: guar seeds are valued for gum from the endosperm, not oil; guar is not used to make biodegradable plastics. Bioplastics come from starch, PLA or PHA.
Correct: guar gum is a thickener in fracking fluid used for shale gas and oil extraction, and this drove its recent demand.
Incorrect: guar leaf extract is not known for antihistamine properties; it is used as green fodder or a vegetable.
Incorrect: guar is not a source of high-quality biodiesel; Jatropha, Pongamia and algae are the usual biodiesel sources.
keyfact: Guar gum (galactomannan from guar seed endosperm) is used in fracking fluid for shale gas extraction, so option (b) is correct.
option_notes: Biodegradable plastics (bioplastics) are made from renewable sources such as starch, cellulose, polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA). They are designed to decompose through microbial action. In India, research has used corn starch, sugarcane bagasse and other feedstocks. Guar is not a recognised raw material for them, and guar seeds are not an oil crop. Guar's industrial product is gum, plus guar meal (korma) as protein-rich cattle feed.

Guar gum is a galactomannan from the endosperm of guar seeds. In hydraulic fracturing, a gel made from guar gum is pumped with water and sand at high pressure into shale formations to fracture the rock and release gas or oil. The gel keeps the sand suspended. The US shale boom raised Indian guar exports and prices sharply from 2011 to 2012, and demand later softened when prices fell and synthetic substitutes emerged.

Antihistamines are drugs that block histamine receptors and are used for allergies, for example cetirizine, loratadine and diphenhydramine. Histamine is released by mast cells during allergic reactions. Guar is not a source of antihistamines. Guar gum does have a medical use as a dietary fibre, helping control blood sugar and cholesterol and acting as a bulk laxative.

Biodiesel is a fuel made by transesterification of vegetable oils or animal fats. India's National Policy on Biofuels (2009, revised 2018) promotes non-edible oilseeds such as Jatropha curcas and Pongamia (Karanja) as feedstocks, and used cooking oil is also encouraged. Guar is a legume grown for gum, vegetable and fodder, and is not a typical biodiesel crop. Guar also fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility.
related: Guar (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba) is a leguminous kharif crop of arid regions.
India produces about 80 percent of the world's guar; Rajasthan is the top state.
Guar gum is a galactomannan extracted from the seed endosperm.
Guar gum thickens fracking fluid in shale gas and oil extraction.
Hydraulic fracturing uses water, sand and chemicals at high pressure to fracture shale rock.
Jatropha and Pongamia are non-edible oilseeds promoted for biodiesel in India.
Guar gum is approved as food additive E412.
SEBI suspended guar futures trading in 2012 to curb speculation.
summary: The correct answer is (b). Guar (cluster bean) seeds yield guar gum, a galactomannan, which is used as a thickener in hydraulic fracturing fluid for extracting shale gas. This is why guar cultivation has gained fresh significance in India, especially in Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat.
topic_notes: Guar or cluster bean (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba) is a hardy, drought-resistant, deep-rooted leguminous kharif crop suited to sandy soils and low rainfall (about 300-500 mm). India is the largest producer and exporter, with Rajasthan (about 70 percent), Haryana, Gujarat and Punjab as major producing states. It is traditionally used as a vegetable and as cattle fodder, and the seed meal (korma) is a protein-rich feed. As a legume it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium, so it is useful in crop rotation. The key industrial product is guar gum, extracted from the endosperm (about 30-35 percent of the seed). It is a galactomannan with exceptional water-binding and thickening ability, and is cheaper and more efficient than many alternatives such as locust bean gum. Uses include food (E412 additive in ice cream, dairy, bakery), pharmaceuticals, textiles, paper, cosmetics, mining explosives, and oil and gas drilling. The shale gas fracking boom in the USA, where guar gum thickens the fracturing fluid, made guar a high-value cash crop during 2011-2014, with price spikes and speculation on commodity exchanges. Trading in guar futures was suspended by SEBI in 2012 to curb speculation. India's guar exports go mainly to the USA, Germany, China and Russia. Related topics UPSC may ask: other industrial gums (gum arabic from Acacia, karaya), hydraulic fracturing and shale gas basins in India (Cambay, Krishna-Godavari, Cauvery), Jatropha and biodiesel policy, nitrogen-fixing legumes, and kharif and rabi crop classification. Guar is also grown in Pakistan, the USA (Texas), Australia and parts of Africa.

ocr: Which of the following -have coral reefs? 1. Andaman and Nicobar Islands 2. Gulf of Kachchh 3. Gulf of Mannar 4 Sunderbans Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b}) 2 and 4 only (ec) 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2, 3 and 4
subject: Environment
detail: Coral reefs need clear, warm (23-29 degrees C), saline, shallow, sunlit water with low sediment, because the symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) in coral polyps need light for photosynthesis. India has four major reef regions: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (fringing reefs, the richest and most diverse), the Gulf of Mannar (fringing and patch reefs around about 21 islands, in the Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park and Biosphere Reserve), the Gulf of Kachchh (the northernmost reefs, in the Marine National Park near Jamnagar, Gujarat) and Lakshadweep (atolls). The Sunderbans lies in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, where huge freshwater and silt discharge makes the water turbid and low in salinity. That is hostile to corals but ideal for mangroves such as Heritiera fomes (sundari) and the Bengal tiger habitat. Elimination: since 1, 2 and 3 are all reef areas, any option leaving out one of them fails. Options (b) and (d) include the Sunderbans, and (b) also omits the Andamans. Only (a) is left. Coral bleaching, caused by thermal stress, expels the zooxanthellae and turns the coral white.
explanations: Correct: it lists exactly the three reef regions among the items, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Mannar, and leaves out the Sunderbans.
Wrong: it includes the Sunderbans, which has mangroves rather than reefs, and it omits the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Gulf of Mannar, which do have reefs.
Wrong: the Andamans and the Gulf of Mannar do have reefs, but it leaves out the Gulf of Kachchh, which also has coral reefs.
Wrong: it includes the Sunderbans, which has no coral reefs because of its turbid, brackish, silt-laden delta waters.
keyfact: India's coral reefs: Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Mannar and Gulf of Kachchh; the Sunderbans has mangroves, not corals.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 3 only, covers the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Mannar. These, with Lakshadweep, are India's four main coral reef regions. The Andamans have the richest reefs, the Gulf of Mannar has fringing and patch reefs, and the Gulf of Kachchh has the northernmost reefs. Lakshadweep has atolls, which are ring-shaped reefs. All of these areas are vulnerable to bleaching caused by rising sea temperatures.

Option (b), 2 and 4 only, pairs the Gulf of Kachchh with the Sunderbans. The Gulf of Kachchh is in Gujarat and has a Marine National Park near Jamnagar with reefs and mangroves. The Sunderbans is a mangrove delta in West Bengal and Bangladesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for the Bengal tiger. Pairing them is wrong because the Sunderbans has no coral reefs.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only, pairs the Andaman and Nicobar Islands with the Gulf of Mannar. Both really have reefs. The Andamans have the richest and most diverse coral, with Wandoor Marine National Park. The Gulf of Mannar is a Biosphere Reserve (1989) with about 21 islands. The option is incomplete because it omits the Gulf of Kachchh.

Option (d), 1, 2, 3 and 4, would add the Sunderbans to the three true reef regions. The Sunderbans is the world's largest contiguous mangrove forest, in the Ganges delta, and is a UNESCO site and tiger reserve. Its low-salinity, silt-laden water suits mangroves and not corals. The option is therefore incorrect.
related: India's four coral reef regions: Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh.
Gulf of Mannar became Asia's first marine Biosphere Reserve in 1989.
The Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park (1982) was India's first marine national park.
Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel zooxanthellae under thermal stress.
Corals are listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
Coral reefs are in CRZ-I under the Coastal Regulation Zone rules.
The Sunderbans is a mangrove UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987) and a Ramsar site.
Lakshadweep islands are coral atolls.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands have extensive fringing and barrier reefs. They are India's most diverse coral area, with over 200 coral species. Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park (Wandoor) and Rani Jhansi Marine National Park are reef-rich protected areas. The reefs face threats from bleaching, as in 1998, 2010 and 2016, from siltation and from the 2004 tsunami's uplift. Surveys also record sea anemones, giant clams and many reef fish.

2 — Correct: The Gulf of Kachchh in Gujarat has the northernmost coral reefs in India. The Marine National Park and Sanctuary near Jamnagar, India's first marine national park (1982), protects 42 islands with reefs, mangroves, mudflats and seagrass. Reefs here are fringing and patch types, with fewer species than the Andamans because of high tides, turbidity and salinity swings. The area is also home to Pirotan Island and the endangered dugong.

3 — Correct: The Gulf of Mannar lies between southeast India (Tamil Nadu) and Sri Lanka. It has about 21 islands with fringing and patch reefs and has about 117 coral species. It is a Marine National Park (1982) and became Asia's first marine Biosphere Reserve in 1989. It is known for dugongs, pearl oysters and sea cucumbers. Major threats include coral mining, overfishing, pollution and bleaching.

4 — Incorrect: The Sunderbans is a mangrove forest in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta, shared by India (West Bengal) and Bangladesh. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987), a Ramsar site and a Biosphere Reserve, and holds a Project Tiger reserve. The water is brackish, turbid and silty, so corals cannot grow. Typical species include sundari, royal Bengal tiger, saltwater crocodile and Irrawaddy dolphin.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3 only. India's four major coral reef areas are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Gulf of Kachchh, the Gulf of Mannar and Lakshadweep. The Sunderbans is a mangrove (tidal delta) ecosystem with no coral reefs.
topic_notes: Coral reefs are underwater structures built by colonial polyps (class Anthozoa) that secrete calcium carbonate. They live in symbiosis with zooxanthellae algae, which give them colour and food. They need clear water at 23-29 degrees C, salinity of about 32-42 ppt and depths under about 50-70 m, and they are mainly found between 30 degrees N and S. Reef types are fringing, barrier and atoll. The Great Barrier Reef (Australia) is the largest. India's main reef areas are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, the Gulf of Mannar and the Gulf of Kachchh. Lakshadweep consists of atolls of coral origin. Coral bleaching happens when heat stress makes corals expel zooxanthellae. Other threats are ocean acidification, pollution, siltation, destructive fishing, coral mining and the crown-of-thorns starfish. Protection comes through the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, where corals are in Schedule I, through the Coastal Regulation Zone notifications, which classify coral reefs as CRZ-I, and through Marine National Parks. The Zoological Survey of India monitors reefs. India has an International Coral Reef Initiative link and the Coral Reef Monitoring network. Related ecosystems are mangroves (the Sunderbans, Bhitarkanika), seagrass beds and mudflats. Mangroves and reefs both buffer coasts against storms. UPSC may ask about the locations of reefs, bleaching causes, CRZ categories, Ramsar and biosphere sites, and which ecosystems are found in which region.

question:
In India, the problem of soil erosion is associated with which of the following?
1. Terrace cultivation
2. Deforestation
3. Tropical climate Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Geography
detail: Soil erosion is the removal of the topsoil by water, wind or ice faster than it forms. In India, the major causes are deforestation, overgrazing, shifting (jhum) cultivation, up-and-down slope ploughing, mining and unplanned construction. Forests protect soil in three ways: the canopy breaks the force of raindrops, leaf litter slows runoff, and roots bind soil and improve infiltration. When forests are cleared, rainsplash, sheet erosion, rill and gully erosion increase, as seen in the Chambal ravines, the Shiwalik foothills and the Western Ghats. Terracing, along with contour ploughing, contour bunding, strip cropping, shelterbelts and check dams, is a recognised method of conserving soil on slopes, so it cannot be listed as a cause. This is why statements 1 and 3 are weak. A tropical climate has high-intensity rain, but the erosion depends on land cover and land management; many tropical areas under dense forest or well-managed terraces have little erosion. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is recognised as a conservation practice, options (a), (c) and (d) all fall, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it counts terrace cultivation as a cause, but terracing is a soil conservation method.
Correct: only deforestation, statement 2, is clearly associated with soil erosion in India, so 2 only is the answer.
Wrong: it includes terrace cultivation (1) and a tropical climate (3), and neither is a recognised cause of erosion.
Wrong: it includes both terrace cultivation and a tropical climate, and the first of these is a conservation measure.
keyfact: Deforestation causes soil erosion in India; terracing is a conservation measure, not a cause.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only, pairs terrace cultivation with deforestation. Terracing is cultivation on stepped, levelled fields on hill slopes, used in the Himalayas, Western Ghats and Northeast to reduce runoff and erosion, hold moisture and enable crops such as rice and tea. Deforestation is the clearing of forest for other uses and is a major driver of erosion, landslides, floods and loss of biodiversity. India's forest policy targets 33 percent cover.

Option (b), 2 only, is the official answer. It identifies deforestation as the cause of soil erosion. Deforestation removes canopy, litter and root systems, which exposes topsoil to rain and wind. Effects include gully formation, loss of fertility, reservoir siltation and desertification. India loses billions of tonnes of soil annually. Remedies include afforestation, agroforestry, check dams, shelterbelts and watershed management under schemes such as the Integrated Watershed Management Programme.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only, combines terrace cultivation and a tropical climate. Terrace farming is a conservation practice. The tropical climate covers regions between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, with high temperatures and, in monsoon areas, seasonal intense rain. India has a tropical monsoon climate. Intense rain raises erosivity, and tropical soils like laterite and red soils are erodible, but climate alone is not a cause of erosion.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, would count every listed factor as a cause. It is wrong because terrace cultivation is a protective measure and a tropical climate is not an independent cause. Soil erosion in India affects roughly 30 percent of land to some degree. Types include sheet, rill, gully and wind erosion, and the main agents are water and wind. Ravines in Chambal, Yamuna and Mahi are examples of gully erosion.
related: Gully erosion produces ravines in Chambal, Yamuna and Mahi valleys.
Terracing, contour bunding and strip cropping are soil conservation measures.
Jhum cultivation is shifting cultivation in the Northeast and contributes to erosion.
CSWCRTI is at Dehradun and CAZRI is at Jodhpur.
World Soil Day is 5 December; World Day to Combat Desertification is 17 June.
The National Forest Policy 1988 targets 33 percent forest cover, 66 percent in hilly areas.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015.
Shelterbelts and windbreaks check wind erosion in arid regions.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Terrace cultivation is a soil-conservation technique that reduces slope length and runoff velocity. Terracing converts steep slopes into step-like level fields. It is widely practised in the Himalayan foothills, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, the Northeast, the Western Ghats and the Nilgiris, for example in tea, rice and fruit farming. Bench terraces cut slope length, hold water and cut erosion. Poorly maintained terraces can fail, but terracing is not itself the cause of erosion. Other conservation measures are contour bunding, contour ploughing, strip cropping, mulching and afforestation.

2 — Correct: Deforestation exposes soil and speeds up erosion. Forest cover reduces the impact of raindrops and binds the soil with roots. Clearing forests for agriculture, settlement, mining, roads and fuelwood leads to sheet, rill and gully erosion, landslides and siltation of reservoirs. India's major affected zones include the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, the Chambal ravines and the Northeast, where jhum cultivation is practised. The National Forest Policy 1988 aims for 33 percent forest cover, with 66 percent in hills. Afforestation, agroforestry and watershed programmes are the remedies.

3 — Incorrect: A tropical climate is not an independent cause of soil erosion. Although tropical regions can receive intense monsoon rainfall, which has high erosivity, erosion actually occurs when land is bare or poorly managed. Dense tropical forests, such as those of the Western Ghats and the Northeast, protect soil well. Tropical soils like laterites are, however, prone to erosion when cleared. UPSC treats climate as only a background factor, whereas human activity is the key driver. Rainfall intensity, slope, soil type and vegetation cover are the natural factors.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Deforestation removes the protective vegetation cover and root binding, which leaves soil exposed to rain and wind erosion. Terrace cultivation is a soil conservation measure, and a tropical climate is not by itself a cause of erosion.
topic_notes: Soil erosion is the detachment and transport of soil particles by water, wind, ice or gravity. In India, water erosion dominates: sheet erosion is uniform removal of a thin layer, rill erosion forms small channels, and gully erosion produces deep channels that create badlands or ravines, as in Chambal, Yamuna and Mahi. Wind erosion is significant in Rajasthan and the arid parts of Gujarat and Haryana. Natural factors include rainfall intensity, slope steepness, soil texture and vegetation cover. Human factors include deforestation, overgrazing, shifting cultivation (jhum in the Northeast, called podu, penda and others elsewhere), up-and-down slope ploughing, mining, construction and poor irrigation practices. Impacts are loss of topsoil and fertility, lower yields, reservoir siltation, floods, desertification and landslides. Conservation measures: contour ploughing, contour bunds, terracing, strip cropping, crop rotation, mulching, cover crops, shelterbelts and windbreaks, check dams, gully plugging, afforestation, agroforestry and controlled grazing. Institutions and programmes: the Central Soil and Water Conservation Research and Training Institute (CSWCRTI) at Dehradun, the Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) at Jodhpur, the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) at Nagpur, the Integrated Watershed Management Programme (now under PMKSY watershed component), the Soil Health Card scheme (2015) and the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture. Soil types often asked: alluvial, black (regur), red, laterite, arid, forest and saline soils. Related concepts: soil horizons, soil salinity and alkalinity, and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD, 1994) with its 17 June observance as the World Day to Combat Desertification. World Soil Day is on 5 December.

ocr: The seasonal reversal of winds is the typical characteristic of ‘ fa) Equatorial climate (b) Mediterranean climate (c) Monsoon climate (d) All of the above climates B-FVS-N-IVUA/58A
subject: Environment
detail: The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season, and it refers to a complete reversal of the prevailing wind system with the seasons. In summer the Asian landmass heats rapidly and develops a low-pressure area, while the Indian Ocean stays relatively cooler and holds higher pressure. Moist southwest winds are therefore drawn onto the land and bring heavy rain. In winter the land cools, a strong high-pressure cell builds over Siberia and Central Asia, and dry winds blow outward from land to sea as the northeast monsoon. The northward shift of the ITCZ to about 20-25 degrees N over the Gangetic plain in summer, the withdrawal of the subtropical westerly jet from the Indian region, and the Tropical Easterly Jet all support this reversal. Equatorial climate has calm, doldrum-type conditions with convectional rain all year and no wind reversal. Mediterranean climate has a seasonal shift of wind belts, with westerlies bringing winter rain and trade winds or subtropical high pressure bringing summer drought. This is a shift of belts, not a reversal of direction. So (a) and (b) are wrong, which also eliminates (d).
explanations: Incorrect: Equatorial climate has weak, variable winds (doldrums), uniform high temperature and daily convectional rainfall throughout the year; there is no seasonal reversal of winds.
Incorrect: Mediterranean climate has dry summers and wet winters because the wind belts and pressure belts shift. Westerlies bring winter rain, but winds do not reverse direction.
Correct: Monsoon climate is defined by the seasonal reversal of winds. Summer winds blow from sea to land (southwest monsoon), and winter winds blow from land to sea (northeast monsoon).
Incorrect: Since equatorial and Mediterranean climates do not show seasonal wind reversal, 'all of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: Seasonal reversal of wind direction is the hallmark of monsoon climate, caused by differential heating of land and sea and the shift of the ITCZ.
option_notes: Equatorial climate lies roughly within 5-10 degrees N and S of the equator, as in the Amazon basin, the Congo basin and Indonesia. It has temperatures of 25-27 degrees C with a very low annual range, and rainfall of 150-250 cm or more spread through the year, mostly convectional in the afternoon. Natural vegetation is tropical evergreen rainforest. The ITCZ (doldrums) dominates, with light, variable winds.

Mediterranean climate occurs on the western margins of continents between about 30 and 45 degrees latitude: the Mediterranean basin, California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa and southwest and south Australia. Summers are hot and dry under subtropical high pressure, and winters are mild and rainy from westerlies and cyclones. Vegetation is evergreen, drought-resistant scrub and woodland, and the region is known for citrus, grapes and olives.

Monsoon climate is found in South and Southeast Asia, northern Australia and parts of East Africa and West Africa. It has distinct wet and dry seasons, with rain mostly in summer. India receives about 75% of its rainfall from the southwest monsoon, which arrives in Kerala around 1 June, and retreats from October. The winter northeast monsoon brings rain to Tamil Nadu. The monsoon is the unifying bond of the Indian economy.

'All of the above climates' would be right only if all three had seasonal wind reversal. Only monsoon climate does. The option works as a distractor because equatorial and Mediterranean climates both show some seasonality in the weather, namely wind belt shifts and rainfall regimes, which students may confuse with reversal.
related: Monsoon comes from the Arabic word 'mausim', meaning season.
The southwest monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by about 8 July.
The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) develops over peninsular India in summer and is linked to monsoon strength.
El Nino generally weakens the Indian summer monsoon, while a positive Indian Ocean Dipole generally strengthens it.
The Mediterranean climate has dry summers and wet winters.
The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is also called the monsoon trough over the Gangetic plain in summer.
Tamil Nadu gets most of its rain from the retreating (northeast) monsoon in October-December.
Koppen's 'Am' and 'Aw' types describe monsoon and savanna climates.
summary: The answer is (c) Monsoon climate. The defining feature of monsoon climate is the seasonal reversal of wind direction, with the southwest monsoon blowing onshore in summer and the northeast monsoon blowing offshore in winter. This reversal results from differential heating of land and sea and the seasonal shift of the ITCZ.
topic_notes: Monsoon winds are planetary-scale seasonal winds that reverse direction between summer and winter. They are strongest in South Asia but also occur in East Asia, Northern Australia and West Africa. The classical theory explains the monsoon by differential heating of land and sea. The modern view stresses the seasonal migration of the ITCZ, which moves to the Gangetic plain in July and is then called the monsoon trough. Other factors include the Tibetan Plateau heating up, the Tropical Easterly Jet over peninsular India, the Somali jet (the Findlater jet), the Southern Oscillation, ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole. El Nino usually weakens the Indian monsoon, while La Nina and a positive IOD usually favour it. The Indian monsoon has two branches: the Arabian Sea branch, which gives heavy rain on the Western Ghats windward side, and the Bay of Bengal branch, which gives heavy rain in the northeast and the Gangetic plain. The break in the monsoon happens when the monsoon trough shifts toward the Himalayas. The retreating monsoon in October-November brings clear skies, 'October heat', and cyclones in the Bay of Bengal. India Meteorological Department (IMD) issues forecasts, with long-range forecasts in April and June. Other climate types UPSC asks about include tropical savanna (Sudan type), temperate (British type), steppe, taiga and tundra, with the Koppen classification as the standard scheme. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya get the highest rainfall because of funnelling of moist winds.
