At this scale, materials show novel optical, electrical, magnetic and catalytic properties because of quantum effects and a huge surface-area-to-volume ratio. Common engineered nanomaterials: nano-silver (antimicrobial), TiO2 and ZnO (sunscreens, paints, self-cleaning glass), carbon nanotubes and graphene (electronics, composites), fullerenes (C60), quantum dots, nano-clay (packaging), nano-iron (groundwater remediation) and gold nanoparticles (diagnostics, drug delivery). Benefits include targeted drug delivery, water purification, efficient solar cells, stronger lightweight materials, and fortified or preserved food. Risks: persistence and accumulation in the environment, entry into food chains, ability to cross biological barriers (lungs, skin, gut, blood-brain barrier), generation of reactive oxygen species leading to oxidative stress, inflammation, genotoxicity and possible carcinogenicity, and occupational inhalation hazards. Ecotoxicity affects algae, soil microbes, fish and invertebrates. Governance: India's Nano Mission was launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology; it supports research, infrastructure and human resource development, including nano-safety studies. The Bureau of Indian Standards has set up nanotechnology standards committees, and FSSAI and CDSCO have issued guidance on nanomaterials in food and drugs. Internationally, the OECD Working Party on Manufactured Nanomaterials, ISO TC 229 and the EU REACH regulation (with nano-specific provisions) cover safety. Related UPSC angles: applications of nanotechnology (drug delivery, water purification, agriculture), nanomaterials in cosmetics, differences between nano and micro scales, the properties of graphene, and the precautionary principle in environmental governance.

question: Which of the following organizations brings out the publication known as World Economic Outlook’?
subject: Economy
detail: The World Economic Outlook is produced by the IMF's Research Department and analyses global growth, inflation, trade, fiscal and external balances, commodity prices and risks, with growth forecasts for advanced, emerging and developing economies and for individual countries. It is released around the Spring Meetings (April) and the Annual Meetings (October) of the IMF and World Bank, with interim WEO Updates typically in January and July. The IMF, headquartered in Washington DC, was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and began operations in 1945; it has 190 members, and India is a founding member. Its mandate covers monetary cooperation, financial stability, trade facilitation, high employment and poverty reduction. Elimination logic: UNDP publishes the Human Development Report; the World Economic Forum (Geneva/Davos) publishes the Global Competitiveness Report, Global Risks Report, Global Gender Gap Report and Energy Transition Index; the World Bank publishes the World Development Report, Global Economic Prospects, Doing Business (discontinued 2021) and Ease-of-doing-business style data. A common trap is confusing WEO with the World Bank's Global Economic Prospects, which is a similar-sounding but separate report.
explanations: Correct: the WEO is the IMF's flagship biannual report on the global economy, with updates in January and July.
Incorrect: UNDP publishes the Human Development Report (HDI) and the Multidimensional Poverty Index (with OPHI), not the WEO.
Incorrect: the WEF publishes the Global Risks Report, Global Gender Gap Report, Travel and Tourism Development Index and formerly the Global Competitiveness Report, not the WEO.
Incorrect: the World Bank publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects; the WEO is an IMF product.
keyfact: World Economic Outlook = IMF (April and October, with January and July updates); Human Development Report = UNDP; World Development Report = World Bank.
option_notes: The IMF is a Bretton Woods institution, set up in 1944 and operational from 1945, headquartered in Washington DC with 190 members. It provides surveillance (Article IV consultations), lending (Stand-By Arrangements, Extended Fund Facility) and technical assistance. Its quota system determines votes and contributions. Its unit of account is the Special Drawing Right (SDR). Publications include the WEO, Global Financial Stability Report, Fiscal Monitor and External Sector Report. Managing Director: Kristalina Georgieva (since 2019).

UNDP is the UN's global development network, established in 1965 and headquartered in New York. It works on poverty eradication, governance, climate and resilience. It publishes the annual Human Development Report, which ranks countries by the Human Development Index (life expectancy, education, per capita GNI), conceptualised by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen in 1990. It also reports on the Multidimensional Poverty Index with OPHI.

The WEF is an international non-profit based in Geneva, Switzerland, founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab as the European Management Forum. It is known for its annual meeting at Davos in January. Reports include the Global Risks Report, Global Gender Gap Index, Travel and Tourism Development Index, Energy Transition Index and the Future of Jobs Report. It was formerly known for the Global Competitiveness Report.

The World Bank (IBRD plus IDA, together the World Bank; with IFC, MIGA and ICSID forming the World Bank Group) was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington DC. It lends for development and poverty reduction. Its publications include the World Development Report, Global Economic Prospects (January and June), International Debt Statistics and formerly Doing Business, discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities.
related: IMF and World Bank were both created at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944.
IMF's Global Financial Stability Report is also published twice a year, in April and October.
World Bank's Global Economic Prospects is released in January and June.
UNDP publishes the Human Development Report; the Human Development Index was introduced in 1990.
WEF publishes the Global Gender Gap Report; the WEF is based in Geneva.
UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report.
Global Hunger Index is published by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe.
The IMF's unit of account is the Special Drawing Right (SDR).
summary: The answer is (a) The International Monetary Fund. World Economic Outlook (WEO) is the IMF's flagship survey of global economic prospects, published twice a year (April and October), with updates in January and July.
topic_notes: International organisations and their flagship reports are a staple of UPSC prelims, and the question types are usually direct 'which body publishes this report' matches. IMF: Bretton Woods institution; flagship reports are World Economic Outlook (April, October), Global Financial Stability Report, Fiscal Monitor, and the External Sector Report. It uses quotas and SDRs; the SDR basket currently has five currencies: US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling (renminbi added in 2016). India's quota is around 2.75 percent. World Bank: World Development Report (annual), Global Economic Prospects, Ease of Doing Business (discontinued), Logistics Performance Index, Human Capital Index, Worldwide Governance Indicators, and the Remittance (Migration and Development Brief). UNDP: Human Development Report and the Multidimensional Poverty Index. WEF: Global Risks Report, Global Gender Gap Report, Future of Jobs, Energy Transition Index, Travel and Tourism Development Index. Other frequently asked: UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report and Trade and Development Report; FAO publishes the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) and State of the World's Forests; UNEP publishes the Emissions Gap Report; WTO publishes World Trade Statistical Review; Transparency International publishes the Corruption Perceptions Index; IFPRI publishes the Global Hunger Index (with Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe); ILO publishes the World Employment and Social Outlook; OECD publishes PISA; UNESCO publishes the Global Education Monitoring Report; WIPO publishes the Global Innovation Index. Tip: associate each organisation with its mandate to eliminate quickly.

question:
With reference to Union Budget, which of the following is/are covered under Non-Plan Expenditure?
1. Defence expenditure
2. Interest payments
3. Salaries and pensions
4. Subsidies Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Until the 2017-18 Budget, the Union Budget divided expenditure into Plan and Non-Plan. Plan Expenditure financed the programmes and projects of the Five Year Plans, i.e. central assistance to state and UT plans and central plan schemes. Non-Plan Expenditure was everything else: the recurring, committed liabilities needed to keep the government running. Its main heads were interest payments (usually the largest single item), defence, subsidies (food, fertiliser, petroleum), salaries, pensions, police, economic services, grants to states and UTs, and loans to public enterprises and states. Because all four items listed in the question fall under these heads, option (c) is correct. Elimination: (a) is wrong because defence is only one of the heads. (b) wrongly leaves out defence and subsidies. (d) is impossible because at least one item is plainly Non-Plan. Note that the Plan/Non-Plan distinction was abolished from 2017-18 on the recommendation of the Rangarajan Committee (2011) and the Kelkar approach, and replaced by Revenue and Capital expenditure. The 12th Plan (2012-17) was the last Five Year Plan, and NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015.
explanations: (a) is wrong: defence is Non-Plan, but it is not the only item. Interest, salaries, pensions and subsidies are also Non-Plan.
(b) is wrong: interest, salaries and pensions are Non-Plan, but the option wrongly excludes defence and subsidies, which are also Non-Plan.
(c) is correct: all four items (defence, interest payments, salaries and pensions, subsidies) were Non-Plan expenditure heads.
(d) is wrong: it says none of the items is Non-Plan, but every one of them was a standard Non-Plan head.
keyfact: Until 2016-17, defence, interest, salaries, pensions and subsidies were all Non-Plan expenditure; from 2017-18 the Plan/Non-Plan split was replaced by Revenue/Capital.
option_notes: Defence expenditure only: defence is a major Non-Plan head, covering pay, allowances, stores, maintenance and capital acquisitions of the Army, Navy and Air Force. It is a committed obligation under the Union List (Entry 1, Seventh Schedule). It is the largest or second-largest central expenditure item along with interest. Defence pensions are budgeted separately. As an option, 'defence only' is incomplete because other committed items are also Non-Plan.

Interest payments, salaries and pensions: these were all Non-Plan, being committed obligations that recur every year. Interest on public debt is charged to the Consolidated Fund under Article 112(3), so it is not voted. Salaries and pensions arise from service conditions and Pay Commission awards. The 7th Pay Commission took effect on 1 January 2016. The option is incomplete because it omits defence and subsidies.

All four items: defence, interest, salaries and pensions, and subsidies are all Non-Plan expenditure. Non-Plan spending is the ongoing, obligatory expenditure not tied to the Five Year Plan. It was divided into revenue and capital components. The Plan/Non-Plan classification was dropped from the 2017-18 Budget, which moved to a revenue versus capital classification. This is the official answer.

None: this would mean no listed item is Non-Plan, which is false. It could only be right if all items were Plan expenditure, which finances developmental schemes under Five Year Plans (central sector schemes, centrally sponsored schemes and central assistance to states). The last Five Year Plan was the 12th (2012-17). The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
related: The Plan/Non-Plan classification was abolished from the 2017-18 Budget.
The Rangarajan Committee (2011) recommended scrapping the Plan/Non-Plan distinction.
Interest payments were usually the largest Non-Plan item.
The Union Budget is presented under Article 112 as the 'Annual Financial Statement'.
Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund is not voted by Parliament, e.g. salary of the President and debt charges.
Revenue expenditure creates no assets, while capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities.
The Railway Budget was merged with the General Budget from 2017-18.
Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
statements: 1 — Correct: Defence expenditure was Non-Plan. Defence revenue spending (pay, allowances, maintenance, stores) was classed as Non-Plan, and defence capital outlay (acquisitions) was also treated as Non-Plan. It is a committed national-security obligation, not a Plan scheme. It has been among the largest items of the Union Budget, alongside interest payments. After 2017-18 it is shown under revenue and capital expenditure of the Ministry of Defence.

2 — Correct: Interest payments were Non-Plan. These are the interest on the government's past borrowings (market loans, small savings, provident funds, external debt). It is a legally binding charge and was usually the single largest Non-Plan item, often around 35-40 percent of the total. Interest is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 112(3) and is not voted by Parliament. It is a key component of the revenue deficit and a determinant of the primary deficit (fiscal deficit minus interest payments).

3 — Correct: Salaries and pensions were Non-Plan. Pay and allowances of central government employees, along with pension liabilities (including defence pensions), were routine administrative commitments classed as Non-Plan revenue expenditure. The Pay Commissions (7th, chaired by Justice A. K. Mathur, reported in 2015, effective 1 January 2016) drive these costs. The 8th Pay Commission was announced in 2025. The New Pension System (now NPS) covers those who joined from 2004, and the Unified Pension Scheme was announced in 2024.

4 — Correct: Subsidies were Non-Plan. Major subsidies are food (under the National Food Security Act 2013, run by FCI), fertiliser and petroleum (LPG), and are classed as Non-Plan revenue expenditure. They are demand-driven or price-driven commitments, not Plan schemes. Subsidies are a revenue expenditure that creates no assets. Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT, started 2013) and the PAHAL scheme (2015) aim to reduce leakages and improve targeting.
summary: The answer is (c): all four items, namely defence expenditure, interest payments, salaries and pensions, and subsidies, were classified as Non-Plan Expenditure in the Union Budget. Non-Plan Expenditure covered the routine, committed and obligatory spending of the government that was not part of Five Year Plan allocations.
topic_notes:
Before 2017-18 the Union Budget classified expenditure as Plan and Non-Plan, and also as Revenue and Capital. Plan expenditure financed the Five Year Plan programmes. It had two parts: Central Plan (Ministries' schemes and public sector enterprises' budgetary support) and Central assistance to State and UT Plans. Non-Plan expenditure was the remainder: committed, routine spending to run government and meet past obligations. Its main heads were interest payments, defence, subsidies, salaries, pensions, police, general and economic services, and grants and loans to states and UTs. Interest payments were usually the biggest item. The Non-Plan share was typically larger than the Plan share.

Reform: the Rangarajan Committee (2011) recommended doing away with the distinction because it created a bias in which Plan spending was equated with development and Non-Plan with wasteful spending, and it hindered outcome-based budgeting. The government implemented this from the 2017-18 Budget. Expenditure is now presented as Revenue and Capital. Revenue expenditure does not create assets (salaries, interest, subsidies, grants). Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities (infrastructure, loans, repayment of debt).

Other angles: the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266) receives all revenues and loans. Charged expenditure (for example the salaries of the President, Judges and CAG, and debt charges) is not voted (Article 112(3)). The Contingency Fund (Article 267) allows urgent advances. The Public Account holds funds such as provident funds. Budget is laid under Article 112, and the Appropriation Bill is covered by Article 114. Deficits: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. The FRBM Act 2003 set deficit targets, and the N. K. Singh Committee (2017) reviewed it. The Union Budget is presented by the Finance Minister, and since 2017 it has been presented on 1 February and merged with the Railway Budget.

ocr: ‘Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana’ has been launched for {a} providing housing’ loan to poor people at cheaper interest rates (b} promoting women’s Self-Help Groups in backward areas (¢) promoting financial inclusion in the country (dj providing financial help to the marginalized communities
subject: Economy
detail: PMJDY was announced by PM Narendra Modi in his Independence Day speech on 15 August 2014 and launched on 28 August 2014. It is described as a National Mission for Financial Inclusion and aims at universal access to banking facilities, with at least one basic bank account for every household. It also covers financial literacy, access to credit, insurance and pension. Accounts are zero-balance basic savings bank accounts. Key features: a RuPay debit card with an inbuilt accident insurance cover (Rs 1 lakh, later raised to Rs 2 lakh for accounts opened after 28 Aug 2018), an overdraft facility (initially Rs 5,000, raised to Rs 10,000), direct benefit transfer (DBT) linkage, and access to micro-insurance and pension products such as APY. It follows a 'banking the unbanked' approach, using Business Correspondents and mobile banking. Elimination logic: (a) housing loans relate to schemes like PMAY; (b) women's SHGs relate to DAY-NRLM; (d) is too narrow because PMJDY covers all households, not only marginalised communities. Option (c) is the broad, correct description.
explanations: Wrong: providing cheap housing loans is the domain of schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (credit-linked subsidy), not PMJDY.
Wrong: promoting women's Self-Help Groups in backward areas is the aim of the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), not PMJDY.
Correct: PMJDY is the National Mission on Financial Inclusion, giving universal access to banking, credit, insurance and pension.
Wrong as the best answer: although the poor and marginalised benefit, PMJDY is aimed at all unbanked households, so this is too narrow. The official answer is (c).
keyfact: PMJDY (28 Aug 2014) = National Mission on Financial Inclusion: universal banking access with zero-balance accounts, RuPay card, overdraft, insurance and pension.
option_notes: Housing loans for the poor: the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY), launched in 2015, provides 'Housing for All'. Its Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS) gives an interest subsidy on home loans to EWS, LIG and MIG households. It has Urban (PMAY-U) and Gramin (PMAY-G) components. PMAY-G replaced the Indira Awaas Yojana in 2016. The National Housing Bank and HUDCO are linked institutions in housing finance.

Women's SHGs: the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) was launched in 2011 as Aajeevika, under the Ministry of Rural Development. It mobilises rural poor women into SHGs and links them to bank credit. The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was started by NABARD in 1992. NULM is the urban counterpart. The World Bank supports NRLM.

Financial inclusion is the delivery of banking and financial services at an affordable cost to all sections of society, especially the weak and low-income. PMJDY, launched 28 August 2014, is its flagship mission. Earlier steps included the Swabhimaan campaign (2011), no-frills accounts and Business Correspondents. The Rangarajan Committee (2008) and the Nachiket Mor Committee (2014) dealt with financial inclusion. RBI and NABARD promote it, and the Financial Inclusion Index was introduced in 2021.

Financial help to marginalised communities is delivered by many schemes: Stand-Up India (2016) gives loans to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs; Post-Matric and Pre-Matric Scholarships serve SC/ST/OBC students; NSFDC and NSKFDC provide concessional finance; and the Mudra Yojana (2015) gives collateral-free loans up to Rs 10 lakh to micro enterprises. These are targeted schemes, unlike PMJDY, which is universal.
related: PMJDY was launched on 28 August 2014; it was announced on 15 August 2014.
PMJDY is the National Mission on Financial Inclusion under the Department of Financial Services.
JAM trinity means Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile, which powers DBT.
PMJDY accounts get a RuPay debit card with accident insurance cover (Rs 2 lakh for accounts opened after 28 Aug 2018).
PMJDY overdraft facility was raised from Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000.
Atal Pension Yojana, PMSBY and PMJJBY were launched in 2015 and are linked to bank accounts.
PM Mudra Yojana (2015) offers loans up to Rs 10 lakh to micro enterprises under Shishu, Kishor and Tarun categories.
India Post Payments Bank was launched in 2018 to extend banking to remote areas.
summary: The answer is (c). Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) is the National Mission on Financial Inclusion, launched to give every household access to banking, credit, insurance and pension services.
topic_notes: PMJDY was launched on 28 August 2014 by the Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance. It was announced on 15 August 2014. It was a mission with six pillars: universal access to banking facilities; basic bank accounts with an overdraft facility and RuPay debit card; financial literacy; a credit guarantee fund; insurance; and pension for the unorganised sector. The first phase ran from 2014 to 2015 and the second from 2015 to 2018, and the scheme was extended beyond 2018 with a shift from 'every household' to 'every adult'. A Guinness World Record was set for the most bank accounts opened in one week (over 18 million accounts in the launch week). Account benefits: zero-balance account, RuPay card with accident insurance of Rs 1 lakh (Rs 2 lakh for accounts opened after 28 August 2018), overdraft up to Rs 10,000 (a limit of Rs 2,000 is allowed without conditions), eligibility for DBT, PM Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY), Atal Pension Yojana (APY) and Mudra loans. Aadhaar and mobile linkage gave rise to the 'JAM trinity' (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile), which drives DBT and reduces leakages. Over 50 crore accounts have been opened, with a majority held in public sector banks and more than half held by women. Related institutions: RBI (Financial Inclusion Index, FI-Index from 2021), NABARD (SHG-Bank Linkage), NPCI (RuPay and UPI), India Post Payments Bank (2018), small finance banks and payments banks. Possible angles: the JAM trinity, differences between PMJDY and Mudra, the SHG programme, and the Rangarajan and Nachiket Mor committees.

question: With reference to the Fourteenth Finance Commission, which of the following statements is/are correct? L It has increased the share of States in the central divisible pool from 32 percent to 42 percent. It has made recommendations concerning sector-specific grants. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Polity
detail: The Fourteenth Finance Commission was constituted in January 2013 under Dr Y.V. Reddy under Article 280 of the Constitution. It submitted its report in December 2014, and it covered 2015-16 to 2019-20. Its landmark recommendation was to increase the States' share of the divisible pool of central taxes from 32% (set by the 13th FC) to 42%. The aim was to expand fiscal autonomy by giving States more untied funds and so reduce dependence on centrally sponsored schemes. Because of this philosophy, the Commission deliberately did not recommend sector-specific grants, which were a feature of the 13th FC and tied States to centrally set priorities. Its grants were confined to revenue deficit grants, grants to local bodies (panchayats and municipalities) and a disaster relief grant. Elimination logic: statement 1 is a well-known headline fact and is correct. Statement 2 contradicts the Commission's untied-funds approach, so it is incorrect. That rules out (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is accurate, since the 14th FC raised the States' share from 32% to 42%, and statement 2 is wrong, so only statement 1 holds.
Incorrect: statement 2 is false. The 14th FC avoided sector-specific grants and favoured untied transfers.
Incorrect: although statement 1 is right, statement 2 is wrong, so the two cannot both be correct.
Incorrect: statement 1 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: 14th Finance Commission (Y.V. Reddy): States' share raised from 32% to 42%, with no sector-specific grants.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: the 14th FC (chair: Y.V. Reddy; report December 2014; period 2015-20) increased the States' share of the divisible pool to 42%, from 32%. This was the biggest jump in devolution ever. It was meant to promote fiscal federalism and States' autonomy, and the Centre accepted it. The Commission also recommended grants for local bodies and disaster relief, and revenue deficit grants for some States.

Option (b), statement 2 only: this would mean the 14th FC recommended sector-specific grants, which is false. Sector-specific grants were a feature of the 13th FC (chair: Vijay Kelkar, 2010-15). They were used to link transfers to areas such as elementary education, health, roads and the environment. The 14th FC moved away from this approach and chose untied devolution, which made this option wrong.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this is wrong because statement 2 is false. The 14th FC's recommended transfers were mostly untied tax devolution, supplemented by revenue deficit grants, local body grants and disaster relief. Students sometimes confuse the 13th and 14th FC features, which is why UPSC tests such differences. The 14th FC also suggested that the Centre and States stay within fiscal deficit targets of 3% of GDP.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong because statement 1 is accurate. The 42% devolution is the most quoted fact about the 14th FC. After this, the Centre's own share in taxes fell, and it changed the funding patterns of centrally sponsored schemes, with States bearing more of the cost. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in January 2015, around the same time that these recommendations came into force.
related: Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, which is constituted every five years.
14th FC: chairman Y.V. Reddy, with a report period of 2015-16 to 2019-20.
13th FC (Vijay Kelkar) recommended a 32% share for States.
15th FC (N.K. Singh) recommended 41% for 2021-26, after adjusting for J&K and Ladakh.
The 16th FC is chaired by Arvind Panagariya.
Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
Article 275 deals with statutory grants-in-aid to States.
The First Finance Commission (1951) was chaired by K.C. Neogy.
statements: 1 — Correct: The 14th FC raised the States' share in the divisible pool from 32% to 42%, the largest increase ever recommended by any Finance Commission. The 13th FC (chair: Vijay Kelkar) had recommended 32% for 2010-15. The 14th FC argued that States should have more untied funds to plan according to local needs. The Centre accepted the recommendation, and it took effect from 2015-16. The share is distributed among States by a formula that uses population (1971 and 2011), income distance, area, forest cover and demographic change. The 15th FC later set it at 41% for 2020-21 after Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory, with 1% reserved for J&K and Ladakh, and kept 41% for 2021-26.

2 — Incorrect: The 14th FC did not recommend sector-specific grants. It recommended revenue deficit grants for 11 States, grants to local bodies and a disaster relief grant. The 13th FC had recommended sector-specific grants for education, health, roads and bridges and the like, but the 14th FC's philosophy was to tilt towards untied transfers. It argued that sector-specific interventions should be handled by the Centre through its own resources and by the Planning Commission's successor processes. The Centre then restructured centrally sponsored schemes, leaving States to find more of their own funding. The 15th FC reintroduced some performance-based and sector-specific grants, for example for health, school education and agriculture reforms.
summary: The correct answer is (a): statement 1 only. The Fourteenth Finance Commission (chair: Y.V. Reddy) raised the States' share in the central divisible pool of taxes from 32% to 42%. It did not recommend sector-specific grants, because it moved towards untied devolution and kept grants limited.
topic_notes: Finance Commission: a quasi-judicial constitutional body under Article 280, appointed by the President every five years (or earlier) to recommend the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and States and among States. It also recommends the principles that govern grants-in-aid under Article 275 and the measures to augment State funds to supplement local bodies' resources. It consists of a chairman and four other members. The First FC was set up in 1951 under K.C. Neogy. The 14th FC (Y.V. Reddy) covered 2015-20, and the 15th FC (N.K. Singh) covered 2021-26 and recommended 41% devolution. The 16th FC is under Arvind Panagariya. Key 14th FC points: 42% devolution; weights in the formula were population (1971) 17.5%, demographic change (2011) 10%, income distance 50%, area 15% and forest cover 7.5%; it recommended grants to panchayats and municipalities, and a disaster relief grant (replacing the earlier National Calamity Contingency Fund approach); and it urged a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP. It advised that the Centre rethink centrally sponsored schemes and suggested the GST council design. The 13th FC (Kelkar) gave 32% and sector-specific grants. The 12th FC (C. Rangarajan) gave 30.5%, and the 11th FC (A.M. Khusro) gave 29.5% (in a 29.5-30.5 range). The FC's recommendations are advisory, and the Centre lays the report before Parliament with an explanatory Action Taken memorandum. The Finance Commission differs from the Planning Commission, which was non-constitutional and was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. The GST Council is under Article 279A. Likely future angles: the terms of reference of the 15th FC, the use of the 2011 census, and the demands of southern States.

question: The Fortaleza Declaration’, recently in the news, is related to the affairs of
subject: Economy
detail: The Fortaleza Declaration was issued at the 6th BRICS Summit at Fortaleza (with the Brasília leg), Brazil, on 15-16 July 2014, under the theme 'Inclusive Growth: Sustainable Solutions'. Its headline outcomes were the signing of the Agreement establishing the New Development Bank, with initial subscribed capital of $50 billion and authorised capital of $100 billion, and the Treaty for the BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement with an initial size of $100 billion. The NDB has its headquarters in Shanghai, and its first president was K.V. Kamath of India. The leaders also called for IMF quota reform and for a reformed UN Security Council. Elimination logic: ASEAN's documents are usually named after places such as Bali, Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur and relate to Southeast Asia. The OECD works through recommendations and guidelines, not summit declarations of this type. The WTO's ministerial outcomes carry names like Doha, Bali and Nairobi. A Brazilian city name together with 2014 and a bank for emerging economies points to BRICS.
explanations: Incorrect: ASEAN summits produce declarations tied to Southeast Asian cities and have no link to Fortaleza.
Correct: The Fortaleza Declaration came out of the 6th BRICS Summit in Brazil in July 2014 and led to the NDB and CRA.
Incorrect: The OECD is a Paris-based grouping of mostly developed economies and does not issue leader summit declarations of this kind.
Incorrect: The WTO's outcomes come from Ministerial Conferences (Doha, Bali, Nairobi), not from Fortaleza.
keyfact: Fortaleza Declaration (July 2014, Brazil) = 6th BRICS Summit, which created the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement.
option_notes: ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, was founded on 8 August 1967 through the Bangkok Declaration. Its Secretariat is in Jakarta. It has 10 members, and Timor-Leste was admitted as the 11th member in 2025. Its charter came into force in 2008. It is built on consensus and non-interference. Related forums include the ARF, the East Asia Summit and RCEP.

BRICS is a grouping of emerging economies. The term BRIC was coined by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs in 2001. South Africa joined in 2010, which made it BRICS. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined in 2024, and Indonesia joined in 2025. It has no secretariat or charter. The chair rotates every year. Its institutions are the New Development Bank (Shanghai) and the CRA.

The OECD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is headquartered in Paris. It evolved from the OEEC, which administered the Marshall Plan, and was formed in 1961. It has about 38 members. It publishes the PISA tests and the Economic Outlook, and works on tax standards such as BEPS. India is not a member but is a key partner.

The WTO was established on 1 January 1995 as the successor to GATT (1947), following the Uruguay Round. It is headquartered in Geneva and has about 166 members. Its decision-making body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets every two years. It runs a Dispute Settlement Body. Key agreements include TRIPS, GATS, the Agreement on Agriculture and the Trade Facilitation Agreement, which was concluded at Bali in 2013.
related: 6th BRICS Summit: Fortaleza, Brazil, July 2014.
New Development Bank is headquartered in Shanghai; its initial authorised capital is $100 billion.
CRA initial size is $100 billion, to counter balance-of-payments problems.
K.V. Kamath of India was the first NDB president.
The term BRIC was coined by Jim O'Neill in 2001.
South Africa joined BRICS in 2010.
India hosted the 8th BRICS Summit at Goa in 2016.
Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined BRICS in 2024.
summary: The answer is (b) BRICS. The Fortaleza Declaration was adopted at the 6th BRICS Summit held in Fortaleza, Brazil, in July 2014, where the leaders also signed the agreement establishing the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA).
topic_notes: BRICS began as BRIC in 2001, a term coined by Jim O'Neill. The first formal summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. South Africa joined in December 2010 and attended the 2011 Sanya summit. The Fortaleza (Brazil) summit of 2014 was the 6th and the first of the second cycle. It created the New Development Bank, headquartered in Shanghai, with equal voting shares for its founding members and a regional office in Johannesburg. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement is a $100 billion financial safety net against balance-of-payments pressures, with China contributing $41 billion, Brazil, India and Russia $18 billion each, and South Africa $5 billion. Later summits include Ufa 2015, Goa 2016 (8th), Xiamen 2017, Johannesburg 2018, Brasília 2019, Russia 2020 (virtual), India 2021 (virtual), China 2022 (virtual), Johannesburg 2023 (15th, where expansion was agreed), Kazan 2024 (16th) and Brazil 2025 (17th). India hosted the 2016 Goa summit and the 2021 virtual summit. BRICS decisions are taken by consensus. Other angles UPSC may ask include the BRICS Youth Summit, the NDB's membership expansion to Bangladesh, the UAE and Egypt, the Kamath presidency followed by Marcos Troyjo and then Dilma Rousseff, BRICS Pay and local-currency trade debates, and the BRICS Business Council. Compare with other groupings such as IBSA (Brasília Declaration, 2003), SCO, G20 and the Quad.

ocr: A decrease in tax to GDP ratio of a country indicates which of the following? 1. Slowing economic growth rate 2. Less equitable distribution of national income B-AQN-O-JUA/63A, Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (ce) Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The tax-to-GDP ratio is total tax revenue (Centre plus States, sometimes only the Centre) divided by nominal GDP. It measures the share of national output that the government captures as taxes and indicates fiscal capacity. When the ratio falls, tax collections are growing more slowly than GDP. Typical causes are a slowdown in output, profits and consumption, lower tax buoyancy, rate cuts or exemptions, weak compliance or higher evasion. Of these, a slowing economy is the cause the question points to, which makes Statement 1 acceptable as an indication. Equity of income distribution depends on the progressivity of the tax structure (direct versus indirect taxes), on the Gini coefficient and on the incidence of taxes. The ratio is an aggregate and says nothing about who pays. A country can have a falling ratio and a more equal distribution, or the reverse. A decline may even come from cutting regressive indirect taxes, which would improve equity. The statement therefore draws an unwarranted inference. Eliminating it leaves only (a). In India the Centre's gross tax-to-GDP ratio has been roughly 10-12 percent, and the general government figure roughly 16-18 percent, which is low compared with OECD economies at around 34 percent.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is a valid inference from a lower tax-to-GDP ratio, and Statement 2 is not, which matches the official answer.
Wrong. Statement 2 is not a valid inference, because the ratio does not measure income distribution.
Wrong. This would require Statement 2 to be valid, but the ratio gives no information about equity of distribution.
Wrong. Statement 1 is a reasonable indication, since slower growth, weaker buoyancy or poorer compliance lowers the ratio, so 'neither' is incorrect.
keyfact: Tax-to-GDP ratio shows fiscal capacity and tax buoyancy, not income distribution; a falling ratio hints at slower growth, not at inequity.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', means that only the slowing-growth inference is valid. This is the official answer. The tax-to-GDP ratio is tax revenue as a share of GDP and is a standard gauge of fiscal capacity. Low ratios restrict public spending on health, education and infrastructure. India's ratio is lower than the OECD average and below that of many emerging peers. Governments raise it by broadening the tax base, improving compliance, using technology and formalising the economy.

Option (b), '2 only', would hold if the ratio revealed distributional equity. It does not. Income inequality is measured with the Gini coefficient (0 is perfect equality, 1 is perfect inequality), the Lorenz curve, and the Palma and Theil indices. Redistribution works through progressive direct taxes and transfers. In India, indirect taxes form roughly half or more of Centre tax revenue, so the system is only mildly progressive. Wealth inequality data come from sources such as the World Inequality Database.

Option (c), 'both 1 and 2', would require both inferences to be valid. Only the first is. Combined statements of this kind are common traps in UPSC economics questions, where an unrelated consequence is attached to a true statement. Always check whether each claim follows directly from the indicator in question.

Option (d), 'neither 1 nor 2', would mean the ratio tells nothing about growth. In fact the ratio is linked to growth through tax buoyancy. Tax buoyancy is the responsiveness of tax revenue to GDP changes, whereas tax elasticity adjusts for discretionary changes. A buoyancy above 1 raises the ratio, and a buoyancy below 1 lowers it. Both concepts are asked about in UPSC prelims from time to time.
related: Tax-to-GDP ratio = total tax revenue divided by GDP, an indicator of fiscal capacity.
Tax buoyancy = percentage change in tax revenue divided by percentage change in GDP.
GST began on 1 July 2017 after the 101st Constitutional Amendment; GST Council is under Article 279A.
Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, constituted every five years.
The Gini coefficient measures inequality, from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).
The Laffer curve shows that beyond a point, raising tax rates reduces revenue.
Agricultural income is exempt from central income tax in India and is a State subject.
The FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 to bring fiscal discipline.
statements: 1 — Correct: A falling tax-to-GDP ratio commonly indicates that tax revenue is growing slower than output, which often goes with an economic slowdown, weaker profits and consumption, or poorer compliance. Tax buoyancy is the percentage change in tax revenue for a 1 percent change in GDP, and it falls when growth slows. India's Centre gross tax revenue was about 11 percent of GDP in 2007-08, fell to about 9.9 percent by 2020-21 after the 2008 crisis and the pandemic, and later recovered to above 11 percent. GST was introduced on 1 July 2017 to widen the base. The Tax Administration Reform Commission and the Kelkar Committee have dealt with improving the ratio.

2 — Incorrect: The ratio is an aggregate of revenue to output and carries no information on how income is distributed. Distribution is measured by indicators such as the Gini coefficient, Lorenz curve, Palma ratio and income shares of deciles. Equity of taxation depends on the mix of direct taxes (income, corporate; progressive) and indirect taxes (GST, excise, customs; often regressive). A fall in the ratio could come from cutting regressive indirect taxes, which improves equity, or from cutting top-bracket rates, which worsens it. The Lorenz curve was developed by Max Lorenz in 1905 and the Gini coefficient by Corrado Gini in 1912. India's Gini on consumption is about 0.35.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. A falling tax-to-GDP ratio usually reflects slower economic activity, lower buoyancy of tax revenue or more evasion and exemptions, so Statement 1 holds. It does not by itself show how national income is distributed, so Statement 2 cannot be inferred.
topic_notes: The tax-to-GDP ratio is tax revenue divided by GDP, and it is the main indicator of how much of the economy the state mobilises through taxation. It can be computed for the Centre alone or for the general government (Centre plus States). India's Centre gross tax-to-GDP has been about 10-12 percent in recent decades, and the combined figure is about 16-18 percent, below the OECD average of about 34 percent. Reasons for a low ratio include a large informal sector, a narrow personal income tax base, agricultural income being exempt from central tax (it is a State subject), many exemptions and evasion. Tax buoyancy measures the responsiveness of tax revenue to GDP growth. India's tax structure comprises direct taxes (personal income tax, corporate tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise on petroleum). GST was launched on 1 July 2017 after the 101st Constitutional Amendment, with the GST Council under Article 279A. Key reform bodies include the Kelkar Task Force on Direct and Indirect Taxes (2002), the Shome Committee on GAAR and the Tax Administration Reform Commission (2014). A ratio can fall because of a slowdown, tax cuts (for example the 2019 corporate tax cut to 22 percent), or higher compliance costs and evasion. Related UPSC themes include the Laffer curve (higher tax rates beyond a point reduce revenue), the fiscal deficit target under the FRBM Act 2003, progressive versus regressive taxes, Article 265 (no tax without the authority of law), Article 270 (distribution of taxes between the Centre and States) and the Finance Commission under Article 280. Revenue receipts include tax and non-tax revenue, and capital receipts include borrowings and disinvestment. The Gini coefficient and the Lorenz curve are used to measure inequality, and they are separate from fiscal indicators.

question: In the South Atlantic and South-Eastem Pacific regions in tropical latitudes, cyclone does not originate. What is the reason?
options: Absence of land in those regions
subject: Geography
detail: Tropical cyclones need several conditions: sea surface temperature above about 26.5 degrees C to a depth of roughly 50 m, a Coriolis force strong enough to give rotation (generally beyond 5 degrees latitude), low vertical wind shear, high humidity in the mid-troposphere, and a pre-existing low-level disturbance with convergence. The ITCZ, a belt of converging trade winds, supplies that disturbance through easterly waves and monsoon-trough vortices. In the South Atlantic and the South-Eastern Pacific, the ITCZ stays north of the equator for almost the whole year because of the cold Benguela and Humboldt (Peru) currents and the cool south-east trades. So the cyclonic seedlings rarely form. Cold upwelling water and strong upper-level shear make it worse, but the official answer rests on the ITCZ. Elimination: (a) is a result of the same cold currents, but it is not the stated reason; (c) is wrong because Coriolis force is adequate away from the equator; (d) is wrong because cyclones form over oceans and need no land.
explanations: Wrong as the official reason. Cold currents do cool parts of these oceans, but low sea surface temperature is a side effect, and UPSC's key points to the missing ITCZ.
Correct. The ITCZ seldom occurs south of the equator in these regions, so the convergence zone and disturbances needed to form cyclones are absent.
Wrong. Coriolis force grows with latitude and is sufficient at tropical latitudes beyond about 5 degrees. It is weak only near the equator.
Wrong. Cyclones form over warm oceans and need no land. Land actually weakens them after landfall.
keyfact: Southern Atlantic and south-eastern Pacific lack tropical cyclones because the ITCZ seldom lies there (cold currents keep it north of the equator).
option_notes: Sea surface temperature: tropical cyclones need SST of at least 26.5 degrees C extending to about 50 m depth, which supplies latent heat and moisture. Cold currents such as the Humboldt (Peru) current in the Pacific and the Benguela current in the Atlantic keep the eastern parts of the southern oceans cool. Warm waters fuel cyclones; cold waters suppress them.

The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is the belt near the equator where trade winds from both hemispheres meet, producing rising air, cloud and heavy rain. It shifts seasonally with the sun and is the birthplace of many tropical disturbances. In the South Atlantic and South-Eastern Pacific it generally stays north of the equator, so the region has few seedlings for cyclones.

Coriolis force is the deflecting force from Earth's rotation. It is zero at the equator and increases toward the poles. It must be adequate, generally beyond 5 degrees latitude, to give cyclones their rotation. This is why cyclones almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator, but it is not the problem in these regions.

Land absence is irrelevant to cyclone genesis. Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans and draw energy from the sea. On crossing land they lose their moisture and energy supply and weaken. Landfall decides where damage occurs, not where cyclones originate.
related: Cyclones rarely form within about 5 degrees of the equator because Coriolis force is too weak.
Cyclone Catarina (2004) was a rare hurricane in the South Atlantic, striking Brazil.
Cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
Tropical cyclones need SST above 26.5 degrees C.
The Humboldt (Peru) current is cold and flows along the west coast of South America.
The Benguela current is a cold current off south-western Africa.
IMD is the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean.
Cyclones are called typhoons in the western North Pacific and willy-willies in Australia.
summary: The answer is (b). In the South Atlantic and South-Eastern Pacific, the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) seldom lies south of the equator, so the low-level convergence and pre-existing disturbances needed to seed tropical cyclones are largely missing. Cold currents and strong wind shear add to this, but UPSC treats the rare ITCZ as the key reason.
topic_notes: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems that form over warm tropical oceans. Conditions for genesis: SST above 26.5 degrees C, Coriolis force beyond about 5 degrees latitude, weak vertical wind shear, high mid-level humidity, and a pre-existing disturbance with low-level convergence, usually along the ITCZ. Regional names: hurricanes in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoons in the western North Pacific, willy-willies in north-west Australia, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific. Direction of rotation: anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Structure: a calm eye with sinking air, surrounded by the eyewall with the strongest winds and rain, then spiral rainbands. Storm surge is the main killer on coasts. In the North Indian Ocean, cyclones form mainly in the pre-monsoon (April to June) and post-monsoon (October to December) seasons, more often in the Bay of Bengal than the Arabian Sea. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for the North Indian Ocean, and a WMO/ESCAP panel names the storms. Naming has been done by a list of 13 member countries since 2004, expanded to 13 members with 169 names. IMD classifies systems by wind speed: depression, deep depression, cyclonic storm, severe, very severe, extremely severe and super cyclonic storm (above 221 km/h). The South Atlantic is the rare case: Cyclone Catarina struck Brazil in 2004, and it is considered the first recorded hurricane there. Tropical cyclones are also absent near the equator because Coriolis force is too weak. Related: extra-tropical (temperate) cyclones form along fronts in mid-latitudes and differ in origin, size and energy source.

ocr: Which one of the following pairs of States of India indicates the easternmost and westernmost State? fa) Assam and Rajasthan (bj) Arunachal Pradesh and Rajasthan (c) Assam and Gujarat (d) Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Easternmost and westernmost points of India are decided by longitude. India's extent runs from about 68°7'E to 97°25'E, a span of roughly 29 degrees, which produces a time difference of nearly two hours between the east and the west; this is why Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise much earlier than Gujarat. The easternmost State is Arunachal Pradesh; its far-eastern village Kibithu in Anjaw district lies near the tri-junction with China and Myanmar, and Dong in the same district is famed as the place that sees the first sunrise. The westernmost State is Gujarat; its westernmost point is Guhar Moti in the Kutch district, near Sir Creek and the Pakistan border. Rajasthan, although bordering Pakistan over a long stretch, lies east of Gujarat's Kutch extremity. Assam is east-central in the northeast, but lies west of Arunachal Pradesh. Elimination logic: any option with Assam is wrong because Arunachal Pradesh is further east; any option with Rajasthan is wrong because Gujarat is further west. Only (d) survives. Remember also that Indira Point (Great Nicobar) is the southernmost point, and Indira Col in Ladakh is the northernmost point of the country in common reference.
explanations: Incorrect: Assam is not the easternmost State, since Arunachal Pradesh lies further east, and Rajasthan is not the westernmost because Gujarat's Kutch extends further west.
Incorrect: Arunachal Pradesh is correct for the east, but Rajasthan is not the westernmost; Gujarat (Guhar Moti, Kutch) lies further west.
Incorrect: Gujarat is correct for the west, but Assam is not the easternmost; Arunachal Pradesh extends further east.
Correct: Arunachal Pradesh is the easternmost State and Gujarat is the westernmost State, matching the official answer.
keyfact: East = Arunachal Pradesh (Kibithu); West = Gujarat (Guhar Moti, Kutch).
option_notes: Assam: the largest State of Northeast India, with the Brahmaputra and Barak valleys, capital Dispur, and well known for tea, one-horned rhinoceros (Kaziranga) and oil (Digboi). It lies west of Arunachal Pradesh and so is not the easternmost. Rajasthan is the largest State by area, with the Thar Desert, the Aravallis and a long border with Pakistan, but lies east of Gujarat's western tip.

Arunachal Pradesh and Rajasthan: Arunachal Pradesh, 'land of the dawn-lit mountains', has capital Itanagar, borders China, Myanmar and Bhutan, and sees India's first sunrise (Dong). It became a State in 1987, formerly NEFA. Rajasthan, capital Jaipur, is the largest State by area (about 342,239 sq km) and contains the Thar Desert and Mount Abu, the Aravalli's highest peak (Guru Shikhar).

Assam and Gujarat: Assam is a northeastern State with ethnic diversity, the Brahmaputra and the Kaziranga and Manas parks; capital Dispur. Gujarat has India's longest coastline among States (about 1,600 km), capital Gandhinagar, the Rann of Kutch, Gir (Asiatic lion) and Kandla and Mundra ports. Gujarat is correctly the westernmost, but Assam is not the easternmost.

Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat: the correct pair. Arunachal's Kibithu is the easternmost village at about 97°25'E, and Gujarat's Guhar Moti in Kutch is the westernmost at about 68°7'E. The 82°30'E meridian is the Indian Standard Time line passing through Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh. Debate exists about a separate time zone for the Northeast because of the roughly two-hour sunrise difference.
related: Easternmost State: Arunachal Pradesh; westernmost State: Gujarat.
Southernmost point of India: Indira Point (Great Nicobar), 6°45'N.
Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 States, including Gujarat, Rajasthan and Mizoram.
Indian Standard Time is based on 82°30'E near Mirzapur.
Gujarat has the longest coastline among Indian States.
Dong in Arunachal Pradesh sees India's first sunrise.
Bangladesh shares India's longest international border.
Rajasthan is the largest State by area; Goa is the smallest.
summary: The answer is (d) Arunachal Pradesh and Gujarat. Arunachal Pradesh lies at the extreme east of India (Kibithu, about 97°25'E) and Gujarat lies at the extreme west (Guhar Moti, Kutch, about 68°7'E). Rajasthan is the westernmost in the sense of being the most western mainland border state only in common misconception; by longitude Gujarat extends further west.
topic_notes: India lies wholly in the northern and eastern hemispheres. Latitudinal extent: 8°4'N (Indira Point, Great Nicobar, southernmost point of India, submerged partly by the 2004 tsunami) to 37°6'N (Indira Col, in the far north). The southernmost tip of the mainland is Kanyakumari at 8°4'N. Longitudinal extent: 68°7'E to 97°25'E. The Tropic of Cancer (23°30'N) passes through eight States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. Standard Meridian: 82°30'E, passing through Mirzapur (near Prayagraj), used for Indian Standard Time, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. The north-south extent is about 3,214 km and the east-west extent is about 2,933 km. Land frontier is about 15,200 km and coastline (with islands) about 7,516 km. Total area is 3.28 million sq km, the seventh largest in the world, about 2.4 percent of the world's land. States sharing the longest international borders: Pakistan borders Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and Jammu and Kashmir/Ladakh; China borders Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and Arunachal; Bangladesh is bordered by West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (longest border with a single country is Bangladesh, about 4,096 km). Largest State by area is Rajasthan and smallest is Goa. Neighbours: Afghanistan, Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. The Radcliffe Line, McMahon Line and Durand Line are key boundary lines. Easternmost point is Kibithu, northernmost is Indira Col, westernmost is Guhar Moti, and southernmost is Indira Point. UPSC often asks about the Tropic of Cancer, the States with the longest coastlines, and international borders.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the Directive Principles of State Policy :
1. The Principles spell out the sacioeconomic democracy in the country.
2. The provisions contained in these Principles are not enforceable by any court. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They embody the ideal of a welfare state and socio-economic democracy, complementing the political democracy guaranteed by Fundamental Rights. Dr B.R. Ambedkar called them 'novel features' meant to establish economic democracy. The Preamble's promise of justice, social, economic and political, is given content through Articles 38 (social order promoting welfare), 39 (equitable distribution of resources, equal pay for equal work), 41 (work, education, public assistance), 42 (just working conditions, maternity relief), 43 (living wage) and 47 (nutrition, public health). Article 37 says the provisions shall not be enforceable by any court, yet the principles are fundamental in the governance of the country, and the State has a duty to apply them in making laws. So they are non-justiciable, unlike Fundamental Rights, which are enforceable under Articles 32 and 226. Elimination logic: Statement 2 is the direct text of Article 37, so (a) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 reflects the settled description of DPSP as socio-economic in character, so (b) falls away. Only (c) remains.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it ignores Statement 2, which is also correct under Article 37.
(b) is wrong because it ignores Statement 1, which correctly describes DPSP as spelling out socio-economic democracy.
(c) is right because both statements are correct: DPSP embody socio-economic democracy and are non-justiciable under Article 37.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so it cannot be 'neither'.
keyfact: DPSP (Part IV, Arts 36-51) aim at socio-economic democracy and are non-justiciable under Article 37.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only would hold if DPSP were justiciable, but they are not. The statement it endorses, that DPSP spell out socio-economic democracy, is true. Socio-economic democracy means equitable distribution of wealth, social justice and welfare, in contrast to the political democracy of universal suffrage and civil liberties. Ambedkar stressed this in the Constituent Assembly, saying political democracy cannot last unless it rests on social democracy. The DPSP are the Constitution's main instrument for this goal.

Option (b) 2 only isolates the non-justiciability point. Article 37 provides that DPSP are not enforceable by courts, unlike Fundamental Rights, which can be enforced through writs under Articles 32 and 226. The reasons given in the Constituent Assembly were limited state resources and the country's diversity and backwardness. The government is still morally and politically bound to implement DPSP, and courts can use them to interpret laws and test the reasonableness of restrictions.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2 is the official answer. DPSP in Part IV (Arts 36-51) are positive instructions to the State for achieving justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. They were influenced by the Irish Constitution and the Gandhian, socialist and liberal ideals of the freedom movement. They are non-justiciable but fundamental to governance. The State must apply them when making laws. Courts have increasingly harmonised them with Fundamental Rights, which has widened Article 21.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2 would require both statements to be false, which is not the case. It would imply DPSP are neither socio-economic in aim nor non-justiciable. In fact the Constitution makes Fundamental Rights justiciable and DPSP non-justiciable. This contrast is a standard UPSC theme, along with the difference between the political rights of Part III and the social and economic goals of Part IV.
related: Article 37: DPSP not enforceable by any court but fundamental to governance.
DPSP were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
Article 44 directs the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code.
Article 40 directs the State to organise village panchayats.
Article 50 requires separation of the judiciary from the executive.
42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A and 48A.
Minerva Mills (1980) held the harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is a basic feature.
Article 51 deals with promotion of international peace and security.
statements: 1 — Correct: DPSP set out the social and economic goals of the Constitution and aim at socio-economic democracy. DPSP are in Part IV, Articles 36-51, and were taken from the Irish Constitution, which in turn drew on Spanish precedents. They are often grouped as socialistic (Arts 38, 39, 41-43, 47), Gandhian (Arts 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) and liberal-intellectual (Arts 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). Granville Austin called Fundamental Rights and DPSP the 'conscience of the Constitution'. They aim at a welfare state, not a police state. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Arts 39A, 43A and 48A. The 44th Amendment (1978) added Art 38(2) on reducing inequalities. The 86th Amendment (2002) changed Art 45 and added Art 21A. The 97th Amendment (2011) added Art 43B.

2 — Correct: Article 37 explicitly says DPSP are not enforceable by any court, so they are non-justiciable. Courts cannot compel the government to implement them, but the principles are 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court held that DPSP must run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights. This changed with Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980), which held that Fundamental Rights and DPSP together form the Constitution's core balance. Article 31C, added by the 25th Amendment, protects laws giving effect to Arts 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Arts 14 and 19. The Supreme Court has also read some DPSP into Article 21, for example the right to education and to livelihood.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51) lay down the goals of socio-economic democracy, and Article 37 states that they are not enforceable by any court.
topic_notes: Part IV (Articles 36-51) contains the DPSP. Article 36 defines 'State' as in Part III. Article 37 declares them non-justiciable but fundamental to governance. Source: the Irish Constitution, with the idea of a welfare state. Classification (not in the text, but by scholars): Socialistic principles include Art 38 (social order, reducing inequalities), 39 (livelihood, equal pay, no concentration of wealth), 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 41 (work, education, public assistance), 42 (just and humane work conditions, maternity relief), 43 (living wage), 43A (workers' participation in management) and 47 (nutrition, public health, prohibition of intoxicants). Gandhian principles include Art 40 (village panchayats), 43 (cottage industries), 43B (cooperative societies), 46 (SC/ST and weaker sections' interests), 47 (prohibition) and 48 (prevention of cow slaughter, improving breeds). Liberal-intellectual principles include Art 44 (Uniform Civil Code), 45 (early childhood care and education up to age 6), 48 (modern agriculture and animal husbandry), 48A (environment, forests and wildlife), 49 (monuments), 50 (separation of judiciary from executive) and 51 (international peace and security). Key amendments: 42nd (1976) added 39A, 43A, 48A and altered Art 39; 44th (1978) added 38(2); 86th (2002) replaced Art 45 and added Art 21A and the Fundamental Duty 51A(k); 97th (2011) added 43B. Key cases: Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980, balance between Part III and IV is a basic feature). Article 31C, as modified, protects laws implementing Art 39(b)-(c) from challenge under Arts 14 and 19. DPSP differ from Fundamental Rights in that they are positive obligations on the State, non-justiciable, and do not directly confer rights on individuals. They have inspired many policies: MGNREGA, the Right to Education, the National Food Security Act and the Equal Remuneration Act.

question: In the ‘Index of Eight Core Industries’, which one of the following is given the highest weight?
subject: Economy
detail: The Index of Eight Core Industries (ICI) measures the combined and individual production performance of eight key infrastructure industries: coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement and electricity. It is compiled and released monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, usually on the 20th of each month with a lag of about one month. These industries together account for about 40.27% of the weight of items in the IIP. Base year was revised from 1993-94 to 2004-05 in 2012, and to 2011-12 in May 2017. Weights in the 2011-12 series are: Refinery Products 28.04%, Electricity 19.85%, Steel 17.92%, Coal 10.33%, Crude Oil 8.98%, Natural Gas 6.88%, Cement 5.37%, Fertilizers 2.63%. In the 2004-05 series that applied in 2015, Electricity had the highest weight at 10.32% of IIP among the eight industries, followed by Steel at 6.68% and Refinery Products at 5.94%. Coal was 4.38% and Fertilizers 1.25%. Elimination: fertilizers is the smallest in either series, coal is mid-ranked, and steel is second. Electricity is therefore the correct choice for the 2015 paper.
explanations: Incorrect: coal weighs about 4.38% of IIP in the 2004-05 base (10.33% within the ICI in 2011-12), below electricity.
Correct: electricity generation had the highest weight, about 10.32% of IIP in the 2004-05 base series, which was current in 2015.
Incorrect: fertilizers has the lowest weight of the eight (about 1.25% of IIP in 2004-05; 2.63% in 2011-12).
Incorrect: steel is second in the 2004-05 series, with about 6.68% of IIP, and is below electricity.
keyfact: In the 2004-05 base ICI that applied in 2015, electricity had the highest weight, while fertilizers had the lowest.
option_notes: Coal production: India is the second-largest coal producer, and Coal India Ltd accounts for most of the output. Coal is the main fuel for thermal power, which supplies about 70% of electricity. Its weight in the ICI is about 10.33% in the 2011-12 base. Coal is a bulk raw material and its output often rises in the second half of the fiscal year.

Electricity generation: This covers generation from thermal, nuclear, hydro and imports from Bhutan, and it now includes renewables. It has the highest weight in the old 2004-05 series of the ICI and a high weight in the 2011-12 base (19.85%). The data is supplied by the Central Electricity Authority. Electricity is a key infrastructure input for every sector.

Fertilizer production: This covers urea, ammonium sulphate, DAP, complex fertilizers and others, and the ICI tracks nitrogen and phosphate production. Fertilizers have the lowest weight among the eight core industries (about 2.63% in the 2011-12 base). Urea is controlled under the Fertilizer Control Order, and the Department of Fertilizers supplies the data. India is a major importer of potash.

Steel production: This covers production of alloy and non-alloy finished steel, and the data comes from the Joint Plant Committee. Steel has the second-highest weight in the older series and about 17.92% in the 2011-12 base. India is the second-largest crude steel producer in the world, after China. The National Steel Policy 2017 targets 300 million tonnes of capacity by 2030-31.
related: ICI covers 8 industries and about 40.27% of IIP weight.
ICI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, around the 20th of each month.
The current ICI base year is 2011-12 (revised in 2017).
In the 2011-12 base, refinery products has the highest weight (28.04%).
Fertilizers has the lowest weight in the ICI.
IIP is compiled by NSO, MoSPI.
WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, while CPI is published by NSO, MoSPI.
summary: The answer is (b) Electricity generation. In the Index of Eight Core Industries (ICI), electricity has the largest weight, about 19.85% in the base 2004-05 series, ahead of steel, refinery products and crude oil. Its weight reflects its share in the Index of Industrial Production (IIP).
topic_notes: The Index of Eight Core Industries is a monthly production volume index, not a value index. It is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, and released around the 20th of the month. Together the eight industries make up about 40.27% of the IIP, so they are a good leading indicator of industrial growth. They are coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilizers, steel, cement and electricity. Base years have been revised over time: 1993-94, then 2004-05 (from 2012), then 2011-12 (from May 2017). A revision to 2022-23 has been discussed. Weights in the ICI (2011-12): Refinery products 28.04, Electricity 19.85, Steel 17.92, Coal 10.33, Crude oil 8.98, Natural gas 6.88, Cement 5.37, Fertilizers 2.63. Weights in the ICI differ from weights in the IIP. The IIP itself is compiled by the National Statistical Office (NSO), MoSPI, and covers mining, manufacturing and electricity. It also has use-based classifications such as basic goods, capital goods, intermediate goods, infrastructure goods and consumer durables and non-durables. Related indices include WPI (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT) and CPI (NSO, MoSPI). Potential angles for UPSC include which industry has the lowest weight, which sources supply the data, the base-year revision, and the relationship between the ICI and the IIP.

question: Which of the following National Parks is unique in being a swamp with floating vegetation that supports a_ rich biodiversity?
subject: Environment
detail: Keibul Lamjao National Park (about 40 sq km) lies on the southern part of Loktak Lake in Manipur and is the only floating national park in the world. Its base is made of phumdis, heterogeneous floating mats of soil, vegetation and decaying organic matter that are thick enough to support animals. It was notified as a sanctuary in 1966 and upgraded to a national park in 1977. Its flagship species is the Sangai or brow-antlered deer (Rucervus eldii eldii), Manipur's state animal, which is Endangered on the IUCN list. Loktak Lake is a Ramsar site (since 1990) and is also on the Montreux Record, which lists Ramsar sites facing ecological damage. The Ithai barrage of the Loktak hydroelectric project disturbed the natural water cycle of the lake. Elimination: Bhitarkanika in Odisha is a mangrove and estuarine system known for saltwater crocodiles. Keoladeo in Rajasthan is a man-made, managed wetland known for birds. Sultanpur in Haryana is a bird sanctuary-turned-national park on a shallow lake. None of these is a floating swamp.
explanations: Incorrect: Bhitarkanika is a mangrove and estuarine ecosystem in Odisha, not a swamp with floating vegetation.
Correct: Keibul Lamjao in Manipur is the only floating national park, sitting on phumdis in Loktak Lake, and it supports the Sangai deer and rich wetland biodiversity.
Incorrect: Keoladeo Ghana is a man-made, seasonally flooded wetland in Bharatpur known for migratory birds, and it has no floating phumdi base.
Incorrect: Sultanpur in Haryana is a shallow-lake bird habitat with fixed ground and no floating vegetation mass.
keyfact: Keibul Lamjao (Manipur, Loktak Lake) is the world's only floating national park, made of phumdis, and it protects the Sangai deer.
option_notes: Bhitarkanika National Park lies in Kendrapara district, Odisha, in the Brahmani-Baitarani delta. It has India's second largest mangrove ecosystem after the Sundarbans. It is famous for saltwater crocodiles, and the Gahirmatha beach nearby is a major Olive Ridley turtle nesting site. It was declared a national park in 1998, and the area was designated a Ramsar site in 2002.

Keibul Lamjao National Park is in Bishnupur district, Manipur, on Loktak Lake, the largest freshwater lake in northeast India. It is the world's only floating national park, resting on phumdis. It protects the Sangai deer, whose population is around 260 or more. It was declared a national park in 1977. Local fishing communities live on the phumdis as huts called phumsangs.

Keoladeo Ghana National Park is in Bharatpur, Rajasthan, and is also called Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary. It was once a royal duck-shooting reserve and is a man-made wetland. It became a national park in 1982 and a Ramsar site in 1981, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985). It is famous for the Siberian crane, which has not visited in recent years, and for many migratory waterfowl.

Sultanpur National Park is in Gurugram district, Haryana, around a shallow seasonal lake. It was declared a bird sanctuary in 1972 and a national park in 1991. It is named after Dr Salim Ali, who helped in its establishment, and is a stopover for migratory birds from Siberia and Europe. It lies near Delhi and is a popular site for birdwatching.
related: Keibul Lamjao is the world's only floating national park.
Sangai deer is the state animal of Manipur and is also called the dancing deer.
Loktak Lake is on the Montreux Record of the Ramsar Convention.
Phumdis are floating mats of vegetation, soil and organic matter.
Chilika Lake is the largest brackish-water lagoon in India.
Keoladeo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Ramsar site.
Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is the largest inland saltwater lake in India.
Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 and India joined in 1982.
summary: The answer is (b) Keibul Lamjao National Park in Manipur. It is the world's only floating national park, built on phumdis, which are floating masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter on Loktak Lake, and it is the last natural home of the Sangai deer.
topic_notes: Wetlands and national parks are frequently tested in UPSC prelims. Loktak Lake in Manipur is the largest freshwater lake in northeast India. It is known for phumdis, which are floating biomass islands. The lake was listed as a Ramsar site on 23 March 1990. It is also on the Montreux Record, which lists Ramsar sites where ecological character has changed or is likely to change. The Loktak Hydroelectric Project and the Ithai barrage have caused phumdi thickening and altered water flow. The Loktak Development Authority manages the lake. Keibul Lamjao is the only floating national park in the world and hosts the Sangai deer (Rucervus eldii eldii), listed as Endangered by IUCN and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. Other notable wetland parks include Keoladeo (Rajasthan), Chilika Lake (Odisha), which is the largest brackish-water lagoon in India and the first Indian Ramsar site along with Keoladeo, and Sundarbans (West Bengal), which has the largest mangrove forest and the Royal Bengal Tiger. Also learn Bhitarkanika (Odisha), Vembanad (Kerala), Sambhar Lake (Rajasthan), the largest inland saltwater lake in India, and Wular Lake (J&K), one of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia. Other related areas are Dachigam (Hangul), Kaziranga (one-horned rhino), Manas (tiger reserve and World Heritage Site) and Namdapha (Arunachal Pradesh). Remember the Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 in Iran and India joined in 1982. The number of Indian Ramsar sites has grown rapidly in recent years, so check the latest total.

ocr: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding National Innovation Foundation-India (NIF}? 1. NIF is an autonomous body of the Department of Science and Technology under the Central Government. 2. NIF is an initiative to strengthen the highly advanced scientific research in India’s premier scientific institutions in collaboration with highly advanced foreign scientific institutions. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Geography
detail: The National Innovation Foundation (NIF), headquartered at Gandhinagar, Gujarat, was set up in March 2000 with support from the DST as India's national initiative to strengthen grassroots technological innovations and outstanding traditional knowledge. It was established as an autonomous society under the DST. Its inspiration was the Honey Bee Network, founded by Prof. Anil K. Gupta of IIM Ahmedabad, which documents, protects and spreads the creativity of ordinary people, farmers and artisans. NIF scouts, documents, validates and adds value to such innovations, helps with patent filing through the Micro Venture Innovation Fund (MVIF), and supports commercialisation and diffusion. It also runs the Grassroots Innovation Augmentation Network (GIAN) in partnership with others, and organises the National Biennial Competition for grassroots innovations. The annual awards were presented by the President at the Festival of Innovation held at Rashtrapati Bhavan. Elimination logic: Statement 1 matches NIF's institutional status. Statement 2 describes high-end research collaboration, which is the opposite of NIF's grassroots, informal-sector focus. So only statement 1 is right, giving (a).
explanations: (a) is correct: statement 1 is right because NIF is an autonomous DST body, and statement 2 is wrong because NIF targets grassroots innovation, not advanced institutional research with foreign partners.
(b) is wrong: it accepts statement 2 and rejects statement 1, which is the reverse of the facts.
(c) is wrong: it requires both statements to be correct, but statement 2 misdescribes NIF's mandate.
(d) is wrong: it rejects both statements, but statement 1 is correct.
keyfact: NIF (2000, Gandhinagar) is an autonomous DST body that supports grassroots innovation and traditional knowledge, not high-end research tie-ups with foreign institutions.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this is the official answer. It reflects NIF as an autonomous DST body, with the second statement rejected. NIF was founded in 2000 and is based at Gandhinagar. It scouts, documents, validates, protects and commercialises grassroots innovations and traditional knowledge. It works closely with the Honey Bee Network and SRISTI, and has helped file patents for innovators in India and abroad. It also administers the MVIF through SIDBI and runs the national competitions and awards for grassroots innovators.

Option (b), 2 only: this would mean NIF is about advanced research in premier institutions with foreign partners, which is incorrect. That description fits other bodies, for example the CSIR laboratories, IISc, IITs and DST's international science collaboration schemes such as the Indo-US Science and Technology Forum (IUSSTF).
