IUSSTF is a bilateral autonomous body set up in 2000 by the Governments of India and the USA to promote science and technology collaboration. NIF is distinct, as its work centres on grassroots creators.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: this is wrong because only statement 1 holds. Treating both as correct would blur NIF's grassroots mission with high-end collaborative research. NIF's distinctive features are its focus on informal-sector inventors, its documentation database of tens of thousands of ideas and traditional practices, its link with the Honey Bee Network founded by Anil Gupta, and its support for patent filing and incubation through the Grassroots Technological Innovation and Traditional Knowledge Awards framework.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong because statement 1 is correct. NIF is indeed an autonomous body under the DST. Established in March 2000 with DST support, it was India's first national initiative to give grassroots innovators institutional backing. It also works with the Technology Development Board, SIDBI, and research and academic institutions. Its Gandhinagar premises host the Grassroots Innovation Augmentation Network activities, and it runs the Micro Venture Innovation Fund.
related: NIF was set up in 2000 and is headquartered at Gandhinagar, Gujarat.
NIF is an autonomous body under the Department of Science and Technology.
The Honey Bee Network was founded by Prof. Anil K. Gupta of IIM Ahmedabad.
NIF's Micro Venture Innovation Fund supports grassroots innovators with early-stage capital.
The Atal Innovation Mission was launched by NITI Aayog in 2016.
TKDL is a database of traditional knowledge meant to prevent biopiracy and wrongful patents.
INSPIRE is a DST scheme to attract talented youth to science.
IUSSTF is a bilateral Indo-US body for science and technology collaboration.
statements: 1 — Correct: NIF is an autonomous body under the DST, Government of India. NIF was established in 2000 at Ahmedabad, later with its campus in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It is registered as a society and funded by the DST. Its mandate is to build a national register of grassroots innovations and traditional knowledge, support their protection through IPR, provide incubation, and help with commercialisation and dissemination. Its work is linked to the Honey Bee Network, and it operates the Micro Venture Innovation Fund and the Gandhian Young Technological Innovation Awards in partnership with SRISTI.

2 — Incorrect: NIF does not exist to strengthen advanced scientific research in premier institutions with foreign collaboration. Its focus is grassroots innovation and traditional knowledge held by farmers, artisans, students and other informal-sector people. Advanced collaborative research is the domain of bodies such as CSIR labs, IISc, IITs and DST schemes like the Indo-foreign joint centres. NIF documents and validates innovations, adds value, protects them through patents, and promotes their diffusion, rather than funding high-end institutional research.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. NIF-India is an autonomous body under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, set up to support grassroots innovation and traditional knowledge. Statement 2 is wrong because NIF does not exist to strengthen advanced research in premier institutions in collaboration with foreign institutions.
topic_notes: The National Innovation Foundation-India was established in 2000 at Ahmedabad and is now based in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. It is an autonomous body under the Department of Science and Technology. Its mission is to help India become creative and innovative by strengthening grassroots technological innovations and traditional knowledge. The founding inspiration was the Honey Bee Network, started in 1989 by Prof. Anil K. Gupta of IIM Ahmedabad, along with SRISTI (Society for Research and Initiatives for Sustainable Technologies and Institutions). The Honey Bee Network's principles include acknowledging the innovator, seeking prior informed consent, sharing benefits, and keeping the knowledge in the public domain through reciprocity. NIF's main functions are: scouting and documenting innovations through shodh yatras, validating and adding value in partnership with research institutions, protecting IP by filing patents on behalf of innovators, supporting business development through the Micro Venture Innovation Fund, and disseminating innovations. NIF has an incubation arm called the Grassroots Innovation Augmentation Network (GIAN). It also runs national competitions and awards for grassroots innovators, and its award ceremonies have been held at Rashtrapati Bhavan during the Festival of Innovation. Related institutions and programmes include the Technology Development Board, the Atal Innovation Mission (NITI Aayog, 2016), the Atal Tinkering Labs, the Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research (INSPIRE) scheme of DST, and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC). Other angles UPSC could examine include the Honey Bee Network, traditional knowledge protection through the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), the Patents Act, the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001, and national awards for innovators.

question:
What can be the impact of excessive / inappropriate use of nitrogenous fertilizers in agriculture?
1. Proliferation of nitrogen-fixing microorganisms in soil can occur.
2. Increase in the acidity of soil can take place.
3. Leaching of nitrate to the groundwater can occur. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Geography
detail: Nitrogenous fertilizers (urea, ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, DAP) supply ammonium or nitrate. Excess ammonium is oxidised by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter (nitrification), releasing H+ ions. This acidifies soil, lowers pH, reduces base cations (Ca, Mg, K) and can mobilise toxic aluminium. Nitrate is negatively charged and not held by negatively charged soil colloids, so it leaches readily with irrigation or rain into groundwater. This causes methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby syndrome) in infants, and when it runs off into water bodies it causes eutrophication and algal blooms. Nitrogen-fixing organisms such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae fix atmospheric N2 only when soil mineral nitrogen is scarce, because nitrogenase is energy-expensive and is repressed by available nitrogen. Excess fertilizer therefore reduces their activity and does not promote them. Also note nitrous oxide emissions, a potent greenhouse gas. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong, so options (a) and (d) go. Statement 3 is certainly right, so (b) goes, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect because excess nitrogen suppresses nitrogen-fixers instead of promoting them.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, and leaching of nitrate to groundwater is a well-established effect of excess nitrogen fertilizer.
Correct: statements 2 (soil acidification) and 3 (nitrate leaching) are both valid impacts, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so the full set cannot be correct.
keyfact: Excess nitrogen fertilizer acidifies soil and leaches nitrate into groundwater, but it suppresses rather than promotes nitrogen-fixing microbes.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 3 only, pairs the false claim of nitrogen-fixer proliferation with the true claim of nitrate leaching. It is wrong because nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium and Azotobacter reduce fixation when soil nitrate or ammonium is abundant. It also omits soil acidification, which is real. Nitrate leaching is the main groundwater pollution route from agriculture, with a 45 mg/L drinking-water limit.

Option (b), 2 only, correctly names soil acidification but ignores nitrate leaching. Acidification comes from nitrification of ammonium, which releases H+. It is a real effect, but nitrate leaching is equally well documented, and both are linked to heavy use of urea and ammonium sulphate. Acid soils are managed with lime, and the Soil Health Card promotes balanced fertilizer use.

Option (c), 2 and 3 only, is the correct answer. Acidification and nitrate leaching are both direct, well-known consequences of excess nitrogen fertilizer. Related consequences are eutrophication, nitrous oxide emissions, blue baby syndrome, and lower nitrogen use efficiency, which in India is about 30-40% for urea. Neem-coated urea, introduced in 2015, aims to slow nitrification and improve efficiency.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, is wrong only because of statement 1. It reflects the common misconception that more nitrogen helps all soil nitrogen microbes. In fact, nitrogenase, the enzyme complex of nitrogen-fixers, is repressed by combined nitrogen. Nitrifiers and denitrifiers may increase with excess fertilizer, but nitrogen-fixers do not, and the overall soil microbial balance is disturbed.
related: Neem-coated urea was made mandatory for all domestic urea production in 2015.
Nitrate limit in drinking water under WHO and BIS is 45 mg/L; excess causes blue baby syndrome.
Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate.
Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion.
Nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential of about 265-298 times CO2, and agriculture is its major source.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015 to promote balanced fertilizer use.
PM-PRANAM (2023) rewards states for reducing chemical fertilizer use.
Nano Urea, developed by IFFCO, was launched in 2021 to improve nitrogen use efficiency.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High soil nitrogen inhibits nitrogenase and the nodulation process, so nitrogen-fixers decline rather than proliferate. Nitrogen-fixing microbes include symbiotic Rhizobium in legume root nodules, Frankia in actinorhizal plants like Alnus, and Anabaena-Azolla in rice fields. Free-living ones include Azotobacter, Azospirillum, Clostridium and cyanobacteria such as Nostoc. They are used as biofertilizers, which cut chemical fertilizer need. Heavy mineral N use reduces the benefit of these biofertilizers and weakens natural soil fertility cycling.

2 — Correct: Ammonium-based fertilizers undergo nitrification (NH4+ to NO2- to NO3-), releasing H+ ions and lowering pH. Urea hydrolyses to ammonium, which then nitrifies. Acidification leaches away calcium and magnesium, raises aluminium and manganese toxicity and harms beneficial microbes. Remedies include liming, balanced NPK use, organic manure, and soil testing through the Soil Health Card scheme (launched 2015). Ammonium sulphate is among the most acidifying fertilizers, while calcium ammonium nitrate is less so.

3 — Correct: Nitrate is highly soluble and mobile in soil, so excess application beyond crop uptake leaches into groundwater. The BIS and WHO limit for nitrate in drinking water is 45 mg/L. High nitrate causes methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby syndrome) and is linked to health risks in adults. Runoff to surface water causes eutrophication, algal blooms, hypoxia and fish kills. Hotspots include Punjab and Haryana. Mitigation includes neem-coated urea (made mandatory in 2015), drip fertigation, split dosing and buffer strips.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 3 only. Excess nitrogenous fertilizer acidifies soil, mainly through nitrification, and nitrate leaches into groundwater. It does not cause proliferation of nitrogen-fixing microbes; high mineral nitrogen actually suppresses them.
topic_notes: Nitrogen is the nutrient needed in the largest quantity by crops, and India is the second-largest consumer of fertilizer after China. Urea (46% N) dominates, and its price is controlled under the Nutrient Based Subsidy for P and K and a separate subsidy regime for urea. Nitrogen use efficiency of applied urea is low, roughly 30-40%, because of leaching, volatilisation of ammonia and denitrification. The nitrogen cycle has five steps: fixation (N2 to NH3, by Rhizobium, Azotobacter, cyanobacteria, and lightning and the Haber-Bosch process), ammonification, nitrification (Nitrosomonas to nitrite, Nitrobacter to nitrate), assimilation and denitrification (Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus return N2 to the air). Environmental impacts of overuse include soil acidification, nitrate contamination of groundwater, eutrophication, hypoxic dead zones, nitrous oxide (about 265-298 times CO2 in GWP over 100 years), ammonia-derived particulate air pollution and loss of soil biodiversity. Health effects include methaemoglobinaemia. Policy responses are neem-coated urea (mandatory since 2015), the Soil Health Card scheme (2015), the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana for organic farming, the Nano Urea launched by IFFCO, Integrated Nutrient Management, the Fertiliser Control Order 1985, the PM-PRANAM scheme (2023) to reduce chemical fertilizer use, and the Gobardhan scheme for biogas and organic manure. Biofertilizers include Rhizobium, Azolla, Azospirillum, phosphate-solubilising bacteria and mycorrhiza. Related global ideas are the planetary boundaries framework, in which nitrogen flow is already beyond the safe limit, and the Kigali-style push to cut nitrogen waste by half under the Colombo Declaration (2019).

question:
With reference to the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. IUCN is an organ of the United Nations and CITES is an international agreement between governments.
2. IUCN runs thousands of field Projects around the world to better manage natural environments.
3. CITES is legally binding on the States that have joined it, but this Convention does not take the place of national laws. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: IUCN, founded in 1948 at Fontainebleau, France, is a hybrid membership organisation. Its members include sovereign states, government agencies and NGOs. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland, and has Observer status at the UN General Assembly, but it is not a UN organ. It publishes the Red List of Threatened Species, and its field work spans thousands of projects worldwide. CITES was drafted following an IUCN resolution of 1963 and signed in Washington DC on 3 March 1973. It entered into force on 1 July 1975, and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) administers its Secretariat. CITES is an international agreement between governments, and it is legally binding on the Parties. It does not replace national laws. Instead, it gives a framework that each Party must implement through its own domestic legislation. For India, the relevant law is the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Species are listed in Appendices I, II and III according to the degree of protection they need. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails because IUCN is not a UN organ. That rules out options (a), (c) and (d), so (b) is the only remaining option.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it accepts statement 1, which is false: IUCN is not a UN organ. It also leaves out statements 2 and 3, which are correct.
(b) is correct because statement 2 (IUCN runs thousands of field projects) and statement 3 (CITES is binding but does not replace national laws) are both true. Statement 1 is false.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 2, which is true.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, since IUCN is not an organ of the United Nations.
keyfact: IUCN (1948, Gland) is a non-UN membership union that runs field projects; CITES (1973) is a binding treaty enforced through national laws.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would hold only if IUCN were a UN body. It is actually a hybrid membership union founded in 1948, with governments and NGOs as members. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland, and has UNGA Observer status. It publishes the Red List and has Species Survival and Protected Areas commissions. It is not part of the UN system, so this option is wrong.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3 only: this is the official answer. It reflects IUCN as a large implementer of conservation field projects. It also reflects CITES (1973, in force 1975) as a legally binding treaty that works through national legislation. CITES is administered by a Secretariat under UNEP, and the Appendices I-III classify the species it covers.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3 only: it correctly treats CITES as binding but not replacing national laws. It wrongly treats IUCN as a UN organ. IUCN is a non-UN union, and it was involved in drafting CITES after a 1963 resolution. Such traps, which turn an independent body into a UN organ, recur in UPSC questions.

Option (d), all three statements: it would require IUCN to be a UN organ, which is false. Remember that CITES has a UNEP-hosted Secretariat but is a treaty, whereas IUCN is an independent union with observer status at the UN. Mixing these up is the usual error, and the option fails on statement 1 alone.
related: IUCN was founded in 1948 and is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland.
CITES was signed in 1973 and came into force in 1975; the CITES Secretariat is hosted by UNEP in Geneva.
World Wildlife Day is celebrated on 3 March, the anniversary of CITES's adoption.
Appendix I of CITES covers species threatened with extinction, with commercial trade generally prohibited.
TRAFFIC is a wildlife trade monitoring network run by WWF and IUCN.
India joined CITES in 1976, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is the main implementing law.
The IUCN Red List categories run from Extinct to Least Concern, including Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable.
IUCN has Observer status at the UN General Assembly but is not a UN organ.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: IUCN is not a UN organ; it is an independent membership union of states and NGOs. CITES is indeed an agreement between governments, but the first half of the statement makes it false. IUCN was founded in 1948 as the International Union for the Protection of Nature, with headquarters at Gland, Switzerland. It has over 1,400 members, including states, government agencies and civil society organisations. It holds Observer status at the UN General Assembly. It is best known for the Red List, and it also advises on the World Heritage Convention for natural sites.

2 — Correct: IUCN describes itself as running thousands of field projects worldwide to manage natural environments better. Its work covers species conservation, protected areas, ecosystem restoration and sustainable livelihoods. It is organised into six commissions, including the Species Survival Commission (SSC) and the World Commission on Protected Areas (WCPA). Its World Congress meets about every four years. It also helped create the Ramsar Convention, CITES and the World Heritage Convention, and it has a regional office in India.

3 — Correct: CITES is legally binding on the Parties, which are the states that have joined it, but it does not take the place of national laws. Parties must adopt domestic legislation to implement it. The Convention was signed in 1973, came into force in 1975, and has about 180+ Parties. India joined in 1976. The Conference of the Parties (CoP) meets every 2-3 years. Appendix I lists species threatened with extinction, and commercial trade in them is generally prohibited. Appendix II lists species where trade is regulated through permits. Appendix III lists species that a Party has asked others to help it protect.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is wrong. IUCN is not an organ of the United Nations; it is a membership union of governments and NGOs. It does run thousands of field projects, and CITES is legally binding on its Parties but works through their national laws.
topic_notes:
IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature) was founded on 5 October 1948 at Fontainebleau, France. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland. It is the world's largest and most diverse environmental network, with governments, NGOs and scientists as members. It issues the Red List of Threatened Species, which uses these categories: Extinct (EX), Extinct in the Wild (EW), Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), Vulnerable (VU), Near Threatened (NT), Least Concern (LC), Data Deficient (DD) and Not Evaluated (NE). The IUCN Green Status of Species assesses recovery. The IUCN also classifies protected areas into categories Ia to VI.

CITES was adopted on 3 March 1973 in Washington DC, so 3 March is World Wildlife Day. It came into force on 1 July 1975. The Secretariat is administered by UNEP and located in Geneva. Appendix I covers species threatened with extinction, with trade permitted only in exceptional circumstances. Appendix II covers species not necessarily threatened but whose trade must be controlled. Appendix III covers species protected in at least one country that has asked other Parties for help in controlling trade. CITES issues permits and certificates, and it works with a 'non-detriment finding' principle.

India is a Party to CITES (since 1976), and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Wildlife Protection Amendment Act, 2022 give effect to it. TRAFFIC is the wildlife trade monitoring network run by WWF and IUCN. Other related conventions are Ramsar (1971), CMS (Bonn, 1979), the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), the World Heritage Convention (1972) and the Nagoya Protocol. UPSC may also ask about Red List status of specific species, Appendices, and the bodies that administer each convention.

question: The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane is approved by the
options: Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices
Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, Ministry of Agriculture
subject: Economy
detail: The Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) is the minimum price that sugar mills must pay sugarcane farmers. It replaced the Statutory Minimum Price (SMP) from the 2009-10 sugar season, under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, which is issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) examines cost of production, returns from alternative crops, the price trend of sugar, the recovery rate and the likely effect on consumers, and then recommends the FRP after consulting the states and stakeholders. The Union Government decides after considering the recommendation, and the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) gives the formal approval. The FRP is linked to a basic sugar recovery rate (it was 9.5% for years, and is 10.25% in recent seasons), with a premium for higher recovery. States may fix a higher State Advised Price (SAP), as Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana do. Elimination: CACP only advises. The Directorate of Marketing and Inspection is a data and grading agency. The APMC regulates mandi trade and fixes no prices.
explanations: Correct. The CCEA gives the final approval of the FRP after taking the CACP's recommendation into account.
Wrong. The CACP is an advisory body that recommends MSP for 22 mandated crops and the FRP for sugarcane, but it has no power to approve or notify them.
Wrong. The DMI is an attached office of the Agriculture Ministry that handles agricultural marketing, grading (Agmark), standardisation and market data. It does not fix prices.
Wrong. APMCs are state-level market bodies regulating mandis under State APMC Acts. They run market yards, license traders and collect fees, and have no role in the FRP.
keyfact: CACP recommends, CCEA approves: the FRP of sugarcane is approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.
option_notes: The CCEA is a Cabinet committee chaired by the Prime Minister. It decides on economic policy matters, including MSPs, the FRP of sugarcane, fertiliser subsidy, and approval of major infrastructure projects above specified cost limits. Its membership consists of senior Union ministers, such as those holding the Home, Finance, Agriculture and Commerce portfolios.

The CACP was set up in January 1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission and was renamed CACP in 1985. It is an attached office of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. It recommends MSPs for 22 crops and the FRP for sugarcane. Its recommendations are not binding on the government. It has a Chairman, a Member Secretary, two official members and two non-official members.

The DMI is an attached office of the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, headquartered at Faridabad, Haryana. It administers the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937, under which Agmark certification is granted. It also works on market intelligence, standardisation and the development of agricultural marketing.

The APMC is a statutory market committee set up under state APMC Acts to regulate the sale of farm produce in notified mandis. It licenses traders and commission agents and collects market fees. The Model APMC Act, 2003 and the Model APLM Act, 2017 aimed at reform. The 2020 farm laws, since repealed, sought to allow trade outside APMC yards.
related: The CACP was set up in 1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission and renamed in 1985.
The CACP recommends MSP for 22 crops and the FRP for sugarcane; the CCEA approves them.
The FRP replaced the SMP from the 2009-10 sugar season.
The FRP is fixed under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
The State Advised Price (SAP) is announced by states such as UP and can exceed the FRP.
Agmark is administered by the DMI under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937.
The Rangarajan Committee (2012) recommended a revenue-sharing model for cane pricing.
The CCEA is chaired by the Prime Minister.
summary: The answer is (a) Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. The CACP only recommends the FRP of sugarcane, and the CCEA, chaired by the Prime Minister, takes the final decision and approves it on the basis of that recommendation.
topic_notes: Sugarcane pricing: Before 2009-10, the Centre announced a Statutory Minimum Price (SMP) under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, which the FRP then replaced. The FRP is a single national floor price payable by mills. It is announced for each sugar season (October to September) by the CCEA on the CACP's recommendation, after consulting state governments. It is linked to a basic recovery rate, with a premium for each 0.1 percentage point above it. Mills must pay it within 14 days of cane delivery, otherwise interest is payable. Several states, including Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand, announce a higher State Advised Price (SAP). The Rangarajan Committee (2012) recommended a revenue-sharing formula, under which cane growers would get 70% of the sugar and by-product revenue. The Sugar Development Fund and ethanol blending policy are related areas, with the blending target of 20% by 2025-26. India is among the world's top sugar producers and consumers, and Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka are the leading producing states. The CACP recommends MSP for 22 mandated crops: 7 cereals, 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds and 4 commercial crops (copra, sugarcane, cotton, raw jute). For sugarcane, however, it recommends the FRP rather than an MSP. MSP is likewise approved by the CCEA. Other angles UPSC can test: the Essential Commodities Act, the Sugar (Control) Order, the Swaminathan Commission's C2+50% formula, the A2+FL and C2 cost concepts, and PM-AASHA.

ocr: What explains the eastward flow of the equatorial counter-current? (a) The Earth’s rotation on its axis (b) Convergence of the two equatorial currents (c) Difference in salinity of water (ad) Occurrence of the belt of calm near the equator
subject: Geography
detail: In the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, the trade winds drive the North Equatorial Current and the South Equatorial Current westward, one on each side of the equator. They carry warm surface water to the western margins of the ocean basins. This piles up water there, so the sea surface on the western side stands higher than on the eastern side. The doldrums (equatorial low-pressure belt) lie between the two currents, where the winds are weak. The accumulated water flows back eastward under gravity and the pressure gradient, in the zone between the two equatorial currents. This eastward flow is the Equatorial Counter-current, and it is narrow, shallow and warm. In the Pacific it lies roughly 3°N-10°N, mainly in the northern hemisphere. In the Atlantic it is called the Guinea Current in the east. The Coriolis force is weak near the equator, so the pressure gradient can drive the flow. Elimination: (a) Earth's rotation, together with the winds, explains the westward flow of the equatorial currents, not the eastward return. (c) Salinity differences produce only minor density-driven flows. (d) The belt of calm only marks where the counter-current runs. It is not the cause of the flow.
explanations: Wrong: rotation and the trade winds explain the westward equatorial currents. The eastward counter-current is a return flow from the water piled up in the west.
Correct: the two equatorial currents converge on the western side of the ocean, raising the sea level there. The excess water flows back east as the counter-current, driven by the pressure gradient.
Wrong: salinity differences cause only minor density-driven flows, and they do not explain an eastward current that is persistent and ocean-wide.
Wrong: the doldrums are the zone in which the counter-current flows, because the weak winds there offer little opposition. The calm is a condition, not the driving force.
keyfact: The equatorial counter-current flows eastward because water piled up in the west by the converging North and South Equatorial Currents flows back down the pressure gradient.
option_notes: Earth's rotation on its axis, from west to east, produces the Coriolis force. This deflects moving objects to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. It shapes the gyres and western intensification of currents. It is also why the trade winds blow from the east. Its effect is weakest at the equator, because the Coriolis force is zero there.

Convergence of the North and South Equatorial Currents happens in the western parts of the oceans. Both currents are driven westward by the trade winds. Water piles up against the continental margins, raising the sea level by several centimetres. The resulting pressure gradient sends the water back east as the counter-current. The same convergence also produces warm pools such as the Indo-Pacific warm pool.

Salinity differences produce density differences. Denser, saltier water sinks and fresher water stays on the surface. This drives thermohaline circulation, the slow deep-ocean 'conveyor belt'. Surface salinity averages about 35 parts per thousand. It is highest in the subtropics, where evaporation is high (the Atlantic is saltier than the Pacific), and lower near the equator and the poles. Salinity influences mainly deep currents, not surface currents.

The belt of calm, or doldrums, is the equatorial low-pressure zone near 0°-5° where the trade winds converge (the ITCZ). The air rises, so the surface winds are light and variable, and there is heavy convectional rain. Sailing ships were often becalmed there. The equatorial counter-current runs through this zone because the weak winds do not oppose it.
related: The Equatorial Counter-current flows eastward between the North and South Equatorial Currents.
The Gulf Stream is a warm current that is part of the North Atlantic gyre.
The Humboldt (Peru) Current is a cold current off the west coast of South America, and its upwelling supports rich fisheries.
The Indian Ocean has seasonally reversing currents because of the monsoon.
The Grand Banks fishing ground lies where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold Labrador Current.
El Niño is the warming of the eastern Pacific, with weaker trade winds and suppressed upwelling off Peru.
The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles.
The Sargasso Sea lies in the calm centre of the North Atlantic gyre.
summary: The correct answer is (b): the equatorial counter-current flows eastward because of the convergence of the North and South Equatorial Currents. Both currents flow westward and pile up water on the western side of the ocean. This raises the sea level there, and the excess water returns eastward along the equator as a counter-current, driven by the pressure gradient.
topic_notes: Ocean currents are large-scale, continuous movements of surface water. They are driven by planetary winds, the Coriolis force, the distribution of land, temperature and salinity differences, and gravity. Currents can be warm or cold, and the main surface circulation forms gyres: clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern. The equatorial currents flow westward on both sides of the equator, driven by the trade winds. The Equatorial Counter-current flows eastward between them, around 3°N-10°N in the Pacific. Warm currents include the Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio, Brazil Current, Agulhas and East Australian Current. Cold currents include the Labrador, California, Humboldt (Peru), Benguela, Canary and West Australian Currents. Cold currents usually flow along the western coasts of continents in the tropics and subtropics. Warm and cold currents meet and create fishing grounds. Examples are the Grand Banks, where the Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current, and the North Sea. The Indian Ocean is special because its currents reverse seasonally with the monsoon: the North-East Monsoon Current in winter and the South-West Monsoon Current in summer. El Niño involves a weakening of the trade winds and warm water flowing east in the Pacific, and it is linked to a stronger counter-current and the suppression of Humboldt upwelling. La Niña is the opposite. The effects of currents include moderating the climate (the North Atlantic Drift keeps NW Europe warm), fog formation where warm and cold currents meet, and influences on deserts such as the Atacama and Namib, which lie next to cold currents.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Place of Pilgrimage Location
1. Srisailam : Nallamala Hills
2. Omkareshwar : Satmala Hills
3. Pushkar : Mahadeo Hills Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a pilgrimage-geography question, and the elimination logic rests on matching each shrine to its river and range. Srisailam (Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh) sits on the Nallamala Hills, part of the Eastern Ghats, on the right bank of the Krishna. It has the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga and is also a Shakti Peetha (Bhramaramba). Omkareshwar is on Mandhata (Shivapuri) island in the Narmada, Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. The island lies in the Narmada valley between the Vindhya range to the north and the Satpura range to the south. The Satmala Hills are in Maharashtra and are associated with the Ajanta range, so pair 2 is wrong. Pushkar, near Ajmer, has the Brahma temple and the sacred Pushkar lake. It lies in the Aravalli range, while the Mahadeo Hills are a Satpura sub-range around Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh, so pair 3 is wrong. Only pair 1 is correct, which leaves option (a). Remember that two Jyotirlingas are on the Narmada (Omkareshwar and, by some traditions, Mamaleshwar) and that Srisailam is the only Jyotirlinga on the Nallamala Hills.
explanations: Correct. Only pair 1 is matched correctly: Srisailam is in the Nallamala Hills, so the answer is 1 only.
Wrong. This option includes pair 2 and pair 3, and both are mismatched. Omkareshwar is on a Narmada island, not in the Satmala Hills, and Pushkar is in the Aravalli range, not the Mahadeo Hills.
Wrong. It accepts pair 3, but Pushkar is in the Aravalli range and the Mahadeo Hills are in Madhya Pradesh. Pair 1 is correct but pair 3 is not.
Wrong. It requires all three pairs to be correct, but pairs 2 and 3 are wrong.
keyfact: Srisailam = Nallamala Hills (Krishna); Omkareshwar = Narmada island; Pushkar = Aravalli; Mahadeo Hills = Satpura (Pachmarhi).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: Srisailam is a major pilgrimage centre in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Nallamala Hills by the Krishna river. It has the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha, the Bhramaramba temple. The Srisailam dam and the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve are nearby. The Chenchu tribe is native to the area. Vijayanagara rulers gave the temple major patronage.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only: it combines two wrong pairs. Omkareshwar is a Narmada island shrine with a Jyotirlinga in Madhya Pradesh, and the Satmala Hills lie in Maharashtra. Pushkar is an Aravalli-region town in Rajasthan with the Brahma temple, while the Mahadeo Hills are in the Satpura range, Madhya Pradesh. Neither pair is correct.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only: pair 1 is right, but pair 3 is wrong. Pushkar, in Ajmer district, Rajasthan, is by the sacred Pushkar lake and is famed for its Brahma temple and the Kartik fair. Its hills belong to the Aravalli range. The Mahadeo Hills, near Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh, include Dhupgarh, the highest peak of the Satpura.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: this would need every pair to be correct, but two are not. It is a typical trap built on the similar-sounding names Satmala and Satpura and on the well-known Mahadeo Hills. Real locations: Srisailam in the Nallamala, Omkareshwar on the Narmada in the Vindhya-Satpura zone, Pushkar in the Aravalli.
related: Srisailam is the only Jyotirlinga that is also a Shakti Peetha.
The Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve is India's largest tiger reserve by area.
Omkareshwar lies on Mandhata island in the Narmada, Madhya Pradesh.
Pushkar's Brahma temple is one of the very few in India; the Pushkar fair is held in Kartik.
Dhupgarh (Mahadeo Hills, Pachmarhi) is the highest peak of the Satpura range.
Guru Shikhar on Mount Abu is the highest peak of the Aravallis.
Tirumala temple stands on the Seshachalam Hills in Andhra Pradesh.
The Nallamala Hills lie between the Krishna and Penneru rivers.
statements: 1 — Correct: Srisailam is in the Nallamala Hills on the Krishna river. Srisailam is in Nandyal district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Nallamala Hills of the Eastern Ghats. The Mallikarjuna Swamy temple is one of the 12 Jyotirlingas and also one of the 18 Shakti Peethas (Bhramaramba Devi), a combination that is rare. The Srisailam dam on the Krishna forms a large reservoir, and the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve, India's largest tiger reserve, surrounds the area. The Chenchu tribe lives in the region. The Vijayanagara rulers, notably Harihara and Krishnadevaraya, patronised the temple.

2 — Incorrect: Omkareshwar is on the Narmada, not in the Satmala Hills. Omkareshwar is on Mandhata island, shaped like the Om symbol, in the Narmada in Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. It hosts the Omkareshwar Jyotirlinga and the Mamleshwar temple on the south bank. It lies in the Narmada valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, and the Omkareshwar dam is nearby. The Satmala (Chandor) Hills are in Maharashtra, linked with the Ajanta range, and form the watershed between the Godavari and Bhima basins.

3 — Incorrect: Pushkar is in the Aravalli range, not the Mahadeo Hills. Pushkar is in Ajmer district, Rajasthan, on the sacred Pushkar lake. It has one of the few Brahma temples in India. The annual Pushkar Fair is held in Kartik Purnima (Oct-Nov) and is known for its camel trade. It lies within the Aravalli range, near Nag Pahar. The Mahadeo Hills are a Satpura sub-range in Madhya Pradesh, containing Pachmarhi, Dhupgarh (the highest point of the Satpura) and the Satpura National Park.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Srisailam lies in the Nallamala Hills on the Krishna river, but Omkareshwar is on an island in the Narmada in the Vindhya/Satpura region of Madhya Pradesh, and Pushkar is beside the Aravalli range in Rajasthan.
topic_notes: Pilgrimage geography questions pair a shrine with a river, hill range or state. The key ranges are as follows. The Nallamala Hills belong to the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, lying between the Krishna and Penneru rivers. Their highest peak is Bhairani Konda. The Satpura range runs south of the Narmada and includes the Mahadeo Hills, Maikal range and Dhupgarh (1,350 m). Anamudi in the Western Ghats is the highest peak in peninsular India. The Vindhyas run north of the Narmada. The Aravallis, among the oldest fold mountains, run from Delhi to Gujarat, with Guru Shikhar on Mount Abu (1,722 m) the highest point. The Satmala-Ajanta ranges lie in Maharashtra, and the Balaghat range lies to the south. The twelve Jyotirlingas are Somnath (Gujarat), Mallikarjuna (Srisailam), Mahakaleshwar (Ujjain), Omkareshwar (MP), Kedarnath (Uttarakhand), Bhimashankar (Maharashtra), Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi), Trimbakeshwar (Nashik), Vaidyanath (Deoghar, Jharkhand, per tradition), Nageshwar (Dwarka area, Gujarat), Rameshwaram (Tamil Nadu) and Grishneshwar (Maharashtra). Tirumala (Tirupati) is in the Seshachalam Hills. Other pairings UPSC may ask: Amarnath in the Himalaya, Vaishno Devi in the Trikuta hills, Sabarimala in the Western Ghats, Palani in the Palani Hills, Gaya on the Phalgu, and Pushkar on a sacred lake near Ajmer. Remember that river-valley pairs such as Omkareshwar-Narmada, Nashik-Godavari and Ujjain-Kshipra also come up.

question:
With reference to Rowlatt Satyagraha, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. The Rowlatt Act was based on the tecommendations of the ‘Sedition Committee’. B-AQN-0-JUA/63A
2. In Rowlatt Satyagraha, Gandhiji tried to utilize the Home Rule League.
3. Demonstrations against the arrival of Simon Commission coincided with Rowlatt Satyagraha. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Modern History
detail: The Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, March 1919) was passed on the recommendations of the Sedition Committee chaired by Justice Sidney Rowlatt, appointed in 1917 to examine revolutionary and seditious conspiracies, especially the Ghadar and Bengal groups. It allowed detention without trial for up to two years, trial by special courts without juries, and arrest without warrant, so it was called the 'Black Act' ('No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal'). Gandhi launched the Rowlatt Satyagraha by founding the Satyagraha Sabha (Feb 1919) and made use of the organisational network of the Home Rule League, whose young activists became its backbone; he also drew on Pan-Islamist and Khilafat sentiment. The nationwide hartal came on 6 April 1919, followed by the Amritsar arrests of Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal, the firing and Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919. The Simon Commission was announced in November 1927 and reached India in February 1928, nine years later, with 'Simon Go Back' protests. Statement 3 fails on chronology, so only 1 and 2 stand, giving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it ignores statement 2, which is correct because Gandhi used the Home Rule League network.
Correct: statements 1 and 2 are right, and statement 3 is wrong because the Simon Commission came in 1928, not 1919.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, and statement 3 is false on chronology.
Wrong: statement 3 is false, so not all three statements can be correct.
keyfact: Rowlatt Act (1919) came from the Sedition Committee; Gandhi used the Home Rule League network; the Simon Commission came in 1928.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would accept only the Sedition Committee link. The Sedition Committee under Justice Rowlatt (1917-18) investigated revolutionary conspiracies and recommended extension of wartime Defence of India Act powers. This option fails because it leaves out the Home Rule League's role in the satyagraha, which is historically accepted.

Option (b), 1 and 2 only: this is the official answer. The Rowlatt Act of March 1919 followed the Sedition Committee report, and Gandhi used the Home Rule League's network to organise the Rowlatt Satyagraha and hartal of 6 April 1919. The Simon Commission is unrelated in time, being a 1928 event.

Option (c), 2 and 3 only: it wrongly accepts the Simon Commission link. The Simon Commission (1927-30) was a seven-member all-British body reviewing the working of the Government of India Act 1919, and it was boycotted by Congress, the Muslim League (Jinnah faction) and others. It had nothing to do with 1919 events.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: this accepts all statements. It is wrong because of statement 3. The Simon Commission was a consequence of the 1919 Act's provision for a review after ten years, advanced to 1927 by the Conservative government fearing a Labour win, so it falls in 1928 India.
related: Rowlatt Act passed 18 March 1919; repealed 1922.
Satyagraha Sabha was founded on 24 February 1919 in Bombay.
Nationwide hartal held on 6 April 1919.
Jallianwala Bagh massacre: 13 April 1919, General Dyer, Amritsar.
Hunter Committee (1919) inquired into the Punjab disturbances.
Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League in 1920.
Simon Commission arrived in India in February 1928 with all-white membership.
Gandhi suspended Rowlatt Satyagraha on 18 April 1919, calling violence a 'Himalayan miscalculation'.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Rowlatt Act rested on the Sedition Committee report. The committee was set up in December 1917 under Justice S.A.T. Rowlatt, a British judge, to investigate revolutionary crime linked to Germany and Bolshevik influence during and after the First World War. It reported in 1918. The Rowlatt Bills were introduced in the Imperial Legislative Council in February 1919; all Indian members opposed them, and Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazharul Haq resigned. The Act passed on 18 March 1919 and was repealed in 1922.

2 — Correct: Gandhi used the Home Rule League. Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League in 1920, but even in 1919 its branches, run by Annie Besant's and Tilak's followers, gave him an all-India organisation. The Satyagraha Sabha was formed on 24 February 1919 in Bombay, and its signatories pledged civil disobedience of the Act. Younger Home Rule activists, along with Khilafat supporters, helped coordinate the 6 April 1919 hartal across towns and cities.

3 — Incorrect: The Simon Commission came much later. The Indian Statutory Commission, headed by Sir John Simon, was announced in November 1927 and landed in Bombay on 3 February 1928. It had seven British members and no Indians, hence the boycott and 'Simon Go Back' slogans. Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi charge at Lahore on 30 October 1928 and died in November. The Rowlatt Satyagraha was in 1919, so the two did not coincide.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct, statement 3 is wrong. The Rowlatt Act (1919) followed the Sedition Committee (Justice Rowlatt) report, and Gandhi used the Home Rule League network for the satyagraha, while the Simon Commission arrived only in 1928.
topic_notes: Background: During the First World War the Defence of India Act 1915 gave sweeping powers. Fearing revolutionary activity after the war, the government appointed the Sedition Committee (1917) under Justice Rowlatt. Its recommendations became the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, passed on 18 March 1919 despite opposition from every elected Indian member of the Imperial Legislative Council. It allowed arrest without warrant, detention without trial for up to two years, and in-camera trials. Gandhi, then new to all-India politics after Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad mill strike and Kheda (1918), launched the Satyagraha Sabha and called a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919 (originally 30 March, advanced in Delhi where firing occurred). Violence broke out in Punjab, Gujarat and elsewhere. Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal were arrested on 10 April in Amritsar. On 13 April 1919 General Dyer ordered firing on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds. The Hunter Committee was appointed to inquire; Congress held its own inquiry. Tagore renounced his knighthood. Gandhi called off the movement on 18 April, admitting a 'Himalayan miscalculation'. The Act was never actually applied and was repealed in 1922. Related: Khilafat movement and Non-Cooperation (1920-22), Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms and the Government of India Act 1919 (dyarchy in provinces), Chauri Chaura (February 1922). Later: Simon Commission 1928, Nehru Report 1928, Lahore Congress 1929, Dandi March 1930. Typical UPSC angles: sequence of events, persons involved, committees and their purposes.

question: Among the following, which were frequently mentioned in the news for the outbreak of Ebola virus recently?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The question refers to the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak. It began in December 2013 in Guinea, in the Guéckédou area (Meliandou village), and spread to neighbouring Sierra Leone and Liberia. The WHO declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 8 August 2014, and the epidemic was declared over in 2016. About 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths were reported, mostly in these three countries. Ebola is caused by a filovirus of the genus Ebolavirus, is named after the Ebola River in the DR Congo (first identified in 1976), and is a zoonotic disease with fruit bats as the likely natural reservoir. It spreads through direct contact with blood and body fluids. Elimination logic: Syria and Jordan are Middle Eastern and were in the news for conflict and refugees. The Philippines and Papua New Guinea are in Asia-Pacific. Jamaica, Haiti and Surinam are in the Americas. Only option (b) is in West Africa, so it is the only possible answer.
explanations: Wrong. Syria and Jordan were in the news for the Syrian civil war, ISIS and refugee flows, not Ebola. Both are in West Asia, far from the outbreak zone.
Correct. Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia were the three worst-hit countries in the 2014 West African outbreak. Guinea was the origin, and the two others saw the largest case counts.

Wrong. The Philippines and Papua New Guinea are in Southeast Asia and Oceania. The Philippines does have a Reston ebolavirus strain in animals, but it is not known to cause illness in humans, and there was no 2014 outbreak there.
Wrong. Jamaica, Haiti and Surinam are in the Caribbean and South America. Haiti was associated with cholera after the 2010 earthquake, not Ebola.
keyfact: The 2014-16 Ebola epidemic hit Guinea (origin), Sierra Leone and Liberia in West Africa, and the WHO declared it a PHEIC on 8 August 2014.
option_notes: Syria and Jordan are West Asian (Levant) countries. Syria has been in civil war since 2011, with ISIS, chemical weapons concerns and millions of refugees. Jordan hosts large numbers of Syrian refugees (for example the Zaatari camp) and is a constitutional monarchy. Neither has had a major Ebola outbreak.

Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia are West African nations. Guinea is the origin of the 2014 epidemic, with Conakry as its capital. Sierra Leone's capital is Freetown, and Liberia's is Monrovia. All three are among the poorest countries, with weak health systems, which let the virus spread widely. They received international aid and were declared Ebola-free in 2015-16.

The Philippines is a Southeast Asian archipelago, and Papua New Guinea is in Oceania and occupies the eastern half of New Guinea island. The Reston ebolavirus was found in monkeys and pigs in the Philippines, but it is not pathogenic to humans. Neither country had the 2014 epidemic.

Jamaica and Haiti are Caribbean island countries, and Surinam (Suriname) is a small country in northeastern South America. Haiti suffered a cholera epidemic after the 2010 earthquake. Chikungunya and Zika spread in the region later. No Ebola epidemic was recorded in these countries in 2014.
related: The 2014 Ebola outbreak began in Guinea in December 2013 and was declared a PHEIC by the WHO on 8 August 2014.
Ebola is caused by a filovirus and is named after the Ebola River in the DR Congo.
Fruit bats are the suspected natural reservoir of Ebola.
Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) was the first licensed Ebola vaccine, approved in 2019.
The 2018-20 Kivu outbreak in the DR Congo was the second-largest Ebola outbreak.
The Reston ebolavirus is not known to cause disease in humans.
The WHO has declared PHEICs for H1N1, polio, Ebola, Zika, COVID-19 and mpox.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with body fluids, not through the air.
summary: The answer is (b) Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. These three West African countries were the epicentre of the 2014-16 Ebola epidemic, the largest ever recorded, and accounted for almost all of its cases and deaths.
topic_notes: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), earlier called Ebola haemorrhagic fever, is a severe, often fatal illness with a fatality rate of about 50% on average (25-90% in different outbreaks). It is caused by viruses of the family Filoviridae. There are six known species: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Taï Forest, Reston and Bombali. The Zaire ebolavirus caused the 2014 epidemic. The virus was first identified in 1976 in two simultaneous outbreaks, one in Nzara, South Sudan, and one in Yambuku, DR Congo, near the Ebola River. Fruit bats of the Pteropodidae family are considered the natural hosts. Transmission to humans is through infected wild animals (chimpanzees, gorillas, antelopes), and then human to human through direct contact with blood, secretions and body fluids, or contaminated surfaces. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in some cases, internal and external bleeding. Incubation is 2 to 21 days. Treatment is supportive care, although monoclonal antibody therapies (Inmazeb, Ebanga) were later approved. The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo, by Merck) was approved in 2019. The 2014 epidemic was declared a PHEIC on 8 August 2014. The 2018-20 outbreak in the DR Congo (Kivu) was the second largest and was also declared a PHEIC in 2019. Other WHO-declared PHEICs include H1N1 (2009), polio (2014), Zika (2016), COVID-19 (2020) and mpox (2022 and 2024). UPSC often asks about the causes of these diseases, whether they are zoonotic, vaccine details and where the outbreaks occurred.

ocr: With reference to ‘fly ash’ produced by the power plants using coal as fuel, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Fly ash can be used in the production of bricks for building construction. 2. Fly ash can be used as a replacement for some of the Portland cement contents of concrete. 3. Fly ash is made up of silicon dioxide and calcium oxide only, and does not contain any toxic & elements. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only feo} 1 and 3 (d) 3 only
subject: Environment
detail: Fly ash is the fine particulate residue carried off in flue gases when pulverised coal is burnt in thermal power plants, and it is collected by electrostatic precipitators. It is a pozzolanic material: it reacts with calcium hydroxide released during cement hydration to form additional cementitious compounds. This is why it is used in Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC), in blended and high-volume fly ash concrete, in fly ash bricks and blocks, in road embankments, in mine-void filling and in soil stabilisation. Its main constituents are silica (SiO2), alumina (Al2O3), iron oxide (Fe2O3) and lime (CaO), with smaller amounts of magnesium oxide, sulphur trioxide and unburnt carbon. It also holds trace toxic elements such as arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and selenium, which can leach into groundwater from ash ponds. Statement 3 is therefore wrong for two reasons: it names only two oxides, and it denies toxic elements. Elimination logic: once statement 3 is rejected, options (c) and (d) fall away. Statement 1 is clearly true, so (b), which says '2 only', also falls away. That leaves (a). In India, MoEF notifications since 1999 require the use of fly ash products within a set radius of thermal plants.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, which matches this option exactly.
Wrong. Statement 1 is also true, since fly ash is used in bricks, so '2 only' leaves out a correct statement.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong. Statement 3 alone is false, and this option rejects both of the true statements.
keyfact: Fly ash is a pozzolanic coal-combustion waste used in bricks and as a partial cement substitute, but it is a mix of oxides with toxic trace metals, not just SiO2 and CaO.
related: Fly ash is a pozzolanic material that reacts with calcium hydroxide to form cementitious compounds.
Portland Pozzolana Cement contains 15-35% fly ash (IS 1489).
Fly ash is captured from flue gas by electrostatic precipitators.
Class F fly ash is low in calcium and comes from bituminous coal; Class C is high in calcium.
The MoEF 1999 notification mandates the use of fly ash bricks within a set radius of thermal power plants.
Fly ash contains trace toxic metals such as arsenic, lead, mercury and cadmium.
Red mud is the waste from alumina (bauxite) refining, and phosphogypsum is a waste from fertiliser production.
Cenospheres are hollow, lightweight spheres recovered from fly ash.
statements: 1 — Correct: Fly ash is a standard raw material for bricks, blocks and tiles used in building construction. Fly ash bricks are made from fly ash, sand or stone dust, lime or cement and gypsum, and are cured by steam or water rather than burnt in kilns. They are lighter and stronger than clay bricks and save topsoil, since no clay is dug. The MoEF fly ash notification of 1999 (amended 2003 and 2009) mandates their use within 100 km (later 300 km) of coal or lignite thermal plants. The BIS standard is IS 12894. Fly ash bricks also help reduce coal-ash disposal problems and kiln emissions.

2 — Correct: Fly ash can replace part of the Portland cement in concrete, typically 15-35% and up to 50-60% in high-volume mixes. Because it is pozzolanic, it reacts with lime from cement hydration to form calcium silicate hydrate, which improves long-term strength, workability and durability, reduces heat of hydration and lowers permeability. Portland Pozzolana Cement (IS 1489) contains 15-35% fly ash. Replacing cement also cuts CO2 emissions, since cement production is highly carbon-intensive. Class F (low calcium, from bituminous coal) and Class C (high calcium) are the two ASTM classes of fly ash.

3 — Incorrect: Fly ash is not made only of SiO2 and CaO. Its principal components are silica, alumina and iron oxide, with lime in varying amounts (low in Class F, high in Class C). It also contains magnesium oxide, sulphates, unburnt carbon and trace heavy metals such as arsenic, lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and selenium. These can leach into soil and groundwater from ash ponds, and fine particles (PM2.5) cause respiratory problems. Ash-pond breaches and ash dumping are recurring environmental issues in India, which is why disposal and utilisation rules exist.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2. Fly ash is widely used in brick manufacture and as a partial replacement for Portland cement in concrete. Statement 3 is wrong because fly ash is not made of silicon dioxide and calcium oxide only, and it contains toxic trace elements.
topic_notes: Fly ash is the main solid waste of coal-based thermal power, and India produces well over 200 million tonnes of it a year. It consists of fine, glassy, spherical particles of silica, alumina, iron oxide and lime. Fly ash is collected from flue gas by electrostatic precipitators, while the coarser bottom ash falls to the bottom of the boiler. ASTM C618 classifies it as Class F (low calcium, from bituminous coal) and Class C (high calcium, from lignite or sub-bituminous coal). Uses include Portland Pozzolana Cement, ready-mix concrete, bricks, blocks and tiles, road and embankment construction, filling of mines and low-lying areas, soil conditioning in agriculture, and extraction of cenospheres. Environmental concerns include air pollution from fine dust, leaching of heavy metals into groundwater from ash ponds, loss of land to ash ponds and ash-dyke failures. Policy: the MoEF&CC notification of 1999, amended in 2003, 2009 and 2021, mandates use of fly ash-based products in construction within a specified radius of thermal plants and requires plants to achieve near-100% utilisation. Fly Ash Mission and the Fly Ash Utilisation Centre under the Department of Science and Technology have promoted its use. Fly ash bricks also help cut the soil erosion and emissions linked to clay brick kilns. Related topics UPSC may ask about include other pozzolanic materials (silica fume, ground granulated blast furnace slag), red mud from aluminium refining, phosphogypsum, and the use of industrial waste in cement. Questions may also cover the pollutants from thermal power plants (SO2, NOx, mercury, PM) and flue gas desulphurisation requirements.

question:
With reference to ‘dugong’, a mammal found in India, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Itis a herbivorous marine animal.
2. Itis found along the entire coast of India.
3. It is given legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Select the correct answer using the cade given below
subject: Environment
detail: The dugong (Dugong dugon) is a large marine mammal of the order Sirenia, which also includes manatees. It is the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, and its diet is almost entirely seagrass, which is why it is called the 'sea cow'. In India its distribution is patchy and confined to the Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay (Tamil Nadu), the Gulf of Kutch (Gujarat), the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and a few other places. It is absent from most of the east and west coast, so statement 2 fails on the word 'entire'. It is listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which gives the highest protection. The IUCN status is Vulnerable, and it is on CITES Appendix I. It is also listed on CMS (Bonn Convention), and India signed the CMS Dugong MoU. Tamil Nadu declared the Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay in 2022, the first in India. Elimination logic: statement 2 is clearly wrong because of 'entire', so (a) and (b) go, and since statement 3 is true, (c) is correct and (d) is incomplete.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 2, which is false because the dugong is found only in specific pockets and not along the entire coast.
Wrong: statement 2 alone is incorrect, and it leaves out the true statements 1 and 3.
Correct: statement 1 (herbivorous marine mammal) and statement 3 (Schedule I protection) are both true, and statement 2 is false.
Wrong: statement 3 is true, but it omits statement 1, which is also true.
keyfact: Dugong: herbivorous marine mammal (seagrass eater), found only in pockets of India, Schedule I of the WPA 1972, so the answer is 1 and 3.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this option pairs the true herbivore statement with the false 'entire coast' claim. The dugong occurs only in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is not found along the whole coastline, and areas without seagrass lack it. Remember the pattern: UPSC often uses absolute words like 'entire' to make a statement false.

2 only: this would claim the dugong occurs along the entire Indian coast, which is false. Its range depends on seagrass meadows, which are found in a few places such as the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Seagrass loss from pollution, trawling and coastal development has shrunk its range further. The Palk Bay Dugong Conservation Reserve (2022) is India's first such reserve.

1 and 3: the official answer. The dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal (order Sirenia) that feeds on seagrass, and it has Schedule I protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I. The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are key habitats. It is also called the sea cow.

3 only: this option is correct about legal protection but incomplete. Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gives absolute protection with the heaviest penalties, and covers species such as the tiger, elephant, Ganges river dolphin and dugong. It ignores that the dugong is also a herbivorous marine mammal, so it fails by omission.
related: The dugong is also called the 'sea cow' and is the state animal of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve was notified in Palk Bay, Tamil Nadu, in 2022.
Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve was India's first marine biosphere reserve (2001).
Gulf of Kutch Marine National Park (1980) was India's first marine national park.
Dugongs are in order Sirenia along with manatees; the dugong has a fluke tail.
Dugongs are IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I.
India signed the CMS Dugong Memorandum of Understanding in 2008.
Seagrass meadows are blue carbon sinks and the dugong's key habitat.
statements: 1 — Correct: the dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal that grazes on seagrass. Facts: it belongs to the order Sirenia, family Dugongidae, and is the only living member of that family. It has a fluke-like tail, unlike the manatee's paddle-shaped tail. It lives in warm coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Australia, and it can live 70 years. Its slow breeding and dependence on seagrass meadows make it vulnerable to habitat loss, fishing nets and boat strikes.

2 — Incorrect: the dugong is not found along the entire coast of India. Facts: its presence is restricted to the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which have seagrass beds. Populations are small, and the Andamans are thought to hold the healthiest numbers. Seagrass degradation, coastal development, trawling and entanglement in gill nets are the main threats. The Wildlife Institute of India and state forest departments run monitoring. The Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay (Tamil Nadu, 2022) covers about 448 sq km.

3 — Correct: the dugong is listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Facts: Schedule I gives the highest protection, with the strictest penalties for hunting or trade. Other Schedule I species include the tiger, Asiatic lion, snow leopard and Ganges river dolphin. The Act was amended in 2022 and now has four schedules in place of the earlier six. The dugong is IUCN Vulnerable and on CITES Appendix I, and India has signed the CMS Dugong Memorandum of Understanding.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct. The dugong is a herbivorous marine mammal that feeds on seagrass, and it is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is not found along the entire Indian coast, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: The dugong (Dugong dugon) is the only strictly marine herbivorous mammal. It belongs to order Sirenia, which includes the manatees (three species) and the extinct Steller's sea cow. Key identification point: the dugong has a whale-like fluke tail, while the manatee has a rounded paddle tail. It feeds on seagrasses such as Halophila and Halodule, so it depends on healthy seagrass meadows. Gestation lasts about 13 to 14 months and calves are born singly at long intervals, which makes recovery from population decline slow. In India it occurs in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, the Gulf of Kutch and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Legal status: Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; IUCN Vulnerable; CITES Appendix I; CMS listing, with India a signatory to the CMS Dugong MoU (2008). Tamil Nadu notified the Dugong Conservation Reserve in Palk Bay in September 2022, covering about 448 sq km. The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, India's first marine biosphere reserve (2001), is a major habitat. Other marine reserves and species to link: Gulf of Kutch Marine National Park (the first marine national park in India, 1980), Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park in the Andamans, and Olive Ridley turtles, whose nesting site is Gahirmatha in Odisha. Threats include seagrass loss, bycatch in gill nets, boat strikes, pollution and traditional hunting for meat and oil. Related angles for UPSC: UN Convention on Migratory Species, seagrass ecosystems as blue carbon sinks, coral reefs and mangroves, and Schedule listing under the 2022 amendment to the Wildlife Act.

question:
Who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of colonialism in India?
1. Dadabhai Naoroji
2. G. Subramania lyer
3. R. C. Dutt Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The early nationalists, often called Moderates, built the economic critique of colonialism that became the intellectual base of the freedom movement. Dadabhai Naoroji presented the 'Drain of Wealth' theory in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), estimating that a large share of India's surplus was transferred to Britain through Home Charges, salaries, pensions and profits. R. C. Dutt, an ICS officer and later Congress president (1899), wrote 'The Economic History of India' (2 vols, 1901-03), blaming heavy land revenue, destruction of handicrafts and free-trade policy for famines and poverty. G. Subramania Iyer, co-founder of The Hindu (1878) and the Tamil weekly Swadesamitran, and a founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884), wrote sharply on the impoverishing effects of British economic policy, and he exposed Indian poverty in his writings. Other critics include M. G. Ranade, G. K. Gokhale, Romesh Dutt, Dinshaw Wacha, and William Digby, a British sympathiser. Since all three statements are true, option (d) follows; any option omitting one of them is wrong.
explanations: Wrong: it omits G. Subramania Iyer and R. C. Dutt, both of whom also criticised colonial economic policy.
Wrong: it omits R. C. Dutt, whose 'Economic History of India' is a classic critique of colonial economics.
Wrong: it omits Dadabhai Naoroji, the best-known proponent of the drain theory, so it cannot be right.
Correct: Naoroji, Subramania Iyer and Dutt all analysed and condemned the exploitative economic effects of British rule.
keyfact: Naoroji (drain theory), R. C. Dutt (Economic History of India) and G. Subramania Iyer were all economic critics of colonialism, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Dadabhai Naoroji alone: he was the pioneer of economic nationalism, author of 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), and propounded the drain theory. He was Congress president three times and the first Indian MP in Britain (1892). He was a Parsi from Bombay, a professor at Elphinstone College, and founder of the Rast Goftar and the Indian National Association's early efforts. This option is incomplete because it ignores the other two critics.

Naoroji and Subramania Iyer: this pairing is half right. Both indeed criticised colonial economics, but it leaves out R. C. Dutt. Subramania Iyer was a founder of The Hindu (1878), of Swadesamitran, and of the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884). He moved from moderate to more assertive politics, and he was known as a social reformer who backed widow remarriage and opposed caste restrictions on sea travel.

Subramania Iyer and R. C. Dutt: this excludes Naoroji, the foremost drain theorist. Dutt wrote the 'Economic History of India' (1901-03), was Congress president in 1899, and served in the ICS. He argued famines were due to heavy taxation and policy rather than only natural causes, and he wrote a famous series of open letters to Lord Curzon in 1900 on land revenue. He also translated the Ramayana and Mahabharata into English verse.

All three: this is the official correct answer. Dadabhai Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer and R. C. Dutt belong to the school of economic nationalism that exposed colonial exploitation through drain of wealth, high land revenue, discriminatory tariffs, and decline of Indian handicrafts. This school shaped the Moderate Congress demands for reduced military expenditure, Indianisation of services, and protection of Indian industry.
related: Drain theory was first put forward by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1867 in 'England's Debt to India'.
R. C. Dutt presided over the 1899 Lucknow Congress session.
Naoroji was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons (1892).
Ranade wrote 'Essays on Indian Economics' (1898).
William Digby wrote 'Prosperous British India' (1901).
Welby Commission (1895) examined Indian expenditure; Naoroji was a member.
G. Subramania Iyer co-founded The Hindu in 1878.
The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in 1884.
statements: 1 — Correct: Naoroji formulated the drain theory, the core economic critique of colonialism. Dadabhai Naoroji (1825-1917), the 'Grand Old Man of India', founded the East India Association (London, 1866) and was thrice Congress president (1886, 1893, 1906). He first stated the drain in 'England's Debt to India' (1867) and in a paper of 1876, then developed it in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901). He estimated India's per capita income, and in 1892 became the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons, as a Liberal MP for Finsbury Central. He also coined 'Swaraj' as a Congress goal in 1906.

2 — Correct: G. Subramania Iyer (1855-1916) criticised British economic exploitation and the impoverishment of India. A Tamil nationalist from Tiruvaiyaru, he was a teacher and journalist, and a founder of The Hindu (1878) with M. Veeraraghavachariar and others. He started Swadesamitran (1882), a Tamil paper, and helped found the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884). He attended the first Congress session in Bombay (1885). He wrote on Indian poverty, and he was later moved towards Extremist ideas; he supported Annie Besant's Home Rule League and wrote to President Wilson in 1917.

3 — Correct: R. C. Dutt gave a detailed economic history showing colonial policies impoverished India. Romesh Chunder Dutt (1848-1909) joined the ICS in 1871, retired in 1897, and became Congress president at Lucknow in 1899. His 'Economic History of India' covered 'Under Early British Rule' (1757-1837) and 'In the Victorian Age' (1837-1900). He criticised high land revenue demand, the permanent settlement's effects, and the ruin of cotton industries. He also wrote 'India in the Victorian Age', and was Dewan of Baroda in his last years.
summary: The answer is (d): all three, Dadabhai Naoroji, G. Subramania Iyer and R. C. Dutt, were economic critics of colonialism. Each analysed British rule as a drain on India's wealth and a cause of poverty and de-industrialisation.
topic_notes: Economic nationalism was the major intellectual contribution of the Moderates (1885-1905). Early writers showed that British rule, far from being benign, drained India's resources. Key idea: the 'drain of wealth', meaning an unrequited export of resources to Britain through Home Charges (interest on public debt, railway guarantees, salaries, pensions, and stores), profits of foreign capital and shipping charges. Naoroji's estimates in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule' were widely quoted; he held that the drain was about a fifth to a half of revenue. R. C. Dutt gave the historical proof; his book is considered the first systematic economic history of British India. Other critics: M. G. Ranade ('Essays on Indian Economics', 1898), G. V. Joshi, G. K. Gokhale, Dinshaw Wacha, P. Ananda Charlu, G. Subramania Iyer, and Digby ('Prosperous British India', 1901). Later Marxist and nationalist writers included R. P. Dutt ('India Today', 1940), and Jawaharlal Nehru's 'Discovery of India'. Colonial economic features: ruin of handicrafts (de-industrialisation), commercialisation of agriculture, land revenue systems (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari, Mahalwari), famines (1770, 1876-78, 1896-97, 1899-1900), railway policy, and free trade policy. The Famine Commissions (1880 Campbell, 1898 Lyall, 1901 MacDonnell) and Indian Famine Codes were responses. The Congress passed resolutions on the salt tax, military expenditure and the Welby Commission (1895), where Naoroji testified. Expect questions on authors versus books, Congress presidencies and the stages of colonial economic exploitation, namely mercantilism, free trade and finance imperialism.

question: Which one of the following issues the ‘Global Economic Prospects’ report periodically?
options: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
subject: Economy
detail: Global Economic Prospects is published by the World Bank's Development Prospects Group, usually in January and June each year. It analyses recent global economic developments, gives growth forecasts for advanced economies and for emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), and covers regions such as East Asia and Pacific, South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, Middle East and North Africa, and Europe and Central Asia. The June edition usually includes a special-focus chapter on a specific policy theme. Elimination logic: the Asian Development Bank publishes the Asian Development Outlook (ADO); the EBRD publishes the Transition Report and Regional Economic Prospects; the US Federal Reserve issues the Beige Book, Monetary Policy Report and FOMC projections, not a global development outlook. The IMF's comparable report is the World Economic Outlook (April and October). Students should link each major institution to its flagship publication, since UPSC frequently tests these pairings. The World Bank was founded in 1944 at Bretton Woods and is headquartered in Washington, D.C.
explanations: Incorrect: the ADB publishes the Asian Development Outlook, focused on developing Asia, not Global Economic Prospects.
Incorrect: the EBRD publishes the Transition Report and regional economic prospects for its countries of operation; it does not issue GEP.
Incorrect: the US Federal Reserve is the US central bank and issues the Beige Book and monetary policy reports, not a global outlook report.
Correct: the World Bank issues Global Economic Prospects twice a year, in January and June.
keyfact: Global Economic Prospects is the World Bank's twice-yearly (January and June) report, whereas the IMF's counterpart is the World Economic Outlook.
option_notes: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) was established in 1966 and is headquartered in Manila, Philippines. It promotes social and economic development in Asia and the Pacific through loans, grants, technical assistance and equity investments. Japan and the US are the largest shareholders, and its presidents have traditionally been Japanese. Its flagship publication is the Asian Development Outlook, with updates during the year. India is a member and one of its larger borrowers.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) was established in 1991, after the fall of communism, to support transition to market economies in Central and Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union. It is headquartered in London. It has since expanded to regions including Central Asia, the Southern and Eastern Mediterranean and Sub-Saharan Africa. India became a member in 2018. Its main publication is the Transition Report, and it also issues Regional Economic Prospects.

The US Federal Reserve System is the central bank of the United States, created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. It is headed by a Board of Governors in Washington, D.C., and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets monetary policy and the federal funds rate.
