It publishes the Beige Book eight times a year, the Monetary Policy Report and the Summary of Economic Projections. Its decisions strongly influence global capital flows and exchange rates.

The World Bank was created at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. The World Bank Group comprises IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. It provides loans and grants for development and poverty reduction. Its major reports include Global Economic Prospects, World Development Report, Doing Business (discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities) and Ease of Doing Business-related datasets, and the Human Capital Index.
related: The IMF's flagship growth forecast report is the World Economic Outlook, released in April and October.
The World Bank's World Development Report has been published annually since 1978.
The Asian Development Outlook is the ADB's flagship economic report.
The Doing Business report was discontinued by the World Bank in 2021 after data irregularities.
The Human Development Report is published by UNDP, not the World Bank.
The World Economic Forum publishes the Global Gender Gap Report and the Global Risks Report.
UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report.
The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID.
summary: The answer is (d) The World Bank. Global Economic Prospects (GEP) is the World Bank Group's flagship twice-yearly report (January and June) assessing the outlook for the global economy and for developing regions.
topic_notes: Prelims often tests which institution publishes which report. World Bank: Global Economic Prospects (January and June), World Development Report (annual, since 1978), Human Capital Index, Logistics Performance Index, Migration and Development Brief, Commodity Markets Outlook. Doing Business was discontinued in September 2021 and was replaced by the Business Ready (B-READY) project. IMF: World Economic Outlook (April and October, with updates in January and July), Global Financial Stability Report, Fiscal Monitor, External Sector Report. UNDP: Human Development Report. UNCTAD: World Investment Report, Trade and Development Report. WEF: Global Competitiveness Report, Global Gender Gap Report, Global Risks Report, Global Information Technology Report. OECD: Economic Outlook (twice a year), PISA. UNEP: Emissions Gap Report. WIPO: Global Innovation Index. FAO: State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World, Food Outlook. WTO: World Trade Report, World Trade Statistical Review. Transparency International: Corruption Perceptions Index. Oxfam: inequality reports released at Davos. ADB: Asian Development Outlook. The World Bank's GEP typically covers growth forecasts, risks such as inflation, debt and geopolitical tension, and policy chapters on topics such as commodity prices or investment slowdown. Know each institution's headquarters, founding year and membership, because questions often mix these facts with publication names.

ocr: When the Reserve Bank of India reduces the Statutory Liquidity Ratio by 50 basis points, which of the following is likely to happen? (a) India’s GDP growth rate increases drastically (b) Foreign Institutional Investors may bring more capital into our country (c) Scheduled Commercial Banks may cut their lending rates fd) It may drastically reduce the liquidity to the banking system
subject: Economy
detail: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is the share of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that it must hold in liquid form: cash, gold, or unencumbered approved securities (G-secs, T-bills, state development loans). It is held with the bank itself, unlike the CRR, which is held with the RBI. The legal basis is Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The statutory floor is 0% and the earlier ceiling was 40%; the RBI sets the actual rate. SLR was 25% from 2007 to 2020. It was cut to 18% in 2020, and it was 18% in 2015 when the question was asked. It has since risen to 18% from a 2020-era dip and is now 18%. A 50 bp cut is only a 0.5 percentage point change. It marginally raises lendable resources and eases pressure on lending rates. It is a modest, gradual measure, not a drastic one. Elimination: (a) GDP growth cannot rise 'drastically' from a small change; (b) FII flows depend on global conditions, returns and the exchange rate more than SLR; (d) a cut increases liquidity, it does not reduce it, and a 50 bp cut would not be 'drastic'.
explanations: Wrong. Growth depends on many factors such as investment, demand and global conditions. A 50 bp SLR cut is a small step, so a 'drastic' rise in GDP growth is unrealistic.

Wrong. FII flows respond to global liquidity, interest differentials, growth prospects and currency outlook. A minor change in domestic SLR is not a direct driver, so this is not the 'likely' outcome.
Correct. A lower SLR lets banks hold fewer government securities and lend more. The higher supply of loanable funds eases pressure on interest rates, so banks may cut lending rates.
Wrong. Cutting SLR increases liquidity available to banks for lending; it does not reduce it. A 50 bp change is also too small to be 'drastic'.
keyfact: Lower SLR frees bank funds for lending, so credit expands and lending rates may fall, but a 50 bp cut is far too small to be 'drastic'.
option_notes: India's GDP growth rate is measured by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), using GDP at constant prices, with base year 2011-12. It is reported quarterly and annually. Growth is driven by consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. Monetary tools such as SLR, CRR and repo rate influence growth only indirectly and with lags. Large swings in growth come from structural or external shocks, not from small policy tweaks.

Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs), now covered under the Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) framework from 2014, are overseas entities such as pension funds, mutual funds and insurers that invest in Indian securities. They are regulated by SEBI, with the RBI also setting limits. FPI flows are portfolio (non-FDI) investments, are volatile ('hot money'), and depend on interest differentials, growth outlook, global risk appetite and exchange rates. Investment of under 10% in a company counts as portfolio investment.

Scheduled Commercial Banks are banks listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934. They must have paid-up capital and reserves of at least Rs 5 lakh and satisfy the RBI that depositors' interests are not at risk. They get access to RBI refinance and the liquidity adjustment facility. They include public sector banks, private banks, foreign banks, Regional Rural Banks and Small Finance Banks. They must maintain CRR and SLR. Since 2016 lending rates are linked to external benchmarks, and the MCLR was introduced in April 2016.

Liquidity in the banking system is the availability of funds, which the RBI manages through the repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, open market operations (OMO), the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) and the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS). Liquidity is injected by cutting CRR or SLR, buying securities through OMO, or lowering the repo rate. It is drained by the opposite actions. The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) handles day-to-day management, and the net position is called surplus or deficit liquidity.
related: SLR is governed by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; CRR by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934.
CRR is held as cash with the RBI; SLR assets are held by the banks themselves.
SLR can be maintained in cash, gold or approved securities such as G-secs.
MSF rate is repo plus 25 bp and lets banks dip into their SLR holdings.
The MPC has six members, of whom three are from the RBI, and the Governor chairs it.
A cut in repo rate makes borrowing cheaper and tends to increase liquidity.
Open market purchases of securities by the RBI inject liquidity; sales absorb it.
MCLR was introduced in April 2016, replacing the base rate system.
summary: The answer is (c): Scheduled Commercial Banks may cut their lending rates. A lower SLR means banks must park less of their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) in liquid assets such as government securities, cash and gold. This frees up funds for lending, which raises credit supply and can push lending rates down.
topic_notes: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is a quantitative monetary tool under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Banks must keep a prescribed percentage of NDTL in liquid assets: cash, gold, and approved securities such as G-secs, T-bills and State Development Loans. These assets stay with the bank itself. The RBI can fix SLR at any level; the statutory ceiling of 40% was removed in 2007 by an amendment to the Act. Purposes of SLR include ensuring bank solvency and liquidity, controlling credit expansion, and creating a captive market for government borrowing. Raising SLR reduces credit and tightens liquidity; cutting it does the opposite. Compare with CRR, which is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934. CRR is a percentage of NDTL that banks keep as cash with the RBI, earns no interest, and cannot be used for lending. The CRR floor of 3% was removed in 2006, so the RBI can set any level. Other tools include the repo rate (rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities), the reverse repo (rate at which the RBI absorbs liquidity), the MSF rate (repo plus 25 bp, allowing banks to borrow overnight against SLR securities), and the Bank Rate (the long-term lending rate). Policy rates are decided by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member body created by the RBI Act amendment of 2016 under the flexible inflation targeting framework, with CPI inflation targeted at 4% (±2%). Qualitative tools include margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit control. The 'liquidity coverage ratio' under Basel III is a separate concept from SLR. A cut in SLR transmits to lower lending rates only if banks pass on the benefit, which depends on transmission efficiency, a point UPSC may probe.

ocr: With reference to the use of nano- technology in health sector, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Targeted drug delivery is made possible by nanotechnology. 2. Nanotechnology can largely contribute to gene therapy. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b} 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Nanotechnology works with materials at 1-100 nm, where properties differ from bulk matter. In health it is used for drug delivery, diagnostics, imaging, tissue engineering and gene therapy. Targeted drug delivery uses liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, gold nanoparticles and carbon nanotubes. These carry a drug to diseased tissue, such as a tumour, either through the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect or by ligands/antibodies on the surface. This raises efficacy and reduces side effects, so Statement 1 is correct. Gene therapy needs safe vectors to deliver DNA, siRNA or CRISPR components into cells. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles and gold nanoparticles serve as non-viral vectors and avoid the immunogenicity risks of viral vectors. Lipid nanoparticles were used in mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, which shows their delivery power. So Statement 2 is correct. Elimination logic: both statements describe well-established applications, so (a), (b) and (d) fail. UPSC questions on this theme are typically straightforward and reward knowing the applications and the risks (nanotoxicity, regulation, environmental concerns).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 2 is also correct; nanotechnology does contribute to gene therapy.
(b) is wrong because Statement 1 is also correct; targeted drug delivery is a core nanomedicine application.
(c) is right because both statements are correct: targeted drug delivery and gene therapy are both enabled by nanotechnology.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: Nanotechnology in health enables both targeted drug delivery (nanocarriers) and gene therapy (non-viral nanoparticle vectors), so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold if only targeted drug delivery were valid. Targeted delivery uses nanocarriers like liposomes and polymeric nanoparticles to concentrate drugs at diseased sites by passive (EPR effect) or active (ligand-receptor) targeting. Doxil, a liposomal doxorubicin, was approved by the US FDA in 1995 as the first nano-drug. Here it is incomplete because gene therapy applications also hold true.

Option (b), '2 only', would hold if only gene therapy were valid. Gene therapy introduces, edits or silences genes to treat disease, using viral vectors (adenovirus, AAV, lentivirus) or non-viral vectors such as nanoparticles. Examples include Luxturna for retinal disease and Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy (both viral vector based). It is wrong here because targeted drug delivery is also a correct statement.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official correct answer. It reflects that nanomedicine covers both drug delivery and gene delivery. Nanoparticles of 1-100 nm can be engineered to carry drugs or nucleic acids, cross biological barriers, target specific cells and release cargo in a controlled way. Applications also include imaging contrast agents, biosensors, antimicrobial coatings, tissue scaffolds and cancer therapy such as photothermal treatment with gold nanoshells.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean nanotechnology had no role in either area, which is false. Nanotechnology is widely researched and used in medicine, with approved products in oncology, vaccines (lipid nanoparticle mRNA), imaging and RNA interference drugs. Concerns exist about nanotoxicity, bioaccumulation and regulation, but these do not negate the applications. India's Nano Mission (2007, DST) supports such research.
related: Nanoscale range is 1-100 nm; 1 nm equals one billionth of a metre.
India's Nano Mission was launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology.
Doxil (liposomal doxorubicin) was the first FDA-approved nano-drug in 1995.
Lipid nanoparticles delivered the mRNA in the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines.
Patisiran (Onpattro, 2018) was the first approved siRNA drug and uses an LNP carrier.
The EPR effect lets nanoparticles accumulate in tumours through leaky blood vessels.
IFFCO's Nano Urea is a nano-fertiliser launched in 2021.
Silver nanoparticles are used for antimicrobial wound dressings and water purification.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nanocarriers can deliver drugs specifically to target cells or tissues. Liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, dendrimers, quantum dots and gold nanoparticles act as carriers. Passive targeting uses the EPR effect in leaky tumour blood vessels, while active targeting uses surface ligands, antibodies or folate that bind receptors on diseased cells. Examples: liposomal doxorubicin (Doxil), the first FDA-approved nano-drug (1995), and albumin-bound paclitaxel (Abraxane). Benefits are lower dose, fewer side effects, controlled release and the ability to cross barriers such as the blood-brain barrier. Challenges are toxicity, cost, clearance by the immune system and regulation.

2 — Correct: Nanoparticles serve as non-viral vectors that carry DNA, RNA or gene-editing tools into cells. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, gold nanoparticles and dendrimers protect genetic material from degradation and aid cell entry. They avoid the immune reactions and insertional mutagenesis risks linked with viral vectors. Lipid nanoparticles carried the mRNA in the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines, and the first siRNA drug, patisiran (Onpattro, 2018), uses an LNP. Nanotechnology is also used with CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. Gene therapy treats genetic disorders by correcting, replacing or silencing faulty genes.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. Nanotechnology enables targeted drug delivery through engineered nanocarriers, and it is a major enabler of gene therapy because nanoparticles can carry genetic material into cells.
topic_notes:
Nanotechnology deals with structures of 1-100 nanometres (1 nm = 10^-9 m). At this scale materials show altered optical, electrical, magnetic and chemical properties because of quantum effects and large surface-area-to-volume ratio. Types of nanomaterials: nanoparticles, nanotubes (carbon nanotubes), fullerenes, quantum dots, nanowires, dendrimers, liposomes and graphene.

Health applications: (1) targeted drug delivery, especially in cancer; (2) gene therapy and RNA delivery, using lipid nanoparticles; (3) diagnostics and imaging, including quantum dots, magnetic nanoparticles for MRI, and nano-biosensors; (4) tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, using nanofibre scaffolds; (5) antimicrobial uses, such as silver nanoparticles in wound dressings; (6) theranostics, combining therapy and diagnosis; (7) nanorobots, which are still experimental; (8) vaccines, such as mRNA-LNP COVID-19 vaccines.

Other sectors: water purification (nano-filters, silver and titanium dioxide), agriculture (nano-fertilisers such as IFFCO's Nano Urea, nano-pesticides), energy (solar cells, batteries), electronics, cosmetics (sunscreens with ZnO or TiO2), textiles and food packaging.

India: the Nano Mission was launched in 2007 by the Department of Science and Technology with Rs 1,000 crore over five years. It promotes basic research, infrastructure, applications, human resources and international collaboration. Nano Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI) preceded it in 2001. Centres exist at institutes such as IISc and IITs.

Risks and regulation: nanotoxicity, bioaccumulation, environmental release, and gaps in specific regulation. India has drafted guidelines for nanopharmaceuticals (2019) and the Department of Biotechnology and ICMR have related guidance. Possible future questions: carbon nanotube properties, graphene, nano-silver, quantum dots, nano urea, and the difference between top-down and bottom-up synthesis.

question: In India, markets in agricultural products are regulated under the
options: Agricultural Produce Market Committee Act enacted by States
Food Products Order, 1956 and Meat and Food Products Order, 1973
subject: Economy
detail: Regulation of agricultural produce markets in India is a State subject (Entry 28, State List: 'Markets and fairs'; Entry 14: Agriculture). Each State therefore passed its own APMC Act (Bombay/Madras/Punjab-type laws from the 1930s-1960s, with a push after the 1960s). These Acts notify agricultural commodities, set up market yards run by Agricultural Produce Market Committees, mandate sale through licensed commission agents/traders, levy market fees and ensure auction-based price discovery. The Centre only offered a Model APMC Act in 2003 and Model APLM Act 2017 for States to adopt; it cannot directly enforce them. In 2020 the Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act created trade areas outside APMC yards, but the three farm laws were repealed in 2021. Elimination: the Essential Commodities Act 1955 controls production, supply, distribution and prices of notified essential items (stock limits), not market yards. The Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act 1937 provides quality standards (Agmark). The Food Products Order 1956 and Meat Food Products Order 1973 concern food-processing licensing and hygiene, not marketing regulation.
explanations: Wrong: the Essential Commodities Act 1955 regulates supply, stock-holding and prices of essential goods, not the functioning of agricultural markets.
Correct: State-enacted APMC Acts establish and regulate market yards, licensing, fees and auctions for agricultural produce.
Wrong: the 1937 Grading and Marking Act deals with quality certification (Agmark), not market regulation.
Wrong: these orders deal with licensing and standards for fruit/vegetable product processors and meat product makers, not mandis.
keyfact: Agricultural markets (mandis) are regulated by State-enacted APMC Acts, since 'markets and fairs' is a State subject.
option_notes: The Essential Commodities Act, 1955 empowers the Centre to control production, supply, distribution, trade and price of notified essential commodities (e.g., pulses, edible oils, onions, foodstuffs, drugs, fertilisers). Tools include stock limits, licensing and price control; violations can lead to penal action. Amended in 2020 to deregulate items except in extraordinary price rises (spike thresholds of 100% for perishables, 50% for non-perishables); the Act is administered by the Department of Food and Public Distribution and State governments under delegation.

APMC Acts are State laws that regulate the first sale of notified agricultural produce, mainly through regulated market yards managed by market committees. Features: licensed traders and commission agents, auction, market fee and commission charges, and dispute resolution. Criticised for cartelisation, high mandi fees and restriction on direct sales. Reform efforts: Model APMC Act 2003, e-NAM (launched April 2016), Model APLM Act 2017; Bihar repealed its APMC Act in 2006; Kerala never had one.

The Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 provides for grading and quality marking of agricultural and allied produce, giving rise to the 'Agmark' certification. It is administered by the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection (DMI) under the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, headquartered at Faridabad, with its head office in Nagpur and regional offices. Agmark grades products like ghee, honey, spices, pulses, oils and cereals. It is voluntary, unlike mandatory BIS standards for certain items.

The Fruit Products Order (FPO) 1955 and related Food Products Order 1956 regulated manufacture of fruit and vegetable products, requiring licences and hygiene standards; the Meat Food Products Order 1973 regulated meat processing units. These were issued under the Essential Commodities Act. They were repealed in 2016 when the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 consolidated food laws, administered by FSSAI. They never governed agricultural marketing.
related: Markets and fairs: Entry 28 of the State List.
e-NAM was launched on 14 April 2016, managed by SFAC.
Model APMC Act was circulated in 2003; Model APLM Act in 2017.
Bihar abolished its APMC Act in 2006.
Agmark is administered by the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection.
Essential Commodities Act 1955 was amended in 2020 and stock limits apply only under price spikes.
The three farm laws were repealed in 2021.
MSP is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP).
summary: The answer is (b). Agricultural markets (mandis) in India are regulated through the Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) Acts enacted by individual States, because 'markets and fairs' and agriculture fall in the State domain under the Constitution's Seventh Schedule.
topic_notes: Agricultural marketing in India is governed mainly by State APMC Acts. Constitutionally, agriculture and markets are State subjects, so the Centre can only advise through model laws. Regulated markets began with the Cotton and Grain Markets Acts in the colonial era, such as the Berar Cotton and Grain Markets Law of 1887 and the Bombay Cotton Markets Act of 1927; the Royal Commission on Agriculture (1928) recommended regulated markets. Post-independence, States passed APMC Acts and the network of mandis grew. Problems: limited mandi density, middlemen, high fees, restrictions on private markets, and farmers being forced to sell in notified yards. Reforms include the Model APMC Act 2003 (contract farming, private markets, direct purchase), e-NAM (April 2016, online trading platform run by SFAC), Model Agricultural Produce and Livestock Marketing (Promotion and Facilitation) Act 2017, and Model Contract Farming Act 2018. The 2020 farm laws (Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce Act, Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, and the Essential Commodities Amendment Act) were repealed in November 2021 after protests. Related pricing tools: MSP announced by the CACP-recommended process for 22 crops plus FRP for sugarcane; procurement by FCI and NAFED. Other institutions: Agri-marketing directorate DMI, Gramin Agricultural Markets (GrAMs), Agri Infrastructure Fund (2020), FPOs, and the Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority, which regulates negotiable warehouse receipts.

ocr: Which one of the following is the national aquatic animal of India? (a) Saltwater crocodile (bj) Olive ridley turtle (c) Gangetic dolphin (ad) Gharial
subject: Environment
detail: India's National Aquatic Animal is the Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica gangetica), notified on 5 October 2009 at the first meeting of the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA), chaired by the Prime Minister. It is a freshwater, nearly blind mammal that navigates by echolocation, and it is found in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu river systems of India, Bangladesh and Nepal. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, placed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and in Appendix I of CITES. It is also covered under CMS (Bonn Convention). The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bhagalpur, Bihar, is the only dolphin sanctuary in India. National Dolphin Day is observed on 5 October, and Project Dolphin was announced in 2020. Elimination logic: the saltwater crocodile and the olive ridley are marine or estuarine species, and neither has been given national status. The gharial is a freshwater, fish-eating crocodilian, but it is Critically Endangered and has no national symbol status. The question asks for a mammal that is truly aquatic and is a national symbol, which points to the dolphin.
explanations: Incorrect: the saltwater (estuarine) crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, is a reptile and is not India's national aquatic animal.
Incorrect: the olive ridley is a marine turtle famous for mass nesting (arribada) at Gahirmatha, Odisha, but it holds no national symbol status.
Correct: the Gangetic dolphin was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009.
Incorrect: the gharial is a fish-eating crocodilian of Himalayan rivers and is Critically Endangered, but it is not the national aquatic animal.
keyfact: Gangetic river dolphin = National Aquatic Animal of India (2009); Endangered; Vikramshila Sanctuary, Bihar.
option_notes: The saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) is the largest living reptile. It lives in estuaries, mangroves and coasts, and in India it is found in Bhitarkanika (Odisha), the Sundarbans and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is listed under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Bhitarkanika has a major crocodile conservation programme begun in the 1975 Crocodile Project.

The olive ridley turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) is the most abundant sea turtle and is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. It is famous for mass nesting (arribada) at Gahirmatha, Rushikulya and Devi river mouth in Odisha. It is listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act and in CITES Appendix I. Odisha uses Turtle Excluder Devices to reduce bycatch in trawl nets.

The Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is a freshwater cetacean that is almost blind and uses echolocation. It is Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. It was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009. It is found in the Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. Vikramshila Sanctuary in Bihar protects it. Project Dolphin was announced in 2020, and 5 October is National Dolphin Day.

The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is a long-snouted, fish-eating crocodilian, listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. It is found in the Chambal, Girwa, Gandak and Ramganga rivers. The National Chambal Sanctuary is its major stronghold. Males have a bulbous snout growth called a ghara.
related: The Gangetic dolphin was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009.
The Gangetic dolphin is listed as Endangered by the IUCN.
Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary is in Bhagalpur, Bihar.
National Dolphin Day is observed on 5 October.
Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020.
The Irrawaddy dolphin is found in Chilika Lake, Odisha.
The Indus river dolphin (Platanista minor) is found in the Beas river, Punjab.
The gharial is Critically Endangered and found in the Chambal sanctuary.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Gangetic dolphin. The Gangetic river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) was declared India's National Aquatic Animal in 2009 by the Government of India (announced via the National Ganga River Basin Authority, NGRBA). It is a flagship species and an indicator of the health of the river ecosystem.
topic_notes: National symbols of India are a frequent UPSC prelims topic. National Animal: Tiger (Panthera tigris), which replaced the lion in 1972. National Bird: Indian peafowl. National Aquatic Animal: Gangetic river dolphin (2009). National Heritage Animal: Elephant (2010). National Reptile: King cobra is sometimes cited, though it is not officially notified, so treat it cautiously. National Flower: Lotus. National Tree: Banyan. National Fruit: Mango. The Gangetic dolphin belongs to the family Platanistidae. Its two subspecies are the Ganges river dolphin and the Indus river dolphin (Platanista minor, found in the Beas in Punjab). Both were treated as separate species in 1998. It is a mammal that breathes air, and it has no functional eye lens, so it relies on sound. Threats include habitat fragmentation by dams and barrages, pollution, entanglement in fishing nets, and poaching for oil used as fish bait. Legal protection includes Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Appendix I of CITES and Appendix II of CMS. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies in the Ganga between Sultanganj and Kahalgaon in Bihar. Project Dolphin, announced on 15 August 2020, resembles Project Tiger and Project Elephant. The first national survey of river dolphins reported roughly 6,000 individuals (2023). Other aquatic fauna questions may cover the Irrawaddy dolphin in Chilika Lake and the dugong in the Gulf of Mannar, which has a Dugong Conservation Reserve in Tamil Nadu (2022). The Namami Gange programme and the NGRBA also relate to the river's ecology.

ocr: With reference to Congress Socialist Party, consider the following statements : 1. It advocated the boycott of British goods and evasion of taxes. It wanted to establish the dicta- torship of proletariat. It advocated separate electorate for minorities and oppressed classes. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 1 and 2 only (a} 3 only (b) fc) 1, 2 and 3 (dj None
subject: Modern History
detail: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 at Bombay (its first conference was held at Patna in May 1934, and Bombay in October 1934) by younger Congress leaders such as Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Minoo Masani, Ram Manohar Lohia, Achyut Patwardhan and Asoka Mehta. It arose after the Civil Disobedience Movement was withdrawn, when many Congressmen felt that the Gandhian leadership lacked a clear economic programme. The CSP aimed to work inside the Congress and give it a socialist, anti-imperialist and peasant-worker orientation. It wanted nationalisation of key industries, elimination of princely states and landlordism, and redistribution of land to peasants. It was Marxist-influenced but did not openly adopt the dictatorship of the proletariat; it favoured democratic socialism. Separate electorates were the demand of the Muslim League and of Ambedkar (Communal Award, 1932), and the Congress and the CSP opposed them. Boycott of British goods and evasion of taxes are Congress methods in the non-cooperation and civil disobedience movements (the no-tax campaign), not the CSP's defining programme. Since every statement fails, (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect (boycott and tax evasion were Congress movement methods) and statement 2 is incorrect (the CSP did not aim at the dictatorship of the proletariat).
(b) is wrong because statement 3 is incorrect; the CSP did not demand separate electorates, which were a feature of communal politics and the Communal Award.
(c) is wrong because none of the three statements describes the CSP accurately, so they cannot all be correct.
(d) is correct because all three statements are incorrect, which is the official answer.
keyfact: The Congress Socialist Party (1934) was a democratic-socialist group inside the Congress; it neither wanted proletarian dictatorship nor separate electorates, so the answer is None.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only: it pairs the boycott-and-tax-evasion statement with the dictatorship-of-the-proletariat statement. The first describes Congress mass agitation such as Swadeshi (1905), Non-Cooperation (1920-22) and the no-tax campaigns of Civil Disobedience (1930). The second describes the Marxist-Leninist aim of the Communist parties, not the democratic socialism of the CSP.

Option (b), 3 only: it refers to the demand for separate electorates for minorities and oppressed classes. Separate electorates for Muslims came with the 1909 Morley-Minto Reforms and were extended to Sikhs, Christians and others in 1919 and 1932. Ambedkar demanded them for the depressed classes, which led to the Communal Award (August 1932) and the Poona Pact (September 1932).

Option (c), 1, 2 and 3: it claims that the CSP combined boycott and tax evasion, proletarian dictatorship and separate electorates. These are three unrelated strands: Congress mass-movement methods, Communist ideology and communal or minority politics. The CSP was a socialist grouping inside the Congress, formed in 1934, so this combination does not describe it.

Option (d), None: this is the correct answer. It reflects that the CSP was formed in 1934 as a socialist group inside the Congress, led by JP Narayan, Narendra Dev, Lohia, Masani and others. Its ideas were Marxist-influenced but democratic, and it stressed workers' and peasants' organisation, land reform and nationalisation, with no separate electorates.
related: The Congress Socialist Party was founded in 1934; its first conference was at Patna under Acharya Narendra Dev.
JP Narayan was the general secretary of the CSP and wrote 'Why Socialism?' (1936).
The All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 at Lucknow with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as president.
The Communist Party of India was formed in 1920 at Tashkent (by M.N. Roy) and organised in India in 1925 at Kanpur.
The Poona Pact (1932) replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes with reserved seats.
The Forward Bloc was founded by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939 after he left the Congress.
The Karachi Congress (1931) adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic programme.
In 1948 the socialists left the Congress and formed the Socialist Party; in 1952 it became the Praja Socialist Party.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Boycott of British goods and tax evasion were methods of the Congress mass movements (Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience), not the CSP's defining aim. The CSP concentrated on organising workers and peasants and on a socialist programme within the Congress. Swadeshi and boycott began with the Bengal partition agitation in 1905. Non-Cooperation (1920-22) included boycott of courts, schools and foreign cloth, and Civil Disobedience (1930) included the salt law violation and no-tax campaigns.

2 — Incorrect: The CSP did not formally seek the dictatorship of the proletariat. That is the Communist Party's goal, and the Communist Party of India (founded 1920 at Tashkent or in 1925 at Kanpur by different accounts) was Marxist-Leninist. The CSP drew on Marxism but favoured democratic socialism and stayed within the Congress, aiming for a socialist society through mass mobilisation and constitutional means. Jayaprakash Narayan wrote 'Why Socialism?' (1936), which set out its approach.

3 — Incorrect: The CSP did not demand separate electorates for minorities and oppressed classes. The Communal Award (1932) gave separate electorates to the depressed classes, and Gandhi's fast led to the Poona Pact (1932), which replaced them with reserved seats in joint electorates. Separate electorates had been granted to Muslims under the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909. The Congress and socialists generally opposed them as divisive.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three statements are incorrect. The Congress Socialist Party (CSP, 1934) was a socialist group within the Congress that aimed at Marxian-influenced socialism and economic equality. It did not advocate boycott and tax evasion as its programme, did not seek the dictatorship of the proletariat, and did not demand separate electorates.
topic_notes: The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934, after the Civil Disobedience Movement was suspended and many young Congressmen, who had been jailed in Nashik jail, concluded that the movement lacked a clear social and economic programme. Key figures were Jayaprakash Narayan (general secretary), Acharya Narendra Dev (president at the first conference, Patna 1934), Minoo Masani, Ram Manohar Lohia, Asoka Mehta, Achyut Patwardhan and Yusuf Meherally. The first conference was presided over by Narendra Dev at Patna in May 1934, and the formal founding was at Bombay in October 1934. Its aims were to give the Congress a socialist outlook, to organise peasants and workers, to nationalise key industries, to abolish landlordism and to end princely rule. It worked inside the Congress, and its members sat on the Congress Working Committee in 1934 and 1936. Nehru sympathised with socialism but did not join. The CSP was Marxist in method, yet it rejected the Communist Party's line, although Communists were admitted to it until 1940, when they were expelled. After 1942 the CSP leaders, particularly JP, Lohia and Aruna Asaf Ali, were prominent in the Quit India Movement underground. In 1948 the socialists left the Congress and formed the Socialist Party; in 1952 it merged with the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party to form the Praja Socialist Party. Related topics UPSC could ask are the Left wing in the Congress, the Forward Bloc (1939, Subhas Bose), the All India Kisan Sabha (1936, Swami Sahajanand), the Communist Party of India (1920/1925), the Lahore Congress 1929 and the Karachi Resolution 1931 on fundamental rights and economic policy, and the Faizpur session 1936.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Rajya Sabha has no power either to reject or to amend a Money Bill. The Rajya Sabha cannot vote on the Demands for Grants. The Rajya Sabha cannot discuss the Annual Financial Statement. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: This question tests the financial powers of the Rajya Sabha under the Indian Constitution. Article 109 governs Money Bills: they can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha must return the bill within 14 days with or without recommendations. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject those recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses in the form the Lok Sabha passed it. So the Rajya Sabha can neither reject nor effectively amend it, which makes statement 1 correct in substance. Article 113 gives the power to vote on Demands for Grants exclusively to the Lok Sabha, so statement 2 is correct. Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses. The Rajya Sabha holds a general discussion on the Budget but does not vote on it, so statement 3 is wrong. Elimination logic: the words 'cannot discuss' in statement 3 are an extreme claim, so any option containing 3 (options c and d) can be dropped. Option (a) leaves out statement 2, which is plainly correct, so only (b) remains. The Speaker's certification is final on whether a bill is a Money Bill (Art. 110).
explanations: Wrong. It leaves out statement 2, which is correct, because only the Lok Sabha votes on Demands for Grants.
Correct. Statements 1 and 2 describe the Rajya Sabha's limited financial powers accurately, and statement 3 is false because the Rajya Sabha can discuss the Budget.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false, and excludes statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, but the Rajya Sabha can discuss the Annual Financial Statement.
keyfact: The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to Money Bills (14 days) and cannot vote on Demands for Grants, but it can discuss the Budget.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would have been right if statement 2 were false. Statement 1 reflects Art. 109, under which the Rajya Sabha gets 14 days to return a Money Bill with recommendations, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill, it is deemed passed. The Rajya Sabha therefore has only a recommendatory role in Money Bills and cannot block them.

Option (b), statements 1 and 2 only: this is the official answer. The Rajya Sabha has no binding say over Money Bills (Art. 109) and cannot vote on Demands for Grants (Art. 113). It can discuss the Budget and recommend changes to Money Bills. Despite these limits, it keeps equal powers with the Lok Sabha on constitutional amendments, on the impeachment of the President, and on the removal of judges. It also holds special powers under Art. 249 and Art. 312.

Option (c), statements 2 and 3 only: this combines a correct statement with a false one and excludes statement 1. Statement 3 is false because the Budget is laid before both Houses and the Rajya Sabha discusses it. The Rajya Sabha has no authority over voting on grants, but its discussion rights on the Budget are real and used each year.

Option (d), all three statements: this would imply the Rajya Sabha has no role at all in the Budget, which is not true. The Rajya Sabha takes part in the general discussion on the Budget and in debates on the working of ministries. It also receives the Appropriation Bill as a Money Bill and may return it with recommendations within 14 days.
related: Art. 109: the Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days.
Art. 110 defines a Money Bill, and the Lok Sabha Speaker's certification is final.
Art. 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement, i.e. the Budget.
Art. 113 deals with the procedure for voting on Demands for Grants in the Lok Sabha.
Art. 114 deals with the Appropriation Bill.
Art. 117 deals with Financial Bills, where the Rajya Sabha has full powers.
Art. 267 provides for the Contingency Fund of India, held by the President.
No joint sitting under Art. 108 for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Rajya Sabha cannot reject a Money Bill or make binding amendments to it; it can only recommend changes within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha may ignore them. A Money Bill (Art. 110) deals only with matters such as taxation, government borrowing, the Consolidated Fund and the Contingency Fund of India. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha and only on the President's recommendation. The Lok Sabha Speaker certifies a bill as a Money Bill, and that decision is final and cannot be questioned in any court or in either House. A Financial Bill under Art. 117 is different, because the Rajya Sabha has full powers over it, apart from its inability to initiate it.

2 — Correct: Demands for Grants are presented to the Lok Sabha alone under Art. 113, and only that House votes on them. The Rajya Sabha has no role in voting on them. The Lok Sabha may assent to, refuse or reduce a demand, but cannot increase it. Demands are voted on in the form of Demands for Grants, and a demand needs the President's recommendation. After the vote, the Appropriation Bill (Art. 114) is passed to authorise withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund. Cut motions, namely policy cut, economy cut and token cut, are moved in the Lok Sabha during this stage. The guillotine is applied to pass all pending demands on the last day.

3 — Incorrect: The Annual Financial Statement, or Budget, is laid before both Houses under Art. 112. The Rajya Sabha can hold a general discussion on it, but it has no power to vote on the Demands for Grants. The Finance Minister presents the Budget, traditionally on 1 February in the Lok Sabha. The budget presentation is followed by a general discussion, then departmental committee scrutiny, then voting on demands, and finally passage of the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill. The Rajya Sabha's role is limited to discussion and, for Money Bills, to making recommendations.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect. The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and cannot vote on Demands for Grants, but it is free to discuss the Annual Financial Statement (Budget).
topic_notes: Financial powers of Parliament are a recurring UPSC theme. Art. 109 sets the special procedure for Money Bills in the Rajya Sabha, and Art. 110 defines a Money Bill. Art. 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before Parliament. Art. 113 covers estimates relating to expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund (not voted) and other expenditure (voted by the Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants). Art. 114 governs Appropriation Bills. Art. 115 covers supplementary, additional and excess grants. Art. 116 covers votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants. Art. 117 covers Financial Bills, which have special provisions. Art. 265 says no tax may be levied or collected except by authority of law. Art. 266 establishes the Consolidated Fund and the Public Account, and Art. 267 the Contingency Fund. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund, such as the salaries of the President, the Speaker and judges, is not voted on but can be discussed. Types of cut motions: policy cut (reduces a demand to Re 1), economy cut (reduces by a specified amount) and token cut (reduces by Rs 100). The Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings oversee finances. In a deadlock over ordinary bills, a joint sitting under Art. 108 is possible, but for Money Bills there is no joint sitting because the Lok Sabha prevails. Constitutional amendments under Art. 368 need both Houses to pass them separately. In a Money Bill case, the Aadhaar Act (2016) was certified as a Money Bill and upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018, with a dissent by Justice D.Y. Chandrachud.

ocr: The Government of India Act of 1919 clearly defined (a) the separation of power between the judiciary and the legislature (b) the jurisdiction of the central and provincial governments the powers of the Secretary of State (e) for India and the Viceroy (d) None of the above B-AQN-O-—JUA/63A
subject: Polity
detail: The Government of India Act, 1919 implemented the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Montagu's Declaration of August 1917 promised 'progressive realisation of responsible government'). Its key feature was the devolution of authority: the Devolution Rules (1920) classified subjects into Central and Provincial lists, so the jurisdiction of the centre and provinces was explicitly defined for the first time. Provincial subjects were further split into 'Transferred' (education, local self-government, public health, agriculture; administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislature) and 'Reserved' (law and order, finance, land revenue, justice; administered by the Governor and his Executive Council) - this is dyarchy. Residuary powers stayed with the centre (Governor-General). The Act introduced a bicameral central legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly), direct elections, communal electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans, and a limited franchise. It provided for a statutory commission after 10 years (the Simon Commission, 1927). Elimination: (a) is wrong because no separation of powers between judiciary and legislature was defined; (c) is wrong because the Secretary of State's and Viceroy's powers were not clearly defined - the Secretary of State retained wide control, though his salary was moved to the British exchequer; (d) is wrong since (b) holds.
explanations: Incorrect: The Act did not provide a separation of powers between the judiciary and legislature; the doctrine of separation of powers was never formally adopted in colonial India, and the Governor-General and executive retained wide authority.

Correct: The Act, via the Devolution Rules, clearly separated Central and Provincial subjects and gave provincial legislatures defined powers - the first clear demarcation of central and provincial jurisdiction.

Incorrect: The powers of the Secretary of State and the Viceroy were not clearly defined; the Secretary of State continued to exercise superintendence, direction and control, with only some functions relaxed, such as the creation of the High Commissioner for India in London.
Incorrect: Since option (b) accurately describes a feature of the 1919 Act, 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: Government of India Act 1919 = dyarchy in provinces + clear Central/Provincial subject lists (Devolution Rules 1920) - answer (b).
option_notes: Separation of powers is the doctrine of dividing government among executive, legislature and judiciary (Montesquieu). Colonial India did not formally adopt it; the Regulating Act 1773 created the Supreme Court at Calcutta, and the Indian High Courts Act 1861 created High Courts. In independent India, the Constitution reflects a functional rather than rigid separation, with judicial independence protected under Articles 50, 121, 124 and 211.

Central-provincial jurisdiction means the division of legislative and executive subjects between the centre and provinces. The 1919 Act began this via the Devolution Rules 1920, with Central and Provincial lists. The Government of India Act 1935 went further with a three-fold Federal, Provincial and Concurrent list. The Indian Constitution's Seventh Schedule gives the Union, State and Concurrent lists (Article 246), with residuary power to the Union.

The Secretary of State for India was a British Cabinet minister who headed the India Office, created by the Government of India Act 1858 after the Crown took over from the Company, assisted by the Council of India (15 members). The Viceroy (Governor-General) represented the Crown in India. The 1919 Act gave the Secretary of State's salary to the British exchequer and created the High Commissioner for India in London (1920). The Secretary's office was abolished in 1947.

'None of the above' is the standard UPSC fallback option; it is correct only if all other options are false. Here it is incorrect because the 1919 Act did define central and provincial jurisdiction. Always test each option on its merits before choosing 'None of the above'.
related: Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces (not at the centre) by the 1919 Act; the 1935 Act introduced it at the centre (never implemented).
Devolution Rules 1920 classified subjects into Central and Provincial lists.
Reserved subjects: law and order, finance, land revenue, justice; Transferred subjects: education, health, local self-government, agriculture.
The 1919 Act created a bicameral Central Legislature: Council of State and Legislative Assembly.
Separate electorates were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans in 1919.
The Act provided for a statutory commission after 10 years - the Simon Commission (1927).
Lee Commission (1924) led to the establishment of the Public Service Commission in 1926.
The Government of India Act 1935 provided for the three-fold Federal, Provincial and Concurrent lists.
summary: The correct answer is (b). The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) clearly demarcated the jurisdiction of central and provincial governments by creating Central and Provincial lists of subjects, and by devolving powers to the provinces.
topic_notes: Background: After the First World War and nationalist pressure, Secretary of State Edwin Montagu announced on 20 August 1917 the goal of 'gradual development of self-governing institutions and progressive realisation of responsible government'. The Montagu-Chelmsford Report was published in 1918 and the Act received Royal Assent in December 1919, taking effect in 1921. Key features: (1) Dyarchy in provinces: Transferred subjects under Indian ministers; Reserved subjects under the Governor and his Executive Council. The Governor could override ministers. (2) Central legislature became bicameral: Council of State (upper house, 60 members, 34 elected, 5-year term) and Legislative Assembly (lower house, 144 members, 3-year term). (3) Direct elections with a limited franchise based on property, tax or education (about 10% of adult population in provinces). (4) Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans. (5) Three Indians in the Viceroy's Executive Council of eight. (6) Public Service Commission: Central Public Service Commission established in 1926 (following Lee Commission 1924). (7) Budget: separation of provincial and central budgets (Railway budget separated in 1924 under the Acworth Committee). (8) Provision for a statutory commission after 10 years, which became the Simon Commission (1927), boycotted in India ('Simon Go Back', 1928). Reactions: The Congress, in its special session at Bombay (Aug 1918, under Hasan Imam), declared the reforms 'disappointing and unsatisfactory'. Moderates (Surendranath Banerjea) welcomed them and left the Congress to form the National Liberal Federation. Related: Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 (separate electorates for Muslims), Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, federation proposed, abolition of dyarchy in provinces and its introduction at the centre), Rowlatt Act 1919, Jallianwala Bagh massacre April 1919.

ocr: Which of the following brings out the ‘Consumer Price Index Number for Industrial Workers’? (a) The Reserve Bank of India (b) The Department of Economic Affairs (c) The Labour Bureau (2) The Department of Personnel and Training
subject: Economy
detail: The Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) measures the change in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by industrial workers. It is compiled by the Labour Bureau, headquartered in Chandigarh (with offices in Shimla, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai, Kanpur and Guwahati), an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of India. The Bureau was set up in 1920 in Shimla. The current base year of CPI-IW is 2016=100 (revised from 2001=100 in 2020). It covers 88 centres and 317 markets in the revised series (earlier 78 centres). It is released monthly, usually on the last working day of the following month. CPI-IW is used to compute Dearness Allowance (DA) for central government employees and public sector workers, and for revising minimum wages in scheduled employments. Elimination: the RBI regulates money and credit and does not compile CPI-IW; the Department of Economic Affairs handles economic policy, budget and the Economic Survey; the Department of Personnel and Training deals with civil service matters. The headline CPI (Combined) is released by the NSO under MoSPI, and WPI by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.
explanations: Incorrect: The RBI uses CPI as a key input for monetary policy and inflation targeting but does not compile CPI-IW.
Incorrect: The Department of Economic Affairs (Ministry of Finance) handles economic policy, the Budget and the Economic Survey, not CPI-IW compilation.
Correct: The Labour Bureau under the Ministry of Labour and Employment compiles and publishes CPI-IW monthly.
Incorrect: The Department of Personnel and Training manages civil service personnel policy; it uses CPI-IW indirectly for DA matters but does not produce it.
keyfact: CPI-IW = Labour Bureau (Ministry of Labour and Employment), base 2016=100, used for Dearness Allowance.
option_notes: The Reserve Bank of India, founded on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act 1934 and nationalised in 1949, is India's central bank. It issues currency notes (except one-rupee notes), manages monetary policy and foreign exchange, and regulates banks. Since 2016 it follows flexible inflation targeting of 4% with a ±2% band, based on CPI (Combined). Headquartered in Mumbai.

The Department of Economic Affairs is one of the departments of the Ministry of Finance. It prepares the Union Budget, publishes the Economic Survey (through the Chief Economic Adviser), monitors the economy, handles external borrowing and multilateral institutions such as the World Bank, IMF and ADB, and oversees capital markets and the Financial Stability issues.

The Labour Bureau is an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, established in 1920 and headquartered in Chandigarh. It compiles CPI-IW and CPI-Agricultural Labourers/Rural Labourers, conducts surveys on employment and unemployment, and collects wage and industrial relations statistics. CPI-IW is used for DA and wage revision.

The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) is under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. It handles recruitment and service conditions of central civil servants, oversees UPSC and SSC-related matters, the Central Vigilance and Lokpal frameworks, the RTI Act administration (via CIC), and training institutions like LBSNAA, Mussoorie.
related: CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau, Chandigarh; base year 2016=100.
Headline retail inflation is measured by CPI (Combined), compiled by NSO under MoSPI; base 2012=100.
WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT; base 2011-12=100; excludes services.
RBI inflation target: 4% with a tolerance band of ±2% using CPI.
CPI-AL and CPI-RL are compiled by the Labour Bureau; base 1986-87=100.
Dearness Allowance for central employees is linked to CPI-IW.
Labour Bureau was established in 1920 and is an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
The Economic Survey is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs under the Chief Economic Adviser.
summary: The correct answer is (c) The Labour Bureau. The Labour Bureau, an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, compiles and publishes the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) every month, using price data collected from 78 industrial centres.
topic_notes: India has several price indices, each with a different compiler and purpose. CPI-IW (Labour Bureau, Ministry of Labour and Employment) tracks retail prices for industrial workers; base year 2016=100; used for Dearness Allowance of central government employees and for wage indexation. CPI-AL and CPI-RL (Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers and Rural Labourers) are also by the Labour Bureau, with base 1986-87=100, used to revise minimum wages under MGNREGA wage indexation (MGNREGA wages have been linked to CPI-AL). CPI (Rural, Urban, Combined) is compiled by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), base year 2012=100, and is the headline inflation measure; the RBI uses CPI-Combined for its inflation target of 4% (±2%) set under the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (2016, amended RBI Act). The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser in the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, with base year 2011-12=100; it has no services component. GDP deflator comes from the NSO. The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is by NSO, base 2011-12. Laspeyres method is typically used for index numbers. The Seventh Pay Commission and DA calculations use the average of CPI-IW over the previous 12 months. Possible future questions: which index is used for inflation targeting, which body compiles WPI, which index has services, base years, and the difference between retail and wholesale indices.

ocr: In the context of modern scientific research, consider the following statements about TceCube’, a particle detector located at South Pole, which was recently in the news : 1. It is the world’s largest neutrino detector, encompassing a cubic kilometre of ice. 2. It is a powerful telescope to search for dark matter. 3. It is buried deep in the ice. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only fc} 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Environment
detail: IceCube Neutrino Observatory is operated by a collaboration led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison and located at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. Construction finished in December 2010. It has 5,160 digital optical modules (DOMs) on 86 vertical strings, frozen into holes melted with hot water at depths of about 1,450 m to 2,450 m. Neutrinos are nearly massless, chargeless particles that rarely interact; when one does, it produces a muon or cascade that emits Cherenkov light in the clear ice, which the DOMs record. This allows reconstruction of the neutrino's direction and energy, so IceCube works as a neutrino telescope for astrophysical sources such as active galactic nuclei, supernovae and gamma-ray bursts. In 2013 it reported the first high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and in 2017-18 it traced one to the blazar TXS 0506+056. It also searches indirectly for dark matter (WIMP annihilation in the Sun or Galactic centre), studies neutrino oscillations, and, via DeepCore, probes lower energies. Elimination logic: statement 1 is the well-known descriptor; statement 3 is factual; statement 2 looks doubtful but dark-matter search is a stated goal, so (d) follows.
explanations: Incorrect: statement 1 is correct, but statements 2 and 3 are also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
Incorrect: statements 2 and 3 are correct, but statement 1 is also correct, so this omits it.
Incorrect: statements 1 and 3 are correct, but dark-matter search (statement 2) is also an IceCube objective, so this omits it.
Correct: all three statements are accurate. It is the largest neutrino detector, it works as a telescope that also searches for dark matter, and it lies buried deep in the South Pole ice.
keyfact: IceCube: the world's largest neutrino detector, a cubic kilometre of ice buried 1.45-2.45 km deep at the South Pole, which also searches for dark matter.
related: IceCube is at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station and is run by a University of Wisconsin-Madison-led collaboration.
IceCube uses 5,160 DOMs on 86 strings at 1.45-2.45 km depth.
In 2018 IceCube traced a high-energy neutrino to the blazar TXS 0506+056.
Neutrino oscillation discovery earned the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics (Kajita and McDonald).
India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) is proposed in Theni district, Tamil Nadu.
Super-Kamiokande is a water Cherenkov neutrino detector in Japan.
Dark matter is about 27% of the universe's mass-energy; dark energy is about 68%.
Cherenkov radiation is light emitted when a charged particle moves faster than light in a medium.
statements: 1 — Correct: IceCube instruments one cubic kilometre of ice and is the largest neutrino detector in the world. It is at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, Antarctica, and is run by an international collaboration led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison with US National Science Foundation funding. It has 86 strings and 5,160 DOMs. Construction was completed in December 2010. Its volume far exceeds that of earlier detectors such as AMANDA, Super-Kamiokande (Japan) and ANTARES (Mediterranean).

2 — Correct: IceCube is described as a neutrino telescope, and one of its science goals is the indirect search for dark matter. If WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) accumulate in the Sun, Earth or Galactic halo and annihilate, they would produce high-energy neutrinos that IceCube could detect. Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy and is detected only through gravity. Other experiments include LUX-ZEPLIN, XENON, and the AMS on the ISS. IceCube has set limits on WIMP cross-sections but has not yet detected dark matter.

3 — Correct: The detector is buried deep in the Antarctic ice, with strings lowered into holes 2.5 km deep drilled using hot water. The sensors sit at depths of 1.45 to 2.45 km, where the ice is extremely clear and free of air bubbles, so Cherenkov light can be seen. The overlying ice also shields against cosmic-ray muons. A surface array called IceTop sits above it to detect cosmic-ray air showers, and a denser infill, DeepCore, lowers the energy threshold.
summary: The correct answer is (d): all three statements are correct. IceCube is the world's largest neutrino detector, it instruments a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice at the South Pole, and it is buried 1.45-2.45 km below the surface. It also serves as a 'telescope' that searches for dark matter, among other things.
topic_notes: Neutrinos are elementary leptons of the Standard Model that come in three flavours: electron, muon and tau. They have extremely small mass, no electric charge, and interact only through the weak force and gravity, so trillions pass through the body each second. Sources include the Sun (fusion), supernovae, cosmic-ray interactions, the Big Bang relic background, and distant astrophysical accelerators. The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald for discovering neutrino oscillations, which show that neutrinos have mass. Detectors must be large and shielded, so they are placed deep underground, underwater or in ice. Examples: Super-Kamiokande (Japan, water Cherenkov), SNO (Canada), KamLAND, ANTARES and KM3NeT (Mediterranean), Baikal-GVD (Siberia's Lake Baikal), and IceCube (Antarctica). India's proposed India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) at Bodi West Hills, Theni district, Tamil Nadu, aims to study atmospheric neutrinos with an iron calorimeter (ICAL) but has faced environmental and legal delays. IceCube uses digital optical modules to detect Cherenkov radiation from charged particles created by neutrino interactions. In 2013 it announced the first detection of very-high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and in 2018 it linked a neutrino to the blazar TXS 0506+056, launching multi-messenger astronomy. In 2023 it mapped neutrinos from the Milky Way plane. An upgrade, IceCube-Gen2, is planned. Dark matter is detected indirectly via annihilation products, directly via nuclear recoils in underground detectors, or at colliders such as the LHC. The Higgs boson (2012) and gravitational waves (LIGO, 2015) are related topics.

ocr: The terms ‘Agreement on Agriculture’, ‘Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures’ and ‘Peace Clause’ appear in the news frequently in the context of the affairs of the (a) Food and Agriculture Organization {b} United Nations Framework Conference on Climate Change (ce) World Trade Organization (ad) United Nations Environment Programme t
subject: Economy
detail: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was created on 1 January 1995 after the Uruguay Round (1986-94), whose Marrakesh Agreement was signed in April 1994. The WTO's headquarters are in Geneva. The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) rests on three pillars: domestic support, market access and export competition. Domestic support is classed into Green Box (non-trade-distorting, permitted), Blue Box (production-limiting programmes) and Amber Box (trade-distorting, capped by the Aggregate Measurement of Support, with a de minimis limit of 10% of production value for developing countries and 5% for developed ones). The SPS Agreement lets members protect human, animal and plant life or health through science-based measures, and these must not become disguised trade barriers. The 'Peace Clause' (Article 13 of the AoA) shielded countries from WTO challenge over agricultural subsidies, provided they stayed within prescribed limits; it expired in 2003. The term resurfaced in the news after the 2013 Bali Ministerial, when India's public stockholding for food security was protected by an interim peace clause. Elimination: FAO, UNFCCC and UNEP do not administer binding trade agreements or dispute settlement, so only the WTO fits.
explanations: Incorrect: the FAO is a UN specialised agency for food security and nutrition. It sets standards through Codex Alimentarius, but it does not administer the AoA or the Peace Clause.
Incorrect: the UNFCCC deals with climate change, with the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement under it. It has no trade agreements on agriculture or SPS measures.
Correct: the AoA, SPS Agreement and Peace Clause are all WTO instruments, and they come up often in news about subsidies, food stockholding and disputes.
Incorrect: UNEP is the UN's environmental programme, headquartered in Nairobi. It does not regulate trade rules or farm subsidies.
keyfact: AoA + SPS + Peace Clause = WTO; the Peace Clause shielded agricultural subsidies from dispute challenge, and the 2013 Bali interim version protected India's food stockholding.
option_notes: The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) was founded in 1945 and is headquartered in Rome. Its motto is 'Fiat Panis' (Let there be bread). It leads international efforts against hunger and publishes The State of Food Insecurity and the Food Price Index. It hosts the Codex Alimentarius Commission, jointly with WHO, and the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources. India is a member. World Food Day is observed on 16 October.

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1994. Its secretariat is in Bonn. It has near-universal membership. The Conference of the Parties (COP) is its supreme body. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) were adopted under it. It rests on the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities'.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) succeeded GATT on 1 January 1995. It is based in Geneva and has about 164 members. Its highest body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets every two years. Its Dispute Settlement Body has an Appellate Body, which has been non-functional since December 2019 because of the US blocking appointments. Key agreements include GATT, GATS, TRIPS, AoA and SPS. India was a founding member.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) was established in 1972 following the Stockholm Conference. Its headquarters are in Nairobi, Kenya. It coordinates UN environmental activities, publishes the Global Environment Outlook and the Emissions Gap Report, and administers secretariats of conventions such as CITES, CBD and the Basel Convention. World Environment Day is observed on 5 June.
related: The WTO came into being on 1 January 1995 and is headquartered in Geneva.
The AoA's three pillars are domestic support, market access and export competition.
Green Box subsidies are non-trade-distorting and are not capped.
The Peace Clause (Article 13 of the AoA) expired in 2003. An interim peace clause was agreed at Bali in 2013.
The Nairobi Ministerial (2015) decided to abolish agricultural export subsidies.
The WTO Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019.
The SPS Agreement refers to standards of Codex Alimentarius, WOAH and IPPC.
The G-33 coalition, in which India is prominent, champions public stockholding and special safeguards.
summary: The correct answer is (c) World Trade Organization. The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA), the SPS Agreement and the 'Peace Clause' are all WTO instruments that govern trade in farm goods, food safety and subsidy disputes.
topic_notes: The WTO is the only global body dealing with the rules of trade between nations. It was formed in 1995 and replaced GATT (1947). Its decisions are by consensus. The Ministerial Conference is its top body, followed by the General Council and the Director-General. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has been Director-General since March 2021, the first woman and the first African to hold the post. Major agreements: the AoA (agriculture), SPS (food safety, animal and plant health), TBT (technical barriers), TRIMS (investment measures), TRIPS (intellectual property), GATS (services) and the Subsidies and Countervailing Measures agreement. Under the AoA, subsidies are classed into boxes: Green (decoupled income support, research, public stockholding for food security under conditions), Blue (payments tied to production-limiting programmes) and Amber (price support, input subsidies, counted in the AMS). The developing-country concerns are that the AMS base period is 1986-88 and that administered prices are compared with fixed external reference prices from that period. The Bali Ministerial (2013) produced the Trade Facilitation Agreement and an interim 'peace clause' on public stockholding. The Nairobi Ministerial (2015) decided to abolish agricultural export subsidies. The Doha Development Round launched in 2001 remains stalled. The Cairns Group is a coalition of agricultural exporters, and the G-33 is led by India and Indonesia, which pushes for the Special Safeguard Mechanism and for public stockholding. Dispute Settlement: panels, then the Appellate Body (which has been defunct since 2019). The SPS Agreement refers to standards of Codex (food), OIE (animal health, now WOAH) and IPPC (plant health). India's key issues include MSP procurement, the PM-GKAY food grain scheme and rice subsidy limits.

question: With reference to ‘Near Field Communication (NFC) Technology’, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1, It is a contactless communication technology that uses electromagnetic radio fields. NFC is designed for use by devices which can be at a distance of even a metre from each other. NFC can use encryption when sending sensitive information. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Near Field Communication is a set of short-range wireless standards based on RFID (ISO/IEC 14443 and related standards). It operates at 13.56 MHz, a globally available unlicensed ISM band. It works through magnetic induction between two loop antennas: an active device (initiator) generates an RF field, and a target can be powered by that field (passive) or have its own power (active). The effective range is about 4 cm or less, and the design is intentionally short so that a tap or touch is needed. That short range is itself a basic security feature. Data rates are low (106, 212 and 424 kbit/s, with higher rates in some modes). Secure applications such as contactless payments, e-ticketing, access cards and e-passports can add encryption and secure elements, so statement 3 is correct. Statement 1 is correct because NFC is contactless and uses electromagnetic radio fields. Statement 2 is wrong because it claims a distance of a metre. Elimination: since 2 is wrong, options (a) and (d) go out. Option (b) leaves out statement 1, which is clearly true. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because NFC range is a few centimetres, not a metre.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is correct, and it covers only statement 3.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true, and statement 2 is false because of the range claim.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which wrongly claims a range of about a metre.
keyfact: NFC = contactless, RFID-based, 13.56 MHz, range about 4 cm or less, supports encryption; the claim of a metre range is false.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only: this option is incorrect for this question. It combines the true statement 1 with the false range claim. It is a useful reminder that NFC is a short-range subset of RFID working at 13.56 MHz, with a range of roughly 4 cm. Anything described as working over a metre or more points to UHF RFID, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, not NFC.

Statement 3 only: this option is incorrect because it misses statement 1. NFC does use electromagnetic induction and radio fields without physical contact. Encryption and secure elements are used in payments, but NFC is above all defined as a contactless, proximity-based technology, so statement 1 must also be counted.

Statements 1 and 3 only: this is the correct option. NFC is a contactless, short-range, RFID-derived technology at 13.56 MHz that supports encrypted data exchange. It is used in mobile payments, transit passes, access control, and quick pairing of Bluetooth or Wi-Fi devices. It is standardised under ISO/IEC 18092 and ISO/IEC 14443, and the NFC Forum maintains the specifications.

Statements 1, 2 and 3: this option is incorrect because statement 2 is false. If NFC worked at a metre, it would lose the security advantage of proximity and be mistaken for Bluetooth or UHF RFID. Remember the 4 cm or less rule of thumb to reject any statement that gives a longer range.
related: NFC operates at 13.56 MHz, in the unlicensed ISM band.
The usual NFC range is 4 cm or less.
NFC is a subset of high-frequency RFID (ISO/IEC 14443 and 18092).
NFC modes: reader/writer, peer-to-peer and card emulation.
Passive NFC tags need no battery and are powered by the reader's field.
The NFC Forum was founded in 2004 by Nokia, Philips and Sony.
India's National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) uses contactless NFC-based technology.
Bluetooth has a longer range than NFC but needs pairing.
statements: 1 — Correct: NFC is a contactless technology using electromagnetic radio fields. NFC grew out of RFID and was developed by Philips and Sony, with the NFC Forum set up in 2004 to promote standards. It works at 13.56 MHz through inductive coupling between two antennas. It has three modes: peer-to-peer, reader/writer and card emulation. Common uses are tap-to-pay (Google Pay, Apple Pay), transit cards, smart posters, device pairing and e-passports.

2 — Incorrect: NFC works only over very short distances, typically 4 cm or less (often described as up to 10 cm at most), not a metre. The short range is deliberate and limits eavesdropping. Longer ranges belong to other technologies: Bluetooth works up to about 10 m for Class 2 devices and up to about 100 m for Class 1, Wi-Fi covers tens of metres, and UHF RFID can read from several metres. Do not confuse NFC with these when answering comparison questions.

3 — Correct: NFC can use encryption and secure channels when sending sensitive data. Payment applications use a secure element (in the SIM, in embedded hardware or in the cloud) and tokenisation, so the real card number is not transmitted. Protocols such as AES-based secure channels and EMV contactless standards are used. Limitations remain: eavesdropping is possible at close range, and relay attacks exist, so encryption at the application layer is recommended. The short range gives a first layer of protection.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. NFC is a contactless short-range technology that works on electromagnetic radio fields and can use encryption for sensitive data, but its range is only a few centimetres (about 4 cm or less), not a metre.
topic_notes: Near Field Communication is a short-range wireless technology derived from RFID. It was jointly developed by Philips (now NXP) and Sony around 2002, and the NFC Forum was formed in 2004. It operates at 13.56 MHz and uses magnetic induction between loop antennas. Typical range is 4 cm or less, and data rates are 106, 212 and 424 kbit/s.
