The Blue Economy and Women's Economic Empowerment are cross-cutting priorities. Bilateral and contentious issues are excluded from its agenda by the Charter's principles. The Secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. IOR-ARC (renamed the Indian Ocean Rim Association, IORA, in 2013) was set up in 1997, not recently, as a platform for economic and trade cooperation. It is not a maritime-security-only alliance, since maritime safety and security is only one of its six priority areas.
topic_notes: IORA (formerly IOR-ARC) is a regional grouping of states bordering the Indian Ocean. It was launched at Mauritius on 6-7 March 1997, building on the 1995 Mauritius initiative. The Charter principles include consensus decision-making, non-interference, and exclusion of bilateral and contentious issues. It was renamed IORA in 2013. Members number 23, including India, Australia, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Iran, Kenya, Madagascar, Malaysia, Maldives, Mauritius, Mozambique, Oman, Seychelles, Singapore, Somalia, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, Thailand, UAE, Yemen, Comoros and, most recently, France (for Réunion) and Saudi Arabia among the newer joiners. Dialogue partners include China, Japan, the US, the UK, Germany, Italy, Egypt, Turkey, Russia, South Korea, and others. Six priority areas: maritime safety and security; trade and investment facilitation; fisheries management; disaster risk management; academic, science and technology cooperation; and tourism and cultural exchanges. Cross-cutting areas: Blue Economy and Women's Economic Empowerment. Key documents: Jakarta Concord (2017), Mauritius Declaration, and the IORA Action Plan 2017-21. The Secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius. Related Indian Ocean frameworks that UPSC may ask: the Indian Ocean Naval Symposium (IONS, 2008, naval heads forum), SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region, 2015), BIMSTEC, the Colombo Security Conclave, the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (2019), and the Quad. Do not confuse IORA with SAARC, ASEAN or Colombo Process. Piracy-related frameworks include the Djibouti Code of Conduct and the Contact Group on Piracy off the Coast of Somalia.

question: Which one of the following movements has contributed to a split in the Indian National Congress resulting in the emergence of ‘moderates’ and ‘extremists’?
subject: Modern History
detail: The Partition of Bengal was announced by Lord Curzon in July 1905 and took effect on 16 October 1905. It triggered the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement. Extremists such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai (Lal-Bal-Pal), along with Aurobindo Ghose, wanted to extend the programme to passive resistance, national education and Swaraj. Moderates such as Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta and Surendranath Banerjee wanted to confine boycott to Bengal and rely on constitutional petitions. At the 1906 Calcutta Session under Dadabhai Naoroji, the goals of Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education were adopted as a compromise. At Surat in December 1907 the venue shift from Nagpur and the choice of president (Rash Behari Ghosh over Lajpat Rai) led to a breakdown and the formal split. Elimination: Non-Cooperation (1920-22), Civil Disobedience (1930-34) and Quit India (1942) all came under Gandhi's leadership, long after the Moderate-Extremist divide had healed (reunion at Lucknow, 1916). Those movements did cause other disagreements, such as the Swarajists (Pro-Changers vs No-Changers) after 1922, but not the Moderate-Extremist split.
explanations: Correct: the Swadeshi movement (1905 onwards) created the methods dispute that produced the Moderate-Extremist split at Surat in 1907.
Wrong: Quit India (August 1942) came 35 years later; by then the Congress was a mass organisation under Gandhi and the old Moderate-Extremist labels were obsolete.

Wrong: Non-Cooperation (1920-22) led to the Swarajist (Pro-Changer) vs No-Changer debate after Chauri Chaura, not a Moderate-Extremist split. Some Moderates, however, left the Congress around 1918-20 and formed the Liberal Federation.
Wrong: Civil Disobedience (1930-34) began with the Dandi March; it did not split the Congress into Moderates and Extremists.
keyfact: Swadeshi Movement (1905) led to the Surat split of 1907 between Moderates and Extremists; they reunited at Lucknow in 1916.
option_notes: Swadeshi Movement: launched against Curzon's Partition of Bengal (announced 20 July 1905, effective 16 October 1905, observed as Rakhi Bandhan day). Featured boycott of British goods, national education (National Council of Education, 1906), Bengal National College and Swadeshi industries. Leaders included Surendranath Banerjee, Tilak, Bipin Pal, Aurobindo and Rabindranath Tagore. Partition was annulled in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar of George V, and the capital shifted to Delhi.

Quit India Movement: launched on 8 August 1942 at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, after the failure of the Cripps Mission, with Gandhi's 'Do or Die' call. The Congress leaders were arrested the next day (Operation Zero Hour). Parallel governments arose in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta (Congress Radio) were prominent. Muslim League, Communists and Hindu Mahasabha did not support it.

Non-Cooperation Movement: began on 1 August 1920 with the Khilafat agitation, after the Calcutta special session (September 1920) and Nagpur session (December 1920) endorsed it. It involved surrender of titles, boycott of courts, schools and councils, and Swadeshi with khadi. Gandhi withdrew it in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura violence (4 February 1922, Gorakhpur). The Swaraj Party was formed in 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.

Civil Disobedience Movement: began with Gandhi's Dandi March (12 March to 6 April 1930) to break the salt law, following the Lahore Congress's Purna Swaraj resolution (December 1929). It included no-tax campaigns and forest law violations. It was suspended by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931). Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in 1931. It was resumed in 1932 and formally withdrawn in 1934.
related: Surat split: December 1907; Tilak and the Extremists were excluded from the Congress.
Reunion of Moderates and Extremists: Lucknow Session, 1916, under A.C. Majumdar.
Partition of Bengal: effective 16 October 1905; annulled 1911.
Calcutta Session 1906 under Dadabhai Naoroji declared Swaraj as the goal.
Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Muslim League was founded in Dhaka in 1906.
Swaraj Party formed in 1923 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru after Non-Cooperation.
Bengal National College of 1906 had Aurobindo as its first principal.
summary: The answer is (a) Swadeshi Movement. The Swadeshi and Boycott agitation that followed the 1905 Partition of Bengal exposed a sharp divide over methods, and at the Surat Session of 1907 the Congress split into Moderates and Extremists.
topic_notes: The Moderate-Extremist divide is a core topic of the early nationalist phase. Moderates (1885-1905) included Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, W.C. Bonnerjee and Surendranath Banerjee. They followed the 'three Ps' of prayer, petition and protest, had faith in British justice, and developed the economic critique of colonial rule, especially the drain theory. Extremists (from about 1905) included Lal-Bal-Pal and Aurobindo. They believed in self-reliance, mass action, boycott and Swaraj, and used festivals such as Ganapati and Shivaji to mobilise people. Key events: Curzon's Partition of Bengal (1905); the Calcutta Session of 1906 (Naoroji used the word Swaraj as the goal); the Surat Session of 1907, held on the banks of the Tapti under Rash Behari Ghosh, where the split occurred; and the government's repression that followed, including Tilak's six-year sentence in Mandalay (1908), the Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms), which gave separate electorates, and the 1911 annulment of partition. The Lucknow Session of 1916, presided over by A.C. Majumdar, saw reunion and the Congress-League pact (Lucknow Pact). Other related splits: the formation of the Swaraj Party (1923) and the Liberal Federation (1919), when Moderates led by Surendranath Banerjee left the Congress, and the Congress Socialist Party in 1934. UPSC often asks about the Swadeshi-era institutions, such as the Anushilan Samiti, Dawn Society, Bengal Chemicals, and Vande Mataram, which became the movement's anthem.

question: In a particular region in India, the local people train the roots of living trees into robust bridges across the streams. As the time passes, these bridges become stronger. These unique ‘living root bridges’ are found in
subject: Environment
detail: Living root bridges are a bio-engineering tradition of Meghalaya, found mainly in East Khasi Hills, West Jaintia Hills and South West Khasi Hills districts, around Cherrapunji (Sohra), Mawsynram, Nongriat and Pynursla. The Khasis and Jaintias guide the secondary aerial roots of Ficus elastica (Indian rubber tree, 'jing kieng jri' in Khasi) across a stream using betel-nut trunks or bamboo scaffolding. Over 10-15 years the roots fuse (inosculation) and thicken, so the bridge strengthens with age. Some are 100-500 years old, and some bridges can carry 50 or more people. The heavy rainfall, flash floods and steep terrain make wooden or steel bridges decay or wash away, while living bridges self-renew. The Umshiang double-decker bridge at Nongriat is the best known. Meghalaya's living root bridges are on UNESCO's Tentative List (2022) for World Heritage status as a cultural landscape. Elimination: Himachal Pradesh is known for Himalayan rope and wooden bridges, Jharkhand is a plateau region with no such tradition, and Tamil Nadu has no living root bridge culture. The rain-soaked northeast, with its rubber fig, is the clue.
explanations: Correct. Living root bridges belong to the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, where Ficus elastica roots are trained across streams.
Wrong. Himachal Pradesh has Himalayan suspension and wooden cantilever bridges, but no tradition of living root bridges.
Wrong. Jharkhand is a plateau state known for tribal culture and minerals, not for root bridges.
Wrong. Tamil Nadu has no such tradition. Its famous bridge is the Pamban rail bridge, which links Rameswaram to the mainland.
keyfact: Living root bridges (Ficus elastica roots) are made by the Khasi and Jaintia peoples of Meghalaya.
option_notes: Meghalaya ('abode of clouds') became a state in 1972. It is home to the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo tribes and has a matrilineal society. Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are among the wettest places on Earth. It has the Sixth Schedule's autonomous district councils, and the living root bridges and Mawlynnong 'cleanest village' are well known. Sacred groves (Law Kyntang) are also found there.

Himachal Pradesh, a Himalayan state with Shimla as its capital, became a full state in 1971. It is known for apple orchards, the Kullu-Manali area, Kinnaur and Spiti, and the Great Himalayan National Park (UNESCO site, 2014). Its traditional bridges are wood or rope. The Kalka-Shimla railway is a UNESCO site.

Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar in 2000, with Ranchi as its capital. It lies on the Chota Nagpur Plateau and is rich in coal, iron ore and mica. Its tribes include the Santhal, Munda and Oraon. Parasnath Hill and Betla National Park are located there, and the Damodar and Subarnarekha are its rivers.

Tamil Nadu, with Chennai as its capital, lies on the south-eastern coast, with the Western and Eastern Ghats and the Kaveri delta. It has Dravidian temple architecture, including the Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO). It also has the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and Pamban Bridge. Jallikattu and Bharatanatyam are part of its culture.
related: Living root bridges use aerial roots of Ficus elastica (Indian rubber fig).
They are found mainly in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya.
The Umshiang double-decker bridge is at Nongriat, near Cherrapunji.
Meghalaya's living root bridges are on UNESCO's Tentative List (2022).
Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are among the wettest places on Earth.
Mawlynnong in Meghalaya is called Asia's cleanest village.
Meghalayan Age (4,200 years ago) is the latest stage of the Holocene.
Apatani valley in Arunachal Pradesh is a traditional agriculture site on the UNESCO Tentative List.
summary: The answer is (a) Meghalaya. Living root bridges are made by the Khasi and Jaintia peoples, who guide the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across streams in the wet southern Khasi and Jaintia Hills. The roots strengthen as they grow and thicken over time.
topic_notes: Living root bridges are a form of 'living architecture' or bio-engineering. The species used is mostly Ficus elastica, which produces strong secondary roots from the trunk and grows well on rocky riverbanks. In the Jaintia Hills, a related practice uses the roots of Ficus benghalensis and similar species. Khasi names include 'jingkieng jri'. Examples: the Umshiang double-decker root bridge at Nongriat (near Cherrapunji), the Riwai root bridge near Mawlynnong, and the Mawsaw root bridge. The bridges are built and maintained by communities, often over generations, and can last for centuries. They are on the UNESCO Tentative List (2022) as the 'Jingkieng Jri: Living Root Bridge Cultural Landscapes of Meghalaya'. The bridges reflect traditional ecological knowledge and the community's relationship with the forest. The region has very heavy monsoon rainfall, which makes conventional bridges decay. Related Meghalaya topics: the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo hills; the Sixth Schedule; the Meghalaya Basin Age (Meghalayan stage of the Holocene, 4,200 years ago); Mawlynnong; Dawki and the Umngot river; sacred groves; and the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve. The Khasi Hills also have limestone caves, such as Krem Liat Prah. UPSC often asks about GI-tagged products, UNESCO sites and traditional practices of the northeast, such as Apatani paddy-cum-fish cultivation in Arunachal Pradesh and Zabo farming in Nagaland.

ocr: Tides occur in the oceans and seas due to which among the following? 1. Gravitational force of the Sun 2. Gravitational force of the Moon 3. Centrifugal force of the Earth Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b}) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: Tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational attraction of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. The Moon, though far smaller, is much nearer, so its tide-generating force is about 2.2 times that of the Sun. Tide-generating force depends on the differential pull, which varies roughly with the inverse cube of distance. On the side of Earth facing the Moon, gravitational pull exceeds the average and water bulges toward the Moon. On the opposite side, the Moon's pull is weaker than average and the centrifugal force, arising from the Earth and Moon revolving about their common centre of mass (barycentre), dominates, producing a second bulge away from the Moon. This is why most coasts have two high tides and two low tides roughly every 24 hours 52 minutes. Spring tides occur at new and full moon when the Sun, Moon and Earth are aligned (syzygy); neap tides occur at the quarter phases when the Sun and Moon are at right angles. Since all three factors (Sun's gravity, Moon's gravity, centrifugal force) contribute, 1, 2 and 3 are all correct and option (d) is the answer. Options (a), (b) and (c) each omit at least one valid cause.
explanations: Incorrect: Option (a) names only the Sun's gravitational force. It ignores the Moon, the dominant influence, and the centrifugal force, so it is incomplete.

Incorrect: Option (b) includes the Moon and centrifugal force but leaves out the Sun's gravity, which is a genuine tide-generating factor, producing spring and neap tides in combination with the Moon.
Incorrect: Option (c) includes the Sun and centrifugal force but omits the Moon, the single most important cause of tides, so it is wrong.
Correct: Option (d) is the official answer. Tides result from the gravitational pull of both the Sun and Moon, together with centrifugal force, which balances gravity and creates the far-side bulge.
keyfact: Tides arise from the gravity of the Moon and Sun plus the centrifugal force of the Earth-Moon system, and the Moon's effect is about 2.2 times the Sun's.
option_notes: Option (a), the Sun's gravity alone: The Sun is a G-type star about 150 million km from Earth, with a mass roughly 27 million times that of the Moon. Despite this, its tidal influence is only about 46% of the Moon's because tide-generating force falls off with the cube of distance. It forms the S2 solar tidal constituent and modifies the lunar tides, creating spring tides at syzygy (new and full moon) and neap tides at quadrature. It also affects seasonal tidal variation, as tides are slightly larger near perihelion in early January and smaller at aphelion in early July.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only: This pairs the Moon's gravity with centrifugal force, which are the two main components of the Earth-Moon tidal mechanism. The Moon's gravity causes the near-side bulge, while the centrifugal force from orbiting the barycentre, about 4,600 km from Earth's centre, causes the far-side bulge. It is incomplete only because it omits the Sun. Without the Sun there would be no spring-neap cycle. Tidal period for the lunar semi-diurnal cycle is about 12 hours 26 minutes, giving two high tides in a lunar day of 24 hours 52 minutes.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only: This leaves out the Moon, the main tide-raising body. It combines the Sun's gravity and centrifugal force. It is wrong because the Moon exerts about 2.2 times the Sun's tidal force, owing to its proximity at around 384,400 km. Solar tides alone would produce a much smaller range, with high tides about every 12 hours. The Moon's orbital motion also explains why tides advance about 50 minutes daily, and why tidal heights vary with perigee and apogee, an effect solar-only reasoning cannot explain.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: This is the UPSC official answer. It includes the Sun's gravity, the Moon's gravity and centrifugal force. The combined effect explains the twin tidal bulges, two high and two low tides daily, and the fortnightly spring-neap cycle. The tidal range varies by location, being highest in places such as the Bay of Fundy, Canada, with ranges up to about 16 m, and lower in enclosed seas like the Mediterranean. Coastline shape, ocean depth and resonance modify local tides.
related: Spring tides occur at new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line (syzygy).
Neap tides occur at the first and last quarters, when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other.
The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the highest tidal range in the world.
Tidal bores in India are noted in the Hooghly River; globally, the Qiantang River in China is famous.
The Moon's tide-generating force is about 2.2 times that of the Sun.
Tides come roughly every 12 h 26 min; successive high tides are about 24 h 52 min apart for the same bulge.
The Gulf of Khambhat and the Gulf of Kutch are potential sites for tidal power in India.
Perigee-spring tides, when the Moon is nearest Earth near new or full moon, produce unusually high tides.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Sun's gravity contributes to tide generation, though weaker than the Moon's because of its much greater distance. The Sun is about 150 million km away and has a tidal effect roughly 46% that of the Moon. When it aligns with the Moon (new and full moon) it reinforces the Moon's pull, producing spring tides with higher high tides and lower low tides. At the quarter phases its pull partly offsets the Moon's, giving neap tides with a smaller range. Solar tides are known as S2 constituent (principal solar semidiurnal) in tidal analysis, while the principal lunar semidiurnal is M2. Perihelion (around 3 January) and aphelion (around 4 July) alter the Sun's effect: tides are slightly higher at perihelion.

2 — Correct: The Moon's gravity is the dominant tide-generating force because of its proximity, about 384,400 km on average. It pulls the water on the near side of Earth toward it, creating a tidal bulge. The Moon takes 27.3 days (sidereal) to orbit Earth, but a lunar day is about 24 hours 50 minutes, so tides arrive roughly 52 minutes later each day. At perigee, when the Moon is closest, tidal ranges are about 20% above average (perigean spring tides); at apogee they are weaker. Tide range is greatest in funnel-shaped bays like the Bay of Fundy, in Canada, with ranges over 15 m. The Moon's declination also causes diurnal inequality in tides.

3 — Correct: Centrifugal force, in the Earth-Moon system, arises from the revolution of Earth and Moon around their common centre of mass (barycentre), which lies about 4,600 km from Earth's centre, inside the Earth. Because the force is the same everywhere on Earth in magnitude and direction (away from the Moon), while gravitational pull varies with distance, it exceeds gravity on the far side, creating the second tidal bulge opposite to the Moon. Thus gravity and centrifugal force are the two counterbalancing forces behind tides. Note that it is not mainly the Earth's daily rotation on its own axis. Textbooks such as NCERT present this centrifugal force as the cause of the far-side bulge.
summary: The correct answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3. Tides are produced by the differential gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth's oceans, together with the centrifugal force arising from the Earth's rotation about the Earth-Moon barycentre, which creates the tidal bulge on the side away from the Moon.
topic_notes: Tides are periodic rises and falls of sea level, driven principally by the gravitational attraction of the Moon and Sun on Earth's oceans, with the centrifugal force of the Earth-Moon system revolving around its barycentre accounting for the far-side bulge. The balance between gravity and centrifugal force yields two bulges, so most places have two high and two low tides per lunar day of 24 h 50 min (hence a delay of about 50-52 minutes daily). Types: spring tides (new and full moon, alignment or syzygy, highest range), neap tides (first and last quarter, about 7 days after springs, lowest range). Perigee gives perigean tides, about 20% higher; apogee gives lower tides. Perihelion (about 3 January) and aphelion (about 4 July) bring seasonal variation. Tidal classification: semi-diurnal (two nearly equal highs and lows, as on the Atlantic coasts of Europe and the US), diurnal (one high and one low daily, as in the Gulf of Mexico), and mixed (unequal highs and lows, as on the Pacific coast of North America and much of the Indian coast). Tidal bore occurs in funnel-shaped estuaries, such as the Hooghly, Qiantang (China) and Amazon (pororoca). The Bay of Fundy has the world's highest tidal range, while in India the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) and Gulf of Kutch have high ranges (the Gulf of Kutch is a potential tidal energy site). Tidal energy sites include La Rance (France), Sihwa Lake (South Korea) and Kislaya Guba (Russia). Tides help navigation, fishing and port operations, for example at Kolkata through the Hooghly; they also clear harbour silt and generate power. Related concepts include ebb and flood tides, tidal currents, and the Earth's tidal friction that slowly lengthens the day and moves the Moon away about 3.8 cm each year.

ocr: In which of the following activities are Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellites used? 1, Assessment of crop productivity 2. Locating grcundwater resources 3. Mineral exploration 4, Telecommunications 5S. Traffic studies Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 4 and 5 only fc) 1 and 2 only (@) 1,2,3,4and5
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme, started in 1988 with IRS-1A, is one of the largest civilian remote sensing constellations in the world. It is managed by ISRO, with data distributed through NRSC (National Remote Sensing Centre), Hyderabad. IRS satellites carry optical and microwave sensors (LISS, PAN, AWiFS, and later RISAT radar) in sun-synchronous polar orbits at roughly 600-900 km. Their data support agriculture (crop acreage and production estimation under FASAL), water resources (groundwater prospects mapping under the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission), geology (mineral targeting), forestry, urban planning, flood and drought monitoring, and ocean studies (Oceansat). By contrast, communication satellites such as INSAT and GSAT sit in geostationary orbit at about 36,000 km and handle telecom, TV broadcasting, and meteorology. Elimination logic: statement 4 (Telecommunications) is clearly wrong, because it belongs to INSAT/GSAT. That removes options (b) and (d). Statement 5 (traffic studies) is likewise not a standard IRS use. Between (a) and (c), groundwater and mineral exploration are well-established IRS applications, so (a) is the answer.
explanations: Correct. Crop assessment, groundwater location and mineral exploration are all established IRS applications, while telecom and traffic are not.
Wrong. Telecommunications is the function of INSAT/GSAT geostationary satellites, and traffic studies are not an IRS use; this option leaves out the three genuine uses.
Wrong. Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but this omits mineral exploration (3), which is also a valid IRS use.
Wrong. It includes telecommunications (4) and traffic studies (5), which are not IRS applications.
keyfact: IRS = earth observation in polar orbit (crops, groundwater, minerals, forests); INSAT/GSAT = geostationary telecom and weather.
option_notes: Option (a) lists crop productivity assessment, groundwater location and mineral exploration. These are three core natural-resource applications of IRS data, supported by NRSC, MNCFC and the Geological Survey of India. Multispectral sensors (LISS-III, LISS-IV, AWiFS) and PAN cameras give the resolution needed. This is the official answer, showing that IRS is an earth-observation, resource-management programme rather than a communication or transport one.

Option (b) lists telecommunications and traffic studies. Telecom belongs to the INSAT/GSAT series in geostationary orbit, launched since 1983, with transponders for telephony, TV and broadband. Traffic and vehicle tracking rely more on navigation systems such as NavIC (IRNSS) and GPS. IRS satellites do neither as core roles, so this option is wrong. It is a typical UPSC trap mixing satellite classes.

Option (c) lists crop productivity and groundwater only. Both are correct IRS uses, but the option is incomplete because mineral exploration also uses IRS data. Remember that UPSC often builds wrong options by partial inclusion. Groundwater prospects maps were produced under the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, and crop forecasts under FASAL by MNCFC.

Option (d) claims all five activities. It is wrong because telecommunications is done by INSAT/GSAT and traffic studies are not a standard IRS role. IRS satellites are in sun-synchronous polar orbits at about 600-900 km, designed for periodic imaging of the same ground area under similar lighting, which is unsuited to telecom relay.
related: IRS-1A, launched in 1988, was India's first operational remote sensing satellite.
IRS satellites orbit in sun-synchronous polar orbits, about 600-900 km up.
INSAT/GSAT satellites are geostationary, at about 36,000 km, used for telecom, TV and meteorology.
NRSC, Hyderabad, is the centre for IRS data acquisition and distribution.
Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre uses remote sensing for crop forecasts under FASAL.
RISAT satellites carry synthetic aperture radar, which can image through clouds and at night.
NavIC (IRNSS) is India's regional navigation system with seven satellites.
Bhuvan is ISRO's geoportal for satellite imagery and geospatial services.
statements: 1 — Correct: IRS data are used for crop acreage and productivity assessment. Under the FASAL programme and the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC), set up in 2012 under the Agriculture Ministry, satellite data from sensors such as AWiFS and LISS-III give pre-harvest forecasts of major crops. Multi-date imagery tracks crop vigour, area sown, drought stress and yield modelling. The programme also covers horticulture assessment (CHAMAN) and agricultural drought assessment (NADAMS). This helps policymakers plan procurement, prices, imports and exports.

2 — Correct: IRS data are used for locating groundwater. Multispectral imagery helps identify geomorphology, lineaments, soil, and drainage patterns that indicate groundwater potential zones. ISRO, together with the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission, produced groundwater prospects maps for the country at 1:50,000 scale. The maps guide well-siting in drought-prone and hard-rock areas. NRSC's Bhuvan portal and the National Water Informatics efforts also use such data.

3 — Correct: IRS data are used for mineral exploration. Satellite imagery helps spot rock types, structural features such as faults and folds, hydrothermal alteration zones and geobotanical anomalies, which guide geologists to likely mineral deposits. The Geological Survey of India and the Atomic Minerals Directorate use remote sensing data from LISS and PAN sensors for targeting. It reduces the cost and time of ground surveys, especially in remote or forested terrain.

4 — Incorrect: Telecommunications is done by communication satellites, not IRS. INSAT (Indian National Satellite System, begun 1983) and GSAT series sit in geostationary orbit about 36,000 km up. They carry transponders for telephony, TV, DTH, VSAT, radio networking, tele-education and telemedicine, and disaster warning. INSAT is among the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the Asia-Pacific. IRS, by contrast, orbits in low sun-synchronous polar orbits for earth observation.

5 — Incorrect: Traffic studies are not a recognised core IRS application. IRS focuses on natural resource management, agriculture, water, geology, forestry, urban and land-use mapping, and disaster monitoring. Traffic monitoring needs very high temporal resolution, continuous coverage and often ground sensors, GPS or navigation data. India's navigation system NavIC (IRNSS, seven satellites, operational name given in 2016) and GPS-based systems are more relevant to transport and vehicle tracking than IRS.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3 only. IRS satellites are earth-observation satellites used for crop assessment, groundwater prospecting and mineral exploration, but telecommunications and traffic studies are not their roles. Telecom is done by INSAT/GSAT series, and traffic studies are not a standard IRS application.
topic_notes: The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) programme began with IRS-1A, launched in March 1988 from Baikonur on a Soviet Vostok launcher. It is among the world's largest civilian remote sensing constellations. ISRO builds and operates the satellites; NRSC in Hyderabad (under the Department of Space) handles data reception, processing and distribution. Ground reception is at Shadnagar near Hyderabad. IRS satellites use sun-synchronous polar orbits, which pass over the same location at the same local solar time. Common sensors are LISS-I to LISS-IV (multispectral), PAN (panchromatic), and AWiFS (wide-field). Later series include Resourcesat, Cartosat (high-resolution mapping, urban and infrastructure planning), Oceansat (ocean colour, wind), RISAT (radar imaging, which sees through cloud and at night, useful in monsoon), and Resourcesat-2/2A. PSLV is the usual launcher; it launched IRS-1D and many later ones. Applications include agriculture (FASAL, NADAMS), groundwater prospects, mineral targeting, forest cover assessment (Forest Survey of India), land use and land cover mapping, wasteland mapping, flood and cyclone monitoring, snow and glacier studies, urban sprawl, and watershed development. The Bhuvan portal gives free access to Indian geospatial data. By contrast, INSAT and GSAT are geostationary communication and meteorological satellites; Kalpana and INSAT-3D/3DR are meteorological; NavIC (IRNSS) is the regional navigation system with seven satellites; GAGAN is the satellite-based augmentation system for aviation. Other angles UPSC could ask are polar vs geostationary orbits, PSLV vs GSLV, the difference between active and passive remote sensing, spatial and spectral resolution, and Cartosat's role in strategic mapping.

ocr: Consider the following States : 1. Arunachal Pradesh 2. Himachal Pradesh 3. Mizoram In which of the above States do ‘Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests’ occur? (a) 1 only () 2 and 3 only (co) 1 and 3 only 1, 2 and 3 (d}
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests (Champion and Seth classification) grow where annual rainfall exceeds about 200 cm, the mean annual temperature is about 22°C, humidity is high and the dry season is short or absent. The trees are tall (often 45-60 m), dense and multi-layered, and they shed leaves at different times, so the forest looks evergreen all year. Typical species are mahogany, rosewood, ebony, dhup, jamun, mesua (ironwood) and gurjan. In India they are found on the windward slopes of the Western Ghats, in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and in the upper Assam valley and the north-eastern hill states (Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Tripura). They also occur in parts of the Terai in the eastern Himalayan foothills. Elimination logic: Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram are both in the North-East with very heavy rainfall, so statement 1 and statement 3 are correct. Himachal Pradesh has tropical dry deciduous and subtropical pine forests in the lower hills, then temperate and alpine forests higher up, and no wet evergreen belt. Statement 2 is therefore wrong, which leaves only (c).
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out Mizoram, which does have tropical wet evergreen forests.
Wrong: it includes Himachal Pradesh, which has no such forests, and it leaves out Arunachal Pradesh.
Correct: Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram both receive very heavy rainfall and have tropical wet evergreen forests, while Himachal Pradesh does not.
Wrong: Himachal Pradesh is a temperate and montane state with no tropical wet evergreen forest, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests (rainfall above about 200 cm) occur in the Western Ghats, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the North-East (Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram), not in Himachal Pradesh.
option_notes: Option (a) names Arunachal Pradesh alone. The state lies in the eastern Himalaya, has over 78% forest cover, and holds tropical wet evergreen forests in its foothills as well as temperate and alpine zones higher up. Namdapha National Park in Changlang is its best-known protected area and is a tiger reserve. It is true for Arunachal but incomplete, because Mizoram qualifies too.

Option (b) names Himachal Pradesh and Mizoram. Himachal Pradesh is a western Himalayan state with dry deciduous, chir pine, deodar, oak and alpine vegetation, and its Great Himalayan National Park is a UNESCO site. Mizoram has heavy-rainfall wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forests and large bamboo areas, and is known for mautam (bamboo flowering). The option is wrong because it includes Himachal Pradesh.

Option (c) names Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram, the correct pair. Both are North-Eastern hill states in the Eastern Himalaya or Purvanchal region, with annual rainfall often above 200 cm. Their forests are dense, multi-layered, evergreen and rich in biodiversity, with species such as mesua, dhup and gurjan. The North-East holds a large share of India's forest cover and part of the Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot.

Option (d) claims all three states. Combining a western Himalayan state with the North-Eastern states ignores the rainfall and climate difference. Himachal Pradesh has monsoon rainfall of about 100-200 cm in places and a strong altitudinal zonation, with no tropical wet evergreen belt. The option is wrong because of statement 2.
related: Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests need rainfall above about 200 cm.
Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests are the largest forest type in India by area and include teak and sal.
Mizoram has one of India's highest forest cover percentages, and Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area.
Sundarbans in West Bengal is the largest mangrove forest in the world.
Himachal Pradesh's Great Himalayan National Park became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
The Forest Survey of India, Dehradun, publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years.
Western Ghats and the Eastern Himalaya are among India's biodiversity hotspots.
Mautam is bamboo flowering in Mizoram, which causes rat floods and famine.
statements: 1 — Correct: Arunachal Pradesh has tropical wet evergreen forest in its low-lying, high-rainfall foothills. Arunachal Pradesh lies in the eastern Himalaya and is one of India's most forested states, with over 78% forest cover. Its vegetation ranges from tropical wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forests in the foothills (below about 900 m), through subtropical and temperate forests, to alpine vegetation at the top. Rainfall is very heavy in the foothills. The state is part of the Eastern Himalaya biodiversity hotspot and is home to Namdapha National Park (Changlang district), which is a tiger reserve, and to Mouling and Dibang Valley biosphere areas.

2 — Incorrect: Himachal Pradesh has no tropical wet evergreen forest. Himachal Pradesh is a western Himalayan state whose rainfall is moderate and whose climate varies strongly with altitude. Its vegetation includes tropical dry deciduous and scrub forests in the Shivalik foothills, subtropical chir pine forests at mid elevations, temperate forests of deodar, oak, blue pine, spruce and fir, and alpine pastures and cold desert (Lahaul-Spiti, Kinnaur) at high elevations. Great Himalayan National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014) and Pin Valley National Park are located here. Forest cover is about 27% of the geographical area.

3 — Correct: Mizoram has tropical wet evergreen and semi-evergreen forests. Mizoram is a hilly state in the North-East with heavy monsoon rainfall, and it has over 84% forest cover, among the highest in India. Its forests include tropical wet evergreen, semi-evergreen, and montane subtropical types, along with large bamboo areas. Bamboo flowering (mautam) is a well-known phenomenon that periodically causes rat population explosions and famine. Dampa Tiger Reserve and Murlen National Park are the main protected areas. Shifting cultivation (jhum) is widely practised and is a conservation concern.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests occur in high-rainfall, warm regions such as the Western Ghats, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and the north-eastern states, including Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram. Himachal Pradesh is a Himalayan state with montane, temperate and alpine vegetation, not tropical wet evergreen forest.
topic_notes: Forest types of India follow the Champion and Seth (1968) classification, which has 16 major types in 5 groups: Moist Tropical, Dry Tropical, Montane Subtropical, Montane Temperate, and Subalpine/Alpine. The Moist Tropical group includes Tropical Wet Evergreen, Semi-Evergreen, Moist Deciduous, Littoral and Swamp forests. Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests need rainfall above about 200-250 cm, a short dry season and warm temperatures. They are found on the Western Ghats (windward side, from Kerala to Maharashtra), the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Upper Assam and the North-East, and parts of the Terai. Trees are tall, with dense canopies and little undergrowth in places, and the species are evergreen hardwoods such as mahogany, ebony, rosewood, mesua, dhup and canes. Tropical Semi-Evergreen Forests occur in transition zones with slightly lower rainfall. Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests (the largest group by area, with teak and sal) occur in areas with 100-200 cm rainfall and cover large parts of peninsular and eastern India. Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests occur at 70-100 cm rainfall, and Thorn Forests below 70 cm, in Rajasthan, Gujarat and parts of the Deccan. Mangroves (Littoral and Swamp forests) occur in deltas, such as the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world. The Forest Survey of India (Dehradun) publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years. Forest cover is about 21-22% and tree cover about 3% of the country's area. States with the largest forest area are Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Manipur and Nagaland have the highest percentage of forest cover. UPSC often asks about forest-type distribution, characteristic species, and links with rainfall, soils and biodiversity hotspots.

ocr: The term IndARC’, sometimes seen in the news, is the name of (aj an indigenously developed radar system inducted into Indian Defence (b) India’s satellite to provide services to the countries of Indian Ocean Rim {¢) a scientific establishment set up by India in Antarctic region (d) India’s underwater observatory to scientifically study the Arctic region 26 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Geography
detail: IndARC is a multi-sensor moored observatory deployed in July 2014 in Kongsfjorden fjord, off Ny-Alesund, Svalbard, Norway, at roughly 78 degrees N. It was set up by the Ministry of Earth Sciences through the National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR), Goa, which is the nodal body for polar research. It was placed after India's Arctic research station Himadri (opened 2008 at Ny-Alesund) and made India one of the few countries with an in-situ underwater Arctic observatory. Its sensors record temperature, salinity, ocean currents, pressure, conductivity and other parameters across the water column, helping scientists study the effect of Arctic sea-ice melt and freshwater input on ocean circulation and on the Indian summer monsoon. Elimination logic: the name carries 'ARC' for Arctic, pointing to polar research; Antarctic establishments have different names (Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri, Bharati), so (c) is wrong. Radar systems (Rajendra, Swathi, Ashwini) and the SAARC/South Asia satellite (GSAT-9) have unrelated names, so (a) and (b) fail. Option (d) is the only one that matches both the name and the Arctic context.
explanations: Incorrect: IndARC is not a radar system. Indigenous Indian radars have names like Rajendra, Ashwini, Swathi (weapon locating radar) and Arudhra.
Incorrect: it is not a satellite. India's regional service satellite is the South Asia Satellite (GSAT-9) for SAARC nations, not for the Indian Ocean Rim.
Incorrect: it is not in Antarctica. India's Antarctic stations are Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri and Bharati; IndARC is in the Arctic, in Svalbard.
Correct: IndARC is India's first underwater moored observatory in the Arctic, in Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, deployed in July 2014 to study Arctic climate and its monsoon links.
keyfact: IndARC = India's first underwater moored observatory in the Arctic (Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, 2014), run by NCAOR under MoES.
option_notes: Indigenous radars inducted by India include Swathi (weapon locating radar, DRDO), Rajendra (phased array radar of the Akash missile system), Ashwini (3D low-level tactical radar) and Arudhra (medium-power radar). They are developed by DRDO and produced by BEL and others. None is called IndARC; the name was a distractor playing on 'radar'.

The South Asia Satellite (GSAT-9) was launched by ISRO on GSLV-F09 on 5 May 2017 as a gift to SAARC nations, offering communication and disaster-support services. Pakistan opted out. It serves South Asia, not the whole Indian Ocean Rim. India has also launched navigation satellites under NavIC (IRNSS) covering India and about 1,500 km around.

India's Antarctic establishments are Dakshin Gangotri (1983, now defunct), Maitri (1989, Schirmacher Oasis) and Bharati (2012, Larsemann Hills). Management is by NCAOR, Goa. India signed the Antarctic Treaty in 1983, became a consultative party the same year, and passed the Antarctic Act in 2022. IndARC is not part of this set.

IndARC is the moored underwater observatory in Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, deployed July 2014 under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, run by NCAOR. It measures temperature, salinity and currents to study Arctic-monsoon links. It sits near Himadri station in Ny-Alesund. A second mooring was later added and the system is upgraded periodically.
related: IndARC was deployed in July 2014 in Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, Norway.
Himadri is India's Arctic research station at Ny-Alesund (2008).
India got Arctic Council observer status in 2013.
Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri and Bharati are India's Antarctic stations.
NCPOR (earlier NCAOR), Goa, is the nodal polar research body under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
India's Arctic Policy was released in March 2022.
The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959; India joined in 1983.
The Arctic Council was set up by the Ottawa Declaration, 1996.
summary: The correct answer is (d). IndARC is India's first underwater moored observatory in the Arctic region, deployed in Kongsfjorden, Svalbard (Norway) in July 2014 by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (NCAOR, Goa). It is used to study Arctic climate processes and their link with the Indian monsoon.
topic_notes: India's polar programme is coordinated by the Ministry of Earth Sciences through the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (NCPOR, formerly NCAOR), Goa. In the Arctic, India has the Himadri research station at Ny-Alesund, Svalbard (opened 2008), and the IndARC moored observatory (2014) in Kongsfjorden. India became an observer in the Arctic Council in 2013 (along with China, Japan, Korea, Italy and Singapore). The Arctic Council has eight member states: Canada, Denmark (Greenland), Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the USA; it was formed by the Ottawa Declaration, 1996. The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gives Norway sovereignty but allows signatories equal rights to research and commerce; India signed in 1920. India released its Arctic Policy in March 2022 with six pillars, including science and research, climate and environment protection, economic and human development, transportation and connectivity, governance and international cooperation, and national capacity building. In the Antarctic, India's stations are Dakshin Gangotri (1983), Maitri (1989) and Bharati (2012). The first Indian Antarctic expedition was in 1981-82 under Dr S.Z. Qasim. India is a consultative party to the Antarctic Treaty (1959, in force 1961) and signed the Madrid Protocol; the Indian Antarctic Act came in 2022. The research vessel Polar Sea and the Himalayan-linked Himadri program help study sea-ice, glaciers and carbon. Other angles: the Northern Sea Route, the Northwest Passage, melting of Arctic ice, the Arctic-monsoon linkage, and the Deep Ocean Mission.

ocr: With reference to ‘Forest Carbon Partnership Facility’, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. It is a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society and indigenous peoples. It provides financial aid to universities, individual scientists and institutions involved in scientific forestry research to develop eco-friendly and climate adaptation technologies for sustainable forest management. It assists the countries in their ‘REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradationt+)’ efforts by providing them with financial and technical assistance. Select
subject: Environment
detail: The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) is a World Bank-hosted global partnership launched in 2008 (announced at the Bali COP-13 in 2007). It focuses on REDD+: Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus conservation, sustainable management of forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks. It works through two funds. The Readiness Fund helps countries prepare REDD+ strategies, reference emission levels, monitoring systems and safeguards. The Carbon Fund pays countries for verified emission reductions through results-based payments. Its participants include developing forest countries, donor governments, businesses, civil society and Indigenous Peoples' organisations, and the World Bank acts as trustee and secretariat. Elimination logic: statement 1 describes the partnership accurately. Statement 3 describes its core function accurately. Statement 2 describes a research-grant body, which the FCPF is not. Its support goes to national governments for REDD+ readiness and results-based payments, not to universities or individual scientists for technology development. Dropping statement 2 eliminates options (b) and (d), and since statement 1 is true, option (a) is eliminated too, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 3 is also correct. Selecting statement 1 alone ignores the FCPF's central role in assisting REDD+.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect and statement 1 is correct. The FCPF does not fund research scientists or universities.
(c) is right because statements 1 and 3 are correct and statement 2 is incorrect. This matches the official answer.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which wrongly says the FCPF funds scientific research bodies.
keyfact: FCPF (World Bank, 2008) = global partnership that gives REDD+ readiness and results-based carbon payments to countries; it does not fund scientific research.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold if the FCPF were just a partnership with no operational assistance role. In fact the FCPF is defined by its REDD+ support work. Its stakeholders are governments, businesses, civil society and Indigenous Peoples. The World Bank hosts it, and it has the Readiness Fund and the Carbon Fund. Statement 3 is therefore also correct, which is why this option is incomplete.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', is wrong because it includes the false claim about funding research. The FCPF is not a scientific grant agency. It is a World Bank-hosted facility created in 2008 that supports REDD+ readiness and pays for verified emission reductions. Research funding for forestry is handled by other organisations, such as CIFOR (Center for International Forestry Research) and national research institutions.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only', is the correct answer. It reflects the FCPF as a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society and Indigenous Peoples, and as an assistance facility for REDD+ countries. It runs a Readiness Fund for preparation and a Carbon Fund for results-based payments, with the World Bank acting as trustee and secretariat. It was launched in 2008 following the Bali COP-13 discussions on REDD.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is wrong because it accepts statement 2. UPSC often adds an invented function like research funding to a genuine description. The FCPF assists national governments, not universities or individual scientists. It supports REDD+ readiness, national strategies, monitoring systems, and payments for verified emission reductions rather than technology development grants.
related: FCPF was launched in 2008 and is hosted by the World Bank.
The FCPF has two funds: Readiness Fund and Carbon Fund.
REDD+ goes beyond REDD by adding conservation, sustainable forest management and enhancement of carbon stocks.
UN-REDD is a joint programme of FAO, UNDP and UNEP.
The Warsaw Framework for REDD+ was adopted at COP-19 in 2013.
The Bonn Challenge targets restoring 350 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
The Green Climate Fund is headquartered in Songdo, South Korea.
CIFOR is headquartered in Bogor, Indonesia, and does forestry research.
statements: 1 — Correct: The FCPF is a multi-stakeholder global partnership. It brings together governments, businesses, civil society and Indigenous Peoples. It was launched in 2008, is hosted by the World Bank, and has about 47 developing country participants across Africa, Asia and Latin America. Donors have included Norway, Germany, the UK, the USA and The Nature Conservancy. Indigenous Peoples and civil society observers take part in its governing Participants Committee, and it has a capacity-building programme for Indigenous Peoples and forest-dependent communities.

2 — Incorrect: The FCPF does not fund universities, individual scientists or research institutions to develop eco-friendly or climate adaptation technologies. Its money goes to national governments for REDD+ readiness and results-based payments. Scientific forestry research funding comes from bodies such as CIFOR, the ICFRE in India, or national research councils. The Green Climate Fund and the Global Environment Facility are the larger multilateral climate funds, though they too work mostly through governments and accredited entities.

3 — Correct: The FCPF helps countries implement REDD+ through financial and technical assistance. The Readiness Fund supports national REDD+ strategies, forest reference emission levels, measurement, reporting and verification systems, and social and environmental safeguards. The Carbon Fund pays for verified emission reductions through Emission Reductions Payment Agreements, typically at about US$5 per tonne of CO2. REDD+ was developed under the UNFCCC, with the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ adopted in 2013.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) is a global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society and Indigenous Peoples that helps countries with REDD+ through financial and technical assistance. It does not give grants to universities or scientists for forestry research, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: REDD+ stands for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus conservation, sustainable management of forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks in developing countries. The idea emerged at UNFCCC COP-11 (2005) and was developed at Bali COP-13 (2007), the Cancun Agreements (COP-16, 2010) and the Warsaw Framework for REDD+ (COP-19, 2013). Developing countries must prepare a national strategy, a forest reference emission level, a national forest monitoring system and a safeguards information system. The FCPF, launched in 2008 and hosted by the World Bank, has two funds. The Readiness Fund helps countries prepare, and the Carbon Fund pays for verified emission reductions at around US$5 per tonne CO2. Related initiatives include UN-REDD, a joint programme of FAO, UNDP and UNEP launched in 2008, and the Forest Investment Program under the Climate Investment Funds. Other forest and climate bodies: the Green Climate Fund (headquartered in Songdo, South Korea), the GEF (set up 1991, hosted by the World Bank), the New York Declaration on Forests (2014), and the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use (2021), which aims to halt and reverse forest loss by 2030. Other angles: the UN Forum on Forests, CIFOR in Bogor, Indonesia, the Bonn Challenge (restore 350 million hectares by 2030), and India's Compensatory Afforestation Fund (CAMPA) and National Mission for a Green India. India is not an FCPF Carbon Fund participant, but it supports REDD+ in principle and has a national REDD+ strategy. UPSC often tests the full forms, host institutions, funding functions and which body funds whom.

question: Which one of the following was given classical language status recently?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Classical language status was introduced in October 2004 with Tamil as the first. The Ministry of Culture (with the Linguistic Experts Committee under the Sahitya Akademi) recommends languages. Criteria (revised in 2005 and again in 2024): high antiquity of early texts/recorded history over 1,500-2,000 years; a body of ancient literature regarded as a heritage by generations of speakers; an original literary tradition not borrowed from another speech community; and the classical language and literature being distinct from the modern form, possibly with discontinuity. Benefits: two major international awards annually for scholars, a Centre of Excellence for Studies in the language, and a UGC request to create professional chairs in central universities. Order of recognition: Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Kannada and Telugu (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014); in October 2024 Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were added, making 11. In 2015, when this question was asked, Odia was the latest. Konkani and Bhojpuri were not recognised, and Assamese only got it in 2024, so (b), (c) and (d) fail for the 2015 context.
explanations: Correct: Odia was notified as a Classical Language in February 2014, the most recent addition at the time of the 2015 paper.
Incorrect: Konkani has never been given classical status; it is an Eighth Schedule language (added 1992) but not classical.
Incorrect: Bhojpuri is not in the Eighth Schedule and has no classical status.
Incorrect for the 2015 context: Assamese was recognised only in October 2024, long after this question.
keyfact: Odia was declared a Classical Language in 2014 (6th after Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam); Assamese, Bengali, Marathi, Pali and Prakrit followed in 2024.
option_notes: Odia: an Indo-Aryan language of Odisha, written in the Odia script, with literature such as Sarala Das's Mahabharata (15th century). It was declared classical in 2014 after a long campaign, and Odisha has a Centre of Excellence for Classical Odia at Berhampur University. It has been in the Eighth Schedule since the original 1950 list.

Konkani: an Indo-Aryan language spoken in Goa, Karnataka and Konkan coast areas, written in Devanagari (official in Goa), Roman, Kannada and other scripts. It was made Goa's official language in 1987 and entered the Eighth Schedule via the 71st Amendment, 1992. It is not a classical language.

Bhojpuri: an Indo-Aryan language spoken in western Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand, and also in Nepal, Mauritius, Fiji and Suriname via the indenture diaspora. It is written in Devanagari and Kaithi historically. It is not in the Eighth Schedule, despite long demands, and not classical.

Assamese: an Indo-Aryan language of Assam, written in the Assamese-Bengali script, with early works like Charyapada claims and Madhav Kandali's Ramayana (14th century), plus Sankardev's works. It is in the Eighth Schedule from 1950. It was declared classical in October 2024, not in 2014-15.
related: Tamil was the first classical language, declared in 2004.
Odia became the 6th classical language in 2014; Malayalam was the 5th in 2013.
In October 2024 Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were declared classical, bringing the total to 11.
The Eighth Schedule has 22 languages; the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.
The 113th Amendment (2011) changed 'Oriya' to 'Odia'.
Classical language benefits include international awards, Centres of Excellence and UGC professional chairs.
Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added to the Eighth Schedule by the 71st Amendment (1992).
Article 351 directs the Union to promote the spread of Hindi.
summary: The answer is (a) Odia. Odia was declared a Classical Language by the Government of India in February 2014 (the 6th language to get the status at that time), after meeting the Ministry of Culture criteria of antiquity and an independent literary tradition.
topic_notes: Classical languages of India: the government created the category in 2004 following demands from Tamil scholars; Tamil was the first, declared on 12 October 2004. Sanskrit followed in 2005, Telugu and Kannada in 2008, Malayalam in 2013, Odia in 2014. In October 2024, Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were added, giving eleven. The criteria were first set at 1,000 years of early texts and were raised to 1,500-2,000 years; a 2024 revision stressed knowledge texts, poetry and inscriptional evidence. The Linguistic Experts Committee, housed under the Sahitya Akademi, examines proposals; the Ministry of Culture notifies status (earlier the Ministry of Home Affairs handled it). Benefits include the annual international President's Awards for Classical Languages, Centres of Excellence (the Central Institute of Classical Tamil in Chennai is a key body, and the Central Sanskrit Universities are linked to Sanskrit), and UGC chairs. Distinguish from the Eighth Schedule: Article 344(1) and 351 relate to it; it lists 22 languages, with Sindhi added in 1967 (21st Amendment), Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali in 1992 (71st Amendment), Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali in 2003 (92nd Amendment). Odia was added in 1950 and renamed from Oriya through the 2011 Constitution (113th Amendment) Act. Classical status is not the same as Eighth Schedule inclusion or official language status. Related: Article 343 (Hindi in Devanagari as official language of the Union), Article 345 (state official languages), Article 350A (mother-tongue instruction), and Article 350B (Special Officer for linguistic minorities).

question:
With reference to an organization known as BirdLife International’, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. It is a Global Partnership of Conservation Organizations.
2. The concept of ‘biodiversity hotspots’ originated from this organization,
3. It identifies the sites known/ referred to as Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas’. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: BirdLife International is the world's largest partnership of nature conservation organisations, with national partners in over 110 countries. In India its partner is the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS). It was founded in 1922 as the International Council for Bird Preservation (ICBP), renamed BirdLife International in 1993, and is headquartered in Cambridge, UK. It is the official Red List authority for birds for the IUCN. Its flagship programme is the identification and monitoring of Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs), sites of global significance for bird conservation using standardised criteria. The 'biodiversity hotspot' concept was proposed by British ecologist Norman Myers in 1988. Conservation International adopted it in 1989 and refined the criteria: at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5% of the world total) and at least 70% of original habitat lost. Elimination logic: statement 2 is wrong, so any option containing it, (b) and (d), is out. Statements 1 and 3 are both correct, so (a) is incomplete and (c) is the answer.
explanations: Incorrect: this option omits statement 3, which is correct because BirdLife identifies Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas.
Incorrect: it includes statement 2, which is false, since the hotspot concept came from Norman Myers and was later developed by Conservation International.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true (global partnership; identifies IBAs), and statement 2 is false.
Incorrect: it wrongly includes statement 2, as BirdLife did not originate the biodiversity hotspots concept.
keyfact: BirdLife International = global NGO partnership that identifies IBAs (BNHS is its Indian partner); hotspots were conceived by Norman Myers and adopted by Conservation International.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: BirdLife International is a global partnership of conservation NGOs, founded in 1922 as ICBP and renamed in 1993. It is headquartered in Cambridge, UK, and has partners in over 110 countries. In India the partner is BNHS. It is the IUCN Red List authority for birds. This option is wrong because it leaves out the IBA role in statement 3.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3 only: Statement 3 is correct, since IBAs are identified by BirdLife. Statement 2 is wrong because the hotspot concept was formulated by Norman Myers in 1988 and popularised by Conservation International. Hotspots need 1,500 or more endemic plant species and 70% or more habitat loss. There are 36 hotspots, four of them in India. The option fails because it excludes statement 1 and includes statement 2.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3 only: this is the official answer. BirdLife is a global partnership of NGOs, with BNHS as its Indian partner. It designates IBAs on standard criteria, with about 550 sites in India and more than 13,000 worldwide. IBAs are now part of the wider Key Biodiversity Areas framework. They are not automatically legally protected. Hotspots, by contrast, are Conservation International's concept.

Option (d), all three statements: this fails because statement 2 is false. The biodiversity hotspot idea originated with Norman Myers in 1988, and Conservation International adopted it in 1989 with quantitative criteria. India's hotspots are the Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland (Nicobar). BirdLife's own area-based concepts are Endemic Bird Areas and IBAs.
related: BirdLife's Indian partner is the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), founded 1883.
Norman Myers proposed the biodiversity hotspot concept in 1988; Conservation International adopted it in 1989.
There are 36 global hotspots; India has four: Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, Sundaland (Nicobar).
BirdLife International is the IUCN Red List authority for birds.
IBAs are not automatically legally protected; many overlap with national parks or sanctuaries.
The Great Indian Bustard is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
Hotspot criteria: 1,500 or more endemic vascular plants and 70% or more habitat loss.
BirdLife International was founded in 1922 as ICBP and renamed in 1993.
statements: 1 — Correct: BirdLife International describes itself as a global partnership of conservation organisations (NGOs), with one lead partner per country. It was founded in 1922 as ICBP and renamed in 1993. Its Cambridge secretariat coordinates over 115 partners. In India the partner is the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), which works with the Indian Bird Conservation Network. BirdLife is the IUCN Red List authority for birds, produces the Handbook of the Birds of the World with Lynx Edicions, and runs the Preventing Extinctions Programme and the Albatross Task Force.

2 — Incorrect: The hotspot concept did not originate with BirdLife. Norman Myers proposed it in 1988 and Conservation International (CI) adopted it in 1989. The criteria are at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and at least 70% loss of primary habitat. There are 36 hotspots worldwide, and four cover India: the Himalaya, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). BirdLife's equivalents are Endemic Bird Areas (EBAs) and IBAs, not hotspots.

3 — Correct: BirdLife identifies Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) using globally standardised criteria, including threatened species, restricted-range species, biome-restricted assemblages and congregations. IBAs are sites of international significance for bird conservation. Over 13,000 IBAs have been identified globally. India has about 550 IBAs, identified by BNHS with BirdLife. IBAs are not legally protected unless they overlap with protected areas. They form the basis for Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs).
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct. BirdLife International is a global partnership of conservation organisations that identifies Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs), but the 'biodiversity hotspots' concept came from Norman Myers (1988) and was later taken up by Conservation International, not from BirdLife.
topic_notes: BirdLife International is a partnership of national conservation NGOs. It was founded in 1922 as ICBP by T. Gilbert Pearson and others, renamed in 1993, and is headquartered in Cambridge, UK. Its Indian partner is the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), founded in 1883. It serves as the IUCN Red List authority for birds and publishes the annual 'State of the World's Birds'. It runs the IBA programme, with IBAs defined by criteria A1 (globally threatened species), A2 (restricted-range species), A3 (biome-restricted assemblages) and A4 (congregations). More than 13,000 IBAs have been identified globally, and India has about 550. IBAs are also part of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs). Endemic Bird Areas are regions where two or more restricted-range species overlap. Biodiversity hotspots: Norman Myers (1988), Conservation International (1989); 36 hotspots; criteria are 1,500 or more endemic vascular plants and 70% or more habitat loss. India's hotspots are the Himalaya, Western Ghats (with Sri Lanka), Indo-Burma and Sundaland (Nicobar). Related bodies and designations: IUCN (founded 1948, Gland, Switzerland; Red List categories from Extinct to Least Concern), Ramsar Convention (1971, wetlands), Wetlands International, WWF, Conservation International, the Convention on Migratory Species (Bonn, 1979) and the Central Asian Flyway. Related Indian bird species include the Great Indian Bustard (Critically Endangered, Rajasthan), the Siberian Crane, the Forest Owlet and the Bengal Florican. Likely angles for the exam are partner organisations, Red List categories, hotspot criteria, Ramsar sites, and IBA versus protected area status.

question: Which one of the following countries of South-West Asia does not open out to the Mediterranean Sea?
subject: Geography
detail: The eastern Mediterranean coast (the Levant) runs from Turkey in the north, through Syria, Lebanon and Israel, then the Palestinian territory of Gaza, to Egypt's Sinai in the south. Jordan lies inland, east of the Jordan River, the Dead Sea and the Israel/West Bank border. Its only coastline is about 26 km at Aqaba on the Gulf of Aqaba, an arm of the Red Sea, so it reaches the Indian Ocean system, not the Mediterranean. Syria has a coast of about 190 km, with the ports of Latakia and Tartus. Lebanon has about 225 km of coast, with Beirut, Tripoli and Sidon. Israel has Haifa and Ashdod on the Mediterranean and Eilat on the Red Sea, so it opens to both. Elimination logic: remember the north-to-south order of Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel along the coast, and then Jordan is the one left behind them to the east. Jordan is also bordered by Syria, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Israel and the West Bank. The Dead Sea is a landlocked salt lake, not a sea outlet.
explanations: Wrong: Syria has a Mediterranean coast with the ports of Latakia and Tartus, so it does open out to the sea.
Correct: Jordan has no Mediterranean coast. Its only sea access is at Aqaba on the Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea).
Wrong: Lebanon lies wholly along the eastern Mediterranean, with Beirut as its main port, so it opens to the sea.
Wrong: Israel has a Mediterranean coast (Haifa, Ashdod, Tel Aviv) and also a short Red Sea coast at Eilat.
keyfact: Jordan is the only West Asian country in the list with no Mediterranean coast; its sea outlet is Aqaba on the Red Sea.
option_notes: Syria: a West Asian republic with its capital at Damascus. It has a coast of about 190 km on the Mediterranean, with the ports of Latakia and Tartus (the latter hosts a Russian naval facility). It borders Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, Israel and Lebanon. The Euphrates flows through it, and the country has been in civil war since 2011.

Jordan: a landlocked-in-effect Hashemite kingdom with its capital at Amman. Its only coast is about 26 km at Aqaba on the Gulf of Aqaba, an arm of the Red Sea. It borders Syria, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Israel and the West Bank. It shares the Dead Sea, the lowest land point on Earth, and the Jordan River with Israel and Palestine. It signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.

Lebanon: a small Levantine republic with its capital at Beirut. It has about 225 km of Mediterranean coast, with the ports of Beirut, Tripoli and Sidon. It borders only Syria and Israel. The Litani is its main river, and Mount Lebanon runs parallel to the coast. It has a confessional power-sharing system.

Israel: a state in the Levant, founded in 1948, with Jerusalem as its declared capital (not recognised by most countries) and Tel Aviv as its economic hub. It has a Mediterranean coast (Haifa, Ashdod) and a small Red Sea coast at Eilat on the Gulf of Aqaba. It borders Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Egypt, the West Bank and Gaza.
related: Jordan's only port is Aqaba on the Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea).
The Dead Sea, shared by Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, is the lowest land point on Earth.
The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
The Black Sea is bordered by Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia.
The Strait of Gibraltar links the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.
The Bosphorus and Dardanelles link the Black Sea to the Mediterranean via the Sea of Marmara.
The Gulf of Aqaba is shared by Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
Cyprus is an island country in the eastern Mediterranean.
summary: The answer is (b) Jordan. Jordan is the only one of the four that has no Mediterranean coastline; its only sea outlet is the short Gulf of Aqaba coast on the Red Sea. Syria, Lebanon and Israel all lie on the eastern Mediterranean shore.
topic_notes: The Mediterranean Sea is bordered by 21 or so countries across Europe, Asia and Africa. It connects to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar, to the Red Sea through the Suez Canal (opened 1869), and to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles, the Sea of Marmara and the Bosphorus. In Asia, the countries on its coast are Turkey, Syria, Lebanon and Israel, plus Palestine (Gaza) and Cyprus as an island country. In Africa the coastal countries are Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. In Europe they are Spain, France, Monaco, Italy, Malta, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania and Greece. West Asian countries with no Mediterranean coast include Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Gulf states. Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Israel and Egypt all touch the Red Sea. The Gulf of Aqaba is shared by Egypt, Israel, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. The Dead Sea (bordered by Jordan, Israel and the West Bank) is a salt lake, about 430 m below sea level. The Jordan River flows from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. Landlocked countries of the wider region include Armenia, Azerbaijan (it borders the Caspian, a lake or sea by definition), and Afghanistan. Turkey borders the Black, Aegean and Mediterranean Seas. UPSC often asks which countries border which seas, such as the Black Sea, the Caspian Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, so learn them as a clockwise list.

ocr: In India, in which one of the following types of forests is teak a dominant tree species? (a) Tropical moist deciduous forest fb) Tropical rain forest (c) Tropical thorn scrub forest (d) Temperate forest with grasslands B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Environment
detail: Teak is a hardwood tree native to South and Southeast Asia. In India it is the characteristic dominant species of tropical moist deciduous forests, also called monsoon forests. These forests receive annual rainfall of roughly 100-200 cm and shed their leaves for about 6-8 weeks in the dry season. They cover the largest area of any forest type in India, in a belt along the Western Ghats' eastern slopes, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Maharashtra and the Shivalik foothills. Sal is the other major dominant species (in the wetter eastern part), alongside shisham, sandalwood, mahua, khair, arjun, mulberry and kusum. Teak also occurs in drier deciduous zones, but the moist type is the textbook association. Elimination: tropical rain forest (tropical wet evergreen) is dominated by evergreen species such as mahogany, ebony, rosewood, and dipterocarps, and has more than 200 cm of rain. Thorn scrub forest has acacias, babool, khejri and euphorbias in areas with less than 70 cm of rain. Temperate forests with grasslands occur in the Himalayas and Nilgiris, with oak, deodar, chir, spruce and shola, and are not teak habitat. So (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct. Teak is the dominant species of tropical moist deciduous (monsoon) forests with 100-200 cm of rainfall; Sal is the other key species.
Incorrect. Tropical rain forests are evergreen and dominated by mahogany, ebony, rosewood, gurjan and dipterocarps, not teak.
Incorrect. Thorn scrub forests have xerophytic species like babool, khejri, ber and euphorbias in arid areas with less than 70 cm of rainfall.
Incorrect. Temperate forests and grasslands (Himalayas, Nilgiri shola) have oak, deodar, chir pine, magnolia and rhododendron, not teak.
keyfact: Teak and sal = tropical moist deciduous (monsoon) forests, 100-200 cm rain, India's largest forest type.
option_notes: Tropical moist deciduous forests are India's most extensive forest type, lying in zones receiving 100-200 cm of rain. Trees shed leaves in the dry season. Key species are teak, sal, shisham, sandalwood, mahua, arjun, kusum and mulberry. They are found in the Western Ghats' eastern slopes, Chhota Nagpur plateau, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Northeast India and the Shivalik foothills. They are economically important for timber.

Tropical wet evergreen (rain) forests occur where rainfall exceeds 200 cm with a short dry season. They are dense, multi-layered, and the trees do not shed leaves at one time. Species include mahogany, ebony, rosewood, gurjan, dhup and mesua. They are found on the Western Ghats' windward slopes, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Biodiversity is very high.

Tropical thorn and scrub forests occur in regions with less than 70 cm of rain: Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana and the semi-arid parts of the peninsula. Vegetation is stunted, with long roots, thorny and small-leaved plants. Typical species are babool (acacia), ber, khejri, wild date palm, neem, cacti and khair. Trees are scattered, with grasses between them.

Temperate (montane) forests occur in the Himalayas and in higher parts of the south such as the Nilgiris, Anamalai and Palani hills. Wet temperate forests have oak, chestnut, maple, birch and rhododendron. In the Western Himalayas, coniferous forests have chir, deodar, blue pine, spruce and silver fir. In the south, the shola forests are interspersed with montane grasslands. Alpine grasslands lie above the tree line.
related: Teak (Tectona grandis) is dominant in tropical moist deciduous forests.
Sal (Shorea robusta) is the other key moist deciduous species, mainly in eastern India.
Champion and Seth classified India's forests into 16 types in 1968.
Tropical wet evergreen forests receive over 200 cm of rainfall.
Thorn scrub forests receive under 70 cm of rainfall; typical trees are babool and khejri.
Sundari (Heritiera fomes) is the dominant mangrove species of the Sundarbans.
National Forest Policy 1988 targets 33% forest and tree cover.
Forest Survey of India, Dehradun, publishes the ISFR every two years.
summary: The answer is (a) Tropical moist deciduous forest. Teak (Tectona grandis) is the dominant species of India's moist deciduous forests, which receive about 100-200 cm of rainfall and are the most widespread forest type in the country.
topic_notes: India's forests are classified by Champion and Seth (1968) into 16 major types and 221 subtypes, grouped as tropical, subtropical, montane temperate, subalpine and alpine. Per the common textbook classification: tropical evergreen (over 200 cm rainfall), tropical deciduous (moist: 100-200 cm; dry: 70-100 cm), thorn and scrub (under 70 cm), montane, and littoral/swamp (mangroves).
