Article 31C gives certain DPSPs (39(b) and (c)) primacy over FRs under Articles 14 and 19.
Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A, Part IVA) were added by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Directive Principles of State Policy. The ideal of a Welfare State, meaning social and economic justice, is enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution (Articles 36-51), which directs the State to secure the well-being of its people and reduce inequalities.
topic_notes: The Welfare State concept in India flows mainly from Part IV (DPSPs), Articles 36-51, which the Constituent Assembly adopted to establish a social and economic democracy alongside the political democracy of Part III. Dr B.R. Ambedkar called them 'Instruments of Instructions' to the legislature and executive. They are borrowed from the Irish Constitution, which itself took the idea from Spain. Granville Austin called Parts III and IV the 'conscience of the Constitution'. Classification: Socialistic (Arts. 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Arts. 40 village panchayats, 43 cottage industries, 43B cooperatives, 46 SC/ST welfare, 47 prohibition, 48 cow protection) and Liberal-Intellectual (Arts. 44 Uniform Civil Code, 45 early childhood care, 48 agriculture and animal husbandry, 48A environment, 49 monuments, 50 separation of judiciary from executive, 51 international peace). Key cases: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) held DPSPs subordinate to FRs; Golaknath (1967); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) established harmony and balance between Parts III and IV; the 25th Amendment (1971) added Art. 31C giving primacy to Arts. 39(b) and (c) over certain FRs. The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to extend 31C to all DPSPs, but this was struck down in Minerva Mills. The Preamble's words 'Justice - social, economic and political' and the word 'socialist' also reflect welfare aims. Other welfare-linked provisions: Art. 21A, Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art. 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation), and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal welfare. Future questions could ask about the classification of particular DPSPs, the amendments adding them, and the DPSP-FR conflict cases.

ocr: The substitution of steel for wooden ploughs in agricultural production is an example of ‘ (a) labour-augmenting technological progress (b) capital-augmenting technological progress fc) capital-reducing technological progress {d) None of the above
subject: Economy
detail: Technological progress in economics is classified by how it changes the productivity of factors of production. Labour-augmenting (Harrod-neutral) progress raises the effective efficiency of labour, for example through education, skills, training or better management, so each worker produces more. Capital-augmenting (Solow-neutral) progress raises the productivity or effectiveness of capital goods, for example through better machines, tools, materials or equipment, so each unit of capital produces more output. Capital-reducing or capital-saving progress means the same output can be produced with less capital. Hicks-neutral progress raises the productivity of both factors equally. Here, steel ploughs replace wooden ploughs. Steel is harder and more durable, it penetrates soil better and needs less repair, so the same plough as a unit of capital gives more output. This is an improvement in the quality and productivity of the capital input itself, hence capital-augmenting. Elimination: (a) is wrong because the worker's skill or efficiency has not been improved directly. (c) is wrong because the change does not reduce the amount of capital needed; if anything, a steel plough is costlier capital. (d) is wrong because (b) is correct and is the official answer.
explanations: Wrong. Labour-augmenting progress improves worker efficiency through skills, education, health or organisation. Switching the plough material changes the tool, not the worker's own capability.

Correct. A steel plough is a better capital good: more durable, more effective at tilling, and lower in maintenance. Each unit of capital therefore produces more output, which is capital-augmenting progress.

Wrong. Capital-reducing (capital-saving) progress would let the same output be produced with less capital. The steel plough improves the productivity of capital rather than reducing the quantity required.
Wrong. The scenario fits one of the listed categories, namely (b), so 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: A better tool or machine (steel plough instead of wooden) makes capital more productive, so it is capital-augmenting progress; skills and training are labour-augmenting.
option_notes: Labour-augmenting technological progress (Harrod-neutral) raises the effective labour input, so each worker produces more. Typical sources are education, skill development, training, better health, and improved management or work organisation. In growth models, output is written as Y = F(K, A·L), where A is the labour-efficiency factor. It is compatible with steady-state growth in neoclassical models, and it is often linked to human capital. Example: training programmes or literacy raising farm worker productivity.

Capital-augmenting technological progress (Solow-neutral) raises the productivity of capital, so each unit of capital produces more output. In growth models it appears as Y = F(A·K, L). Examples include steel ploughs replacing wooden ones, better quality machinery, higher-yield seeds embodied in capital, and more efficient engines. It is also called embodied technical progress when the improvement is built into new capital goods. This is the category used for the question's example.

Capital-reducing, or capital-saving, technological progress lets the same output be produced with less capital, so the capital-output ratio falls. Examples are lighter machines, cheaper materials, or processes that need fewer machines. It is related to the Hicks and Harrod classifications of technical change: Hicks defined capital-saving change as one that raises the marginal product of labour relative to that of capital at a constant capital-labour ratio. It is not the case in the steel plough example.

'None of the above' is the fourth option, and it is incorrect because option (b) is the official UPSC 2015 answer. Related classifications of technical change that students should know are Hicks-neutral (raises the productivity of both factors equally), Harrod-neutral (labour-augmenting) and Solow-neutral (capital-augmenting). Hicks also distinguished labour-saving and capital-saving innovations by their effect on factor shares.
related: Labour-augmenting progress is also called Harrod-neutral technical progress.
Capital-augmenting progress is also called Solow-neutral technical progress.
Hicks-neutral progress raises the productivity of both capital and labour in equal proportion.
Solow residual is the measure of total factor productivity (TFP) growth.
ICOR stands for incremental capital-output ratio.
Embodied technical progress enters the economy through new capital goods.
Green Revolution in India began in the mid-1960s with HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation.
summary: The answer is (b), capital-augmenting technological progress. Replacing wooden ploughs with steel ones makes the capital input (the plough) more productive and durable, so each unit of capital yields more output. It does not mainly save labour or reduce the capital needed.
topic_notes: Technological progress means improvements in how inputs are converted into output, shifting the production function upward. Economists classify it by its effect on factor productivity and factor shares. Hicks classification: neutral (the ratio of marginal products is unchanged at a given capital-labour ratio), labour-saving (it raises the marginal product of capital relatively more) and capital-saving (it raises the marginal product of labour relatively more). Harrod-neutral progress is labour-augmenting, Y = F(K, AL), and it is the only form consistent with steady-state growth in the neoclassical Solow model. Solow-neutral progress is capital-augmenting, Y = F(AK, L). Hicks-neutral progress is Y = A·F(K, L). Embodied technical progress enters through new capital goods, such as a better plough or machine, whereas disembodied progress improves the efficiency of all inputs, for example through better organisation. The Solow residual measures total factor productivity (TFP), the part of output growth not explained by growth in labour and capital. Endogenous growth theory (Romer, Lucas) treats technology and human capital as products of investment in R&D and education. In the Indian context, the Green Revolution (from the mid-1960s) combined HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation and mechanisation, raising agricultural productivity in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Related ideas include the capital-output ratio, ICOR (incremental capital-output ratio), labour productivity, and the difference between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques. UPSC often asks such conceptual economics questions using everyday examples, so students should be able to map an example to its category: training or skill raises labour efficiency, while better tools or machines raise capital efficiency.

question: There is a Parliamentary System of Government in India because the
options: Lok Sabha is elected directly by the ‘| people
Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha
subject: Polity
detail: The defining feature of a parliamentary system is the executive's responsibility to the legislature, with a nominal head of state (President) and a real executive (Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister). Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers with the PM at its head to aid and advise the President. Article 75(3) says the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People. The government must resign if it loses a no-confidence motion or a money bill, or if a major policy measure is defeated in the Lok Sabha. Ministers are drawn from Parliament (Article 75(5) allows a non-member for up to six months), so executive and legislature overlap, unlike the presidential system of the USA. Elimination: direct election of the Lok Sabha (Article 81) is also true in presidential systems; the amending power (Article 368) exists in nearly every constitution, parliamentary or not; and the Rajya Sabha being a permanent House (Article 83(1)) is a feature of federal bicameralism, not of the form of government. Only (d) captures the executive-legislature link.
explanations: Wrong: direct popular election of the lower House (Article 81) is found in presidential systems too, such as the US House of Representatives, so it does not define a parliamentary system.
Wrong: the power to amend the Constitution (Article 368) is common to parliamentary and presidential systems and says nothing about executive accountability.
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha's non-dissolution (Article 83(1)) reflects its permanent character in a federal structure, not the type of government.
Correct: Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, which is the essence of parliamentary government.
keyfact: Parliamentary government in India rests on Article 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
option_notes: Direct election of the Lok Sabha: Article 81 provides for up to 530 members from states and up to 20 from Union Territories, with the Constitution's present sanctioned strength being 543 (plus a possible 2 Anglo-Indian nominees until the 104th Amendment, 2019, ended it). Voting is by universal adult suffrage (Article 326, voting age 18 since the 61st Amendment, 1988). The term is five years unless dissolved earlier (Article 83(2)).

Parliament's amending power: Article 368 allows amendment by addition, variation or repeal. Some amendments need a special majority only, others need that plus ratification by half the states (federal provisions). Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established the basic structure doctrine, limiting this power. The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part, including Fundamental Rights.

Rajya Sabha not subject to dissolution: Article 83(1) makes it a permanent House. One-third of members retire every second year. Maximum strength is 250 (238 elected from states and UTs, 12 nominated by the President for literature, science, art and social service). The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman. Members serve six-year terms, and the House has special powers under Articles 249 and 312.

Responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha: Article 75(3) establishes collective responsibility; Article 74 provides for the Council headed by the PM. The 44th Amendment (1978) allows the President to ask the Council to reconsider advice once, but he must then act on the reconsidered advice. Individual responsibility operates through the President's pleasure (Article 75(2)). The Council can be removed by a no-confidence motion passed by the Lok Sabha.
related: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Article 74: Council of Ministers with PM at the head aids and advises the President.
91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House's strength.
44th Amendment (1978) lets the President return ministerial advice once for reconsideration.
A non-member can be minister for a maximum of six months (Article 75(5)).
The Constitution does not mention no-confidence motions; they arise from Lok Sabha rules (Rule 198).
State analogue: Article 164(2) makes ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
India's parliamentary model is derived from Britain (Westminster).
summary: The answer is (d). India has a parliamentary system because the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), so the executive stays in office only while it commands the confidence of the directly elected lower House.
topic_notes: India adopted the Westminster model of parliamentary government, with a nominal head (President, Article 52) and a real executive (Council of Ministers headed by the PM). Key features: nominal and real executive; majority-party rule; collective responsibility; political homogeneity of the Council; double membership (ministers belong to both legislature and executive); leadership of the PM; dissolution of the Lok Sabha; and secrecy of proceedings. Differences from the British model: India is a republic with an elected head of state, not a monarchy; Parliament is not fully sovereign because there is a written Constitution, judicial review and federalism; and ministers can be non-members for up to six months. Differences from the presidential system: the executive is not separate from the legislature, it is accountable to the legislature, and ministers are not outsiders to Parliament. Dr B.R. Ambedkar defended the parliamentary form on the ground that it ensures greater responsibility, even at the cost of stability, as compared with the presidential system. The Constituent Assembly preferred responsibility over stability. Related provisions: Article 74 (Council of Ministers), Article 75 (appointment, responsibility and size, capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength by the 91st Amendment, 2003), Article 78 (PM's duty to communicate decisions to the President), Article 85 (summoning and dissolution), Article 163 (state Council of Ministers) and Article 164 (state ministers responsible to the Legislative Assembly). Instruments for accountability include Question Hour, Zero Hour, adjournment motion, calling attention notice, no-confidence motion (Rule 198 of Lok Sabha rules) and cut motions. UPSC can also ask about the Westminster model's origin, differences from the US system, and the roles of the Speaker and the Leader of the Opposition.

question: H1N1 virus is sometimes mentioned in the news with reference to which one of the following diseases?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: H1N1 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus. The name comes from two surface glycoproteins: Haemagglutinin (H, 18 subtypes known) and Neuraminidase (N, 11 subtypes known). The strain that emerged in Mexico in March-April 2009 was a novel reassortant containing genes from swine, avian and human influenza viruses. It was called 'swine flu' because its genes resembled those of viruses found in pigs. WHO declared a pandemic in June 2009 (Phase 6) and announced the post-pandemic period in August 2010. The strain, called A(H1N1)pdm09, now circulates as a seasonal flu virus. It spreads human-to-human through respiratory droplets, not by eating pork. Symptoms are fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and sometimes diarrhoea. Treatment uses neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and zanamivir. Elimination logic: AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus. Bird flu is caused mainly by H5N1 (also H7N9), which is a different subtype. Dengue is caused by a flavivirus (DENV 1-4) and spread by Aedes mosquitoes. Only swine flu matches H1N1.
explanations: Wrong. AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus that attacks CD4 T-cells. It has no connection with H1N1, an influenza virus.
Wrong, though it is a tempting choice. Bird (avian) flu is mainly linked to H5N1 and H7N9. H1N1 is the swine-origin human pandemic strain of 2009.
Wrong. Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus disease spread by Aedes aegypti, not an influenza.
Correct. H1N1 is the virus behind swine flu, which became a pandemic in 2009 and has since been a seasonal flu strain.
keyfact: H1N1 = Influenza A subtype behind swine flu (2009 pandemic); bird flu is H5N1.
option_notes: AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is caused by HIV-1 and HIV-2, which are retroviruses. They spread through blood, sexual contact and mother-to-child transmission. They destroy CD4+ T-helper cells. It was first recognised in 1981. Treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART). India's NACO runs the national programme, and World AIDS Day is on 1 December. It is not an influenza disease.

Bird flu (avian influenza) is caused by Influenza A viruses adapted to birds. The major strains are H5N1 (first human cases in Hong Kong, 1997), H7N9 (China, 2013) and H5N8. It spreads through poultry contact. India has reported outbreaks, for example in Navapur, Maharashtra in 2006. Control is by culling infected birds. Human-to-human spread is rare.

Dengue is caused by dengue virus (DENV-1 to 4), a flavivirus. It is spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, which bite by day. Symptoms are high fever, joint pain and low platelets. Severe forms are dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. There is no specific antiviral. Vaccines include Dengvaxia and Qdenga. National Dengue Day in India is 16 May.

Swine flu is the disease caused by H1N1 influenza A. The 2009 pandemic strain A(H1N1)pdm09 emerged in Mexico and the USA. It is a triple reassortant of swine, avian and human flu genes. It spreads through droplets between humans. Oseltamivir is the treatment, and vaccines exist. India had major outbreaks in 2009, 2015 (Gujarat and Rajasthan) and 2017. It is now a seasonal flu virus.
related: H = Haemagglutinin, N = Neuraminidase: surface proteins that name flu subtypes.
The 1918 Spanish flu was also H1N1.
Bird flu is mainly H5N1 and H7N9.
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is a neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza.
Antigenic shift (reassortment) causes pandemics; antigenic drift causes seasonal epidemics.
WHO declared the swine flu pandemic in June 2009.
The National Institute of Virology (Pune) is a key ICMR lab for virus testing in India.
Pigs are 'mixing vessels' for influenza reassortment.
summary: The answer is (d) Swine flu. H1N1 is a subtype of Influenza A virus, named for its haemagglutinin (H1) and neuraminidase (N1) surface proteins, and it caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic.
topic_notes: Influenza viruses belong to the family Orthomyxoviridae and have a segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA genome. There are four types: A, B, C and D. Only Influenza A is divided into subtypes, based on H and N proteins, and it causes pandemics. Type B causes seasonal epidemics, and type C gives mild illness. Antigenic drift (small point mutations) causes seasonal epidemics. Antigenic shift (reassortment of gene segments) produces new subtypes and pandemics. Pandemics include the 1918 Spanish flu (H1N1), 1957 Asian flu (H2N2), 1968 Hong Kong flu (H3N2) and 2009 swine flu (H1N1). Pigs are called 'mixing vessels' because they have receptors for both avian and human viruses. WHO declared the 2009 pandemic on 11 June 2009. Treatment uses oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and zanamivir, and the pandemic strain is included in seasonal flu vaccines. Prevention measures are hand hygiene, masks and isolation. In India, the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) monitors outbreaks, and the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) and the National Institute of Virology, Pune, do the testing. Other viral outbreaks UPSC asks about include SARS-CoV (2003), MERS-CoV (2012), Ebola (West Africa 2014-16), Zika (2015-16), Nipah (Kerala 2018) and COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2, 2019). Related ideas are zoonosis, the One Health approach, and the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005), under which WHO declares a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC).

ocr: With reference to bio-toilets used by the Indian Railways, consider the following statements : 1. The decomposition of human waste in the bio-toilets is initiated by a fungal inoculum. 2. Ammonia and water vapour are the only end products in this decomposition which are released into the atmosphere. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Environment
detail: The Indian Railways bio-toilet was developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) in collaboration with Indian Railways. Each toilet is fitted with a bio-digester tank beneath it. The tank is seeded with an inoculum of anaerobic bacteria, originally collected from the Antarctic (cold-adapted psychrophilic/mesophilic consortia), which are capable of working in a wide temperature range. The bacteria digest human waste in the absence of oxygen (anaerobic digestion). The process converts the waste mainly into methane, carbon dioxide and water; the gases escape into the atmosphere through a vent, and the water is chlorinated and discharged. Hence the process is initiated by bacteria, not fungi, so Statement 1 fails. Statement 2 claims ammonia and water vapour are the ONLY end products; this is wrong because methane and CO2 are the principal gaseous products, and there is also treated effluent water. The word 'only' is the classic UPSC trap. Elimination logic: once either statement is found false, options (a), (b), (c) fall away. Knowing that anaerobic digestion yields biogas (methane + CO2) kills Statement 2, and knowing the inoculum is bacterial kills Statement 1. Bio-toilets support Swachh Bharat and prevent track corrosion and manual scavenging.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong: the inoculum is bacterial (anaerobic), not fungal, so Statement 1 is incorrect.
(b) 2 only is wrong: methane and carbon dioxide are also released, and the word 'only' makes the statement false.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong because both statements contain factual errors.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is correct: the process uses anaerobic bacteria and yields methane, CO2 and water, so both statements fail. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: Railway bio-toilets (DRDO) use anaerobic bacteria (Antarctic origin) and release methane, CO2 and water, not fungi or only ammonia and vapour.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would mean the fungal inoculum claim is right. In reality, the bio-digester uses anaerobic bacteria. Fungi are mostly aerobic decomposers and are important in composting and soil, but they are not used in the DRDO bio-toilet. Remember that a statement claiming a fungal role is a distractor, and that the bacteria were first isolated from Antarctic soil and lake sediments.

Option (b) '2 only' would mean ammonia and water vapour are the sole outputs. Actually anaerobic digestion yields biogas (methane and CO2) plus water. Ammonia can form from protein breakdown but is not the main product. Methane is a greenhouse gas about 25-28 times more potent than CO2 over 100 years. Biogas is used as a renewable fuel in India's biogas programme.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' would require both statements to be correct. Neither is. It is a typical option UPSC uses to test whether a student knows precise details of the process. The bio-toilet uses bacteria and produces methane, CO2 and water. A student who guesses on partial knowledge may choose this, so verify each claim separately.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is the correct answer. It reflects that the bio-toilet uses an anaerobic bacterial inoculum from Antarctica and that the end products are methane, carbon dioxide and water. The technology was developed by DRDO with Indian Railways to stop direct discharge of human waste on tracks, cut corrosion, and improve hygiene and sanitation.
related: Bio-toilets in Indian Railways were developed by DRDO.
The bio-digester uses anaerobic bacteria originally from Antarctica.
Anaerobic digestion produces methane, CO2 and water.
Methanogens are archaea, responsible for methane formation.
Biogas typically has 55-65% methane.
GOBAR-Dhan scheme was launched in 2018 to convert cattle dung and waste into biogas.
Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014.
Manual scavenging was prohibited by the 2013 Act.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The inoculum is an anaerobic bacterial culture, not fungal. The DRDO bio-digester uses bacteria (originally sourced from Antarctica) to break down human waste. Facts: The bio-toilet technology was developed by DRDO's lab at Gwalior (Defence Research and Development Establishment) with Indian Railways. The bacteria work without oxygen, tolerate temperatures from sub-zero to high, and are self-multiplying, so the tank needs only occasional topping up. Waste is digested within the tank, preventing discharge onto railway tracks, which reduces corrosion of rails and eliminates the need for manual cleaning of tracks. Indian Railways aimed to fit all coaches with bio-toilets, a goal largely achieved by 2019.

2 — Incorrect: Ammonia and water vapour are not the only end products; anaerobic digestion yields methane, carbon dioxide and water, with treated effluent. Facts: Anaerobic digestion occurs in four stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis, the last carried out by methanogenic archaea producing methane. Biogas typically contains about 55-65% methane and 35-45% CO2, with traces of hydrogen sulphide. The gases are vented out, while the liquid effluent is chlorinated before release. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, but in the bio-toilet it is released in small quantities. The same principle underlies biogas plants under the National Biogas Programme and the GOBAR-Dhan scheme.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. The Indian Railways bio-toilet (developed by DRDO) uses an anaerobic bacterial inoculum, not a fungal one, and the decomposition releases methane, carbon dioxide and water vapour (with treated water), not just ammonia and water vapour.
topic_notes: Bio-toilets are a sanitation technology developed by DRDO and adopted by Indian Railways to end the discharge of untreated human waste onto tracks. Each toilet has a bio-digester tank under the floor holding an inoculum of anaerobic bacteria. The microbes were originally sourced from Antarctica, where they survive extreme cold, and the culture was adapted to function across Indian temperatures. The bacteria digest the waste anaerobically into methane, carbon dioxide and water. The gases are vented, and the water is chlorinated before it is released. Benefits include avoiding corrosion of rails, reducing manual cleaning (linked to the abolition of manual scavenging), improved hygiene at stations, and water savings. The bio-toilets need no electricity and little maintenance. Indian Railways has fitted these in nearly all coaches, and 'bio-vacuum toilets' have been introduced in some trains and aircraft-style designs. Related concepts: anaerobic versus aerobic decomposition. Aerobic decomposition needs oxygen and yields CO2, water and heat (composting), while anaerobic digestion yields biogas. Methanogens are archaea, not bacteria. Biogas plants include the KVIC (floating drum) and Deenbandhu (fixed dome) designs. Government programmes: Swachh Bharat Mission (2014), GOBAR-Dhan (2018) and SATAT (2018) for compressed biogas. DRDO's other environmental technologies include bio-digesters for high-altitude regions, such as those used by the Army in Siachen and Ladakh. Possible future angles are the role of extremophiles, bioremediation, biogas composition, greenhouse gases, sewage treatment (STPs, decentralised wastewater treatment systems, DEWATS), and the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers Act, 2013.

question: The problem of international liquidity is related to the non-availability of
subject: Economy
detail: International liquidity refers to the total official reserves a country or the world can use to settle international obligations: foreign exchange (mainly hard, freely convertible currencies like the US dollar, euro, pound, yen), gold, IMF reserve position and Special Drawing Rights (SDRs). The 'problem of international liquidity' arises when countries do not have enough of these widely accepted currencies to pay for imports, repay external debt or defend their exchange rate. Post-1944 Bretton Woods, the dollar (convertible to gold at $35 per ounce) became the main reserve asset, and the Triffin dilemma showed that supplying dollars to the world required US deficits, undermining confidence in the dollar. To ease the shortage the IMF created SDRs in 1969 ('paper gold'). Elimination: (a) and (d) concern real trade capacity, not payment means; goods shortage is a supply problem. (b) Gold and silver are no longer the main settlement medium after the Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971 (Nixon shock) and the Jamaica Accords of 1976 demonetised gold. Hence (c).
explanations: Incorrect: shortage of goods and services is a real-economy supply problem, not a liquidity problem, which concerns means of international payment.

Incorrect: gold and silver once served as monetary metals, but since the end of the gold standard and the 1976 Jamaica Accords, international settlement relies on convertible currencies; silver has no reserve role.

Correct: international liquidity is the availability of dollars and other hard (freely convertible) currencies and reserve assets needed to settle international payments; their scarcity is the liquidity problem.
Incorrect: exportable surplus affects a country's capacity to earn foreign exchange, which is a trade competitiveness issue, not the definition of international liquidity.
keyfact: International liquidity problem = shortage of dollars and other hard currencies (reserve assets) to settle international payments; SDRs (1969) were created to ease it.
option_notes: Goods and services: the real output of an economy. Their trade is recorded in the current account of the balance of payments (merchandise and services). Shortage of goods leads to inflation or import dependence, not to a lack of internationally accepted payment means. India's services exports (IT, business services) are a major surplus item in its current account.

Gold and silver: gold was the base of the classical gold standard (until 1914) and, indirectly, Bretton Woods (dollar pegged at $35/oz). The US ended dollar-gold convertibility in August 1971; the 1976 Jamaica Accords removed gold's official monetary role. Central banks still hold gold as a reserve asset; India holds several hundred tonnes with the RBI. Silver has no reserve role.

Dollars and other hard currencies: hard currencies are stable, freely convertible and widely accepted, such as the US dollar, euro, pound sterling, yen and Swiss franc. They form most official foreign exchange reserves. The IMF's SDR basket (dollar, euro, yuan, yen, pound) supplements them. Shortage of these currencies causes balance-of-payments crises, as India experienced in 1991.

Exportable surplus: the portion of domestic output left after meeting domestic needs that can be sold abroad. It determines export capacity and foreign-exchange earnings. Lack of it is a structural trade problem, often cited for developing economies, but is distinct from the international liquidity problem of reserve asset availability.
related: SDRs were created by the IMF in 1969 and are called 'paper gold'.
The Bretton Woods conference took place in 1944 and produced the IMF and the IBRD.
The Triffin dilemma describes the conflict between US domestic goals and supplying global reserve currency.
The Jamaica Accords (1976) formalised floating exchange rates and ended gold's official role.
The Chinese renminbi joined the SDR basket in October 2016.
The SDR basket currently comprises the US dollar, euro, Chinese yuan, Japanese yen and pound sterling.
The US ended dollar-gold convertibility in August 1971.
The BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement provides liquidity support against balance-of-payments pressures.
summary: The answer is (c): dollars and other hard currencies. International liquidity means the stock of internationally acceptable reserve assets that countries need to settle cross-border payments and finance balance-of-payments deficits, so its problem is a shortage of hard currencies such as the dollar.
topic_notes: International liquidity is the supply of reserve assets acceptable in settling international payments: foreign exchange reserves, gold, SDRs and reserve positions in the IMF. Under the gold standard (to 1914), gold was the reserve. The Bretton Woods conference (July 1944, New Hampshire) created the IMF and World Bank (IBRD); currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar was convertible to gold at $35 an ounce. Robert Triffin (1960) pointed out the dilemma: the world needs growing dollar supply, which requires US deficits, but those deficits erode confidence in the dollar's gold backing. To supplement liquidity, the IMF introduced Special Drawing Rights in 1969, called 'paper gold'. In August 1971 the US suspended gold convertibility (Nixon shock); the Smithsonian Agreement (1971) failed, and the Jamaica Accords (1976, effective 1978) legalised floating exchange rates and demonetised gold. The SDR is not a currency but a claim on IMF members' freely usable currencies; its basket is reviewed every five years, and the Chinese renminbi was added in October 2016. Its value is reported in US dollars. Hard currency means a currency that is stable and freely convertible; soft currency is the opposite, weak and with restricted convertibility. India's forex reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position with the IMF, and were precariously low in 1991 (about two to three weeks of imports), prompting reforms. Related angles: the balance of payments (current and capital accounts), the IMF quota system, the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement of BRICS, and bilateral swap lines among central banks.

ocr: With reference to ‘fuel cells’ in which hydrogen-rich fuel and oxygen are used to generate electricity, consider the following statements : 1, If pure hydrogen is used as a fuel, the fuel cell emits heat and water as by-products. Fuel cells can be used for powering buildings and not for small devices like laptop computers. Fuel cells produce electricity in the form of Alternating Current (AC). Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only 1, 2 and 3 {dj
subject: Science & Tech
detail: A fuel cell is an electrochemical device that converts the chemical energy of a fuel, usually hydrogen, directly into electricity without combustion. It has an anode, a cathode and an electrolyte. Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode, releasing electrons that flow through an external circuit and give DC electricity. Protons (or ions) cross the electrolyte and combine with oxygen at the cathode to form water. With pure hydrogen the only by-products are water and heat, so there are no CO2 or NOx emissions at the point of use. Fuel cells are scalable: milliwatt-scale units for laptops and mobile phones (for example direct methanol fuel cells), kilowatt units for vehicles (Toyota Mirai, Honda Clarity), and megawatt units for buildings, hospitals, data centres and power plants (phosphoric acid, molten carbonate and solid oxide types). Their output is DC, and an inverter is needed to obtain AC for the grid. Elimination logic: statement 2 is wrong because of its word 'not', since small devices are a recognised application. Statement 3 is wrong because the output is DC. That leaves only 1, which is option (a). Options (b), (c) and (d) each include 2 or 3 and so fail.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is true: pure hydrogen gives only water and heat. Statements 2 and 3 are false, so only 1 is correct.
Incorrect. It includes 2 and 3, and both are false. Fuel cells do power small devices, and they give DC, not AC.
Incorrect. Statement 1 is true, but statement 3 is false because fuel cell output is DC. It cannot be paired with 1.
Incorrect. Statements 2 and 3 are false, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: Fuel cell = electrochemical, no combustion; hydrogen + oxygen gives DC electricity, water and heat; usable from laptops to power plants.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only': this is the correct choice. It says that a pure-hydrogen fuel cell emits only water and heat, which is the basic principle of clean fuel cell operation. It rejects the claims that fuel cells cannot power small devices and that they give AC. A fuel cell works electrochemically, with no combustion, and is not a heat engine, so it is not limited by the Carnot efficiency.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only': this is wrong because both statements are false. Statement 2 wrongly excludes small devices such as laptops, and statement 3 wrongly gives the current as AC. A student choosing this option has misunderstood both the range of fuel cell applications and the nature of the electrical output. Fuel cells produce DC, and the DC must be inverted for AC loads.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only': this is wrong because statement 3 is false. The fuel cell has two electrodes with a fixed polarity, and the electrons flow in one direction, so the output is DC. This option is a tempting trap for students who know statement 1 is right but assume that power from a 'plant' must be AC. Only an inverter or power-conditioning stage produces AC.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3': this is wrong because only statement 1 is true. Fuel cells are used from small portable electronics to large stationary power stations, and they give DC. Accepting all three would imply that fuel cells cannot power small devices and that they generate AC, and both claims are factually incorrect.
related: A fuel cell produces DC electricity; an inverter is required to obtain AC.
Pure hydrogen fuel cells emit only water and heat.
William Grove invented the fuel cell in 1839.
NASA used alkaline fuel cells in Apollo and Gemini missions.
India's National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023, targeting 5 MMT by 2030.
Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity.
PEM fuel cells use a solid polymer electrolyte and platinum catalyst.
Direct methanol fuel cells are suited for portable electronics such as laptops.
statements: 1 — Correct: With pure hydrogen the overall reaction is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, releasing electrical energy and heat. Water vapour and heat are the only by-products. The reaction is the reverse of electrolysis. The Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) fuel cell is the usual example: it operates at about 60–80°C and is used in vehicles and portable power. NASA used alkaline fuel cells in the Gemini and Apollo missions, and the astronauts drank the water the cells produced. If the hydrogen is made from natural gas reforming (grey hydrogen), emissions occur upstream, but not in the cell itself. Green hydrogen comes from renewable-powered electrolysis, and India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) promotes it.

2 — Incorrect: Fuel cells are not limited to buildings. They are used in laptops, mobile chargers, drones, forklifts, buses, cars, trains, submarines and spacecraft. Direct methanol fuel cells (DMFC) suit portable electronics. Stationary units such as Bloom Energy servers and the PAFC plants power buildings, hospitals and data centres. Fuel cells therefore cover a very wide power range, from watts to megawatts. Their modular design lets cells be stacked in series to raise voltage and power. Because they are efficient (about 40–60 percent electrical efficiency, and up to 80–90 percent in combined heat and power use) and quiet, they are used in many settings.

3 — Incorrect: A fuel cell produces direct current (DC), because electrons flow in one direction from anode to cathode through the external circuit. An inverter is needed to convert the output to AC for grid use or for AC appliances. Batteries, solar PV cells and fuel cells all give DC. A single cell yields about 0.6–0.8 V under load, so cells are stacked to raise the voltage. The theoretical maximum is about 1.23 V for a hydrogen-oxygen cell. Power plants and alternators, by contrast, naturally produce AC.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. A hydrogen-fed fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen electrochemically, giving electricity, heat and water. It produces direct current (DC), not AC, and fuel cells power devices from laptops to buildings.
topic_notes: A fuel cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a fuel (hydrogen, methanol, natural gas or biogas) and an oxidant (oxygen or air) directly into electricity. It was invented by William Grove in 1839. Unlike a battery it does not run down or need recharging as long as fuel is supplied. The main types are: PEMFC (proton exchange membrane, 60–80°C, used in vehicles), AFC (alkaline, used in Apollo and the Space Shuttle), PAFC (phosphoric acid, about 200°C, stationary), MCFC (molten carbonate, about 650°C), SOFC (solid oxide, 600–1000°C) and DMFC (direct methanol, portable). High-temperature cells allow combined heat and power and internal reforming. The anode reaction in an acidic cell is H2 → 2H+ + 2e-, and the cathode reaction is ½O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O. Electrical efficiency is about 40–60 percent, which is higher than that of internal combustion engines. Key challenges are the cost of the platinum catalyst, hydrogen production, storage and distribution, and durability. Hydrogen is classed by colour: grey (from natural gas), blue (grey plus carbon capture), green (from renewable electrolysis) and brown (from coal). India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (January 2023) targets 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen production a year by 2030. India has also launched hydrogen buses and trial hydrogen trains. Fuel cells appear in current affairs through hydrogen vehicles, green hydrogen and the clean energy transition. UPSC could next ask about the types of fuel cells, the by-products of different fuels (methanol gives CO2), the difference between a fuel cell and a battery, hydrogen colour codes, and energy storage devices such as supercapacitors and lithium-ion batteries.

ocr: Kalamkari painting refers to fa) a hand-painted cotton textile in South India (b) a handmade drawing on bamboo handicrafts in North-East India a] a block-painted woollen cloth in Western Himalayan region of India (a) a hand-painted decorative silk cloth in North-Western India
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Kalamkari is an ancient Indian textile art in which cotton fabric is painted or block-printed with natural vegetable and mineral dyes. The word is Persian-derived: 'qalam' (pen) and 'kari' (craftsmanship). Two main styles survive in Andhra Pradesh. The Srikalahasti style is freehand painting with a bamboo or date-palm pen (kalam), and its themes are Hindu epics and deities, often as temple hangings. The Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam) style uses carved wooden blocks together with some hand painting, shows Persian-influenced floral and tree-of-life motifs, and was historically exported to Persia, Europe and Southeast Asia. The process involves about 17 steps, including treating the cloth with myrobalan (harda) and buffalo milk, using mordants such as alum, and dyeing with indigo, madder (alizarin) and iron acetate (kasimi). Kalamkari has a Geographical Indication tag, and Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam are registered separately. Elimination: bamboo drawing, woollen block-painting in the Himalayas, and silk in the north-west do not match. Cotton plus South India is the key identifier, so only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct: Kalamkari is hand-painted (Srikalahasti) or block-printed (Machilipatnam) cotton cloth made in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, in South India.
Wrong: Kalamkari is not drawing on bamboo and is not from North-East India. Bamboo and cane crafts are associated with Assam, Tripura and Manipur.
Wrong: Kalamkari is not on woollen cloth and is not from the Western Himalayas. Himalayan wool traditions include Kullu shawls and Chamba rumal (embroidery).
Wrong: Kalamkari is not on silk and is not from the North-West. Silk is not its characteristic medium, and the region named is wrong.
keyfact: Kalamkari = pen-work on cotton, Srikalahasti (hand-painted) and Machilipatnam (block-printed), Andhra Pradesh, South India.
option_notes: Kalamkari is a cotton textile art of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. It has two schools: Srikalahasti, which is freehand painting with a pen and depicts temple narratives, and Machilipatnam, which is block printing influenced by Persian taste. Natural dyes and mordants are used. Both schools hold GI tags, and the art flourished under the Golconda Sultanate and in the Coromandel trade.

Bamboo handicrafts belong to the North-East: Assam, Tripura, Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland. Products include baskets, mats, furniture and utensils. Cane and bamboo work is central to the region's economy. Tripura and Assam are prominent producers, and the National Bamboo Mission supports the sector. This is not Kalamkari, which is a textile art.

Woollen block-printed or crafted textiles of the Western Himalayas include Kullu and Kinnauri shawls in Himachal Pradesh, which are woven with geometric patterns and hold GI tags. Pashmina belongs to Kashmir. Chamba rumal is embroidery on cotton or muslin. None of these is Kalamkari, which is cotton and South Indian.

Hand-painted decorative silk in the North-West is not a Kalamkari tradition. North-western India is known for Phulkari (Punjab embroidery), Bandhani (Gujarat and Rajasthan tie-dye), Ajrakh (Gujarat/Sindh block print) and Sanganeri and Bagru prints (Rajasthan). Silk painting traditions such as Tussar silk Madhubani exist elsewhere. This is a distractor.
related: Kalamkari means pen-work (qalam + kari).
Two styles: Srikalahasti (freehand pen) and Machilipatnam (block print).
Dyes are natural; the cloth is treated with myrobalan and buffalo milk.
Pattachitra is cloth and palm-leaf painting from Odisha and West Bengal.
Phad is a Rajasthan scroll painting devoted to folk deities like Pabuji.
Cheriyal scroll painting is from Telangana.
Pochampally Ikat is from Telangana and holds a GI tag.
Phulkari is Punjab embroidery; Kantha is Bengal embroidery.
summary: The answer is (a): Kalamkari is a hand-painted (and block-printed) cotton textile tradition of South India, centred in Andhra Pradesh. The name comes from 'kalam' (pen) and 'kari' (work), meaning pen-work, and the art uses natural dyes on cotton cloth.
topic_notes: Kalamkari means pen-work. The craft uses natural dyes on cotton: indigo for blue, madder for red, myrobalan for yellow, and iron acetate for black. Preparation soaks the cloth in a solution of buffalo milk and myrobalan to fix the dyes and prevent bleeding. Alum is the mordant for reds. The process involves about 17 steps of bleaching, mordanting, washing, painting, dyeing and drying. Srikalahasti (Chittoor district, Andhra Pradesh) is the freehand kalam style, with themes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas, drawn on temple cloth. Machilipatnam (Krishna district) is the block-printing style, once patronised by the Golconda Sultanate and exported widely, with Persian-influenced floral designs. Both have GI tags. Telangana has its own Kalamkari tradition, and Gujarat has the related Mata ni Pachedi, which is temple cloth for the Goddess. Related Indian textile traditions include Ikat (Odisha, Telangana, Gujarat), Bandhani (Gujarat and Rajasthan), Ajrakh (Kutch), Bagh and Dabu prints (Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan), Sanganeri (Jaipur), Phulkari (Punjab), Kantha (Bengal), Chikankari (Lucknow), Kasuti (Karnataka), Pochampally (Telangana), Patola (Patan, Gujarat), Kalamezhuthu and Pattachitra (Odisha, painting on cloth), Phad (Rajasthan scroll painting) and Cheriyal scrolls (Telangana). UPSC often asks about the matching of art forms to regions and mediums, and about GI-tagged crafts.

question: Which one of the following best describes the main objective of Seed Village. Concept”? Encouraging the farmers to use
options: their own farm seeds = and discouraging them to buy the seeds from others Involving the farmers for training
in quality seed production and thereby to make available quality seeds to others at appropriate time and affordable cost Earmarking some villages
exclusively for the production of certified seeds
Identifying the entrepreneurs in villages and providing them technology and finance to set up seed companies
subject: Economy
detail: The Seed Village Concept was launched by the Government of India (Ministry of Agriculture) under the National Food Security Mission and the Integrated Scheme of Oilseeds, Pulses, Oil palm and Maize (ISOPOM), and it continues under the Sub-Mission on Seeds and Planting Material (SMSP). Its core idea is that farmers are trained to produce seed of foundation and certified grade, and also truthfully labelled seed, for their own use and for sale to neighbours in the same village or nearby villages. The aims are to improve the Seed Replacement Rate (SRR) and Varietal Replacement Rate, to ensure timely availability, to cut cost, and to reduce dependence on distant public or private suppliers. State Agricultural Universities, ICAR institutes, KVKs and State Seed Corporations give technical support, and the seed is typically of self-pollinated crops such as paddy, wheat, pulses and oilseeds. Elimination: (a) is wrong because the scheme does not discourage buying seed, only seeks to improve quality and access. (c) is wrong because production is not limited to certified seed and the village is not set aside exclusively for that. (d) is wrong because the scheme trains existing farmers and does not create seed companies. Option (b) matches the stated objective of training, quality and affordable access.
explanations: Incorrect: the concept does not aim to stop farmers buying seed from others. It aims to make quality seed available locally, including to farmers who buy it. Farm-saved seed is also often of poor quality for hybrids.

Correct: this matches the official objective. Farmers are trained in quality seed production, and seed is supplied to other farmers on time and at affordable cost, which raises the Seed Replacement Rate.

Incorrect: villages are not reserved exclusively for certified seed. Seed of foundation, certified and truthfully labelled categories may be produced, and the emphasis is on farmer participation and not on earmarking villages.
Incorrect: the scheme does not select entrepreneurs to set up seed companies with technology and finance. It builds the capacity of ordinary farmers within a village.
keyfact: Seed Village Concept = farmers trained to produce quality seed, so that others get it on time at affordable cost, raising the Seed Replacement Rate.
option_notes: Use of farm-saved seed is the traditional practice of keeping part of the harvest for the next sowing. It is common in self-pollinated crops such as wheat, paddy and pulses, but yields fall over time through loss of purity and disease build-up. Hybrids cannot be saved because the next generation segregates. Farmers' rights to save and exchange seed are protected under the PPV&FR Act 2001.

Farmer training in quality seed production is the heart of the Seed Village Concept. Trained farmers produce seed, sometimes under certification, with technical help from ICAR, KVKs, State Agricultural Universities and State Seed Corporations. Seed is distributed locally at reasonable cost. The aim is to raise the Seed Replacement Rate and make seed available at the right sowing time, reducing dependence on distant sources.

Earmarking villages exclusively for certified seed would mean a seed-producing cluster. Certification is a formal process under the Seeds Act 1966 and the Seeds Rules 1968, run by State Seed Certification Agencies. Certified seed is produced from foundation seed, which comes from breeder seed. Seed villages involve certified seed but are not limited to it, so the option is incomplete.

Seed entrepreneurship is a different idea, found in schemes such as the Agri-Clinics and Agri-Business Centres scheme, run by MANAGE with NABARD support, and in startup and private seed sector promotion. The National Seeds Corporation, set up in 1963, and the State Farms Corporation are public-sector seed bodies. These are not the Seed Village approach.
related: Seed Village Concept is run under the Sub-Mission on Seeds and Planting Material (SMSP).
Seeds Act 1966 classifies seed as Breeder, Foundation and Certified, with Truthfully Labelled also in use.
National Seeds Corporation was established in 1963.
PPV&FR Act 2001 lets farmers save, use, exchange and sell farm-saved seed except branded seed.
Bt cotton (2002) is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India.
GEAC is the regulator for GM organisms and products under the Environment Protection Act 1986.
National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (NBPGR), New Delhi, houses the National Gene Bank.
Seed Replacement Rate is the share of area sown with certified or quality seed instead of farm-saved seed.
summary: The answer is (b). The Seed Village Concept trains farmers to produce quality seed themselves, so that good seed reaches other farmers at the right time and at an affordable price. It aims to raise the Seed Replacement Rate through decentralised, village-level seed production.
topic_notes: Seed system in India: seed is classified into four classes under the Seeds Act 1966: Nucleus, Breeder, Foundation and Certified, with Truthfully Labelled seed also in circulation. Breeder seed is produced under ICAR and agricultural universities, with the breeder's indent being supervised by the Department of Agriculture. Foundation seed is produced from breeder seed by the National Seeds Corporation (NSC), State Seeds Corporations and State Farms. Certified seed is produced from foundation seed, often by registered growers, and is certified by State Seed Certification Agencies. The Central Seed Committee and the Central Seed Certification Board are statutory bodies under the 1966 Act. The National Seeds Corporation was set up in 1963. The Seeds Bill 2004 and later drafts have not yet become law, and the Seeds Act 1966 is still in force. Seed Replacement Rate (SRR) is the percentage of area sown with certified or quality seed instead of farm-saved seed. Varietal Replacement Rate (VRR) is the share of area under varieties of less than ten years of age. The Seed Village Programme began in 2006-07 and now sits under the Sub-Mission on Seeds and Planting Material (SMSP), which is part of the National Mission on Agricultural Extension and Technology. Related legislation includes the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001, which established the PPV&FR Authority (New Delhi) and recognised farmers' rights to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm-saved seed, except branded seed. The National Gene Bank is at NBPGR, New Delhi. Other topics UPSC may ask about include GM crops (Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation, in 2002; GEAC is the regulator under the Environment Protection Act 1986) and the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway.

ocr: There has been a persistent deficit budget year after year. Which of the following actions can be taken by the government to reduce the deficit? 1. Reducing revenue expenditure 2. Introducing new welfare schemes 3. Rationalizing subsidies 4. Expanding industries Select the correct answer using the code given below. 1 and 3 only (a) (b) 2 and 3 only (c} 1 only 1, 2, 3 and 4 (d} 36 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Economy
detail: A budget deficit arises when government expenditure exceeds receipts. Persistent deficits are tackled through fiscal consolidation, which means either raising revenue or cutting expenditure. India's framework is the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003, which set deficit targets. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor and a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP. Revenue expenditure covers salaries, interest, pensions, subsidies and routine running costs. It creates no assets, so trimming it improves the revenue and fiscal balance directly. Subsidies, such as food, fertiliser and fuel subsidies, are a large part of it, and rationalizing them through targeting, DBT and removing leakages reduces the burden. New welfare schemes add recurring commitments, so they widen the deficit. Expanding industries is a long-term growth measure. It may raise tax revenue later, but it usually involves immediate spending, incentives or capital outlay, so it is not a direct remedy. Elimination: statement 2 is clearly wrong, which rules out (b) and (d). Statement 4 is also not a direct measure, which rules out (d). Statement 1 is correct, so (c), which omits 3, is incomplete. That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 3 both reduce government expenditure and so help reduce a persistent deficit, while 2 and 4 do not.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 (new welfare schemes), which raises expenditure and widens the deficit, and it omits statement 1.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but the option leaves out statement 3, rationalizing subsidies, which is also a valid deficit-reducing action.
Wrong: it includes statements 2 and 4. New welfare schemes increase spending, and expanding industries is not a direct deficit-reduction action.
keyfact: Deficits shrink by cutting revenue expenditure and rationalizing subsidies; new welfare schemes raise spending, so answer (a) 1 and 3 only.
option_notes: Options (a) 1 and 3 only: combines cutting revenue expenditure with rationalizing subsidies. These are the standard expenditure-side fiscal consolidation tools. Revenue expenditure covers non-asset-creating spending such as salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies. Subsidy rationalization works through DBT, Aadhaar seeding, targeting and price deregulation. This pairing reflects FRBM Act, 2003 priorities, under which the government commits to reducing the revenue and fiscal deficits through expenditure control and better quality of spending. It is the UPSC-approved answer here.

Option (b) 2 and 3 only: pairs new welfare schemes with subsidy rationalization. Welfare schemes such as MGNREGA, NFSA and PM-KISAN raise recurring commitments, so they work against deficit reduction. Subsidy rationalization alone is valid. The mix is wrong because it treats expansion of spending as a remedy. Governments must weigh social-protection objectives against fiscal discipline, and welfare spending is a major reason deficits persist in developing economies.

Option (c) 1 only: reducing revenue expenditure alone. It is a correct measure, but incomplete, because subsidy rationalization is another correct step. Revenue expenditure includes interest payments, defence revenue spending, salaries, pensions and subsidies. The Revenue Deficit equals revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, and the Effective Revenue Deficit (introduced in 2011-12) subtracts grants for capital asset creation from the revenue deficit. Cutting it improves public savings and reduces borrowing needs.

Option (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4: includes every statement. It is wrong because new welfare schemes add expenditure and industrial expansion is a long-term growth step rather than a direct deficit fix. Deficit measures include fiscal deficit (total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings), primary deficit (fiscal deficit minus interest payments) and revenue deficit. Fiscal consolidation relies mainly on expenditure control and revenue mobilisation, such as GST (2017) and wider tax compliance.
related: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 and amended in 2018 to adopt a debt-to-GDP anchor.
N.K. Singh Committee recommended a 3% fiscal deficit target and 60% general government debt-to-GDP.
DBT was launched in January 2013 to cut subsidy leakages.
Diesel prices were deregulated in October 2014; petrol in June 2010.
Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
Capital expenditure creates assets, while revenue expenditure does not.
statements: 1 — Correct: Reducing revenue expenditure cuts government spending and so narrows the revenue and fiscal deficit. Revenue expenditure is spending that creates no assets or liabilities-reducing effect, such as salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies and grants. In India it forms the larger share of total expenditure, with interest payments a major item. Measures include austerity, curbing non-plan or unproductive spending, and expenditure rationalization. The Revenue Deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Reducing it is a key FRBM objective, and the original FRBM Act aimed to eliminate it. Lower revenue deficit means less borrowing for consumption.

2 — Incorrect: New welfare schemes mean additional recurring expenditure, which raises the deficit unless matched by new revenue. Welfare schemes include MGNREGA (2005), the National Food Security Act (2013) and PM-KISAN (2019). They serve inclusion and social-justice goals and are part of revenue expenditure, often centrally sponsored with cost shared with states. They can be desirable on social grounds, but they work against deficit reduction in the short run. Governments must balance welfare commitments against fiscal prudence, and some argue that well-targeted welfare raises productivity over time.

3 — Correct: Rationalizing subsidies lowers the subsidy bill, a major part of revenue expenditure. Major subsidies in India are food (through the FCI and PDS), fertiliser and petroleum (LPG and kerosene). Rationalization means better targeting, removing ghost beneficiaries, and linking Aadhaar to Direct Benefit Transfer (launched 2013, expanded from 2014-15). The PAHAL scheme for LPG (2014-15) and the Give It Up campaign reduced leakages. Fuel prices were deregulated: petrol in 2010 and diesel in October 2014. The Economic Survey regularly urges subsidy reform. Rationalization does not mean abolition, only more efficient spending.

4 — Incorrect: Expanding industries is a long-term growth strategy, not a direct deficit-reduction step. It may raise tax revenue eventually through higher output and employment, but initially it often requires public investment, incentives or capital expenditure, which can increase the deficit. Examples of industrial policy include the 1991 reforms, Make in India (2014) and the PLI schemes (2020). Capital expenditure builds assets, and its economic effects come later. Hence it is not treated as an immediate fiscal consolidation tool, and the official answer excludes it.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 3 only. A persistent budget deficit is reduced by cutting revenue expenditure and rationalizing subsidies, both of which lower government spending. Introducing new welfare schemes raises spending, and expanding industries is not a direct deficit-reduction measure, since it needs capital outlay and pays off only slowly.
topic_notes: Budget deficits and fiscal consolidation. A budget deficit exists when expenditure exceeds receipts. Types: Revenue Deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal Deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, and it shows the government's borrowing requirement. Primary Deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Effective Revenue Deficit = revenue deficit minus grants for creating capital assets. Budget deficit in the old sense was total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowing, and it was discontinued after 1997. Legal framework: the FRBM Act, 2003 aimed at fiscal discipline, with a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP and elimination of the revenue deficit. It was suspended in 2008-09 after the global financial crisis and in 2020-21 because of Covid-19. The N.K. Singh Committee (2016-17) proposed debt-to-GDP of 60% (40% for the Centre and 20% for states), a fiscal council and a medium-term path. The 2018 amendment adopted debt as the anchor. Ways to reduce a deficit: expenditure side includes cutting non-merit subsidies, curbing wasteful spending, DBT, disinvestment-linked reform, and reducing interest costs through debt management. Revenue side includes GST, widening the tax base, better compliance, non-tax revenue and disinvestment or asset monetisation. Monetising the deficit (RBI printing money) is discouraged, and the FRBM Act restricts RBI's direct subscription to government securities. Capital expenditure is considered of higher quality than revenue expenditure because it creates assets, so the Union Budget has stressed raising capex. Crowding out: heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment. The Twin Deficit problem refers to the fiscal deficit and the current account deficit moving together. Fiscal deficit is financed through market borrowings, treasury bills, external assistance, small savings and the like. Related bodies include the Finance Commission (Article 280), the CAG, and the Comptroller's audit of fiscal data. Expect questions on definitions, deficit types and FRBM targets.

ocr: Which of the following has/have been accorded ‘Geographical Indication’ status? 1. Banaras Brocades and Sarees 2. Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma 3. Tirupathi Laddu Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (@j 1, 2 and 3
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Geographical Indications in India are governed by the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, which came into force on 15 September 2003 and is administered by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, with the GI Registry in Chennai. India's obligation comes from the TRIPS Agreement (WTO), Articles 22-24, and GI sits within the Paris Convention's industrial property framework. A GI identifies goods as originating from a territory where quality, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to that origin. Registration is valid for 10 years and is renewable indefinitely. Darjeeling Tea (2004-05) was the first GI-tagged product in India. Only goods (agricultural, natural, handicraft, manufactured, and foodstuff) qualify, and a registered GI can be used by authorised users. Elimination logic: Banaras Brocades and Sarees were registered in 2009 (statement 1 correct), which rules out (b) and (d) only if statement 2 is wrong. Tirupathi Laddu got GI status in 2009 (statement 3 correct), which eliminates (a). Daal-Bati-Churma has no GI tag, so statement 2 is wrong, which eliminates (b) and (d). That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it omits Tirupathi Laddu, which does hold a GI tag.
Wrong: it includes Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma, which has no GI status, and it omits Banaras Brocades and Sarees.
Correct: Banaras Brocades and Sarees and Tirupathi Laddu are both GI-registered, while Daal-Bati-Churma is not.
Wrong: it wrongly includes Daal-Bati-Churma, which is not a registered GI.
keyfact: Banaras Brocades and Sarees plus Tirupathi Laddu are GI-tagged (2009); Daal-Bati-Churma is not, so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a) names only Banaras Brocades and Sarees, which are a GI-registered handloom product of the Varanasi region of Uttar Pradesh. They are made of silk with zari work and have Mughal-inspired designs. The GI was registered in 2009 and protects against power-loom imitations. The option is wrong only because it leaves out Tirupathi Laddu. Banarasi weaving clusters cover Varanasi, Mirzapur, Bhadohi, Chandauli and Jaunpur, and the craft is hundreds of years old.

Option (b) pairs Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma with Tirupathi Laddu. Daal-Bati-Churma is a classic Rajasthani meal of baked wheat balls, lentils and sweet crumbled wheat. It is a cultural food item but has no GI registration. Tirupathi Laddu is the GI-registered temple prasadam of Tirumala made by the TTD. The option fails because it includes the unregistered dish and excludes the Banaras GI.

Option (c) is the official answer: Banaras Brocades and Sarees and Tirupathi Laddu. Both were GI-registered in 2009 under the 1999 Act. Banaras Brocades are handwoven silk textiles with zari from the Varanasi region, and Tirupathi Laddu is the prasadam of the Sri Venkateswara Temple, Tirumala. Together they show that GI covers both handicrafts and foodstuffs, including religious offerings.

Option (d) claims all three items are GI-tagged. It is wrong because Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma has no GI registration. The dish is a traditional Rajasthani preparation with baked bati, spiced dal and sweet churma, and it is widely popular in Rajasthan and Gujarat. GI tags in Rajasthan include Bikaneri Bhujia and Kota Doria, but not this dish.
related: India's first GI product was Darjeeling Tea (2004-05).
The GI Act came into force on 15 September 2003 and the GI Registry is in Chennai.
GI registration is valid for 10 years and is renewable.
GI is covered under TRIPS Articles 22-24 of the WTO.
Banaras Brocades and Sarees and Tirupathi Laddu got GI tags in 2009.
GI is a collective right and cannot be owned by an individual.
GI is administered by the DPIIT under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Kanchipuram silk, Basmati and Pochampally Ikat are well-known GI examples.
statements: 1 — Correct: Banaras Brocades and Sarees hold a GI tag (registered 2009). The GI covers handwoven silk brocades and sarees from Varanasi and nearby districts such as Mirzapur, Chandauli, Bhadohi and Jaunpur. The craft features intricate zari (gold and silver thread) work, Mughal-inspired motifs and fine silk. The tag protects weavers against power-loom imitations and false labelling. Banaras weaving is among India's oldest heritage textile crafts, with roots in the Mughal era, and the cluster is associated with the Varanasi weaver community.

2 — Incorrect: Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma is a traditional regional dish and is not a registered GI. It consists of baked wheat balls (bati), spiced lentils (dal) and sweetened crushed wheat (churma). It is a staple of Rajasthani and Marwari cuisine, linked to desert-region cooking traditions and associated with festive meals. Although foodstuffs can legally get GI tags, this dish has no registration. Rajasthan's registered GIs include Bikaneri Bhujia, Kota Doria, Sanganeri prints and Molela clay work.

3 — Correct: Tirupathi Laddu has a GI tag (registered 2009). It is the prasadam sweet offered at the Sri Venkateswara Temple at Tirumala, Andhra Pradesh, and is prepared in the temple kitchen (potu) by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD). It is made from gram flour, ghee, sugar, cashews, cardamom and raisins. The GI means only TTD can use the name Tirupathi Laddu, which prevents commercial imitation. Selling the laddu is a major source of temple revenue.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Banaras Brocades and Sarees and Tirupathi Laddu are registered Geographical Indications under the GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. Rajasthani Daal-Bati-Churma is a regional dish with no GI registration.
topic_notes: A Geographical Indication (GI) is an intellectual property right that identifies goods with a specific geographical origin and with qualities, reputation or characteristics essentially due to that origin. Internationally, GIs fall under TRIPS (Articles 22-24) of the WTO, and the Paris Convention covers industrial property. In India the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, in force from 15 September 2003, governs them. The GI Registry is at Chennai under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Registration is valid for 10 years and is renewable. Darjeeling Tea was the first Indian GI (2004-05). Goods covered include agricultural products, natural goods, handicrafts, manufactured goods and foodstuffs. Wines and spirits get enhanced protection under TRIPS Article 23. Applicants are associations of persons, producers or organisations, not individuals. A GI is a collective right, cannot be assigned or licensed like a trademark, and is different from a trademark, which identifies a business rather than a place. Examples of Indian GIs include Basmati rice, Kanchipuram silk, Mysore silk, Pochampally Ikat, Alphonso mango, Nagpur orange, Kullu shawl, Madhubani paintings, Kangra tea, Malabar pepper, Tirupathi Laddu, Banaras Brocades and Sarees, Bikaneri Bhujia, Hyderabadi Haleem and Rasgulla (West Bengal and Odisha disputes). NABARD supports GI registration through facilitation. Related instruments: the Lisbon Agreement for appellations of origin and the Geneva Act (2015). Other IPR topics UPSC may ask about include patents, trademarks, copyright, the Plant Variety Protection (PPV&FR) Act and the National IPR Policy 2016.

ocr: With reference to the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA), which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. It is a Public Limited Government Company. 2. It is a Non-Banking Financial Company. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b} 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: IREDA (Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited) was established in 1987 and incorporated on 11 March 1987 under the Companies Act, 1956. It is a Mini Ratna (Category-I) Public Sector Enterprise under the administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). Its legal form is a Public Limited Government Company, meaning the Government of India holds the equity and the company is not privately held. It is also notified as a Public Financial Institution under Section 4A of the Companies Act, 1956, and is registered with the RBI as a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC), now classified as an Infrastructure Finance Company (NBFC-IFC). Its role is to promote, develop and extend financial assistance for renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, waste-to-energy) and energy efficiency/conservation projects. Its motto is 'Energising the Future'. IREDA was listed on the stock exchanges in November 2023 through an IPO. Elimination logic: once a student knows IREDA is a government-owned lender, statement 1 (government company) is clearly right, and statement 2 follows because it lends but does not take demand deposits like a bank, so it is an NBFC. Options (a), (b) and (d) each reject one true statement.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it accepts only statement 1 and rejects statement 2, but IREDA is also an RBI-registered NBFC.
(b) is wrong because it accepts only statement 2 and rejects statement 1, but IREDA is a Public Limited Government Company.
(c) is right because both statements are true: IREDA is a Public Limited Government Company and an NBFC.
(d) is wrong because it rejects both statements, although both are factually correct.
keyfact: IREDA (1987, under MNRE) = Public Limited Government Company + RBI-registered NBFC (IFC) + Mini Ratna-I, financing renewable energy.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would hold only if IREDA were a government company but not a regulated financial company. In fact IREDA is a government-owned Mini Ratna PSU under MNRE, set up in 1987 to finance renewable energy, and it is also an RBI-registered NBFC and Public Financial Institution. Government companies are those in which at least 51 percent of paid-up capital is held by the Central or State Governments (Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013).

Option (b), 2 only: this would hold only if IREDA were an NBFC but not a government company. An NBFC is a company registered under the Companies Act that lends and invests but does not hold a banking licence and cannot accept demand deposits. NBFCs are regulated by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934. IREDA does meet this definition, but it is also government-owned, so 'NBFC only' wrongly excludes statement 1.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: this is the official answer. IREDA, incorporated 11 March 1987 and headquartered in New Delhi, is a Public Limited Government Company under MNRE, a Mini Ratna Category-I PSU, and an RBI-registered NBFC (IFC category). It finances renewable energy and energy efficiency projects, raises funds from multilateral agencies and bond markets, and has been listed on the stock exchanges since November 2023.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: this would mean IREDA is neither government-owned nor a financial company, such as a purely private or purely regulatory body. That is false. IREDA is a government-owned financial institution, so it is both a government company and an NBFC. Students sometimes confuse IREDA with regulators like CERC or with bodies like SECI (Solar Energy Corporation of India), which is a CPSU that does project and trading work rather than lending.
related: IREDA was established in 1987 and works under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy.
IREDA is a Mini Ratna Category-I PSU and an RBI-registered NBFC (NBFC-IFC).
A government company is one in which the government holds at least 51 percent of paid-up share capital.
NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits and are regulated by the RBI.
SECI (Solar Energy Corporation of India) is the CPSU under MNRE for solar tendering and trading.
The International Solar Alliance has its headquarters in Gurugram and was launched in 2015.
India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030.
IREDA was listed on the stock exchanges in November 2023.
statements: 1 — Correct: IREDA is a Public Limited Government Company, with the Government of India as the owner, under MNRE. IREDA was incorporated on 11 March 1987 under the Companies Act, 1956 and is headquartered in New Delhi. It is a Mini Ratna Category-I PSU, an award that gives greater financial and operational autonomy.
