It was listed on NSE and BSE in November 2023 after an IPO, yet the Government of India still holds the majority stake. Its Chairman and Managing Director is appointed by the government. It is under MNRE, the nodal ministry for solar, wind, biomass and small hydro.

2 — Correct: IREDA is registered with the RBI as a Non-Banking Financial Company. It is notified as a Public Financial Institution under Section 4A of the Companies Act and is classified as an NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Company (NBFC-IFC). It raises funds from domestic and international markets (bonds, multilateral lines of credit from World Bank, ADB, KfW, JICA) and lends for renewable energy and energy efficiency projects. It does not accept demand deposits and cannot issue cheques drawn on itself, which distinguishes an NBFC from a bank. It also provides loans, and promotes the sector through credit and advisory services.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. IREDA is a Public Limited Government Company under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and is also registered with the RBI as a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) that lends to renewable energy and energy efficiency projects.
topic_notes: IREDA is the leading public financial institution dedicated to renewable energy in India. It was established in 1987 as a Public Limited Government Company, is headquartered in New Delhi, and works under the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). It holds Mini Ratna Category-I status, is notified as a Public Financial Institution under Section 4A of the Companies Act, and is registered with the RBI as an NBFC (Infrastructure Finance Company). Its mandate is to promote, develop and extend financial assistance for renewable energy and energy efficiency projects, including solar, wind, small hydro, biomass, bagasse cogeneration and waste-to-energy. Its motto is 'Energising the Future'. It borrows from multilateral and bilateral agencies such as the World Bank, ADB, KfW (Germany), JICA (Japan) and the European Investment Bank, and also issues tax-free and taxable bonds. IREDA was listed on NSE and BSE through an IPO in November 2023. Related institutions: MNRE, the nodal ministry, which runs the National Solar Mission (2010, launched under NAPCC) and sets targets such as 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; SECI, a CPSU under MNRE that tenders and trades solar power; NTPC and NHPC, which run renewable capacity; and the International Solar Alliance (ISA), headquartered in Gurugram, launched in 2015 by India and France. Related finance: Power Finance Corporation (PFC) and REC Limited are also NBFCs under the Ministry of Power. Other angles UPSC may ask: the difference between a bank and NBFC (NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, are not part of the payment and settlement system, and deposit insurance is not available to their depositors), the definition of a government company, the Navratna/Maharatna/Miniratna categories, and India's renewable targets and green financing instruments such as sovereign green bonds.

ocr: Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its prorogation. 2. A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha, which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha, shall not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: The rule on lapsing of Bills comes from Article 107 of the Constitution. Article 107(3) says a Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses. Prorogation only ends a session; it does not end the life of the House or its pending business. Article 107(5) says a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or one passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha. Article 107(4) says a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse on dissolution, because the Rajya Sabha is a continuing House under Article 83(1). Bills that do not lapse include: a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha; a Bill passed by both Houses and awaiting Presidential assent; a Bill returned by the President to the Houses for reconsideration; and a Bill on which a joint sitting has been notified (Article 108). Elimination logic: Statement 1 confuses prorogation with dissolution, so options (a), (c) are out. Statement 2 is correct, so (d) is out. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because prorogation does not cause a pending Bill to lapse (Article 107(3)); only dissolution of the Lok Sabha does.
(b) is right: Statement 1 is wrong, and Statement 2 is correct under Article 107(4), since the Rajya Sabha is a continuing House and its pending Bills survive dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
(c) is wrong: It requires Statement 1 to be correct, but a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha does not lapse on prorogation.
(d) is wrong: Statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: Lok Sabha Bills lapse on dissolution, not prorogation; Rajya Sabha-pending Bills not passed by the Lok Sabha do not lapse (Art. 107).
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would hold if prorogation caused lapsing, but it does not. Prorogation is the termination of a session by the President under Article 85(2)(a), on the advice of the Council of Ministers. After prorogation, the House stands ended for that session until summoned again. It differs from adjournment (by the presiding officer) and dissolution (end of the Lok Sabha's life). Pending Bills survive prorogation, though pending motions, such as no-confidence motions, are generally affected.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' is the correct choice. It reflects Article 107(4): a Bill that has been pending in the Rajya Sabha and has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. This follows from the Rajya Sabha being a permanent House. Bills that began in the Rajya Sabha are therefore kept alive until the new Lok Sabha considers them. Bills that originated in or were passed by the Lok Sabha and are pending, in either House, lapse on dissolution.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is wrong because it asserts that a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on prorogation. In fact, Article 107(3) says that the pendency of a Bill is unaffected by prorogation. Only dissolution of the Lok Sabha ends pending Lok Sabha Bills (Article 107(5)). The option serves as a trap for students who confuse prorogation, adjournment and dissolution.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is wrong because Statement 2 is a correct application of Article 107(4). It tests whether the student knows that the Rajya Sabha is a continuing chamber and that its pending Bills, which have not been passed by the Lok Sabha, are not affected by the Lok Sabha's dissolution.
related: Article 107 deals with the introduction and passing of Bills; Article 108 provides for joint sittings.
Only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved; the Rajya Sabha is a permanent House (Article 83).
Prorogation is by the President; adjournment is by the presiding officer.
Joint sittings have been held in 1961, 1978 and 2002.
A Bill returned by the President for reconsideration does not lapse on dissolution.
A Bill passed by both Houses and awaiting Presidential assent does not lapse.
A Money Bill cannot be the subject of a joint sitting; the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return it.
The gap between two sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months (Article 85).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Under Article 107(3), a pending Bill does not lapse on prorogation; lapsing happens on dissolution of the Lok Sabha. Prorogation is the end of a session, ordered by the President (Article 85(2)). It ends a sitting session but not the House's life. Pending Bills and notices of motions continue, though committees and some pending items may need procedural revival. Adjournment, by contrast, suspends a sitting for hours, days or weeks and is done by the presiding officer. Adjournment sine die ends a sitting without a fixed date for reassembly, but only the President prorogues. Dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha, and only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved, either on completion of its five-year term (Article 83(2)) or earlier by the President under Article 85(2)(b). Under Article 352, the term can be extended by one year at a time during a National Emergency.

2 — Correct: Under Article 107(4), a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House under Article 83(1), with one-third of its members retiring every two years, and each member serving a six-year term. It has a maximum of 250 members, of whom 12 are nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service. The Lok Sabha has a maximum of 550 members (530 from the states and 20 from the Union Territories), though the present strength is 543. A Bill originating in the Rajya Sabha and passed there, then sent to the Lok Sabha and pending there, lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. The Rajya Sabha's chairman is the Vice-President, who is ex officio chairperson.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha, not on prorogation, so Statement 1 is wrong. A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse, because the Rajya Sabha is a permanent House that is never dissolved, so Statement 2 is correct.
topic_notes: The topic is the fate of Bills in Parliament, which is governed by Article 107 (ordinary Bills) and Article 108 (joint sittings). Article 107(1) says a Bill other than a Money Bill or Financial Bill may originate in either House. Article 107(2) says a Bill is not passed unless both Houses agree on it, with or without amendments. Article 107(3): a Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse on prorogation. Article 107(4): a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse on dissolution. Article 107(5): a Bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses on dissolution. Article 108 provides for a joint sitting if there is a deadlock between the Houses on an ordinary Bill or a Financial Bill (Article 117(1) type). The joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker. It does not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. A Bill that has been notified for a joint sitting does not lapse on dissolution, as the President's notification of the joint sitting keeps it alive. Joint sittings have been held three times: 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill), 1978 (Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill) and 2002 (Prevention of Terrorism Bill, POTA). Related angles include: Money Bills (Article 110), in which the Rajya Sabha has only a recommendatory role and must return the Bill within 14 days; the President's options on Bills (assent, withhold, return, with a pocket veto not being bound by a time limit); the distinction between Money Bills and Financial Bills; Constitution Amendment Bills (Article 368); the Lok Sabha's maximum term of five years; and Article 85, under which the President summons, prorogues and dissolves. The gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months (Article 85(1)).

ocr: Which of the following is/are the indicator/indicators uscd by IFPRI to compute the Global Hunger Index Report? 1. Undernourishment 2. Child stunting 3. Child mortality Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1,2 and 3 (a) 1 and 3 only
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Global Hunger Index is a peer-reviewed annual report that measures and tracks hunger at the global, regional and national levels. IFPRI (International Food Policy Research Institute, Washington DC) first produced it in 2006 with Welthungerhilfe; Concern Worldwide joined in 2007. Since 2018 the GHI has been calculated from four component indicators: (1) undernourishment, the share of the population with insufficient calorie intake; (2) child wasting, the share of children under five with low weight for their height; (3) child stunting, the share of children under five with low height for their age; and (4) child mortality, the mortality rate of children under five. Undernourishment carries one-third of the weight, and the other three carry one-sixth each. Scores run from 0 to 100, where 0 is best. Scores of 9.9 or less are 'low', 10-19.9 'moderate', 20-34.9 'serious', 35-49.9 'alarming' and 50 or more 'extremely alarming'. Before 2015 the indicators were undernourishment, child underweight and child mortality. Because all three listed items are used, options (a), (b) and (d) are wrong by elimination, and only (c) includes every item.
explanations: (a) Wrong. It recognises only undernourishment and leaves out child stunting and child mortality, which are also GHI indicators.
(b) Wrong. Stunting and mortality are indeed indicators, but it wrongly omits undernourishment, which is the most heavily weighted.
(c) Correct. Undernourishment, child stunting and child mortality are all GHI indicators, along with child wasting.
(d) Wrong. It omits child stunting, which is a GHI component.
keyfact: GHI = 4 indicators: undernourishment (1/3), and child wasting, stunting and mortality (1/6 each); scale 0-100, lower is better.
option_notes: Option (a), 'undernourishment only', would describe an index based solely on calorie deficiency. Undernourishment is the FAO's Prevalence of Undernourishment (PoU), the share of people whose habitual food intake is below the minimum energy requirement. It is also the basis for the UN SDG indicator 2.1.1. FAO publishes it in the SOFI report. It is only one of the four GHI components, though it carries one-third of the weight, so this option is incomplete.

Option (b), 'stunting and mortality only', describes two child-focused indicators. Child stunting means low height for age and reflects chronic undernutrition, while under-five mortality is the probability of dying before age five. Both are GHI components, but the option omits undernourishment and so is incomplete. Stunting data in India come from NFHS, and mortality estimates come from UN IGME. Both are tracked under SDG 2 and SDG 3.

Option (c), 'all three', is the official answer. The GHI uses four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting and child mortality. The index is published each October by Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide (with IFPRI as a partner in earlier editions). The scale is 0 to 100. The weights are 1/3 for undernourishment and 1/6 each for the other three. The index is used to rank countries and to track progress toward Zero Hunger (SDG 2) by 2030.

Option (d), 'undernourishment and child mortality only', leaves out child stunting. Both included indicators are real GHI components, which makes the option tempting. The GHI is intended to capture both calorie deficiency and child undernutrition, and stunting captures chronic child undernutrition. Dropping it would fail to reflect long-term nutrition deprivation, so the option is incomplete.
related: GHI is published annually, and its indicators are undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting and child mortality.
IFPRI is headquartered in Washington DC and is a research centre of CGIAR.
The GHI scale runs from 0 (best) to 100 (worst).
Undernourishment carries a 1/3 weight in the GHI; each of the other three indicators carries 1/6.
POSHAN Abhiyaan was launched in 2018 to reduce stunting, undernutrition, anaemia and low birth weight.
The National Food Security Act 2013 covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
SDG 2 aims for Zero Hunger by 2030.
NFHS is the Indian survey that provides data on stunting and wasting among children.
statements: 1 — Correct: Undernourishment is a GHI indicator and carries the highest weight, one-third. It means the share of the population whose caloric intake is insufficient. The data come mainly from FAO, which estimates it as the Prevalence of Undernourishment (PoU) in its State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report. It reflects chronic food deprivation at the population level and is the only GHI indicator that covers the whole population, not just children under five. A high PoU signals that food availability or access is inadequate.

2 — Correct: Child stunting is a GHI indicator with a weight of one-sixth. It means the share of children under five whose height is too low for their age, which reflects chronic undernutrition. It is measured against WHO Child Growth Standards, with stunting defined as more than two standard deviations below the median height for age. Data come from surveys such as DHS, MICS and, in India, NFHS. Stunting causes lasting physical and cognitive damage. The related indicator, child wasting (low weight for height), reflects acute undernutrition and is also part of the GHI.

3 — Correct: Child mortality is a GHI indicator with a weight of one-sixth. It is the under-five mortality rate, meaning the share of children who die before their fifth birthday. The data come from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME). It partly reflects the deadly combination of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments, and it captures the fatal effect of undernutrition. Along with stunting and wasting, it is a child-focused indicator in the GHI.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1, 2 and 3. The Global Hunger Index (GHI), published by IFPRI (and, in later years, with Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide), combines four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting and child mortality. All three items listed in the question are therefore GHI indicators.
topic_notes:
The Global Hunger Index (GHI) is an annual report on hunger at the global, regional and national levels. It was first published in 2006 by IFPRI and Welthungerhilfe. Concern Worldwide became a co-publisher in 2007. IFPRI withdrew as a co-publisher after 2018, and the GHI is now published by Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide. Its purpose is to raise awareness of hunger, compare countries and track progress toward Zero Hunger (SDG 2).

The index uses four indicators. Undernourishment (the share of the population with insufficient calorie intake) has a weight of 1/3. Child wasting (low weight for height), child stunting (low height for age) and child mortality (under-five death rate) each have a weight of 1/6. Scores run from 0 to 100, where 0 is the best. The severity categories are: low (9.9 or less), moderate (10-19.9), serious (20-34.9), alarming (35-49.9) and extremely alarming (50 and above).

Data sources are FAO (undernourishment), UNICEF, WHO and the World Bank (stunting and wasting), and UN IGME (mortality). India has typically ranked in the 'serious' category. Its ranking has drawn discussion and government objections about methodology, and in the 2023 edition India was ranked 111 out of 125 countries, with a score of 28.7. India's child wasting rate is among the world's highest, at over 18 percent.

Other angles UPSC could ask: other indices from IFPRI (such as the Global Food Policy Report), other global indices (Human Development Index from UNDP, Multidimensional Poverty Index from UNDP and OPHI, Global Gender Gap Index from the World Economic Forum), Indian schemes (POSHAN Abhiyaan, the National Food Security Act 2013, Mid-Day Meal / PM POSHAN, ICDS, Mission Poshan 2.0) and the NFHS surveys. IFPRI is part of CGIAR and headquartered in Washington DC.

ocr: There has been a persistent deficit budget year after year. Which action/actions of the following can—be— taken by the Government to reduce the deficit? af 1. Reducing revenue expenditure 2. Introducing new welfare’ schemes 3. Rationalizing subsidies 4. Reducing import duty B-APM-P-CKB/65A 2 Select the correct answer using the code given below, {a) 1 only {b) 2 and 3 only fc) 1 and 3 only (dj 1, 2, 3 and 4
subject: Economy
detail: A budget deficit arises when government expenditure exceeds receipts. India tracks the revenue deficit (revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts), the fiscal deficit (total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings) and the primary deficit (fiscal deficit minus interest payments). The FRBM Act, 2003 set the legal framework for fiscal consolidation. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60 percent for the general government, with the Centre at 40 percent. To reduce a deficit, the government has two levers: raise receipts (tax and non-tax revenue, disinvestment) or cut expenditure. Revenue expenditure covers salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies. It creates no assets, so trimming it is the standard consolidation step. Subsidies, mainly on food, fertiliser and fuel, form a large part of that spending, so rationalizing them through targeting and DBT saves money. Elimination logic: new welfare schemes add to expenditure, so statement 2 is wrong, which removes (b) and (d). Customs duty is a tax revenue source, so lowering import duty reduces receipts and widens the deficit. That makes statement 4 wrong and leaves (c), with 1 and 3 correct.
explanations: Incorrect: Statement 1 is right, but the option leaves out statement 3. Rationalizing subsidies is also a valid way to cut the deficit.
Incorrect: Statement 2 is wrong, because new welfare schemes increase expenditure. Statement 1 is correct but is missing from this option.
Correct: Reducing revenue expenditure and rationalizing subsidies both cut spending and narrow the deficit. New welfare schemes and lower import duty do the opposite.
Incorrect: This includes statements 2 and 4. New welfare schemes raise spending and lower import duty reduces revenue, so both widen the deficit.
keyfact: Cutting revenue expenditure and rationalizing subsidies narrow a deficit; new welfare schemes and lower import duty widen it.
option_notes: Option (a) is 1 only: reducing revenue expenditure. Revenue expenditure is spending that creates no assets, such as salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies. It is a large part of the Union Budget, and interest payments alone take a big share of revenue receipts. Cutting it reduces the revenue deficit and the fiscal deficit. Capital expenditure, in contrast, builds assets such as roads, railways and defence equipment. The option is incomplete here because it ignores subsidy rationalization, which also reduces the deficit. FRBM discipline generally favours improving the quality of expenditure.

Option (b) is 2 and 3 only: new welfare schemes and subsidy rationalization. New welfare schemes include MGNREGA (2005), PM-KISAN (2019) and Ayushman Bharat (2018), and they raise expenditure. Subsidy rationalization, on the other hand, curbs expenditure through DBT (from 2013) and better targeting. The two measures pull in opposite directions on the deficit. The option fails because it includes statement 2 and omits statement 1. Welfare schemes can be funded without worsening the deficit only if they are matched by additional revenue or by savings elsewhere.

Option (c) is 1 and 3 only: reducing revenue expenditure and rationalizing subsidies. This is the official UPSC answer. Both measures cut government spending without hurting receipts, so they narrow the deficit. Revenue expenditure covers non-asset-creating spending, and subsidies on food, fertiliser and fuel are among its largest items. Tools include DBT, Aadhaar-linked targeting, PAHAL for LPG, and market-linked fuel pricing. The FRBM Act, 2003 guides this consolidation, and the 2018 amendment made debt-to-GDP the anchor. India's fiscal deficit target is 4.5 percent of GDP or less by 2025-26.

Option (d) is 1, 2, 3 and 4: all the measures. It is wrong because it adds new welfare schemes, which raise expenditure, and a cut in import duty, which reduces customs revenue. Customs duty is levied under the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and is a significant source of indirect tax revenue. Lower duties make imports cheaper but cut government receipts. A deficit-reduction plan would need to raise revenue or cut expenditure, and statements 2 and 4 do neither.
related: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 and amended in 2018 to make debt-to-GDP the anchor.
N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a 60 percent debt-to-GDP ceiling for the general government.
Article 112 requires the annual financial statement (Union Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
Direct Benefit Transfer was launched on 1 January 2013 to reduce subsidy leakages.
Ad hoc Treasury Bills were discontinued in 1997 and replaced by Ways and Means Advances.
GST came into force on 1 July 2017.
statements: 1 — Correct: Reducing revenue expenditure lowers total spending and so narrows the deficit. Revenue expenditure is spending that creates no assets or liabilities, such as salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies and grants. It is shown in the Union Budget as a separate category from capital expenditure. Interest payments, defence revenue spending, pensions and subsidies are its major components. The revenue deficit is the gap between revenue expenditure and revenue receipts. Economists prefer cuts here over cuts in capital expenditure, because capital expenditure builds assets and supports growth. The 'effective revenue deficit' concept appeared in the 2011 budget, and it removes grants for creating capital assets from the revenue deficit.

2 — Incorrect: New welfare schemes raise government expenditure and widen the deficit unless they are matched by new revenue. Examples of welfare schemes include MGNREGA (2005, Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act), the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana, PM-KISAN (2019, Rs 6,000 per year in three instalments) and Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (2018). These are mostly funded as revenue expenditure. They carry social and developmental value, but in fiscal terms they push the deficit up. They can be accommodated only by raising taxes, cutting other spending or borrowing more. Fiscal policy therefore balances welfare objectives against the FRBM consolidation targets.

3 — Correct: Rationalizing subsidies means targeting them better, eliminating leakages and removing unwarranted ones, which cuts the subsidy bill. India's three main subsidies are food (administered through the FCI and the Public Distribution System under the National Food Security Act, 2013), fertiliser and petroleum (LPG and kerosene). Direct Benefit Transfer, launched on 1 January 2013, and the PAHAL scheme for LPG (2015) reduce leakages. The JAM trinity, Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile, supports this targeting. Diesel prices were deregulated in October 2014 and petrol prices in 2010. Subsidy rationalization is a core recommendation of the Kelkar Committee and the Economic Survey.

4 — Incorrect: Reducing import duty lowers customs revenue, which falls under indirect tax receipts, and so enlarges the deficit. Customs duties are levied under the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and are a Union subject under Entry 83 of the Union List. Basic customs duty, the social welfare surcharge and the IGST on imports are the main components. Lower import duties may help consumers and industry, and may spur trade, but they cut the government's revenue in the short run. Raising duties would improve receipts, though it may raise prices and invite retaliation.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. A persistent budget deficit is reduced by cutting government spending (especially unproductive revenue expenditure) and by rationalizing subsidies. Launching new welfare schemes and cutting import duty would both widen the deficit.
topic_notes: Types of deficit: the revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. The fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, and it measures the government's total borrowing need. The primary deficit is the fiscal deficit minus interest payments, and it shows the current year's borrowing excluding the burden of past debt. The budget deficit concept was dropped after 1997, when the practice of automatic monetization of deficits through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended. Deficit financing sources: market borrowings through G-secs, small savings, external borrowing and RBI support. Since 1997, ad hoc T-bills have been replaced by Ways and Means Advances (WMA). FRBM Act, 2003 (in force from 2004): it aimed at eliminating the revenue deficit and reducing the fiscal deficit to 3 percent of GDP. Targets were deferred many times, including during the 2008 crisis and the COVID-19 shock. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt ceiling of 60 percent of GDP for the general government, 40 percent for the Centre and 20 percent for the states, plus a Fiscal Council. The 2018 amendment replaced the revenue deficit target with the fiscal deficit and debt anchors. The escape clause allows deviation in cases of national security, war, calamity, or a sharp fall in output. Ways to reduce the deficit: raise tax revenue through GST (launched on 1 July 2017) and improve compliance; raise non-tax revenue through dividends and spectrum auctions; push disinvestment; cut subsidies and unproductive expenditure; and shift spending toward capital expenditure. Related concepts: crowding out, where heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment; the Ricardian equivalence argument; the debt trap; and the quality of fiscal adjustment, meaning the ratio of revenue deficit to fiscal deficit. Likely UPSC angles include definitions of each deficit, the FRBM thresholds, the N.K. Singh Committee, the Union Budget's classification into revenue and capital accounts, the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266), and Article 112, which requires the annual financial statement.

ocr: The establishment of ‘Payment Banks’ is being allowed in India to promote financial inclusion. Which of the following statements is/are correct in this context? 1. Mobile telephone companies and supermarket chains that are owned and controlled, by residents are eligible to be promoters of Payment Banks, 2. Payment Banks can issue both credit cards and debit cards. 3. Payment Banks cannot undertake lending activities. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 and 2 only {b) 1 and 3 only (c} 2 only (aj) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Economy
detail: Payment Banks are a differentiated category of bank created to advance financial inclusion by serving migrant workers, low-income households, small businesses and other unorganised-sector entities. The Nachiket Mor Committee (2013-14) recommended them, and RBI issued the Guidelines for Licensing of Payment Banks in November 2014. Eligible promoters include existing non-bank PPI issuers, individuals or professionals, NBFCs, corporates, mobile telephone companies, supermarket chains, real sector cooperatives and public sector entities, provided they are owned and controlled by residents. Payment Banks are registered as public limited companies under the Companies Act 2013 and licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949. They can accept demand deposits (originally capped at Rs 1 lakh per customer, raised to Rs 2 lakh in 2021), issue ATM and debit cards, offer payments and remittance services, and distribute simple financial products such as insurance and mutual funds. They cannot lend, cannot issue credit cards, and cannot accept NRI deposits. They must maintain CRR with RBI and invest at least 75% of demand deposit balances in government securities with maturity up to one year. Elimination logic: statement 3 is certainly correct because lending is barred. Statement 2 is wrong because credit cards are barred, which removes (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: It includes statement 2, but Payment Banks cannot issue credit cards, which would amount to lending.
Correct: Statements 1 and 3 are right. Resident-controlled mobile telecom companies and supermarket chains are eligible promoters, and Payment Banks cannot lend.
Wrong: It says only statement 2 is correct, but statement 2 is false while statements 1 and 3 are true.
Wrong: It includes statement 2, which is false because credit cards cannot be issued by Payment Banks.
keyfact: Payment Banks can accept deposits (up to Rs 2 lakh per customer) and offer debit cards and payments, but cannot lend or issue credit cards.
related: Payment Banks were recommended by the Nachiket Mor Committee in 2014.
RBI issued its final Payment Bank licensing guidelines in November 2014.
Minimum paid-up capital for a Payment Bank is Rs 100 crore.
The deposit cap per customer is Rs 2 lakh, raised from Rs 1 lakh in 2021.
Airtel Payments Bank was the first to commence operations, in January 2017.
India Post Payments Bank was launched in September 2018 under the Department of Posts.
Payment Banks must invest at least 75% of demand deposit balances in government securities.
Small Finance Banks can lend, but Payment Banks cannot.
statements: 1 — Correct: Mobile telephone companies and supermarket chains owned and controlled by residents are expressly listed as eligible promoters in the 2014 RBI guidelines. Eligible promoters also include NBFCs, corporate business correspondents, PPI issuers, real sector cooperatives and public sector entities. The promoter must be 'fit and proper' with a sound track record of at least five years. The minimum paid-up equity capital is Rs 100 crore. The promoter or promoter group must hold at least 40% of the paid-up equity for the first five years, and foreign shareholding follows FDI norms for private sector banks. The Payment Bank must list on stock exchanges within three years of reaching a net worth of Rs 500 crore. Examples include Airtel Payments Bank, Paytm Payments Bank, India Post Payments Bank and Jio Payments Bank.

2 — Incorrect: Payment Banks can issue debit cards and ATM cards but cannot issue credit cards, because credit cards involve extending credit, which is a lending activity. Credit cards are a revolving line of credit, so the issuer lends to the cardholder. Debit cards simply draw on the customer's own deposited balance. Payment Banks can also offer mobile banking, internet banking, prepaid instruments, and payment and remittance services. They may act as business correspondents of other banks, which is how they can distribute loans or credit products of other lenders without lending themselves. They cannot set up subsidiaries to carry out non-banking financial services.

3 — Correct: Payment Banks cannot undertake lending activities, which is their defining restriction. They accept deposits but cannot advance loans. Their funds are mainly parked in Statutory Liquidity Ratio-eligible government securities (at least 75% of demand deposit balances) and in balances with other scheduled commercial banks (up to 25%). They must keep a Cash Reserve Ratio with RBI. They also cannot accept fixed or recurring deposits and cannot accept NRI deposits. The maximum balance per customer was Rs 1 lakh, raised to Rs 2 lakh in April 2021. Their income comes largely from fees, commissions and interest on investments. This distinguishes them from Small Finance Banks, which can lend.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 1 and 3 only. Under RBI's 2014 Guidelines for Licensing of Payment Banks, resident-controlled entities such as mobile telecom companies and supermarket chains are eligible promoters. Payment Banks can accept deposits and offer payments services but cannot lend or issue credit cards.
topic_notes: Payment Banks are niche banks meant to deepen financial inclusion, especially through small savings accounts and payments and remittance services. The Nachiket Mor Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low Income Households (2013-14) proposed them. RBI released final guidelines in November 2014 and granted in-principle approval in August 2015 to 11 applicants, including Airtel M Commerce Services, India Post, Paytm, Fino PayTech, Aditya Birla Nuvo, National Securities Depository Ltd, Reliance Industries, Vodafone m-pesa, Tech Mahindra, Cholamandalam and Dilip Shanghvi's group. Airtel Payments Bank was the first to start operations, in January 2017. India Post Payments Bank was launched in September 2018 and has the largest physical reach through post offices. Key rules are a minimum paid-up capital of Rs 100 crore, a leverage ratio of at least 3% (later 3.0% on exposure), promoter holding of at least 40% for five years, and a voting-rights cap for foreign shareholders under FDI rules. They can accept demand deposits (current and savings) up to Rs 2 lakh per customer, issue debit cards, handle remittances, and distribute third-party financial products. They cannot lend, issue credit cards, accept NRI deposits or set up NBFC subsidiaries. A Payment Bank can convert into a Small Finance Bank after five years of operation, subject to RBI approval. Related categories include Small Finance Banks, which can lend to underserved sectors and were announced in 2014, as well as Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks and cooperative banks. Possible future questions concern the difference between Payment Banks and SFBs, the role of the Payments Banks in direct benefit transfer, UPI and mobile wallets, PPI regulation, Jan Dhan Yojana, and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007.

ocr: With reference to ‘LiFi’, recently in the news, which of the following statements” is/are correct? 1, It uses light as the medium for high- speed data transmission. 2. It is a wireless technology and is several times faster than ‘WiFi’. Select the correct answer using the code ‘given below. \ fa) 1 only fb) 2 only~ ‘(c) Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Li-Fi, or Light Fidelity, is a bidirectional, high-speed, networked wireless communication technology that belongs to the family of Visible Light Communication (VLC) or Optical Wireless Communication (OWC). The term was coined by Prof. Harald Haas of the University of Edinburgh, who demonstrated it in his 2011 TED talk. It works by modulating the intensity of LED light at rates too fast for the human eye to notice. A photodetector at the receiver converts the flickering into an electrical signal and then into data. Wi-Fi uses radio waves in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, whereas Li-Fi uses the visible light spectrum (roughly 400-800 THz), which is about 10,000 times wider than the entire radio-frequency spectrum. Laboratory speeds of over 224 Gbps have been reported, and the technology is considered several times, even up to 100 times, faster than typical Wi-Fi. Limitations: light cannot pass through walls, so range is short and line-of-sight is needed, and it does not work without light. Elimination logic: statement 1 (light as the medium) is the defining feature, so (b) and (d) are out. Statement 2 is also true, since Li-Fi is wireless and faster, so (a) is out. That leaves (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it says only statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also true, because Li-Fi is wireless and much faster than Wi-Fi.
(b) Wrong: it says only statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is also true, because light is the transmission medium in Li-Fi.
(c) Correct: Li-Fi uses visible light (LEDs) to transmit data wirelessly and achieves speeds several times higher than Wi-Fi, so both statements hold.
(d) Wrong: it says neither statement is correct, but both are factually accurate descriptions of Li-Fi.
keyfact: Li-Fi = Light Fidelity: wireless data via modulated LED visible light, far faster than Wi-Fi (radio) but short-range and line-of-sight.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be right only if Li-Fi were not clearly wireless or not faster than Wi-Fi. In fact Li-Fi is a wireless optical technology. Its speed advantage comes from the huge visible-light bandwidth, which is about 10,000 times the RF spectrum. Lab speeds exceed 200 Gbps, while real-world deployments usually give around 1 Gbps or more. UPSC often builds such options as partial-truth traps, so a student must check each statement independently.

Option (b), '2 only', would be right only if Li-Fi did not use light as its medium. Li-Fi is a subset of Visible Light Communication, which modulates LED light intensity, and the receiver is a photodetector. It does not use radio waves, which is the key difference from Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11). Its drawbacks are that it cannot pass through opaque walls, has limited range and needs line of sight. Its advantages are security and freedom from electromagnetic interference.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official answer. Li-Fi uses visible light from LEDs for bidirectional, high-speed, networked wireless communication. The idea was demonstrated by Harald Haas in 2011, and the IEEE 802.15.7 and 802.11bb standards govern it. Its speed is many times that of Wi-Fi, and its bandwidth is much wider than the radio spectrum. It suits places where radio is restricted, such as aircraft, hospitals, hazardous industrial sites and underwater, and it also lets street lighting double as a data network.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is wrong because both statements describe Li-Fi accurately. Students may confuse Li-Fi with Wi-Fi (radio-based, 802.11) or with Bluetooth, NFC or WiMAX, which also use radio frequencies. Li-Fi is distinct because it uses optical rather than radio frequencies. Related but different technologies are fibre optics (guided light through glass cables) and free-space optical communication (FSO), which uses lasers over long line-of-sight links.
related: Li-Fi stands for Light Fidelity and was popularised by Harald Haas in 2011.
Li-Fi is a subset of Visible Light Communication (VLC), with standards IEEE 802.15.7 and 802.11bb.
Wi-Fi uses radio waves (IEEE 802.11); Li-Fi uses visible light from LEDs.
Li-Fi cannot penetrate walls, so it is more secure but has short range.
Visible-light spectrum is about 10,000 times wider than the radio spectrum.
Lab Li-Fi speeds have exceeded 200 Gbps.
Optical fibre uses total internal reflection to guide light in cables.
NFC works over a few centimetres at 13.56 MHz.
statements: 1 — Correct: Li-Fi uses light, specifically modulated LED visible light, as the medium for data transmission. Li-Fi stands for Light Fidelity and is a form of Visible Light Communication. The term was popularised by Prof. Harald Haas (University of Edinburgh) at TED Global in 2011. LEDs are switched on and off at extremely high rates, which is imperceptible to the human eye, and a photodiode receiver decodes the signal. The IEEE 802.15.7 standard covers short-range optical wireless communication, and IEEE 802.11bb covers Li-Fi. The firm pureLiFi, a spin-off from Edinburgh, commercialised it. Trials were run in Tallinn, Estonia, in 2015 for offices and industrial areas, and India has also conducted pilot tests.

2 — Correct: Li-Fi is wireless and is several times faster than Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi relies on radio waves (IEEE 802.11, 2.4/5/6 GHz), while Li-Fi exploits the visible spectrum, which is far larger and uncongested. Laboratory tests have reached about 224 Gbps, and some field trials showed about 1 Gbps, which is up to roughly 100 times faster than average Wi-Fi. It is also more secure, because light cannot pass through walls, and it does not cause radio interference, so it suits hospitals, aircraft and underwater use. Its drawbacks are limited range, the need for line of sight, and dependence on a light source.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Li-Fi (Light Fidelity) is a wireless technology that transmits data through visible light (LED illumination) and can reach speeds that are many times faster than Wi-Fi in lab and field tests.
topic_notes: Li-Fi (Light Fidelity) is a wireless communication technology that uses light, typically LED lamps, to carry data. It is a form of Visible Light Communication (VLC) under the broader Optical Wireless Communication (OWC) group. Prof. Harald Haas (University of Edinburgh) introduced the idea publicly in 2011 and co-founded pureLiFi. Standards: IEEE 802.15.7 (VLC) and IEEE 802.11bb (Li-Fi, light communications). How it works: the LED's brightness is varied at very high speed, creating binary signals (on is 1, off is 0) that the eye cannot perceive, and a photodetector decodes them. The visible spectrum (about 380-780 nm, 400-800 THz) offers a bandwidth about 10,000 times larger than the radio spectrum used by Wi-Fi. Lab speeds above 200 Gbps have been shown. Advantages: very high speed, no radio interference (useful in aircraft, hospitals, nuclear and mining sites), better security since light does not pass through walls, and reuse of existing lighting infrastructure. Limitations: short range, line-of-sight needs, it does not work in the dark unless the light is dimmed but kept on, and interference from sunlight or other lights. Trials: Estonia (2013-15, Velmenni), and in India the IIT Madras and some pilot projects, as well as the Telecom authorities' interest. Comparisons: Wi-Fi uses radio waves (2.4, 5, 6 GHz); Bluetooth uses 2.4 GHz; NFC works at 13.56 MHz over a few centimetres; WiMAX is an IEEE 802.16 wide-area wireless standard; fibre optics is guided light. Other angles UPSC could ask: 5G and its spectrum bands, the Internet of Things, Wi-Fi versus Li-Fi, optical fibre, BharatNet, and satellite internet.

question: The term ‘Intended Nationally Determined Contributions’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of
options: pledges made by the European countries to rehabilitate refugees from the war-affected Middle East
plan of action outlined by the countries of the world to combat climate change
capital contributed by the member countries in the establishment of Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
plan of action outlined by the countries of .the world regarding Sustainable Development Goals
subject: Economy
detail: INDCs were introduced by the Warsaw COP19 (2013), which invited Parties to prepare and communicate their intended post-2020 climate contributions before COP21 in Paris (December 2015). They are 'intended' because they were pre-agreement proposals; once a country ratifies the Paris Agreement (adopted 12 December 2015, in force 4 November 2016), its INDC becomes its first Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under Article 4. They are nationally determined, so they are bottom-up and not legally binding in target, unlike Kyoto Protocol targets, which were top-down for Annex I countries. India submitted its INDC on 2 October 2015, with three headline goals for 2030: reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 33-35% from 2005 levels, achieve about 40% cumulative electric power capacity from non-fossil sources, and create an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forests and tree cover. Elimination: refugee pledges, AIIB capital subscriptions and the SDGs (2030 Agenda, 17 goals, adopted September 2015) are unrelated to the INDC mechanism, which sits wholly within the UNFCCC process.
explanations: Incorrect: refugee rehabilitation pledges by European states relate to the migration crisis and have nothing to do with INDCs, which are a UNFCCC mechanism.
Correct: INDCs are the national plans of action, submitted by countries before COP21 Paris, to cut emissions and build climate resilience.
Incorrect: AIIB capital is subscribed by members under its Articles of Agreement, not through INDCs; the term 'contribution' here refers to emission actions, not money.
Incorrect: SDGs are a separate UN framework (2030 Agenda, 17 goals); INDCs concern climate action, which only overlaps with SDG 13.
keyfact: INDCs = countries' pre-Paris (COP21, 2015) voluntary national climate action pledges under the UNFCCC; they became NDCs on ratification.
option_notes: European refugee pledges: the 2015 influx from war-hit Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan prompted EU relocation quotas, the Dublin Regulation debates and the EU-Turkey deal of March 2016. Germany under Merkel accepted over a million asylum seekers. These are governed by EU asylum law and the 1951 Refugee Convention, not by climate processes.

Climate action plans: INDCs, now NDCs, are national pledges under the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, covering mitigation and optionally adaptation, finance and technology. Over 160 INDCs covering about 190 countries were submitted by COP21. NDCs are to be updated every five years, with progress reviewed through the global stocktake.

AIIB: the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, proposed by China in 2013, was launched with its Articles signed in 2015 and began operating in January 2016, headquartered in Beijing. Authorised capital is $100 billion. China is the largest shareholder, India the second largest. Its first president was Jin Liqun.

Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals with 169 targets adopted by the UN General Assembly in September 2015 as the 2030 Agenda, replacing the MDGs (2000-2015). SDG 13 is climate action. India's NITI Aayog publishes the SDG India Index. The SDGs are not delivered through INDCs.
related: INDC became NDC once a country ratified the Paris Agreement.
Paris Agreement: adopted 12 Dec 2015, in force 4 Nov 2016; Article 4 covers NDCs.
India's INDC (2 Oct 2015): 33-35% emissions intensity cut by 2030 from 2005 levels.
Warsaw COP19 (2013) introduced the concept of INDCs.
Kyoto Protocol had binding targets only for developed (Annex I) countries; Paris is universal.
International Solar Alliance was launched at COP21 by India and France.
India's net-zero target year is 2070, announced at COP26 Glasgow.
Green Climate Fund is headquartered in Songdo, South Korea.
summary: The answer is (b). Intended Nationally Determined Contributions (INDCs) are the climate action plans that countries submitted ahead of the 2015 Paris Conference (COP21) under the UNFCCC, stating how they would curb greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to climate change.
topic_notes: Climate change governance runs through the UNFCCC, adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and in force from 1994, with its secretariat in Bonn. The COP is its supreme body. The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set binding targets for developed countries on the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR); its Doha Amendment extended it to 2020. The Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015) aims to hold the global temperature rise well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts for 1.5°C. It moved to a universal, bottom-up model in which every country submits NDCs. Key features include a five-year ratchet cycle, the global stocktake (first concluded at COP28 Dubai, 2023), transparency framework, and the $100 billion a year climate finance goal for developing nations. The Green Climate Fund (headquartered in Songdo, South Korea) and Loss and Damage fund (agreed at COP27 Sharm el-Sheikh) are related finance mechanisms. India's updated NDC (2022) raised its targets to a 45% reduction in emissions intensity by 2030 from 2005 levels and 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030, and India announced a net-zero target for 2070 at COP26 Glasgow along with the Panchamrit commitments. India's initiatives include the International Solar Alliance (launched with France at COP21), the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008, eight missions) and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure. UPSC may ask about the differences between INDC and NDC, Kyoto and Paris, or the roles of the IPCC and the UNEP Emissions Gap Report.

ocr: Which one of the following is a purpose of ‘UDAY’, a scheme of the Government? fa) Providing technical and financial assistance to. start-up entre- preneurs in the field of renewable sources of energy fb) Providing electricity to every houschold in the country by 2018 (c) Replacing the coal-based power plants with natural gas, nuclear, solar, wind and tidal power plants over a period of time {d) Providing for financial turnaround and revival of power distribution companies
subject: Science & Tech
detail: UDAY was launched by the Ministry of Power in November 2015 as an optional scheme for states to rescue loss-making state-owned DISCOMs, whose accumulated debt was about Rs 4.3 lakh crore. Under it, states take over 75% of DISCOM debt over two years (50% in 2015-16 and 25% in 2016-17). The states issue non-SLR bonds, and the DISCOMs issue bonds for the remaining debt. The state also bears future losses of the DISCOMs in a graded manner. The operational targets are: reducing AT&C (aggregate technical and commercial) losses to 15% by 2019 (it was around 22%), closing the ACS-ARR gap (average cost of supply minus average revenue realised) by 2019, universal smart metering, feeder metering, and distribution transformer metering, and promoting energy efficiency such as LED bulbs. Elimination logic: (a) describes the start-up and renewable energy support idea, which is not a UDAY feature. (b) matches 'Power for All' / 24x7 power, and the electrification schemes DDUGJY and Saubhagya. (c) is a coal phase-out policy, which UDAY does not contain. Only (d) deals with DISCOM finances, so it is correct. The key words to remember are 'Ujwal DISCOM' and 'debt restructuring'.
explanations: Wrong: Support for renewable start-up entrepreneurs is not part of UDAY. UDAY deals with DISCOM finances, not with start-up assistance.
Wrong: Electricity to every household is the aim of 'Power for All' and of electrification schemes like DDUGJY and Saubhagya. UDAY is not an electrification scheme.
Wrong: UDAY does not replace coal plants with gas, nuclear or renewable plants. Coal remains the mainstay of Indian power, and UDAY has no phase-out agenda.
Correct: UDAY provides for the financial turnaround and revival of state power distribution companies through debt takeover by states, bond issuance, and operational reforms.
keyfact: UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, 2015) = financial turnaround of state power distribution companies, with states taking over 75% of DISCOM debt.
option_notes: Support for renewable energy start-ups is associated with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and with schemes and bodies such as IREDA (financing), the National Solar Mission (2010, under which India set a target of 100 GW of solar by 2022) and the Start-up India initiative (2016). MNRE also runs incubation and innovation programmes. None of these is UDAY, which concerns DISCOM finances and not entrepreneurship.

'Power for All' (24x7 power) is a joint initiative of the Centre and states, begun in 2014-15 with the aim of supplying uninterrupted power to all households, industry and commerce. Related schemes: DDUGJY (Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana, 2014, rural feeder separation and electrification) and Saubhagya (2017, last-mile household connections). Electrification of villages was declared complete in April 2018. These are supply and access schemes, not DISCOM bailouts.

India's power mix is still dominated by coal, which supplies roughly 70% of electricity generation. Policy directions are the International Solar Alliance (2015), the target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, the National Solar Mission, and the 2070 net-zero pledge. India has not announced a complete replacement of coal plants. Coal plants are retired selectively on grounds of age and emissions norms, and no UDAY provision covers this.

UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana) is a Ministry of Power scheme, launched in November 2015 and opted into by most states (Jharkhand was the first state to join). Its objectives are to improve DISCOM operational and financial efficiency, reduce the cost of power, and cut interest costs through state takeover of debt. It was a successor to the 2012 Financial Restructuring Plan (FRP) for DISCOMs. Later schemes include the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (2021), which offers results-linked, reform-based assistance.
related: UDAY stands for Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, launched in November 2015 by the Ministry of Power.
Under UDAY, states take over 75% of DISCOM debt, over two years.
The UDAY target was to reduce AT&C losses to 15% by 2019.
UJALA (2015) distributes LED bulbs, implemented by EESL.
Saubhagya (2017) provides last-mile household electricity connections.
DDUGJY (2014) focused on rural feeder separation and village electrification.
The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) was launched in 2021 to improve DISCOM finances.
The Electricity Act 2003 is the main law governing the power sector, including open access and regulators.
summary: The answer is (d). UDAY (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana), launched in November 2015, is meant for the financial turnaround and revival of state-owned power distribution companies (DISCOMs). It does this by having states take over most of the DISCOM debt and by requiring operational improvements.
topic_notes: India's power sector has three segments: generation, transmission and distribution. Distribution is the weakest, because state-owned DISCOMs have long suffered from high AT&C losses, tariffs below cost, subsidised or free power to farmers, theft, and poor billing and collection. By 2015 they had accumulated debt of about Rs 4.3 lakh crore. An earlier rescue, the 2012 Financial Restructuring Plan, failed to solve the problem. UDAY, launched in November 2015, was the next attempt. Its four main elements: (1) improving operational efficiency through smart meters, feeder and transformer metering, and cutting AT&C losses to 15%; (2) reducing the cost of power through coal linkage rationalisation, higher coal washing, and LED and other energy-efficiency measures; (3) reducing interest costs, with states taking over 75% of DISCOM debt and issuing bonds; (4) enforcing financial discipline through regular tariff revisions and quarterly reporting. Participation is voluntary for states, and the scheme is run through MoUs between the Centre, the state and the DISCOM. Other power reforms include the Electricity Act 2003 (delicensing of generation, open access, regulatory commissions), the Ujala scheme (LED distribution by EESL, 2015), Saubhagya (2017), DDUGJY (2014), Integrated Power Development Scheme (IPDS, 2014, urban distribution), and the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS, 2021). Regulatory bodies: CERC (central regulator), SERCs (state regulators), CEA, PFC and REC (financiers), and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency. UPSC often asks the objectives of schemes by name, so remember the expansion of each acronym and the ministry in charge.

ocr: With reference to ‘IFC Masala Bonds’, * sometimes seen in the news, which of the statements given below is/are correct?’ ~~ 1. The International Finance Corpora- tion, which offers these bonds, is an arm of the World Bank. 2. They are the rupee-denominated bonds and are a source of debt financing for the public and private sector. B-APM-P-CKB/65A Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only {b) 2 only (fc) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: Masala Bonds are bonds issued by Indian entities in overseas markets but denominated in Indian rupees, not in foreign currency. Because investors, not the issuer, bear the currency risk, the issuer is shielded from rupee depreciation. The term 'Masala' was coined by the IFC to evoke Indian culture. The IFC issued the first Masala Bond in November 2014, raising Rs 1,000 crore for infrastructure projects. In July 2016, the IFC issued a Rs 1,000 crore green Masala Bond listed on the London Stock Exchange. In August 2016, NTPC issued the first Masala green bond by an Indian corporate. HDFC was among the early large issuers. The IFC, founded in 1956, is a member of the World Bank Group and focuses on private-sector development in developing countries. Elimination logic: statement 1 is true because the IFC is a World Bank Group institution, so (b) and (d) fall. Statement 2 is true because Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated and are used by both public and private bodies, so (a) falls. The answer is (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct. Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated and finance public and private sector entities.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct. The IFC is a World Bank Group institution.
(c) is right because both statements are correct: the IFC is part of the World Bank Group and Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated debt instruments.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so it cannot be 'neither'.
keyfact: Masala Bonds: rupee-denominated, issued overseas, investor bears currency risk; first issued by the IFC (World Bank Group) in 2014.
option_notes: Option (a), 'Statement 1 only': this would hold only if Masala Bonds were not rupee-denominated. The IFC, founded in 1956, is the World Bank Group's private-sector arm. Its membership is over 180 countries. It provides loans, equity, guarantees and advisory services. It first issued Masala Bonds in 2014 to raise rupee funds for Indian infrastructure, and in 2016 it issued a green Masala Bond.

Option (b), 'Statement 2 only': this would hold only if the IFC were not part of the World Bank Group. Statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is also correct. Masala Bonds are issued offshore but denominated in rupees. The investor bears the exchange-rate risk, which reduces the issuer's currency exposure. The RBI regulates them under the ECB framework.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2': this is the official answer. The IFC is a World Bank Group member and Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas. They are used by public and private entities to raise debt. Examples are the IFC's 2014 issue, NTPC's 2016 green Masala Bond and the HDFC issue. The RBI treats them as rupee-denominated ECB.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2': this would require both statements to be false, which is not the case. The IFC belongs to the World Bank Group and Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated. This option is a typical distractor for students who confuse Masala Bonds with foreign-currency bonds such as Eurobonds or Dollar bonds.
related: Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India.
The IFC issued the first Masala Bond in November 2014.
NTPC issued the first corporate green Masala Bond in 2016.
In Masala Bonds the investor bears the currency risk.
The IFC was set up in 1956 and is the World Bank Group's private-sector arm.
Panda Bonds are yuan-denominated bonds issued in China.
Samurai Bonds are yen-denominated bonds issued in Japan.
Masala Bonds are regulated by the RBI under the ECB framework.
statements: 1 — Correct: The IFC, which offers these bonds, is part of the World Bank Group, so it is correctly described as an arm of the World Bank. The IFC was established in 1956 and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. It is the largest global development institution focused on the private sector in developing countries. It lends, invests in equity, mobilises resources and gives advisory services. The World Bank Group also includes IBRD, IDA, MIGA and ICSID. The IFC issued the first Masala Bond in November 2014 (Rs 1,000 crore) to fund Indian infrastructure projects.

2 — Correct: Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India, so they work as a source of debt finance for public and private sector borrowers. The currency risk lies with the investor, not the issuer. The IFC issued the first one in 2014, and NTPC issued the first green Masala Bond in 2016, listed in London. Other issuers include HDFC and NHAI, which raised funds through such bonds. RBI regulates Masala Bonds under the ECB framework, which has set minimum maturity rules. In 2016 the RBI also eased the tax and withholding provisions for them.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) is the private-sector lending arm of the World Bank Group, and Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India that raise debt finance for Indian public and private sector entities.
topic_notes: Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities in overseas capital markets. The name was coined by the IFC to link the instrument to Indian culture. Because they are denominated in rupees, investors bear the currency risk, not the Indian borrower. The IFC issued the first Masala Bond in November 2014, raising Rs 1,000 crore for infrastructure. In 2016 it issued a green Masala Bond listed on the London Stock Exchange. NTPC issued the first corporate green Masala Bond in 2016. HDFC was an early large issuer. They count as a form of External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and are regulated by the RBI under the ECB framework. The RBI has revised the rules several times, with changes in minimum maturity, eligible borrowers and end-use restrictions. In 2019 the government exempted interest on Masala Bonds issued between 2017 and 2019 from withholding tax. The IFC is a member of the World Bank Group, which comprises IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. The IFC was set up in 1956 and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. Other angles UPSC could ask: Dollar-denominated ECBs, Eurobonds, Green bonds, Sovereign Gold Bonds, Panda Bonds (yuan-denominated, issued in China), Samurai Bonds (yen-denominated, issued in Japan), Yankee Bonds (dollar-denominated, issued in the US), Formosa Bonds (Taiwan), and Kangaroo Bonds (Australia). Also relevant: the difference between FDI, FPI and ECB, as well as the role of the RBI and FEMA in regulating foreign borrowing.

question:
Regarding the taxation system of Krishna Deva, the ruler of Vijayanagar, consider the following statements :
1. The tax rate on land was fixed depending on the quality of the land.
2. Private owners of workshops paid an industries tax. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? :
subject: Economy
detail: Vijayanagara revenue administration, as described by foreign travellers (Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz) and by inscriptions, rested mainly on land revenue (called sist or sishtu), which was usually between one-sixth and one-third of produce, varying with the fertility and type of land. Land was classified as wet land (irrigated by tanks, canals, wells), dry land, and garden or orchard land, and the rates differed. Besides land revenue there were many other levies: the Amarnayaka-related dues, customs and port duties (the empire was active in maritime trade with Portuguese, Arabs and others), professional taxes, taxes on marriages, and taxes on artisans such as weavers, potters, oil-pressers, goldsmiths and others. Krishnadevaraya's Telugu work Amuktamalyada discusses statecraft and taxation. Elimination logic: since the official key is (c), and both statements match the standard textbook account of Vijayanagara taxation (land assessed by quality; industries and workshops taxed), options (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out. Remember that Vijayanagara was a revenue-rich state, with Nayankara system tying military chiefs to land revenue assignments.
explanations: Incorrect: it ignores statement 2, which is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
Incorrect: it ignores statement 1, which is also true, since land tax depended on land quality.
Correct: both the quality-based land tax and the industries tax on private workshop owners are recorded features of Krishnadevaraya's taxation.
Incorrect: since both statements are valid, 'neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: Under Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara, land tax varied with soil quality and workshop owners paid an industries tax, so both statements are correct.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would apply if only land revenue were graded by quality. Vijayanagara did grade land (wet, dry, garden) and charged different rates, but this option wrongly excludes the industrial taxes. Land revenue (sist) was the principal income, generally one-sixth to one-third of produce, collected in cash or kind. Remember it as only a part of the full tax structure.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' would apply if only workshops were taxed. Artisans and workshop owners did pay occupational and industrial taxes, including on looms, but the state also graded land by quality. Vijayanagara's non-agricultural taxes covered crafts, markets, customs, marriage fees and professions. This option is wrong because it denies the land-quality principle.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is the official answer. Under Krishnadevaraya, land was assessed by fertility and irrigation, and craftsmen and workshop owners paid industry-related taxes. The empire's revenue system combined land revenue, customs, professional taxes and special levies, supporting the large army and temple endowments. Nuniz and Paes describe the wealth of the empire, and the Amuktamalyada addresses governance.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' would be correct only if Vijayanagara had a flat land tax and exempted industry. Both are contradicted by evidence: rates varied with the quality of land, and craft production was taxed. The state was highly commercialised, with active ports and guilds, so exempting industry would be historically inaccurate.
related: Krishnadevaraya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty and ruled 1509-1529.
His Telugu work Amuktamalyada deals with polity and statecraft.
Battle of Talikota (1565) ended Vijayanagara's power.
Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz were Portuguese visitors to Vijayanagara.
Nayankara system tied military chiefs to land revenue assignments.
Abdur Razzaq visited during Deva Raya II's reign.
Vijayanagara's gold coin was the varaha, also called hun or pagoda.
Krishnadevaraya's court poets were known as the Ashtadiggajas.
statements: 1 — Correct: Land tax rates varied with soil quality and productivity. Vijayanagara surveyed and classified land into wet, dry and orchard types, and the state's share (commonly one-sixth of produce, sometimes more) varied with fertility and irrigation. Revenue was collected in cash and kind. The land revenue was known as sist or sishtu. Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva dynasty, 1509-1529) improved irrigation by building tanks and canals, such as those near Hampi and the Basavanna canal, which increased the revenue base. Village officials (karanams, the accountants) maintained records, and the Athavane department handled revenue administration.

2 — Correct: Owners of private workshops and artisans paid an industries tax. The Vijayanagara state levied taxes on crafts and manufactures, including on weavers, potters, smiths, oil-mongers, leather workers and others, as well as on professions and trade. Inscriptions mention dues such as the loom tax and other occupational levies. Trade guilds like the Manigramam and Nanadesis operated, and the empire earned much from ports like Bhatkal, Mangalore and Calicut-linked trade. Temples also received donations from guilds and shared in revenues. These non-agricultural taxes supplemented land revenue and funded a large standing army.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Under Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509-1529) of Vijayanagara, land revenue was assessed according to soil quality and productivity, and artisans and owners of workshops paid a separate tax on industries and crafts.
topic_notes: Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty, with Hampi as the capital on the Tungabhadra. Dynasties in order: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu. Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva, 1509-1529) was its greatest ruler. He won against Orissa's Gajapatis, the Bahmani successors, and the Adil Shah of Bijapur (Raichur, 1520). He wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu (and a Sanskrit work, Jambavati Kalyanam, is attributed to him), and was called Andhra Bhoja. His court had the Ashtadiggajas (eight poets), including Allasani Peddana. He built the Vithala and Hazara Rama temples and the town Nagalapuram. Foreign visitors: Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese), Abdur Razzaq (Persian, under Deva Raya II), Nicolo de Conti, and Duarte Barbosa. Administration: the empire was divided into rajyas, mandalams, nadus, sthalas and gramas. The Nayankara system gave military chiefs (nayakas) land assignments (amaram) in return for troops. Ayagar system governed villages with twelve hereditary village officials. Revenue: land revenue (sist), plus taxes on professions, marriages, customs, and others. Land was classified as wet, dry, and orchard. Currency: gold varaha (pagoda or hun), pratapa, and fanam. The empire fell after the Battle of Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when the Deccan sultanates defeated Aliya Rama Raya. Architecture: Vijayanagara style with large gopurams, and carved pillared halls (kalyana mandapas), and the Vittala temple's stone chariot. Related later questions can ask about the Nayaka successor states (Madurai, Thanjavur, Gingee), and the Portuguese relations under Albuquerque in Goa.

ocr: Which one of the following books of ancient India has the love story of the son of the founder of Sunga dynasty? {a) -Swapnavasavadatta (b) Malavikagnimitra {c) Meghadoota {ad} Ratnavali
subject: Ancient History
detail: The Sunga dynasty (c. 185-73 BCE) was founded by Pushyamitra Sunga, the commander-in-chief of the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha, whom he assassinated. His son Agnimitra ruled as viceroy at Vidisha. Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitram (Malavika and Agnimitra) is a five-act Sanskrit romantic drama about Agnimitra's love for Malavika, a maidservant who is actually a princess in exile. The queens Dharini and Iravati are rivals in the plot. The play also offers historical glimpses: Pushyamitra's Ashvamedha sacrifice, the conflict with Vidarbha, and the Greek (Yavana) clash on the Sindhu river, which his grandson Vasumitra won. Elimination logic: Swapnavasavadatta is by Bhasa and concerns King Udayana of Vatsa and Vasavadatta. Meghaduta is a lyrical poem by Kalidasa about a Yaksha sending a message through a cloud, and it has no Sunga link. Ratnavali is a drama by Harsha (Harshavardhana) about Udayana and Ratnavali. So only (b) matches the Sunga connection. Remember that Kalidasa is traditionally linked with the Gupta period, but this play deals with the earlier Sunga king.
explanations: Wrong: Swapnavasavadatta is by Bhasa. It is about Udayana of Vatsa and Vasavadatta, with no Sunga connection.
Correct: Malavikagnimitram by Kalidasa tells the love story of Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra Sunga (founder of the Sunga dynasty), and Malavika.
Wrong: Meghaduta is Kalidasa's lyrical poem in which an exiled Yaksha sends a message to his wife through a cloud. It is not a love story of a Sunga prince.
Wrong: Ratnavali is a Sanskrit play by Harsha, about King Udayana and Princess Ratnavali of Sri Lanka. It has no Sunga link.
keyfact: Malavikagnimitram (Kalidasa) = love story of Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra Sunga, and Malavika.
option_notes: Swapnavasavadatta is a Sanskrit play attributed to Bhasa, one of the earliest known Sanskrit dramatists, who is placed before Kalidasa. It is the best known of the 13 Trivandrum plays discovered by T. Ganapati Sastri in 1912. It is about King Udayana of Vatsa, his queen Vasavadatta, and his marriage to Padmavati, arranged by the minister Yaugandharayana. The title refers to a dream in which Udayana sees Vasavadatta.

Malavikagnimitram is a five-act Sanskrit play by Kalidasa, thought to be his first drama. Its hero is the historical Sunga king Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra Sunga, who falls in love with Malavika, a princess who has been in disguise as a servant. The queens Dharini and Iravati are rivals in the plot. The play contains references to Sunga history, including the Ashvamedha sacrifice and war against Vidarbha.

Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger) is a lyrical poem in Sanskrit by Kalidasa, in two parts (Purvamegha and Uttaramegha) and about 111 verses, written in the Mandakranta metre. A Yaksha is exiled by Kubera to Ramagiri and asks a cloud to carry his message of love to his wife in Alaka on Mount Kailash. It describes the geography of India along the route, including Ujjain and Vidisha.

Ratnavali is a Sanskrit drama (natika) in four acts attributed to Harsha (Harshavardhana, 7th century CE) and is a court comedy. It is about King Udayana of Vatsa and Sagarika, who is actually Ratnavali, princess of Simhala (Sri Lanka). Queen Vasavadatta is the jealous wife. Harsha also wrote Priyadarshika and Nagananda. It reflects the courtly romance of the early 7th century.
related: Pushyamitra Sunga founded the Sunga dynasty after killing Brihadratha, the last Maurya, c. 185 BCE.
Kalidasa's three plays: Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam, Abhijnanashakuntalam.
Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha) was erected by a Greek ambassador and is dedicated to Vasudeva.
Patanjali, author of the Mahabhashya, was a contemporary of Pushyamitra Sunga.
Last Sunga king Devabhuti was overthrown by Vasudeva Kanva, founder of the Kanva dynasty.
Bhasa wrote Swapnavasavadatta and Pratijnayaugandharayana.
Harsha wrote Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.
Bharhut stupa railings and Sanchi stupa expansion belong to the Sunga period.
summary: The answer is (b) Malavikagnimitra, a Sanskrit play by Kalidasa. It narrates the love story of Malavika and King Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra Sunga, who founded the Sunga dynasty.
topic_notes: The Sungas succeeded the Mauryas around 185 BCE when Pushyamitra Sunga, a Brahmin general, killed Brihadratha. The capital was Pataliputra, with Vidisha as a prominent centre. Agnimitra, his son, was viceroy at Vidisha. Sources: Malavikagnimitram, Patanjali's Mahabhashya (Patanjali was a contemporary and reportedly officiated at Pushyamitra's sacrifices), the Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva, the Puranas, and Buddhist works such as the Divyavadana. Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices. He is traditionally described as hostile to Buddhism, though the Bharhut stupa and the expansion of Sanchi stupa happened in the Sunga period. The dynasty fought the Indo-Greeks (Menander is associated with this era) and Kharavela of Kalinga. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha) is a Garuda pillar erected by the Greek ambassador Heliodorus in the reign of Bhagabhadra, showing Bhagavatism. The last Sunga ruler, Devabhuti, was killed by his minister Vasudeva Kanva about 73 BCE, which began the Kanva dynasty. Art: Bharhut, Sanchi (stupa 2) and Bodh Gaya railings. Literature and language: Sanskrit revived, and Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya. Manusmriti is often dated to this period. Other Sanskrit dramatists to know: Bhasa, Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram), Shudraka (Mrichchhakatika), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa, Devichandraguptam), Bhavabhuti (Mahaviracharita, Malatimadhava), and Harsha (Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda).

ocr: In the context of which of the following —______——do—you--sometimes—find the. terms ‘amber box, blue box and green box’ in the news? fa} WTO affairs (b) SAARC affairs {c} UNFCCC affairs {d) India-EU negotiations on FTA
subject: Economy
detail: The WTO Agreement on Agriculture (Uruguay Round, 1994, in force from 1 January 1995) classifies domestic support by its trade-distorting effect, using traffic-light colours. Amber box covers trade-distorting support linked to production or prices, such as Market Price Support, input subsidies and fertiliser or power subsidies. It is subject to reduction commitments and de minimis limits: 5% of the value of production for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.
