Blue box covers amber-type support that is tied to production-limiting programmes, such as direct payments under acreage or headage limits, and has no spending cap. Green box covers minimally or non-trade-distorting support (Annex 2 of the AoA), such as research, extension, pest control, infrastructure, environmental programmes, decoupled income support and public stockholding for food security, and it is uncapped. India's MSP-based procurement is counted as amber support, which is the source of disputes over the Bali (2013) 'Peace Clause' and public stockholding. Elimination logic: SAARC, UNFCCC and FTA talks do not use this colour-coded subsidy vocabulary, so (a) is the only fit.
explanations: Correct. Amber, blue and green boxes are WTO Agreement on Agriculture categories of domestic farm subsidies, so they appear in news on WTO affairs.
Incorrect. SAARC deals with South Asian regional cooperation, such as SAFTA, SAARC Development Fund and the South Asian University. It has no subsidy 'boxes'.
Incorrect. UNFCCC news deals with climate terms such as COP, NDCs, the Green Climate Fund and Kyoto. Its 'green' term is the Green Climate Fund, not a green box.

Incorrect. India-EU FTA talks (the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement, BTIA) involve market access, tariffs, IPR and data security. They do not use the box classification, which belongs to the WTO.
keyfact: Amber, blue and green boxes are WTO Agreement on Agriculture categories of domestic farm subsidies: amber is trade-distorting, blue is production-limiting, and green is non-distorting.
option_notes: The WTO was established on 1 January 1995, succeeding GATT (1947), and is headquartered in Geneva. It has 164 members (as of 2023). Its Ministerial Conference is the highest decision-making body. Its core agreements are GATT, GATS, TRIPS and the AoA. It runs a Dispute Settlement Body with an Appellate Body, which has been non-functional since December 2019 because of the US blocking appointments. Decisions are taken by consensus. Key rounds: Doha (2001), Bali (2013), Nairobi (2015).

SAARC was founded in 1985 in Dhaka and has its secretariat in Kathmandu. It has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. SAFTA came into force in 2006. The South Asian University is in New Delhi. The last summit was held in Kathmandu in 2014 (18th), and the 2016 Islamabad summit was postponed after India and others withdrew. The body is largely dormant, and India now favours BIMSTEC.

The UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1994. Its secretariat is in Bonn. Its supreme body is the Conference of the Parties (COP). Key outcomes are the Kyoto Protocol (1997), the Paris Agreement (2015), and principles such as Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR). Related funds include the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund. COP28 was held in Dubai in 2023.

India-EU FTA talks, formally the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement (BTIA), began in 2007 and stalled in 2013 over differences on auto and wine tariffs, services and data-security status. Talks resumed in June 2022. The EU is one of India's largest trading partners. The EU also has a Trade and Technology Council with India, set up in 2022. India signed an FTA with EFTA in 2024. Related issues include CBAM, the EU carbon border tax.
related: Amber box: trade-distorting subsidies subject to reduction commitments, such as MSP and input subsidies.
Blue box: subsidies tied to production-limiting programmes, uncapped.
Green box: non-trade-distorting subsidies in Annex 2 of the AoA, uncapped.
De minimis limits: 5% of production value for developed countries and 10% for developing ones.
The Bali Ministerial (2013) produced the Peace Clause on public stockholding and the Trade Facilitation Agreement.
The Nairobi Ministerial (2015) decided to abolish agricultural export subsidies.
The WTO Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019.
India leads the G-33 on the Special Safeguard Mechanism and food security.
summary: The answer is (a) WTO affairs. 'Amber box, blue box and green box' are the categories of domestic agricultural subsidies under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture (AoA), classified by how much they distort trade. They come up in news around WTO negotiations on farm subsidies, public stockholding and the Doha Round.
topic_notes: The WTO Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) rests on three pillars: market access (converting non-tariff barriers into tariffs, called tariffication), domestic support, and export competition (export subsidies). Domestic support is classified by colour. Amber box: Aggregate Measurement of Support (AMS), including market price support, which is measured against an external reference price fixed in 1986-88. De minimis exemption: 5% for developed and 10% for developing countries of the value of production. Blue box: payments under production-limiting programmes, with no limit. Green box: Annex 2 measures with no or minimal trade distortion, such as direct income support decoupled from production, government services, food-security stockholding and disaster relief. Special and Differential Treatment (Article 6.2) exempts developing-country investment and input subsidies. Disputes over India: MSP for wheat and rice is calculated using the 1986-88 reference price, which makes India's AMS appear high; India has invoked the Peace Clause (Bali, 2013, confirmed at Nairobi 2015) to shield public stockholding programmes from legal challenge until a permanent solution is reached. The Nairobi Ministerial (2015) decided to eliminate agricultural export subsidies. Other concepts: Special Safeguard Mechanism (SSM) for developing countries to counter import surges, the G-33 grouping led by India and Indonesia, the Cairns Group of agricultural exporters, and the G-20 (developing countries) in agriculture. The Doha Development Round (2001) remains deadlocked over agriculture. UPSC could next ask about MSP and the National Food Security Act, the Peace Clause, the Nairobi decisions, GATT vs WTO, TRIPS or the Trade Facilitation Agreement (2017).

ocr: Which of the following is/are included in the capital budget of the Government of India? 1. Expenditure on acquisition of - assets like roads, buildings, machinery, etc. 2. Loans received from foreign — governments 3. Loans and advances granted to the States and Union Territorics Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (a) 1,2 and 3
subject: Economy
detail: The Union Budget, under Article 112 (Annual Financial Statement), is split into the Revenue Budget and the Capital Budget. The Revenue Budget covers revenue receipts (tax and non-tax) and revenue expenditure, which does not create assets or reduce liabilities (salaries, subsidies, interest payments, grants). The Capital Budget covers capital receipts and capital expenditure. Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset: borrowings (market loans, T-bills, external loans, loans received from foreign governments and institutions), recovery of loans granted, and disinvestment or PSU stake sales. Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities: acquisition of land, buildings, machinery and roads, investments in shares, loans and advances to States, UTs, PSUs, and repayment of borrowings. Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus revenue receipts minus non-debt capital receipts, so it is essentially the borrowing requirement. Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly capital expenditure, so (b) falls. Statement 2 is a borrowing, which is a capital receipt, so (a) and (c) fall. Statement 3 is a capital disbursement, so (d) is the only option that includes all three. Grants to States for creating assets are still treated as revenue expenditure, but loans are capital.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes only statement 1, but statements 2 and 3 are also capital budget items.
(b) is wrong because it omits statement 1, which is clearly capital expenditure on asset creation.
(c) is wrong because it omits statement 2; loans received from foreign governments are capital receipts as they create liabilities.
(d) is correct because asset acquisition, loans received (a liability-creating capital receipt) and loans granted to States and UTs (a capital disbursement) all belong to the Capital Budget.
keyfact: Capital Budget = capital receipts (borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment) + capital expenditure (asset creation, loans and advances, debt repayment); anything that changes assets or liabilities is capital.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would limit the capital budget to expenditure on asset creation. Capital expenditure does cover land, buildings, roads, machinery, defence equipment and investments, and it creates assets. But the Capital Budget has two sides: capital receipts (borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment) and capital expenditure (asset creation, loans and advances, repayment of debt). Treating only asset-creation as capital ignores the receipts side and loan disbursements.

Option (b) '2 and 3 only' pairs foreign loans received with loans advanced to States and UTs. Both are real capital items: the first is a capital receipt creating a liability and the second is a capital disbursement creating a financial asset. The option fails only by leaving out asset-creating expenditure. Note that interest on those loans is revenue expenditure (interest payments), while interest received on loans given is a non-tax revenue receipt.

Option (c) '1 and 3 only' groups capital expenditure on assets with loans granted to States and UTs, both capital disbursements. It excludes loans received from foreign governments, but borrowings from any source are capital receipts. The common mistake is thinking only expenditure items belong in the capital budget. Capital receipts such as market borrowings, external loans, recoveries of loans and disinvestment proceeds also form part of it.

Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the official answer. It reflects the full scope of the Capital Budget: capital receipts (loans received, including from foreign governments, recoveries, disinvestment) and capital payments (asset creation, loans and advances to States, UTs and PSUs, debt repayment). The test is whether the transaction creates or reduces assets or liabilities. Revenue items, such as taxes, salaries, subsidies and interest, are in the Revenue Budget.
related: Article 112 requires the President to lay the Annual Financial Statement before Parliament each year.
Loans received from foreign governments are capital receipts; interest paid on them is revenue expenditure.
Disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts, as they reduce government assets.
Recovery of loans given earlier is a capital receipt.
Grants to States are revenue expenditure even when used to create assets.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
The Railway Budget was merged with the General Budget from 2017-18.
statements: 1 — Correct: Expenditure on acquiring assets such as roads, buildings and machinery is capital expenditure because it creates durable assets. Capital expenditure is shown in the Capital Budget and also includes investments in shares, defence equipment and infrastructure. It is distinguished from revenue expenditure, which is recurring and consumed within the year (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies). The government has sharply raised capital expenditure (capex) since 2020-21, with the Union Budget capex outlay rising to over Rs 10 lakh crore in recent years, to boost growth through the multiplier effect. A related concept is 'effective capital expenditure', which includes grants-in-aid given to States for creating capital assets.

2 — Correct: Loans received from foreign governments are borrowings, so they create a liability and are capital receipts in the Capital Budget. Other external capital receipts include loans from multilateral bodies such as the World Bank, ADB and the IMF, and bilateral aid from countries like Japan (JICA loans for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train). Internal borrowings include dated securities, Treasury Bills, and small savings. Repayment of such loans is capital expenditure. Fiscal deficit is financed by these borrowings, and India's FRBM Act 2003 sets the deficit targets, with the glide path now framed around reducing fiscal deficit to 4.5% of GDP by 2025-26.

3 — Correct: Loans and advances granted to States and Union Territories are capital disbursements because they create a financial asset (a claim on the borrower), and their repayment later appears as a capital receipt (recovery of loans). The Centre also gives loans to PSUs and other bodies. Examples include the 50-year interest-free capital investment loans to States introduced in 2020-21 and Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment. Under Article 293, the Centre may make loans to States, and States need Centre's consent to borrow if a loan to them remains outstanding. Such loans differ from grants-in-aid under Article 275, which are generally revenue expenditure.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. All three items are capital-budget items of the Government of India: spending that creates assets, receipts that create liabilities (loans received), and loans and advances given by the Centre (which are recoveries and disbursements that change assets). The test is whether the transaction changes the government's assets or liabilities.
topic_notes:
The Union Budget (Annual Financial Statement) is mandated by Article 112, presented by the Finance Minister, and passed by Parliament through the Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill. Government accounts are in three parts: the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266(1)), the Contingency Fund (Article 267) and the Public Account (Article 266(2)). The budget is divided into the Revenue Budget and the Capital Budget.

Revenue receipts: tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs, excise) and non-tax revenue (interest receipts, dividends, profits, fees, grants). Revenue expenditure: spending that does not create assets, such as salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest payments, defence revenue expenditure and grants to States (even where used for asset creation).

Capital receipts: borrowings (market loans, T-bills, external loans, small savings, provident funds), recovery of loans, and other receipts such as disinvestment (PSU stake sale). Capital expenditure: acquisition of assets, investments, loans and advances to States, UTs and PSUs, and repayment of debt.

Deficit concepts: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings (i.e., total borrowing requirement). Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. The FRBM Act 2003 (amended 2018 following the N.K. Singh Committee) targets a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP and a debt-to-GDP ratio of 40% for the Centre, though these targets have been deferred.

Other likely angles: the 2017 merger of the Railway Budget with the General Budget; the shift of the budget date to 1 February; the removal of the Plan/Non-Plan classification from 2017-18; Article 113 (votes on demands for grants), Article 114 (appropriation), Article 116 (vote on account); Article 265 (no tax without authority of law); Article 109 (Money Bills); and the Outcome Budget, Gender Budget and zero-based budgeting.

ocr: What is/are the importance/importances of the ‘United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification’? 1. It aims to promote effective action through innovative national programmes and supportive inter- national partnerships. 2. It has a special/particular focus on South Asia and North Africa regions, and its Secretariat facilitates the allocation of major = portion of financial ‘resources to these regions. 3. It is committed to bottom-up approach, encouraging the partici- pation of local people in combating the desertification. Select the correct answer using the code given below, {aj 1 only (b
subject: Economy
detail: The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted in Paris on 17 June 1994 and came into force in December 1996. It is one of the three Rio Conventions, alongside the UNFCCC and the CBD, all arising from the 1992 Earth Summit. It is the only legally binding international agreement linking environment and development to sustainable land management. It addresses desertification, land degradation and drought in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas, collectively called drylands. Its core approach is bottom-up: National Action Programmes (NAPs) are prepared with the participation of local communities, supported by sub-regional and regional programmes and by partnerships between developed and developing countries. Its original focus was on Africa, reflected in the full title 'particularly in Africa', and it has regional annexes for Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Northern Mediterranean, and Central and Eastern Europe. The Secretariat is in Bonn, Germany. The Global Mechanism, hosted by IFAD, helps mobilise resources. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong because the special focus is on Africa and the Secretariat does not allocate money, so options (b) and (d) go. Statement 1 is correct, so option (a), which omits statement 3, is also incomplete. That leaves (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but this option leaves out statement 3, which is also correct.
(b) Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because the focus is on Africa and the Secretariat does not allocate funds, and it leaves out statement 1.
(c) Correct: statements 1 and 3 are accurate, and statement 2 is the only false one.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 2, which wrongly states a special focus on South Asia and North Africa and a Secretariat role in allocating funds.
keyfact: The UNCCD (1994, Secretariat in Bonn) is a bottom-up, participatory treaty with a special focus on Africa, and its action runs through National Action Programmes.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 alone: the UNCCD's objective of promoting effective action through national programmes and international partnerships. It is a legally binding treaty adopted in 1994 and in force since 1996. It deals with desertification, land degradation and drought in drylands. National Action Programmes are its main instrument. The Secretariat is in Bonn, and there are about 197 Parties, including India, which ratified in 1996. The option is incomplete because statement 3 is also true.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3: statement 3 describes a true feature, the bottom-up approach with local participation. Statement 2 is false because the Convention's special focus is on Africa. The Convention has five regional implementation annexes, for Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Northern Mediterranean, and Central and Eastern Europe. Funds are not allocated by the Secretariat; they flow through donor Parties, the Global Mechanism and the GEF.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3: this is the official answer. It reflects the UNCCD's two defining features. The first is action through national programmes and international partnerships. The second is the bottom-up, participatory approach. Together they distinguish the Convention from top-down environmental treaties. Land degradation neutrality (SDG 15.3) is now its central goal. COP14 was held in India in 2019, and the Delhi Declaration was adopted there. The 2022 COP15 was in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire.

Option (d), all three statements: this is wrong because statement 2 is false. The UNCCD has a special focus on Africa, which is why the full title contains 'Particularly in Africa'. It does not single out South Asia and North Africa. Its Secretariat in Bonn provides administrative and technical support, while financing is provided by Parties and by mechanisms such as the GEF. The Global Mechanism is hosted by IFAD in Rome.
related: The UNCCD was adopted in 1994 and entered into force in 1996, and its Secretariat is in Bonn.
The three Rio Conventions are the UNCCD, UNFCCC and CBD.
World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on 17 June.
India hosted UNCCD COP14 in 2019 at Greater Noida.
India's pledge is to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
The Global Mechanism of the UNCCD is hosted by IFAD.
The Great Green Wall is an initiative across the Sahel to combat desertification.
SDG 15.3 targets land degradation neutrality by 2030.
statements: 1 — Correct: The UNCCD's objective is to promote effective action through innovative local programmes and supportive international cooperation and partnerships. Its Article 2 states the objective of combating desertification and mitigating drought through long-term integrated strategies focused on improved land productivity and on the rehabilitation, conservation and sustainable management of land and water resources. Parties prepare National Action Programmes (NAPs), supported by sub-regional (SRAP) and regional (RAP) programmes. Developed countries commit to supporting affected countries financially and technically. The Convention was adopted on 17 June 1994, which is why 17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought. It has about 197 Parties and its Secretariat is in Bonn.

2 — Incorrect: The Convention's special focus is on Africa, not South Asia and North Africa. Its full title is 'Convention to Combat Desertification in Those Countries Experiencing Serious Drought and/or Desertification, Particularly in Africa'. Annex I covers Africa, Annex II Asia, Annex III Latin America and the Caribbean, Annex IV the Northern Mediterranean, and Annex V Central and Eastern Europe. The Secretariat in Bonn does not allocate large financial portions to regions. Funding comes through developed-country Parties, the Global Mechanism (hosted by IFAD) and the GEF, which became a financial mechanism of the UNCCD in 2003. India hosted COP14 in September 2019 at Greater Noida.

3 — Correct: The UNCCD is committed to a bottom-up approach that encourages participation of local people, especially women, farmers and NGOs, in designing and implementing programmes against desertification. Article 3 sets out the principles of participation, partnership and decentralised decision-making. It is the only Rio Convention that explicitly stresses community participation in NAP preparation. Local communities, civil society organisations and scientific bodies take part through the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) and the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention (CRIC). Related ideas include land degradation neutrality (LDN), which was adopted as a target under SDG 15.3.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. The UNCCD promotes action through innovative national programmes and supportive international partnerships, and it follows a bottom-up approach with local participation. Statement 2 is wrong because the Convention's special focus is on Africa, not South Asia and North Africa, and its Secretariat does not allocate funds.
topic_notes: The UNCCD is one of the three Rio Conventions that came out of the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, together with the UNFCCC (climate change) and the CBD (biodiversity). African countries pushed for it because of the severe droughts they had suffered. It was adopted on 17 June 1994 in Paris and came into force on 26 December 1996. It has about 197 Parties, including the EU. India ratified it in 1996, and the nodal ministry in India is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The Secretariat is in Bonn, Germany. Its governing body is the Conference of the Parties (COP), which meets every two years. It has two subsidiary bodies: the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) and the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention (CRIC). The Global Mechanism, hosted by IFAD, mobilises financial resources. The Global Environment Facility (GEF) serves as a financial mechanism of the Convention. Key concepts include desertification, defined as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variations and human activities, and Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN), which is linked to SDG 15.3. Its instruments are National Action Programmes (NAPs). India hosted COP14 at Greater Noida in September 2019. At that meeting India pledged to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030, up from the earlier 21 million hectare target. COP15 was held in Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, in 2022 and COP16 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December 2024. World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on 17 June. Related Indian programmes include the Bonn Challenge, the National Afforestation Programme, the Desert Development Programme and the Green India Mission. The Great Green Wall initiative in the Sahel is an African initiative to fight desertification. The Space Applications Centre (ISRO) has published a Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas of India.

question: Recently, which one of the following currencics has been proposed to be added to the basket of IMF’s SDR?
subject: Economy
detail: The Special Drawing Right (SDR) is an international reserve asset created by the IMF in 1969 to supplement members' official reserves under the Bretton Woods system. It is not a currency; it is a potential claim on the freely usable currencies of IMF members. Its value is based on a basket of currencies, reviewed roughly every five years. Until 2015 the basket had four currencies: US dollar, euro, pound sterling and Japanese yen. In the November 2015 review the IMF Executive Board concluded that the Chinese renminbi met both criteria for inclusion: (1) the country must be among the world's largest exporters of goods and services, and (2) the currency must be 'freely usable' (widely used for international transactions and widely traded). The RMB was added with effect from 1 October 2016, with an initial weight of 10.92%. The weights were USD 41.73%, euro 30.93%, RMB 10.92%, yen 8.33%, pound 8.09%. Elimination: the rouble, rand and rupee were never formally proposed because their issuing economies' currencies do not meet the freely usable test. Only the renminbi was added in the 2015 review.
explanations: Incorrect: The Russian rouble is not freely usable, is not widely traded internationally, and was not proposed for the SDR basket in the 2015 review.
Incorrect: The South African rand is not an SDR basket currency; it lacks the global reserve and trading usage needed for the freely usable criterion.
Incorrect: The Indian rupee is not in the SDR basket. India has called for reforms in IMF governance but the rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account and so does not meet the criteria.
Correct: The Chinese renminbi was approved by the IMF Executive Board in November 2015 for inclusion in the SDR basket from 1 October 2016, as the fifth currency.
keyfact: The Chinese renminbi became the fifth SDR basket currency on 1 October 2016, joining the USD, euro, yen and pound.
option_notes: The rouble is the currency of Russia, issued by the Central Bank of Russia and divided into 100 kopeks. It was heavily affected by the 2014 crisis and sanctions. It is not part of the SDR basket, though Russia is a BRICS member and a significant IMF member.

The rand is the currency of South Africa, issued by the South African Reserve Bank, named after the Witwatersrand gold region and introduced in 1961. It is divided into 100 cents. It is a freely floating emerging-market currency but is not in the SDR basket.

The Indian rupee is issued by the Reserve Bank of India (Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934), with the symbol ₹ adopted in 2010. It is fully convertible on the current account since 1994 (Article VIII status) but only partially convertible on the capital account. It is not in the SDR basket.

The renminbi ('people's currency') is the official currency of China, issued by the People's Bank of China, with the yuan as its main unit. It joined the SDR basket on 1 October 2016 with a 10.92% weight, the first emerging-market currency included, which marked its recognition as a global reserve currency.
related: SDR was created by the IMF in 1969.
Before 2016 the SDR basket had four currencies: USD, euro, pound sterling and yen.
The renminbi joined the SDR basket on 1 October 2016.
The SDR basket is reviewed roughly every five years.
The renminbi was the first emerging-market currency in the SDR basket.
SDR criteria: major exporter status and a freely usable currency.
India's IMF quota is about 2.75% and the IMF is headquartered in Washington, D.C.
summary: The answer is (d) Renminbi. The IMF Executive Board decided in November 2015 to add the Chinese renminbi (yuan) as a fifth currency in the SDR basket, effective 1 October 2016, because it met the 'freely usable' criterion and China is a leading exporter.
topic_notes: The SDR was created in 1969 by the IMF as a supplementary international reserve asset to address concerns about the adequacy of gold and dollar reserves under Bretton Woods. It is neither a currency nor a claim on the IMF itself; it is a potential claim on members' freely usable currencies. Holders can exchange SDRs for currencies through voluntary trading arrangements or by IMF designation. The SDR is the IMF's unit of account and is also used by some other international organisations. Its value is set daily in US dollars, and the SDR interest rate is based on a weighted average of representative short-term interest rates in the basket currencies. The basket is normally reviewed every five years. The criteria for inclusion are: export criterion (the issuer is among the top exporters) and the freely usable criterion. Before 1999 the basket included the German mark and French franc, which were replaced by the euro. The 2015 review added the renminbi, effective 1 October 2016. The next review in 2022 kept the same five currencies but changed weights to USD 43.38%, euro 29.31%, RMB 12.28%, yen 7.59%, pound 7.44%. The IMF was established at Bretton Woods in 1944 and began operations in 1947. It is headquartered in Washington, D.C. India's quota share is about 2.75%. Quota determines voting power, financial contribution and access to financing. Related ideas include IMF quota reforms (2010 reforms effective in 2016) and the AIIB and New Development Bank as alternative institutions.

ocr: With reference to the International Monetary and Financial Committce (IMFC}, consider the following é statements : 1. IMFC discusses matters of concern affecting the global economy, and . advises the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the direction of its work, 2. The World Bank participates as observer in IMFC’s meetings. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only ‘(b} -2-only ' {ce} Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2 . ‘Rashtriya Garima een: spa is a national campaign to (a) rehabilitate the ‘homeless and destitute persons and provide them with suitable sources of livelih
subject: Economy
detail: The International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) is the IMF Board of Governors' advisory body, created in 1999 as the successor to the Interim Committee of 1974. It has 24 members, drawn from the governors of the IMF's 190 member countries (central bank governors or ministers) and structured on the same constituency basis as the 24-member Executive Board. It meets twice a year, in spring and during the annual meetings in autumn. Its main roles are to advise and report to the Board of Governors on the supervision and management of the international monetary and financial system, including adjustment and liquidity, and to consider proposals by the Executive Board to amend the Articles of Agreement. It also deals with disturbances that might threaten the system. It is advisory only and takes no binding decisions, issuing a communique at the end of each meeting. Observers include the World Bank, BIS, OECD, WTO, UN, ILO and FSB. The Development Committee is the parallel World Bank-IMF body on development finance. Elimination logic: statement 1 is the textbook description of the IMFC's role, so (b) and (d) go out. Statement 2 is also true because the World Bank regularly attends, so (a) goes out and (c) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, since the World Bank attends IMFC meetings as an observer, so '1 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, because advising the IMF on the direction of its work is the core IMFC function, so '2 only' is incomplete.
Correct: both statements are accurate. The IMFC discusses global economic concerns and advises the IMF, and the World Bank is an observer at its meetings.
Wrong: neither statement is false, so this option cannot be right.
keyfact: The IMFC (24 members, since 1999) advises the IMF on the direction of its work, and the World Bank attends as an observer.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would mean the IMFC's advisory role is correct but World Bank observer participation is not. UPSC often uses this trap by leaving out a true statement. In fact the IMFC is advisory to the IMF Board of Governors, was created in 1999, has 24 members and meets twice a year. Observers from other international organisations, including the World Bank, attend. So '1 only' fails.

Option (b) '2 only' would mean World Bank observer participation is correct but the IMFC's advisory function is not. This is wrong because the advisory function is the IMFC's main purpose. The World Bank does attend as an observer. The IMFC advises and reports to the IMF Board of Governors on the international monetary system, including adjustment, liquidity and systemic disturbances, and it considers proposals to amend the Articles of Agreement.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is the official answer. The IMFC is the IMF's key policy advisory committee, with 24 members. It succeeded the Interim Committee in 1999 and meets in spring and at the annual meetings in autumn. It issues a communique, which sets the IMF's strategic direction, but has no formal decision-making powers. Observers include the World Bank, BIS, OECD, WTO, UN and FSB.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' would mean both statements are false, which is not so. The IMFC is a real, active advisory body of the IMF with a clear mandate, and the World Bank is among the regular observers. Do not confuse the IMFC with the IMF Executive Board, which handles day-to-day operations, or with the Development Committee, which is a joint IMF-World Bank forum on development issues.
related: The IMFC replaced the Interim Committee in 1999.
The IMFC has 24 members and meets twice a year.
The IMFC is advisory and issues a communique; it makes no binding decisions.
The IMF was established at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is based in Washington DC.
The Development Committee is the joint IMF-World Bank forum on development finance.
The yuan was added to the SDR basket in October 2016.
The IMF's World Economic Outlook is published twice a year, in April and October.
The IMF Executive Board has 24 directors.
statements: 1 — Correct: The IMFC's mandate is to discuss matters of concern to the global economy and to advise the IMF on the direction of its work. IMFC facts: it was established in 1999, replacing the Interim Committee (set up in 1974). It has 24 members, who are governors of the Fund, ministers or others of similar rank, and it mirrors the Executive Board's 24 constituencies. It meets twice a year, in April and October. Its chair is selected by the committee, and the IMF Managing Director takes part. It issues a communique but takes no formal decisions. It advises the Board of Governors on the supervision and management of the international monetary system and on proposals to amend the Articles of Agreement.

2 — Correct: The World Bank attends IMFC meetings as an observer, along with other international organisations. Observers include the World Bank, BIS, OECD, WTO, UN, ILO, FSB, and others. The World Bank (IBRD and IDA) was founded at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington DC, like the IMF. The two institutions are separate but closely linked, and they hold joint annual meetings. The Development Committee (formally the Joint Ministerial Committee of the Boards of Governors of the Bank and the Fund) is their joint forum on the transfer of real resources to developing countries. The World Bank president attends IMFC meetings, and both institutions jointly release some reports.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. The IMFC is the IMF's advisory committee: it discusses global economic concerns and advises the IMF on the direction of its work, and the World Bank takes part in its meetings as an observer, along with other international bodies.
topic_notes: The IMF was created at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944 and began operations in 1945. It is headquartered in Washington DC and has 190 member countries. India is a founding member. Its purposes are to promote international monetary cooperation, exchange rate stability, and the balanced growth of trade, and to provide temporary financial assistance to countries with balance-of-payments problems. Governance runs on three levels. The Board of Governors is the highest authority, with one governor per member. The Executive Board has 24 directors and handles day-to-day work. The IMFC is the advisory committee that sets strategic direction. The Managing Director heads the staff, and the post has traditionally gone to a European. Quotas determine each member's subscription, voting power and access to financing. Quota reforms have raised the share of emerging economies, and India's share has increased. The Special Drawing Right (SDR) is the IMF's reserve asset, valued against a basket of currencies that includes the US dollar, euro, yuan (added in 2016), yen and pound sterling. Key IMF publications are the World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report and Fiscal Monitor. Key lending facilities include the Stand-By Arrangement, the Extended Fund Facility and the Flexible Credit Line. The Development Committee is the joint IMF-World Bank forum on development finance. The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. UPSC can ask about the World Bank's reports, such as Ease of Doing Business (discontinued in 2021), the Human Capital Index and the Logistics Performance Index. Other international economic bodies to know are the WTO, BIS, OECD, G20, FSB, NDB (BRICS) and AIIB.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only ‘(b} -2-only ' {ce} Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2 . ‘Rashtriya Garima een: spa is a national campaign to (a) rehabilitate the ‘homeless and destitute persons and provide them with suitable sources of livelih
subject: Economy
detail: Rashtriya Garima Abhiyan (National Campaign for Dignity) was launched in 2001 by the Safai Karmachari Andolan (SKA), co-founded by Bezwada Wilson, to end manual scavenging, meaning the manual cleaning, carrying, disposal or handling of human excreta from insanitary latrines, open drains or pits. The practice is linked to caste, and the campaign stresses dignity under Article 21 and the abolition of untouchability under Article 17. The legal framework has two Acts. The Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 was the first. The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 now applies, and it bans insanitary latrines, manual cleaning of sewers and septic tanks without protection, and hazardous cleaning. The Supreme Court in Safai Karamchari Andolan v. Union of India (2014) directed rehabilitation and compensation of Rs 10 lakh for sewer deaths. The government's rehabilitation scheme is SRMS (Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers), and NAMASTE (2022) now covers sewer and septic tank workers. Elimination logic: the word 'Garima' means dignity, which points to sanitation workers. Options (a), (b) and (d) describe other schemes or laws such as SMILE, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, and the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956.
explanations: Wrong: rehabilitation of the homeless and destitute is the focus of schemes such as SMILE (Support for Marginalised Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise) and shelter programmes under DAY-NULM, not this campaign.
Wrong: release and rehabilitation of sex workers falls under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, the Ujjawala scheme and NGO programmes. It is not the aim of Rashtriya Garima Abhiyaan.
Correct: the campaign works to eradicate manual scavenging and rehabilitate manual scavengers. It was launched by Safai Karmachari Andolan.

Wrong: bonded labour is handled under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 and the Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers. Bharat Bachao Andolan and similar groups work on it, but the Garima campaign does not.
keyfact: Rashtriya Garima Abhiyaan (SKA, 2001) = campaign to end manual scavenging and rehabilitate manual scavengers.
option_notes: Homeless and destitute rehabilitation: addressed through shelter homes under DAY-NULM (Shelter for Urban Homeless), the SMILE scheme (2022) of the Ministry of Social Justice for beggars, and Supreme Court directions on night shelters. Homelessness is counted in the Census, which records houseless households. Article 21 (right to life) has been read by the Supreme Court to include shelter. This is a different policy area from sanitation work.

Sex workers: the legal framework is the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (ITPA), which criminalises trafficking, brothel-keeping and soliciting in public places. Ujjawala (2007) is a scheme against trafficking and for rescue and rehabilitation. NACO runs targeted HIV-prevention interventions for sex workers. In 2022 the Supreme Court said sex work is a profession and that police should not harass consenting adult sex workers.

Manual scavenging: employing people to clean insanitary latrines or sewers by hand. It was banned by the 1993 Act and then by the 2013 Act, which defines insanitary latrines and hazardous cleaning. Rashtriya Garima Abhiyaan, run by Safai Karmachari Andolan under Bezwada Wilson, campaigns against it. Wilson received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2016. The National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK) monitors the issue, and its tenure was extended to 2025. The government now uses the NAMASTE scheme for mechanised sanitation.

Bonded labour: forced work to repay a debt, abolished under Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour) and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. District magistrates must identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers, with the rehabilitation scheme revised in 2016 to give Rs 1 to 3 lakh depending on the category. Bandhua Mukti Morcha, founded by Swami Agnivesh, led the key case, Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984). The National Human Rights Commission also monitors it.
related: Rashtriya Garima Abhiyaan was launched in 2001 by Safai Karmachari Andolan (SKA).
Bezwada Wilson, the SKA leader, won the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2016.
The 2013 Act bans employment of manual scavengers and hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks.
The Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 was the first law.
NAMASTE scheme (2022) targets mechanised sanitation and zero sewer deaths.
Supreme Court in 2014 ordered Rs 10 lakh compensation for families of sewer deaths.
Article 23 prohibits forced labour; the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act dates from 1976.
National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK) was set up in 1993.
summary: The answer is (c): Rashtriya Garima Abhiyaan is a national campaign to eradicate the practice of manual scavenging and to rehabilitate manual scavengers. It was launched by Safai Karmachari Andolan (SKA), a civil-society movement led by Bezwada Wilson, and is not a government scheme for the homeless, sex workers or bonded labourers.
topic_notes: Manual scavenging is a caste-linked form of occupational exploitation. It is defined in the 2013 Act as the manual cleaning, carrying or disposal of human excreta from insanitary latrines, open drains, pits or railway tracks. Legal timeline: the 1993 Act was the first law against it, and the 2013 Act (in force from December 2013) widened the definition, made hazardous sewer and septic tank cleaning an offence, and mandated rehabilitation. The Act was passed after the 2013 Supreme Court order that directed states to implement it. The Supreme Court in 2014 (Safai Karamchari Andolan case) ordered that families of those who died in sewers be paid Rs 10 lakh compensation. Constitutional links: Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), Article 21 (dignity), Article 23 (forced labour) and Article 15. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 are also relevant. Institutions: National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK, set up in 1993 as a statutory body, later non-statutory), the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, and the National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC). Schemes: SRMS (2007, revised 2013) provides one-time cash assistance, skill training and subsidised loans. NAMASTE (National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem, 2022-23) aims at zero fatalities in sanitation work and covers sewer and septic tank workers. Swachh Bharat Mission built toilets, with a focus on eliminating insanitary latrines. Civil society: Safai Karmachari Andolan (founded in 1994 by Bezwada Wilson and others) and its Garima Yatra and Bhim Yatra. Other angles UPSC can ask: the Ramon Magsaysay Award, Census 2011 data on insanitary latrines, the Dalit rights movement, sewer deaths statistics, and the differences between manual scavenging and sanitation work.

ocr: With reference to the cultural history of medieval India, consider the following Statements : 1. Siddhas (Sittars} of Tamil region were monotheistic and condemned idolatry. 2. Lingayats of Kannada _ region questioned the theory of rebirth and rejected the caste hierarchy. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b} 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Medieval History
detail: This question tests heterodox and bhakti-era protest movements of medieval South India. The Siddhars (Tamil Siddha tradition, roughly 9th-15th century CE) were mystic-poets and alchemists-cum-physicians. They preached one formless God, rejected temple idol worship, ritualism, Brahmanical authority and caste, and stressed yogic discipline, inner purity and moral conduct. Their verses are in Tamil, with Sivavakkiyar and Tirumular (author of the Tirumantiram) among the best known. The Lingayats, or Virashaivas, were founded or consolidated by Basavanna (Basaveshwara) in 12th-century Karnataka, under the Kalachuri king Bijjala. They worship Shiva only in the form of the Ishtalinga, worn on the body, and reject temple worship, Vedic ritual, caste hierarchy, untouchability and child marriage. They also reject the doctrine of rebirth and karma-based birth hierarchy: death means merging with Shiva, not return to the cycle. They stressed the dignity of labour (kayaka) and wrote vachanas in Kannada. Elimination logic: since both statements match the standard NCERT/Spectrum descriptions of these movements, options (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out, which leaves (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it accepts only statement 1. Statement 2 is also correct, since the Lingayats rejected rebirth and caste.
(b) is wrong because it accepts only statement 2. Statement 1 is also correct, since the Siddhars were monotheistic and condemned idolatry.
(c) is correct because both statements match the established descriptions of the Siddhars and the Lingayats.
(d) is wrong because it says neither statement is correct, but both are.
keyfact: Siddhars (Tamil) rejected idol worship and caste; Lingayats (Basavanna, Karnataka) rejected rebirth and caste hierarchy, so both statements are correct.
option_notes: Statement 1 alone: it is true about the Siddhars. The Siddhars were Tamil mystic-poets and healers (about 9th-15th century) who preached one formless God and rejected idol worship, rituals and caste distinctions. Tirumular's Tirumantiram, Sivavakkiyar and Pambatti Siddhar are key names. Agastya is traditionally credited with the Siddha medicine system. Their ideas shaped later Tamil dissent, and Siddha medicine is now a recognised AYUSH system with its national institute in Chennai.

Statement 2 alone: it is true about the Lingayats. The Lingayats (Virashaivas) were led by Basavanna in 12th-century Karnataka under the Kalachuri king Bijjala. They worship Shiva through the Ishtalinga, reject caste, untouchability, Vedic ritual and rebirth, and promote kayaka (dignified labour) and dasoha (service). Their teachings are in Kannada vachanas, and the Anubhava Mantapa was their forum for debate. Their social reforms included widow remarriage and opposition to child marriage.

Both statements: this is the correct choice. It combines the Siddhars' monotheism and anti-idolatry with the Lingayat rejection of rebirth and caste. Both are part of the broader medieval South Indian protest tradition, along with the Alvars, Nayanars and the Bhakti poets. Such movements questioned Brahmanical dominance and used regional languages, such as Tamil and Kannada, to spread their messages to ordinary people.

Neither statement: this option is wrong because both statements are accurate. It would be true only if the statements wrongly attributed ideas to these groups. The Siddhars did oppose idol worship, and the Lingayats did reject caste hierarchy and rebirth. UPSC often uses this option as a trap for students who confuse the Siddhars with orthodox Shaiva Nayanars or the Lingayats with Vaishnava sects.
related: Basavanna founded or revived the Lingayat movement in 12th-century Karnataka.
Anubhava Mantapa was the Lingayat forum for spiritual and social discussion.
Tirumular's Tirumantiram is a major Tamil Siddha text.
Alvars were Vaishnava saints, and Nayanars were Shaiva saints, of early medieval Tamil Nadu.
Nalayira Divya Prabandham is the Alvar compilation, compiled by Nathamuni.
Ramanuja propounded Vishishtadvaita, and Shankara propounded Advaita.
Vachanas are Kannada devotional verses of the Lingayat saints.
Akka Mahadevi was a prominent woman Virashaiva saint-poet.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Siddhars of Tamil Nadu preached one formless God and condemned idol worship, ritualism and caste. Siddhars (Tamil Siddha tradition) were mystic-poets, yogis and healers who were active roughly from the 9th century onward. Their Tamil verses stress the oneness of God, self-discipline, and inner realisation over temple ritual. Tirumular wrote the Tirumantiram, and Sivavakkiyar and Pambatti Siddhar were other well-known figures. Agastya is traditionally seen as the father of the Siddha system of medicine, which uses herbs, minerals and metals. Their rationalist, anti-Brahmanical tone influenced later Tamil protest and reform thought. Today the Siddha system is a recognised AYUSH system, with the National Institute of Siddha in Chennai.

2 — Correct: The Lingayats of Karnataka rejected the theory of rebirth and caste hierarchy. The Virashaiva or Lingayat movement arose in 12th-century Karnataka under Basavanna, a minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala. Followers wear the Ishtalinga and worship Shiva alone. They reject Vedic authority, temple worship, caste distinctions, untouchability and pollution beliefs, and they permit widow remarriage and oppose child marriage. They hold that the soul merges with Shiva after death rather than being reborn. Their teachings are in Kannada vachanas, composed by Basavanna, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi and others. Anubhava Mantapa was their assembly for spiritual and social discussion. Karnataka has a large Lingayat community, and the demand for a separate religion status has been a recurring political issue.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The Siddhars of Tamil Nadu were monotheistic and condemned idol worship, and the Lingayats (Virashaivas) of Karnataka questioned rebirth and rejected caste hierarchy.
topic_notes: Medieval South India saw two parallel religious currents: the devotional Bhakti movement and the more radical, heterodox protest traditions. The Alvars (Vaishnava) and Nayanars (Shaiva) in Tamil Nadu, from about the 6th to 9th century, used Tamil hymns, and their works were compiled in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham and the Tirumurai. The Siddhars went further: they were non-conformist, rationalist, and focused on yoga, alchemy and medicine, rejecting idol worship and caste. In Karnataka the Virashaiva or Lingayat movement of Basavanna (12th century) challenged the caste system, ritualism, the Vedas' authority and rebirth, and championed labour and gender equality. Women saints such as Akka Mahadevi took part. Other South Indian traditions include Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita (11th-12th century), Madhva's Dvaita (13th century) and Shankara's Advaita (8th century). Later Bhakti and Sufi figures in the north include Kabir, Nanak, Ravidas, Chaitanya, Mirabai and Tulsidas. Kabir and Nanak also attacked idolatry and caste, but they belong to the north. Vachana literature is Kannada, Tirumantiram is Tamil, and Basavanna's temple-free Shaivism is central to Lingayat identity. Other angles UPSC could ask: the Nathpanthis and Tantric traditions, the Sufi orders (Chishti, Suhrawardi), the Bhakti saints of Maharashtra (Tukaram, Namdev, Eknath), Assam's Sankaradeva, and the languages in which these figures composed.

ocr: Which of the following best describes the term ‘import cover’, sometimes seen in the news? (a) It is the ratio of value of imports to the Gross Domestic Product of a country (b) It is the total value of imports of a country in a year (fc) It is the ratio between the value of exports and that of imports between two countries (d) It is the number of months of imports that could be paid for by a country’s international reserves
subject: Economy
detail: Import cover = Foreign exchange reserves / (Annual imports/12), i.e. the number of months for which a country could pay for its imports from its reserves if no other foreign exchange inflow occurred. It is one of the key indicators of reserve adequacy, along with the ratio of reserves to short-term external debt, reserves to GDP and reserves to broad money (the Greenspan-Guidotti rule says reserves should equal short-term external debt). A common rule of thumb is that reserves should cover at least 3 months of imports; below this a country risks a balance-of-payments crisis. India's 1991 crisis occurred when reserves covered only about 2-3 weeks of imports (roughly 3 weeks), whereas in recent years India's cover has been about 10-11 months, and it was higher during 2020-21 (above 17 months). The RBI publishes reserves and cover figures in its Annual Report and Weekly Statistical Supplement. Elimination: (a) describes the import-to-GDP ratio, a measure of trade openness/import dependence. (b) is simply the import bill. (c) is the export-import ratio, similar to an export-import cover or trade balance indicator. Only (d) links imports to reserves and is expressed in months.
explanations: Incorrect: the ratio of imports to GDP is the import intensity or import penetration ratio, a measure of openness, not import cover.
Incorrect: the total value of imports in a year is the import bill; it is one input to import cover but not the concept itself.
Incorrect: the ratio of exports to imports between two countries is a bilateral trade ratio (export-import ratio / export cover of imports), not import cover.
Correct: import cover is the number of months of imports that can be paid for from a country's international (foreign exchange) reserves.
keyfact: Import cover = number of months of imports that a country's foreign exchange reserves can pay for (India: ~3 weeks in 1991, ~10-11 months recently).
option_notes: Imports-to-GDP ratio: it shows how dependent an economy is on imports and, with exports added, forms the trade-to-GDP ratio, a measure of openness. Small open economies such as Singapore have very high ratios, while large economies like India, the USA and Japan have much lower ones. India's merchandise imports are roughly 20-25% of GDP. It says nothing about the ability to finance imports.

Import bill: the total value of goods (and sometimes services) a country buys from abroad in a given period, usually a year. In India it is reported by the Ministry of Commerce and DGCI&S. Crude oil, gold, electronics and coal are the largest items. A higher import bill, especially oil, widens the current account deficit and the trade deficit and pressures the rupee.

Export-import ratio (export cover of imports): exports divided by imports, showing how much of the import bill is financed through export earnings. A ratio below 1 implies a trade deficit; above 1 implies a surplus. India usually runs a ratio of about 0.6-0.7 for merchandise trade. It can be computed bilaterally, for example India-China, where India has a large deficit.

Import cover: foreign exchange reserves divided by monthly average imports, expressed in months. It measures the external liquidity cushion. Reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position at the IMF. India's cover was about 3 weeks in 1991, about 11 months in 2021-22 and about 10-11 months in recent years. A cover of 3 months is the traditional minimum.
related: Import cover = foreign exchange reserves divided by average monthly imports, expressed in months.
India's 1991 balance-of-payments crisis: reserves covered only about 3 weeks of imports.
Traditional safe minimum import cover is about 3 months.
Greenspan-Guidotti rule: reserves should equal short-term external debt (ratio of 1).
India's forex reserves consist of foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the IMF reserve tranche.
The RBI is the custodian and manager of India's foreign exchange reserves.
The SDR basket comprises USD, Euro, Chinese yuan, Japanese yen and British pound.
Imports-to-GDP is a measure of openness, not of reserve adequacy.
summary: The correct answer is (d). Import cover is the number of months of imports that a country's foreign exchange (international) reserves can finance. It is a standard measure of external-sector vulnerability and reserve adequacy.
topic_notes: Foreign exchange reserves are external assets held by the central bank (RBI in India) for settling international payments, intervening in the currency market and maintaining confidence. Components: foreign currency assets (the largest, about 80-90%), gold, Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) held with the IMF, and the Reserve Tranche Position in the IMF. India's reserves crossed about USD 600 billion in 2021 and peaked at roughly USD 640-700 billion in 2021-24, among the largest in the world after China, Japan and Switzerland. In 1991 reserves fell to about USD 1 billion-ish levels, enough for around 3 weeks of imports, forcing gold pledging and the launch of economic reforms. Reserve adequacy indicators: import cover (months), reserves to short-term debt (the Greenspan-Guidotti rule, 1:1), reserves to total external debt, reserves to GDP, and the IMF's ARA (Assessing Reserve Adequacy) metric. The Malegam and the Tarapore committees dealt with reserve and capital account issues; the Tarapore Committee advocated capital account convertibility. Reserves rise through FDI, FPI inflows, NRI deposits, external commercial borrowings and RBI purchases of dollars; they fall when RBI sells dollars to defend the rupee. Valuation changes also matter, as reserves are reported in USD, so gold price or currency movements change their value. The RBI reports reserves weekly in its Weekly Statistical Supplement and half-yearly in its Report on Foreign Exchange Reserves. Related ideas: current account deficit, balance of payments, trade deficit, currency intervention, sterilisation through MSS, and the Special Drawing Right basket (USD, Euro, Yuan, Yen, Pound).

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Community sometimes In the affairs of mentioned in the news 1. Kurd : Bangladesh 2. Madhesi : Nepal . 3. Rohingya : Myanmar - -— Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? fa) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 (a) 3 only B-APM-P-CKB/65A .
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests ethnic and minority communities that were prominent in the news, a recurring UPSC current-affairs theme. The key is to link each community to its homeland. The Kurds are a stateless Indo-European (Iranian-language) people of about 30-40 million who live in the highland region called Kurdistan, spread across southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, northeastern Syria and western Iran. They were promised a state in the Treaty of Sevres (1920), but the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) dropped this. Iraqi Kurdistan has an autonomous region with Erbil as its capital. The Madhesi live in Nepal's southern Terai plains and have close cultural and kinship links with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Their agitation over federal boundaries and citizenship accompanied Nepal's 2015 Constitution. The Rohingya are a Muslim minority in Rakhine (Arakan) state, Myanmar, denied citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law, and displaced in large numbers in 2016-17 to Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh. Elimination: Kurd-Bangladesh is wrong, so any option containing 1 (option a) is out. Options (b) and (d) each leave out one correct pair, so only (c) works.
explanations: Wrong: it includes pair 1, but Kurds are not associated with Bangladesh.
Wrong: pair 2 is correct, but pair 3 is also correct, so '2 only' is incomplete.
Correct: Madhesi-Nepal and Rohingya-Myanmar are correct, and Kurd-Bangladesh is wrong.
Wrong: pair 3 is correct, but pair 2 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
keyfact: Madhesi = Terai, Nepal; Rohingya = Rakhine, Myanmar; Kurds = Turkey/Iraq/Syria/Iran (not Bangladesh).
related: Rohingya are concentrated in Rakhine (Arakan) state, Myanmar.
Madhesi live in Nepal's Terai region.
Kurdistan spans Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran; Erbil is the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan.
Nepal's current Constitution was promulgated on 20 September 2015.
India is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention.
Yazidis are a minority of northern Iraq (Sinjar) persecuted by ISIS.
Uighurs are a Turkic Muslim minority of Xinjiang, China.
Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh hosts the largest Rohingya refugee settlement.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Kurds are not linked with Bangladesh; they live in Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran. The Kurds are an Iranian-language ethnic group of roughly 30-40 million, the largest stateless nation. Their homeland, Kurdistan, covers mountain regions of four countries. The Treaty of Sevres (1920) proposed a Kurdish state, but Lausanne (1923) ended the idea. Iraq's Kurdistan Regional Government (capital Erbil) is autonomous under the 2005 constitution. Kurdish groups such as the PKK (Turkey) and the YPG (Syria) have been in conflict or have fought ISIS. Most Kurds are Sunni Muslims.

2 — Correct: Madhesi are the people of Nepal's Terai plains. The Madhesi are people of the Terai, the southern lowland strip of Nepal bordering Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, with deep roti-beti (kinship and marriage) ties to India. They make up a large share of Nepal's population. Their grievances concern citizenship, representation and the demarcation of provinces in the 2015 Constitution, which led to protests and a border blockade in 2015-16. Parties include the Madhesi Janadhikar Forum and the Rastriya Janata Party Nepal. Languages include Maithili, Bhojpuri and Awadhi.

3 — Correct: Rohingya are from Myanmar. The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim ethnic minority concentrated in Rakhine (Arakan) state in western Myanmar, bordering Bangladesh. Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law excludes them from the 135 recognised ethnic groups, making them effectively stateless. Violence in 2012, 2016 and especially August 2017 forced hundreds of thousands to flee to Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh. The UN described the military action as ethnic cleansing. The case is before the International Court of Justice (The Gambia v. Myanmar, 2019). India has also hosted Rohingya refugees without being party to the 1951 Refugee Convention.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 3. Madhesi are a people of the Terai plains of Nepal, and Rohingya are a Muslim minority of Rakhine state in Myanmar. Kurds are not associated with Bangladesh; they are an ethnic group spread across Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran.
topic_notes:
UPSC repeatedly asks about communities, minorities and refugees that feature in the news, usually as matching pairs. Method: link each group to its country and its main issue.

Kurds: stateless people across Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran; Kurdistan Regional Government in Iraq (Erbil); the Peshmerga fought ISIS; Turkey's PKK conflict; the Syrian YPG.

Madhesi: Terai people of Nepal; Nepal's Constitution was promulgated on 20 September 2015 and established a federal republic with seven provinces; Madhesi and Tharu protests demanded changes to boundaries, citizenship and proportional representation; India-Nepal border trade was disrupted in 2015-16.

Rohingya: Rakhine state, Myanmar; denied citizenship in 1982; major exodus in 2017; Cox's Bazar hosts nearly a million, and Bhasan Char island was used for relocation by Bangladesh; ICJ case filed by The Gambia in 2019; the ICC has also examined the situation. India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and handles refugees through domestic law and policy.

Other communities that are often asked: Yazidis (Iraq, Sinjar, targeted by ISIS in 2014); Uighurs (Xinjiang, China); Tamils (Sri Lanka); Chakma (Bangladesh, Mizoram and Tripura); Hazaras (Afghanistan, Pakistan); Rohingya and Moro (Philippines, Mindanao); Tibetans in exile; Bodo and Gorkha in India; Pashtuns (Afghanistan and Pakistan; Durand Line).

Also know: the principle of non-refoulement; the UNHCR, headquartered in Geneva; the Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 (for persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Pakistan and Bangladesh).

ocr: With reference to ‘Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), consider the following statements ; 1. It is an organization of European Union in working relation with NATO and WHO. 2. It monitors chemical industry to prevent new weapons from emerging. 3. It provides assistance and protection to States (Parties) against chemical weapons threats. : Which of the statements given above is/are correct? ° fa) 1 only. ; (b) 2 and 3 only {c} 1 and 3 only é {d} 1, 2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) is the implementing body of the Chemical Weapons Convention, which was adopted in 1993, entered into force on 29 April 1997, and has its seat at The Hague, Netherlands. It is an autonomous international organization with 193 States Parties. It has a working relationship with the UN through a Relationship Agreement, but it is not part of the UN system. It was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013. Its core functions are: (1) verifying the destruction of chemical weapon stocks and former production facilities; (2) monitoring the chemical industry through declarations and inspections so that toxic chemicals are not diverted to new weapons, which is the non-proliferation function under the CWC Schedules 1, 2 and 3; (3) assistance and protection under Article X, and (4) international cooperation in peaceful uses of chemistry under Article XI. Elimination logic: statement 1 is plainly wrong because the OPCW is global, not an EU organ, and it is not tied to NATO. Once 1 is eliminated, only (b) remains, since (b) contains 2 and 3 and excludes 1.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1 only, which is false because the OPCW is not an EU body or a NATO partner, and it leaves out the correct statements 2 and 3.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 describe the OPCW's industry-verification and assistance and protection roles under the CWC, while statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 2, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: The OPCW is the Hague-based implementing body of the CWC (in force 1997, Nobel Peace Prize 2013). It verifies destruction, monitors industry, and gives assistance and protection, and it is not an EU or NATO body.
related: The OPCW is headquartered at The Hague, Netherlands.
The CWC entered into force on 29 April 1997.
The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013.
India's National Authority for the CWC is under the Cabinet Secretariat.
The Geneva Protocol of 1925 banned the use of chemical weapons, but not their possession.
The Australia Group is an export-control regime on chemical and biological items.
The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 has no formal verification body.
The CWC's destruction of declared stockpiles was completed in 2023.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The OPCW is an independent global body, not an organization of the European Union, and it has no working relation with NATO as stated. Facts: it has its headquarters at The Hague and has 193 member states from all continents. It implements the CWC, which entered into force in 1997. It cooperates with the UN under a 2001 Relationship Agreement and reports to the UN General Assembly and Security Council. Its decision-making organs are the Conference of the States Parties, the Executive Council of 41 members, and the Technical Secretariat headed by a Director-General.

2 — Correct: The OPCW monitors the chemical industry to prevent new chemical weapons from emerging. Facts: the CWC Verification Annex classifies chemicals into Schedules 1, 2 and 3, plus unscheduled discrete organic chemicals (DOCs). Member states declare relevant facilities, and the Technical Secretariat conducts routine inspections of the industry. The aim is to ensure that toxic chemicals and their precursors are used only for purposes not prohibited by the Convention. The Convention's general purpose criterion bans any toxic chemical used as a weapon. This is the non-proliferation pillar alongside destruction of stockpiles.

3 — Correct: The OPCW provides assistance and protection to States Parties against chemical weapons threats. Facts: Article X of the CWC provides for assistance and protection, including detection equipment, protective gear, decontamination, medical antidotes, and training. The OPCW coordinates emergency assistance if a state is attacked or threatened with chemical weapons. It maintains a voluntary assistance network and runs capacity-building programmes. Article XI promotes economic and technological cooperation in chemistry for peaceful purposes. The OPCW also runs investigations, such as the Investigation and Identification Team created in 2018 to attribute chemical attacks in Syria.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. The OPCW is an independent international organization based in The Hague that implements the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC). It is not an EU body, and it verifies the chemical industry and provides assistance and protection to States Parties.
topic_notes: The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) was opened for signature in Paris in January 1993 and entered into force on 29 April 1997. It bans the development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, transfer and use of chemical weapons. It is the first multilateral disarmament treaty with a time-bound destruction schedule and a verification regime. The OPCW, at The Hague, is its implementing body. Its organs are the Conference of the States Parties (all members), the Executive Council (41 members elected for two-year terms), and the Technical Secretariat headed by the Director-General (Fernando Arias of Spain since 2018). The OPCW won the 2013 Nobel Peace Prize for its extensive work to eliminate chemical weapons, as the Syrian chemical disarmament was under way. The CWC has 193 States Parties. Egypt, North Korea and South Sudan remained outside it, while Israel has signed but not ratified. Syria joined in 2013. India ratified the CWC in 1996, and its national authority is the National Authority for Chemical Weapons Convention (NACWC) under the Cabinet Secretariat. India declared and destroyed its stockpile by 2009. In 2023 the OPCW announced that all declared stockpiles had been verifiably destroyed, with the USA the last possessor to finish. Schedule 1 covers chemicals with few or no peaceful uses, such as sarin and mustard gas. Schedule 2 covers chemicals with some peaceful use, and Schedule 3 covers chemicals with large-scale industrial use, such as phosgene. Related regimes: the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972, which has no verification body, the NPT, and the Australia Group, an export-control group on chemical and biological items. UPSC may also ask about the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use but not the possession of chemical weapons, and about Syria's use of chemical weapons.

ocr: With reference to ‘Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana’, consider the following statements : 1. Under this scheme, farmers will have to pay a uniform premium of two percent for any crop they cultivate in any season of the year. _ 2. This scheme covers post-harvest losses arising out of cyclones and unseasonal rains, Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only fc) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) was launched in January 2016 (approved by the Union Cabinet on 13 January 2016, effective from Kharif 2016). It replaced the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS) and the Modified NAIS, and aimed to provide comprehensive risk cover at low, uniform premium rates. The premium is differentiated by crop type and season, not uniform for all crops: 2% of sum insured for Kharif food grains, pulses and oilseeds; 1.5% for Rabi food grains, pulses and oilseeds; and 5% for annual commercial and annual horticultural crops. The balance of the actuarial premium is shared equally by the Centre and States (subsidy), with no upper cap on government subsidy. The scheme covers the full crop cycle: prevented sowing/planting, standing crop losses (drought, dry spell, flood, inundation, pests and diseases, landslide, natural fire, lightning, storm, hailstorm, cyclone), post-harvest losses and localised calamities (hailstorm, landslide, inundation). Post-harvest cover applies for a maximum of 14 days from harvesting for crops that are cut and left to dry in the field. Elimination: statement 1 uses the absolute words 'uniform' and 'any crop', which are wrong, so options (a) and (c) fall. Statement 2 is true, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the 2% premium is limited to Kharif food and oilseed crops, not any crop in any season.
Correct: statement 1 is wrong, and statement 2 is right because post-harvest losses from cyclone and unseasonal rain are covered for up to 14 days after harvest.
Wrong: this needs both statements to be true, but statement 1 fails on the 'uniform premium for any crop' claim.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: PMFBY (2016): premium 2% Kharif, 1.5% Rabi, 5% commercial/horticultural; covers post-harvest losses up to 14 days, so only statement 2 is correct.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would be right only if the premium were a flat 2% for every crop and season. In reality, PMFBY has a three-tier farmer premium structure of 2% (Kharif), 1.5% (Rabi) and 5% (commercial/horticultural). It would also require post-harvest cover to be absent, which is untrue. The scheme was launched in 2016 and is run by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The option is a trap built on the partly true number 2%.

Option (b) '2 only' is the official answer. It reflects PMFBY's comprehensive coverage, which includes post-harvest losses up to 14 days from harvest for crops drying in the field, due to cyclone, cyclonic rain and unseasonal rain. PMFBY covers pre-sowing (prevented sowing), standing crop, post-harvest and localised calamity risks. It is a yield-index based scheme with area approach for widespread risks and individual farm approach for localised ones. It replaced NAIS and MNAIS from Kharif 2016.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is wrong because statement 1 overgeneralises the premium rate. Remember the structure: 2% Kharif food/oilseed, 1.5% Rabi food/oilseed, 5% annual commercial/horticultural. Statement 2 alone is true. UPSC often builds a two-statement question where one statement is accurate and the other has an absolute word such as 'uniform', 'any' or 'all', which is exactly what happened here.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is wrong because statement 2 is factually correct. PMFBY explicitly provides post-harvest cover for losses from cyclone, cyclonic rain and unseasonal rain for 14 days after harvest on crops kept in the field to dry. Students who believe crop insurance covers only standing crops, as with earlier schemes such as NAIS, might choose this option, but PMFBY expanded the cover.
related: PMFBY launched in 2016 replacing NAIS and MNAIS.
Farmers' premium: 2% Kharif, 1.5% Rabi, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops.
Post-harvest loss cover lasts up to 14 days after harvest for crops drying in the field.
Localised calamities covered include hailstorm, landslide and inundation.
Loss must be reported within 72 hours; helpline number is 14447.
Enrolment became voluntary for all farmers from Kharif 2020.
RWBCIS uses weather parameters instead of yield as the index trigger.
Centre and States share the balance premium subsidy equally under PMFBY.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The 2% rate applies only to Kharif food crops (cereals, millets, pulses) and oilseeds; Rabi is 1.5% and annual commercial/horticultural crops pay 5%. Premium is therefore not uniform across crops or seasons. PMFBY was launched in 2016 and replaced NAIS and MNAIS. Farmers' premium is capped at these low rates, and the rest of the actuarial premium is borne by Centre and State in equal shares (50:50 in most states; the Centre pays more in the North-East and hilly states). Enrolment was compulsory for loanee farmers originally and became voluntary from Kharif 2020. Claims are settled using Crop Cutting Experiments (CCE), supplemented by remote sensing, smartphones and drones for yield estimation. Implementation is by empanelled insurance companies selected by the states through bidding.

2 — Correct: PMFBY covers post-harvest losses for up to 14 days after harvest for crops drying in the field ('cut and spread'), caused by cyclone, cyclonic rain and unseasonal rain (and, in the original guidelines, also hailstorm). This is one of its five coverage stages besides prevented sowing, standing crop, and localised calamities. Post-harvest cover was absent or limited under earlier schemes such as NAIS. Localised calamities cover hailstorm, landslide, inundation, and later cloud burst and natural fire are also covered under individual farm-level assessment.
