NASA's Kepler and TESS missions search for exoplanets. PRL Ahmedabad, in 2018, discovered a planet-like object around a Sun-like star using the PARAS spectrograph.

New Educational Policy: the National Education Policy 2020 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020. It was drafted by a committee under K. Kasturirangan and replaced the NPE 1986. It adopted a 5+3+3+4 school structure, a 3-language formula, a four-year undergraduate programme, a target of 50% Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education by 2035, and the setting up of the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) as a single regulator.
related: Mission Indradhanush was launched on 25 December 2014 by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
India was certified polio-free by the WHO on 27 March 2014.
Intensified Mission Indradhanush was launched in 2017 for 90% full immunization coverage.
The Universal Immunization Programme began in 1985.
eVIN (Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network) tracks vaccine stocks and cold-chain temperature.
Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25 June 2015 with 100 cities.
NEP 2020 was drafted by a committee under K. Kasturirangan.
Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005), under the NRHM, promotes institutional delivery.
summary: The answer is (a): Mission Indradhanush is a Government of India immunization programme for children and pregnant women. It was launched on 25 December 2014 to raise full immunization coverage against vaccine-preventable diseases.
topic_notes: Immunization in India: the Expanded Programme on Immunization began in 1978 and became the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) in 1985, expanded to all districts by 1990. The UIP covers 12 vaccine-preventable diseases (nationally for 9 and in selected areas for 3). Mission Indradhanush was launched on 25 December 2014 to push full immunization coverage up, as the annual rate of increase was only 1% a year. The first phase covered 201 districts, and the second phase covered 352 districts in 2015. Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI) was launched in 2017 to reach 90% coverage and covered 173 districts and 17 urban areas. IMI 2.0 in 2019-20 targeted 272 districts across 27 states. IMI 3.0 was launched in 2021 to cover children missed during COVID-19 disruptions. The vaccines originally included BCG, DPT, polio, measles and hepatitis B. Others were added over time, including rotavirus vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), measles-rubella (MR) and the injectable inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). Mission Indradhanush also used a cold-chain monitoring tool, eVIN, to track vaccine stock and storage temperature. India was declared polio-free by the WHO on 27 March 2014, with the last case in January 2011 in West Bengal. Maternal and neonatal tetanus was eliminated in 2015. Related health programmes include the National Health Mission (2013, merging NRHM and NUHM), Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005), Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (2016), Ayushman Bharat (2018) and Poshan Abhiyaan (2018). UPSC often tests the launch year, ministry and target group of such schemes.

ocr: With reference to pre-packaged items in India, it is mandatory to the manufacturer to put which of the following information on the main label, as per the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011? l. List of ingredients including additives 2. Nutrition information 3. Recommendations, if any, made by the medical profession about the possibility of any allergic reactions 4, Vegetarian/non-vegetarian Select the correct answer using the code given below. {a) 1, 2 and 3 (b} 2, 3 and 4 (c) 1, 2 and 4 {dj} 1 and 4 only B-APM~-P-CKB/65A
subject: Economy
detail: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 created the FSSAI (headquartered in Delhi, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare). The Packaging and Labelling Regulations, 2011 set out the mandatory particulars on a pre-packaged food label. These include the name of the food, the list of ingredients (including additives), nutritional information, the veg/non-veg declaration, the name and address of the manufacturer, net quantity, lot/batch number, date of manufacture or packing, best before/use by date, and the country of origin for imported food. The veg declaration uses a green-filled circle inside a green-outlined square for vegetarian food and a brown-filled triangle inside a brown-outlined square for non-vegetarian food. The regulations require no statement of medical-profession recommendations. Medical advice is not part of the label, though allergen declarations and some specific advisory statements are required for particular products. Elimination logic: statement 3 is the odd one out and clearly not a mandatory item, so every option containing 3 (a and b) is wrong. Between (c) and (d), nutrition information is certainly mandatory, so (d), which leaves out statement 2, is wrong. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 3, and medical recommendations on allergic reactions are not a mandatory label item.
Wrong: it includes statement 3 and omits statement 1, but list of ingredients is mandatory.
Correct: ingredients list, nutrition information and veg/non-veg symbol are all mandatory under the 2011 regulations, and statement 3 is not.
Wrong: it omits nutrition information, which is also a mandatory label requirement.
keyfact: FSSAI labels must carry ingredients, nutrition information and the veg/non-veg symbol, but not any medical-profession recommendations on allergies.
option_notes: Statements 1, 2 and 3: this combination wrongly adds the medical recommendations. Items 1 and 2 are real mandatory labelling requirements under FSSAI. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated earlier food laws such as the PFA Act, 1954 and the Fruit Products Order, and created the Food Authority. The regulations are made under Section 92 of the Act, and FSSAI is the regulator for labelling, standards and licensing.

Statements 2, 3 and 4: this combination mixes two mandatory requirements, nutrition information and the veg symbol, with one non-mandatory item. Nutrition info is expressed per 100 g/ml or per serving, and the veg/non-veg mark is a green dot or brown triangle. The FSSAI also regulates claims, such as 'low fat' or 'sugar free', through the Advertising and Claims Regulations, 2018.

Statements 1, 2 and 4: this is the correct combination. The label must carry the ingredient list in descending order by weight, nutrition information and the veg/non-veg symbol. Other mandatory particulars include the name of the food, the FSSAI licence number and logo, the manufacturer's address, net quantity, batch number, date marking, and the country of origin for imports. FSSAI also requires allergen declaration.

Statements 1 and 4 only: this is incomplete because it drops nutrition information. Nutrition labelling is mandatory for most packaged foods, with limited exemptions. FSSAI's 2020 Labelling and Display Regulations replaced the 2011 rules for many provisions, requiring bold declarations of total sugar, salt and saturated fat. A front-of-pack labelling system has been under discussion.
related: FSSAI was established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and is headquartered in New Delhi.
The vegetarian symbol is a green dot in a green square, and the non-vegetarian symbol is a brown triangle or dot in a brown square.
Ingredients must be listed in descending order of weight or volume.
Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 require the MRP and net quantity declaration.
Eat Right India is FSSAI's campaign for safe, healthy and sustainable food.
The +F logo identifies fortified foods under FSSAI.
AGMARK certifies agricultural commodities, and BIS hallmarks certify standards for gold, among other products.
The Codex Alimentarius is the international food standards body of FAO and WHO.
statements: 1 — Correct: The list of ingredients, including additives, is mandatory in descending order of composition by weight or volume at the time of manufacture. Ingredients must be listed in descending order of weight. Added colours and flavours must be declared, and class titles such as 'emulsifier' are used with INS numbers for additives. Single-ingredient foods are exempt. This helps consumers identify allergens, additives and composition, and it is a core FSSAI labelling requirement.

2 — Correct: Nutrition information per 100 g or 100 ml (or per serving) is mandatory on the label. It must state energy value, protein, carbohydrate (with sugars), fat (with saturated fat and trans fat), and any other nutrient claimed. Later FSSAI labelling rules (2020 regulations) strengthened this, requiring declaration of added sugar, salt and saturated fat, and proposing front-of-pack labelling. Some foods, such as raw or single-ingredient items, are exempt.

3 — Incorrect: There is no requirement to print medical-profession recommendations about allergic reactions. Labelling rules do require declaration of known allergens in the ingredients, as well as specific statements for certain products, such as cautions on sweeteners, caffeine-containing drinks and irradiated food. But advice attributed to the medical profession is not part of the mandatory declaration. Hence this item makes options (a) and (b) wrong.

4 — Correct: The vegetarian/non-vegetarian declaration is mandatory. Vegetarian food carries a green dot inside a green-bordered square, and non-vegetarian food carries a brown dot or triangle inside a brown-bordered square. The symbol must appear on the main label near the product name, with specified size and contrasting background. Eggs are treated as non-vegetarian, and a vegetarian claim has to be accurate. The rule dates to 2011 and was later refined.
summary: The answer is (c) 1, 2 and 4. Under the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, a pre-packaged food label must carry the list of ingredients including additives, nutrition information and the vegetarian/non-vegetarian declaration (green dot or brown triangle). Medical recommendations on allergic reactions are not a mandatory label item.
topic_notes: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 integrated eight older food laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Fruit Products Order 1955, the Meat Food Products Order 1973, the Edible Oils Packaging Order and the Milk and Milk Products Order. It established the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), a statutory body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, headquartered in New Delhi, headed by a Chairperson appointed by the Centre. FSSAI sets science-based standards, regulates manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, and licenses and registers food business operators. The Packaging and Labelling Regulations, 2011 laid down the label particulars: name of the food, ingredients list, nutrition information, veg/non-veg logo, additives declaration, manufacturer details, net quantity, batch number, date marking, country of origin and the FSSAI logo and licence number. The 2020 Labelling and Display Regulations later consolidated the labelling rules. Related regimes include the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, which require declaration of MRP, net quantity, the manufacturer or packer, consumer care details and the month and year of manufacture. Other FSSAI initiatives include Eat Right India, Fortified Rice and the +F logo for fortified food, the Food Safety Mitra scheme, the Hygiene Rating, the RUCO (Repurpose Used Cooking Oil) initiative, the Clean Street Food Hub programme, the State Food Safety Index and the FoSCoS licensing portal. Possible next questions concern the Codex Alimentarius, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Central Consumer Protection Authority, plus the standards marks AGMARK (agricultural produce) and BIS/ISI.

question: Project Loon’, sometimes seen in the news, is related to
subject: Environment
detail: Project Loon was launched by Google X in June 2013 with a pilot in Canterbury, New Zealand. It placed solar-powered balloons about 18-20 km above Earth, in the stratosphere, well above weather and air traffic. Each balloon carried a transceiver and relayed signals between ground stations, user antennas and other balloons, forming a aerial mesh network. Balloons were steered by riding wind layers moving in different directions, guided by algorithms and later machine learning. Connectivity was typically 4G/LTE through partner telecom operators on their spectrum. Loon became a separate Alphabet subsidiary in 2018, provided emergency coverage in Peru (2017) and Puerto Rico (2017, after Hurricane Maria), and began commercial service in Kenya with Telkom Kenya in 2020. Alphabet shut it down in January 2021 because it was not commercially viable. Elimination logic: the name 'Loon' (from balloon) and its association with Google point to technology and telecom, not waste, solar generation or water. Solar panels only powered the balloons, so (c) is a trap.
explanations: Incorrect: Loon had nothing to do with waste processing or disposal.
Correct: Loon provided internet access through stratospheric balloons acting as floating cell towers, which is wireless communication technology.
Incorrect: Balloons used solar panels for their own power, but the project was not about producing solar power.
Incorrect: It had no link to water conservation or harvesting.
keyfact: Project Loon = Google/Alphabet stratospheric balloons providing internet (wireless communication); closed in 2021.
option_notes: Waste management technology covers segregation, recycling, composting, waste-to-energy and landfill management. In India, the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 and Swachh Bharat Mission govern this area. Technologies include bioremediation, plasma gasification and biomethanation. It is unrelated to Project Loon, which is a common distractor in questions on tech projects.

Wireless communication technology transmits information without physical cables, using radio waves, microwaves or satellites. Examples are 4G/5G, Wi-Fi, Li-Fi, satellite internet (Starlink, OneWeb) and high-altitude platforms. Project Loon belonged here, using stratospheric balloons to extend internet to remote areas. Facebook's Aquila drone project was a comparable effort, later abandoned.

Solar power production technology converts sunlight into electricity through photovoltaic cells or concentrated solar power. India's National Solar Mission (2010) and the International Solar Alliance (launched 2015 by India and France, HQ Gurugram) are key. Project Loon's balloons used small solar panels only for their own power, not to supply electricity to others.

Water conservation technology includes rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation, watershed management, desalination and greywater recycling. Indian schemes include Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Atal Bhujal Yojana, Namami Gange and PMKSY. It is unrelated to Project Loon, which concerned internet connectivity.
related: Project Loon: Alphabet/Google X stratospheric balloon internet, shut down January 2021.
First Loon pilot was in Canterbury, New Zealand, in 2013.
Loon's commercial launch was in Kenya with Telkom Kenya in 2020.
Facebook's Aquila was a solar-powered drone for internet, cancelled in 2018.
Starlink is SpaceX's low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation.
BharatNet aims to connect gram panchayats with optical fibre.
PM-WANI is India's scheme for public Wi-Fi access networks.
Li-Fi transmits data using visible light.
summary: The answer is (b) wireless communication technology. Project Loon was an Alphabet (Google X) initiative that used high-altitude balloons in the stratosphere to deliver internet connectivity to rural and remote areas.
topic_notes: Project Loon belongs to the group of attempts to extend internet access using non-terrestrial platforms. It was developed at Google X (now X Development) under Alphabet, announced in 2013 and tested first in New Zealand. Balloons were polyethylene, about 12 m wide, flown at 18-25 km in the stratosphere. Each had solar panels, batteries, an avionics unit and an antenna. Ground-to-balloon links used the 2.4 and 5.8 GHz ISM bands, while the balloon-to-user links used licensed LTE spectrum from telecom partners. Navigation relied on adjusting altitude to catch winds blowing in desired directions. Records included a 312-day single-balloon flight in 2020. It served disaster zones in Peru and Puerto Rico and began commercial service in Kenya in July 2020. Alphabet closed Loon in January 2021 because costs were too high. Other connectivity projects: Facebook's Internet.org and Aquila solar drones (cancelled 2018), SpaceX Starlink and Amazon Kuiper (low Earth orbit satellite constellations), OneWeb (Bharti-backed), and Google's Project Titan (drones, abandoned). In India, relevant programmes include BharatNet (rural optical fibre), Digital India, and PM-WANI (public Wi-Fi hotspots). Related terms: stratosphere (about 12-50 km), High Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS), 5G, Li-Fi (light-based data transmission), and net neutrality. UPSC often frames such questions around technology projects in the news, so remember the sponsor company and the purpose.

question: Nct metering’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of promoting the
options: production and use of solar energy by the houscholds/consumers
use of piped natural gas in the kitchens of households
installation of CNG kits in motorcars
installation of water meters in urban households
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Net metering is a billing mechanism under which a consumer who generates electricity, typically from rooftop solar PV, feeds surplus power into the distribution grid. A bi-directional meter records both import and export. At the end of the billing cycle the consumer pays only for net consumption, and any surplus is carried forward as credit or settled as per the regulator's rules. It encourages decentralised renewable generation, reduces the consumer's bill and eases peak load on the grid. In India, electricity is a Concurrent List subject, so State Electricity Regulatory Commissions notify net-metering regulations under the Electricity Act, 2003. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) promotes it through the Rooftop Solar Programme Phase II (2019, target 40 GW rooftop solar by 2022, later extended) and the National Solar Mission (JNNSM, 2010). The Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 also support it, with net metering available for loads up to 500 kW or the sanctioned load, whichever is lower. Elimination: piped natural gas, CNG kits and water meters have no link to a net-billing concept. 'Metering' there would simply mean measuring consumption, with no export or credit element, so (b), (c) and (d) fail.
explanations: Correct: net metering credits households and consumers for surplus solar power exported to the grid, which promotes solar production and use.
Wrong: piped natural gas supply (City Gas Distribution) uses ordinary consumption meters, with no export or netting of gas by consumers.
Wrong: CNG kits are retrofits that convert vehicles to run on compressed natural gas, a vehicular fuel measure with no relation to net metering.
Wrong: water meters measure household water use for volumetric billing. They involve no generation by consumers, so net metering does not apply.
keyfact: Net metering = bi-directional meter that bills a rooftop-solar consumer only for net units after exporting surplus power to the grid.
option_notes: Solar energy production and use by households and consumers: rooftop solar PV systems turn sunlight into electricity for self-use. India's solar target is 280 GW by 2030 within the 500 GW non-fossil goal. Schemes include PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024), which targets 1 crore households, and the Rooftop Solar Programme. Net metering and gross metering are the two main billing models for such systems.

Piped natural gas (PNG) in kitchens: natural gas is supplied through pipelines to homes under City Gas Distribution (CGD) networks. These are authorised by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB). PNG is cleaner than LPG cylinders and is metered by volume. India aims to raise natural gas to 15% of its energy mix. Mahanagar Gas, Indraprastha Gas and Adani Total Gas are well-known CGD operators.

CNG kits in motorcars: Compressed Natural Gas is natural gas stored at about 200-250 bar and used as a cleaner vehicle fuel. Delhi's Supreme Court-ordered shift of public transport to CNG (1998 onwards, M.C. Mehta case) is a landmark. Kits retrofit petrol engines for bi-fuel use. The SATAT scheme (2018) promotes compressed biogas (CBG) production and supply as an alternative.

Water meters in urban households: these devices measure volumetric water consumption so that utilities can charge by use and discourage wastage. They are promoted under urban reforms such as AMRUT and the Jal Jeevan Mission (Urban). Water is a State subject. Metering helps reduce non-revenue water, but it has nothing to do with net metering, which concerns electricity.
related: Net metering: consumer pays only for net units (import minus export).
Gross metering: all solar power is sold to the utility at a fixed tariff.
PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) targets rooftop solar for 1 crore households.
International Solar Alliance was launched at COP21 in Paris in 2015 and is headquartered in Gurugram.
India's targets by 2030: 500 GW non-fossil capacity, of which 280 GW is solar.
MNRE is the nodal ministry for solar and renewable energy.
Virtual net metering lets housing societies or multiple consumers share the benefit of a solar plant.
summary: The answer is (a). Net metering is a billing arrangement that lets households and consumers with rooftop solar (or other renewable) systems export surplus electricity to the grid and be billed only for the net units, which is the difference between import and export.
topic_notes: Net metering is part of India's push for distributed renewable energy. Under it, a bi-directional meter records the electricity a consumer imports from and exports to the grid, and the bill reflects the net units. It differs from gross metering, where all generated power is sold to the utility at a fixed tariff and the consumer's own consumption is billed separately. Policy and legal framework: the Electricity Act, 2003 (electricity is in the Concurrent List); State Electricity Regulatory Commissions notify the detailed rules; the National Tariff Policy 2006 (amended 2016) and the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 support it. MNRE runs the schemes. The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (2010) was the start, and the Rooftop Solar Programme Phase II (2019) offers Central Financial Assistance to residential consumers (20% for most areas of the country, in a 40% subsidy slab for the first 3 kW). PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (Feb 2024) aims at rooftop solar for 1 crore households with subsidies and up to 300 units of free electricity per month. India's targets: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 280 GW solar. The International Solar Alliance (launched 2015 by India and France at COP21, headquartered at Gurugram) promotes solar globally. Related ideas for future questions: net billing, virtual net metering (for housing societies), group net metering, open access, Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO), Renewable Energy Certificates (REC), smart meters and the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme. Challenges include DISCOM revenue loss, grid stability, a lack of bi-directional meters, and caps on system size.

ocr: India’s ranking in the ‘Ease of Doing Business Index’ is sometimes seen in the news, Which of the following has declared that ranking? fa) Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) (b) World Economic Forum (ce) World Bank (d) World Trade Organization (WTO) 8. Banjaras during the medieval period of Indian history were generally {a) agriculturists (b) warriors (c) weavers {d) traders
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) index was compiled by the World Bank Group's Doing Business project, launched in 2002, with the first report in 2003. It ranked about 190 economies on a scale of 0 to 100 using indicators across the life cycle of a business: starting a business, dealing with construction permits, getting electricity, registering property, getting credit, protecting minority investors, paying taxes, trading across borders, enforcing contracts and resolving insolvency. A lower rank number means a better regulatory environment. India rose from 142 in 2014 to 130 in 2017, 100 in 2018 and 77 in 2019, and reached 63 in the 2020 report. The World Bank discontinued the series in September 2021 after data irregularities were found in the 2018 and 2020 reports (China, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Azerbaijan were involved). It announced a successor, the Business Ready (B-READY) report. Elimination: the OECD publishes economic surveys and PISA, the WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Report and Global Gender Gap Index, and the WTO administers trade rules. None of these publishes EoDB.
explanations: Incorrect: the OECD publishes economic surveys, the PISA tests and the Better Life Index, not the EoDB ranking.
Incorrect: the WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Report, Global Gender Gap Report and Global Risks Report, and its Davos meeting is the best-known event. It does not publish EoDB.
Correct: the World Bank Group's Doing Business report published the Ease of Doing Business ranking.
Incorrect: the WTO administers trade agreements and settles disputes. It publishes trade statistics, not a business-climate ranking.
keyfact: Ease of Doing Business ranking = World Bank (Doing Business report, 2003–2020, discontinued 2021); India was 63rd in 2020.
option_notes: The OECD was founded in 1961 (successor to the OEEC of 1948) and is headquartered in Paris. It is a club of about 38 mostly developed, market-economy members. India is not a member but is a key partner. It publishes the Economic Outlook, PISA (education assessment), the Better Life Index and tax policy work such as BEPS. It is a policy forum and data source rather than a lender.

The World Economic Forum is a non-profit based in Geneva, Switzerland, founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab and best known for its annual Davos meeting. Its reports include the Global Competitiveness Report, Global Gender Gap Index (India ranked 129th in 2022 and 127th in 2023), Global Risks Report, Energy Transition Index and Travel & Tourism Development Index.

The World Bank was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington, DC. The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. It lends for development and publishes the Human Capital Index, World Development Report, Logistics Performance Index and the former Doing Business report. It is discontinuing Doing Business and moving to B-READY.

The WTO was established on 1 January 1995, succeeding GATT (1947), and is headquartered in Geneva. It has about 164 members, and its highest body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets every two years. It runs the Dispute Settlement Body and administers agreements such as GATS, TRIPS, the Agreement on Agriculture and TRIMS. It does not rank business environments.
related: Doing Business report was published by the World Bank Group; the series was discontinued in 2021.
The successor to Doing Business is the B-READY (Business Ready) report.
The Global Competitiveness Report is published by the World Economic Forum.
The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO, with Cornell University and INSEAD.
The Logistics Performance Index is published by the World Bank.
The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was enacted in 2016 and boosted India's EoDB 'resolving insolvency' score.
summary: The correct answer is (c) World Bank. The Ease of Doing Business Index was published by the World Bank Group in its annual 'Doing Business' reports, which ranked economies on how easy it was to do business. India's rank was the one regularly reported in the news.
topic_notes: The Doing Business project of the World Bank Group began in 2002. It measured business regulation for domestic small and medium-sized firms in the largest business city of each economy (Delhi and Mumbai for India). The Doing Business 2020 report covered 190 economies and used 10 indicator sets. Top performers were New Zealand, Singapore and Hong Kong. India's rank was 63 in 2020, up from 77 in 2019, and the country was among the top ten improvers for several years. The Government of India, through DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade), pushed reforms such as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, GST, single-window clearances and online registration. In 2021 the World Bank withdrew the report after data irregularities, and an external review found that data had been changed in earlier editions. The replacement, Business Ready (B-READY), assesses the regulatory framework, public services and operational efficiency. Other well-known indices and their publishers: the Global Competitiveness Index (WEF), Global Innovation Index (WIPO, Cornell and INSEAD), Human Development Index (UNDP), Logistics Performance Index (World Bank), Global Hunger Index (Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide), Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International), World Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders), Economic Freedom Index (Heritage Foundation) and Global Peace Index (Institute for Economics and Peace). UPSC often asks which body publishes which index, so link each index to its publisher.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q38.
ocr: India’s ranking in the ‘Ease of Doing Business Index’ is sometimes seen in the news, Which of the following has declared that ranking? fa) Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) (b) World Economic Forum (ce) World Bank (d) World Trade Organization (WTO) 8. Banjaras during the medieval period of Indian history were generally {a) agriculturists (b) warriors (c) weavers {d) traders
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Banjaras (also called Lambadis, Lamans, Gor or Gormati) were the most important nomadic trading community of medieval India. They carried bulk goods such as grain, salt, ghee, timber and forest produce across regions where there were few good roads, using large herds of pack bullocks organised into caravans called tandas. Their services were especially valued by armies on campaign. Sikandar Lodi's period is cited for their grain trade, and Alauddin Khalji's market control used Banjara carriers to supply grain to Delhi markets. The Mughal armies depended on them as well, and Emperor Jahangir's memoirs mention them carrying grain on the Deccan routes. The 17th-century traveller Peter Mundy also described their trade. The trade-based reading of the term is the one UPSC follows, and it is a commonly repeated fact in the Medieval India section. Elimination logic: agriculturists were settled peasants (the opposite of nomadic), warriors were Rajputs, Marathas and similar groups, and weavers were artisan castes such as Julahas. Only the long-distance carrier trade fits the Banjaras. In the colonial period their livelihood declined with railways and the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, which wrongly labelled many Banjara groups as criminal.
explanations: Incorrect: Agriculturists were settled cultivators tied to land. Banjaras were nomadic and moved in caravans, though some took up farming after the decline of their trade in the colonial period.
Incorrect: Warriors were groups like the Rajputs, Marathas and Jats. Banjaras supplied armies with grain but were not the fighting force themselves.
Incorrect: Weavers were artisans, such as the Julahas, Tantis and Koshtis. Banjaras were not a weaving community.
Correct: Banjaras were nomadic grain and goods carriers who moved in tandas and supplied markets and armies. This is the official UPSC answer.
keyfact: Banjaras were medieval nomadic traders who carried grain and goods in tandas, and they supplied armies and markets.
option_notes: Agriculturists were the settled peasant classes (such as Jats, Kurmis, Reddys and Vellalas), who formed the base of the medieval land revenue system. They paid revenue under systems such as Alauddin Khalji's measurement-based assessment, Sher Shah's rai and Akbar's zabt (Todar Mal's dahsala). Khud-kasht and pahi-kasht were the two peasant categories in Mughal sources. Many of them lived in villages and were bound to the land. Banjaras differed in being mobile and trade-oriented.

Warriors in medieval India included Rajput clans (Chauhans, Sisodias, Rathores), Marathas, Jats, Sikhs and Afghans, as well as the mansabdar-based Mughal military. The Rajputs formed clan-based kingdoms and followed a code of chivalry. Mughal mansabdari with zat and sawar ranks organised military service. Banjaras were not a martial caste, though their grain supply was vital for armies on campaign.

Weavers were artisans in textile production. Examples include the Julahas (Muslim weavers), Tantis, Koshtis, Salis and Devangas. Famous centres included Dhaka (muslin), Banaras (silk and brocade), Surat, Kanchipuram, Masulipatnam and Ahmedabad. Indian textiles were exported widely through European trading companies. Banjaras did not weave, though they carried goods including textiles and other commodities.

Traders here means the Banjaras, a nomadic community found across north, west and central India and the Deccan. They carried grain, salt and other goods in large caravans (tandas) on pack bullocks. They were also known as Lambadis or Lamans in the south and Gor in some regions. Alauddin Khalji, Sikandar Lodi and the Mughals used their services, and Jahangir mentions them in his memoirs. In the colonial period they lost their livelihood and were notified under the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871. Many are now classed as Scheduled Tribes or Scheduled Castes or Denotified Tribes, depending on the state.
related: Banjaras carried grain in caravans called tandas.
Alauddin Khalji used Banjara carriers to supply grain to Delhi markets.
Banjaras are also known as Lambadis or Lamans in the south.
Criminal Tribes Act 1871 branded many nomadic groups; it was repealed in 1952.
Hundi was the credit instrument used by merchants in medieval India.
Manigramam and Ayyavole 500 were South Indian merchant guilds.
Bakarwals and Gujjars are pastoral nomads of Jammu and Kashmir.
Ease of Doing Business Index (Q37 of the same paper) was published by the World Bank, option (c).
summary: The answer is (d) traders. During the medieval period in India, the Banjaras were best known as nomadic trader-carriers who moved grain and other goods in large caravans (tandas). Their role was most prominent in transporting foodgrains to armies and to distant markets.
topic_notes: Trade and commerce in medieval India depended on both settled merchants and itinerant communities. Banjaras were the best-known nomadic carriers. They moved in large tandas, often with thousands of pack animals, and were crucial where road and river transport was limited. Sultanate rulers such as Alauddin Khalji used them for grain supply in the Delhi market, and the Mughals relied on them for provisioning their armies. Other commercial groups included Multanis and Marwaris in north and west India, Chettiars and Komatis in the south, Gujarati Banias, Armenians and Jews in port trade, and the Bohras and Khojas. Prominent trade items included textiles, spices, indigo, saltpetre, horses (imported from Central Asia and Arabia) and silver (bullion inflow from the New World). Important ports were Surat, Cambay, Calicut, Cochin, Masulipatnam and Hooghly. Merchant organisations included the Manigramam and Ayyavole 500 in the south in the earlier medieval period. The hundi was used as a credit instrument. Banjara communities were later affected by railways, the colonial forest laws and the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 (repealed in 1952; the groups were then called Denotified Tribes). Other nomadic and pastoral groups UPSC may ask about include the Gaddis (Himachal Pradesh), Gujjars and Bakarwals (Jammu and Kashmir), Maldharis (Gujarat) and Dhangars (Maharashtra). Peasant and artisan categories, along with revenue systems, are also often asked in the medieval section.

ocr: Who of the following had first deciphered the edicts of Emperor Ashoka? fa) Georg Bihler (b) James Prinsep (c) Max Miller (a) William Jones
subject: Ancient History
detail: The edicts of Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) are inscribed on rocks and pillars in Brahmi (most of the subcontinent), Kharosthi (northwest), Greek and Aramaic (Kandahar, Afghanistan). For centuries the Brahmi script was unreadable. James Prinsep, assay master at the Calcutta Mint and Secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, deciphered Brahmi in 1837, building on the work of Christian Lassen, Ramchandra and others, who had studied Brahmi-Greek bilingual coins. Prinsep also worked out that the 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' of the edicts was a Mauryan ruler. The ruler was confirmed as Ashoka only in 1915, when the Maski edict (Karnataka) used the name 'Asoka' explicitly. He also published in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Elimination: Georg Bühler was an Austrian Indologist who later worked on Ashokan inscriptions, Brahmi origins and the Indian Antiquary, but he did not first decipher them. Max Müller edited the Rig Veda and the Sacred Books of the East. William Jones founded the Asiatic Society (1784), translated Shakuntala and proposed the Indo-European language family, but he died in 1794, long before the deciphering.
explanations: Incorrect: Georg Bühler studied and edited the Ashokan inscriptions and wrote on the origin of the Indian alphabet, but this came after Prinsep's decipherment.
Correct: James Prinsep first deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837, which unlocked the Ashokan edicts.
Incorrect: Max Müller was a Sanskritist and philologist known for the Rig Veda edition and the Sacred Books of the East, not for epigraphy.
Incorrect: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in 1784 and died in 1794, well before the edicts were deciphered.
keyfact: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 and so first read Ashoka's edicts.
option_notes: Georg Bühler (1837-1898) was a German-Austrian Indologist and epigraphist. He was a professor at Elphinstone College, Bombay, and searched for Sanskrit manuscripts. He wrote 'Indian Palaeography' and 'On the Origin of the Indian Brahma Alphabet', edited the Ashokan edicts and helped with the Sacred Books of the East series. He also edited the Apastamba Dharmasutra and translated the Laws of Manu. He founded the Bombay Sanskrit Series. He died in 1898, drowning in Lake Constance.

James Prinsep (1799-1840) was an English scholar and official. He was assay master at the Calcutta Mint, editor of the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, and secretary of the Society. He deciphered Brahmi in 1837 and also Kharosthi, with coins as clues. He studied Indo-Greek coins and Gupta coins, and drew up Benares maps and surveys. Ill health forced him back to England, and he died in 1840.

Friedrich Max Müller (1823-1900) was a German-born philologist and Orientalist at Oxford. He edited the Rig Veda with Sayana's commentary, edited the 50-volume Sacred Books of the East, and promoted comparative philology and religion. He is associated with the Aryan invasion idea, which he later modified. He was called 'Moksha Mulara' in India. Bhavan in Delhi, Max Mueller Bhavan, is named for him and used by the Goethe-Institut.

Sir William Jones (1746-1794) was a British judge at the Calcutta Supreme Court and a philologist. He founded the Asiatic Society (Calcutta) in 1784 and proposed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin share a common origin, which led to Indo-European linguistics. He translated Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam and the Manusmriti ('Institutes of Hindu Law'), and promoted the Hindu and Muslim law digests.
related: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837 and was Secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal.
The Maski edict (Karnataka) names 'Asoka' explicitly; Gujarra (MP) also does.
Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts are in Kharosthi; Kandahar has Greek and Aramaic ones.
Rock Edict XIII records the Kalinga war and mentions Hellenistic rulers like Antiochus II.
The Asiatic Society was founded in 1784 by William Jones.
The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman (c. 150 CE) is the earliest long Sanskrit inscription.
Ashoka's Dhamma Mahamattas were appointed in his 13th regnal year.
Sarnath Lion Capital is India's national emblem.
summary: The correct answer is (b) James Prinsep. In 1837, this British scholar and Asiatic Society of Bengal secretary first deciphered the Brahmi script, and then the Ashokan edicts, which were written in it. The edicts called their ruler 'Devanampiya Piyadasi', and the identification of this ruler with Ashoka came later.
topic_notes: Ashokan inscriptions are the earliest deciphered, datable Indian written records on a large scale. Ashoka (r. c. 268-232 BCE), the Mauryan emperor, issued Major Rock Edicts (14, with variants at Girnar, Kalsi, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Dhauli and Jaugada), Minor Rock Edicts (Maski, Gujarra, Brahmagiri, Rupnath, Sasaram and others), Pillar Edicts (seven at Delhi-Topra, Meerut, Allahabad, Lauriya-Araraj and Lauriya-Nandangarh) and Cave Edicts (Barabar). Languages and scripts: Prakrit in Brahmi in most places; Kharosthi in Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (written right to left); Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan (Kandahar, Laghman). Ashoka calls himself 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' (beloved of the gods) and he is named Ashoka only in Maski and Gujarra edicts, along with the edict at Nittur and Udegolam. Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war (261 BCE) and conversion to Dhamma; Edict II mentions the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras; Edict XIII also names Hellenistic kings such as Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas and Alexander. Dhamma included tolerance, non-violence and welfare, with Dhamma Mahamattas appointed in the 13th regnal year. Epigraphy milestones: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi (1837); Kharosthi was deciphered through Indo-Greek coins by Prinsep and Lassen (1830s); the Piyadasi-Ashoka identification came in 1915 (Maski); the Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman (150 CE) is the earliest long Sanskrit inscription; Cunningham's ASI (1861) and Epigraphia Indica carry this work forward. The Brahmi script is the ancestor of most Indian scripts.

question:
With reference to the ‘Gram Nyayalaya Act’, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. As per the Act, Gram Nyayalayas can hear only civil cases and not criminal cases.
2. The Act allows local social activists as mediators/reconciliators. Select the correct answer uning the code given below
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 was enacted on the basis of the 114th Law Commission Report and came into force on 2 October 2009. Its aim is to give access to justice at the village level, in line with Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid). A Gram Nyayalaya is established for a group of villages at the intermediate panchayat level. It is presided over by a Nyayadhikari, who has the same salary and powers as a Judicial Magistrate of First Class and is appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court. The court has jurisdiction over both civil and criminal matters. It can try offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding two years. It can also hear civil disputes under the Schedule, such as property, wages and some rights-related matters. Procedure is summary, and the court may sit at places other than its headquarters (mobile courts). It must first try conciliation, and for this it appoints conciliators, who are social workers of integrity. Elimination: statement 1 is false because the Act covers criminal cases. That removes (a) and (c). Statement 2 is true, so (b) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is false because Gram Nyayalayas hear both civil and criminal cases.
Correct: statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true, since the Act allows social workers to serve as conciliators.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so the pair cannot both be correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: Gram Nyayalayas (Act 2008, in force 2 Oct 2009) have both civil and criminal jurisdiction and use social-worker conciliators.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would mean Gram Nyayalayas are purely civil courts. They are not. Under the 2008 Act they exercise both civil and criminal jurisdiction, as set out in the First and Second Schedules. The Nyayadhikari holds powers equal to a Judicial Magistrate of First Class. A student must remember that the statement that they hear only civil cases is a common distractor used in UPSC, and that these courts are mobile and meant to bring justice to the villager's doorstep.

Option (b), 2 only, is the correct answer. The Act provides for conciliators, who are social workers with integrity and suitable qualifications. Conciliation is mandatory as a first step in civil matters. The Gram Nyayalayas Act came into force on 2 October 2009. Each court is established for a village group at intermediate panchayat level, and the State Government appoints the Nyayadhikari in consultation with the High Court. The Act follows the Law Commission's 114th report and Article 39A of the Constitution.

Option (c), 1 and 2, is wrong because statement 1 is false. The Act does give a role to social workers as conciliators, but it does not limit the courts to civil cases. A student should note how UPSC mixes one true and one false statement. Gram Nyayalayas try offences with punishment up to two years, and civil disputes such as property, wages, and rights under various welfare laws are also within their jurisdiction.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2, is wrong because statement 2 is true. The Act expressly appoints conciliators drawn from social workers. The Gram Nyayalaya is a court of the first instance with summary procedure. The Act allows evidence to be recorded in a simplified manner, and the court is not strictly bound by the Indian Evidence Act, instead being guided by principles of natural justice. The Centre supports setting up these courts through financial assistance to States, though adoption has been slow.
related: Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 came into force on 2 October 2009.
Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
The Nyayadhikari has the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of First Class.
Gram Nyayalayas try civil and criminal cases and use conciliation first.
Lok Adalats were given statutory status by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
NALSA was constituted in 1995 and is headed by the Chief Justice of India as Patron-in-Chief.
The 114th Law Commission Report recommended Gram Nyayalayas.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Gram Nyayalayas have both civil and criminal jurisdiction. Under the Act, they try criminal offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment above two years. They also hear civil disputes listed in the Second Schedule. The First Schedule lists the criminal matters and the Second Schedule the civil ones. The Central and State Governments can amend the jurisdiction. Appeals in criminal cases go to the Sessions Court, which must dispose of them within six months. Appeals in civil cases go to the District Court. The court follows summary procedure and gives priority to plea bargaining and conciliation. Judgments are to be delivered within 30 days of the trial's conclusion and are subject to a time-bound disposal norm, with civil cases ideally decided within six months.

2 — Correct: The Act provides for conciliators, who are appointed by the High Court-approved process, and these are social workers with integrity and suitable qualifications. Section 27 of the Act deals with conciliators. The Gram Nyayalaya must first try to settle civil disputes through conciliation, and it uses the services of these conciliators. A conciliator is a person with a record of social service, and retired judicial officers or others may be considered. Their appointment is intended to reduce litigation and keep justice informal and local. The Nyayadhikari is not a conciliator but may take their help. Conciliation settlements are recorded and treated as decrees of the court, which makes them enforceable like court judgments.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 lets these courts try both civil and criminal cases, so statement 1 is wrong. It also provides for appointing social workers with suitable qualifications as conciliators, so statement 2 is correct.
topic_notes: The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 was passed to provide inexpensive and speedy justice at the grassroots, implementing Article 39A, which directs the State to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied because of economic or other disabilities. It rests on the Law Commission's 114th Report (1986). The Act came into force on 2 October 2009. Key features: the State Government, after consulting the High Court, establishes one or more Gram Nyayalayas for each Panchayat at the intermediate level or for a group of contiguous Panchayats. The presiding officer is the Nyayadhikari, who has the same salary, authority and powers as a Judicial Magistrate of First Class, and is appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court. The court sits at its headquarters but may hold proceedings in villages, so it works as a mobile court. It exercises civil and criminal jurisdiction. Criminal cases include offences not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding two years. Civil cases are those listed in the Second Schedule. Summary procedure applies, and the court tries to resolve matters through conciliation and plea bargaining. Appeals in criminal cases lie to the Sessions Court and in civil cases to the District Court, to be disposed of within six months. Conciliators are social workers. Related ideas that UPSC may ask: Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which give binding awards; Nyaya Panchayats; the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), created in 1995; Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive); the Fast Track Courts; and Family Courts. Implementation has been limited, as only a limited number of States have operationalised the courts because of funding and infrastructure constraints.

subject: Current Affairs
detail: The TPP was signed on 4 February 2016 in Auckland by 12 countries: the USA, Japan, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Peru, Chile, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Vietnam. It grew out of the P4 agreement (2005) of Chile, New Zealand, Singapore and Brunei. Its scope covered tariff elimination, services, investment, intellectual property, e-commerce, labour and environment standards, state-owned enterprises and dispute settlement (including ISDS). Statement 1 is wrong because 'all Pacific Rim countries except China and Russia' overstates membership. Many Pacific Rim states, such as South Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Taiwan, Colombia and Ecuador, were never members, so the exclusion was not limited to China and Russia. Statement 2 is wrong because the TPP was not a security alliance; it was a trade pact, and maritime security 'only' is plainly incorrect. Elimination: once either statement is shown false, only (d) can stand, and here both fail. In January 2017 the USA withdrew, and the remaining 11 signed the CPTPP in March 2018 (in force 30 December 2018).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false: the TPP had only 12 members, and many Pacific Rim countries were never part of it, so it was not 'all except China and Russia'.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false: the TPP was a trade and investment agreement, not a maritime-security alliance.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be true.
(d) is correct because statement 1 misstates the membership and statement 2 misdescribes the nature of the agreement.
keyfact: TPP = 12-nation Pacific Rim trade pact (signed 2016, US quit 2017, became 11-member CPTPP in 2018); not a security alliance and not open to all Pacific Rim states.
option_notes: Option (a), 'Statement 1 only', would hold only if the TPP covered every Pacific Rim state apart from China and Russia. It did not: it had 12 signatories, and countries like South Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand were outside it. The TPP was signed on 4 February 2016 in Auckland, never entered into force in that form because the USA withdrew in January 2017, and was succeeded by the CPTPP with 11 members.

Option (b), 'Statement 2 only', would describe the TPP as a maritime-security alliance. That is wrong. Maritime or strategic alliances in the region include ANZUS (Australia, NZ, US, 1951), the Quad (India, US, Japan, Australia), AUKUS (2021) and US bilateral treaties with Japan, the Philippines and South Korea. The TPP, by contrast, was purely a trade, investment and regulatory-standards agreement, though it had strategic subtext for the US.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', would require both statements to be true. Both are false. It is a typical UPSC distractor combining a partly plausible claim about geography with a wrongly framed purpose. The TPP's reality: 12 members, covering about 40% of world GDP and about a third of world trade, negotiated since 2010 and signed in 2016, with 30 chapters on trade and related rules.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is the official answer. The TPP was a 12-nation mega-regional trade deal: the USA, Japan, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Peru, Chile, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Vietnam. China and India were not members. After the US withdrawal in 2017, the remaining 11 concluded the CPTPP (signed in Santiago, 8 March 2018, in force 30 December 2018). The UK joined CPTPP in 2023.
related: TPP was signed in Auckland on 4 February 2016 by 12 countries.
The US formally withdrew from the TPP on 23 January 2017 under President Trump.
CPTPP was signed in March 2018 and came into force on 30 December 2018 with 11 members.
India is not a member of TPP, CPTPP or APEC, and withdrew from RCEP negotiations in November 2019.
RCEP came into force on 1 January 2022 and includes ASEAN plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand.
IPEF was launched in May 2022 by the USA, and India is a member.
The UK acceded to the CPTPP, with the accession protocol signed in July 2023.
The P4 agreement of 2005 (Brunei, Chile, New Zealand, Singapore) was the origin of the TPP.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Membership was 12 specific countries, not all Pacific Rim states, and the exclusion was not simply China and Russia. The TPP was negotiated from 2010 to 2015 and signed in Auckland on 4 February 2016. Members were the USA, Japan, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Peru, Chile, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Vietnam. China was not part of it, and the US framed it as a way to set trade rules in the Asia-Pacific. Several Pacific Rim economies (South Korea, Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand, Taiwan) stayed out, though some expressed interest. The 12 together accounted for about 40% of global GDP. After the US withdrawal on 23 January 2017, the others continued as the CPTPP.

2 — Incorrect: The TPP was a trade and economic integration agreement, not a strategic or maritime-security alliance. It covered market access, rules of origin, services, investment, intellectual property, labour, environment, SOEs and e-commerce. Strategic motives (balancing China's rise, part of the US 'pivot to Asia') were discussed by commentators, but the treaty text had no defence or maritime security obligations. Maritime and security cooperation in the region is handled by arrangements like ANZUS, the Quad, bilateral US alliances and ASEAN-led forums. The TPP's comparable counterpart on the Chinese side was RCEP, which is also a trade pact.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. The Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) was a mega-regional trade and investment agreement among 12 Pacific Rim countries, not a pact covering all Pacific Rim countries, and it was an economic agreement, not a maritime-security alliance.
topic_notes: The Trans-Pacific Partnership originated from the P4 (Trans-Pacific Strategic Economic Partnership) agreement of 2005 between Brunei, Chile, New Zealand and Singapore. The USA joined negotiations in 2008-2010 under Presidents Bush and then Obama, who made the TPP the economic pillar of the 'pivot to Asia'. Negotiations concluded in October 2015 in Atlanta, and the deal was signed on 4 February 2016 in Auckland by 12 countries. Together they represented roughly 40% of global GDP. The text had 30 chapters covering tariff cuts, services, investment, intellectual property, labour, environment, state-owned enterprises, e-commerce and investor-state dispute settlement. Critics raised concerns about IP rules, medicine prices, sovereignty and ISDS. On 23 January 2017 President Trump withdrew the US, so the agreement could not enter into force because the ratification threshold needed the US and Japan. The remaining 11 countries negotiated the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), signed 8 March 2018 in Santiago and in force from 30 December 2018. Some of the original provisions, especially on IP, were suspended. The UK acceded in December 2024 (after accession talks concluded in 2023). China, Taiwan, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Uruguay, Ukraine and Indonesia have applied or expressed interest. India is not a member. Related groupings: RCEP (15 members, in force January 2022, India withdrew in November 2019), APEC (21 economies, India not a member), USMCA (replaced NAFTA in 2020), and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF, launched May 2022, India is a member). UPSC may also ask about the WTO, plurilateral and mega-regional trade agreements, rules of origin and ISDS.

ocr: Consider the following statements : The India-Africa Summit 1. held in 2015 was the third such Summit 2. was actually initiated by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1951 -— Which of the statements given above is/are correct? faj 1 only (b}) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 fd) Neither 1 nor 2 16 B-APM-P-CKB/65A
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The India-Africa Forum Summit (IAFS) is the institutional framework for India's engagement with the African continent. The first summit was held in New Delhi in April 2008, the second in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia in May 2011, and the third in New Delhi in October 2015. The 2015 summit was the largest diplomatic gathering hosted by India since the 1983 NAM summit, with all 54 African countries invited and most represented by heads of state or government. Its theme was 'Partnership, Shared Agenda'. Outcomes included a Delhi Declaration, a Framework for Cooperation, a concessional credit line of USD 10 billion over five years and a grant assistance of USD 600 million, including 50,000 scholarships. Nehru was a strong supporter of decolonisation in Africa and Asia and of Afro-Asian solidarity (Bandung Conference 1955), but no India-Africa Summit was initiated by him in 1951. Elimination logic: statement 1 is verifiably correct, so (b) and (c) are out; statement 2 is a fabricated historical claim, so (d) is out. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is true (2015 was the third IAFS) and statement 2 is false (Nehru did not initiate it in 1951), so only 1 is correct.
Incorrect. Statement 2 is false, since no India-Africa Summit was initiated by Nehru in 1951. The formal series began in 2008.
Incorrect. It would require statement 2 to be correct, but the claim about Nehru in 1951 is historically baseless.
Incorrect. Statement 1 is correct: the October 2015 summit was the third IAFS, so 'neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: IAFS: 2008 Delhi, 2011 Addis Ababa, 2015 Delhi (third, all 54 African states); not initiated by Nehru in 1951.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: The 2015 IAFS-III in New Delhi was the third summit in the series (2008 New Delhi, 2011 Addis Ababa, 2015 New Delhi). It had all 54 African nations invited, a USD 10 billion credit line offer, USD 600 million grants and 50,000 scholarships. It is the official answer because only the first statement is accurate.

Option (b) 2 only: This would mean Nehru started the summit in 1951 and that the 2015 summit was not the third. Both are wrong. Nehru's Africa policy was about anti-colonialism, support for independence movements, opposition to apartheid and Afro-Asian solidarity (Bandung 1955), but not a summit-format engagement. The structured IAFS began only in 2008.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: This would need Nehru's 1951 initiative to be true. No such summit existed in 1951. Nehru's engagement with Africa was via the UN, the Asian Relations Conference (1947), Bandung (1955) and NAM (founded 1961 in Belgrade, with Nehru as a co-founder). The 1951 claim is a distractor invented by the question setter.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: This would deny that the 2015 summit was the third. In fact it was: the first IAFS was in April 2008 in New Delhi, the second in May 2011 in Addis Ababa, and the third in October 2015 in New Delhi. So at least statement 1 is correct, ruling this option out.
related: IAFS-I was held in New Delhi in 2008, IAFS-II in Addis Ababa in 2011 and IAFS-III in New Delhi in 2015.
IAFS-III (2015) invited all 54 African countries; theme 'Partnership, Shared Agenda'.
India offered USD 10 billion in concessional credit and USD 600 million grant at IAFS-III.
The African Union became a permanent member of the G20 at the 2023 New Delhi summit.
The African Union is headquartered in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
The Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC) is an India-Japan initiative announced in 2017.
The Pan-African e-Network (2009) provides tele-education and telemedicine services to African nations.
The Bandung Conference (1955) was the first large Afro-Asian conference, and Nehru was a key figure.
statements: 1 — Correct: The 2015 summit in New Delhi was indeed the third IAFS, after 2008 (New Delhi) and 2011 (Addis Ababa). Facts: IAFS-III was held on 26-29 October 2015 at New Delhi, with participation from all 54 African states, and about 40 were represented at head of state or government level. Its theme was 'Partnership, Shared Agenda'. India announced USD 10 billion concessional credit and USD 600 million grant, including an India-Africa Development Fund and Health Fund, and 50,000 scholarships over five years. The summit adopted the Delhi Declaration 2015 and the India-Africa Framework for Strategic Cooperation. The 2015 summit was postponed from 2014 due to the Ebola outbreak. A fourth summit has been repeatedly delayed.

2 — Incorrect: Nehru did not initiate the India-Africa Summit in 1951. The summit process began in 2008. Facts: Nehru championed anti-colonialism, Afro-Asian unity and the Non-Aligned Movement, and India supported African independence movements and opposed apartheid in South Africa, raising it at the UN as early as 1946. The Asian Relations Conference was held in 1947, and the Bandung Afro-Asian Conference in 1955 was a key milestone where Nehru played a central role. However, the structured IAFS, with a formal summit-level format, was launched in 2008 under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, building on earlier engagements like the Techno-Economic Approach for Africa-India Movement (TEAM-9) in 2004 and the Pan-African e-Network in 2009.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. The India-Africa Forum Summit held in New Delhi in October 2015 was the third such summit (after Delhi 2008 and Addis Ababa 2011). Statement 2 is wrong because the summit series was not initiated by Nehru in 1951; the formal IAFS process began in 2008 under Manmohan Singh.
topic_notes: India-Africa Forum Summit (IAFS) is the apex framework of India-Africa relations. IAFS-I: New Delhi, April 2008, with 14 African countries (representing regional groupings) and adoption of the Delhi Declaration and Framework for Cooperation. IAFS-II: Addis Ababa, May 2011, with the Addis Ababa Declaration and a USD 5 billion credit offer. IAFS-III: New Delhi, 26-29 October 2015, all 54 African countries, USD 10 billion credit and USD 600 million grants. Historical background: India's links with Africa go back through Indian Ocean trade; Gandhi's South African years (1893-1914) shaped his satyagraha; Nehru backed decolonisation and opposed apartheid, and India was the first country to impose a trade embargo on South Africa (1946). Key initiatives: Pan-African e-Network (2009, for tele-education and telemedicine), Team-9 initiative (2004, West Africa), Focus Africa Programme (2002), India-Africa Skills Development Centres, and the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) programme. India also co-founded the International Solar Alliance (ISA) with France in 2015, in which many African countries are members. India's trade with Africa is above USD 90 billion, with India among the top trading partners of the continent. Major imports from Africa are crude oil, gold and pulses. In 2023, the African Union was made a permanent member of the G20 at the New Delhi G20 summit, under India's presidency. Other related frameworks: Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), a joint India-Japan vision announced in 2016-17. Africa is also a major focus of India's Lines of Credit under EXIM Bank, and India has opened many new embassies in African countries since 2018. UPSC could ask about AU headquarters (Addis Ababa), AfCFTA, Bandung Conference, NAM, ISA, AAGC and G20 membership.

ocr: What is/are the purpose/ purposes of the ‘Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)’ announced by RBI? 1. These guidelines help improve the transparency in the methodology followed by banks for determining _ the interest rates on advances. 2. These guidelines help ensure availability of bank credit at interest rates which are fair to the borrowers as well as the banks. Select the correct answer aca the code given below. (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither’ 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) was introduced by the RBI on 1 April 2016 as the internal benchmark for banks' lending rates, replacing the Base Rate system (in force since July 2010, which had replaced the BPLR). The Base Rate was criticised because it was based on average cost of funds, so cuts in the repo rate were transmitted to borrowers slowly and the method was opaque. MCLR is computed from four components: marginal cost of funds (the largest weight, mainly deposit rates and borrowings), negative carry on CRR, operating costs, and a tenor premium. Banks publish MCLR for overnight, 1-month, 3-month, 6-month, 1-year and longer tenors, and review it monthly. Loans are priced as MCLR plus a spread, with reset periodically. Because marginal cost reflects current funding conditions, policy rate changes pass through faster, and the published methodology improves transparency. The framework aims for fairness to borrowers (quicker rate cuts) and to banks (viable margins, sustaining credit supply). Both statements reflect the stated objectives, so (c). Options (a), (b) and (d) each wrongly deny one or both of these objectives. Later, from 1 October 2019, external benchmark-linked lending (repo rate etc.) became mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSME loans.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is also a stated purpose of MCLR, so 'Statement 1 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, since MCLR was designed to make the rate-setting methodology transparent, so '2 only' is incomplete.
Correct: both the transparency of methodology and fair, available credit for borrowers and banks are stated objectives of the MCLR guidelines.
Wrong: at least one, in fact both, statements describe the real purposes of MCLR.
keyfact: MCLR (1 April 2016) replaced the Base Rate to make loan pricing transparent, speed up transmission of policy rates, and keep credit fair for both borrowers and banks.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' covers transparency in methodology. Transparency is a real aim of MCLR, as banks must disclose a defined formula built from marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating costs and tenor premium. Alone the option is incomplete, because the guidelines also aim at fair credit availability and better monetary policy transmission. The MCLR regime started on 1 April 2016, replacing the Base Rate, and banks publish MCLR for several tenors and review it monthly.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' covers fairness of rates to borrowers and banks and the availability of credit. This reflects MCLR's goal of better transmission of policy rates while keeping bank margins viable. It is incomplete alone because transparency is also an explicit aim. Before MCLR the Base Rate (July 2010) used average cost of funds, which responded slowly to repo rate changes, one reason RBI moved to a marginal-cost approach in 2016.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is the correct answer. MCLR, effective 1 April 2016, is the internal benchmark below which banks cannot normally lend, with exceptions such as certain government-sponsored schemes. Loans are priced as MCLR plus spread. It improves transparency and transmission and keeps credit flowing at fair rates. Later, from 1 October 2019, external benchmarks (repo rate, T-bill yields) became mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSME loans, complementing MCLR.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is wrong because it denies both real purposes. MCLR replaced the Base Rate system, itself introduced in July 2010 in place of the Benchmark Prime Lending Rate (BPLR, 2003). Each reform tried to make loan pricing more transparent and policy transmission more effective. Rejecting both statements ignores the central aim of the 2016 reform, so this option is eliminated.
related: MCLR came into effect on 1 April 2016, replacing the Base Rate.
Base Rate system started in July 2010; BPLR in 2003.
MCLR components: marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating costs, tenor premium.
From 1 October 2019, new floating-rate retail and MSME loans must be linked to an external benchmark such as the repo rate.
The Monetary Policy Committee (six members) was statutorily formed in 2016 to set the repo rate.
Inflation target is 4% with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%.
Negative carry on CRR arises because banks earn no interest on CRR balances kept with RBI.
FBIL (Financial Benchmarks India Pvt. Ltd.) publishes benchmark rates such as T-bill yields.
statements: 1 — Correct: The MCLR guidelines were meant to improve transparency in how banks determine lending rates, because the formula's components are defined and disclosed. Fact note: Before MCLR, the Base Rate (from 1 July 2010) was calculated on the average cost of funds, which was opaque and made transmission of policy rate changes sluggish. RBI's April 2016 guidelines, following an internal study group, specified that MCLR comprises marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating costs and tenor premium. Banks must publish MCLR for several tenors and review it monthly. The board-approved methodology must be disclosed, which improves clarity for borrowers.

2 — Correct: The guidelines aim to ensure credit availability at rates fair to both borrowers and banks, and to improve monetary policy transmission. Fact note: Using marginal rather than average cost of funds means that when deposit rates and the repo rate fall, lending rates fall faster, benefiting borrowers, while banks keep their cost-based margins and so remain willing to lend. MCLR-linked loans reset at intervals (often annually), and the spread over MCLR cannot be changed arbitrarily for existing borrowers except on credit-risk grounds. Since 1 April 2016 MCLR has been the internal benchmark; since 1 October 2019 external benchmarks are mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSME loans.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. RBI's MCLR framework, effective 1 April 2016, replaced the Base Rate system to make banks' loan pricing more transparent and to ensure credit is available at rates fair to both borrowers and banks.
topic_notes: MCLR is the internal benchmark lending rate system of Indian scheduled commercial banks, introduced by the RBI with effect from 1 April 2016 following the report of an internal study group on the marginal cost methodology. It replaced the Base Rate regime (July 2010), which had itself replaced the BPLR (2003). Components: (1) marginal cost of funds, with the highest weight, consisting of marginal cost of borrowings (about 92% weight) and return on net worth (about 8%); (2) negative carry on CRR, arising because banks earn no interest on CRR balances; (3) operating costs; (4) tenor premium, reflecting the longer maturity of loans. Banks publish MCLR for overnight, one month, three months, six months, one year and, in some cases, longer tenors, and review it monthly. Actual lending rate equals MCLR plus a spread, which includes credit risk premium and other charges. The reset frequency of the loan, often one year, determines how soon borrowers get the benefit of changes. Exceptions: loans to employees, fixed-rate loans, and certain loans under government schemes can be priced outside the MCLR floor. Limitations: transmission remained slow because deposit rates are sticky and banks' cost of funds includes legacy deposits. Hence RBI moved to external benchmark-linked lending rates (EBLR) from 1 October 2019 for new floating-rate retail loans and MSME loans, with benchmarks such as the repo rate, 91-day or 182-day T-bill yield, or another benchmark published by FBIL. Related concepts for prelims: repo rate, reverse repo, marginal standing facility (MSF), bank rate, CRR, SLR, monetary transmission, Monetary Policy Committee (set up in 2016 under the RBI Act amendment), and the shift to inflation targeting (4% with a ±2% band).

ocr: What is/are unique about ‘Kharai camel’, a breed found in India? 1. It is capable of swimming up to three kilometres in seawater. 2. It survives by grazing on mangroves, 3. It lives in the wild and cannot be domesticated. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (cj) 1 and 3 only {d) 1,2 and 3
subject: Environment
detail: Kharai (meaning 'salty' in Gujarati) is a camel breed of the coastal Kachchh (Kutch) region and nearby areas of Gujarat. It is among the few camel populations in the world that is adapted to a saline, tidal, mangrove ecosystem. It can swim in seawater for long distances, reported up to about 3 km, to reach islands with mangrove vegetation, and it survives mainly by browsing on mangroves such as Avicennia marina (and halophytic plants). It is a domesticated breed, looked after by pastoral communities such as the Fakirani Jats and Rabaris, and is not a wild animal. Kharai was recognised by the National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources (NBAGR, Karnal) as India's 8th camel breed (2015). Its numbers have dropped because of restricted access to mangroves (forest-department curbs, Kutch coastal protected areas), industrial development and a shift in pastoral livelihoods. Elimination logic: statement 3 is false because the breed is domesticated and managed by herders, which rules out (b), (c) and (d). Only (a) remains, consistent with the official answer.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true (swimming in seawater and grazing on mangroves), and statement 3 is false. This matches the official answer.
Incorrect. It says only statement 3 is true, but the Kharai is domesticated, so statement 3 is false. It also leaves out statements 1 and 2, which are true.
Incorrect. It pairs statement 1 (true) with statement 3 (false). Statement 2, about mangrove grazing, is true and is left out.
Incorrect. It includes statement 3, which is false because the breed is domesticated and managed by herders.
keyfact: Kharai camel (Kutch, Gujarat): a domesticated breed that swims in the sea and eats mangroves; the answer is 1 and 2 only.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 and 2 only', is the official answer, and it gives the correct combination for this question. The Kharai camel is a Kutch breed that swims and feeds on mangroves, and it is a domesticated breed.

Option (b), '3 only', would suggest the Kharai is a wild animal that cannot be domesticated. That is false. The Kharai is a domesticated breed, reared by pastoral communities, and was recognised as a breed by NBAGR.
Option (c), '1 and 3 only', combines the correct swimming claim with the incorrect wild-animal claim. It is wrong because it omits the mangrove diet and includes the false claim about being wild.
Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', adds the false statement 3 to the true statements 1 and 2. It is wrong because the Kharai is not a wild animal.
related: The Kharai camel is native to Kachchh (Kutch), Gujarat.
Kharai means 'salty' in Gujarati.
The breed is recognised by NBAGR (Karnal), which registers India's animal genetic resources.
Rajasthan has the largest camel population in India; the National Research Centre on Camel is at Bikaner.
Fakirani Jats and Rabaris are the main Kharai herders.
The Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park (1982) was India's first marine national park.
Avicennia marina is the main mangrove species eaten by Kharai camels.
The wild Bactrian camel (Camelus ferus) is critically endangered and is not found in India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Kharai camels are well known for swimming through shallow sea and creeks to reach mangrove islands, reported up to about 3 km. This is a rare trait among camels. Kharai means 'salty' in Gujarati, and the swimming ability is the breed's most distinctive feature. The animals live in the Kachchh coastal belt (Bhachau, Rapar, Lakhpat, Abdasa and Mundra talukas) and move between mainland pastures and mangrove islands with the tides. Herders let them swim, and the camels may remain at sea for hours. The ability reflects adaptation to a tidal, saline ecosystem and is the basis of the breed's recognition as a genetic resource.

2 — Correct: Kharai camels feed mainly on mangrove foliage, especially Avicennia marina (grey mangrove), along with salt-tolerant shrubs, and are among the few large mammals to rely on mangroves. They can tolerate saline water and a high-salt diet. Mangroves in Kutch are part of the Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park and Sanctuary (India's first marine national park, 1982) region and the Indus delta fringe. Restriction on grazing in protected mangroves has been a serious threat to the breed, which led to herders' legal petitions and to conservation attention from groups such as Sahjeevan, which works on pastoralist rights and the breed's conservation.

3 — Incorrect: The Kharai camel is not wild; it is a domesticated breed reared by pastoralist communities such as the Fakirani Jats and Rabaris, who keep it for milk, breeding and transport and sometimes for wool. The only wild camel found in India historically is not the Kharai; true wild camels are the Bactrian (Camelus ferus) of Central Asia, so Indian camels are domesticated types. The Kharai was accepted in 2015 by the NBAGR as a registered camel breed, which would not apply to a wild animal. Other Indian breeds include Bikaneri, Jaisalmeri, Kachchhi, Mewari and Marwari.
