It oversees the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) in Mumbai. It also oversaw CIPAM, created in 2016 as a Section 8-type body for implementing the policy. In January 2019 DIPP was renamed the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). Copyright, however, is handled by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, and the Copyright Office, which is a nuance UPSC may test.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The National IPR Policy 2016 explicitly reiterates India's commitment to the Doha Development Agenda and the TRIPS Agreement (with their flexibilities), and DIPP (now DPIIT) is the nodal department for IPR matters in India.
topic_notes: The National IPR Policy 2016 was approved by the Union Cabinet on 12 May 2016. It followed a think-tank and draft stage in 2014-15 and is a vision document, not legislation. Its slogan is 'Creative India; Innovative India'. It has seven objectives: IPR awareness; creation of IPRs; legal and legislative framework; administration and management; commercialisation; enforcement and adjudication; and human capital development. DIPP, now DPIIT, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, is the nodal department, and CIPAM, set up in 2016, is the implementing cell. The policy covers all IPR forms: patents, copyright, trademarks, industrial designs, geographical indications, plant varieties, semiconductor integrated circuit layouts, and traditional knowledge. It recommended bringing all IP offices under one roof. The CGPDTM, based in Mumbai, administers the Patents Act 1970 (amended 2005), the Trade Marks Act 1999, the Designs Act 2000 and the Geographical Indications of Goods Act 1999. Copyright Act 1957 is administered by the Ministry of Education. The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001 is under Agriculture. The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000 is under MeitY. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) was abolished in 2021 by the Tribunals Reforms Act, and its functions moved to High Courts. Internationally, WIPO (Geneva, 1967 convention, UN agency since 1974) administers IP treaties, including the Patent Cooperation Treaty, Madrid Protocol and Berne Convention. India joined the Budapest Treaty and Madrid Protocol in 2013. Section 3(d) of the Patents Act prevents evergreening, as in the Novartis v. Union of India case (2013). Section 84 provides for compulsory licensing, first used for Natco's sorafenib (Nexavar) in 2012. India is on the USTR Special 301 Priority Watch List. National IPR Awareness Mission and the IP Yatra are related initiatives.

question:
According to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which of the following animals cannot be hunted by any person except under some provisions provided by law ? ly Gharial
2. Indian wild ass
3. Wild buffalo Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: Section 9 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 prohibits hunting of any wild animal listed in Schedules I to IV. Hunting is permitted only under Section 11 (animals dangerous to human life or property, or disabled or diseased beyond recovery, on the Chief Wildlife Warden's order) and Section 12 (capture or hunting for education, scientific research, scientific management, or collecting specimens for zoos or museums, with permission). Section 11 also allows killing in self-defence. Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II carry the highest protection, with the severest penalties under Section 51: imprisonment of three to seven years and a fine of at least Rs 10,000 for a first offence. The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus), the Indian wild ass or khur (Equus hemionus khur) and the wild buffalo (Bubalus arnee) are all Schedule I species. Elimination logic: once a candidate knows that even one of 2 or 3 is on Schedule I, options (a) and (c)/(b) become doubtful, and the three-animal combination in (d) holds. Schedule VI covers protected plants, and Schedule V covers vermin, which may be hunted.
explanations: Wrong: it names only the gharial, but the Indian wild ass and wild buffalo are also on Schedule I and equally protected.
Wrong: it omits the gharial, which is Schedule I, so the set is incomplete.
Wrong: it omits the Indian wild ass, also a Schedule I species.
Correct: the gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo are all Schedule I animals, which cannot be hunted except under the exceptions in Sections 11 and 12.
keyfact: Gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo are all Schedule I animals under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, so hunting is barred except under Sections 11 and 12.
option_notes: Gharial alone: a fish-eating crocodilian with a long thin snout, found in the Chambal, Gandak and Girwa rivers. It is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and on Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. Project Crocodile began in 1975. The National Chambal Sanctuary is its major stronghold. It is also in CITES Appendix I.

Indian wild ass and wild buffalo: the Indian wild ass (khur) lives in the Little Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, and is Near Threatened on the IUCN list. The wild buffalo is Endangered and found mainly in Assam's Kaziranga and Manas. Both are on Schedule I. Neither is on its own the full answer, because the gharial is also protected.

Gharial and wild buffalo: both are Schedule I species. The wild buffalo (Bubalus arnee) is the ancestor of domestic water buffalo and is Endangered. The gharial is Critically Endangered. This pair omits the khur, which is the Indian wild ass of Gujarat's Little Rann of Kutch, a species protected under Schedule I.

All three: gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo. Together they show Schedule I covering a reptile and two mammals. Schedule I species get the strongest legal protection, with penalties of three to seven years in prison and a fine of at least Rs 10,000 for a first offence. Hunting is permitted only under Sections 11 and 12.
related: Section 9 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act bans hunting; Sections 11 and 12 give the exceptions.
The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 cut the schedules from six to four.
Wildlife was moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
The Little Rann of Kutch Wild Ass Sanctuary protects the Indian wild ass (khur).
Gharial is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List; its stronghold is the National Chambal Sanctuary.
The National Board for Wildlife is chaired by the Prime Minister.
Section 35 deals with national parks, Section 36A with conservation reserves and Section 36C with community reserves.
statements: 1 — Correct: The gharial is on Schedule I of the Act, so hunting is banned except under Sections 11 and 12. The gharial is a fish-eating crocodilian of the Indian subcontinent, with a long narrow snout and, in males, a bulbous 'ghara' at the snout tip. The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. It lives in the Chambal, Girwa, Gandak and Ramganga rivers, and the National Chambal Sanctuary is the main stronghold. Project Crocodile, launched in 1975, ran captive breeding and release programmes. It is also protected under CITES Appendix I.

2 — Correct: The Indian wild ass (khur) is on Schedule I. It is a subspecies of the Asiatic wild ass and is found only in the Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, with some in adjoining areas. The Wild Ass Sanctuary in the Little Rann of Kutch was established in 1972 and is the last home of the species in India. The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened, an improvement from earlier Endangered status. Its population has risen to more than 6,000. It is a fast runner, reaching about 70 km/h.

3 — Correct: The wild buffalo (Bubalus arnee) is on Schedule I. It is also called the Asiatic wild buffalo or arna, and is the wild ancestor of the domestic water buffalo. The IUCN lists it as Endangered. In India it survives mainly in Assam (Kaziranga, Manas), with small numbers in Meghalaya, Chhattisgarh (Udanti-Sitanadi) and Arunachal. It is Assam's state-linked flagship species in Manas. Threats include hybridisation with domestic buffalo, habitat loss and disease. It is also in CITES Appendix III (Nepal) and is protected by the Act.
summary: The answer is (d): Gharial, Indian wild ass and wild buffalo all cannot be hunted except under the narrow exceptions the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 allows. All three are listed on Schedule I, which gives the highest protection and the heaviest penalties.
topic_notes: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted to protect wild animals, birds and plants and to regulate trade in wildlife products. It was passed by Parliament under Article 252, with states adopting it, and Jammu and Kashmir adopted it later. The Act was moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976), when forests and protection of wild animals and birds were transferred from the State List. Key amendments came in 1991, 2002 and 2006, and the 2022 amendment reduced schedules from six to four and gave effect to CITES. The 2006 amendment created the National Tiger Conservation Authority and the Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control Bureau (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau). Original schedules: Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II give absolute protection with the highest penalties; Schedule III and IV give protection with lesser penalties; Schedule V lists vermin (such as common crow, fruit bats, rats and mice); Schedule VI lists protected plants (such as beddomes cycad, blue vanda, pitcher plant, red vanda, Kuth). The 2022 amendment restructured these as Schedule I (higher protection), Schedule II (lower protection), Schedule III (plants) and Schedule IV (CITES appendices), with vermin dropped. Protected areas under the Act: national parks (Section 35), wildlife sanctuaries (Section 26A), conservation reserves (Section 36A) and community reserves (Section 36C). Section 9 bans hunting; Section 11 allows hunting of dangerous animals; Section 12 allows hunting for scientific purposes; Section 51 prescribes penalties. Chief Wildlife Warden is the key state authority. Related bodies: the National Board for Wildlife, chaired by the Prime Minister, and the Central Zoo Authority.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are true of the Fundamental Duties of an Indian citizen ?
1. A legislative process has been provided to enforce these duties.
2. They are correlative to legal duties. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976), through a new Part IVA containing Article 51A. Originally there were 10 duties; the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the 11th (duty of parents/guardians to provide education opportunities to children aged 6-14). They are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR. Unlike Fundamental Rights, they are non-justiciable: the Constitution provides no direct sanction or legal process for enforcement, and Parliament has not been compelled to legislate. Statement 1 is wrong because the Constitution itself provides no legislative process to enforce them; Parliament may enact laws on specific matters (for example, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971), but this is not a general enforcement process within the duties. Statement 2 is wrong because duties are moral and civic obligations, not correlative legal duties; the Verma Committee (1999) identified existing laws related to some duties, but the duties themselves remain unenforceable. Eliminating both statements leaves (d). Courts use them as interpretive aids (AIIMS Students Union case, 2001; Ranganath Misra case).
explanations: (a) is wrong because no legislative process is provided in the Constitution to enforce the duties; they are non-justiciable.
(b) is wrong because duties are moral obligations and not correlative to enforceable legal duties.
(c) is wrong because both statements are false.
(d) is correct: neither statement is true, as the duties lack enforcement machinery and are not legally correlative duties.
keyfact: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, Part IVA, 42nd Amendment 1976) are non-justiciable moral obligations with no enforcement machinery, so both statements are false.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: it would imply a legislative enforcement process exists. In fact, enforcement is left to ordinary laws on specific matters, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. There is no general constitutional mechanism, and the duties remain non-justiciable.

Option (b), 2 only: it would imply duties are correlative to legal duties. Fundamental Duties are moral and civic obligations in Part IVA. They are not directly enforceable by courts, though judges may use them as interpretive aids in deciding cases and testing statutes.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: it would treat duties as enforceable and legally correlative. This confuses duties with Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable under Articles 32 and 226. Fundamental Duties lack such remedies, which makes this option wrong.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2: this is the correct answer. Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, Part IVA) were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. They are non-justiciable, lack sanctions, and apply only to citizens. The 11th duty was added in 2002.
related: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A.
They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the 11th duty on education of children aged 6-14.
The idea of Fundamental Duties was borrowed from the USSR Constitution.
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and apply only to citizens.
The Justice Verma Committee (1999) examined their implementation.
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 relates to respect for the flag, anthem and Constitution.
Fundamental Rights are justiciable under Articles 32 and 226.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Constitution provides no legislative process or sanction to enforce Fundamental Duties; they are non-justiciable. Detail: Article 51A in Part IVA was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. The Committee suggested penalties for non-compliance, but this was not accepted. Parliament may legislate on specific matters, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (covering the Constitution, flag and anthem) and the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955. Yet there is no general enforcement machinery, and courts cannot compel citizens to perform duties. The Verma Committee (1999) listed existing legal provisions for some duties and recommended implementation strategies. The Supreme Court has held that duties help interpret laws and the constitutionality of statutes (Article 51A cited in AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS, 2001).

2 — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties are moral obligations and are not correlative to legal duties in the sense of being legally enforceable. Detail: They are described as moral and civic duties of citizens only, not aliens. The original list had 10 duties; the 86th Amendment (2002) added clause (k) on duty of parents to educate children aged 6-14. They include respecting the Constitution, the national flag and anthem, cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle, defending the country, promoting harmony, preserving composite culture, protecting the environment, developing scientific temper, safeguarding public property, and striving for excellence. Unlike rights, they have no direct legal sanction, though courts may take them into account when deciding the reasonableness of restrictions.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is true. Fundamental Duties in Part IVA (Article 51A) are non-justiciable moral obligations with no built-in legislative enforcement mechanism, and they are not correlative to legal duties in the sense of being legally enforceable.
topic_notes: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (the 'mini-Constitution'), during the Emergency. They followed the Swaran Singh Committee, which recommended eight duties; the Amendment added ten. The idea is borrowed from the USSR Constitution. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the 11th duty, clause (k): parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6-14. Key features: they apply only to citizens, not foreigners; they are non-justiciable; they have no direct sanction; and Parliament can legislate on them, but the Constitution does not require it. The Committee's recommended penalties and the proposal to include the duty to pay taxes were not accepted. Duties in Article 51A include abiding by the Constitution and respecting the national flag and anthem; cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle; upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity; defending the country; promoting harmony and renouncing practices derogatory to women; preserving the composite culture; protecting the natural environment; developing scientific temper and humanism; safeguarding public property and abjuring violence; striving for excellence; and the duty regarding children's education. The Justice Verma Committee (1999) on Fundamental Duties of Citizens identified legal provisions for some duties (for example, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967). Court cases: Hanif Quareshi, AIIMS Students Union (2001), Ranganath Misra (2003) and Bijoe Emmanuel (1986, national anthem). Compare with Directive Principles (Part IV, non-justiciable) and Fundamental Rights (Part III, justiciable). Duties are a reminder that rights come with responsibilities, as the Preamble and Part IV also emphasise.

question:
Consider the following pairs :
1. Radhakanta Deb — First President of the British Indian Association
2. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty — Founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha
3. Surendranath Banerjee — Founder of the Indian Association Which of the above pairs is/are correctly matched ?
subject: Polity
detail: This question tests early political associations in India before the Indian National Congress (1885). The British Indian Association was formed in Calcutta on 31 October 1851 by merging the Landholders' Society and the Bengal British India Society. Radhakanta Deb was its first President and Debendranath Tagore its first Secretary. It was dominated by landlords and petitioned Parliament on the Charter Act of 1853. The Indian Association (Indian Association of Calcutta) was founded on 26 July 1876 by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose, and it represented the middle class. It campaigned against lowering the ICS age limit (1877) and organised the Indian National Conference in 1883. The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in May 1884 by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty founded the Madras Native Association (1852) and edited the Crescent. Elimination logic: knowing that pair 2 is wrong removes (c) and (d). Knowing that pair 1 is right removes (a). That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: this option omits pair 3, which is also correct because Surendranath Banerjee did found the Indian Association.
Correct: pairs 1 and 3 are accurate, and pair 2 is wrong because the Madras Mahajana Sabha was not founded by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty.
Wrong: this option includes pair 2, which is incorrect, and leaves out pair 1, which is correct.
Wrong: this option includes pair 2, but Chetty is not the founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha.
keyfact: Radhakanta Deb headed the British Indian Association (1851) and Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876), but the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) was not founded by G. L. Narasu Chetty.
option_notes: Option (a), pair 1 only: Radhakanta Deb (1784-1867) was a conservative Bengali leader who headed the British Indian Association from 1851. He was a Sanskrit scholar, compiled the encyclopedic Sabdakalpadruma, and was an early president of the Calcutta School Book Society. He led the orthodox Dharma Sabha against the abolition of Sati in 1829 but supported female education. The British Indian Association he led was a landlord body that lobbied the British Parliament on the Charter Act of 1853.

Option (b), pairs 1 and 3 only: this is the official answer. It combines two accurate matches. Radhakanta Deb headed the British Indian Association (1851), the first all-Bengal political association of Indians. Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876), the most prominent pre-Congress middle-class body. Both were Calcutta-based. Together they show the shift from landlord politics to middle-class nationalism, which culminated in the Congress in 1885.

Option (c), pairs 2 and 3 only: it wrongly accepts pair 2. Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty (1806-1868) was a Madras merchant and early public figure. He founded the Madras Native Association (1852) and the Crescent newspaper, and he opposed the Company's policy on missionary education and the torture practices of revenue officials. The Madras Mahajana Sabha belongs to the later 1884 generation of leaders, namely Veeraraghavachariar, Subramania Iyer and Anandacharlu.

Option (d), all three pairs: it is wrong because pair 2 fails. Together the three pairs show how political bodies emerged in Bengal and Madras. These were the British Indian Association (1851), the Madras Native Association (1852), the Indian Association (1876), the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884), the Bombay Presidency Association (1885) and the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870). Pre-Congress associations were regional and class-based, and they petitioned rather than agitated.
related: British Indian Association was founded in 1851; Radhakanta Deb was its President and Debendranath Tagore its Secretary.
The Indian Association was founded in 1876 by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose.
The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in 1884 by Veeraraghavachariar, Subramania Iyer and Anandacharlu.
The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was founded in 1870 by Ranade and others.
The East India Association was founded in London in 1866 by Dadabhai Naoroji.
Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty founded the Madras Native Association in 1852.
The Bombay Presidency Association was formed in 1885 by Mehta, Telang and Tyabji.
The Landholders' Society (1838) was the first organised political association in British India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Radhakanta Deb was the first President of the British Indian Association. The Association was founded in Calcutta on 31 October 1851 by merging the Landholders' Society (1838) and the Bengal British India Society (1843). Deb was a conservative Hindu leader and Sanskrit scholar who opposed Derozio's followers but supported female education. Debendranath Tagore was Secretary. It sent a petition to Parliament in 1852 before the Charter Act 1853, seeking separation of executive and judicial functions and Indian representation in legislative councils. It mainly represented landlord interests.

2 — Incorrect: Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty was not the founder of the Madras Mahajana Sabha. He was a Madras merchant and public figure who founded the Madras Native Association in 1852 and published the Crescent newspaper. He was an early critic of the East India Company on issues such as the missionary role in education and the torture inquiry in Madras. The Madras Mahajana Sabha was founded in May 1884 by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu, and it helped prepare the ground for the Congress in 1885.

3 — Correct: Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association on 26 July 1876 with Ananda Mohan Bose. It was more representative of the middle class than the landlord-dominated British Indian Association. It led the agitation against reducing the maximum age for the ICS examination from 21 to 19 in 1877, and Banerjee toured India for it. It also protested the Vernacular Press Act 1878 and the Arms Act, and supported tenants' rights. It convened the Indian National Conference in 1883. It later merged into the Congress movement. Banerjee became Congress President in 1895 (Pune) and 1902 (Ahmedabad).
summary: The answer is (b): pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched, while pair 2 is not. Radhakanta Deb was the first President of the British Indian Association (1851) and Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian Association (1876). Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty did not found the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884), which was founded by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Anandacharlu.
topic_notes: Political associations before the Indian National Congress were regional and mostly petition-based. The Landholders' Society (1838, Calcutta) was founded by Dwarkanath Tagore and others as the first organised political body. The Bengal British India Society (1843) was led by William Adam and George Thompson. The two merged into the British Indian Association in 1851. The East India Association (1866) was founded in London by Dadabhai Naoroji. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) was led by Mahadev Govind Ranade, G. V. Joshi and S. H. Chiplunkar. The Indian League (1875) was started by Sisir Kumar Ghosh. The Indian Association (1876) was founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose. The Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) was founded by Veeraraghavachariar, Subramania Iyer and Anandacharlu. The Bombay Presidency Association (1885) was founded by Pherozeshah Mehta, K. T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji. The Indian National Association Conference (1883) was the first all-India gathering of its kind. The Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay by A. O. Hume, with W. C. Bonnerjee as first President. Early demands were expansion of legislative councils, simultaneous ICS examinations in India and Britain, and reduction in military expenditure. The early leaders were called Moderates and used the 'prayer and petition' method. Related other angles are the Ilbert Bill agitation (1883), the Vernacular Press Act (1878), the Arms Act (1878), the ICS age limit agitation (1877), the Indian Councils Act 1861 and the Indian Councils Act 1892.

question: Which one of the following objectives is not 41. embodied in the Preamble to the Constitution of India ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Preamble resolves to secure to all citizens: JUSTICE (social, economic and political); LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship); EQUALITY (of status and of opportunity); and to promote FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation. Liberty in the Preamble therefore has exactly five components: thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Economic appears only with Justice, not with Liberty. The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. It was adopted with the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and amended once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'. The Berubari Union case (1960) held the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled this and held it is a part and can be amended without altering the basic structure. Elimination: options (a), (c) and (d) are word-for-word in the Preamble, leaving (b) as the only item missing from it. Economic liberty is only indirectly protected through Article 19(1)(g) and Article 300A.
explanations: Incorrect as an answer: 'Liberty of thought' is expressly listed in the Preamble, so it is embodied.
Correct answer: 'Economic liberty' is not in the Preamble's list of liberties. Only 'economic' Justice is mentioned.
Incorrect as an answer: 'Liberty of expression' is expressly listed in the Preamble.
Incorrect as an answer: 'Liberty of belief' is expressly listed in the Preamble.
keyfact: Preamble's Liberty = thought, expression, belief, faith, worship; 'economic' appears only under Justice, not Liberty.
option_notes: Liberty of thought is the first of the five liberties in the Preamble. It is the foundation for freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). The Preamble's liberty ideal was inspired by the French Revolution (Liberty, Equality, Fraternity). These liberties are made enforceable through Fundamental Rights (Articles 19-22 and 25-28). The Preamble itself is not enforceable in court.

Economic liberty is not named in the Preamble. The Preamble includes 'economic' only in 'Justice, social, economic and political'. Economic freedoms are protected indirectly: Article 19(1)(g) gives the right to practise any profession or carry on any trade or business, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6). The right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a legal right under Article 300A.

Liberty of expression is part of the Preamble's liberty clause. It is given legal force by Article 19(1)(a), the freedom of speech and expression, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) (sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency, defamation, contempt of court, incitement to an offence and others). The press freedom is read into it, as in Romesh Thappar and Indian Express cases.

Liberty of belief is part of the Preamble's liberty clause, along with faith and worship. It connects to the freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion under Articles 25-28. The word 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), although secularism was already a basic feature of the Constitution, as the S.R. Bommai case (1994) confirmed.
related: The Preamble lists five liberties: thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
The Preamble has been amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
42nd Amendment added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held the Preamble to be a part of the Constitution.
Berubari Union case (1960) held the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
The Preamble is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution of 13 December 1946.
Right to property is now under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right (44th Amendment, 1978).
The Preamble's Justice ideal comes from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality and Fraternity from the French Revolution.
summary: The answer is (b) Economic liberty. The Preamble secures to all citizens 'Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship', but it does not mention economic liberty. It speaks of 'Justice, social, economic and political', which is a different concept.
topic_notes: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution and sets out its philosophy and objectives. Its opening words are 'We, the People of India', showing that sovereignty rests with the people. It describes India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. The four objectives are Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. Justice (social, economic, political) is drawn from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality and Fraternity from the French Revolution. The Preamble's date of adoption is stated as 26 November 1949. The Objectives Resolution (Nehru, 13 Dec 1946) was its basis. The Preamble was drafted largely by Nehru, and the Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar. Constituent Assembly's President was Dr Rajendra Prasad. Judicial views: In re Berubari Union (1960) said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) said it is a part; LIC of India case (1995) affirmed this. The Preamble is neither a source of power nor a limitation on power, and it is non-justiciable. It can be amended under Article 368, but the basic structure cannot be changed. It has been amended only once, in 1976 (42nd Amendment). Other angles: sources of different Constitutional features; the difference between the Preamble's liberty and Fundamental Rights; the Directive Principles (Articles 38 and 39) which address economic justice; the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A); and the concepts of 'Socialist' and 'Secular' as interpreted by the courts.

ocr: With reference to ‘Quality Council of India (QCI)’, consider the following statements : QCI was set up jointly by the is Government of India and the Indian Industry. Chairman of QCI is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendations of the industry to the Government. Which of the above statements is/are correct ? lonly (a) 42. 2 only (b) Both 1 and 2 (c) Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Economy
detail: The Quality Council of India (QCI) is a non-profit autonomous organisation, registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and set up in 1997 following a decision of the Government of India, acting with the Indian industry, to create a national body for accreditation and quality promotion. Its design is a public-private partnership: the founding industry associations are ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI. The nodal ministry is the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. QCI has 38 members in its council, with equal government and industry representation among them, and its Chairman is nominated by the Prime Minister on the recommendation of the industry; the Chairman is not chosen by the government alone. Its constituent boards include the National Accreditation Board for Certification Bodies (NABCB), the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL), the National Accreditation Board for Education and Training (NABET), the National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH), and the Quality Certification arm. Elimination logic: if a student knows the PPP origin (statement 1), options (b) and (d) go out; the Prime Minister's role in appointing the Chairman then confirms (c) over (a).
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 2 is also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) Wrong: Statement 1 is correct, so '2 only' omits a true statement.
(c) Correct: QCI is a Government-industry joint initiative (1997), and the PM appoints the Chairman on the industry's recommendation.
(d) Wrong: Both statements are correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: QCI (1997) = joint Government–industry body (ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI); its Chairman is appointed by the PM on industry's recommendation.
option_notes: 1 only: This option would imply that the Chairman is chosen in some other way, e.g. by the Commerce Minister or by the council itself. In reality the PM appoints him. Facts to remember about QCI: it is autonomous, was set up in 1997, and has its headquarters in New Delhi. It is the national accreditation body for conformity assessment, has equal representation from government and industry, and is the nodal agency for several quality schemes such as the Zero Defect Zero Effect (ZED) certification and Swachh Bharat Mission surveys.

2 only: This would mean QCI was not a joint set-up, which is false. QCI was a PPP creation, not a purely governmental body such as BIS (statutory, under the BIS Act, 2016) or a purely industry body. The Chairman's appointment by the PM adds a government role. QCI's work covers accreditation (NABCB, NABL), education (NABET), healthcare (NABH), and certification (ZED, Ayush Mark, Indian Certification of Medical Devices Plus). It is also the nodal body for the Pradhan Mantri Ayush initiatives of certification.

Both 1 and 2: This is the official answer. QCI was set up jointly in 1997 by the Government and the three industry associations ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI, and the Chairman is appointed by the PM on the recommendation of the industry. QCI is autonomous, non-profit and works under DPIIT. It runs accreditation boards (NABCB, NABL, NABET, NABH) and national schemes such as ZED, Ayush Mark, Swachh Survekshan evaluation and the National Quality Campaign. It represents India in international accreditation forums such as ILAC and IAF.

Neither 1 nor 2: This would portray QCI as a purely governmental or purely private body with an unrelated appointment process. That is incorrect. QCI is not a statutory body like BIS or the Competition Commission; it is a registered society. It nevertheless holds a quasi-official role as India's national accreditation body, with international recognition by the Asia Pacific Accreditation Cooperation (APAC) and the International Accreditation Forum (IAF) through its boards NABCB and NABL.
related: QCI was established in 1997 as a PPP between Government of India and Indian industry.
QCI founding industry bodies: ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI.
QCI is under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (Ministry of Commerce and Industry).
NABH accredits hospitals; NABL accredits labs; NABET covers education and training; NABCB covers certification bodies.
The BIS is a statutory body (BIS Act 2016) that sets standards and runs the ISI mark and Hallmarking.
ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect) certification for MSMEs is run by QCI.
QCI's Chairman is appointed by the Prime Minister on the industry's recommendation.
QCI is a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, not a statutory body.
statements: 1 — Correct: QCI was established jointly by the Government of India and the Indian industry. QCI was set up in 1997 as an autonomous, non-profit body registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The three founding industry associations are ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI. It was created to establish a national accreditation structure and promote quality through national campaigns. The idea arose from the need for a credible third-party assessment of conformity, aligned with WTO (TBT) requirements after 1995. It functions under the administrative control of DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Its first Chairman was Mr. Rahul Bajaj's era successor Dr. ... (recall just the structure, not names); the present chair is Jaxay Shah (since 2019).

2 — Correct: The Chairman of QCI is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendation of the industry to the Government. The council has 38 members, split among government, industry and other stakeholders, with the three industry bodies (ASSOCHAM, CII, FICCI) nominating a panel. The Chairman is a leader from industry, not a bureaucrat. Appointment by the PM gives the body high-level backing while keeping it autonomous. Jaxay Shah was appointed Chairman in 2018 (term started in 2019 and renewed later). QCI also has a Secretary General who runs day-to-day administration. Its boards include NABL, NABCB, NABET and NABH.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. QCI was set up in 1997 as an autonomous body jointly by the Government of India and the Indian industry (represented by ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI), and its Chairman is appointed by the Prime Minister on the recommendations of the industry to the Government.
topic_notes: The Quality Council of India was set up in 1997 as an autonomous non-profit society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, to give India a national quality infrastructure. It followed the Government's recognition after the 1995 WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) that third-party conformity assessment needed credible, internationally accepted accreditation. The founding industry partners are ASSOCHAM, CII and FICCI. The nodal ministry is Commerce and Industry (DPIIT). The Council has 38 members with a mix of government, industry and consumer or other stakeholder representation, and the Chairman is appointed by the Prime Minister on the industry's recommendation. Jaxay Shah has been Chairman since 2018-19. Constituent boards: NABCB (certification bodies), NABL (testing and calibration labs), NABET (education and training), NABH (hospitals and healthcare providers), and the National Board for Quality Promotion (NBQP). Major initiatives: ZED (Zero Defect Zero Effect) certification for MSMEs, Ayush Mark, Indian Certification for Medical Devices (ICMED), Swachh Bharat Mission surveys and Swachh Survekshan, Voluntary Compliance Scheme, and the PM's national quality campaigns. Related bodies: the Bureau of Indian Standards (statutory, BIS Act 2016, formulates standards and runs ISI mark and Hallmarking), FSSAI (food safety), the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), the Export Inspection Council, and the National Productivity Council. UPSC could ask about the difference between accreditation (QCI) and standardisation (BIS), the agencies under QCI, QCI's role in WTO-TBT compliance, its international membership (ILAC, IAF, APAC), or its autonomy and funding.

question:
What is the purpose of setting up of Small Finance Banks (SFBs) in India ? To supply credit to small business units L.
2. To supply credit to small and marginal farmers 43. To encourage young entrepreneurs to set up business particularly in rural areas. _ Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: The RBI's 2014 Guidelines for Licensing of Small Finance Banks in the Private Sector state the objective: to further financial inclusion by providing (a) savings vehicles to underserved and unserved sections and (b) supply of credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and other unorganised sector entities, through high technology-low cost operations. Statements 1 and 2 mirror this wording almost exactly. Statement 3 is a plausible-sounding distractor: SFBs do not have a youth-entrepreneur or rural-only mandate, and their focus is on underserved segments, not a particular age group. Key rules: SFBs are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and registered as public limited companies under the Companies Act, 2013. Minimum paid-up capital is Rs 200 crore (later Rs 200 crore for new; Rs 1,000 crore for transition to Universal Bank is a different matter). They must lend 75% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit to priority sectors, and at least 50% of the loan portfolio must consist of loans up to Rs 25 lakh. Elimination: once 1 and 2 are known to be correct, only (a) and (d) remain, and rejecting 3 gives (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 match the RBI's stated objectives for SFBs, namely credit to small business units and to small and marginal farmers, and statement 3 is not one of them.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is not a purpose of SFBs, and it leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is not a stated purpose, and it leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is incorrect. The SFB mandate is financial inclusion through savings and credit, not youth rural entrepreneurship promotion.
keyfact: SFBs aim at financial inclusion: savings for the underserved and credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers and the unorganised sector, not youth rural entrepreneurship.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: This is the official answer, covering credit to small business units and to small and marginal farmers. It reflects the SFB objective of financial inclusion through high-technology, low-cost operations. SFBs were announced in the 2014-15 Budget, guidelines were issued in November 2014, and in-principle licences went to 10 entities in 2015. They are licensed under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

2 and 3 only: This pairs the farmer credit objective with the youth-entrepreneur claim, which is not in RBI guidelines. Youth entrepreneurship is the domain of schemes like Start-up India, Stand-Up India, MUDRA and PMEGP. The option is wrong because statement 3 is not a purpose of SFBs and statement 1 is left out.

1 and 3 only: This pairs small business credit with the youth-entrepreneur claim. It is wrong because it drops farmers, who are explicitly named in the RBI objectives, and includes a purpose that is not stated. SFB lending also has priority sector requirements, with 75% of ANBC going to priority sectors.

1, 2 and 3: This is the all-inclusive option, which UPSC often uses as a trap. It is wrong because statement 3 is an add-on not found in the guidelines. Always check each statement against the official wording of RBI guidelines or the relevant Act.
related: SFBs are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
Minimum paid-up capital for SFBs is Rs 200 crore.
SFBs must lend 75% of ANBC to priority sectors.
Payments Banks can accept deposits but cannot lend.
The Nachiket Mor Committee recommended differentiated banks.
AU Small Finance Bank was the first SFB to be granted a universal bank in-principle approval in 2024-25 process stage.
Ten entities received in-principle SFB licences in 2015.
At least 25% of SFB branches must be in unbanked rural centres.
statements: 1 — Correct: Supplying credit to small business units is an explicit objective in the RBI's 2014 SFB guidelines. SFBs focus on micro and small enterprises, which are often underserved by large banks. Examples include AU Small Finance Bank, Equitas, Ujjivan, Jana, Capital, ESAF, Utkarsh, Suryoday, Fincare and North East SFB. The first 10 in-principle licences were granted in September 2015. SFBs can accept deposits, lend, distribute mutual funds and insurance, but cannot set up subsidiaries for non-banking activity. They must open at least 25% of branches in unbanked rural centres. Promoters need 5 years of experience and the minimum capital is Rs 200 crore.

2 — Correct: Supplying credit to small and marginal farmers is also an explicit objective in the guidelines. Small farmers hold 1-2 hectares and marginal farmers hold less than 1 hectare of land. SFBs help meet priority sector lending requirements, including agriculture, which has sub-targets for small and marginal farmers. They operate alongside Regional Rural Banks, cooperative banks and Payments Banks. Unlike Payments Banks, which cannot lend, SFBs can lend. The Nachiket Mor Committee (2013-14) recommended differentiated banks for financial inclusion, which led to the creation of both categories.

3 — Incorrect: Encouraging young entrepreneurs to set up business in rural areas is not stated in the RBI's SFB objectives. Youth entrepreneurship is promoted by other schemes such as Start-up India (2016), Stand-Up India (2016, for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, with loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore), MUDRA Yojana (2015, loans up to Rs 10 lakh in Shishu, Kishor and Tarun categories) and PM Employment Generation Programme. SFBs are not restricted to youth or rural areas, and their focus is on underserved segments generally.
summary: The answer is (a): 1 and 2 only. Small Finance Banks were set up to extend basic banking and credit to underserved sections, namely small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and the unorganised sector. Encouraging young entrepreneurs in rural areas is not a stated purpose of SFBs.
topic_notes: Background: The Nachiket Mor Committee (Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low Income Households, 2013-14) recommended differentiated banks, leading to Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks. The Union Budget 2014-15 announced them, and RBI issued final guidelines in November 2014. In September 2015 RBI gave in-principle approval to 10 entities for SFBs (and 11 for Payments Banks). Eligibility: resident-owned and controlled, including individuals with 10 years of banking and finance experience, companies, societies, NBFCs, microfinance institutions and local area banks. Legal form: public limited company with a licence under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Capital: minimum paid-up equity of Rs 200 crore, with promoter holding of at least 40% initially, reduced to 26% over 12 years. Lending norms: 75% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit to priority sectors, and 50% of the loan portfolio in loans up to Rs 25 lakh. Operations: they can accept deposits, lend, and distribute mutual funds, insurance and pension products, and they must list within three years of reaching net worth of Rs 500 crore. Restrictions: they cannot set up subsidiaries to undertake non-banking financial activities, and they must open at least 25% of branches in unbanked rural centres. Comparison with Payments Banks: Payments Banks (initial deposit cap Rs 1 lakh, raised to Rs 2 lakh) cannot lend or issue credit cards, and their capital requirement is Rs 100 crore. Other related areas: Regional Rural Banks (1975), NABARD (1982), Local Area Banks, cooperative banks and the PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014). Possible future angles include voluntary transition of SFBs to universal banks, the 2019 on-tap licensing guidelines, and the conversion of Ujjivan and AU into universal bank candidates.

ocr: With reference to ‘Asia Pacific Ministerial Conference on Housing and Urban Development (APMCHUD), consider the following statemerits : : iL, The first APMCHUD was held in India in 2006 on the theme ‘Emerging Urban Forms — Policy Responses and Governance Structure’. 2: India hosts all the Annual Ministerial Conferences in partnership with ADB, APEC and ASEAN. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (ce) Both 1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Democracy’s superior virtue lies in the fact that it calls into activity (a) the intelligence and character of ordinary men and w
subject: Economy
detail: APMCHUD is a ministerial forum for Asia-Pacific countries on housing and urban development. It was launched on India's initiative, and the first conference was held in New Delhi in December 2006 on the theme 'Emerging Urban Forms – Policy Responses and Governance Structure'. This matches statement 1. The forum is convened with UN-Habitat and UNESCAP as the key partners, and it is held roughly every two to four years in different member countries, not every year. Statement 2 therefore fails on three counts. India does not host all the conferences, they are not annual, and the named partners (ADB, APEC, ASEAN) are wrong, because the partners are UN-Habitat and UNESCAP. India's Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs acts as the secretariat or permanent-member lead, and the 2016 Habitat III context and the 'New Urban Agenda' feed into the later sessions. Elimination logic: reject any option that endorses statement 2, which leaves (a). Absolute words like 'all' and 'annual' in a statement are a red flag in UPSC questions. Note the discrepancy: option (d) would require statement 1 to be false, which contradicts the 2006 New Delhi record.
explanations: (a) 1 only: matches the facts, because statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong. By standard sources this is the logically correct option.
(b) 2 only: wrong, because statement 2 is factually incorrect (it is not India alone, not annual, and the partners are wrong).
(c) Both 1 and 2: wrong, because statement 2 is incorrect.

(d) Neither 1 nor 2: the supplied key marks this as correct, but it would require statement 1 to be false. That conflicts with the first APMCHUD being held in New Delhi in 2006, so verify against the official key.
keyfact: APMCHUD: first held in New Delhi in 2006 with UN-Habitat and UNESCAP; it rotates among hosts and is not annual or India-only. The supplied key (d) conflicts with this, so verify it.
option_notes: 1 only: the option that accepts the 2006 New Delhi first conference and rejects the claim that India hosts all annual meetings. It reflects the rotating hosting and the UN-Habitat/UNESCAP partnership. Related facts: India's Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs leads participation, and the forum feeds into global urban agendas such as the New Urban Agenda adopted at Habitat III in Quito in 2016. UN-Habitat is headquartered in Nairobi and UNESCAP in Bangkok.

2 only: would mean the claim about India hosting all annual conferences with ADB, APEC and ASEAN is true. It is not. ADB (Manila, 1966) finances development projects, APEC (1989) is a 21-economy trade forum, and ASEAN (Bangkok Declaration, 1967) has 10 members. None of them organises APMCHUD, so this option is a distractor.

Both 1 and 2: would require both statements to be true. It fails because statement 2 is wrong. UPSC often builds such options by adding an exaggerated second statement with absolute terms like 'all'. APMCHUD sessions are periodic and rotate among Asia-Pacific hosts.

Neither 1 nor 2: the key supplied with the question says this is the official answer. On standard facts statement 1 is true, so this option looks inconsistent. Treat it with caution and confirm against the official UPSC key. If it is the official key, the likely reasoning would be a disputed detail in statement 1, such as the exact theme or wording.
related: The first APMCHUD was held in New Delhi in 2006.
APMCHUD partners are UN-Habitat and UNESCAP.
UN-Habitat is headquartered in Nairobi and was created in 1978.
SDG 11 covers sustainable cities and communities.
Habitat III was held in Quito in 2016 and adopted the New Urban Agenda.
The 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) inserted Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule.
PMAY-Urban and Smart Cities Mission were both launched in 2015.
World Habitat Day falls on the first Monday of October.
statements: 1 — Correct: India hosted the first APMCHUD in New Delhi in 2006 on the theme 'Emerging Urban Forms – Policy Responses and Governance Structure'. APMCHUD is a forum of Asia-Pacific housing and urban development ministers, set up on India's initiative with UN-Habitat and UNESCAP support. It aims to promote sustainable urbanisation, affordable housing and slum upgrading, and to share best practices. The Indian ministry (now Housing and Urban Affairs) is a permanent-member lead. Later sessions were held in other countries, including Indonesia, Jordan and Colombo-based or regional venues, with declarations on urban development goals.

2 — Incorrect: India does not host all the conferences. They rotate among member countries and are not strictly annual. The partners are UN-Habitat and UNESCAP, not ADB, APEC and ASEAN. ADB is a development bank, APEC a trade-economic forum, and ASEAN a regional political-economic grouping, and none of them is the organiser of APMCHUD. Absolute claims like 'all' are a classic UPSC trap, so memorise that the forum rotates and its partners are UN bodies.
summary: The image shows two questions; this note covers the first one, on APMCHUD. Your supplied key says (d), but by the standard facts statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong, which gives (a) 1 only. Please re-check the key against the official UPSC answer sheet before relying on this note.
topic_notes:
APMCHUD (Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Housing and Urban Development) is an intergovernmental platform for housing and urban ministers of Asia-Pacific countries. It was initiated by India, with the first session in New Delhi in 2006. UN-Habitat and UNESCAP are the main technical partners. It promotes inclusive, sustainable urbanisation, affordable housing, slum upgrading, urban governance and the implementation of global agendas such as the Sustainable Development Goals (especially SDG 11) and the New Urban Agenda (Habitat III, Quito, 2016). It works through ministerial declarations and action plans, and a secretariat arrangement in which India's Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs plays a lead role.

Related Indian urban schemes that UPSC often links to this topic: Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban), launched 2015 with the aim of 'Housing for All'; Smart Cities Mission (2015, 100 cities); AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation, 2015); Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban); HRIDAY for heritage cities; and DAY-NULM for livelihoods. Constitutional context: the 74th Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule (18 functions) for urban local bodies. UN-Habitat was created in 1978, its HQ is at Nairobi, and it runs the World Urban Forum and World Habitat Day (first Monday of October). Habitat I was in Vancouver (1976), Habitat II in Istanbul (1996), and Habitat III in Quito (2016). UNESCAP (founded 1947, HQ Bangkok) is the regional UN commission. Likely future angles: the host and year of the first session, the partner bodies, and linkage with SDG 11. Remember also the elimination habit of rejecting absolute words such as 'all' and 'annual'.

question: Which of the following is a most likely consequence of implementing the ‘Unified Payments Interface (UPI)’?
options: Mobile wallets will not be necessary for online payments
Digital currency will totally replace the physical currency in about two decades
Direct transfer of subsidies to poor people will become very effective
subject: Economy
detail: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), regulated by the RBI, and launched publicly in April 2016 (pilot) with the first apps going live in August 2016. It is built over the Immediate Payment Service (IMPS) and works 24x7x365. A user creates a Virtual Payment Address (VPA), links one or more bank accounts to a single app, and authorises payments with a UPI PIN. Money moves directly between bank accounts in real time, supporting both push (pay) and pull (collect) transactions, and it merges several bank accounts into one mobile app. Because the funds stay in the bank account, a prepaid wallet (Paytm, MobiKwik, etc.), which needs pre-loaded balance, becomes redundant for many users. That is why (a) is the most plausible consequence. Elimination: (b) is an extreme claim, since cash still dominates and no such timeline exists. (c) FDI depends on policy, ease of doing business and the macroeconomy, not on a retail payment system. (d) Direct Benefit Transfer works mainly through Aadhaar-linked accounts (JAM trinity, AEPS, APBS), not UPI, so UPI is not the main driver.
explanations: Correct. UPI links bank accounts directly to the payment app, so pre-loaded wallets are not needed for online payments. This is the most direct and plausible effect.
Wrong. It is an absolutist prediction ('totally replace', 'two decades'). Cash remains widely used, and UPI is a way to move bank money, not a new digital currency.
Wrong. FDI inflows depend on investment policy, regulation and macroeconomic conditions. A domestic retail payment interface has no direct link to a drastic rise in FDI.
Wrong. Subsidy transfers rely on DBT infrastructure such as Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and APBS. UPI may help, but it is not the most likely consequence of its implementation.
keyfact: UPI = NPCI's real-time system linking bank accounts directly via VPA and UPI PIN, so a pre-loaded mobile wallet is no longer necessary.
option_notes: Mobile wallets are prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) regulated by the RBI under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Users load money into the wallet from a bank account or card and spend from that balance. Examples are Paytm, MobiKwik, FreeCharge and PhonePe wallet. They can be semi-closed or open and are subject to KYC limits. After UPI, many wallets began offering UPI themselves, and wallet usage declined relative to UPI.

Digital currency means money existing only in electronic form. India's RBI launched the e-rupee (CBDC) pilots: wholesale in November 2022 and retail in December 2022. A CBDC is legal tender issued by the central bank, unlike private cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin. Cash in circulation has continued to grow in value, so total replacement of physical currency is not happening on any set timeline.

Foreign Direct Investment is investment by a non-resident into an Indian enterprise with lasting interest, generally a 10 percent or greater stake. It is governed by FEMA 1999, the DPIIT's FDI policy and RBI rules, via the automatic route or the government route. FDI trends depend on sectoral caps, ease of doing business, and global conditions. Payment system innovation has only a marginal link to FDI.

Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) was launched on 1 January 2013 to send subsidies and benefits straight to beneficiaries' bank accounts, reducing leakages. It rests on the JAM trinity: Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile. The Aadhaar Payment Bridge System and Aadhaar-enabled Payment System are the key tools. Examples include PAHAL for LPG subsidy and PM-KISAN. It operates independently of UPI.
related: UPI was developed by NPCI and launched in April 2016.
UPI is built on top of the IMPS infrastructure.
BHIM app was launched in December 2016 and is named after B. R. Ambedkar.
UPI uses a Virtual Payment Address and a UPI PIN for authentication.
RBI regulates prepaid payment instruments (wallets) under the PSS Act 2007.
The RBI launched retail e-rupee (CBDC) pilot in December 2022.
DBT began on 1 January 2013; JAM stands for Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile.
NPCI was incorporated in 2008 as a not-for-profit company.
summary: The answer is (a). UPI lets users send money directly from one bank account to another through a single mobile app using a Virtual Payment Address, without first loading money into a wallet. The most likely consequence is therefore that separate mobile wallets become unnecessary for online payments.
topic_notes: UPI is a real-time inter-bank payment system created by NPCI, an umbrella organisation for retail payments set up in 2008 as a not-for-profit company under the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association. UPI was launched on 11 April 2016 under Dr Raghuram Rajan's RBI governorship, with the BHIM app released in December 2016. Key features: single mobile app for multiple bank accounts, VPA instead of account number and IFSC, two-factor authentication (device binding plus UPI PIN), QR code payments, peer-to-peer and merchant payments, mandates for recurring payments, and 24x7 operation. It runs on top of IMPS. Other NPCI products: RuPay card, IMPS, NETC (FASTag), Bharat BillPay, AePS, NACH, and the BHIM Aadhaar. Related payment systems: NEFT (batch settlement, now 24x7 since December 2019), RTGS (real-time gross settlement, minimum Rs 2 lakh), and the Payments Infrastructure Development Fund. UPI 123PAY enables feature-phone payments, and UPI Lite supports small-value offline-style transactions. UPI has expanded internationally through links with Singapore (PayNow), UAE, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius and France. The RBI regulates PPIs (wallets) and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 governs the entire framework. Future questions may cover CBDC (e-rupee), the difference between wallets and UPI, DBT and the JAM trinity, Bharat Interface for Money, and the demonetisation of November 2016 that boosted digital payments.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q43.
ocr: Which of the following is a most likely consequence of implementing the ‘Unified Payments Interface (UPI)’? (a) Mobile wallets will not be necessary for online payments. (b) Digital currency will totally replace the physical currency in about two decades. (c) FDI inflows will drastically increase. (d) Direct transfer of subsidies to poor people will become very effective.
subject: Economy
detail: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) and launched in April 2016 (pilot), with Reserve Bank of India backing. It is built on top of the Immediate Payment Service (IMPS) and allows several bank accounts to be linked in one mobile app. Payments are made with a Virtual Payment Address (VPA), so account numbers and IFSC codes need not be shared. It supports peer-to-peer 'push' and 'pull' requests, works 24x7 on all days, and uses two-factor authentication (device binding plus UPI PIN). Because money moves straight from bank account to bank account, a user does not need to preload money into a wallet such as Paytm Wallet or Mobikwik, which is why option (a) is the most likely consequence. Elimination: (b) is an extreme prediction ('totally replace', 'two decades') and UPI is not a digital currency, it only moves existing bank money. (c) FDI inflows depend on policy, markets and investor sentiment, not a domestic payment rail. (d) Direct Benefit Transfer relies on Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and mobile (JAM) and the Aadhaar Payments Bridge, not mainly on UPI. Extreme words like 'totally' and 'drastically' are a warning sign in UPSC options.
explanations: Correct. UPI links bank accounts directly to the app and allows instant transfers, so a prepaid wallet is no longer required for online payments. This is the official answer.

Incorrect. UPI is not a digital currency but a payment system that moves existing bank deposits. The claim that physical currency will be 'totally' replaced within two decades is an extreme and unsupported prediction.
Incorrect. FDI depends on investment climate, sectoral caps and macroeconomic policy. A domestic retail payment interface has no direct link to FDI surges.
Incorrect. Subsidy transfer is handled by Direct Benefit Transfer using the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile) and the Aadhaar Payments Bridge. UPI is not the key enabler of this.
keyfact: UPI (NPCI, 2016, on IMPS) enables direct bank-to-bank mobile payments through a VPA, reducing the need for mobile wallets.
option_notes: Mobile wallets are prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) regulated by the RBI under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Users load money into the wallet and spend from the balance. Examples include Paytm, MobiKwik and PhonePe wallet. They are issued by banks and non-banks, and KYC norms decide the limits (minimum-KYC and full-KYC wallets). Wallets can now be made interoperable through UPI.

Digital currency means money that exists only in electronic form. Bitcoin is a private cryptocurrency, which the RBI has cautioned against and which is not legal tender in India. The RBI's own Central Bank Digital Currency, the e-rupee (e₹), began pilots in December 2022 (wholesale from November 2022, retail from December 2022). It is a digital form of legal tender, unlike UPI, which is a payment rail.

Foreign Direct Investment is investment by a non-resident into the productive assets or equity of an Indian firm with lasting interest, usually a 10 percent or greater stake. It is governed by FEMA 1999 and the FDI policy of DPIIT. Routes are Automatic and Government approval. Inflows depend on sectoral caps, ease of doing business and global conditions, not payment systems.

Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) was launched on 1 January 2013 to send subsidies and benefits straight into beneficiaries' bank accounts, reducing leakages and middlemen. It uses the JAM trinity: Jan Dhan accounts (August 2014), Aadhaar and mobile numbers. The Cabinet Secretariat's DBT Mission coordinates it. LPG's PAHAL scheme is a well-known example.
related: UPI was developed by NPCI, which was set up in 2008 with RBI guidance.
UPI is built on the IMPS (Immediate Payment Service) infrastructure.
BHIM app launched December 2016 is a UPI-based app.
RuPay is NPCI's domestic card payment network.
The e-rupee is the RBI's Central Bank Digital Currency, piloted from late 2022.
Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 gives the RBI power to regulate payment systems.
JAM trinity = Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile, the basis of DBT.
UPI uses a Virtual Payment Address, so no need to share account number or IFSC.
summary: The answer is (a). UPI is an interoperable, real-time, bank-to-bank payment system run by NPCI, so users can pay directly from any bank account through any UPI app. This makes separate prepaid mobile wallets largely unnecessary for online payments.
topic_notes: UPI is a real-time payment system created by NPCI, the umbrella organisation for retail payments in India. NPCI was set up in 2008 as a not-for-profit company under Section 25 (now Section 8) of the Companies Act, promoted by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association. UPI was launched in April 2016 and is built on IMPS. Features: a single mobile app can hold multiple bank accounts; use of a Virtual Payment Address; push and pull transactions; QR code payments; 24x7 operation; and UPI PIN with device binding. UPI 2.0 (2018) added overdraft accounts, one-time mandates, invoice in the inbox and signed intent/QR. UPI Lite is for small-value offline-style payments. UPI 123PAY lets feature-phone users pay via IVR. UPI is now linked with cross-border systems such as Singapore's PayNow, and has been accepted in places like Bhutan, Nepal, UAE, Sri Lanka, Mauritius and France. NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL) is its overseas arm. Other NPCI products: RuPay cards, IMPS, NACH, NETC (FASTag), Bharat BillPay, BHIM app (December 2016, named after B. R. Ambedkar) and the Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS). Related RBI concepts: Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007, the Payments Regulatory Board, prepaid payment instruments, NEFT, RTGS, the e-rupee (CBDC), and the Digital Payments Index. Likely UPSC angles: which body runs UPI, what it is built on, differences between UPI, wallets and cryptocurrency, JAM trinity, DBT, and international expansion of UPI.

question: The terms ‘Event Horizon’, ‘Singularity’, 47. ‘String Theory’ and ‘Standard Model’ are sometimes seen in the news in the context of
options: Observation and understanding of the Universe
Study of the solar and the lunar eclipses
Placing satellites in the orbit of the Earth
Origin and evolution of living organisms on the Earth
subject: Science & Tech
detail: All four terms belong to modern physics and cosmology. An event horizon is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape; its radius is the Schwarzschild radius. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration released the first image of a black hole shadow (M87*) in April 2019 and of Sagittarius A* in May 2022. A singularity is a point of infinite density and spacetime curvature predicted by general relativity at a black hole's centre and at the Big Bang. String theory is a candidate theory of quantum gravity which proposes that fundamental particles are tiny vibrating strings, and it needs extra dimensions. The Standard Model describes the elementary particles (quarks, leptons, gauge bosons, Higgs boson) and three of the four fundamental forces; it excludes gravity. The Higgs boson was confirmed at CERN's LHC in 2012. Elimination: eclipses concern the Sun-Moon-Earth geometry, which uses none of these terms. Satellite placement involves orbital mechanics and launch vehicles. Origin of life involves biology and evolution. Only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct. Black holes (event horizon, singularity), quantum gravity (string theory) and particle physics (Standard Model) all serve to understand the structure, origin and workings of the Universe.
Wrong. Eclipses involve the alignment of the Sun, Moon and Earth (umbra, penumbra, syzygy); none of these four terms is used for them.
Wrong. Satellite placement concerns launch vehicles, orbits (LEO, GEO, polar) and rocket science, not these theoretical physics concepts.
Wrong. Origin and evolution of life belongs to biology and uses terms like abiogenesis, natural selection and the Miller-Urey experiment, not these terms.
keyfact: Event horizon, singularity, string theory and the Standard Model belong to astrophysics and particle physics, which are about understanding the Universe.
option_notes: Observation and understanding of the Universe is the field of astronomy, astrophysics and cosmology. It covers telescopes (Hubble, JWST, EHT, Astrosat), gravitational waves (LIGO detected them in 2015), the Big Bang (about 13.8 billion years ago), dark matter and dark energy. Theoretical frameworks include general relativity, quantum field theory, the Standard Model and string theory. India contributes through ISRO's Astrosat (2015), LIGO-India and the GMRT at Pune.

Study of solar and lunar eclipses covers the geometry of the Sun, Moon and Earth. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth at new moon; a lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth lies between them at full moon. Related terms include umbra, penumbra, annular eclipse, totality, Baily's beads and the diamond ring effect. The Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees, so eclipses are not monthly. The Saros cycle is about 18 years.

Placing satellites in Earth orbit involves launch vehicles and orbital mechanics. India's PSLV serves polar and sun-synchronous orbits, while GSLV serves geostationary transfer orbits (about 36,000 km). LEO is up to about 2,000 km. Key terms include apogee, perigee, escape velocity (11.2 km/s for Earth) and cryogenic engines. SSLV is for small satellites. The first Indian satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975.

Origin and evolution of living organisms is the domain of evolutionary biology. Key ideas include Darwin's natural selection (On the Origin of Species, 1859), Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters, the Oparin-Haldane hypothesis, the Miller-Urey experiment (1953), mutation theory (de Vries), and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Homologous and analogous organs, fossils and molecular phylogeny serve as evidence. Terms like genetic drift and speciation belong here.
related: Event horizon: the boundary of a black hole beyond which light cannot escape.
The first black hole image (M87*) was released by the Event Horizon Telescope in April 2019.
LIGO first detected gravitational waves on 14 September 2015.
The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN's LHC in 2012.
The Standard Model does not include gravity.
Chandrasekhar limit is about 1.4 solar masses, the limit for white dwarfs.
Hawking radiation is the theoretical emission from black holes.
ISRO's Astrosat (2015) is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory.
summary: The answer is (a): Observation and understanding of the Universe. Event Horizon, Singularity, String Theory and Standard Model are all concepts from astrophysics, cosmology and particle physics, used to explain black holes, the origin of the Universe, and the fundamental forces and particles.
topic_notes: This question tests science-and-technology vocabulary from cosmology and particle physics. Black holes: regions where gravity is so strong that escape needs speed greater than light. Stellar black holes form from the collapse of massive stars; supermassive ones sit in galactic centres. The Schwarzschild radius defines the event horizon. Hawking radiation (Stephen Hawking, 1974) is the theoretical thermal emission from black holes. The first direct image came from the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019 (M87*), followed by Sgr A* in 2022. Gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein in 1916, were first detected by LIGO on 14 September 2015 from merging black holes; the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured Weiss, Barish and Thorne. The Standard Model has 6 quarks, 6 leptons, gauge bosons (photon, W, Z, gluon) and the Higgs boson. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the 2013 Nobel Prize. CERN is near Geneva, and its Large Hadron Collider is the largest particle accelerator. Gravity, dark matter and dark energy lie outside the Standard Model. String theory and M-theory aim at a 'theory of everything' unifying gravity with quantum mechanics. Related Indian items: Satyendra Nath Bose (bosons, Bose-Einstein statistics), Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses), India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) proposal, and LIGO-India in Maharashtra. Other possible topics: the Big Bang, cosmic microwave background, the James Webb Space Telescope (launched December 2021), Chandrayaan, Aditya-L1 and Astrosat.

question:
With reference to agriculture in India, how can the technique of ‘genome sequencing’, 4g often seen in the news, be used in the immediate future ?
1. Genome sequencing can be used to identify genetic markers for disease resistance and drought tolerance in various crop plants.
2. This technique helps in reducing the 49 time required to develop new varieties of crop plants.
3. It can be used to decipher the host-pathogen relationships in crops. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: Genome sequencing determines the complete DNA sequence of an organism. In agriculture it supports genomics-assisted breeding. Sequencing many varieties reveals SNPs, QTLs and genes linked to useful traits such as resistance to blast or rust, drought and salinity tolerance, and yield. These markers are used in marker-assisted selection (MAS), which lets breeders screen seedlings in the lab instead of waiting for the plant to mature and show the trait in the field. This shortens the breeding cycle, which usually takes 8-12 years, and permits faster backcrossing and genomic selection. Sequencing both crop and pathogen genomes (for example rice and Magnaporthe oryzae, or wheat and rust fungi) helps identify resistance (R) genes, pathogen effector genes and the molecular basis of infection. It also helps track new virulent strains. Indian milestones include the pigeonpea genome (2011, ICRISAT and ICAR), the chickpea genome (2013), the tomato genome and the rice genome (IRGSP, 2005), the Indian-led 3,000 Rice Genomes project, and the 2017 mango and jute efforts. Elimination logic: statement 1 is textbook, so (b) fails. Statement 2 is the central benefit of MAS, so (a) and (c) fail. Statement 3 is a recognised application, which leaves (d).
explanations: Wrong: it covers only statement 1, but statements 2 and 3 are also valid applications.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is a core and correct use of genome sequencing.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, but marker-assisted breeding does shorten variety development time.
Correct: all three statements describe real applications, namely marker discovery, faster breeding and host-pathogen studies.
keyfact: Genome sequencing gives markers for traits, speeds breeding via marker-assisted selection, and reveals host-pathogen interactions, so all three statements are correct.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: statement 1 on markers for disease resistance and drought tolerance is true, but this option wrongly excludes the other two. Such markers (SNPs, SSRs, QTLs) underpin marker-assisted selection. Examples include the Sub1A gene for submergence tolerance in rice and Xa21 for bacterial blight resistance. ICRISAT, ICAR and NIPGR lead Indian crop genomics, and the pigeonpea genome was sequenced in 2011.

Option (b) 2 and 3 only: this is wrong because it omits statement 1. Statement 2 refers to faster variety development through marker-assisted breeding, and statement 3 to host-pathogen studies. These are valid, but genetic marker identification is the most basic use of sequencing. Related techniques include genomic selection, speed breeding, and CRISPR genome editing, which India has used for rice varieties released in 2025.

Option (c) 1 and 3 only: this is wrong because it excludes statement 2. Statement 3 on host-pathogen relationships is correct, as sequencing both genomes reveals R genes and effectors. However, sequencing also shortens breeding time, since MAS reduces the need for several field generations. Breeding a new crop variety conventionally takes about 8-12 years.

Option (d) 1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. Genome sequencing is the reading of an organism's full DNA. In crops it supports marker discovery, accelerated breeding and pathogen interaction studies. Key milestones: the rice genome in 2005 (IRGSP), pigeonpea in 2011, chickpea in 2013, and the 3,000 Rice Genomes Project. In 2000 Arabidopsis became the first plant genome sequenced.
related: Bt cotton is India's only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation (2002).
GEAC under MoEFCC regulates GM organisms in India.
