detail: Dyarchy (from Greek 'di-archia', rule by two) was introduced in the provinces of British India by the Government of India Act, 1919, based on the Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918), and it came into force in 1921. Provincial subjects were split into two lists. Transferred subjects (local self-government, education, public health, agriculture, public works, excise) were administered by the Governor with Indian ministers responsible to the provincial legislative council. Reserved subjects (law and order, police, justice, land revenue, finance, irrigation) stayed with the Governor and his Executive Council, who were not answerable to the legislature. The Governor held overriding powers and control of finance. The scheme was withdrawn by the Government of India Act 1935, which granted provincial autonomy. Elimination: (a) describes bicameralism, which the 1919 Act did introduce at the Centre (Council of State and Legislative Assembly), but that is not dyarchy. (b) confuses dyarchy with federal division of powers (the central-provincial devolution rules). (c) is a political caricature with no constitutional basis. Only (d) matches the actual meaning of the term.
explanations: Incorrect: the bicameral central legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly) was a separate feature of the 1919 Act; it is not what dyarchy means.

Incorrect: Central and State governments reflect a federal division of powers. Dyarchy operated inside the provinces, not between Centre and provinces; the Centre remained unitary and non-responsible.
Incorrect: there were never two sets of rulers in London and Delhi in this sense; the Secretary of State and Viceroy were part of one imperial hierarchy, so this is not dyarchy.

Correct: provincial subjects were divided into Transferred (under Indian ministers responsible to the legislature) and Reserved (under the Governor and his Executive Council). This is the official answer.
keyfact: Dyarchy (GoI Act 1919, effective 1921) = provincial subjects split into Transferred (ministers) and Reserved (Governor); ended in 1937 by provincial autonomy.
option_notes: Bicameralism at the Centre: the 1919 Act created a bicameral Imperial Legislature, with the Council of State (upper house, 60 members, 34 elected, tenure 5 years) and the Legislative Assembly (lower house, 145 members, 3-year term). The franchise was very restricted and the Governor-General kept certification and veto powers. Before this there was a unicameral Imperial Legislative Council. Bicameralism was a different reform from dyarchy.

Central and State governments: this describes a federal structure. The Government of India Act 1919 began separating central and provincial subjects through the Devolution Rules 1920, and the 1935 Act formalised federal lists (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent). The 1919 provincial dyarchy was a different concept. Federation under the 1935 Act never fully came into operation because the princely states did not join. Independent India has a Union-State federation under Article 1 and the Seventh Schedule.

Two sets of rulers in London and Delhi: this is a distractor with no constitutional meaning. In reality authority flowed from the British Parliament to the Secretary of State for India in London (assisted by the India Council) and to the Viceroy/Governor-General in Delhi. This was a chain of command, not a dual rule. Dual government in Bengal (1765-72) under Robert Clive is a different historical idea, in which the Company held diwani and the Nawab nizamat.

Division of provincial subjects into two categories: dyarchy, introduced by the 1919 Act and effective from 1921 in the nine provinces, divided subjects into Transferred and Reserved. Lionel Curtis is regarded as its architect. Ministers for Transferred subjects were elected members of the legislative council, answerable to it, and appointed by the Governor. The Governor could override ministers and controlled finance. It failed because ministers lacked financial power, and it was ended in 1937 by provincial autonomy.
related: Dyarchy in the provinces was introduced by the Government of India Act 1919 and took effect in 1921.
Dyarchy was abolished by the Government of India Act 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy in 1937.
Transferred subjects: education, local self-government, public health, agriculture; Reserved: law and order, finance, land revenue, justice.
Lionel Curtis is regarded as the architect of dyarchy.
The Government of India Act 1919 created the Council of State and Legislative Assembly at the Centre.
The Government of India Act 1935 proposed dyarchy at the Centre, but this part was never implemented.
The Simon Commission (1927) was the statutory commission due under the 1919 Act.
Montagu's August 1917 declaration promised 'progressive realisation of responsible government'.
summary: The official answer is (d): the principle of 'Dyarchy (diarchy)' refers to the division of the subjects delegated to the provinces into two categories, Transferred and Reserved. It was introduced by the Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) and applied only at the provincial level, not the Centre.
topic_notes: Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms): Secretary of State Edwin Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford. It followed the August 1917 declaration promising 'progressive realisation of responsible government'. Features: (1) Dyarchy in the provinces, with Transferred subjects under ministers and Reserved subjects under the Governor's Executive Council. (2) Bicameral Centre, with a Council of State and a Legislative Assembly. (3) Devolution Rules separated central and provincial subjects and revenues. (4) Franchise extended but still limited, with communal electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans. (5) A High Commissioner for India in London, which relieved the Secretary of State of some functions. (6) The Public Service Commission was provided for (set up 1926). (7) A statutory commission was to be appointed after 10 years, which led to the Simon Commission (1927). Dyarchy was introduced in Bengal, Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Punjab, Bihar and Orissa, Central Provinces, Assam, and later Burma. Ministers such as Surendranath Banerjee in Bengal and the Swarajists' stance (Council entry, 1923) shaped its working. The Muddiman Committee (1924) examined its working. The Government of India Act 1935 abolished provincial dyarchy and introduced provincial autonomy, while proposing dyarchy at the Centre for some subjects (never implemented). Other related ideas: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) with separate electorates; Indian Councils Act 1892; Government of India Act 1858 (Crown rule). Nehru Report (1928) and Cabinet Mission (1946) are later steps in the constitutional story. Also remember that the Congress at first rejected the 1919 reforms as 'inadequate and disappointing'.

question:
Consider the following in respect of ‘National Career Service’ : 1, National Career Service is an initiative of the Department of Personnel and Training, Government of India. 66.
2. National Career Service has been launched in a Mission Mode to improve the employment opportunities to uneducated youth of the country. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The National Career Service (NCS) was launched by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of India, on 20 July 2015 (the Prime Minister launched the NCS portal in 2015 and it was initially rolled out as a Mission Mode Project). It is a digital platform (www.ncs.gov.in) that links job seekers, employers, skill providers, career counsellors and training institutes. It works through the Directorate General of Employment (DGE), which transformed the traditional employment exchanges into Model Career Centres. It is not under the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), which sits in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and deals with civil service personnel policy, recruitment rules and training, so Statement 1 fails. Statement 2 fails because the NCS serves all job seekers, including graduates, diploma holders, ITI pass-outs and skilled workers. Its services include job matching, career counselling, vocational guidance, information on skill courses and internships, and it is not restricted to the uneducated. Elimination: once you remember that NCS belongs to the Labour Ministry, (a) and (c) go out. Since it is not a scheme only for the uneducated, (b) goes out as well. That leaves (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 1 is incorrect: NCS belongs to the Ministry of Labour and Employment, not the DoPT.
(b) is wrong because Statement 2 is incorrect: NCS serves job seekers at all education levels, not only the uneducated.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both hold.
(d) is correct because both statements are factually wrong: the Labour Ministry runs NCS and it is open to all job seekers.
keyfact: NCS = Ministry of Labour and Employment portal for all job seekers (2015), not a DoPT scheme and not only for the uneducated.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would imply NCS is a DoPT initiative. The DoPT is a department of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. It deals with the Central Civil Services, recruitment, training (via the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration and ISTM), the Central Vigilance Commission and Lokpal matters, and the Right to Information Act. It has no role in running a national employment service, which is the job of the Labour Ministry.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' would imply NCS is meant for uneducated youth. In fact NCS serves everyone from school pass-outs to professionals. Schemes aimed at the less-educated or unskilled include PMKVY (Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, launched 2015 under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship), which gives short-term skill training and certification, and MGNREGA, which guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' would require both statements to be right. In reality NCS has one parent ministry, Labour and Employment, and one broad aim: to bridge the gap between job seekers and employers through a technology-driven platform. It is part of the digital India and e-governance push and replaced the older, paper-based employment exchange system with online services.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is the official answer. The NCS portal (ncs.gov.in) was launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment through the DGE. It provides job matching, career counselling, listings of skill courses and apprenticeships, and links employers with seekers. It is open to all, with special attention to disadvantaged groups, and its Model Career Centres are the upgraded employment exchanges.
related: NCS was launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
The NCS portal address is ncs.gov.in.
The Directorate General of Employment (DGE) implements NCS.
Employment exchanges are being converted into Model Career Centres.
DoPT falls under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
PMKVY was launched in 2015 under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.
The e-Shram portal is a national database of unorganised workers, launched in 2021.
The four labour codes subsume 29 central labour laws.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: NCS is an initiative of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, not DoPT. The NCS Project was launched in 2015 as a Mission Mode Project under the National e-Governance Plan to transform the National Employment Service. It is run by the Directorate General of Employment (DGE). The portal offers job matching, career counselling, and information on skill courses, apprenticeships and internships. DoPT, by contrast, sits under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and handles civil service matters. Employment Exchanges have been converted into Model Career Centres under the NCS.

2 — Incorrect: NCS is not meant only for uneducated youth. It is an open platform for all job seekers regardless of educational level, as well as employers, placement organisations, training providers and counsellors. It was launched as a Mission Mode Project to provide a national, online, transparent and efficient job-matching system. Its services include registration, job search, career counselling, vocational guidance, and information on skilling and entrepreneurship. Special features include a focus on persons with disabilities, women and rural youth, and links with DigiLocker, Aadhaar and Skill India. The portal has also been used for Covid-era job support and for hosting job fairs.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. The National Career Service (NCS) is an initiative of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, not the Department of Personnel and Training, and it is a portal for job matching and career guidance open to all job seekers, not only uneducated youth.
topic_notes: The National Career Service is a flagship employment-facilitation initiative of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, launched in 2015 as a Mission Mode Project. It aims to reform the old National Employment Service, a network of employment exchanges set up under the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959. The NCS portal (ncs.gov.in) offers online registration, job search, job matching, career counselling, vocational guidance, and information on training, apprenticeships and internships. Its stakeholders are job seekers, employers, skill providers, counsellors, and government departments and agencies. The Directorate General of Employment (DGE) implements it, and the old employment exchanges are being upgraded into Model Career Centres (MCCs). NCS is integrated with other digital initiatives such as Aadhaar, DigiLocker and Skill India, and it supports special groups including persons with disabilities, women and rural youth. Related Labour Ministry bodies and laws: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC), the Code on Wages 2019, the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Social Security Code 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020, which consolidate 29 earlier labour laws into four codes. The e-Shram portal (2021) builds a national database of unorganised workers. Other employment and skills schemes UPSC may ask about: PMKVY (skilling), MGNREGA (rural wage employment), PM-SVANidhi (street vendor credit), Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (rural skills, Ministry of Rural Development), the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme, and the Employment Linked Incentive scheme. Always match the scheme with its ministry and its target group, since UPSC frequently tests exactly that.

question: Which of the following statements best describes the term ‘Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A)’, recently seen in the news ?
options: It is a procedure for considering ecological costs of developmental schemes formulated by the Government
It is a scheme of RBI for reworking the financial structure of big corporate 67. entities facing genuine difficulties
It is a disinvestment plan of the Government regarding Central Public Sector Undertakings
It is an important provision in ‘The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code’ recently implemented by the Government
subject: Current Affairs
detail: S4A (Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets) was issued by the Reserve Bank of India in June 2016 as one of its tools for dealing with the non-performing asset problem in the banking sector, alongside the Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR), the Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) mechanism, the Joint Lenders' Forum and the Asset Quality Review. It applies to large borrowers with total exposure of at least Rs 500 crore whose projects have already started commercial operations. The firm's debt is divided into two parts. Part A is the sustainable debt, which the company can service from its cash flows. Part B is the unsustainable debt, which is converted into equity or redeemable cumulative optionally convertible preference shares. An independent evaluation agency must certify the debt-sustainability level, and the resolution plan needs approval from 75 percent of creditors by value and 50 percent by number. The scheme is meant for genuine business difficulties, not wilful default. Elimination: S4A has nothing to do with ecological costing, so (a) is out. It is not a disinvestment plan, which is the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management's remit, so (c) is out. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is a separate statute, and S4A is an RBI circular, not a provision of that Code, so (d) is out. The RBI later withdrew S4A in February 2018 and replaced it with a revised framework.
explanations: Incorrect: S4A is a debt-resolution tool for banks. It is not a procedure for assessing the ecological cost of government development schemes.
Correct: S4A is an RBI scheme for reworking the debt and financial structure of large corporates whose projects are viable but facing genuine difficulties.
Incorrect: Disinvestment of Central Public Sector Undertakings is a government policy handled by DIPAM and has no link to S4A.
Incorrect: S4A is an RBI regulatory scheme issued in 2016 and is not a provision of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, which is a separate law.
keyfact: S4A (RBI, June 2016): split a stressed large borrower's debt (Rs 500 crore or more) into sustainable and unsustainable parts, converting the latter into equity or preference shares; withdrawn in 2018.
summary: The correct answer is (b). S4A, announced by the RBI in June 2016, is a resolution scheme that lets banks restructure the debt of large stressed corporate borrowers whose projects are operationally viable but over-leveraged, by splitting the debt into a sustainable part and an equity or quasi-equity part.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) to Reduce Short Lived Climate Pollutants is a unique initiative of G20 group of countries. 2; The CCAC focuses on methane, black carbon and hydrofluorocarbons. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Environment
detail: The Climate and Clean Air Coalition to Reduce Short-Lived Climate Pollutants was launched on 16 February 2012 by Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden and the United States, together with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), which hosts its Secretariat in Paris. It is a voluntary partnership of governments, intergovernmental organisations, businesses, scientific institutions and civil society. It is not a G20 body, so statement 1 fails on the word 'G20'. SLCPs stay in the atmosphere for a short time (days to about a decade) but have a strong warming effect. The main ones are methane, black carbon (soot), tropospheric ozone and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). Cutting them can slow near-term warming and also improve air quality, public health and crop yields. India joined the CCAC in 2019. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is recognised as wrong because the CCAC is not a G20 initiative, options (a) and (c) go out. Statement 2 matches the CCAC's core focus, which rules out (d). That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 1, but the CCAC is not a G20 initiative. It was launched by a small group of countries and UNEP in 2012.
Correct: statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true. The CCAC addresses methane, black carbon and HFCs, which are all SLCPs.
Wrong: it needs statement 1 to be true, and it is not.
Wrong: statement 2 correctly describes the CCAC's focus on methane, black carbon and HFCs, so it cannot be rejected.
keyfact: CCAC (2012, UNEP-hosted, founded by six countries and UNEP) targets SLCPs: methane, black carbon, HFCs and tropospheric ozone; it is not a G20 initiative.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would make the CCAC a G20 initiative, which is false. The G20 is a forum of 19 countries plus the EU and the African Union (admitted 2023). It started in 1999 as a finance ministers' forum and was upgraded to a leaders' summit in 2008. India hosted the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023. The G20 has no permanent secretariat and works through rotating presidencies and a troika.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the correct answer. The CCAC focuses on SLCPs: methane, black carbon, HFCs and tropospheric ozone. It was launched in February 2012, and its Secretariat is hosted by UNEP in Paris. It is a voluntary coalition of states and non-state partners. The aim is to cut near-term warming and improve air quality. India joined in 2019. It funds action through a Trust Fund.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this is wrong because statement 1 is false. The CCAC is a coalition of governments, organisations, businesses and civil society, not a G20 programme. Its partners include many non-G20 countries such as Ghana and Bangladesh, which were founding partners. Statement 2 is right, but a statement-based answer needs both to be correct for (c).

Option (d), neither: this is wrong because statement 2 is correct. The CCAC's work covers methane, black carbon and HFCs. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a short lifetime. HFCs are phased down under the Kigali Amendment (2016, in force 2019). Black carbon comes from incomplete combustion and speeds melting of snow and ice when it settles on them.
related: The CCAC was launched on 16 February 2012 and is hosted by UNEP, with its Secretariat in Paris.
India joined the CCAC in 2019.
The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol phases down HFCs, and entered into force on 1 January 2019.
The Global Methane Pledge (COP26, 2021) targets a 30% cut in methane by 2030 from 2020 levels.
Black carbon is soot from incomplete combustion; it warms the air and darkens snow and ice, speeding melt.
Methane has a lifetime of about 12 years and a 100-year GWP of about 28-30.
Tropospheric ozone is a secondary pollutant and not emitted directly.
The G20 has no permanent secretariat; the African Union became a permanent member in 2023.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the CCAC was not created by the G20. It was launched in 2012 by six countries and UNEP. Facts: The first partners were Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden and the US. The announcement came from US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. The Secretariat is hosted by UNEP in Paris. Membership is voluntary and open to states and non-state partners, and now covers well over 70 state partners. It works through sector initiatives on methane from oil and gas, waste, agriculture, brick kilns, HFCs, diesel and household energy. It has no binding obligations and is not a treaty.

2 — Correct: the CCAC targets methane, black carbon and HFCs, along with tropospheric ozone. Facts: SLCPs have atmospheric lifetimes much shorter than CO2. Methane lasts about 12 years and has a global warming potential (GWP) of about 28-30 over 100 years. Black carbon comes from incomplete combustion of diesel, biomass and cookstoves. HFCs are replacements for ozone-depleting substances and are controlled under the Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol. Cutting SLCPs could avoid roughly 0.5°C of warming by 2050 and prevent millions of premature deaths from air pollution.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The CCAC targets short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs) such as methane, black carbon and HFCs, but it is not a G20 initiative. It was launched in 2012 by a small group of countries led by the US, along with UNEP.
topic_notes:
Short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs) are agents that have a strong warming effect but stay in the atmosphere for only days to about a decade, unlike CO2, which lasts centuries. The main SLCPs are methane (about 12 years), black carbon (days to weeks), tropospheric ozone (a secondary pollutant formed from precursors such as NOx and VOCs) and HFCs (lifetimes vary, average about 15 years). Cutting them is seen as the fastest way to slow near-term warming and could avoid about 0.5°C by mid-century. It also brings co-benefits for public health, because fine particulate matter causes millions of premature deaths, and for crop yields.

The CCAC was launched on 16 February 2012. The founding partners were Bangladesh, Canada, Ghana, Mexico, Sweden, the US and UNEP. Its Secretariat is in Paris, hosted by UNEP. It has state partners, intergovernmental organisations and non-state partners. India joined in 2019. It runs sector initiatives on methane in oil and gas, waste, agriculture, brick production, HFCs and household energy, and it has a Trust Fund.

Related frameworks include:
- The Montreal Protocol (1987) on ozone-depleting substances. Its Kigali Amendment (2016, in force 1 January 2019) phases down HFCs.
- The Global Methane Pledge, launched at COP26 in Glasgow (2021) by the US and EU, aims to cut methane emissions by 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.
- The Gothenburg Protocol, under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution, covers black carbon.
- India's National Clean Air Programme (2019) aims for a 20-30% cut in PM concentrations, later raised to 40%.
- The Arctic Council works on black carbon and methane.

UPSC may ask about the GWP of gases, the Kigali Amendment, the sources of black carbon and the Global Methane Pledge.

question:
With reference to ‘Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) sometimes mentioned in the news while forecasting Indian monsoon, which of the following statements is/are correct ? 1 10D phenomenon is characterised by a difference in sea surface temperature between tropical Western Indian Ocean and tropical Eastern Pacific Ocean.
2. An IOD phenomenon can influence an El Nino’s impact on the monsoon. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), also called the Indian Nino, is an irregular oscillation of sea surface temperatures within the Indian Ocean. It is measured by the Dipole Mode Index (DMI), the SST anomaly difference between the western pole (50°E-70°E, 10°S-10°N) and the eastern pole (90°E-110°E, 10°S-equator). In a positive phase the western Indian Ocean (near Africa) is warmer and the eastern part (near Indonesia) is cooler. This brings more rain to East Africa and India and drought to Indonesia and Australia. In a negative phase the pattern reverses. Statement 1 is wrong because it names the Eastern Pacific as the second pole. A west-Pacific versus east-Pacific temperature contrast is the ENSO (El Nino-Southern Oscillation) mechanism, not the IOD. Statement 2 is right because the IOD and ENSO interact. A positive IOD can suppress the drying effect of El Nino on the Indian monsoon, as in 1997, while a negative IOD can worsen it. IOD events typically peak in September-October and are linked to changes in Walker circulation and winds along the equator. Elimination: once statement 1 is seen to be wrong, only (b) or (d) remain, and the well-known IOD-ENSO interplay settles it as (b).
explanations: Wrong: this accepts statement 1, which wrongly places the IOD's second pole in the Eastern Pacific, and it rejects the correct statement 2.
Correct: statement 1 is wrong because the IOD is an Indian Ocean east-west SST difference. Statement 2 is right because the IOD can modify the effect of El Nino on the monsoon.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, since the Eastern Pacific is part of the ENSO system, not the IOD.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, since the IOD and ENSO interact and a positive IOD can offset El Nino's impact on the monsoon.
keyfact: IOD is an Indian Ocean west-minus-east SST gradient (not Pacific), and a positive IOD can offset El Nino's drying effect on the Indian monsoon.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would have made the IOD a Western Indian Ocean versus Eastern Pacific phenomenon, which is incorrect. The Eastern Pacific is central to ENSO, where Pacific SST anomalies and the Southern Oscillation (the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin) drive El Nino and La Nina. The IOD operates only within the Indian Ocean. This confusion is the trap in the question.

Option (b), statement 2 only: this is the correct answer. It reflects the fact that the IOD, an Indian Ocean mode, interacts with ENSO and modifies its effect on the Indian monsoon. A positive IOD tends to enhance monsoon rainfall even in El Nino years, as in 1997, while a negative IOD tends to suppress it. The IOD is measured by the Dipole Mode Index.

Option (c), both statements: this is wrong because statement 1 mislocates the IOD's poles. Statement 2 alone is valid. Remember that the IOD has a western pole near the Arabian Sea and East Africa and an eastern pole near Sumatra and Indonesia, both in the Indian Ocean.

Option (d), neither statement: this is wrong because statement 2 is correct. The IOD and ENSO are known to interact. A positive IOD can compensate for an El Nino's drying effect on the Indian monsoon, which is why the IMD and other forecasters monitor both when predicting seasonal rainfall.
related: IOD is also called the Indian Nino or Dipole Mode.
DMI measures the IOD as the western minus eastern tropical Indian Ocean SST anomaly.
A positive IOD usually boosts Indian monsoon rainfall and can offset El Nino.
In 2019 a very strong positive IOD coincided with heavy monsoon rain in India and bushfires in Australia.
El Nino is warming of the central and eastern Pacific and usually weakens the Indian monsoon.
La Nina is Pacific cooling that usually strengthens the Indian monsoon.
The Southern Oscillation Index measures the Tahiti-Darwin pressure difference.
IOD events typically peak in September-October.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The IOD is defined by the SST gradient between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean, not the Eastern Pacific. The IOD is an ocean-atmosphere coupled phenomenon in the Indian Ocean, first described in detail by Saji et al. in 1999. The DMI is the SST anomaly in the western pole (50-70°E, 10°S-10°N) minus the eastern pole (90-110°E, 10°S-equator). A positive phase gives a warm west and cool east, with more rainfall over East Africa and the Indian subcontinent. A negative phase gives the opposite. The Pacific-based temperature contrast belongs to ENSO, which includes El Nino and La Nina.

2 — Correct: A positive IOD can counteract an El Nino's adverse effect on the monsoon. In 1997 a strong El Nino coincided with a strong positive IOD, and the Indian monsoon was near normal. In 2019 a very strong positive IOD helped produce heavy late-season monsoon rainfall in India. A negative IOD combined with El Nino can deepen monsoon deficits. The two phenomena are partly independent but can reinforce or offset each other through changes in the Walker circulation and the winds over the equatorial Indian Ocean. Forecasters, including the IMD, therefore track the IOD alongside ENSO.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The IOD is the difference in sea surface temperature between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean, not the Eastern Pacific, and a positive IOD can offset the weakening effect of El Nino on the Indian monsoon.
topic_notes: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), also called the Indian Nino or Dipole Mode, is a coupled ocean-atmosphere oscillation in the tropical Indian Ocean. It was formally identified in 1999 by Saji and colleagues. It is measured by the Dipole Mode Index (DMI), the SST anomaly gradient between the western pole (50-70°E, 10°S-10°N) and the eastern pole (90-110°E, 10°S-equator). Phases: positive (warm west, cool east; stronger easterly winds along the equator weaken or reverse; more rain over East Africa and India, drought in Indonesia and Australia, including bushfire risk in Australia) and negative (the reverse; drier for East Africa and India, wetter for Australia). Events usually develop in May-June, peak in September-October and decay by December. ENSO is the Pacific counterpart. El Nino is warming of the central and eastern Pacific, usually weakening the Indian monsoon. La Nina is cooling there, usually strengthening it. The Southern Oscillation Index measures the Tahiti-Darwin pressure difference. A positive IOD can offset El Nino, as in 1997, while a negative IOD can worsen El Nino-linked deficits. Other related ideas include the Walker circulation, Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), Equatorial Indian Ocean Oscillation (EQUINOO), and the IMD Monsoon Mission. Other related ocean-atmosphere patterns include the North Atlantic Oscillation, Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Atlantic Nino. UPSC often tests the contrast between the IOD and ENSO, the locations of the poles, and the effects on rainfall in India, Africa and Australia.

question: If you want to see gharials in their natural habitat, which one of the following is the best place to visit ?
subject: Environment
detail: The gharial is a fish-eating, long-snouted crocodilian found in clean, fast-flowing rivers with sandy banks for nesting. It is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Historically it ranged across the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and Mahanadi systems, but it has vanished from most of them. Today the Chambal holds the bulk of the world's population, with smaller groups in the Girwa (Ghaghara), Gandak, Son and Ramganga rivers. The National Chambal Sanctuary, a tri-state protected area, was notified in 1979 (Madhya Pradesh in 1978) and also protects the Ganges river dolphin, mugger, red-crowned roof turtle, and skimmers. Elimination: Bhitarkanika in Odisha is a mangrove area famous for saltwater crocodiles and Olive Ridley nesting at Gahirmatha. Pulicat is a brackish coastal lagoon on the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu border known for flamingos and other migratory birds. Deepor Beel in Assam is a freshwater wetland and Ramsar site known for birds. None of these is a gharial stronghold, so only the Chambal fits.
explanations: Incorrect: Bhitarkanika's mangrove creeks are known for the saltwater crocodile, not for the freshwater, river-dwelling gharial.
Correct: the National Chambal Sanctuary protects the largest wild breeding population of gharials, so it is the best place to see them.
Incorrect: Pulicat is a brackish coastal lagoon known for flamingos and migratory waterbirds, not gharials.
Incorrect: Deepor Beel is a freshwater wetland in Assam known for birds and elephants nearby, not gharials.
keyfact: Gharial stronghold = National Chambal Sanctuary (Rajasthan-MP-UP); Bhitarkanika = saltwater crocodile.
option_notes: Bhitarkanika Mangroves lie in Kendrapara district, Odisha, in the Brahmani-Baitarani delta. The sanctuary was declared in 1975 and became a Ramsar site in 2002. It has India's second-largest mangrove ecosystem and is home to the largest population of saltwater crocodiles in India. The adjoining Gahirmatha beach is a major mass-nesting site for Olive Ridley turtles. Also notable for the king cobra and many resident and migratory birds.

Chambal River is a tributary of the Yamuna that rises near Mhow in the Vindhyas of Madhya Pradesh. It flows through MP, Rajasthan and UP. The National Chambal Sanctuary, notified in 1979, protects the gharial, mugger, Ganges river dolphin, smooth-coated otter and several turtle species including the red-crowned roof turtle. It is known for its badlands (ravines) and relatively low pollution. It is a tri-state protected area and a key Indian conservation site for gharials.

Pulicat Lake is India's second-largest brackish water lagoon, after Chilika. It lies on the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu coast, separated from the Bay of Bengal by the Sriharikota barrier island, which hosts ISRO's launch centre. The Pulicat Lake Bird Sanctuary is famous for greater flamingos, pelicans, and migratory ducks. It supports fisheries and local livelihoods, and is threatened by siltation and mouth closure.

Deepor Beel is a permanent freshwater lake in a former channel of the Brahmaputra, located southwest of Guwahati, Assam. It was designated a Ramsar site in 2002 and is an Important Bird Area. It supports many resident and migratory birds, including the greater adjutant stork, and is important for fish. Threats include a nearby landfill, railway line, encroachment, and urban pollution.
related: The gharial is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
National Chambal Sanctuary spans Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
Project Crocodile was launched in 1975 for gharial, mugger and saltwater crocodile.
Bhitarkanika, Odisha has the largest saltwater crocodile population in India, and nearby Gahirmatha hosts Olive Ridley mass nesting.
The Chambal is a tributary of the Yamuna, rising near Mhow in Madhya Pradesh.
Ganges river dolphin is the national aquatic animal and also lives in the Chambal.
Pulicat is the second-largest brackish lagoon in India; Chilika is the largest.
Deepor Beel in Assam is a Ramsar site.
summary: The answer is (b) Chambal River. The National Chambal Sanctuary, spread across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, holds the largest surviving wild breeding population of the critically endangered gharial (Gavialis gangeticus), and it was set up mainly to protect this species.
topic_notes: The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is a fish-eating crocodilian whose male has a bulbous growth at the snout tip called the 'ghara'. IUCN: Critically Endangered; Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972: Schedule I; CITES: Appendix I. Its population has declined sharply due to riverine habitat loss, dams and barrages, sand mining, fishing nets and pollution. Its range has shrunk to under 5 percent of historical distribution. The main remaining population is in the Chambal, with others in the Girwa river in Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary, Son river, Gandak, Ramganga in Corbett, and the Mahanadi's Satkosia gorge in Odisha. Other Indian crocodilians: mugger (marsh crocodile, Vulnerable), found across the subcontinent in freshwater lakes and rivers; saltwater crocodile (Least Concern), found in Bhitarkanika, Sundarbans and Andaman and Nicobar. Project Crocodile was launched in 1975 with FAO and UNDP support to protect all three Indian species and had captive breeding and rearing centres. The National Chambal Sanctuary covers about 5,400 sq km along a roughly 400 km stretch, and also protects the Ganges river dolphin, the national aquatic animal. Related wetlands: Chilika (Odisha, the largest brackish lagoon, with Irrawaddy dolphins), Loktak (Manipur, with Keibul Lamjao floating national park and the sangai), Sundarbans (Bengal tigers), Kolleru, Vembanad. UPSC often links species with their habitat and protected area, so memorise matches such as gharial-Chambal, saltwater crocodile-Bhitarkanika, sangai-Keibul Lamjao, and Olive Ridley-Gahirmatha.

question:
Consider the following in respect of Indian 71. Ocean Naval Symposium (IONS) :
1. Inaugural IONS was held in India in 2015 under the chairmanship of the Indian Navy. 3 IONS is. a voluntary initiative that seeks to increase maritime co-operation among navies of the littoral states of the Indian Ocean Region. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Ocean Naval Symposium (IONS) was launched by the Indian Navy in New Delhi in February 2008, with the Chief of the Naval Staff as its first Chairman (2008-10). It is a voluntary, non-binding forum that gives navies of Indian Ocean littoral states a platform to discuss regional maritime issues, build mutual understanding and promote cooperation. It is not a treaty body and has no formal secretariat obligations or binding decisions. Membership is organised into four sub-regional groups: South Asian, West Asian, East African and South East Asian/Australian littorals. The chair rotates every two years. Later chairs included the UAE (2010-12), South Africa (2012-14), Australia (2014-16), Bangladesh (2016-18), Iran (2018-21), and France (2021-23). India took over again in 2023 and the Indian Navy hosted the Conclave of Chiefs in Kochi in 2025. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails because of the wrong year (2015 instead of 2008), which removes (a) and (c). Statement 2 is a correct description, which removes (d), leaving (b). Note that the International Fleet Review of 2016 and MILAN are separate events and should not be confused with the inaugural IONS.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is false because the inaugural IONS was in 2008, so 'statement 1 only' cannot be correct.
Correct: statement 2 accurately describes IONS as a voluntary maritime cooperation initiative among Indian Ocean littoral navies, while statement 1 is false.
Wrong: this requires statement 1 to be true, but the inaugural IONS was in 2008, not 2015.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be right.
keyfact: IONS was launched by the Indian Navy in New Delhi in 2008 as a voluntary forum for Indian Ocean littoral navies, not in 2015.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would mean the inaugural IONS took place in 2015. In fact it took place in New Delhi in February 2008, hosted by the Indian Navy. The Navy's chief was the first chair for 2008-10. Chairmanship rotates biennially. Selecting this option confuses the date with later events such as the 2016 International Fleet Review at Visakhapatnam, or with the 2015 maritime activities. It is therefore wrong on both counts since it also omits the correct statement 2.

Option (b), statement 2 only: this is the official answer. IONS is a voluntary, non-binding forum of Indian Ocean littoral navies, launched in 2008 by India. It promotes maritime cooperation, shared understanding of maritime issues and regional security. Members are drawn from four sub-regions: South Asia, West Asia, East Africa and South East Asia/Australia. Chairs rotate every two years, including UAE, South Africa, Australia, Bangladesh, Iran, France and India. Working groups address HADR, information sharing and interoperability.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this would require the inaugural IONS to be in 2015 under Indian chairmanship. While India did chair the inaugural IONS, it was in 2008, not 2015. The correct recognition of statement 2 as true is not enough because statement 1 contains the wrong year. UPSC often alters a single fact such as a date in an otherwise correct statement, so check each element carefully.

Option (d), neither: this would mean IONS is not a voluntary initiative for cooperation. That is incorrect, since IONS is explicitly a voluntary, non-binding forum for cooperation among Indian Ocean littoral navies. Statement 2 is a standard description of the organisation. IONS is distinct from treaty-based or military alliance structures, and it has no collective defence obligations or binding decisions.
related: IONS was launched in February 2008 in New Delhi by the Indian Navy.
IONS is voluntary and non-binding, with chairmanship rotating every two years.
IONS has four sub-regional groups: South Asia, West Asia, East Africa, South East Asia and Australia.
IORA was founded in 1997 and is headquartered in Ebene, Mauritius.
MILAN is a biennial multilateral naval exercise hosted by India at Visakhapatnam.
SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) was announced by PM Modi in 2015.
IFC-IOR is based in Gurugram and was set up in 2018.
The Western Pacific Naval Symposium (WPNS) is the Pacific counterpart of IONS.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The inaugural IONS was held in 2008, not 2015. IONS was conceived and launched by the Indian Navy at New Delhi in February 2008, with India as the first chair for 2008-10. The Chief of the Naval Staff holds the chair role. Chairmanship rotates every two years among members, and India later chaired again (2023 onwards). The 2015 date is a distractor, likely confused with other maritime events. Later symposia and conclaves of chiefs are held during each chair's tenure.

2 — Correct: IONS is a voluntary initiative that seeks to increase maritime cooperation among navies of littoral states of the Indian Ocean Region. Its aim is to promote regional maritime security through a open and inclusive forum for discussing regional issues. It has no binding commitments. Working groups cover areas such as HADR (humanitarian assistance and disaster relief), information sharing and interoperability, and anti-piracy. Members are grouped in four sub-regions: South Asia, West Asia, East Africa, and South East Asia and Australia.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. IONS is a voluntary initiative for maritime cooperation among navies of Indian Ocean littoral states, but the inaugural IONS was held in New Delhi in February 2008, not in 2015.
topic_notes: IONS was launched in New Delhi in February 2008 by the Indian Navy. Its objective is to enhance maritime cooperation among navies of Indian Ocean littoral states by providing an open and inclusive platform for discussing regional maritime issues. It is voluntary and non-binding. The members are divided into four sub-regional groupings: South Asian littorals (including India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Maldives), West Asian littorals (including Iran, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Oman), East African littorals (including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa, Mozambique, Madagascar), and South East Asian and Australian littorals (including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Australia). The chair rotates every two years, and each chair hosts a Conclave of Chiefs and a seminar. IONS works through working groups on HADR, information sharing and interoperability, and anti-piracy, and it has produced a charter of business that was adopted in 2014. Related Indian maritime initiatives include MILAN, a biennial multilateral naval exercise at Visakhapatnam hosted by the Eastern Naval Command since 1995; the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA), founded in 1997 and headquartered in Ebene, Mauritius; SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region), announced by PM Modi in 2015; the Colombo Security Conclave; and the Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) at Gurugram, established in 2018. UPSC may also ask about Quad, Malabar exercise, Western Pacific Naval Symposium (WPNS) and the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative. Always check dates, hosts and membership when answering such questions.

question: The painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani is one of the most famous and oft-illustrated paintings at
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Ajanta, near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) in Maharashtra, has 30 rock-cut Buddhist caves cut into a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora river. They were built in two phases: the Satavahana phase (c. 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE, Hinayana/Theravada) and the Vakataka phase (c. 5th to 6th century CE, Mahayana, under Harishena). The caves were rediscovered in 1819 by John Smith, a British army officer, and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983). Cave 1 holds the famous Padmapani and Vajrapani paintings, and the Padmapani figure is shown with a lotus, a tall crown, and a graceful tribhanga pose. The paintings are done in a tempera technique on dry plaster and illustrate Jataka tales and the Buddha's life. Elimination: Badami (Karnataka) has Chalukyan rock-cut caves, both Brahmanical and Jain, with some paintings, but is not known for Padmapani. Bagh (Madhya Pradesh) has Buddhist murals that are similar but are more secular and less famous. Ellora (Maharashtra) is known for the Kailasa temple and its mix of Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, with few paintings.
explanations: Correct: Padmapani is in Cave 1 at Ajanta, a Mahayana-phase cave of the Vakataka period, and is the most illustrated Ajanta mural.
Wrong: Badami has 6th-century Chalukyan cave temples, including Vaishnava, Shaiva and Jain ones, with sculptures such as Vishnu and Nataraja, but it is not associated with Padmapani.
Wrong: Bagh has Buddhist cave murals in Madhya Pradesh that are similar in style to Ajanta's, but Padmapani is not their famous figure.
Wrong: Ellora is known for sculpture and monolithic architecture such as the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), not for the Padmapani painting.
keyfact: Padmapani (and Vajrapani) paintings are in Cave 1 at Ajanta, Maharashtra.
option_notes: Ajanta: 30 Buddhist rock-cut caves in the Waghora gorge, Maharashtra. They date from the 2nd century BCE to c. 6th century CE and were rediscovered in 1819 by John Smith. They are a UNESCO site (1983) and are famous for murals of Jataka stories, Padmapani and Vajrapani, and the dying princess. Caves 9, 10, 19, 26 and 29 are chaityas, and the others are viharas.

Badami: the ancient Vatapi, capital of the Early Chalukyas under Pulakeshin I and II, in Karnataka. It has four rock-cut cave temples of the 6th century (Shaiva, Vaishnava, Jain and possibly Buddhist), cut in red sandstone. It is also known for structural temples at nearby Aihole and Pattadakal, and Cave 3 (Vishnu) has some murals.

Bagh: a group of nine Buddhist rock-cut caves on the Bagh river in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, dating from c. 5th to 6th century CE. The murals are similar to Ajanta's but are considered more earthly and robust, and the site was rediscovered in 1818. It is protected by the ASI.

Ellora: 34 caves at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Maharashtra, with 12 Buddhist (Caves 1-12), 17 Hindu (13-29) and 5 Jain (30-34). It was built under the Rashtrakutas and others from c. 600 to 1000 CE. Cave 16, the Kailasa temple, is a monolith carved from the top down under Krishna I. It is a UNESCO site (1983).
related: Ajanta caves were rediscovered in 1819 by John Smith of the Madras Regiment.
Ajanta and Ellora were both inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1983.
Ajanta has 30 caves, with Caves 9, 10, 19, 26 and 29 as chaityas.
Ajanta paintings use the tempera technique on dry plaster.
Sittanavasal in Tamil Nadu has Jain cave paintings.
The Kailasa temple at Ellora (Cave 16) was built by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
Bagh caves are in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh.
Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is at Udayagiri, Odisha.
summary: The answer is (a) Ajanta. The painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani, the lotus-bearing Avalokiteshvara, is in Cave 1 at Ajanta in Maharashtra and is among the most celebrated examples of Indian Buddhist mural art of the Gupta and Vakataka period.
topic_notes: Indian rock-cut architecture and cave paintings are a favourite UPSC topic. Ajanta: a horseshoe gorge on the Waghora, with 30 caves. Phase I (Satavahana, Hinayana) has Caves 9, 10, 8, 12 and 13. Phase II (Vakataka, Mahayana) has Caves 1, 2, 16, 17, 19 and 26. Painting is in tempera on dry plaster. Cave 1 has Padmapani and Vajrapani, and Cave 17 has the Mahajanaka Jataka and Buddha's return to Kapilavastu. Cave 16 has the famous 'dying princess' (Sundari). Cave 26 has the large reclining Buddha. Chinese pilgrims, including Hiuen Tsang, are linked to the region. Ellora has Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, the Kailasa temple (Rashtrakuta, Krishna I) and the Indra Sabha. Elephanta, near Mumbai, has the Trimurti/Maheshvara Shiva sculpture (Shaiva, c. 5th to 6th century). Other cave sites include Bagh (MP), Badami (Karnataka), Udayagiri and Khandagiri (Odisha, Jain, Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela), Barabar caves (Bihar, Mauryan, Ajivikas, polished surfaces), Karla, Bhaja and Kanheri (Maharashtra, Buddhist chaityas), Mahabalipuram (Pallava, rathas and Descent of the Ganga), Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu, Jain murals), and Lepakshi (Vijayanagara murals). Types: a chaitya is a prayer hall with a stupa, and a vihara is a monastery. Mural traditions reappear in the Pallavas, Pandyas, Cholas (Brihadisvara murals) and Vijayanagara. Ajanta's Mahayana phase shows Bodhisattva imagery, and the Gupta-era aesthetic can be seen in the graceful bends of the figures.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Traditions Communities a Chaliha Sahib Festival — Sindhis zi Nanda Raj Jaat Yatra -— Gonds
3. Wari-Warkari — Santhals Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched ?
subject: Art & Culture
detail: This question tests the matching of cultural traditions with the communities or regions that practise them. Chaliha Sahib (Chaliho) is a 40-day thanksgiving observance by Sindhi Hindus to Jhulelal (Uderolal), the patron deity associated with Varuna, the water god. It marks deliverance from the Sindh ruler Mirkhshah, who is said to have forced conversions. Nanda Raj Jaat is a long Himalayan pilgrimage in Uttarakhand, held roughly every 12 years, honouring Goddess Nanda Devi. It is associated with Garhwali and Kumaoni people, not the Gonds, who are a central Indian tribe. The Wari is the Vaishnava pilgrimage to Pandharpur in Maharashtra, followed by the Warkari sect devoted to Vitthal (Vithoba), with saints such as Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram. It is not a Santhal tradition. The Santhals are an eastern Indian tribe known for the Hul rebellion of 1855 and the Sarhul and Karam festivals. Elimination: once pair 1 is known to be correct and either pair 2 or 3 is known to be wrong, only (a) survives. Options (b), (c) and (d) all fail because of pair 2, pair 3, or pair 1.
explanations: Correct. Only pair 1 is right: Chaliha Sahib is a Sindhi festival, while pairs 2 and 3 are mismatched.
Wrong. Pair 2 is incorrect because Nanda Raj Jaat is a Uttarakhand pilgrimage, not Gond. Pair 3 is also incorrect.
Wrong. Pair 1 is correct, but pair 3 is incorrect because Wari-Warkari is Maharashtrian, not Santhal.
Wrong. Pair 1 is correctly matched, so 'none' cannot be correct.
keyfact: Chaliha Sahib = Sindhi; Nanda Raj Jaat = Uttarakhand; Wari-Warkari = Maharashtra (Vitthal).
option_notes: Pair 1 only: Chaliha Sahib is the 40-day Sindhi festival devoted to Jhulelal (Uderolal), the water deity identified with Varuna or Khwaja Khizr. It commemorates deliverance from Mirkhshah's oppression. Devotees fast and offer prayers near water, and the festival ends in thanksgiving. Sindhis also celebrate Cheti Chand, their new year, as Jhulelal's birth anniversary. Since pair 1 is accurate, this is the official answer.

Pairs 2 and 3 only: this combines Nanda Raj Jaat with the Gonds and Wari-Warkari with the Santhals, both of which are wrong. Nanda Raj Jaat is a Himalayan pilgrimage in Uttarakhand, and Wari is a Maharashtra Vaishnava pilgrimage to Pandharpur. The Gonds and Santhals are separate tribal communities of central and eastern India respectively.

Pairs 1 and 3 only: this treats Wari-Warkari as Santhal, which is wrong. The Warkari sect is a Maharashtra-based Bhakti movement devoted to Vitthal, whose saints include Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram. The Wari is the annual pilgrimage to Pandharpur around Ashadhi Ekadashi. Santhals have their own traditions such as Sarhul, Karam and Baha.

None of the above: this would hold only if all three pairs were wrong. Because Chaliha Sahib is truly a Sindhi festival, this option fails. It is a common distractor in matching questions, where at least one pair is often correct.
related: Chaliha Sahib is a 40-day Sindhi thanksgiving to Jhulelal.
Nanda Raj Jaat is held roughly every 12 years in Uttarakhand for Nanda Devi.
Wari goes to Pandharpur for Vitthal on Ashadhi Ekadashi.
Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram are core Warkari saints.
Santhals led the Hul rebellion of 1855 under Sidhu and Kanhu.
Cheti Chand is the Sindhi new year.
Nanda Devi National Park is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Uttarakhand.
Kumbh Mela is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
statements: 1 — Correct: Chaliha Sahib is indeed a Sindhi festival. It is a 40-day thanksgiving by Sindhi Hindus, observed in July-August after the monsoon sets in. Devotees worship Jhulelal (Uderolal, Daryalal), the incarnation of Varuna, who is believed to have saved the community from the tyranny of the ruler Mirkhshah. Devotees fast and pray beside water. It ends with Chaliha Sahib thanksgiving prayers. Sindhis also celebrate Cheti Chand as their new year and Jhulelal's birth day.

2 — Incorrect: Nanda Raj Jaat is not a Gond tradition. It is a major pilgrimage of Uttarakhand dedicated to Nanda Devi, the patron goddess of Garhwal and Kumaon, and is held about every 12 years. The yatra passes through Chamoli district, travelling roughly 280 km with a four-horned ram (chausingha khadu) leading the procession, and reaches Roopkund and Homkund. Nanda Devi National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Gonds are a central Indian Dravidian tribe of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra.

3 — Incorrect: Wari-Warkari belongs to the Maharashtra Bhakti tradition, not the Santhals. Warkaris are devotees of Vitthal (Vithoba) of Pandharpur, who walk in groups (dindis) carrying palanquins of saints Dnyaneshwar from Alandi and Tukaram from Dehu, reaching Pandharpur on Ashadhi Ekadashi. The Santhals are one of India's largest tribes, living in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and Bihar, and they led the Santhal Hul of 1855-56 under Sidhu and Kanhu.
summary: The answer is (a): only pair 1 is correctly matched. Chaliha Sahib is a festival of the Sindhis, while Nanda Raj Jaat is a Garhwal-Kumaon Himalayan pilgrimage and Wari-Warkari is a Maharashtra Vaishnava tradition.
topic_notes: This question covers matching of traditions, festivals and pilgrimages to communities or regions, a recurring UPSC Art and Culture theme. Chaliha Sahib (Chaliho) is the Sindhi festival of 40 days of thanksgiving to Jhulelal, the water deity. Sindhis also mark Cheti Chand (new year), Thadri and Teejri. Nanda Raj Jaat (Nanda Devi Raj Jat) is a Himalayan pilgrimage of about 280 km in Chamoli, Uttarakhand, held roughly every 12 years, with a four-horned ram leading the procession. It ends near Homkund, and Roopkund and its skeleton lake lie on the route. Nanda Devi National Park and the Valley of Flowers together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Wari is a Vaishnava pilgrimage in Maharashtra to Pandharpur on the Chandrabhaga (Bhima) river, dedicated to Vitthal. Warkari saints include Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram and Janabai. The palanquins leave Alandi and Dehu. Tribal links to remember: the Santhals live in Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha, and their festivals include Sarhul, Karam and Baha. The Gonds are central Indian tribes known for the Gondwana kingdoms, with the Gond art style (Pardhan Gond). Other tribal and regional pairs UPSC may ask: Bhil (Bhagoria), Toda (Nilgiris), Bodo (Bihu-related Assam communities), Khasi (Nongkrem dance), Naga (Hornbill festival). Similar UPSC questions have covered Kumbh Mela, Rath Yatra, Pongal, Onam, Chapchar Kut (Mizo), Hemis (Ladakh) and Losar. Intangible Cultural Heritage items of UNESCO from India include Kumbh Mela, Kalbelia, Chhau, Ramlila and Durga Puja in Kolkata. For prelims, always link each festival to its deity, region, season and community.

question:
Which of the following practices can help in water conservation in agriculture ?
1. Reduced or zero tillage of the 1 and 2. ' Applying gypsum before irrigating the field
3. Allowing crop residue to remain in the field Select.the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: Conservation agriculture rests on three principles: minimum or zero soil disturbance, permanent soil cover (mulch or crop residue), and crop diversification or rotation. Zero tillage keeps soil structure and organic matter intact, which improves infiltration and water-holding capacity. It also lowers evaporation and cuts the water used for pre-sowing irrigation. In India it is widely used for wheat after rice in the Indo-Gangetic plains, and it also saves fuel and time. Crop residue left in the field acts as mulch. It shades the soil, reduces evaporation, moderates soil temperature, checks runoff and erosion, and adds organic carbon, so the soil holds more water. Burning residue destroys these benefits. Gypsum (calcium sulphate) is applied to reclaim sodic or alkaline soils. It replaces exchangeable sodium with calcium and so improves soil structure and permeability. Its purpose is soil reclamation and better water penetration, not saving water, and in fact it is applied together with irrigation to leach out sodium. Elimination logic: once statement 2 is rejected, options (a) and (d) fall, leaving (b) and (c). Since zero tillage is a standard conservation practice, statement 1 is correct, which rules out (b) and leaves (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 2, gypsum application, which is not a water-conservation practice, and it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
(b) is wrong because statement 3 is correct but statement 1, reduced or zero tillage, also conserves water, so 3 alone is incomplete.
(c) is correct because reduced or zero tillage and residue retention both conserve soil moisture, while gypsum does not.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 2, and gypsum is meant for sodic soil reclamation, not for saving water.
keyfact: Conservation agriculture (zero tillage + residue mulch + crop rotation) saves water; gypsum only reclaims sodic soils.
statements: 1 — Correct: Reduced or zero tillage preserves soil structure and moisture, reduces evaporation and lowers irrigation needs.
2 — Incorrect: Gypsum reclaims sodic soils by displacing sodium. It is a soil amendment, not a water-saving practice.
3 — Correct: Crop residue left on the field works as mulch, cutting evaporation and runoff and improving soil moisture retention.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Reduced or zero tillage and leaving crop residue on the field both conserve soil moisture. Gypsum is a soil amendment for sodic soils, not a water-conservation practice.

question: Consider the following statements : The nation-wide ‘Soil Health Card Scheme’ aims at 1. expanding the cultivable area under irrigation. 2. enabling the banks to assess the quantum. of loans to be granted to farmers on the basis of soil quality. 3. checking the overuse of fertilizers in ' farmlands. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan. It is implemented by the Department of Agriculture, Cooperation and Farmers Welfare, Ministry of Agriculture, with State Governments. Under it, soil samples are tested every two years (cycle-based) for 12 parameters: N, P, K (macro-nutrients); S (secondary); Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B (micro-nutrients); and pH, EC, organic carbon (physical parameters). The card advises farmers on the dose of fertilizers and soil amendments needed for specific crops, which promotes Integrated Nutrient Management, reduces input cost, and checks overuse of urea and other chemical fertilizers. Elimination logic: Statement 1 confuses SHC with irrigation schemes like PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana), whose motto is 'Har Khet Ko Pani'. Statement 2 invents a link with bank credit; farm credit is assessed through the Scale of Finance fixed by District Level Technical Committees and the Kisan Credit Card, not soil quality. Only statement 3 matches the scheme's objective, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, but SHC neither expands irrigation nor guides bank loans.
Correct: only statement 3 is true, since SHC aims to check overuse of fertilizers through crop-specific nutrient advice.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because banks do not use SHC to determine loan quantum.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are both false, so all three cannot be correct.
keyfact: Soil Health Card (2015): soil-test-based nutrient advice to check fertilizer overuse, not irrigation or bank loan assessment.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only is a statement-number option, but its content is wrong. Statement 1 relates to irrigation schemes such as PMKSY, and statement 2 relates to farm credit instruments such as Kisan Credit Card and Scale of Finance. Neither is an SHC objective. SHC is a soil-nutrient advisory scheme launched in 2015 by the Agriculture Ministry, covering 12 soil parameters and a two-year testing cycle.

3 only is the correct option. It reflects the scheme's main aim: promoting balanced fertilizer use based on soil testing. The cards provide farmers with the soil's nutrient status, recommended doses of fertilizers and amendments, helping raise productivity, lower input cost, and protect soil health from excess chemical use, especially urea.

2 and 3 only is incorrect because of statement 2. Bank lending to farmers is based on the cropping pattern, Scale of Finance, and Kisan Credit Card limits, assessed through District Level Technical Committees and NABARD norms, not soil quality. The scheme gives agronomic advice only, though statement 3 in this option is right.

1, 2 and 3 is incorrect because it accepts both false statements. Irrigation expansion is the domain of PMKSY and the Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme, and credit assessment is that of banks and NABARD. SHC is limited to soil testing and nutrient recommendations, and extends to no other area.
related: SHC Scheme launched 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan.
SHC tests 12 parameters and is issued on a two-year cycle.
PMKSY motto: 'Har Khet Ko Pani' (2015).
Neem-coated urea was made mandatory for domestic urea production in 2015.
Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) policy for P and K fertilizers began in April 2010.
Kisan Credit Card scheme was introduced in 1998.
PM-KISAN gives Rs 6,000 per year in three instalments to farmer families.
2015 was declared the International Year of Soils by the UN.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: SHC is about nutrient management, not irrigation expansion. Irrigation coverage is the aim of PMKSY (launched 2015, merging AIBP, IWMP and On-Farm Water Management), with components like Per Drop More Crop and Watershed Development. SHC only tells farmers soil nutrient status and the right fertilizer and amendment doses, and it does not add any irrigated area.

2 — Incorrect: SHC has no role in determining bank loans. Farm credit is guided by the Scale of Finance set by District Level Technical Committees under NABARD guidelines, and delivered through the Kisan Credit Card (introduced 1998). The soil health card is an advisory document for farmers and carries no banking or credit-assessment function.

3 — Correct: SHC's core aim is balanced, judicious fertilizer use. It gives crop-wise recommendations of nutrients and fertilizers based on tests of 12 parameters, which reduces overuse of urea and cuts cultivation cost. Launched 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan, it works on a two-year cycle and is linked to the Soil Health Management scheme under the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). Related efforts include neem-coated urea, promoted to curb overuse and diversion.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. The Soil Health Card Scheme gives farmers a card with soil nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations, so it promotes balanced and judicious fertilizer use. It does not expand irrigation, and it is not a tool for banks to set loan quantum.
topic_notes: The Soil Health Card Scheme was launched on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan, by PM Narendra Modi, with the slogan 'Swasth Dharaa to Khet Hara'. It is run by the Department of Agriculture, Cooperation and Farmers Welfare under the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA). Soil samples are collected by state governments, often through agriculture colleges, and tested in static or mobile labs, and the cycle is two years. Cards report 12 parameters: N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC and organic carbon. Based on these, the card recommends fertilizer doses and soil amendments (such as gypsum or lime) for chosen crops. Aims: promote Integrated Nutrient Management, reduce input cost, avoid overuse of urea, raise productivity, and build local capacity such as testing by rural youth and women's groups. Later initiatives include a mobile app and portal, and the Soil Health Card Portal. Related schemes: Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (organic farming clusters), PM-KISAN (income support of Rs 6,000 a year, 2019), PMFBY (crop insurance, 2016), PMKSY (irrigation, 2015), neem-coated urea (made mandatory in 2015), the e-NAM electronic market (2016) and Kisan Credit Card (1998). Soil topics UPSC can ask: soil types in India (alluvial, black, red, laterite), soil degradation, salinity and alkalinity, role of organic carbon, nitrogen fixation, biofertilizers like Rhizobium, Azolla and blue-green algae, and the International Year of Soils (2015). Also note the nutrient-imbalance concerns in Punjab and Haryana caused by excessive NPK ratios, and nutrient-based subsidy (NBS) policy from 2010.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Commonly used / Unwanted or consumed materials controversial chemicals likely to be found in them Lipstick — Lead 2. Soft drinks — Brominated vegetable oils 3. Chinese — Monosodium fast food glutamate Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched ? (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (ec) land 3 only (d) 1,2and3
subject: Geography
detail: This question tests awareness of controversial additives and contaminants in everyday consumer products, a recurring theme in UPSC Environment and Science and Technology. Lead is a toxic heavy metal that appears as a contaminant in lipsticks, as shown by studies from the US FDA and Indian NGOs such as the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) and Toxics Link. Brominated vegetable oil is vegetable oil modified with bromine. It was used as an emulsifier to keep citrus flavouring evenly dispersed in soft drinks. It has been controversial because bromine can accumulate in body tissue. The US FDA revoked its authorisation in 2024, and many countries, including India under FSSAI norms, restrict or prohibit it. MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid. It is added as a flavour enhancer (umami) and is widely used in Chinese-style food, in the seasoning known as Ajinomoto, and in instant noodles. It became controversial after the 2015 Maggi episode and because of the so-called 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'. Elimination logic: once a student knows that any one of the pairs is correct, options that exclude it fall away. Since all three are factually established, (d) is the only option that holds. FSSAI regulates additives and contaminants under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts only pair 1, but pairs 2 and 3 are also correct.
Wrong: it leaves out pair 1 (lead in lipstick), which is correct.
Wrong: it leaves out pair 2 (brominated vegetable oils in soft drinks), which is correct.
Correct: lead in lipstick, BVO in soft drinks and MSG in Chinese fast food are all valid matches, so all three pairs are right.
keyfact: Lead in lipstick, brominated vegetable oils in soft drinks and MSG in Chinese fast food are all valid pairs, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a), pair 1 only: lead in lipstick is a valid pair. Lead is a toxic heavy metal and neurotoxin that accumulates in the body. It occurs as a contaminant in pigments, and studies by the US FDA, CSE and Toxics Link have detected it in lipsticks. In India, cosmetics fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and BIS standards. Lead has been phased out of petrol and paints in most countries. It remains a concern in water, batteries and some imported toys.

Option (b), pairs 2 and 3 only: BVO and MSG are both valid pairs. BVO is an emulsifier once used in citrus soft drinks and banned in the EU, Japan and (since 2024) the USA. MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, a flavour enhancer first isolated by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and sold as Ajinomoto. It is widely used in Chinese-style food, soups and instant noodles. FSSAI regulates it and requires a label warning for infants.

Option (c), pairs 1 and 3 only: lead in lipstick and MSG in Chinese fast food are both valid. Lead is a heavy metal toxin found in some cosmetics, and MSG is a flavour enhancer (umami). Both were in the news during the 2015 Maggi controversy, when FSSAI tested noodles for lead and MSG. The option is wrong only because it excludes pair 2, since BVO is indeed linked to soft drinks. Recall that the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 created FSSAI.

Option (d), all three pairs: this is the official answer. Lipstick can contain lead, soft drinks have used brominated vegetable oils as emulsifiers, and Chinese fast food often uses MSG as a flavour enhancer. These are the 'unwanted or controversial' chemicals in the question. FSSAI, set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, regulates additives in food, while cosmetics fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
related: FSSAI was established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and is under the Union Health Ministry.
BVO is a vegetable oil bonded with bromine used as an emulsifier; the US FDA revoked it in 2024.
MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, first isolated by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and sold as Ajinomoto.
Maggi noodles were banned in 2015 over excess lead and undeclared MSG claims, and the ban was later lifted.
FSSAI banned potassium bromate in 2016 after CSE findings.
Lead is a neurotoxin, especially harmful to children, and India phased out leaded petrol in 2000.
Minamata disease is caused by mercury; Itai-itai disease by cadmium.
CSE reports on pesticide residue in soft drinks came out in 2003 and 2006.
statements: 1 — Correct: Lipstick is a recognised source of lead exposure. Lead is a heavy metal that occurs as a trace contaminant in pigments and mineral colourants. Facts: Lead is a neurotoxin and is especially harmful to children and pregnant women, and no safe exposure level is established. Studies by the US FDA (2010 and later) and Indian groups such as Toxics Link found lead in many lipsticks. India's Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets limits for heavy metals in cosmetics (IS 4707), and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 governs cosmetics in India. Lead can also be found in old paints, petrol (now phased out) and water pipes.

2 — Correct: Brominated vegetable oil (BVO) was used in some citrus-flavoured soft drinks. Facts: BVO is vegetable oil bound with bromine and acts as an emulsifier and clouding agent, preventing flavour oils from separating. Concerns include bromine build-up in tissues and effects on the thyroid and nervous system. It was banned in the EU and Japan, and in 2024 the US FDA revoked its authorisation for use in food. Companies like Coca-Cola and PepsiCo had earlier removed it from their products. In India, the CSE raised concerns about soft drink additives and pesticide residues in 2003 and 2006.

3 — Correct: Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is commonly found in Chinese fast food. Facts: MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, an amino acid, and gives the savoury 'umami' taste. It was first isolated by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and is marketed as Ajinomoto. It is used in soups, sauces, instant noodles and snacks. The US FDA classifies it as 'generally recognised as safe', but it remains controversial because of reports of headache and flushing ('Chinese restaurant syndrome'). In India, FSSAI requires a label warning that it is not recommended for infants under 12 months, and the 2015 Maggi controversy involved MSG and lead.
summary: The answer is (d): all three pairs are correctly matched. Lipstick can contain lead, brominated vegetable oils (BVO) have been used in some soft drinks, and Chinese fast food often contains monosodium glutamate (MSG) as a flavour enhancer.
topic_notes: The topic is controversial chemicals and additives in everyday consumer goods, and the regulatory framework around them. Food in India is regulated by FSSAI, a statutory body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with its headquarters in Delhi. Cosmetics and drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 through the CDSCO, and BIS sets standards. Key chemicals: lead (neurotoxic heavy metal, found in old paints, some cosmetics, contaminated water and leaded petrol, which India phased out in 2000); BVO (emulsifier in citrus soft drinks, banned in the EU, Japan, and the US from 2024); MSG (flavour enhancer, umami, Kikunae Ikeda 1908, Ajinomoto); potassium bromate (a flour improver banned by FSSAI in 2016 after CSE findings, and a possible carcinogen); Sudan dyes (illegal industrial dyes in chilli powder); calcium carbide (illegal fruit ripener, acetylene gas); and formalin in fish. Other angles: CSE reports on pesticides in soft drinks (2003, 2006) and in honey (2020), and on antibiotics in honey; Toxics Link studies on cosmetics; trans fats, with FSSAI capping industrial trans fat at 2 per cent by 2022; the Eat Right India movement; fortification of staples; and the labelling rules for HFSS foods. Related international bodies: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO and WHO), the Stockholm Convention on POPs, the Minamata Convention on mercury, and the Basel Convention. Heavy metals and their effects: lead (neurotoxicity), mercury (Minamata disease), cadmium (Itai-itai disease), arsenic (blackfoot disease), and chromium.

question:
Organic Light Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) are 76, used to create digital display in many devices. What are the advantages of OLED displays over Liquid Crystal displays ?
1. OLED displays can be fabricated on flexible plastic substrates.
2. Roll-up displays embedded in clothing can be made using OLEDs. 3; Transparent displays are possible using OLEDs. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
options: None of the above statements is correct
subject: Science & Tech
detail: An Organic Light Emitting Diode (OLED) uses thin films of organic compounds, placed between two electrodes, that emit light when current passes through them (electroluminescence). Because each pixel produces its own light, an OLED needs no backlight, colour filter-heavy stack or rigid glass layers of the kind an LCD requires. An LCD works differently: liquid crystals only modulate light from an LED or CCFL backlight, which needs a rigid, thick assembly with polarisers. This difference gives OLEDs their advantages: thinner and lighter panels, true blacks, high contrast, wide viewing angles and fast response. Because the organic layers are thin and can be deposited at low temperature, plastic (for example polyimide) substrates can be used, so flexible, foldable and rollable displays are possible. Such displays can be woven or embedded into fabrics and clothing (wearables). If the electrodes are made transparent (for example ITO), the panel itself becomes see-through, which allows transparent displays. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all recognised OLED applications, so options (a), (b) and (d) are wrong. Drawbacks of OLEDs include shorter lifetime of blue emitters, burn-in, moisture sensitivity and higher cost.
explanations: Incorrect: this option omits statement 2, which is also correct, since roll-up displays embedded in clothing are possible with OLEDs.
Incorrect: it accepts only statement 2, but statements 1 and 3 are also valid OLED advantages.
Correct: flexible substrates, roll-up and wearable displays and transparent displays are all advantages of OLEDs over LCDs.
Incorrect: the statements are correct, so this option cannot be true.
keyfact: OLEDs are self-emissive organic films with no backlight, enabling flexible, rollable, wearable and transparent displays that LCDs cannot easily match.
option_notes: Options (a) 1 and 3 only: a partial answer. Flexible and transparent OLEDs are both real technologies.
