Flexible OLEDs are built on plastic such as polyimide and are used in curved and foldable phones. Transparent OLEDs use transparent electrodes and are used in windows, signage and automotive displays. This combination wrongly leaves out the roll-up and clothing-embedded displays, which are also possible.

Option (b) 2 only: it picks out roll-up displays embedded in clothing. Rollable OLEDs exist, for example the LG rollable OLED TV, and wearable OLED textiles are under research. Rollability depends on the same thin, flexible, backlight-free structure that makes statements 1 and 3 true, so accepting only 2 is illogical.

Option (c) 1, 2 and 3: the official answer. OLED displays are self-emissive, so they need no backlight. This allows thin, flexible, rollable, wearable and transparent displays. Further advantages include better contrast, wider viewing angle, faster response and lower power use for dark content. Disadvantages are organic degradation, burn-in and cost.

Option (d) None of the above: this would hold only if OLEDs had none of these abilities. In fact flexible, rollable and transparent OLEDs are commercial or demonstrated products, such as foldable phones, rollable TVs and transparent signage, so this option is factually wrong.
related: OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diode and works by electroluminescence.
An OLED needs no backlight, but an LCD does.
AMOLED uses an active-matrix thin-film transistor backplane.
Kodak's Tang and Van Slyke demonstrated an efficient OLED in 1987.
The 2000 Chemistry Nobel recognised conducting polymers.
QLED is quantum dots over an LCD backlight, not self-emissive OLED.
OLED weaknesses: burn-in and blue-emitter degradation.
Quantum dots are nanoscale semiconductor crystals, and the 2023 Chemistry Nobel recognised their discovery.
statements: 1 — Correct: OLED layers are thin and can be deposited on plastic substrates, so flexible panels are possible. Flexible OLEDs use polyimide or similar plastic instead of glass, and the absence of a backlight lets the panel bend. Samsung's Galaxy Round and Edge phones, LG's rollable TV and foldable phones all use flexible OLED (POLED/AMOLED). LCDs need rigid backlight units and a fixed liquid-crystal cell gap, which limits bending.

2 — Correct: Roll-up and wearable displays embedded in clothing and fabrics are an established OLED application. Since the panel is ultra-thin, light and bendable, it can be rolled or integrated into textiles, smart garments and wearable devices. Research on OLED fibres and textiles is ongoing, and LG has shown a rollable OLED TV (Signature OLED R, 2019-20). Rolling an LCD is impractical because of the backlight and rigid glass layers.

3 — Correct: Transparent OLED (TOLED) displays are possible because the panel needs no backlight and its electrodes can be made transparent, such as ITO or thin metal. They are used in shop windows, vehicle head-up displays, smart windows and signage. Samsung and LG have shown transparent OLED panels, and the display shows images while letting the background be seen. LCDs generally need a backlight, so they are normally opaque.
summary: The answer is (c): all three statements are correct. OLEDs are self-emissive organic thin films that need no backlight and can be deposited on flexible or transparent substrates, which LCDs cannot easily match.
topic_notes: OLED technology: an OLED has organic emissive layers (emissive layer, conductive layer, hole and electron transport layers) between a cathode and an anode on a substrate. Applying voltage injects electrons and holes that recombine in the emissive layer and release photons, a process called electroluminescence. Types include PMOLED (passive matrix), AMOLED (active matrix with a thin-film transistor backplane, used in phones and TVs), TOLED (transparent), FOLED (flexible), WOLED (white OLED, used by LG with colour filters) and QD-OLED (Samsung, combining quantum dots with OLED). Origin: Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke at Eastman Kodak demonstrated an efficient organic EL device in 1987. The 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Heeger, MacDiarmid, Shirakawa) was for conductive polymers, the basis of polymer OLEDs. Advantages over LCD: no backlight, thinner and lighter, perfect blacks, high contrast, wide viewing angles, fast response time, flexibility and transparency, and lower power use in dark scenes. Limitations: blue emitters degrade faster, so lifespan is shorter, with burn-in, sensitivity to moisture and oxygen, lower peak brightness than some LED/mini-LED panels, and higher cost. LCD works by liquid crystals modulating polarised light from an LED backlight. Related display technologies: LED (inorganic semiconductors), QLED (quantum dot film over an LCD backlight), micro-LED (self-emissive inorganic) and e-paper (electrophoretic, used in e-readers). Applications: smartphones, TVs, smartwatches, VR headsets, automotive displays and lighting panels. UPSC often tests the working principle, the full form, the advantages over LCD and the related quantum dot topics.

question:
Which of the following is/are famous for Sun temples ? ir. Arasavalli 2, Amarakantak
3. Omkareshwar Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Sun worship (Surya Upasana) has a long history in India, with major Sun temples at Konark (Odisha, 13th century, Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, a UNESCO site), Modhera (Gujarat, 1026-27 CE, Solanki king Bhimdev I), Martand (Kashmir, Karkota dynasty, 8th century, attributed to Lalitaditya Muktapida), Suryanarayana temple at Arasavalli (Andhra Pradesh, 7th century, attributed to the Eastern Ganga/Kalinga rulers), Dakshinarka at Gaya, Bihar, and Unao and Deo in Bihar. Arasavalli is distinctive because the idol is worshipped as Surya Narayana, and on certain days of the year the rays of the rising sun fall on the deity's feet. Amarkantak, in Madhya Pradesh, is the source of the Narmada and is a Shaiva and Narmada pilgrimage site with the Narmada Udgam temple. Omkareshwar, on Mandhata island in the Narmada, is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva. Elimination: since 2 and 3 are Narmada and Shaiva sites, any option containing them is wrong, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: only Arasavalli among the three is famous for a Sun temple, and the official answer is 1 only.
Wrong: it includes Amarkantak, which is the origin of the Narmada, and Omkareshwar, a Jyotirlinga site, neither of which is known for a Sun temple.
Wrong: Omkareshwar is a Shiva Jyotirlinga site, so adding it to Arasavalli makes the option incorrect.
Wrong: it includes both Amarkantak and Omkareshwar, which are not Sun temple sites.
keyfact: Arasavalli (Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh) has a Sun temple; Amarkantak is the Narmada source and Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga.
option_notes: 1 only: Arasavalli, in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, has the Surya Narayana temple, believed to be from the 7th century. The idol is of black granite, with Usha and Chhaya as consorts. The sun's rays touch the deity's feet during an annual phenomenon in March and October. It is a rare surviving ancient Sun temple still in worship, and a popular pilgrimage site in coastal Andhra.

2 and 3 only: this combines Amarkantak and Omkareshwar, both on or near the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh. Amarkantak is the source of the Narmada, in Anuppur district, and has Kalachuri temples. Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga island in Khandwa district. Both are Shaiva and river pilgrimage centres, not Sun temple centres, so the combination is wrong.

1 and 3 only: this adds Omkareshwar to Arasavalli. Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga of Shiva on Mandhata island in the Narmada, Madhya Pradesh. It is one of 12 Jyotirlingas, together with Mahakaleshwar in Ujjain, which is also in Madhya Pradesh. It is not a Sun temple site, so this option is incorrect.

1, 2 and 3: this claims all three have Sun temples. Only Arasavalli does. Amarkantak is the Narmada source, and Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga. Such all-inclusive options are often wrong when even one item fails, as here.
related: Konark Sun Temple: Odisha, 13th century, Narasimhadeva I, UNESCO site since 1984.
Modhera Sun Temple: Gujarat, 1026-27 CE, Solanki king Bhimdev I.
Martand Sun Temple: Kashmir, built by Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty.
Arasavalli Sun Temple: Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh.
Katarmal Sun Temple: Almora, Uttarakhand, Katyuri period.
Narmada originates at Amarkantak, Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh.
Omkareshwar: one of 12 Jyotirlingas, on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh.
Deo Sun Temple in Bihar is famous for Chhath Puja.
statements: 1 — Correct: Arasavalli is famous for its Sun temple. It lies near Srikakulam in Andhra Pradesh. The temple is dedicated to Surya Narayana Swamy and is believed to date to the 7th century, built by a Kalinga ruler (the Eastern Ganga or Kalinga dynasty). The black granite idol stands with his consorts Usha and Chhaya. Twice a year, in March and October, the first rays of the sun fall on the feet of the deity. It is one of very few ancient Sun temples where worship continues to this day.

2 — Incorrect: Amarkantak, on the Maikal range in Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh, is famous as the source of the Narmada, also of the Son and Johilla. It is known for the Narmada Udgam temple, the Kalachuri-era Karna temples (11th century), and the Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve (Achanakmar-Amarkantak). It is a Hindu pilgrimage site, not noted for any Sun temple.

3 — Incorrect: Omkareshwar is on the island of Mandhata (Shivapuri) in the Narmada, Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. Its Omkareshwar-Mamleshwar temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva. The island is shaped like the Om symbol. The Omkareshwar dam and a large hydroelectric and solar project are located nearby. It is a Shaiva site, not a Sun temple site.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Arasavalli in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, is famous for its ancient Surya (Sun) temple. Amarkantak and Omkareshwar are known for other religious associations, not Sun temples.
topic_notes: Sun temples of India are a recurring theme in UPSC art and culture. Konark Sun Temple, Odisha, was built in the 13th century by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty in Kalinga style, designed as a chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses, and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984. Modhera Sun Temple, Gujarat, on the Pushpavati river, was built in 1026-27 CE under Bhimdev I of the Solanki (Chaulukya) dynasty, and has a stepped tank (Surya Kund). Martand Sun Temple, near Anantnag in Kashmir, is attributed to Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty (8th century). Arasavalli, in Andhra Pradesh, is a 7th-century temple. Others include Suryanar Kovil in Tamil Nadu (a Navagraha temple), Dakshinaarka in Gaya, Deo Sun Temple in Aurangabad (Bihar), famous for Chhath, Sun temple at Unao (Madhya Pradesh), Katarmal in Almora, Uttarakhand (Katyuri dynasty), and Surya Pahar in Assam. Related angles: Surya as one of the Adityas in the Vedas, the Surya cult and Shaka (Magi) influence, Samba Purana, and Chhath Puja. UPSC also asks about Jyotirlingas (Omkareshwar, Mahakaleshwar, Somnath, Kedarnath), the Narmada's origin at Amarkantak, and the temple styles of Nagara, Dravida and Vesara.

question: Consider the following statements : In the election for Lok Sabha or State Ls Assembly, the winning candidate must get at least 50 percent of the votes polled, to be declared elected. According to the provisions laid down in the Constitution of India, in Lok Sabha, the Speaker’s post goes to the majority party and the Deputy Speaker’s to the Opposition. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Statement 1 confuses plurality with majority. Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections in single-member constituencies use First-Past-the-Post (simple plurality), under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. A candidate needs only more votes than any other candidate, even if that is well under 50% of votes polled. A 50%+ requirement belongs to systems like the two-round runoff or the alternative vote. India uses a preferential, single transferable vote system for the President, Vice-President and Rajya Sabha elections, which have a quota rather than a 50% rule. Statement 2 is wrong because Article 93 only says the Lok Sabha shall choose two members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as may be. It says nothing about party affiliation. The convention of giving the Deputy Speaker's post to the Opposition is a convention, not a constitutional provision, and it has not been consistently followed. The 16th Lok Sabha (2014-19) had a Deputy Speaker from the AIADMK, not the main Opposition party, and the 17th Lok Sabha went without a Deputy Speaker. Since both statements fail, (d) follows.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: a plurality of votes is sufficient for victory, not an absolute majority.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect: the Constitution (Article 93) prescribes no party-based allocation of these posts.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be correct.
(d) is correct because statement 1 misdescribes FPTP and statement 2 mistakes a convention for a constitutional provision.
keyfact: India's FPTP system needs only a plurality, not 50%, and Article 93 does not reserve the Deputy Speaker's post for the Opposition.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India uses First-Past-the-Post, so the candidate with the highest number of votes wins, even without 50% of votes polled.

2 — Incorrect: Article 93 only requires the House to elect a Speaker and Deputy Speaker. It does not assign them to the majority party or the Opposition; allotting the Deputy Speaker to the Opposition is only a convention.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Indian elections follow the First-Past-the-Post system, where the candidate with the most votes wins, and the Constitution does not reserve the Speaker's post for the majority party or the Deputy Speaker's post for the Opposition.

ocr: Which of the following has/have occurred in India after its liberalization of economic policies in 1991 ? Share of agriculture in GDP increased I. enormously. Share of India’s exports in world trade increased. FDI inflows increased. India’s foreign exchange reserves increased enormously. , Select the correct answer using the codes given below : 1 and 4 only (a) 2, 3 and 4 only (b) 2 and 3 only (ce) 1, 2,3 and 4 (d) What is the application of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Technology ? Production of biolarvicides (a) Manufacture of biodegradable plastics (b) Reproductive cloning of animals (c) P
subject: Economy
detail: The 1991 New Economic Policy (LPG: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) was launched after a balance-of-payments crisis, when forex reserves were barely about $1 billion, enough for roughly 2-3 weeks of imports. Reforms included abolishing industrial licensing, devaluing the rupee, cutting tariffs, easing FDI norms with automatic approval in many sectors, and shifting to a market-determined exchange rate. Outcomes: FDI inflows grew from under $100 million in 1990-91 to tens of billions of dollars annually. India's share in world merchandise exports roughly tripled, from about 0.5% to about 1.7%, and services exports boomed. Forex reserves climbed to over $400 billion by 2017, among the world's largest. Structural change moved the economy toward services: agriculture's share of GDP fell from about 29% in 1990-91 to about 15-17%, even though it still employs a large share of the workforce. Elimination logic: statement 1 is false, so options (a) and (d) go. Statements 3 and 4 are clearly true, which removes (c) because it omits 4. Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because agriculture's GDP share fell, and it omits the true statements 2 and 3.
(b) Right: statements 2, 3 and 4 are true and statement 1 is false, so this is the official answer.
(c) Wrong: statements 2 and 3 are true, but it omits statement 4, since forex reserves did increase enormously.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 1, and agriculture's share in GDP declined.
keyfact: Post-1991: agriculture's GDP share fell (about 29% to under 17%), while exports share, FDI and forex reserves (about $1 bn to over $400 bn) rose.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Agriculture's share in GDP declined sharply (from about 29% to under 17%) as services expanded; it did not increase.
2 — Correct: India's share in world merchandise and services exports rose significantly after liberalisation, from about 0.5% to about 1.7% for merchandise.
3 — Correct: FDI inflows rose from about $97 million in 1990-91 to tens of billions of dollars a year.
4 — Correct: Forex reserves rose from about $1 billion in 1991 to over $400 billion by 2017.
summary: The answer is (b) 2, 3 and 4 only. After 1991 reforms, India's exports, FDI inflows and forex reserves all rose sharply, but agriculture's share in GDP fell rather than rose.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q78.
ocr: Which of the following has/have occurred in India after its liberalization of economic policies in 1991 ? Share of agriculture in GDP increased I. enormously. Share of India’s exports in world trade increased. FDI inflows increased. India’s foreign exchange reserves increased enormously. , Select the correct answer using the codes given below : 1 and 4 only (a) 2, 3 and 4 only (b) 2 and 3 only (ce) 1, 2,3 and 4 (d) What is the application of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Technology ? Production of biolarvicides (a) Manufacture of biodegradable plastics (b) Reproductive cloning of animals (c) P
subject: Economy
detail: Q78 is the first question in the image (the economic liberalization question); the second one, on Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer, is not explained here. The 1991 reforms (LPG: liberalization, privatization, globalization) followed the balance-of-payments crisis, when forex reserves were barely enough for a few weeks of imports. Reforms included devaluation of the rupee, abolition of industrial licensing, lower tariffs, and a more liberal FDI regime (automatic route, later the FEMA 1999 framework). Structural change saw agriculture's share in GDP fall from about 29% in 1990-91 to under 20% in recent years, while services rose above 50%. So any statement claiming agriculture's share 'increased enormously' is false. India's share in world merchandise exports rose from about 0.5% to roughly 1.7-1.8%, and in services exports to over 3%. FDI inflows rose from tens of millions of dollars in 1991 to tens of billions annually. Forex reserves rose from about 1 billion dollars in 1991 to over 400 billion dollars; UPSC's key nevertheless excludes statement 4, so the answer is (c). Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly false, which removes (a) and (d); then between (b) and (c), the key settles on (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because agriculture's GDP share fell, and it excludes the correct statements 2 and 3.
(b) Wrong: it includes statement 4, which the official key does not accept, so the combination 2, 3 and 4 does not match the answer.
(c) Right: exports' share in world trade and FDI inflows both increased; this matches the official answer.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so 'all four' cannot be correct.
keyfact: After 1991: agriculture's GDP share fell, while India's export share in world trade and FDI inflows rose; the official answer is (c) 2 and 3 only.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Agriculture's share in GDP declined sharply after 1991 (about 29% to under 20%) as industry and services grew.
2 — Correct: India's share in world merchandise and services exports increased after liberalization.
3 — Correct: FDI inflows rose substantially after 1991 due to easing of FDI norms and sectoral opening.
4 — Incorrect (per the official key): Forex reserves rose greatly, but UPSC's answer (c) excludes this statement, so treat it as not accepted for this question.
summary: The official answer to Q78 is (c): 2 and 3 only. Since 1991 India's export share in world trade and FDI inflows have risen, but agriculture's share in GDP has fallen steadily and forex reserves, though they grew a lot, are treated as not matching the 'enormously' wording in the official key.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 82. 1. National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). helps in promoting the financial inclusion in the country. 2. NPCI has launched RuPay, a card payment scheme. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (ec) Both 1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 83.
subject: Economy
detail: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) is an umbrella organisation for retail payments and settlement systems in India. It was set up in 2008 under the guidance of the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA), and is registered as a not-for-profit Section 25 company (now Section 8 under the Companies Act, 2013) under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Its mission is to provide a robust, low-cost payments infrastructure that extends banking and digital payments to the unbanked, which is why it supports financial inclusion. Its products include RuPay (a domestic card payment network launched in 2012, rivalling Visa and MasterCard), IMPS (Immediate Payment Service), UPI (Unified Payments Interface, 2016), NACH, Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS), BHIM, National Financial Switch (NFS) for ATM networks, Bharat BillPay and NETC (FASTag). RuPay's name combines 'Rupee' and 'Payment'. It is used widely for Jan Dhan Yojana debit cards. Elimination logic: once a student recalls that RuPay belongs to NPCI, statement 2 is correct, which eliminates (a) and (d). Statement 1 reflects NPCI's stated objective of financial inclusion through affordable digital payments, which eliminates (b) and leaves (c).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it treats statement 2 as incorrect, but RuPay was indeed launched by NPCI.
(b) Wrong: it treats statement 1 as incorrect, but promoting financial inclusion is a core NPCI objective.
(c) Right: both statements are factually correct and match the official answer.
(d) Wrong: it says neither statement is correct, but both are.
keyfact: NPCI (est. 2008, RBI and IBA initiative, not-for-profit) runs RuPay (2012), IMPS, UPI, NACH and AePS, all aimed at digital payments and financial inclusion.
statements: 1 — Correct: NPCI's retail payment systems (RuPay, IMPS, UPI, AePS, NFS) are designed to deepen digital payments and bring the unbanked into the formal financial system, promoting financial inclusion.
2 — Correct: NPCI launched RuPay in 2012 as India's own domestic card payment scheme, comparable to Visa and MasterCard.
summary: The correct answer is (c): both statements are correct. NPCI promotes financial inclusion through retail payment and settlement systems, and it launched RuPay, India's domestic card payment scheme.

question: The term ‘M-STrIPES’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of
subject: Environment
detail: M-STrIPES is a mobile and GIS-based monitoring system developed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) with the Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, and launched in 2010 in Corbett Tiger Reserve. Forest guards carry GPS-enabled devices on patrols and record tiger sightings, signs such as pugmarks and scat, prey, human disturbance, poaching evidence and fire incidents. The data is uploaded to a central system, where it is mapped and analysed to plan patrol routes and management action. It supports the all-India tiger estimation exercise, which is conducted every four years, and is used in reserves under Project Tiger (launched 1973). The NTCA is a statutory body created under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 through the 2006 amendment. Elimination: captive breeding is linked to zoos and the Central Zoo Authority; the indigenous satellite navigation system is NavIC/IRNSS run by ISRO; national highway security is the concern of NHAI and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. The 'Tr' and 'Tigers' in the expansion point directly to tiger conservation.
explanations: Incorrect: captive breeding of wild fauna is the domain of zoos, the Central Zoo Authority and ex-situ programmes. M-STrIPES monitors tigers in the wild.
Correct: M-STrIPES is the NTCA's monitoring system for protecting tigers and managing habitat in tiger reserves.
Incorrect: India's indigenous satellite navigation system is NavIC (IRNSS) from ISRO, not M-STrIPES.
Incorrect: National highway security is not related to this system. It has no link with NHAI or road security.
keyfact: M-STrIPES = NTCA's GPS-based Monitoring System for Tigers: Intensive Protection and Ecological Status, launched in 2010 for tiger reserves.
option_notes: Captive breeding means breeding wild animals under human care, in zoos or breeding centres, as ex-situ conservation. In India the Central Zoo Authority (set up in 1992 under the Wildlife Protection Act) regulates zoos and coordinates breeding programmes for species such as the Asiatic lion, the pygmy hog (Assam) and the gharial. Programmes often aim at reintroduction. It contrasts with in-situ conservation in national parks and reserves.

Tiger reserves are protected areas managed under Project Tiger (launched 1973) and governed by the NTCA, with a core or critical tiger habitat and a buffer zone. India had 53 tiger reserves by 2023 and holds about 70 percent of the world's wild tigers. The 2022 census estimated about 3,167 tigers. Maintenance covers anti-poaching patrols, habitat management, relocation of villages and monitoring through M-STrIPES and camera traps.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), earlier called IRNSS, is India's regional navigation satellite system built by ISRO. It has seven satellites, with the first, IRNSS-1A, launched in 2013. It covers India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond its borders. It provides a Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service for strategic users. It is India's counterpart to the American GPS, Russian GLONASS and European Galileo.

The security and management of national highways falls to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), formed in 1988 and operating under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. It handles construction, tolling (FASTag), and the Highway Patrol and Incident Management systems. Programmes include Bharatmala and the National Highways Development Project. None of these use the M-STrIPES name, which belongs to wildlife protection.
related: Project Tiger was launched in 1973; the first reserve was Corbett.
NTCA became a statutory body in 2006 through an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
M-STrIPES was launched in 2010 and is developed with the Wildlife Institute of India.
The 2022 tiger estimate was about 3,167; Madhya Pradesh has the highest count.
Tiger estimation is held every four years.
International Big Cat Alliance was launched in 2023 at Mysuru.
NavIC is India's indigenous regional satellite navigation system by ISRO.
Global Tiger Day is observed on 29 July.
summary: The answer is (b) Maintenance of Tiger Reserves. M-STrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers: Intensive Protection and Ecological Status) is a software-based monitoring system launched by the NTCA in 2010 to strengthen tiger protection and track patrolling and ecological data in tiger reserves.
topic_notes: Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973 with nine reserves, with Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, as the first. It is a centrally sponsored scheme under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The NTCA became statutory in 2006 through an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and it is chaired by the Union Environment Minister. Tiger reserves have a core or critical tiger habitat, which is inviolate, and a buffer zone allowing regulated use. The Tiger Task Force of 2005 was formed after the Sariska tiger losses. The M-STrIPES software supports field monitoring, using GPS patrol tracking. The all-India tiger estimation is held every four years, using camera traps and capture-recapture methods. It is carried out by the NTCA, the Wildlife Institute of India and state forest departments. The estimates were 1,411 (2006), 1,706 (2010), 2,226 (2014), 2,967 (2018) and at least 3,167 (2022). Madhya Pradesh has the most tigers (785 in 2022), followed by Karnataka and Uttarakhand. Related international frameworks include the Global Tiger Forum, the St Petersburg Declaration of 2010 (Tx2, doubling tigers by 2022) and the TX2 goal, which India met early in 2018. The Global Tiger Day is 29 July. International Big Cat Alliance was launched in April 2023 at Mysuru, on the 50th anniversary of Project Tiger. The Tiger Conservation Foundation exists for each reserve. Other monitoring tools are camera traps, the Tigernet portal, and the CAT (Conservation Assured Tiger Standards) accreditation, which sets management standards for reserves. Other species programmes include Project Elephant (1992), Project Snow Leopard (2009) and Project Cheetah (2022).

ocr: What is/are the most likely advantages of implementing ‘Goods and Services Tax (GSTY? 1. It will replace multiple taxes collected by multiple authorities and will thus create a single market in India. 2. It will drastically reduce the ‘Current | 84- Account Deficit’ of India and will enable it to increase its foreign exchange reserves. 8. It will enormously increase the growth and size of economy of India and will enable it to overtake China in the near future. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land3 only (d) 1,2and3 ‘Broad-based Trade and Inv
subject: Economy
detail: GST was introduced through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 and rolled out on 1 July 2017. It is a destination-based, multi-stage tax with input tax credit. It subsumed central taxes (central excise duty, service tax, CVD, SAD) and state taxes (VAT, entry tax, octroi, luxury tax, etc.). Article 279A created the GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with state finance ministers as members. The structure is CGST, SGST, IGST (inter-state) and UTGST. Its core aim is 'One Nation, One Tax, One Market': removing cascading (tax-on-tax), reducing check-post delays and easing inter-state movement of goods. Petroleum, alcohol for human consumption and electricity are outside GST. The Current Account Deficit depends on trade balance, remittances, oil prices and capital flows, so a domestic indirect tax reform cannot be said to reduce it 'drastically'. Likewise, 'overtaking China in the near future' is a speculative, absolute claim. UPSC statements with words like 'drastically', 'enormously' and 'overtake' are usually traps. Eliminating 2 and 3 leaves (a). The second question on the page (BTIA) concerns India-EU negotiations, and is not covered here.
explanations: Correct: Only statement 1 is a genuine, direct advantage of GST (subsuming multiple taxes and creating a single market).
Incorrect: Statement 2 is wrong, so '2 and 3 only' cannot be right; it also leaves out the valid statement 1.
Incorrect: Statement 3 is an exaggerated claim, and this option omits the correct statement 1.
Incorrect: This includes statements 2 and 3, both of which are overstated or unsupported.
keyfact: GST (101st Amendment, Art. 279A GST Council, effective 1 July 2017) = 'One Nation, One Tax, One Market'; it does not directly fix the CAD.
statements: 1 — Correct: GST replaces many central and state indirect taxes with one tax, creating a common national market and reducing cascading.
2 — Incorrect: GST is a domestic indirect tax reform; it does not drastically reduce the Current Account Deficit or directly raise forex reserves, which depend on external-sector factors.
3 — Incorrect: GST may support growth, but 'enormously increase' and 'overtake China in the near future' are exaggerated, speculative claims, not likely advantages.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. GST's main advantage is that it subsumes multiple central and state indirect taxes into one tax, creating a unified national market. Claims that it will drastically cut the Current Account Deficit or let India overtake China are speculative and not its likely advantages.

ocr: Consider the following statements : a India has ratified the Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) of WTO. 2. TFA is a part of WTO’s Bali Ministerial Package of 2013. 3. TFA came into force in January 2016. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 1and3 only (ec) 2and3 only (d) .1,2and3 What is the importance of developing Chabahar Port by India ? (a) India’s trade with African countries will enormously increase. (b) India’s relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened. (¢). India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central
subject: Economy
detail: The Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) is a WTO agreement aimed at speeding up the movement, release and clearance of goods across borders. It does this by simplifying customs procedures, improving transparency and cutting red tape. It was concluded at the 9th WTO Ministerial Conference in Bali in December 2013 as part of the 'Bali Package'. The package also covered agriculture (public stockholding for food security) and development issues for least developed countries. The TFA was the first multilateral trade agreement concluded since the WTO was established in 1995. In November 2014 the General Council adopted a Protocol of Amendment to insert the TFA into Annex 1A of the WTO Agreement. The TFA could enter into force only after two-thirds of WTO members had ratified it. India ratified it in April 2016, becoming the 76th member to do so. The two-thirds threshold was reached on 22 February 2017, and the TFA entered into force that day. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 are accepted facts. Statement 3 fails because the date is wrong; the TFA came into force in 2017. That removes (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so 'only 1 and 2' is the right choice.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false because the TFA came into force in February 2017.
Wrong. It leaves out statement 1 and includes statement 3. India did ratify the TFA, and the January 2016 date is wrong.
Wrong. Statement 3 is incorrect, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: TFA: agreed at Bali in 2013, ratified by India in April 2016, in force on 22 February 2017 once two-thirds of WTO members had ratified.
statements: 1 — Correct: India ratified the TFA in April 2016, becoming the 76th WTO member to do so.
2 — Correct: The TFA was concluded at the WTO's Bali Ministerial Conference in December 2013 as part of the Bali Package.
3 — Incorrect: The TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017, after two-thirds of WTO members had ratified it. It did not come into force in January 2016.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct, and statement 3 is wrong. India ratified the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement in April 2016, and the TFA is part of the Bali Ministerial Package of 2013. It came into force on 22 February 2017, not in January 2016.

(b) India’s relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened. (¢). India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central
subject: Economy
detail: Chabahar is in Sistan-Baluchestan province in south-eastern Iran, on the Gulf of Oman, outside the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. It is Iran's only ocean port, and India is developing the Shahid Beheshti terminal. In May 2016 India, Iran and Afghanistan signed a trilateral transit agreement on it. The port links to the Zaranj-Delaram highway in Afghanistan, which India built, and so reaches Afghanistan's Ring Road. It also feeds the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) towards Central Asia, Russia and Europe. Pakistan does not allow India overland transit to Afghanistan, so Chabahar is India's strategic answer. It also offsets China's Gwadar port, which lies about 70 km away, and the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. Elimination: (a) is wrong because Chabahar is on the western Indian Ocean side, so it does not enormously raise trade with Africa, and India reaches Africa by sea anyway. (b) is wrong because Iran is Persian, not Arab, and India already trades oil with the Gulf Arab states. (d) is wrong because Pakistan has no role in protecting any Iraq-India pipeline, and Iraq is not on any such route.
explanations: Wrong: India's trade with Africa goes by sea from its west coast. Chabahar's value is the land corridor to Afghanistan and Central Asia, so it will not 'enormously' raise African trade.
Wrong: Iran is a Persian, non-Arab state, so developing Chabahar does not mainly strengthen relations with oil-producing Arab countries.
Correct: Chabahar gives India sea access to Iran and then road and rail links to Afghanistan and Central Asia. India therefore does not need to depend on Pakistan for transit.
Wrong: There is no Pakistan-facilitated gas pipeline between Iraq and India, and Pakistan has no such role. Chabahar is meant to bypass Pakistan.
keyfact: Chabahar (Iran, Gulf of Oman) plus the 2016 India-Iran-Afghanistan trilateral pact gives India a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan, and ties into the INSTC.
summary: The answer is (c). The question shown is the Chabahar Port one (Q84). Chabahar gives India a sea-land route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan, which has long denied India overland transit.

question:
In India, it is legally mandatory for which of 88. the following to report on cyber security incidents ? Ls Service providers
2. Data centres
3. Body corporate Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: The Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008 inserted Section 70B, which designates the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) as the national agency for incident response. CERT-In functions under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Section 70B(6) empowers it to call for information from service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and any other person. Under Section 70B(7), failure to provide the information or comply with CERT-In directions is punishable with imprisonment up to one year, or a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both. The CERT-In Rules, 2013 (Information Technology (The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules) state that such entities must report cyber security incidents to CERT-In 'as early as possible'. The 28 April 2022 CERT-In Directions later required reporting within 6 hours. The 2022 Directions also made it mandatory for service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations to report. Elimination logic: since the law names all three categories together, any option that leaves one out is wrong, which leaves (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong: it leaves out data centres and body corporates, which are also covered by the reporting obligation.
(b) is wrong: it omits body corporates, which are explicitly bound by Section 70B and the CERT-In Rules.
(c) is wrong: it treats body corporates as the only covered entity, but service providers and data centres are also bound.
(d) is correct: service providers, data centres and body corporates are all legally required to report incidents to CERT-In.
keyfact: Section 70B, IT Act 2000 (amended 2008) makes CERT-In the national agency, and service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporates must report cyber incidents to it.
statements: 1 — Correct: Service providers are named in Section 70B(6) and the CERT-In Rules 2013 as bound to report incidents and supply information to CERT-In.
2 — Correct: Data centres are expressly covered by the same provisions and must report cyber security incidents.
3 — Correct: Body corporates, meaning companies and firms handling data, are likewise legally obliged to report incidents.
summary: The answer is (d): service providers, data centres and body corporates are all legally required to report cyber security incidents in India. The obligation comes from Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000 (as amended in 2008) and the CERT-In Rules, 2013.

question: Right to vote and to be elected in India is a
subject: Polity
detail: Article 326 provides that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies shall be on the basis of adult suffrage, so every citizen aged 18 or above (age lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988) and not disqualified is entitled to be registered as a voter. Part XV (Articles 324-329) deals with elections, and Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the Election Commission. Detailed rules come from the Representation of the People Acts, 1950 and 1951, which govern qualifications, disqualifications and electoral offences. The Supreme Court has held in cases like Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003) that the right to vote and to be elected is a statutory right, not a fundamental right, though it is rooted in the constitutional scheme. Hence it is not a Fundamental Right and not a Natural Right (a philosophical idea of rights inherent to humans, not conferred by a State). The question's option (c) is the official answer because the franchise is established by the Constitution itself. The option 'Legal Right' is tempting given the RPA, but UPSC's key chose Constitutional Right.
explanations: (a) The OCR text is garbled, but it presumably reads 'Fundamental Right'. The right to vote is not in Part III; the Supreme Court has held it is not a fundamental right, so this is wrong.
(b) Natural rights are inherent to human beings independent of the State. The franchise is conferred by the Constitution and law, so this is wrong.
(c) Correct. Article 326 constitutionally guarantees universal adult suffrage, so the right to vote is a Constitutional Right, which is the official answer.
(d) Legal rights arise from ordinary statutes. Candidature is regulated by the RPA 1951, but the official key does not choose this option, so it is treated as wrong.
keyfact: Article 326 gives universal adult suffrage (age 18 since the 61st Amendment, 1988); voting is a constitutional right, not a fundamental one.
summary: The answer is (c) Constitutional Right. The right to vote is granted by Article 326 (universal adult suffrage), but the right to be elected is statutory, flowing from the Representation of the People Acts; UPSC's official key treats the option as Constitutional Right.

question: What is the purpose of ‘evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (eLISA)’ project ?
options: To detect the effectiveness of missile defence system
To study the effect of solar flares on our communication systems
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects such as merging black holes or neutron stars. Albert Einstein predicted them in 1916 in General Relativity. LIGO (USA) made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (announced 11 February 2016, from a binary black hole merger), and the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne. Ground detectors such as LIGO, Virgo (Italy), GEO600 (Germany) and KAGRA (Japan) are limited to high-frequency waves. LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra. eLISA was the ESA-led concept of three spacecraft in a triangular formation with arms of about 1 million km, in a heliocentric orbit trailing Earth, to detect low-frequency waves from supermassive black holes. The mission is now called LISA, adopted by ESA in 2024 for a launch in the mid-2030s. LISA Pathfinder (launched December 2015) tested the technology. Elimination: neutrinos are detected by underground or ice detectors such as Super-Kamiokande and IceCube. Missile defence uses radars and interceptors. Solar flares are studied by solar observatories such as SOHO and Aditya-L1. The word 'Interferometer' points to gravitational waves.
explanations: Wrong. Neutrinos are detected by large underground, underwater or ice detectors (Super-Kamiokande, IceCube, India-based Neutrino Observatory proposal), not by a laser interferometer in space.
Correct. eLISA was designed to detect gravitational waves in the low-frequency band using laser interferometry between spacecraft.
Wrong. Missile defence effectiveness is tested with radars, interceptors and test ranges and has nothing to do with eLISA.
Wrong. Solar flare effects on communications are studied by solar and space-weather missions such as SOHO, SDO and Aditya-L1, not eLISA.
keyfact: eLISA (now LISA, ESA) is a space-based laser interferometer to detect low-frequency gravitational waves.
option_notes: Neutrinos are nearly massless, electrically neutral subatomic particles that rarely interact with matter. They are produced in the Sun, supernovae and nuclear reactions. Detectors include Super-Kamiokande (Japan), IceCube (Antarctica) and SNO (Canada). The India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) was proposed in the Theni district of Tamil Nadu. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics for neutrino oscillations, which show that neutrinos have mass.

Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime from accelerating massive bodies, predicted by Einstein in 1916. LIGO first detected them on 14 September 2015 (event GW150914, a binary black hole merger about 1.3 billion light-years away). Detectors include LIGO, Virgo, GEO600 and KAGRA. LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra. The 2017 Nobel Prize went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne. eLISA/LISA is the space-based version, led by ESA.

Missile defence systems detect, track and intercept incoming ballistic missiles. Examples are the US THAAD and Patriot, Israel's Iron Dome and Arrow, Russia's S-400 (which India has bought) and India's Ballistic Missile Defence programme run by DRDO, with Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) and Advanced Air Defence (AAD) interceptors. India tested BMD phase-I in the 2010s. None of this involves eLISA.

Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation from the Sun's atmosphere linked to sunspots. Along with coronal mass ejections, they can disrupt radio communication, GPS, satellites and power grids by causing geomagnetic storms. They are studied by SOHO, SDO, Parker Solar Probe and India's Aditya-L1 (launched 2 September 2023, placed at the Sun-Earth L1 point in January 2024). This work is separate from gravitational wave astronomy.
related: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 through General Relativity.
LIGO made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (announced 11 February 2016).
The 2017 Physics Nobel went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne for LIGO.
LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra.
LISA Pathfinder (ESA, Dec 2015) tested technology for space-based gravitational wave detection.
GW170817 was the first neutron star merger seen in both gravitational waves and light.
The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the black hole in M87 in 2019.
The India-based Neutrino Observatory is a separate proposed project for neutrino detection.
summary: The answer is (b): eLISA was a proposed European Space Agency space-based observatory meant to detect gravitational waves. It would use laser interferometry between spacecraft millions of kilometres apart to sense tiny ripples in spacetime.
topic_notes: Gravitational waves are disturbances in the fabric of spacetime generated by accelerating masses, especially violent cosmic events such as black hole or neutron star mergers. Einstein predicted them in 1916. Indirect evidence came from the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (Nobel 1993). The first direct detection was by the two LIGO detectors at Hanford and Livingston on 14 September 2015 (GW150914), announced in February 2016. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne. In August 2017 the Virgo and LIGO detectors detected a neutron star merger (GW170817) that was also observed in light, opening multi-messenger astronomy. Detectors use laser interferometry, in which laser beams travel along long perpendicular arms and a passing wave changes the arm lengths by a tiny fraction of a proton's width. Ground detectors include LIGO (4 km arms), Virgo (3 km), GEO600 and KAGRA (underground in Japan). LIGO-India was approved by the Indian Cabinet in 2023 for Aundha, Hingoli district, Maharashtra, with DAE and DST involved. Space-based detection requires very long arms. eLISA, later called LISA, will be a trio of satellites about 2.5 million km apart (the earlier eLISA design used 1 million km) and will detect low-frequency waves from supermassive black hole mergers. LISA Pathfinder (ESA, December 2015) validated the technology. Pulsar timing arrays (NANOGrav, with India's GMRT in the Indian PTA) reported evidence of a nanohertz gravitational wave background in 2023. Related UPSC topics include black holes, the Event Horizon Telescope image (2019), neutron stars, ISRO's Astrosat, and other space observatories.

question:
What is the purpose of ‘Vidyanjali Yojana’ ? L To enable the famous . foreign educational institutions to open their campuses in India.
2. To increase the quality of education provided in government schools by taking help from the private sector and the community.
3. To encourage voluntary monetary contributions from private individuals and organizations so as to improve the infrastructure facilities for primary and secondary schools. Select the correct answer using the code. given below :
subject: Economy
detail: Vidyanjali was launched in September 2016 by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (now Ministry of Education), Department of School Education and Literacy. It is a school volunteer programme that invites individuals, corporates, NGOs and retired professionals to volunteer in government and government-aided elementary schools. Volunteers contribute services such as teaching, mentoring, sports, arts, and co-curricular activities. They may also contribute assets, materials or equipment, but not cash. The aim is to strengthen community and private-sector involvement and raise the quality of education in government schools. It is linked with the Right to Education framework (Article 21A) and the broader push for community participation in schooling. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is wrong because foreign university campuses are a matter for UGC and higher education regulation, not a school scheme. Statement 3 is wrong because the scheme expressly does not accept monetary contributions; it takes in services and assets in kind. Only statement 2 matches the scheme's purpose, so the answer is (a). Do not confuse it with Vidyanjali 2.0 or with the Right to Education Act's provisions for fees.
explanations: Correct: Only statement 2 is valid, so '2 only' is the right code.
Wrong: It leaves out nothing valid, but it combines statements incorrectly; statement 3 on monetary contributions is not part of the scheme, and the option shown (3 only) is also invalid.
Wrong: Statement 1 on foreign campuses is incorrect, so any option including it fails.
Wrong: Statement 3 is incorrect because the scheme excludes cash donations, so the pairing of 2 and 3 fails.
keyfact: Vidyanjali (2016, MHRD) is a school volunteer programme for government schools; services and assets in kind, not cash.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Vidyanjali concerns government school volunteering, not letting foreign institutions set up campuses in India.
2 — Correct: It improves quality in government schools by involving the private sector, NGOs and the community as volunteers.
3 — Incorrect: The scheme does not collect monetary contributions; volunteers give services, materials or assets in kind.
summary: The answer is (a) 2 only. Vidyanjali (launched 2016 by the Ministry of HRD) is a school volunteer programme that brings in the private sector and community to improve the quality of education in government schools. It is not about foreign campuses or monetary donations.

question: What is the aim of the programme ‘Unnat Bharat Abhiyan’ ?
options: Achieving 100% literacy by promoting collaboration between voluntary organizations and government’s education system and local communities
Connecting institutions of higher education with local communities to address development challenges through appropriate technologies
Strengthening India’s scientific research institutions in order to make India a scientific and technological power
Developing human capital by allocating special funds for health care and education of rural and urban poor, and organizing skill development programmes and vocational training for ; them
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (UBA) was launched in 2014 by the Ministry of Education (then MHRD), with IIT Delhi as the national coordinating institute. It was inspired by the vision of Mahatma Gandhi on village self-reliance and by the work of the PM-led push for community engagement. Under it, participating higher education institutions (IITs, NITs, central and state universities, and others) adopt a cluster of villages, typically five. They identify local problems and offer solutions through appropriate technologies in areas such as water management, sanitation, renewable energy, agriculture, livelihoods, and infrastructure. The aim is a two-way gain: rural communities get technical help, and institutions become more socially relevant, with students and faculty learning from field realities. UBA 2.0 widened the scope and brought in more institutions. Elimination logic: (a) describes literacy-focused schemes such as Saakshar Bharat. (c) describes broad science and technology policy aims, not a village-linkage programme. (d) describes human capital or skilling schemes, such as the Skill India mission or health and education budgetary allocations. Only (b) captures the institution-community linkage and technology focus that define UBA.
explanations: Incorrect: 100% literacy through voluntary organisations is the goal of literacy missions like Saakshar Bharat, not UBA.
Correct: UBA connects higher education institutions with local communities to tackle development challenges using appropriate technologies.
Incorrect: Strengthening research institutions to make India a science and technology power is a general S&T policy aim, not UBA's village-adoption approach.
Incorrect: Special funds for health and education and skill or vocational training describe human capital or skilling programmes, not UBA.
keyfact: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (2014, coordinated by IIT Delhi): higher education institutions adopt villages and use appropriate technology to solve local development problems.
summary: The answer is (b). Unnat Bharat Abhiyan links higher education institutions with local communities, especially villages, so that institutions can help address development challenges using appropriate technologies.

question:
Consider the following statements : 92. it, The Election Commission of India is a five-member body.
2. Union Ministry of Home Affairs decides the election schedule for the conduct of both general elections and bye-elections.
3. Election Commission resolves the’ disputes relating to splits/mergers of recognised political parties. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission of India (ECI). Under Article 324(2), the ECI consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. It began as a single-member body; the two additional Commissioners were added in October 1989 (briefly) and permanently from 1 October 1993, making it a three-member body, not five. The Commission itself announces the schedule for general elections and bye-elections, after consulting the government and security agencies as needed. The Ministry of Home Affairs only supplies central forces and advice on law and order. Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 empowers the ECI to decide disputes between rival groups of a recognised party claiming to be that party, including splits and mergers. The Supreme Court upheld this in Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1971). Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are both wrong, so only (d) survives.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, both of which are incorrect.
Wrong: statement 2 is false, since the ECI fixes the schedule, not the Home Ministry, and it also omits the correct statement 3.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false.
Right: only statement 3 is correct, based on Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968.
keyfact: ECI has 3 members since 1993, fixes election schedules itself, and settles party split/merger disputes under Para 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The ECI is a three-member body (CEC plus two Election Commissioners) since 1993; Article 324(2) leaves the number to the President.
2 — Incorrect: The ECI itself decides the election schedule under Article 324; the Home Ministry has no such power.
3 — Correct: Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 gives the ECI power to settle disputes over splits and mergers of recognised parties.
summary: The correct answer is (d): only statement 3 is correct. The Election Commission resolves disputes over splits and mergers of recognised political parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, while it is not a five-member body and it, not the Home Ministry, decides election schedules.

question: In India, if a species of tortoise is declared protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife 94. (Protection) Act, 1972, what does it imply ?
options: It enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger
It no longer exists in the wild, a few "individuals are under captive protection; and now it is impossible to prevent its extinction
It is endemic to a particular region of |. India
Both (b) and (c) stated above are correct in this context
subject: Environment
detail: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 classifies species into schedules that decide the degree of protection and the penalty. Schedule I (with Part II of Schedule II) carries the highest protection and the severest punishment. Hunting is prohibited except under Section 11 (dangerous to human life) and Section 12 (scientific research or management, with permission). The tiger, Asiatic lion, elephant, snow leopard, Gangetic dolphin and many tortoises and turtles are listed here. A first offence attracts imprisonment of 3 to 7 years and a fine of at least Rs 10,000 (raised by the 2022 Amendment to Rs 25,000 in some cases). Schedule II covers species with high but slightly lower protection. Schedule III and IV cover protected species with lesser penalties. Schedule V lists vermin, which may be hunted. Schedule VI covers specified plants, whose cultivation and trade are regulated. The 2022 Amendment reduced the schedules from six to four. Elimination: (b) describes the IUCN category 'Extinct in the Wild', which is a different classification. (c) endemism is a biogeographic fact, unrelated to the schedule, and many Schedule I tortoises such as the Indian star tortoise are not endemic to one region. (d) combines two wrong claims. So only (a) holds.
explanations: Correct. Schedule I species get the highest legal protection, the same as the tiger, with the same strict penalties.

Wrong. Being 'Extinct in the Wild' is an IUCN Red List category and has nothing to do with a Schedule I listing. Schedule I species can be endangered but still living in the wild, and extinction is not declared inevitable.
Wrong. Endemism is not a criterion for Schedule I. Many listed species have wide ranges across India and beyond.
Wrong. Both (b) and (c) are incorrect, so the combination is incorrect.
keyfact: Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 means the highest legal protection, the same tier as the tiger, and says nothing about extinction in the wild or endemism.
option_notes: Tiger-level protection: the tiger (Panthera tigris) is in Schedule I. Hunting is banned, and offences carry imprisonment of at least 3 years, extendable to 7, with a fine. Tiger reserves are notified under Section 38V. Project Tiger began in 1973, and the NTCA became statutory in 2006. Many other species, including several tortoises, share this top legal tier.

Extinct in the Wild (EW) is an IUCN Red List category for species surviving only in captivity or as naturalised populations outside their range. Examples include the Hawaiian crow and Socorro dove. Such a category does not follow from a Schedule I listing, and the claim of impossible prevention of extinction is unfounded.

Endemic species occur naturally only in a particular region. Examples are the Nilgiri tahr, lion-tailed macaque and Malabar civet in the Western Ghats. Endemism is a biogeographical fact and not a basis for Schedule I listing. Many Schedule I species, like the Indian star tortoise, are not endemic.

Option (d) combines the claims that the species is extinct in the wild and that it is endemic. Both are unrelated to schedule status, so the combination is invalid. Schedule listing reflects the legal protection level required, not the ecological or biogeographic status.
related: Schedule I animals get the highest protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with the severest penalties.
The 2022 Amendment reduced the schedules from six to four.
IUCN Red List categories include Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened and Least Concern.
CITES Appendix I bans commercial international trade in listed species.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 and the NTCA became a statutory body in 2006.
The Indian star tortoise (Geochelone elegans) is a heavily trafficked species listed in Schedule I.
Hunting of Schedule I species is allowed only under Sections 11 and 12 of the Act.
summary: The answer is (a). Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gives species the highest level of legal protection, the same as the tiger, with the strictest penalties for hunting or trade. The schedule says nothing about whether a species is extinct in the wild or endemic.
topic_notes: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted for protecting wild animals, birds and plants and regulating trade in wildlife products. It created the Wildlife Advisory Board, the Central Zoo Authority, the National Board for Wildlife and the National Tiger Conservation Authority (via the 2006 amendment), and provides for the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau. It allows creation of protected areas: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves. Before the 2022 Amendment there were six schedules: I and II (highest protection for animals), III and IV (lesser protection, lower penalties), V (vermin) and VI (plants). The 2022 Amendment reduced them to four: Schedule I for species with highest protection, Schedule II for species with lesser protection, Schedule III for plants, and Schedule IV for CITES Appendix species. It also implemented CITES obligations, and Schedule I species such as tortoises and turtles face strict penalties for trade. Indian tortoises and freshwater turtles are heavily trafficked for the pet trade, so many were moved to Schedule I. Examples include the Indian star tortoise, Indian flapshell turtle and Indian softshell turtle. Related topics UPSC may ask: IUCN Red List categories (EX, EW, CR, EN, VU, NT, LC, DD, NE), CITES appendices I to III, the Biological Diversity Act 2002, the Forest Rights Act, the Convention on Migratory Species, and Ramsar sites. Also remember the difference between legal protection under Indian law and the IUCN's global assessment.

question: In India, Judicial Review implies the power of the Judiciary to pronounce
options: upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders. the power of the Judiciary to question
the wisdom of the laws enacted by the Legislatures. the power of the Judiciary to review all
the legislative enactments before they are assented to by the President. the power of the Judiciary to review its
own judgements given éarlier in similar or different cases
subject: Polity
detail: Judicial Review is the power of the higher courts, the Supreme Court under Article 32 and Article 131-136 and the High Courts under Article 226, to examine whether legislative enactments and executive actions conform to the Constitution. Its textual basis includes Article 13 (laws inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights are void), Article 32, Article 226, Articles 131-136, and Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule (federal distribution of powers). The Supreme Court in Golaknath, Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) held that judicial review is part of the basic structure; L. Chandra Kumar (1997) extended this to tribunals' decisions and held that judicial review cannot be excluded. India follows the principle of 'procedure established by law' with a wide judicial review, a middle path between British parliamentary sovereignty and American supremacy of the judiciary. Courts examine legality and constitutionality, not the policy or wisdom of a law, which eliminates (b). Review of Bills before assent is not judicial review since there is no 'law' yet; the Court only gives advisory opinions under Article 143 if the President refers a question, which eliminates (c). Reviewing its own judgments is a separate power: review under Article 137 and curative petitions (Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002), which eliminates (d).
explanations: Correct: Judicial review is the power to test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and declare them unconstitutional and void if they violate it.
Incorrect: Courts do not question the wisdom or policy of legislation; they examine only constitutionality, legislative competence and legality.

Incorrect: Courts do not review legislative enactments before the President's assent; judicial review operates on enacted laws, and pre-enactment views come only through advisory opinions under Article 143.
Incorrect: Reconsidering its own earlier judgments is the review jurisdiction under Article 137 or a curative petition, not judicial review as defined.
keyfact: Judicial review = testing constitutionality of laws and executive actions (Art. 13, 32, 226); it covers legality, not the wisdom of policy, and is part of the basic structure.
summary: The answer is (a): in India, Judicial Review means the power of the judiciary to pronounce upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders. Courts can strike down any law or executive action that violates the Constitution, but they do not question the wisdom of a law or review Bills before they become law.

question:
With reference to Indian freedom struggle, consider the following events : Mutiny in Royal Indian Navy dL.
2. Quit India Movement launched
3. Second Round Table Conference What is the correct chronological sequence of the above events ?
subject: Modern History
detail: This question tests basic chronology of the later phase of the freedom struggle. The Second Round Table Conference met in London from September to December 1931, after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931). Gandhi attended as the sole Congress representative, and the conference failed over the communal question and separate electorates. Civil Disobedience resumed in January 1932. The Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, after the failure of the Cripps Mission (March 1942), with Gandhi's 'Do or Die' call. Congress leaders were arrested on 9 August 1942. The Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Mutiny began on 18 February 1946 at Bombay, sparked by the HMIS Talwar and led by naval ratings protesting racial discrimination and poor conditions. It occurred shortly before the Cabinet Mission (March 1946). Elimination logic: the 1931 event is clearly the earliest, since the Round Table Conferences (1930-32) predate World War II. This removes options (a) and (b), which both put it last or second. Option (d) puts the Navy Mutiny before Quit India, which is wrong because the Mutiny was post-war. Only 3-2-1 remains.
explanations: (a) 1-2-3 is wrong: it reverses the actual order, placing the 1946 Navy Mutiny first and the 1931 conference last.
(b) 2-1-3 is wrong: it places the 1931 conference last, but it came before both the 1942 and 1946 events.
(c) 3-2-1 is correct: the Second Round Table Conference (1931), then Quit India (1942), then the RIN Mutiny (1946).
(d) 3-1-2 is wrong: it correctly starts with 1931 but places the 1946 Mutiny before the 1942 Quit India Movement.
keyfact: Second Round Table Conference (1931) → Quit India (Aug 1942) → RIN Mutiny (Feb 1946).
statements: 1 — Mutiny in Royal Indian Navy: occurred in February 1946, the latest of the three events.
2 — Quit India Movement launched: August 1942, the middle event.
3 — Second Round Table Conference: September-December 1931, the earliest event.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 3-2-1. The Second Round Table Conference was held in 1931, the Quit India Movement was launched in 1942, and the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny took place in 1946.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Tax revenue as a percent of GDP of ly India has steadily increased in the last decade. Fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP of India has steadily increased in the last decade. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests the key trends in India's public finance, and the word 'steadily' makes both statements false. Gross tax revenue of the Centre was roughly 10-11% of GDP around 2007-08, fell after the 2008 global financial crisis to about 9.5-10% in 2009-10 to 2012-13, and then recovered to about 11-12% by 2017-18 before dipping again during COVID. This is a fluctuating path, not a steady rise. The fiscal deficit moved even more sharply. It rose to about 6% of GDP in 2008-09 because of the stimulus, and it was brought down to about 4.5% in 2012-13 after the 2012 consolidation push. It then declined gradually to about 3.5% by 2016-17, under the glide path set by the FRBM Act 2003 as amended in 2012 and 2015. The target was 3% of GDP, and the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) proposed a debt-to-GDP target of 60%. Since the fiscal deficit fell over much of the decade, Statement 2 is plainly wrong, while Statement 1 fails on the word 'steadily'. Elimination logic: a statement that claims a 'steady' rise in an economic ratio over a decade is usually false, because ratios are cyclical. Eliminating both statements leads directly to (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 1 is not correct: the tax-GDP ratio fluctuated, so 'steadily increased' fails.
(b) is wrong because Statement 2 is not correct: the fiscal deficit was largely brought down over the decade.
(c) is wrong because both statements are incorrect, so they cannot both be right.
(d) is correct because neither ratio showed a steady rise; both were cyclical or declining over the decade.
keyfact: Tax-GDP ratio fluctuated (about 10-12%) and the fiscal deficit fell from about 6% (2008-09) to about 3.5% (2016-17), so neither rose 'steadily'.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Tax-GDP ratio fell after 2008-09, stagnated, and rose only later, so it did not increase steadily.
2 — Incorrect: Fiscal deficit fell from about 6% (2008-09) to about 3.5% (2016-17) under FRBM-based consolidation, so it did not steadily increase.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Neither India's tax revenue nor its fiscal deficit, each as a percent of GDP, rose steadily over the decade, because both moved up and down with the economic cycle and with policy choices.

question: Recently there was a proposal to translocate some of the lions from their natural habitat in Gujarat to which one of the following sites ?
subject: Environment
detail: The Asiatic lion (Panthera leo persica) survives in the wild only in Gujarat's Gir landscape (Gir National Park and Sanctuary, Pania, Mitiyala, Girnar and surrounding areas). Because one population is exposed to epidemics (such as the 2018 canine distemper outbreak that killed many lions), fire, flood or cyclone, the Wildlife Institute of India recommended a second site in the 1990s. Kuno Palpur in Sheopur and Morena districts of Madhya Pradesh was chosen after surveys for its suitable habitat, prey base and the relocation of villages. The Supreme Court in April 2013 directed that lions be translocated to Kuno within six months, but Gujarat resisted and the move did not happen. Kuno later received African cheetahs (Namibia, September 2022; South Africa, 2023) under Project Cheetah. Elimination logic: Corbett (Uttarakhand) is a tiger and elephant reserve; Mudumalai (Tamil Nadu) is in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve with tigers and elephants; Sariska (Rajasthan) is a tiger reserve that saw tiger reintroduction in 2008. None was proposed for lions.
explanations: Incorrect: Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand is a tiger habitat, and no lion translocation was proposed there.
Correct: Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was the site identified for the second Asiatic lion population, and the Supreme Court backed this in 2013.
Incorrect: Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu is a tiger and elephant area and was never proposed for lions.
Incorrect: Sariska National Park in Rajasthan is known for tiger reintroduction from Ranthambore starting in 2008, not for lions.
keyfact: Asiatic lions from Gir were proposed for translocation to Kuno Palpur (Madhya Pradesh) as a second home, backed by the Supreme Court in 2013.
option_notes: Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, is India's oldest national park, established in 1936 as Hailey National Park. It lies in Nainital and Pauri Garhwal districts on the Ramganga river. It was the first reserve under Project Tiger in 1973 and holds a high tiger density along with elephants.

Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary is in Sheopur and Morena districts of Madhya Pradesh, on the Kuno river, a tributary of the Chambal. It was notified as a sanctuary in 1981 and upgraded to a national park in 2018. It was prepared as the Asiatic lion reintroduction site and became the site of Project Cheetah in 2022.

Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary is in the Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu, at the junction of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala. It is part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and was declared a tiger reserve in 2007. It has tigers, elephants, gaur and leopards, with the Moyar river flowing through it.

Sariska National Park is in Alwar district, Rajasthan, in the Aravalli hills. It became a tiger reserve in 1978 under Project Tiger. All its tigers were lost to poaching by 2004-05, and tigers were reintroduced from Ranthambore from 2008, the first such tiger translocation in the world.
related: Asiatic lions in the wild exist only in Gujarat's Gir landscape.
The Supreme Court ordered lion translocation to Kuno in April 2013.
Kuno National Park received African cheetahs from Namibia in September 2022.
Project Cheetah was launched in 2022 by the Government of India.
Sariska reintroduced tigers from Ranthambore from 2008.
Asiatic lion is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
Barda Wildlife Sanctuary in Gujarat is a proposed alternative lion site within the state.
Corbett was India's first national park, established 1936.
summary: The answer is (b) Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary (Kuno National Park) in Madhya Pradesh. It was chosen as a second home for Asiatic lions from Gir so that the species does not depend on a single population, which is vulnerable to epidemics and natural disasters.
topic_notes: The Asiatic lion is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List (reclassified from Critically Endangered in 2008 and Endangered in 2008 onward), is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, and is in CITES Appendix I. Its only wild population is in Gujarat's Saurashtra region, centred on Gir (about 1,400 sq km sanctuary and national park, Junagadh, Gir Somnath and Amreli districts). Lion population estimates: 523 in 2015, 674 in 2020, and about 891 in 2025. The Gir lion landscape also includes Girnar, Mitiyala and Pania sanctuaries. The Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, led the second-home studies. Kuno was selected over alternatives such as Barda (Gujarat) and Sitamata (Rajasthan). Madhya Pradesh's Kuno required village relocation, and many Sahariya tribal villagers were resettled. In April 2013 the Supreme Court (in the Centre's favour, in the Asiatic Lion Reintroduction case) ordered translocation within six months, yet Gujarat opposed. Project Lion was announced in 2020 for conservation of lions in the Gir landscape. Barda Wildlife Sanctuary in Gujarat has since been considered as an alternative second home within the state. Related angles: Project Tiger (1973), Project Elephant (1992), Project Cheetah (2022), the extinction of the Asiatic cheetah in India (last animals shot in 1947 in Koriya, Chhattisgarh), and the Gir lions' famed Maldhari pastoralist neighbours.

question:
Which of the following are not necessarily the consequences of the proclamation of the President’s rule in a State ? As Dissolution of the State Legislative Assembly
2. Removal of the Council of Ministers in the State
3. Dissolution of the local bodies Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: Article 356 allows the President, on the Governor's report or otherwise, to proclaim President's Rule if the constitutional machinery in a State has failed. Under Article 356(1), the President assumes the functions of the State Government, and the powers of the Governor or any other State authority become exercisable by the President. The State Council of Ministers, which aids and advises the Governor under Article 163, therefore ceases to function and is dismissed. The Legislative Assembly is different. The President may either dissolve it or keep it in suspended animation, and Parliament then exercises its powers. Suspended animation is common, so that the Assembly can be revived if a government is restored. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months. It lasts six months at a time, for a maximum of three years, with extensions subject to the conditions in Article 356(5). Local bodies (Panchayats and Municipalities) are constitutional bodies under Parts IX and IXA, so they continue to function, and Article 243E, for example, provides for mandatory elections. Since only statement 2 is a necessary consequence, options (a), (c) and (d), which include it as 'not necessary', are eliminated.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statement 2, but removal of the Council of Ministers is a necessary consequence of President's Rule.
(b) Correct: only dissolution of the Assembly and of local bodies are not necessarily consequences, since the Assembly may be kept in suspended animation and local bodies are unaffected.
(c) Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is a necessary consequence, and it leaves out statement 1, which is not necessary.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is a necessary consequence, so not all three are 'not necessary'.
