The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the UN. It was established in 1945 under the UN Charter and began work in 1946. It sits in the Peace Palace at The Hague and has 15 judges elected for 9-year terms by the UNGA and UNSC. It decides contentious cases between states and gives advisory opinions. Its working languages are English and French. India's Kulbhushan Jadhav case was heard here.

The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) was created in 1993 after the Vienna World Conference on Human Rights. It is headquartered in Geneva. It leads UN human rights work, supports treaty bodies and special rapporteurs, and backs the Human Rights Council. The post is held by Volker Türk since 2022. It reports on rights situations but does not rank countries on rule of law.

The World Justice Project is an independent, multidisciplinary non-profit organisation founded in 2006 by William H. Neukom. It is based in Washington DC. It works to advance the rule of law worldwide. Its main publication is the annual Rule of Law Index, first released in 2008. It also publishes the Global Insights and Open Government Index. Its work rests on the principles of accountability, just laws, open government and accessible justice.
related: WJP Rule of Law Index scores run from 0 to 1, and 1 is the strongest adherence.
WJP was founded in 2006 by William H. Neukom and is based in Washington DC.
The index uses 8 factors and 44 sub-factors.
Corruption Perceptions Index is published by Transparency International.
Democracy Index is published by the Economist Intelligence Unit.
World Press Freedom Index is published by Reporters Without Borders.
Global Hunger Index is published by Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide.
The ICJ has 15 judges with 9-year terms and sits at The Hague.
summary: The correct answer is (d) World Justice Project. The WJP Rule of Law Index is its annual flagship report, which measures how far countries adhere to the rule of law as experienced by ordinary people. Amnesty International, the ICJ and the UN human rights office do not publish this index.
topic_notes: The rule of law is the principle that all persons, institutions and the state itself are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced and independently adjudicated. The concept is associated with A. V. Dicey, who held that no one is punished except for a breach of law, that everyone is equal before the law, and that the constitution is the result of ordinary law. In India, the rule of law is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. It is reflected in Article 14 (equality before law), Article 21 (life and liberty by procedure established by law) and Article 32 (right to constitutional remedies). The WJP Rule of Law Index is based on four universal principles: accountability, just law, open government and accessible and impartial justice. Data comes from general population polls and qualified respondents' questionnaires. The 8 factors are constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Scores run from 0 to 1. Nordic countries lead the rankings, and in recent years India has been placed roughly 77th to 79th. Other indices that UPSC often asks about include the Global Hunger Index (Welthungerhilfe and Concern Worldwide), the Corruption Perceptions Index (Transparency International), the Democracy Index (Economist Intelligence Unit), the World Press Freedom Index (Reporters Without Borders), the Human Development Index (UNDP), the Global Gender Gap Index (WEF), the Ease of Doing Business report (World Bank, discontinued in 2021), and the Global Innovation Index (WIPO). Match each index with its publisher.

question: Which one of the following links all the ATMs in India ?
subject: Economy
detail: NPCI is an umbrella organisation for retail payments and settlement systems in India. It was set up in 2008 under the guidance of the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks' Association, and incorporated as a not-for-profit company under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013). The National Financial Switch (NFS) was launched in 2004 by IDRBT (Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology) and was transferred to NPCI in 2009. It is the largest network of shared ATMs in India and enables inter-bank ATM transactions. NPCI also runs other retail payment systems: RuPay card, IMPS (Immediate Payment Service), UPI (Unified Payments Interface, 2016), NACH, Bharat BillPay, FASTag and the AePS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System). Elimination logic: the RBI is the regulator and central bank, and it authorises payment systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, but it does not operate the ATM switch. IBA is an industry association of banks and does not operate payment networks. NSDL is a depository for securities (demat holdings), unrelated to ATMs.
explanations: Incorrect: The Indian Banks' Association is a representative body of banks and management; it promoted NPCI but does not link ATMs.
Incorrect: NSDL is India's first depository, holding securities in dematerialised form; it has no role in ATM networks.
Correct: NPCI operates the National Financial Switch, which links the ATMs of all participating banks in India.
Incorrect: The RBI regulates and supervises payment systems and guided NPCI's creation, but the ATM interconnection is operated by NPCI, not the RBI.
keyfact: NPCI (set up 2008) runs the National Financial Switch (NFS), which links all bank ATMs in India, along with RuPay, IMPS and UPI.
summary: The answer is (c) National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). NPCI operates the National Financial Switch (NFS), which interconnects the ATMs of different banks across India so that a customer of any bank can use any bank's ATM.

question: Consider the following statements : Ls Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) is the amount that banks have to maintain in the form of their own funds to offset any loss that banks incur if the account-holders fail to repay dues. 2: CAR is decided by each individual bank. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: Capital Adequacy Ratio (also called Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio, CRAR) = (Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital) / risk-weighted assets. It acts as a cushion that protects depositors and keeps the banking system stable by ensuring a bank can absorb losses, notably those arising from credit risk when borrowers fail to repay. The framework comes from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Bank for International Settlements): Basel I (1988), Basel II (2004), Basel III (after the 2008 crisis). In India the Reserve Bank of India, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, prescribes the norm. Indian scheduled commercial banks must maintain a minimum CRAR of 9%, higher than the Basel minimum of 8%, and under Basel III the total is 9% plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, giving 11.5%. Statement 1 matches this definition. Statement 2 is wrong because CAR is a regulatory requirement set by the central bank, applied uniformly, though a bank may hold more than the minimum. Hence only statement 1 is correct, and (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) Correct: statement 1 correctly describes CAR as a capital buffer against losses, and statement 2 is wrong because the regulator sets the norm.
(b) Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect, since individual banks do not decide CAR; the RBI prescribes it.
(c) Wrong: it would require statement 2 to be correct, but CAR is set by the regulator.
(d) Wrong: statement 1 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: CAR = (Tier 1 + Tier 2 capital) / risk-weighted assets, prescribed by RBI per Basel norms (India minimum 9%; Basel III total with conservation buffer 11.5%).
statements: 1 — Correct: CAR is the minimum own capital a bank must hold against its risk-weighted assets, serving as a buffer against losses including borrower defaults.
2 — Incorrect: CAR is prescribed by the regulator (RBI, based on Basel norms), not decided by each individual bank.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. CAR is the minimum capital a bank must hold from its own funds against its risk-weighted assets to absorb losses, including those from borrowers' defaults. It is prescribed by the regulator (RBI, following Basel norms), not decided by each bank.

question:
The identity platform ‘Aadhaar’ provides open “Application Programming Interfaces (APIs)”. What does it imply ?
1. It can be integrated into any electronic device.
2. Online authentication using iris is possible. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: Aadhaar is the 12-digit unique identity number issued by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), set up in 2009 and given statutory backing by the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016. UIDAI describes Aadhaar as an open identity platform that exposes open Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). An open API is a published, standard interface that lets third-party developers, agencies and device makers plug Aadhaar services into their own software or hardware, so it can be integrated into any electronic device such as a smartphone, a biometric scanner, a point-of-sale terminal or a micro-ATM. Aadhaar authentication supports several modes: demographic authentication, one-time password (OTP), fingerprint biometric, iris biometric, and face authentication (added later). Authentication is done online by sending the data to the Central Identities Data Repository (CIDR), which replies with a yes/no answer or an e-KYC response. Elimination logic: Statement 1 follows directly from the meaning of open APIs, and statement 2 is a recognised authentication mode, so (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out. The Supreme Court's 2018 Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) judgment later limited private-entity use of Aadhaar authentication.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it counts only statement 1, but statement 2 is also correct because iris authentication is supported.
(b) Wrong: it counts only statement 2, but statement 1 is also correct because open APIs imply integration into any device.
(c) Right: both statements are correct, so this matches the official answer.
(d) Wrong: it says neither statement is correct, but both are.
keyfact: Aadhaar is an open identity platform with open APIs, so it can be integrated into any device, and it supports online iris, fingerprint, OTP and face authentication.
statements: 1 — Correct: Open APIs let Aadhaar authentication services be integrated into any electronic device or application that meets the technical specifications.
2 — Correct: Aadhaar supports online biometric authentication, including iris scans (alongside fingerprint, OTP, demographic and face authentication).
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Aadhaar's open APIs allow its authentication services to be built into any electronic device or application, and the platform supports online authentication using biometrics such as iris scans as well as fingerprints.

ocr: Very recently, in which of the following | 21. countries have lakhs of people either suffered from severe famine/acute malnutrition or died due to starvation caused by war/ethnic conflicts ? (a) Angola and Zambia (b) Morocco and Tunisia (ec) Venezuela and Colombia (d) Yemen and South Sudan
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a current-affairs question on conflict-induced hunger. Yemen has been in civil war since 2014-15, when the Houthi movement took over Sanaa and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. Air strikes, blockades of the Hodeidah port and the collapse of the economy left millions food insecure. The UN repeatedly called it the world's worst humanitarian crisis, with famine-like conditions and acute malnutrition among children. South Sudan became independent from Sudan in July 2011. It fell into civil war in December 2013 (Salva Kiir vs Riek Machar, with a Dinka-Nuer ethnic dimension). Famine was formally declared in parts of Unity State in February 2017, the first declaration anywhere in the world since Somalia in 2011. The same year the UN warned of famine risk in four countries: Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and north-east Nigeria. For elimination, the key is the phrase 'war/ethnic conflicts'. Morocco and Tunisia are relatively stable North African states, Angola and Zambia are not in a famine-causing conflict, and Venezuela and Colombia have had economic or political crises, not war-driven mass starvation at this scale. Venezuela's crisis was economic, not war.
explanations: Incorrect: Angola's civil war ended in 2002 and Zambia is politically stable. Neither has had recent war-driven famine on this scale.
Incorrect: Morocco and Tunisia have no war or ethnic conflict causing mass starvation. Tunisia's post-2011 issues were political and economic.
Incorrect: Venezuela has had an economic collapse with shortages, and Colombia has had a long insurgency that ended in the 2016 peace deal. Neither has seen lakhs die of war-induced famine.
Correct: Yemen (civil war and Saudi-led intervention since 2015) and South Sudan (civil war since 2013, famine declared in 2017) both had mass famine and acute malnutrition caused by conflict.
keyfact: Famine from conflict: Yemen (civil war since 2015) and South Sudan (civil war since 2013, famine declared Feb 2017).
summary: The answer is (d) Yemen and South Sudan. Both countries have recently seen lakhs of people suffer severe famine or acute malnutrition, or die of starvation, as a direct result of prolonged war and ethnic conflict.

question:
Regarding Wood’s Dispatch, which of the following statements are true ?
1. Grants-in-Aid system was introduced.
2. Establishment of universities was recommended.
3. English as a medium of instruction at all levels of education was recommended. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Wood's Dispatch of 1854, named after Sir Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control, is often called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'. It set out a comprehensive scheme for the education system. Its main recommendations were: creation of a Department of Public Instruction in each province (headed by a Director); establishment of universities on the London University model at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (founded in 1857), with Senate-based governance; a graded structure of schools, from vernacular primary schools to Anglo-vernacular high schools, affiliated colleges and universities; a system of grants-in-aid to encourage private effort, with aid given on the basis of secular education, adequate management and government inspection; teacher training institutions; promotion of female and vocational education; and the policy of religious neutrality. On language, the Dispatch supported English for higher education but emphasised vernaculars for school-level education, so it did not recommend English as the medium at all levels. Statement 3 is therefore incorrect, which eliminates (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a).
explanations: (a) is right: statements 1 and 2 are true, and statement 3 is false, so only 1 and 2 qualify.
(b) is wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 1, which is true.
(c) is wrong: it pairs statements 1 and 3, but statement 3 is false and statement 2 is true, so it omits 2.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement 3, and the Dispatch did not recommend English as the medium at all levels.
keyfact: Wood's Dispatch (1854): grants-in-aid, universities at the three presidencies (1857), Department of Public Instruction, vernacular for schools and English for higher education.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Dispatch introduced the grants-in-aid system to encourage private enterprise in education, with aid linked to secular instruction, proper management and inspection.
2 — Correct: It recommended establishing universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras on the model of London University; they were set up in 1857.
3 — Incorrect: It favoured English for higher education but vernacular languages at the primary and school levels, so English was not prescribed at all levels.
summary: The correct answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are true. Wood's Dispatch (1854) introduced the grants-in-aid system and recommended universities at the presidency towns, but it did not make English the medium at all levels.

question: With reference to the Parliament of India, 22. which of the following Parliamentary Committees scrutinizes and reports to the House whether the powers to make regulations, rules, sub-rules, by-laws, etc. conferred by the Constitution or delegated by the Parliament are being properly exercised by the Executive within the scope of such delegation ?
subject: Polity
detail: Parliament cannot legislate on every detail, so it passes broad enabling Acts and delegates the power to frame rules, regulations, sub-rules and by-laws to the Executive. This is called delegated or subordinate legislation. To keep the Executive from exceeding its delegated authority, each House has a Committee on Subordinate Legislation. The Lok Sabha committee has 15 members and the Rajya Sabha committee has 15 members. Ministers are not members. The committee checks whether the rules conform to the Constitution and the parent Act, whether they are within the scope of the delegation, whether they trespass on fundamental rights, whether they have retrospective effect, and whether they should be dealt with by an Act of Parliament instead. Rules framed under an Act must be laid before the House, which can modify or annul them. Elimination: the Committee on Government Assurances monitors the implementation of promises made by Ministers on the floor of the House. The Rules Committee is not a standing committee of the kind that scrutinises delegated legislation; the relevant Lok Sabha body is the Committee on Rules, which considers matters of procedure and conduct of business and suggests amendments to the Rules of Procedure. The Business Advisory Committee recommends the time allocation for Bills and other business.
explanations: Incorrect: The Committee on Government Assurances follows up on assurances, promises and undertakings given by Ministers in the House and checks whether they have been fulfilled. It does not examine rule-making powers.

Correct: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation scrutinises whether the powers to make regulations, rules, sub-rules and by-laws conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament are being properly exercised by the Executive within the scope of the delegation, and it reports to the House.

Incorrect: The Rules Committee considers matters of procedure and conduct of business in the House and recommends amendments to the House's Rules of Procedure. It does not review executive rules made under delegated powers.

Incorrect: The Business Advisory Committee recommends the time to be allotted for discussion of Bills and other business, and it is headed by the Speaker (or the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha). It has no role in scrutinising delegated legislation.
keyfact: Committee on Subordinate Legislation = watchdog over delegated legislation (rules, regulations, by-laws) made by the Executive; Government Assurances Committee = ministers' promises.
summary: The answer is (b) Committee on Subordinate Legislation. This committee examines whether the rule-making powers conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament to the Executive are being properly exercised within the scope of the delegation, and it reports to the House.

question: Consider the following statements : As per the Right to Education (RTE) i Act, to be eligible for appointment as a teacher in a State, a person would be required to possess the minimum qualification laid down by the concerned State Council of Teacher Education. As per the RTE Act, for teaching primary classes, a candidate is required to pass a Teacher Eligibility Test conducted in accordance with the National Council of Teacher Education guidelines. In India, more than 90% of teacher education institutions are directly under the State Governments. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Section 23(1) of the Right to Education Act, 2009 says that a person with the minimum qualifications laid down by an academic authority authorised by the Central Government shall be eligible for appointment as a teacher. The National Council of Teacher Education (NCTE) was notified as this authority on 23 August 2010. The NCTE is a statutory body, set up under the NCTE Act, 1993, that regulates and maintains norms and standards in teacher education. A State Council of Teacher Education (SCERT or equivalent) has no power to prescribe the minimum qualification, so statement 1 is wrong. The NCTE guidelines of 2011 made the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) a minimum requirement for teachers of Classes I to VIII. The Central TET (CTET) is conducted by the CBSE, and States conduct their own TETs. Candidates must pass the TET for primary (Classes I-V) and upper primary (Classes VI-VIII) teaching, so statement 2 is correct. On statement 3, the large majority of teacher education institutions in India are privately managed, many of them self-financed, and government institutions are a small minority. Statement 3 is therefore wrong. Eliminating 1 and 3 leaves only 2.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which wrongly gives the State Council of Teacher Education the power to set qualifications.
(b) is right because only statement 2 holds: the TET is conducted in accordance with NCTE guidelines.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 3, which is factually incorrect since private institutions dominate teacher education.
(d) is wrong because statement 3 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct, so 3 alone cannot be the answer.
keyfact: RTE Act Section 23: the NCTE (the Centre's authorised academic authority) sets teacher qualifications, and the TET is mandatory for Classes I-VIII.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The minimum qualification is laid down by the academic authority authorised by the Central Government (the NCTE), not by State Councils of Teacher Education.
2 — Correct: Under NCTE guidelines (2011), passing the TET (CTET or a State TET) is mandatory for teachers of Classes I-VIII, including primary classes.
3 — Incorrect: Most teacher education institutions are private; far fewer than 90% are directly under State Governments.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under the RTE Act, 2009 (Section 23), the minimum qualifications are laid down by the academic authority authorised by the Central Government (the NCTE), not by State Councils of Teacher Education, and the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) follows NCTE guidelines.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Tradition State 1. Chapchar Kut festival _— Mizoram 2. Khongjom Parba ballad — Manipur 3. Thang-Ta dance — Sikkim Which of the pairs given above is/are correct ? 1 only (a) land 2 (b) 3 only (c) (d) 2 and 3 25. 23. Consider the following statements :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: This question tests the cultural traditions of the North-East, which UPSC asks about regularly. Chapchar Kut is the Mizo festival celebrated in March after jungle clearing (jhum cultivation) and before sowing. It is marked by dance, music and feasting. Khongjom Parba is an epic ballad of the Meitei people of Manipur. It narrates the Battle of Khongjom (1891), the last battle between Manipur and British forces, in which Major Paona Brajabashi died. It is sung with the dholak-like pung and accompanied by the singer's own narration. Thang-Ta is the Manipuri martial art. 'Thang' means sword and 'Ta' means spear, and it is also called Huyen Lallong. It is not a dance, and it is not from Sikkim. Elimination logic: pair 1 and pair 2 are both correct, so options (a), (c) and (d) fall away. Option (a) omits pair 2. Options (c) and (d) both include pair 3, which is wrong. Remember the rule: when a pair has two correct items and one wrong item, check the weakest one first. The Thang-Ta confusion is the trap, because it is a martial art, not a dance, and it belongs to Manipur, not Sikkim.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out pair 2, since Khongjom Parba is indeed a ballad of Manipur.
Right: pairs 1 and 2 are both correct, and pair 3 is incorrect because Thang-Ta is a Manipuri martial art, not a Sikkimese dance.
Wrong: pair 3 is incorrect, and this option also rejects the two correct pairs.
Wrong: it includes pair 3, which is incorrect, and it leaves out pair 1, which is correct.
keyfact: Chapchar Kut = Mizoram festival; Khongjom Parba = Manipur ballad; Thang-Ta = Manipuri martial art (not a Sikkim dance).
option_notes: Option (a), pair 1 only: Chapchar Kut is Mizoram's spring festival, celebrated in March after the jhum clearing. It features Cheraw (bamboo dance), Chai and Khuallam dances, along with songs and feasting. It was revived in 1973 after being discouraged under missionary influence. Other Mizo festivals are Mim Kut and Pawl Kut. Mizoram is a Christian-majority state, so festivals also include Christmas, but Chapchar Kut remains its main cultural festival.

Option (b), pairs 1 and 2: this is the correct answer. It joins Mizoram's Chapchar Kut spring festival to Manipur's Khongjom Parba ballad. The ballad narrates the Battle of Khongjom of 1891 between Manipuri forces and the British. Both pairs are matched correctly, and the option rightly excludes the wrongly paired Thang-Ta. Remember: festival, Mizoram; ballad, Manipur; Thang-Ta, Manipuri martial art.

Option (c), pair 3 only: this is the wrong pairing. Thang-Ta is the martial art of Manipur, with 'Thang' meaning sword and 'Ta' meaning spear. It is also called Huyen Lallong. Sikkim is known for the Singhi Chham (snow lion dance), Yak Chham, Kagyed dance and the Maruni dance. Sikkim has no tradition called Thang-Ta, so this option fails.

Option (d), pairs 2 and 3: it combines the correct pair 2 with the incorrect pair 3. Khongjom Parba is a Manipuri ballad about the 1891 battle. Thang-Ta is a Manipuri martial art, so it cannot match Sikkim. Because it excludes pair 1 as well, which is correct, the option fails on two counts.
related: Chapchar Kut is a Mizoram spring festival celebrated in March.
Khongjom Day is observed on 23 April in Manipur.
Thang-Ta is a Manipuri martial art, also known as Huyen Lallong.
Sattriya dance of Assam became a classical dance in 2000.
Sankirtana of Manipur is on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list (2013).
Singhi Chham is the snow lion dance of Sikkim.
Hornbill Festival is held in Nagaland every December.
Cheraw is the bamboo dance of Mizoram.
statements: 1 — Correct: Chapchar Kut is a festival of Mizoram. It is the most important spring festival of the Mizos, celebrated in March after the jungle clearing for jhum cultivation, when there is little farm work. It was traditionally celebrated for the first time in 1450 AD at Suaipui village (as per tradition), and it was suppressed during the Christian missionary period. It was revived in 1973. Dances include Cheraw (bamboo dance), Chai and Khuallam. Other Mizo festivals are Mim Kut (maize, after harvest) and Pawl Kut (harvest).

2 — Correct: Khongjom Parba is a ballad form of Manipur, belonging to the Meitei oral tradition (Dhol Dholak Cholom style as an accompanying tradition). It recounts the Battle of Khongjom of April 1891 in the Anglo-Manipur War. Manipuri forces under Paona Brajabashi fought the British at Khongjom and he died there. The ballad is sung with the pung (drum) by a lead singer. Khongjom Day is observed on 23 April every year. Manipur also has Lai Haraoba, Ras Lila and Pung Cholom traditions.

3 — Incorrect: Thang-Ta is not a dance of Sikkim. It is a martial art of Manipur, practised by the Meitei people. 'Thang' means sword and 'Ta' means spear. It is also called Huyen Lallong and combines armed and unarmed combat, with a ritual and spiritual dimension. The British banned it after the 1891 Anglo-Manipur War, and it was revived later. It is related to Sarit Sarak (the unarmed form). Sikkim's traditional dances include Singhi Chham (snow lion dance), Yak Chham and Maruni, and festivals include Losar and Saga Dawa.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 1 and 2. Chapchar Kut is a spring festival of Mizoram, and Khongjom Parba is a ballad of Manipur. Thang-Ta is a martial art of Manipur, not a dance of Sikkim, so pair 3 is wrong.
topic_notes: This question belongs to Indian culture, specifically the traditions of the North-East. The North-East is a repeated source of UPSC pairs, so link each tradition to its state and its type: festival, dance, martial art or ballad. Mizoram: Chapchar Kut (spring), Mim Kut (maize), Pawl Kut (harvest); dances are Cheraw (bamboo), Khuallam and Chai. Manipur: Lai Haraoba (ritual festival of the Meitei gods), Ras Lila (Manipuri classical dance, one of the eight classical forms), Pung Cholom (drum dance), Thang-Ta (martial art), Khongjom Parba (ballad), and Yaoshang (Holi) festival. Also note Kang (Rath Yatra) and Ningol Chakouba. Sikkim: Losar, Saga Dawa, Pang Lhabsol, with Singhi Chham and Yak Chham dances. Nagaland: Hornbill Festival, Sekrenyi, Moatsu. Assam: Bihu (Bohag, Magh, Kati), with Bihu dance and Sattriya (classical dance recognised in 2000). Arunachal: Losar, Solung, Mopin, with Ponung dance. Meghalaya: Wangala (Garo), Nongkrem (Khasi), Shad Suk Mynsiem. Tripura: Garia, Kharchi puja. Manipur's Loktak lake and Keibul Lamjao National Park (sangai deer) are tied to the cultural identity. Battle of Khongjom (23 April 1891) ended the Anglo-Manipur War. Intangible Cultural Heritage: UNESCO has listed Sankirtana of Manipur (2013). Remember that martial arts include Kalaripayattu (Kerala), Gatka (Punjab), Thang-Ta (Manipur), Silambam (Tamil Nadu), Mardani Khel (Maharashtra) and Paika Akhada (Odisha). Know the distinction between classical dance, folk dance, martial art and festival, because UPSC often deliberately mixes categories.

question: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 replaced the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAD is under the charge of Director General of Health Services in the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act) consolidated eight older food laws, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA), the Fruit Products Order 1955, the Meat Food Products Order 1973, the Vegetable Oil Products (Control) Order 1947, the Edible Oils Packaging (Regulation) Order 1998, the Solvent Extracted Oil, De-oiled Meal and Edible Flour (Control) Order 1967, and the Milk and Milk Products Order 1992. It was passed in 2006 and notified in 2011, when the PFA Act was repealed. Section 4 of the FSS Act establishes the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) as a statutory body. It is headquartered in New Delhi and administratively linked to the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It is led by a Chairperson, appointed by the Central Government, who is of the rank of Secretary to the Government of India, and a Chief Executive Officer. The Director General of Health Services (DGHS) is a separate technical wing of the Ministry, so statement 2 is wrong. The elimination logic is that statement 1 is verifiably correct and statement 2 confuses administrative linkage with direct charge. This leaves option (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true because the FSS Act, 2006 replaced the PFA Act, 1954, and statement 2 is false, so only 1 holds.
Wrong: statement 2 is not correct, because FSSAI is an autonomous statutory body headed by a Chairperson, not under the DGHS.
Wrong: this needs both statements to be true, but statement 2 is false.
Wrong: this needs both statements to be false, but statement 1 is true.
keyfact: The FSS Act, 2006 replaced the PFA Act, 1954, and FSSAI is an autonomous statutory body, not under the DGHS.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this is the correct choice. It recognises that the FSS Act, 2006 repealed the PFA Act, 1954, and that FSSAI is not under the DGHS. The FSS Act subsumed eight food laws and was enforced from 2011. FSSAI, set up under Section 4, is headquartered in Delhi and works under the Health Ministry's administrative control. Its Chairperson is of Secretary rank, and a CEO handles the executive work.

Option (b), 2 only: this is wrong because it accepts the DGHS claim and rejects the replacement of the PFA Act. The DGHS is the principal technical adviser of the Union Health Ministry on medical and public health matters, and runs the Central Government Health Scheme, hospitals and the Central Health Services. It does not run FSSAI, which has its own Chairperson and CEO. The PFA Act was repealed by the FSS Act.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this is wrong because it endorses both statements. Statement 1 is correct, but FSSAI's structure is a statutory authority with a Food Authority, Chairperson and CEO, not a directorate under the DGHS. Many aspirants wrongly assume that anything under the Health Ministry is under the DGHS, but administrative linkage to a ministry is not the same as being under a subordinate office.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong because statement 1 is true. The PFA Act, 1954 was India's first comprehensive food adulteration law and was repealed once the FSS Act, 2006 came into force on 5 August 2011. Choosing this would imply the older Act is still in force, which is not the case. FSSAI now works as the single regulator of food safety.
related: The FSS Act, 2006 subsumed eight earlier food laws and orders, including the PFA Act, 1954.
The FSS Act came into force on 5 August 2011.
FSSAI is a statutory body established under Section 4 of the FSS Act, 2006.
FSSAI is administratively linked to the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
FSSAI is headquartered in New Delhi.
Eat Right India is FSSAI's campaign for safe, healthy and sustainable food.
FoSTaC is FSSAI's Food Safety Training and Certification programme.
The Codex Alimentarius is the international food standards body of FAO and WHO.
statements: 1 — Correct: The FSS Act, 2006 repealed the PFA Act, 1954 and the other food-related orders it subsumed. The PFA Act, 1954 was India's first comprehensive food law, based on a Central Committee for Food Standards, with a public analyst and food inspector system. It was criticised as outdated, penal-heavy and fragmented across several ministries and orders. The FSS Act was enacted in 2006 to create a single reference point, a science-based standard-setting regime and a unified regulator. FSSAI was established under it in 2008 and the Act came into force on 5 August 2011, with the FSS Rules and Regulations of 2011. It covers manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import of food.

2 — Incorrect: FSSAI is a statutory autonomous body, not a unit under the Director General of Health Services. It is administratively linked to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and its Chairperson is of Secretary rank. The Chairperson is Rajesh Bhushan-era Secretary-level, and a separate CEO runs daily work. FSSAI has Food Authority members drawn from the Centre, States, industry, farmers and consumers. Its functions include framing regulations on standards, licensing and registration of food business operators, accrediting labs, a Food Safety Appellate Tribunal link, and running schemes like Eat Right India, FoSTaC and the Food Safety Connect app. The DGHS is the technical advisor to the Ministry and heads institutions like the Central Health Services.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 did repeal and replace the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, but FSSAI is not under the Director General of Health Services. It is a statutory autonomous body headed by a Chairperson and administered through the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
topic_notes: The FSS Act, 2006 is the central law on food safety in India. It consolidated eight earlier laws and orders, among them the PFA Act, 1954, and created a single regulator and a science-based standards regime. FSSAI was established in 2008, under Section 4, and the Act came into force on 5 August 2011. FSSAI is headquartered in New Delhi, with regional offices, and is administratively linked to the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It is headed by a Chairperson, appointed by the Central Government, of Secretary rank, with a CEO who is of Joint Secretary level or above. Its main functions are laying down science-based standards for food articles, regulating their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, setting guidelines for the accreditation of laboratories, advising the government, collecting data on contamination, and promoting general awareness. Food businesses need a licence or registration, and the FSSAI licence number must appear on labels. State Commissioners of Food Safety, designated officers and food safety officers handle enforcement at state and district levels. Adjudicating officers, and a Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, deal with penalties and appeals. Key initiatives include Eat Right India, the Food Safety and Standards (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, the Food Safety Connect app, the FoSTaC training programme, the Clean Street Food Hub, the Hygiene Rating scheme, the Safe and Nutritious Food (SNF) initiative, and the Food Safety Mitra scheme. The FSSAI logo and the Jaivik Bharat logo for organic food are related features. Possible future angles are the powers of food safety officers, the Codex Alimentarius link, the FSS Act's provision for improvement notices, and the roles of the Food Authority members.

ocr: The term “two-state solution” is sometimes mentioned in the news in the context of the affairs of (a) China (b) Israel (ce) Traq (d) Yemen (138A) With reference to the provisions made under the National Food Security Act, 2013, consider the following statements : t. The families coming under the category of ‘below poverty line (BPL) only are eligible to receive subsidised food grains. 2. . The eldest woman in a household, of age 18 years or above, shall be the head of the household for the purpose of issuance of a ration card. 3. | Pregnant women and lactating mothers are entitled to a ‘take-h
subject: Economy
detail: The 'two-state solution' refers to the proposed resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, under which an independent State of Palestine would exist alongside the State of Israel, living in peace and security. It is based on UN Security Council Resolution 242 (1967), which called for Israeli withdrawal from territories occupied in the Six-Day War, and on the Oslo Accords (1993-95) between Israel and the PLO, which created the Palestinian Authority. The Palestinian territories envisaged are the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) and the Gaza Strip, generally along the pre-1967 lines (the Green Line), with issues such as the status of Jerusalem, Israeli settlements, borders, security and the right of return of refugees remaining unresolved. UN General Assembly Resolution 181 (1947) first proposed partition of Mandatory Palestine into Arab and Jewish states. India officially supports a negotiated two-state solution and recognised Palestine in 1988. Elimination logic: China has Taiwan and Tibet issues, which are not framed as two states; Iraq's issues involve Kurdistan and sectarian governance; Yemen has a civil war involving Houthis and the government, with the historic North-South division reunified in 1990. Only Israel is tied to the phrase 'two-state solution'.
explanations: Incorrect: China's disputes (Taiwan, Tibet, South China Sea) are not described as a 'two-state solution'.
Correct: The two-state solution means independent Israel and Palestine coexisting side by side, based on pre-1967 lines.
Incorrect: Iraq's issues concern Kurdish autonomy and sectarian power-sharing, not a two-state solution.
Incorrect: Yemen's conflict is a civil war between the Houthis and the government; the term is not used for it.
keyfact: Two-state solution = independent Israel and Palestine (West Bank and Gaza, East Jerusalem as capital) living side by side, based on pre-1967 borders.
summary: The image shows two questions; the numbered Q24 is the 'two-state solution' question, whose answer is (b) Israel. The NFSA 2013 question that follows is the one carrying the official answer (b) '2 only', so only that is treated as the item to explain here. Hmm, the instruction says to explain only Q24, and the official answer given is (b); both questions have (b) as the answer under this reading, so the note covers Q24: the two-state solution concerns Israel and Palestine.

question: India enacted The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 in order to comply with the obligations to
subject: Economy
detail: India became a founding member of the WTO in 1995 and so had to accept the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS), which sets minimum standards for IPR protection. Part II, Section 3 (Articles 22-24) of TRIPS deals with Geographical Indications, with extra protection for wines and spirits. To comply, India passed the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. It came into force on 15 September 2003, and the GI Registry is in Chennai. Darjeeling Tea was the first Indian product to get a GI tag (2004-05). The Act is administered by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade. GI protection is generally valid for 10 years and can be renewed. Elimination logic: the ILO deals with labour standards, the IMF with monetary stability and balance-of-payments support, and UNCTAD with trade and development policy. None of them administers a binding IPR agreement. Only the WTO, through TRIPS, imposes enforceable IPR obligations on members. Note that the key supplied with this question marks (b), but this is inconsistent with the facts. The UPSC's published answer for this question is (d).
explanations: (a) ILO - Incorrect: the International Labour Organization sets labour standards and has no connection to geographical indications.

(b) IMF - Incorrect on the facts: the IMF handles monetary cooperation and financial stability and has no IPR or GI obligations. The supplied key marks this option, but it conflicts with the TRIPS basis of the Act.
(c) UNCTAD - Incorrect: UNCTAD is a UN forum on trade and development that produces recommendations, not binding IPR obligations.
(d) WTO - Correct: the Act implements India's obligations under the WTO's TRIPS Agreement (Articles 22-24) on geographical indications.
keyfact: GI Act, 1999 (in force 2003) implements WTO-TRIPS obligations; Darjeeling Tea was India's first GI; the GI Registry is in Chennai.
summary: The correct answer is (d) WTO, not (b) IMF as the supplied key says. The GI Act, 1999 was enacted to meet India's obligations under the WTO's TRIPS Agreement (Articles 22-24), which requires member countries to protect geographical indications. The IMF has no role in intellectual property, so (b) cannot be justified. Please check the key before saving this note.

question:
Consider the following statements : A In India, State Governments do not have the power to auction non-coal mines.
2. Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand do not have gold mines.
3. Rajasthan has iron ore mines. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The question tests mining law and the geography of minerals. Under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR), as amended in 2015 and 2021, the State Governments are the auctioning authority for mineral blocks, including non-coal ones such as iron ore, bauxite and limestone. The Centre auctions coal and lignite blocks under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, and has the power to auction in certain situations (e.g. if a State fails to hold auctions within a stipulated time). Since the 2015 amendment, auctions have replaced first-come-first-served for major minerals, and District Mineral Foundations were created for affected communities. Gold: Karnataka (Kolar, Hutti, Uti), Andhra Pradesh (Ramagiri in Anantapur district) and Jharkhand (Rakha Mines, Singhbhum, and the Sonapet area) have gold deposits or past or present mining. Hence statement 2 fails. Rajasthan's iron ore is mined mainly in Jaipur, Dausa, Sikar, Alwar, Bhilwara and Udaipur, so statement 3 holds. Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are false, which leaves 3 alone; the OCR printed '8 only' for '3 only'.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 is wrong because both statements are factually false: States can auction non-coal minerals, and Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand have gold mines.
(b) 2 only is wrong because statement 2 is false; Ramagiri in Andhra Pradesh and Singhbhum in Jharkhand have gold.
(c) 1 and 3 is wrong because statement 1 is false, as States conduct non-coal mineral auctions under the MMDR Act.
(d) 3 only is correct because only statement 3 is true: Rajasthan has iron ore mines, and the other two statements are false.
keyfact: States auction non-coal major minerals under the MMDR Act; Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand have gold; Rajasthan has iron ore, so the answer is 3 only.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2: this would hold only if States lacked auction power and the two states had no gold. In fact, the MMDR Act (1957, amended 2015 and 2021) gives States the auction power for major minerals, and gold is found in Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand, so neither claim holds. The option is a distractor created from the two false statements.

Option (b), 2 only: this would require Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand to lack gold. Gold is found at Ramagiri (AP) and in Singhbhum (Jharkhand), while Karnataka leads in production. Andhra Pradesh also has Chigargunta and Bisanatham gold fields. This choice tests knowledge of gold distribution, which is contradicted by facts.

Option (c), 1 and 3: this would be right if statement 1 were true. It is false because States run auctions for non-coal minerals such as iron ore, bauxite and limestone, under rules framed by the Centre. Only the Centre auctions coal blocks, through the Ministry of Coal and the nominated authority. This option pairs a false claim with a true one.

Option (d), 3 only (OCR printed as 8 only): this is the official answer. Rajasthan hosts iron ore mines, mainly hematite and magnetite, in Jaipur, Dausa, Alwar, Sikar, Bhilwara and Udaipur. The state is more famous for zinc, lead, copper and marble, but iron ore is present, and the other two statements are false.
related: MMDR Act was enacted in 1957 and was substantially amended in 2015 and 2021.
The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 followed the 2014 Supreme Court cancellation of 204 coal blocks.
Mines and Minerals fall under Union List Entry 54 and State List Entry 23.
District Mineral Foundation funds are used for welfare in mining-affected areas.
Karnataka is the largest gold producer; Kolar Gold Fields closed in 2001.
Rajasthan is the sole producer of zinc and a leading producer of lead.
Odisha is the largest producer of iron ore in India.
The Geological Survey of India was established in 1851.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: State Governments do have the power to auction non-coal mines under the MMDR Act, as amended. The Act of 1957 governs the regulation of mines and the development of minerals other than petroleum, natural gas and atomic minerals. After the 2015 amendment, major mineral concessions are granted by competitive auction conducted by States, with the Centre prescribing rules. The 2021 amendment further empowered the Centre to auction when States do not act and removed the distinction between captive and merchant mines. Coal is separately auctioned by the Centre under the 2015 Act and the Ministry of Coal.

2 — Incorrect: Both states have gold mines. Andhra Pradesh has the Ramagiri gold field in Anantapur district, and Jharkhand has gold in Singhbhum (Rakha, Kundarkocha and Sonapet areas), where mining was historically conducted. Karnataka remains India's largest gold producer (Hutti and Uti mines), with Kolar Gold Fields closed in 2001. Gold is a metallic mineral found in Archaean rocks (the Dharwar craton), and India's gold output is small relative to its massive imports.

3 — Correct: Rajasthan has iron ore, mined in Jaipur and Dausa (Morija-Banol), Udaipur, Bhilwara, Sikar and Alwar districts, mostly hematite and magnetite. The state is better known for zinc, lead (Zawar, Rampura Agucha), copper (Khetri), marble (Makrana), sandstone and gypsum, and is the sole producer of zinc and a leading producer of lead. Major iron ore producers are Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand, and Rajasthan contributes a smaller share.
summary: The correct answer is (d), statement 3 only. Rajasthan does have iron ore mines (e.g., in Jaipur, Dausa, Alwar, Bhilwara and Udaipur districts), while statements 1 and 2 are factually wrong: States auction non-coal (major mineral) blocks under the MMDR Act, and both Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand have gold mines.
topic_notes: Mining in India is governed by the MMDR Act, 1957, which covers all minerals except petroleum, natural gas and atomic minerals. Minerals are divided into major minerals (iron ore, bauxite, coal, limestone, manganese and others) and minor minerals (building stone, sand, gravel, ordinary clay), with the Centre notifying major ones and States controlling minor ones. Mines and minerals are in the Union List (Entry 54) subject to Union control, and States have power under State List Entry 23, subject to Entry 54. The 2015 amendment introduced auctions for major minerals, created District Mineral Foundations (DMF) for affected areas and established the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET). The 2021 amendment removed the distinction between captive and merchant mines and allowed captive mines to sell up to 50% of production after meeting their needs. Coal: nationalised in 1972-73, auctioned under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015, with commercial mining opened to private players in 2020. The Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal blocks allotted since 1993 in the 2014 Manohar Lal Sharma case. Atomic minerals include uranium, thorium and lithium (until 2023), which was later removed from the atomic list and made auctionable by the 2023 amendment. Critical minerals are listed in the Seventh Schedule, and the Centre auctions them. Distribution: iron ore in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa; bauxite in Odisha and Gujarat; copper in Rajasthan (Khetri), Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand) and Jharkhand (Ghatsila); gold in Karnataka (Hutti), Andhra Pradesh (Ramagiri) and Jharkhand; mica in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan; manganese in Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. Institutions: Geological Survey of India (1851), the Indian Bureau of Mines (Nagpur) and the Ministry of Mines.
