ocr: Which of the following is/are the aim/aims of “Digital India” Plan of the Government of India ? i. Formation of India’s own Internet companies like China did. 2. Establish a policy framework to encourage overseas multinational corporations that collect Big Data to build their large data centres within our national geographical boundaries. 3. Connect many of our villages to the Internet and bring Wi-Fi to many of our schools, public places and major tourist centres. Select the correct answer using the code given below : 1 and 2 only (a) 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1,2 and 3 (d)
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 by PM Narendra Modi as an umbrella programme to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy. It rests on three vision areas: (1) digital infrastructure as a core utility for every citizen, covering high-speed Internet, a digital identity, mobile banking and a shareable private space on a public cloud; (2) governance and services on demand, with integrated and real-time online services; and (3) digital empowerment of citizens through universal digital literacy and accessible digital resources. It has nine pillars: Broadband Highways, Universal Access to Mobile Connectivity, Public Internet Access Programme, e-Governance, e-Kranti, Information for All, Electronics Manufacturing, IT for Jobs, and Early Harvest Programmes. BharatNet (earlier NOFN) connects Gram Panchayats by optical fibre, and Wi-Fi in schools, universities, public places and tourist centres is an Early Harvest item. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is a comparison with China and is not a stated aim of the programme. Statement 2 describes a policy to attract foreign firms' data centres, which is not an aim. Data localisation debates exist elsewhere, but they are not part of the Digital India aims. Only statement 3 matches the programme's stated goals, so (b) is correct.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong because both statements fall outside the stated aims of Digital India and it omits statement 3, which is correct.
(b) 3 only is correct because only statement 3, rural connectivity and public Wi-Fi, is a stated aim of Digital India.
(c) 2 and 3 only is wrong because statement 3 is correct but statement 2, the policy for MNC data centres, is not an aim of the programme.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because statements 1 and 2 are not aims of Digital India.
keyfact: Digital India (1 July 2015) aims at digital infrastructure, e-governance and digital empowerment (rural broadband, public Wi-Fi), not at building Chinese-style Internet companies or attracting MNC data centres.
related: Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015.
It is coordinated by MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology).
Nine pillars of Digital India include Broadband Highways and Early Harvest Programmes.
BharatNet (formerly NOFN) connects Gram Panchayats by optical fibre.
Puttaswamy judgment (2017) made privacy a fundamental right under Article 21.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023.
UPI is operated by NPCI and was launched in 2016.
CSCs are the front-end delivery points for digital services in rural India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Digital India has no stated aim of creating Indian Internet companies on the Chinese model. Its goals are infrastructure, services and empowerment. Facts: China built home-grown platforms such as Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent behind its 'Great Firewall'. Digital India instead relies on public digital infrastructure, such as Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker, and on programmes such as Startup India (2016) to support private innovation. It is not a programme for creating national champions modelled on another country.

2 — Incorrect: Digital India does not set out a policy framework to encourage overseas MNCs that collect Big Data to build data centres in India. Facts: data localisation is a separate policy debate. The RBI's 2018 circular required payment data to be stored in India. The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017-18) report led to the Personal Data Protection Bill, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023. A Data Centre Policy was drafted by MeitY in 2020. These are not listed aims of the 2015 Digital India vision.

3 — Correct: connecting villages to the Internet and providing Wi-Fi in schools, public places and tourist centres is an explicit aim. Facts: BharatNet aims to connect about 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats by optical fibre. It is implemented through Bharat Broadband Network Limited (BBNL), now merged into BSNL. The Public Internet Access Programme covers Common Services Centres (CSCs), and Post Offices are to become multi-service centres. Wi-Fi hotspots at tourist centres, railway stations and universities were part of the Early Harvest programmes. PM-WANI (2020) later expanded public Wi-Fi.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. Digital India (launched 1 July 2015) aims at digital infrastructure, e-governance and digital empowerment, which includes connecting villages and providing Wi-Fi in schools, public places and tourist centres. It does not aim to create Indian Internet companies 'like China did', and it does not set a policy to attract foreign MNCs to build data centres.
topic_notes: Digital India is a flagship programme of the Government of India, launched on 1 July 2015 and coordinated by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Its three vision areas are digital infrastructure as a utility, governance and services on demand, and digital empowerment of citizens. Its nine pillars are Broadband Highways, Universal Access to Mobile Connectivity, Public Internet Access Programme, e-Governance (reforming government through technology), e-Kranti (electronic delivery of services), Information for All, Electronics Manufacturing (Net Zero Imports target), IT for Jobs, and Early Harvest Programmes. Key components and related schemes: BharatNet connects Gram Panchayats with optical fibre and was earlier called the National Optical Fibre Network (NOFN). Common Services Centres (CSCs) deliver services in rural areas. Aadhaar is the digital identity, run by UIDAI (statutory under the Aadhaar Act 2016). UPI, run by NPCI, was launched in 2016. DigiLocker stores documents digitally. UMANG is a single mobile app for government services. BHIM is the payments app. e-Sign, MyGov and the National Scholarship Portal also belong here. Related areas UPSC may ask about include the Personal Data Protection debate. This covers the Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) judgment recognising privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21, the Srikrishna Committee, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023. The IT Act 2000 is the main cyber law. CERT-In is the national cyber security agency. Other connected programmes are the National Digital Communications Policy 2018, the National Broadband Mission, PM-WANI public Wi-Fi, Startup India, Make in India, the Production Linked Incentive scheme for electronics and semiconductors, and the India Semiconductor Mission (2021). The India Stack is the public digital infrastructure.

question:
Consider the following pairs : 40. Towns sometimes Country mentioned in news
1. Aleppo — Syria
2. Kirkuk — Yemen
3. Mosul — Palestine
4. Mazar-i-sharif — Afghanistan Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests West Asian geography that often appears in the news. Aleppo is in northern Syria and was one of the country's largest cities and a major battleground in the Syrian civil war, especially in 2012-2016, ending with government recapture in December 2016. Kirkuk is an oil-rich city in northern Iraq, and its status is disputed between the Iraqi central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government. Iraqi forces retook it in October 2017 after the Kurdish independence referendum. Mosul is Iraq's second-largest city on the Tigris, near ancient Nineveh. ISIS declared its caliphate there in 2014, and Iraqi forces retook the city in July 2017. Mazar-i-Sharif is in northern Afghanistan, the capital of Balkh province, known for the Blue Mosque, and is a Taliban-contested area. Palestine's main cities are Gaza, Ramallah and Hebron, while Yemen's are Sana'a, Aden and Hodeidah. Elimination logic: Kirkuk is wrongly placed in Yemen, so any option containing pair 2 (a, c) is out. Mosul is wrongly placed in Palestine, so any option containing pair 3 (c, d) is out. Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes pair 2, but Kirkuk is in Iraq, not Yemen.
(b) Right: Aleppo-Syria and Mazar-i-Sharif-Afghanistan are both correct, and this is the official answer.
(c) Wrong: both pairs 2 and 3 are mismatched, since Kirkuk and Mosul are in Iraq.
(d) Wrong: it includes pair 3, but Mosul is in Iraq, not Palestine.
keyfact: Aleppo = Syria; Kirkuk and Mosul = Iraq; Mazar-i-Sharif = Afghanistan.
statements: 1 — Correct: Aleppo is a major city in northern Syria, central to the Syrian civil war.
2 — Incorrect: Kirkuk is in northern Iraq, not Yemen.
3 — Incorrect: Mosul is in northern Iraq, not Palestine.
4 — Correct: Mazar-i-Sharif is in northern Afghanistan, in Balkh province.
summary: The correct answer is (b): pairs 1 and 4 are correctly matched. Aleppo is in Syria and Mazar-i-Sharif is in Afghanistan, whereas Kirkuk and Mosul are both in Iraq, not Yemen or Palestine.

question: In the Federation established by The Government of India Act of 1935, residuary powers were given to the
subject: Polity
detail: The Government of India Act, 1935 proposed an All-India Federation of British Indian provinces and princely states, though the federal part never came into operation; provincial autonomy took effect in 1937. It divided legislative subjects into three lists: the Federal List (59 items), the Provincial List (54 items) and the Concurrent List (36 items). Unlike the Canadian model, where residuary powers go to the Centre, and unlike the US model, where they go to the states, the 1935 Act gave them to neither legislature. Section 104 authorised the Governor General, in his discretion, to empower the Federal Legislature or a Provincial Legislature to enact a law on any matter not enumerated in the lists, and he could decide whether a given matter was within the residuary field. This reflected the Act's strong centralising and safeguard-oriented character, with the Governor General holding special powers. In contrast, the Constitution of India (Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List) vests residuary powers in the Union Parliament. Elimination logic: provincial bodies (c) and (d) are ruled out because the Act was centralising, and (a) is ruled out because the legislature was not given the power directly; it was the Governor General's discretion.
explanations: Incorrect: The Federal Legislature had no automatic residuary power; it could legislate on residuary matters only if the Governor General authorised it.
Correct: Section 104 of the 1935 Act gave the Governor General discretionary power to allot residuary legislative power to the Federal or a Provincial Legislature.
Incorrect: Provincial Legislatures had power only over the Provincial and Concurrent Lists, and residuary subjects reached them only by the Governor General's authorisation.
Incorrect: Provincial Governors had no residuary powers; the power was held at the federal level by the Governor General.
keyfact: 1935 Act: residuary powers went to the Governor General (Sec. 104), whereas the Indian Constitution gives them to Parliament (Art. 248).
summary: The answer is (b) Governor General. Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the residuary powers (subjects not listed in any of the three legislative lists) were not given to the federal or provincial legislatures but to the Governor General, who could empower either the Federal or a Provincial Legislature to legislate on them at his discretion.

question:
Consider the following statements : 42.
1. The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly shall vacate his/her office if he/she ceases to be a member of the Assembly.
2. Whenever the Legislative Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker shall vacate his/her office immediately. 43. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 179 governs the vacation, resignation and removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly. Clause (a) says the Speaker vacates office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly. Clause (b) allows resignation by writing to the Deputy Speaker. Clause (c) allows removal by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Assembly, with at least 14 days' notice. The proviso to Article 179 is the key to this question: whenever the Assembly is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office until immediately before the first meeting of the Assembly after the dissolution. This ensures continuity and that the office is never vacant. Article 94 is the parallel provision for the Lok Sabha Speaker. A related point is that the Speaker does not preside over the sitting when a resolution for his or her removal is under consideration, though he or she can speak and take part in the proceedings, and vote only in the first instance (not in a tie). Elimination logic: statement 1 is a plain textual rule, so (b) and (d) fall away. Statement 2 contradicts the proviso, so (c) falls away, leaving (a).
explanations: (a) Correct: statement 1 is right under Article 179(a) and statement 2 is wrong because of the dissolution proviso.
(b) Wrong: it accepts statement 2, which is false because the Speaker stays in office after dissolution until the new Assembly's first meeting.
(c) Wrong: it counts statement 2 as correct, but the Speaker does not vacate office immediately on dissolution.
(d) Wrong: statement 1 is correct, since ceasing to be a member ends the Speaker's tenure.
keyfact: Article 179 (and Article 94 for the Lok Sabha): the Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be a member, but after dissolution continues until just before the new House's first meeting.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 179(a) requires the Speaker to vacate office on ceasing to be a member of the Assembly.

2 — Incorrect: Under the proviso to Article 179, on dissolution the Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the new Assembly, so the Speaker does not vacate immediately.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. The Speaker must vacate office on ceasing to be an Assembly member, but on dissolution of the Assembly the Speaker continues in office until the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly.

question: Which one of the following reflects the most appropriate relationship between law and liberty ?
options: If there are more laws, there is less liberty
Ifthere are no laws, there is no liberty
If there is liberty, laws have to be made by the people
If laws are changed too often, liberty is in danger
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question comes from the political theory of liberty (NCERT Class 11, Political Theory, Chapter 2). There are two broad conceptions. Negative liberty (Isaiah Berlin, J.S. Mill) means absence of external constraints, but even Mill's harm principle accepts that restrictions are justified to prevent harm to others. Positive liberty (T.H. Green, Rousseau) means the capacity to develop one's potential, which requires enabling conditions that law can provide. Thinkers such as Locke argued that where there is no law there is no freedom, because without law the strong dominate the weak (a state of nature in which rights are insecure). Law makes liberty equal and secure by restraining the harm one person can do to another. Hence liberty is not licence. In the Indian context, Article 19 grants freedoms subject to reasonable restrictions, and Article 21 protects life and personal liberty through procedure established by law. Elimination: (a) wrongly treats law and liberty as inversely proportional, since the quality of laws matters more than their number. (c) describes democratic or self-government, not the basic relationship. (d) is a concern about stability and legal certainty, not the essential link. Only (b) states the necessary relationship.
explanations: Incorrect: Liberty depends on the quality and justice of laws, not their quantity. Many laws, such as those protecting rights, can enhance liberty.
Correct: Without laws there would be no protection against arbitrary power or the strong, so liberty could not be secured. Law is a precondition of liberty.

Incorrect: Popular law-making relates to democracy and positive or political liberty, but it is not the most basic relationship. Liberty can exist under laws not made directly by the people, such as a rights-respecting constitution.
Incorrect: Frequent change harms certainty and the rule of law, but this is a secondary concern and does not define the relationship between law and liberty.
keyfact: Law does not oppose liberty but secures it: no law, no liberty (liberty is not licence).
summary: The answer is (b): if there are no laws, there is no liberty. Liberty means freedom within a framework of rules that protect each person's freedom from the arbitrary interference of others, so law is a condition of liberty rather than its opposite.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted against the Governor of a State in any court during his term of office.
2. The emoluments and allowances of the Governor of a State shall not be diminished during his term of office. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Governor's position is protected by constitutional safeguards in Part VI. Article 361 gives the President and Governors immunity: they are not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of official powers and duties (361(1)). Under 361(2), no criminal proceedings whatsoever can be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor in any court during the term of office. Under 361(3), no process for arrest or imprisonment can be issued against a Governor during the term. Under 361(4), civil proceedings in respect of personal acts need two months' prior written notice. Article 158 lays down the conditions of the Governor's office. The Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature (158(1)). He is entitled to use of an official residence without paying rent (158(3)), and to emoluments, allowances and privileges fixed by Parliament (158(3)). Article 158(4) states that these emoluments and allowances shall not be diminished during the term of office. The Second Schedule Part B originally dealt with Governors' salaries, now fixed by law; the current salary is Rs 3.5 lakh per month. Since both statements track the constitutional text, (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct under Article 158(4), so statement 1 alone is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct under Article 361(2), so statement 2 alone is incomplete.
(c) is right because Article 361(2) gives immunity from criminal proceedings and Article 158(4) protects emoluments and allowances from diminution during the term.
(d) is wrong because both statements are supported by explicit constitutional provisions.
keyfact: Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings against the President or a Governor during the term; Article 158(4): the Governor's emoluments and allowances cannot be diminished during the term.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 361(2) bars the institution or continuation of criminal proceedings against a Governor in any court during the term of office.
2 — Correct: Article 158(4) provides that the Governor's emoluments and allowances shall not be diminished during the term of office.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Article 361(2) bars criminal proceedings against a Governor during the term of office, and Article 158(4) says the Governor's emoluments and allowances shall not be diminished during the term of office.

question: The well-known painting “Bani Thani” belongs to the
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Bani Thani is the iconic Kishangarh miniature, often called the 'Mona Lisa of India'. It is traditionally dated to c. 1750 and attributed to the master painter Nihal Chand, who served the court of Maharaja Sawant Singh (1699-1764) of Kishangarh in Rajasthan. Sawant Singh was a poet-devotee of Krishna who wrote under the name Nagari Das. Bani Thani, a singer-poetess in his court, is said to have inspired his depiction of Radha, and Sawant Singh himself is shown as Krishna. The style is marked by exaggerated features: elongated body, lotus-petal (almond-shaped) eyes, arched eyebrows, thin pointed nose, thin lips, sharp chin, and a slender neck. Themes are Radha-Krishna love (Rasa Lila, the Vaishnava Pushtimarg tradition) set in lyrical landscapes and boat scenes. Elimination: Bundi is known for hunting scenes, lush forests and the court of Rao Surjan; Jaipur for Mughal-influenced court and portrait work; Kangra is a Pahari school known for delicate, lyrical Radha-Krishna and Gita Govinda themes under Sansar Chand. The Radha-Krishna theme can confuse students with Kangra, but the Bani Thani name settles it as Kishangarh.
explanations: Incorrect: Bundi school is known for vivid colours, dense vegetation, hunting scenes, rain and night skies, not Bani Thani.
Incorrect: Jaipur school is known for court portraits, Mughal-influenced style, large murals and Krishna-themed works, but Bani Thani is not from it.
Incorrect: Kangra school is a Pahari school from Himachal known for soft, naturalistic Radha-Krishna themes, but it does not include Bani Thani.
Correct: Bani Thani was painted by Nihal Chand at Kishangarh under Sawant Singh (Nagari Das), c. 1750, and is the signature work of the Kishangarh school.
keyfact: Bani Thani = Kishangarh school, painted by Nihal Chand (c. 1750) under Sawant Singh (Nagari Das).
option_notes: Bundi school: a Rajasthani school flourishing from the 17th century in Bundi (Hadoti region). It features bright colours, rich greenery, hunting and court scenes, animals, and monsoon skies with clouds and lightning. The Ragamala series from Bundi (1591, Chunar) is famous. Rao Surjan and Rao Chhatrasal were notable patrons. It influenced neighbouring Kota painting, known for hunting scenes.

Jaipur school: Also called Amber/Dhundhar school, developed under Kachwaha rulers such as Sawai Jai Singh II and Sawai Pratap Singh. It shows strong Mughal influence, with court portraits, religious themes (Krishna Leela, Ragamala), and mural/fresco work. Natural dyes, gold and silver were used, and the style is known for large-scale paintings and detailed ornament.

Kangra school: A Pahari school from Himachal Pradesh that rose in the late 18th century under Raja Sansar Chand of Kangra, evolving from Guler painting (Nainsukh, Manaku). It is known for soft colours, delicate lines, lyrical naturalism, and themes like Gita Govinda, Bhagavata Purana, and Bihari Satsai. Women's depiction is graceful, with a straight nose-forehead profile.

Kishangarh school: Rajasthani school of Kishangarh, flourishing under Sawant Singh (Nagari Das) in the 18th century. Its master Nihal Chand created Bani Thani. Features include elongated faces, lotus-shaped eyes, arched brows and pointed chins, with Radha-Krishna devotion (Pushtimarg) as the central theme. Landscapes show lakes and boats. India issued a postage stamp on Bani Thani in 1973.
related: Bani Thani is attributed to Nihal Chand of Kishangarh, c. 1750.
Kishangarh's patron Sawant Singh wrote poetry as Nagari Das.
Basohli is considered the earliest Pahari school, known for bold colours.
Kangra painting flourished under Raja Sansar Chand.
Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad began Mughal painting under Humayun.
Hamzanama was the major painting project under Akbar.
Mansur was Jahangir's famed animal and bird painter.
Bundi and Kota belong to the Hadoti group of Rajasthani painting.
summary: The answer is (d) Kishangarh school. Bani Thani is the celebrated Rajasthani miniature portrait associated with Kishangarh, painted around 1740-1750 by Nihal Chand under the patronage of Raja Sawant Singh (Nagari Das).
topic_notes: Indian miniature painting has several traditions. Rajasthani schools include Mewar (Udaipur; Sahibdin, Ragamala, early Rasikapriya), Marwar (Jodhpur, Bikaner, Jaisalmer), Hadoti (Bundi, Kota, Jhalawar), Dhundhar (Jaipur, Amber, Alwar) and Kishangarh. Mewar's Chawand Ragamala (1605) was painted by Nisardin. Bikaner was strongly influenced by Mughal artists (Ustads) and Deccani styles. Kishangarh's peak was under Sawant Singh with Nihal Chand, who painted Bani Thani c. 1750. Pahari schools include Basohli (bold colours, earliest, late 17th century, Bhanu Datta's Rasamanjari), Guler (Nainsukh, Manaku), Kangra (the most lyrical, Sansar Chand), Chamba, Mankot, Nurpur and Garhwal (Mola Ram). Mughal painting began under Humayun with Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, flourished under Akbar (Hamzanama) and Jahangir (naturalism, bird and animal portraits by Mansur, Bishandas), and declined under Aurangzeb. Deccani schools include Bijapur (Ibrahim Adil Shah II), Golconda, and Ahmednagar. Other forms include Pala (Buddhist manuscripts on palm leaf), Jain (Kalpasutra), Madhubani (Bihar), Pattachitra (Odisha, Bengal), Kalamkari, Warli, Tanjore, and Mysore. Themes in Rajasthani art: Ragamala, Barahmasa, Rasikapriya, Gita Govinda, hunting and court life. Bani Thani is considered a defining icon of Indian Rajasthani art and appeared on an Indian postage stamp in 1973.

question: What is “Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD)”, sometimes seen in the news ?
options: <A defence collaboration between Japan and South Korea
subject: Geography
detail: THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) is a US land-based missile defence system that destroys incoming ballistic missiles during their terminal (descent) phase using hit-to-kill technology: the interceptor has no explosive warhead and destroys the target by kinetic collision. Prime contractor is Lockheed Martin; the radar is the AN/TPY-2 (made by Raytheon). A battery typically has launchers, interceptors, the radar and a fire control unit. Interception altitude is roughly 40-150 km, range about 200 km. It was first deployed by the US Army in 2008. It came into the news in 2016-17 when the US deployed it in South Korea (Seongju) against North Korean missile threats, which angered China and Russia. UAE and Saudi Arabia have also bought it, and it was deployed in Israel in 2024. Elimination: (a) wrong because it is not Israeli and is not merely a radar; Israel's systems are Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow. (b) wrong because India's programme is the Ballistic Missile Defence (Prithvi Air Defence, Advanced Air Defence) run by DRDO. (d) wrong because it is a US system, not a Japan-South Korea collaboration.
explanations: Wrong: THAAD is not Israeli and is a complete interceptor system, not only a radar. Israel's systems are Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow.
Wrong: India's indigenous programme is the DRDO Ballistic Missile Defence (PAD/AAD, now Phase-II), not THAAD.
Correct: THAAD is a US anti-ballistic-missile system made by Lockheed Martin and operated by the US Army.

Wrong: It is not a Japan-South Korea collaboration. The US deployed it in South Korea, and Japan and South Korea have separate defence arrangements such as GSOMIA, which lapsed and was later restored.
keyfact: THAAD = US (Lockheed Martin) hit-to-kill terminal-phase anti-ballistic missile system, deployed in South Korea in 2017.
option_notes: Israel's missile defence is layered: Iron Dome (short-range rockets, with Rafael), David's Sling (medium-range), and Arrow 2 and 3 (long-range ballistic missiles, with Israel Aerospace Industries and Boeing). Israeli radars include the EL/M-2080 Green Pine used with Arrow. Iron Dome became operational in 2011. The US funds much of this cooperation. THAAD is not among these, though the US deployed a THAAD battery in Israel in October 2024.

India's Ballistic Missile Defence programme was started by DRDO after the 1999 Kargil war. Phase-I has a two-tier shield: Prithvi Air Defence (PAD, exo-atmospheric, over 80 km) and Advanced Air Defence (AAD, endo-atmospheric, 15-30 km). It can counter missiles up to roughly 2,000 km range. Phase-II aims at 5,000 km threats, with systems like AD-1 and AD-2. India also bought the Russian S-400 Triumf, with deliveries starting in 2021.

THAAD is a US system developed from the 1990s, first deployed in 2008. It is a hit-to-kill interceptor for the terminal phase, with a 200 km range and an interception altitude of 40-150 km. It uses the AN/TPY-2 radar. Operators include the US, UAE, Saudi Arabia (purchase) and South Korea (US forces). Its 2017 deployment in South Korea strained relations with China.

Japan and South Korea have no joint missile defence system. Their key defence arrangement is GSOMIA, the General Security of Military Information Agreement signed in 2016. South Korea announced withdrawal in 2019 and suspended that decision. Japan relies on Aegis BMD and PAC-3 with the US. South Korea has KAMD (Korea Air and Missile Defense) and hosts the US THAAD battery. In 2023, the US, Japan and South Korea agreed on real-time missile warning data sharing.
related: THAAD uses hit-to-kill technology with no explosive warhead.
THAAD's radar is the AN/TPY-2, made by Raytheon; the interceptor is made by Lockheed Martin.
THAAD was deployed in Seongju, South Korea, in 2017 against North Korea's missile threat.
India signed the S-400 Triumf deal with Russia in October 2018.
India's BMD uses PAD (exo-atmospheric) and AAD (endo-atmospheric) interceptors, developed by DRDO.
Israel's Iron Dome is made by Rafael, and Arrow by Israel Aerospace Industries.
CAATSA is the US law imposing sanctions on buyers of Russian defence equipment; Turkey was sanctioned in 2020.
summary: The answer is (c): THAAD is an American anti-ballistic-missile system developed by Lockheed Martin for the US Army and Missile Defense Agency. It is designed to intercept short-, medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles in their terminal phase, both inside and just outside the atmosphere.
topic_notes: Missile defence systems are built in layers. Exo-atmospheric (outside the atmosphere) interceptors like Aegis BMD SM-3 and India's PAD work in the midcourse phase. Endo-atmospheric interceptors like PAC-3 and India's AAD operate in the terminal phase. THAAD sits between them and can intercept both inside and outside the atmosphere. The US also has the Ground-based Midcourse Defense (GMD) in Alaska and California for ICBMs, and Patriot (PAC-3) for lower-altitude terminal defence. Hit-to-kill means kinetic collision, no warhead. Other countries: Russia has the S-400 Triumf (range up to 400 km, 4 missile types) and S-500, plus the A-135 around Moscow; China has the HQ-9 and HQ-19; Israel has Iron Dome, David's Sling and Arrow; Turkey bought the S-400, leading to US CAATSA sanctions in 2020 and removal from the F-35 programme. India signed the S-400 deal in October 2018 (about $5.43 billion) and got a CAATSA waiver debate. India's DRDO developed Akash (surface-to-air), Barak-8/MRSAM (with Israel), QRSAM, and the Project Kusha long-range SAM. The BMD programme was tested from Abdul Kalam Island (Odisha). Exam angles: country-system matching, interception altitude, hit-to-kill, CAATSA, South Korea's 2017 deployment and China's objections, and the Indian BMD phases.

question:
With reference to cultural history of India, 46, consider the following statements :
1. Most of the .Tyagaraja Kritis are devotional songs in praise of Lord Krishna.
2. Tyagaraja created several new ragas. 3s Annamacharya and Tyagaraja are contemporaries.
4. Annamacharya kirtanas are devotional songs in praise of Lord Venkateshwara. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Art & Culture
detail: This question tests the cultural history of Carnatic music and the Bhakti tradition in South India. Tyagaraja (1767-1847), born at Tiruvarur and settled at Thiruvaiyaru on the Kaveri, is one of the Trinity of Carnatic music along with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri. He composed thousands of kritis, mostly in Telugu, and the large majority are devotional songs to Lord Rama; this makes statement 1 wrong. He is credited with creating or popularising ragas such as Harikambhoji-related forms, Manohari, Kharaharapriya-based phrases, Jayantasree, Garudadhvani, Sri Ranjani and others, so statement 2 is accepted. Annamacharya (1408-1503), a Telugu composer at Tallapaka in present-day Andhra Pradesh, composed sankirtanas, said to number about 32,000, in praise of Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala; statement 4 is correct. Since he lived roughly 300 years before Tyagaraja, statement 3 is wrong. Elimination logic: rejecting 3 removes (c) and (d), and rejecting 1 removes (a), leaving (b). Spotting that either 1 or 3 is wrong is enough to eliminate three options.
explanations: Wrong: it treats statement 1 as correct, but Tyagaraja's kritis are mostly about Rama, and statement 3 is also wrong because Annamacharya and Tyagaraja lived about three centuries apart.
Correct: statements 2 and 4 are accurate. Tyagaraja created several new ragas, and Annamacharya's kirtanas are devotional songs to Venkateswara.
Wrong: statement 1 (Krishna) and statement 3 (contemporaries) are both false, and it leaves out statement 4, which is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false because the two composers were separated by about 300 years, even though statements 2 and 4 are right.
keyfact: Tyagaraja (1767-1847) sang mainly of Rama and created new ragas; Annamacharya (1408-1503) sang of Venkateswara, about 300 years earlier.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 3: this combines two false claims. Tyagaraja's devotion centred on Rama, and Annamacharya was a 15th-century composer, not his contemporary. Krishna-centred works by Tyagaraja exist, such as the opera Nauka Charitam, but they are a small part of his output. Other Krishna-focused composers include Purandaradasa and Narayana Teertha, whose Krishna Leela Tarangini is a well-known Sanskrit work.

Statements 2 and 4: this is the official answer. It correctly links Tyagaraja with the creation of ragas and Annamacharya with songs to Venkateswara. Tyagaraja (1767-1847) belongs to the Carnatic Trinity, and Annamacharya (1408-1503) is the Telugu pada-kavita pioneer of Tirumala. Remember the century gap: Annamacharya in the 15th century and Tyagaraja in the 18th-19th.

Statements 1, 2 and 3: this accepts the Krishna claim and the contemporaneity claim, both wrong, and omits the correct Venkateswara statement. Tyagaraja's chief deity was Rama, as seen in Pancharatna Kritis such as 'Endaro Mahanubhavulu' in Sri raga. Tyagaraja's contemporaries were Dikshitar and Syama Sastri, not Annamacharya.

Statements 2, 3 and 4: this is close to the answer but wrongly adds statement 3. The chronology is the trap: Annamacharya (1408-1503) is placed in the Vijayanagara period, while Tyagaraja lived under Maratha-ruled Thanjavur and the early colonial period. Keeping the chronology of Bhakti and Carnatic composers clear (Annamacharya, Purandaradasa, then the Trinity) avoids this trap.
related: Tyagaraja (1767-1847) composed the Pancharatna Kritis and is one of the Carnatic Trinity.
The Carnatic Trinity: Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri, all born at Tiruvarur.
Annamacharya (1408-1503) composed about 32,000 sankirtanas to Venkateswara at Tirumala.
Purandaradasa is called the Pitamaha of Carnatic music and composed in Kannada.
Bhadrachala Ramadasu composed devotional songs to Rama at Bhadrachalam.
Venkatamakhin's Chaturdandi Prakashika codified the 72 melakarta ragas.
Swati Tirunal of Travancore was a ruler-composer in the 19th century.
Thyagaraja Aradhana is held every year at Thiruvaiyaru.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Most of Tyagaraja's kritis are in praise of Rama, not Krishna. Tyagaraja (1767-1847) was born in Tiruvarur and lived at Thiruvaiyaru in the Thanjavur region. He composed in Telugu and some Sanskrit, with thousands of compositions, of which about 700 survive. Famous works include the Pancharatna Kritis in Adi tala, beginning with 'Jagadanandakaraka' in Nata raga. He also wrote the operas Prahlada Bhakti Vijayam and Nauka Charitam, the latter on Krishna. His guru was Sonti Venkataramanayya, and he declined royal patronage from the Thanjavur court. The Thyagaraja Aradhana is held every year at Thiruvaiyaru.

2 — Correct: Tyagaraja is credited with creating or popularising several ragas, including Garudadhvani, Pratapavarali, Sri Ranjani, Jayantasree, Chenchukambhoji and Manohari. He is regarded as a great innovator in sangati (melodic variations) in kritis and enriched the form of the kriti. He belongs to the Trinity of Carnatic music, with Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri, all born in Tiruvarur and flourishing in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The Trinity's period is often called the golden age of Carnatic music. Tyagaraja's sishya parampara carried his compositions forward.

3 — Incorrect: Annamacharya (1408-1503) lived in the Vijayanagara era in the 15th century, while Tyagaraja (1767-1847) lived in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. They were about three centuries apart. Annamacharya was born at Tallapaka in Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh, and is regarded as the Pada-kavita Pitamaha (grandsire of Telugu song-writing). He served the Saluva and Tuluva rulers and was a contemporary of the Bhakti saints of his period. His descendants kept his work alive, and copper plates containing his compositions were preserved at Tirumala.

4 — Correct: Annamacharya's kirtanas are devotional songs in praise of Lord Venkateswara (Venkateshwara) of Tirumala-Tirupati. He is said to have composed about 32,000 sankirtanas, of which roughly 12,000 survive on copper plates preserved in the Tirumala temple library. They fall into two themes: adhyatma (spiritual) and sringara (romantic devotion). He is regarded as an incarnation of Nandaka, the sword of Vishnu. The Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) has promoted his works, and the Annamacharya Project is run by TTD. He is also credited with the Telugu work Sankirtana Lakshanamu.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 4 are correct. Tyagaraja created several new ragas, and Annamacharya's kirtanas praise Lord Venkateshwara of Tirupati. Most of Tyagaraja's kritis praise Rama, not Krishna, and Annamacharya (15th century) lived about 300 years before Tyagaraja (18th-19th century), so they were not contemporaries.
topic_notes: Carnatic music has a long history, with many composers each tied to a period and a deity. Purandaradasa (1484-1564) is called the Pitamaha of Carnatic music. He systematised teaching with graded exercises such as sarali varisai and janta varisai, and composed in Kannada in praise of Krishna and Vitthala. Annamacharya (1408-1503) wrote Telugu sankirtanas to Venkateswara at Tirumala. Kshetrayya composed padams, and Bhadrachala Ramadasu (17th century) composed songs to Rama at Bhadrachalam. Narayana Teertha wrote the Krishna Leela Tarangini. The Trinity of the late 18th and early 19th centuries were Tyagaraja (Rama, Telugu), Muthuswami Dikshitar (Sanskrit, with the signature 'Guruguha', and the raga-mudra style) and Syama Sastri (Tamil and Telugu, Goddess Kamakshi, the swarajatis). Swati Tirunal, the ruler of Travancore (1813-1846), was also a notable composer. Other musical forms include the varnam, kriti, padam, javali and tillana. The Tamil Trinity (Muthu Thandavar, Arunachala Kavi, Marimutha Pillai) came earlier. Hindustani music had Tansen, Amir Khusrau, and Swami Haridas. The Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952) is the national academy for music, dance and drama, and the Madras Music Academy holds its December season annually. The Sangita Kalanidhi title is the highest honour of the Madras Music Academy. Musical treatises include Natya Shastra (Bharata), Brihaddeshi (Matanga), Sangita Ratnakara (Sharngadeva, 13th century) and Chaturdandi Prakashika (Venkatamakhin, 17th century), which codified the 72 melakarta scheme. Next time UPSC could ask about composers' deities, languages, chronology, or musical forms.

question:
Which of the following are regarded as the main features of the “Rule of Law” ? 1 Limitation of powers
2. Equality before law
3. People’s responsibility to the Government 48. 4, Liberty and civil rights Select the correct answer using the code given below :
options: 1, 2,3 and 4 Which one of the following statements correctly describes the meaning of legal tender money ? The money which is tendered in courts
of law to defray the fee of legal cases
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Rule of Law was systematised by A.V. Dicey in 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution' (1885). It has three pillars: supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power, equality before law, and individual rights flowing from ordinary law and court decisions. The idea is that no one is above the law and that the state itself must act within legal limits. In India it is a basic structure feature of the Constitution. It is reflected in Article 14 (equality before law and equal protection of laws), Article 21 (life and personal liberty through 'procedure established by law'), Articles 32 and 226 (judicial remedies) and judicial review. Its core features are therefore limitation of governmental powers, equality before law, and protection of liberty and civil rights. Elimination logic: statement 3 reverses the relationship, since in a rule-of-law or democratic system the government is answerable to the people and to the law. Any option containing 3, namely (a) and (d), is therefore wrong. Option (b) omits limitation of powers, which is the central idea, so (c) is the only complete option. The OCR text has garbled option labels; the correct option is '1, 2 and 4 only'.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it includes statement 3, which is not a feature, and it leaves out equality before law and civil liberties.
(b) is wrong: statements 2 and 4 are correct but it omits limitation of powers, which is a core feature.
(c) is right: 1, 2 and 4 together capture limited power, equality before law and protected liberty and civil rights, and it correctly excludes 3.
(d) is wrong: it includes statement 3, which reverses the accountability relationship between government and people.
keyfact: Rule of Law (Dicey): limited government power, equality before law, and protection of liberty and rights. Accountability runs from the government to the people, not the reverse.
statements: 1 — Correct: Limitation of powers is central to the Rule of Law, because the state and its officials must act within law and arbitrary power is excluded.
2 — Correct: Equality before law, Dicey's second pillar and Article 14 in India, means that all persons are subject to the same law and the same courts.
3 — Incorrect: The Rule of Law makes the government accountable to the people and to the law. It does not impose a 'responsibility of the people to the Government'.
4 — Correct: Liberty and civil rights are protected by law and enforced by independent courts, as in Articles 21 and 32.
summary: The answer is (c): 1, 2 and 4 only. The Rule of Law means that government power is limited by law, everyone is equal before law, and liberty and civil rights are protected. 'People's responsibility to the Government' is not a feature, because accountability runs from the government to the people.

subject: Economy
detail: The question is: 'Increase in absolute and per capita real GNP do not connote a higher level of economic development, if...'. The idea is that growth (a rise in output or income) is not the same as development, which also needs structural balance, wider distribution of gains and better living standards. In developing countries such as India, a large share of the population depends on agriculture. If agricultural output lags behind industrial output, rural incomes stagnate, food supply and food prices come under pressure, and sectoral imbalance and inequality widen. GNP can still rise because of industry, but the mass of people see little improvement, so the rise does not indicate real development. Elimination logic: (a) is the reverse case. Agriculture outpacing industry is not usually seen as a sign of backwardness in this framing, though it could suggest weak industrialisation. (c) Rising poverty and unemployment would also undermine development, and this is a tempting option, but UPSC's official key is (b), which treats balanced sectoral growth as the point being tested. (d) Imports growing faster than exports concerns the balance of payments, not the quality of development. Remember: growth is not the same as development, and sectoral balance matters.
explanations: Incorrect: industrial output failing to keep pace with agricultural output is not the condition the question points to. It would suggest slow industrialisation, but it does not make a rise in GNP fail to reflect development.

Correct: if agriculture lags behind industry, growth is imbalanced and the large agriculture-dependent population gains little, so higher absolute and per capita GNP does not imply a higher level of development. This matches the official key.
Incorrect as the official answer: rising poverty and unemployment are indeed signs of poor development, but they are not the answer UPSC's key accepts. The key takes sectoral imbalance as the reason.
Incorrect: imports growing faster than exports points to a trade or balance-of-payments problem. It says little about whether the structure and quality of development have improved.
keyfact: Growth is not the same as development: if agriculture lags behind industry, rising GNP and per capita GNP do not indicate higher development.
summary: The official answer is (b). Increases in absolute and per capita real GNP do not signal a higher level of economic development if agricultural output fails to keep pace with industrial output, because growth is then imbalanced and the large agriculture-dependent population does not share in it.

question: Despite being a high saving economy, capital formation may noé result in significant increase in output due to
options: high capital-output ratio 54. 51. After the Santhal Uprising subsided, what was/were the measure/measures taken by the colonial government ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Incremental Capital-Output Ratio (ICOR) is the units of capital needed to produce one extra unit of output (ICOR = Investment/GDP ratio divided by growth rate). In the Harrod-Domar framework, growth rate = savings rate / capital-output ratio. So if the saving rate is high but the capital-output ratio is also high, growth stays low. A high ratio reflects low capital productivity: inefficient use of capital, project delays and cost overruns, poor technology, capacity under-utilisation, and infrastructure bottlenecks. India's planners used ICOR to estimate the investment needed for target growth rates. For example, with an ICOR of about 4 and a target growth of 8%, the investment rate required is about 32% of GDP. Elimination logic: options (a), (b) and (c) are general developmental constraints, and none is the direct technical link between capital formation and output. The question asks what directly weakens the translation of capital into output, and that is the capital-output ratio. A lower ICOR means more efficient capital use and faster growth for the same saving rate.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: weak administration can hinder implementation, but it is not the direct economic measure linking capital to output, so it is not the best answer.
(b) Incorrect: illiteracy limits human capital quality, but it is not the specific reason capital formation fails to raise output; it is a broader constraint.
(c) Incorrect: high population density does not directly determine how much output each unit of capital produces; the effect is ambiguous and indirect.
(d) Correct: a high capital-output ratio means more capital is required per unit of extra output, so high savings and capital formation give only a small rise in output.
keyfact: Growth rate = saving rate ÷ ICOR (Harrod-Domar): a high ICOR means low capital productivity and weak output gains despite high savings.
summary: The answer is (d) high capital-output ratio. A high ICOR means each additional unit of output needs a large amount of capital, so even high saving and capital formation yield only a small rise in output.

ocr: The territories called ‘Santhal Paraganas’ were created. 2: It became illegal for a Santhal to transfer land to a non-Santhal. ; Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 Economically, one of the results of the British rule in India in the 19*" century was the (a) increase in the export of Indian handicrafts (b) growth in the number of Indian owned factories (c) commercialization of Indian agriculture (d) rapid increase in the urban population
subject: Economy
detail: Colonial land revenue systems (Permanent Settlement 1793, Ryotwari, Mahalwari) demanded high revenue in cash. This forced peasants to sell produce in the market and to grow cash crops instead of food grains. Raw materials such as cotton, jute, indigo, opium, tea and oilseeds were exported to feed British industry. The result was the commercialization of agriculture, with greater market dependence, indebtedness to moneylenders, and recurrent famines. The Deccan Riots of 1875 and the indigo revolt of 1859-60 are consequences of this. Alongside it came deindustrialization: cheap Manchester machine-made goods flooded India after the Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly, and Indian handicrafts such as Dhaka muslin declined. Elimination: (a) is wrong because handicraft exports fell, not rose. (b) is wrong because Indian-owned factories were few in the 19th century. Cotton mills in Bombay (1854) and jute mills began, but there was no significant growth, and modern industry was mostly British-controlled. (d) is wrong because urbanisation was slow and old towns decayed, and the urban population remained roughly 10 percent or less. Only (c) matches the established historical consensus. The Santhal question in the image, partly cut off, concerns the Santhal Pargana Tenancy arrangements after the 1855 Santhal rebellion. Its likely answer is (c) both 1 and 2, but treat that as a separate item.
explanations: Incorrect: Indian handicraft exports declined in the 19th century because British machine-made goods displaced them (deindustrialization).
Incorrect: There was no significant growth in Indian-owned factories in that century. Modern industry was limited and mostly British-owned, and Indian entrepreneurship grew mainly later.
Correct: Cash-based revenue demands and the needs of British industry pushed peasants toward cash crops like cotton, indigo, jute, opium and tea. This is the commercialization of agriculture.
Incorrect: Urbanisation was slow, and many traditional craft towns declined, so there was no rapid increase in the urban population.
keyfact: 19th-century colonial rule brought commercialization of agriculture (cash crops for export) along with deindustrialization and the decline of handicrafts.
summary: The image has two questions. The one numbered Q51 in this task is the second: 'Economically, one of the results of British rule in India in the 19th century was the...'. The official answer is (c), commercialization of Indian agriculture. Under colonial rule, cultivators were pushed to grow cash crops for the market and for export, such as cotton, indigo, jute, opium and tea.

ocr: If the President of India exercises his power as provided under Article 356 of the Constitution in respect of a particular State, then (a) the Assembly of the State is automatically dissolved. (b) the powers of the Legislature of that State shall be exercisable by or under the authority of the Parliament. (ec) Article 19 is suspended in that State. (d) the President can make laws relating to that State. Consider the following pairs : Craft Heritage of 1. Puthukkulishawls — Tamil Nadu 2; Sujni embroidery — Maharashtra 3. Uppada Jamdani saris — Karnataka Which of the pairs given above is/are cor
subject: Polity
detail: Article 356 applies when the President is satisfied, on the Governor's report or otherwise, that the State government cannot be carried on according to the Constitution. The President may then assume the functions of the State government, except those of the High Court. The President may also declare that the State Legislature's powers are exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament. This is the text of Article 356(1)(b), which is why (b) is correct. The Proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months. It lasts six months at first, can be extended in six-month steps, and cannot exceed three years in total. Extension beyond one year needs a National Emergency in force or Election Commission certification. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held the Proclamation is subject to judicial review. It also held that the Assembly should not be dissolved until Parliament approves the Proclamation, so the Assembly can be kept in suspended animation instead of being dissolved. Article 357 allows Parliament to delegate its law-making power for the State to the President or another authority, so the President has no independent law-making power. Article 19 can be suspended only under a National Emergency (Articles 352 and 358), not under Article 356.
explanations: (a) Wrong. Dissolution is not automatic. The Assembly may be kept in suspended animation, and under Bommai it cannot be dissolved before Parliament approves the Proclamation.
(b) Correct. Article 356(1)(b) says the State Legislature's powers become exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.
(c) Wrong. Article 19 is suspended only during a National Emergency (Article 358), not during President's Rule.

(d) Wrong, and the least precise option. The President has no independent power to make laws for the State. Parliament exercises the legislative power and may delegate it to the President under Article 357.
keyfact: Article 356: State Legislature's powers pass to Parliament (not automatic dissolution); Article 19 is suspended only under a National Emergency (Art. 358); Bommai (1994) allows judicial review.
summary: The answer is (b). Under Article 356 (President's Rule), the President can declare that the powers of the State Legislature are exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament. The Assembly is not automatically dissolved, and Article 19 is not suspended.

subject: Polity
detail: This question tests the geographical indication (GI) and craft-heritage map of India, a favourite UPSC theme. Puthukkuli is the traditional embroidered shawl of the Toda pastoral community of the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu. It has red and black thread work on white cloth, and it has a GI tag. Sujni (Sujini) embroidery is a quilted, running-stitch craft from Bhusura village in Muzaffarpur district, Bihar. It was traditionally used to make quilts from old cloth, and it also has a GI tag. Uppada Jamdani is a lightweight handloom silk sari from Uppada in East Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh. It uses the Jamdani technique of discontinuous supplementary weft, and it received a GI tag in 2009. To eliminate options, spot that pair 2 (Maharashtra) is wrong because Sujni is Bihar's craft. That removes (b) and (d). Pair 3 (Karnataka) is wrong because Uppada is in Andhra Pradesh. That removes (c). Only pair 1 survives, so (a) is correct. For revision, link each craft to its state and GI status, and watch for traps where a craft is attributed to a neighbouring state.
explanations: Correct. Only pair 1 is right: Puthukkuli is from Tamil Nadu, while pairs 2 and 3 are mismatched.
Wrong. Pair 2 is incorrect because Sujni is from Bihar, not Maharashtra, so '1 and 2' cannot hold.
Wrong. Pair 3 is incorrect because Uppada Jamdani is from Andhra Pradesh, not Karnataka, and pair 1 is also correct, so '3 only' fails.
Wrong. Both pairs 2 and 3 are incorrect, so '2 and 3' is false.
