In the temperate zone, westerlies make the eastern sections of oceans warmer than the western sections. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: Ocean surface temperature patterns follow the planetary wind system and the gyres it drives. In the tropics (roughly 0-30 degrees), the north-east and south-east trade winds blow from east to west. They drive the North and South Equatorial Currents westward, and warm water accumulates on the western margins of the ocean basins. Examples are the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio origins, the Brazil Current and the East Australian Current. The thermocline is deeper in the west. On the eastern sides, Ekman transport moves surface water away from the coast and cold water upwells, as with the Peru (Humboldt), Canary, California and Benguela currents. In the temperate zone (30-60 degrees), the westerlies blow from west to east. They carry warm currents such as the North Atlantic Drift and the Alaska Current to the eastern sides of oceans, which warms north-west Europe and British Columbia. Western margins at these latitudes carry cold currents such as the Labrador and Oyashio. Elimination logic: statement 1 is the standard trade-wind effect, and statement 2 is the standard westerly effect. Both are textbook statements, so (c) is correct. This also explains the El Nino and La Nina contrast, where the Pacific warm pool normally sits in the west.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it rejects statement 2, but statement 2 is correct because westerlies carry warm water to the eastern sides of temperate oceans.
(b) Wrong: it rejects statement 1, but trade winds do pile warm water on the western sides of tropical oceans.
(c) Correct: both statements describe the wind-driven pattern of ocean temperatures, trades in the tropics and westerlies in the temperate zone.
(d) Wrong: both statements are correct, so neither can be rejected.
keyfact: Tropics (trade winds): west warmer. Temperate zone (westerlies): east warmer. Warm boundary currents are narrow and fast in the west, and cold ones are broad and slow in the east.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be right only if the tropical statement held and the temperate one failed. The tropical statement describes the western intensification of warm water, as in the Pacific warm pool (above 28 degrees C). It drives Walker circulation and the ENSO cycle. Western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) are narrow, deep, fast and warm. Eastern boundary currents are broad, shallow, slow and cold. This option is wrong only because it leaves out the temperate pattern.

Option (b), '2 only', would be right only if the westerly statement held and the tropical one failed. The temperate pattern gives warmer eastern margins. The North Atlantic Drift keeps north-west Europe about 10-15 degrees C warmer than other places at the same latitude. Warm water arrives with the westerlies and the Gulf Stream extension. Cold western boundary currents include the Labrador and Oyashio, which meet warm currents to form fog and rich fishing grounds (Grand Banks, off Newfoundland). This option is wrong because it denies the tropical pattern.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official answer. It captures the full wind-driven asymmetry of ocean basins. Planetary winds (trades and westerlies), the Coriolis effect and continental barriers produce the subtropical gyres. These circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern. Warm water is thrown to the west in the tropics and to the east in mid-latitudes, while cold water lies on the opposite sides in each case. It is a standard NCERT geography result.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean that winds do not shape ocean temperature asymmetry. That is false, since surface currents are driven mainly by prevailing winds, with temperature and salinity density differences driving deep circulation (thermohaline). Other factors are the Coriolis force, the shape of the coastline and bottom relief. Wind-driven currents occupy the upper few hundred metres. Thermohaline circulation, the 'global conveyor belt', moves deep water over centuries. This option is wrong because both statements are correct.
related: The Sargasso Sea lies in the middle of the North Atlantic gyre and has no land boundary.
The Peru (Humboldt) Current is a cold eastern boundary current linked with upwelling and anchovy fisheries.
The Gulf Stream, Kuroshio and Agulhas are warm western boundary currents.
The Labrador (cold) and Gulf Stream (warm) meet near Newfoundland, forming fog and the Grand Banks fishing grounds.
The Antarctic Circumpolar (West Wind Drift) is the only current that completely encircles the Earth.
The Somali Current reverses direction with the monsoon and is the fastest ocean current in the Indian Ocean.
El Nino weakens the trade winds and warms the eastern Pacific.
The Canary, Benguela and California currents are cold eastern boundary currents.
statements: 1 — Correct: Trade winds push warm surface water westward, so the western tropical ocean is warmer than the eastern. Facts: the trade winds blow from the subtropical highs (about 30 degrees) toward the equatorial low, deflected by the Coriolis force into north-east (Northern Hemisphere) and south-east (Southern Hemisphere) winds. They drive the equatorial currents westward, which build up the Pacific warm pool near Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. Sea level there is higher and the thermocline deeper. Warm currents formed include the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil and East Australian. Eastern margins have cold upwelling currents (Peru, Canary, Benguela, California). When trade winds weaken, El Nino results.

2 — Correct: In the temperate zone, the westerlies drive warm currents eastward and poleward, so eastern sections are warmer than western ones. Facts: the westerlies blow from the subtropical highs toward the sub-polar lows between 30 and 60 degrees latitude and are strongest in the Southern Hemisphere (Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties). They carry the North Atlantic Drift and North Pacific Current to the west coasts of Europe and North America. As a result Norway's ports stay ice-free, and western Europe has a mild maritime climate. Western margins at these latitudes are chilled by the cold Labrador and Oyashio currents.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. In the tropics, trade winds blow from east to west and pile warm surface water against the western sides of oceans. In the temperate zone, westerlies push warm water to the eastern sides of oceans.
topic_notes: Ocean currents are large-scale movements of surface water. They are driven by planetary winds, the Coriolis force, the distribution of landmasses, and density differences caused by temperature and salinity. Winds produce the large subtropical gyres, which turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern. Within a gyre, the equatorial currents flow westward under the trade winds, the western boundary current carries warm water poleward, the westerly drift carries it eastward, and the eastern boundary current returns cold water toward the equator. Western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, East Australian, Agulhas) are narrow, fast and warm. Eastern boundary currents (Canary, California, Peru or Humboldt, Benguela, West Australian) are broad, slow and cold, and they are associated with upwelling and rich fisheries and with coastal deserts (Atacama, Namib, Sahara coast). In the Indian Ocean the monsoon reverses the currents seasonally: the north-east monsoon drift flows in winter and the south-west monsoon drift in summer. The Somali Current is the strongest. Equatorial counter-currents flow eastward in the doldrums belt. El Nino occurs when the trade winds weaken, the warm pool shifts east, and Peru's upwelling is suppressed. La Nina is the opposite. The Indian Ocean Dipole is a similar east-west SST asymmetry. Currents also affect climate: warm currents raise temperature and rainfall on the coasts they touch, while cold currents lower temperature and cause fog where they meet warm ones. Other possible angles are the Sargasso Sea at the centre of the North Atlantic gyre, the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (the only current encircling the globe), and thermohaline circulation.

question:
In the context of India’s preparation for Climate-Smart Agriculture, consider the following statements :
1. The ‘Climate-Smart Village’ approach in India is a part of a project led by the Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS), an international research programme.
2. The project of CCAFS is carried out under Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR) headquartered in France.
3. The International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) in India is one of the CGIAR’s research centres. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: CCAFS (Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security) was a global research programme launched in 2010 by CGIAR and Future Earth. It aimed to tackle climate change and food security together. Its flagship Climate-Smart Village (CSV) model tests and scales up climate-smart agricultural practices, technologies, services and local institutions in selected villages. In India the CSVs were developed in states such as Bihar, Punjab and Haryana, and Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, with partners including ICAR, state agricultural universities and ICRISAT. CGIAR (Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research), set up in 1971, is a global partnership of agricultural research centres, with its System Organization headquartered in Montpellier, France. Its centres include ICRISAT (Patancheru, Hyderabad, India), IRRI (Philippines), CIMMYT (Mexico), IFPRI (Washington DC), CIFOR and ICRAF. Elimination logic: each option omits at least one true statement. Since statements 1, 2 and 3 are each factually correct, only (d) survives. Students should remember that CGIAR has its headquarters in France and that ICRISAT is the only CGIAR centre headquartered in India, a point UPSC frequently tests.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement 3, which is correct: ICRISAT is a CGIAR centre.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement 1, which is correct: the CSV approach is a CCAFS-led initiative.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, which is correct: CCAFS is carried out under CGIAR, headquartered in France.
(d) is correct because all three statements are factually accurate.
keyfact: CCAFS's Climate-Smart Villages sit under CGIAR (HQ Montpellier, France), whose centres include ICRISAT, Hyderabad.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Climate-Smart Village approach is a flagship of the CCAFS programme and has been implemented in India.
2 — Correct: CCAFS ran under CGIAR, whose headquarters is in Montpellier, France.
3 — Correct: ICRISAT, based in Patancheru, Hyderabad, is one of CGIAR's research centres.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. The Climate-Smart Village approach in India is part of the CCAFS programme, CCAFS operates under CGIAR (headquartered in Montpellier, France), and ICRISAT, Hyderabad, is one of CGIAR's research centres.

question: “Leaf litter decomposes faster than in any other biome and as a result the soil surface is often almost bare. Apart from trees, the vegetation is largely composed of plant forms that reach up into the canopy vicariously, by climbing the trees or growing as epiphytes, rooted on the upper branches of trees.” This is the most likely description of
subject: Environment
detail: Tropical rain forests lie roughly between 10°N and 10°S of the equator (Amazon, Congo basin, Southeast Asia, parts of the Western Ghats and Northeast India). They have high temperatures (about 25-27°C year-round), heavy rainfall (over 200 cm, evenly spread) and high humidity. These conditions favour rapid activity by bacteria, fungi and termites, so litter decomposes within weeks and nutrients are recycled almost immediately into living biomass. The soil is therefore nutrient-poor (laterite/oxisol), leached and often bare of litter. Dense, multilayered canopies (emergent, canopy, understorey, shrub and ground layers) cut off sunlight to the floor, so little ground vegetation grows. Plants compete for light by climbing (lianas, rattans) or by growing as epiphytes (orchids, bromeliads, ferns) on upper branches. Elimination: coniferous forests (taiga) are cold, with slow decomposition and thick needle litter and acidic podzol soils. Dry deciduous forests shed leaves in the dry season and have slower, seasonal decomposition with a visible litter layer. Mangroves are coastal halophytic forests with waterlogged saline soil and pneumatophores, not climbers and epiphytes as the dominant forms.
explanations: Wrong: coniferous (boreal/taiga) forests are cold, so decomposition is the slowest of the major forests, needle litter accumulates thickly, and epiphytes and lianas are rare.

Wrong: dry deciduous forests have a marked dry season, leaf fall and slower seasonal decomposition, so litter accumulates on the floor. Lianas and epiphytes are far less prominent than in rain forests.

Wrong: mangroves grow in tidal, saline, waterlogged soils and are characterised by stilt roots and pneumatophores. Their litter is exported or broken down by tides and crabs, and climbers and epiphytes are not the main vegetation.
Correct: the tropical rain forest has the fastest litter decomposition, bare soil because nutrients are rapidly recycled, and abundant lianas and epiphytes that reach the canopy for light.
keyfact: Tropical rain forest: fastest litter decomposition, nutrients locked in biomass, bare soil, lianas and epiphytes reaching the canopy.
option_notes: Coniferous forest (taiga or boreal forest) occurs in high northern latitudes (Siberia, Canada, Scandinavia) and in Himalayan highlands. Dominant trees are pine, spruce, fir and larch, with needle leaves and conical shapes that shed snow. Soils are acidic podzols, litter decomposes slowly, and species diversity is low. It is the largest terrestrial biome and a major carbon store. Timber and softwood for pulp and paper come from it.

Dry deciduous forest occurs in areas with about 70-100 cm rainfall, covering much of peninsular India, such as Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Trees such as teak, sal (in part), tendu, mahua and palas shed leaves in the dry season to conserve water. The canopy is open, so undergrowth is dense, grass is common and litter is seasonal. It is the most widespread forest type in India.

Mangrove forests are salt-tolerant (halophytic) forests of tropical and subtropical tidal coasts and deltas. They are found in the Sundarbans (the largest mangrove area in the world), Bhitarkanika, Godavari-Krishna deltas and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Features include pneumatophores (breathing roots), prop or stilt roots and viviparous germination. They protect coasts against cyclones and erosion, and are breeding grounds for fish. Species include Rhizophora, Avicennia and Heritiera fomes.

Tropical rain forest (tropical wet evergreen forest) has year-round warmth and rainfall above about 200 cm. It has the highest terrestrial biodiversity and a layered structure with emergent trees reaching 40-60 m. Lianas, epiphytes (orchids, ferns), buttress roots and drip-tip leaves are typical. Nutrients are held in the biomass rather than in the soil. Major examples are the Amazon, Congo and Indo-Malayan forests, and in India the Western Ghats, Assam and the Andamans.
related: Epiphytes (orchids, bromeliads) use host trees only for support, while parasites (e.g. Cuscuta) draw nutrients from the host.
Amazon basin holds the world's largest tropical rain forest.
Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Taiga (boreal forest) is the largest terrestrial biome, dominated by conifers.
In India, tropical wet evergreen forests occur in the Western Ghats, Northeast and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Tropical rain forests have most of their nutrients in the biomass, not the soil.
Sal and teak are characteristic trees of moist and dry deciduous forests respectively.
Buttress roots and drip-tip leaves are adaptations of rain forest trees.
summary: The answer is (d) tropical rain forest. Only the tropical rain forest combines the fastest leaf-litter decomposition of any biome, a nearly bare soil surface, and vegetation dominated by lianas (climbers) and epiphytes that reach the canopy.
topic_notes: Forest biomes are distinguished by climate, soil, decomposition rate and vegetation structure. Tropical rain forests (equatorial; temperature 20-28°C, rain over 200 cm) cover only about 6-7% of land but hold over half of all species. Their features: evergreen broadleaf trees with no distinct leaf-fall season, multiple strata, buttress roots, cauliflory, drip-tip leaves, lianas and epiphytes. Because of rapid decomposition and heavy leaching, soils are poor (oxisols/laterites), and clearing the forest leads to quick fertility loss, so shifting cultivation (jhum) leaves fallow periods. Other tropical types: moist deciduous (100-200 cm rain; sal, teak), dry deciduous (70-100 cm), thorn and scrub (below 70 cm; acacia, babul), and montane forests. Temperate forests include temperate deciduous (oak, beech, maple) and Mediterranean scrub. Boreal coniferous forest has the slowest decomposition and carbon-rich peaty soils. Mangroves and swamp forests are edaphic (soil-determined) formations. In India, forest cover is about 21.7% of the area (ISFR 2021), with Madhya Pradesh having the largest forest area and Mizoram the highest percentage. Tropical wet evergreen forests are in the Western Ghats, Northeast and Andaman and Nicobar Islands. UPSC often asks about the characteristics of biomes, stratification, epiphytes versus parasites versus lianas, nutrient cycling, and the distribution of mangroves, so compare biomes systematically on rainfall, temperature, soil and dominant species.

ocr: The vegetation of savannah consists of grassland with scattered small trees, but extensive areas have no trees. The forest development in such areas is generally kept in check by one or more or a combination of some conditions. Which of the following are such conditions? dl ame Nes Burrowing animals and termites Fire Grazing herbivores Seasonal rainfall Soil properties Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 4 and 5 (c) 2, 3 and 4 (@j24%.3 and’5
subject: Environment
detail: Savannas are tropical grasslands with scattered trees, found in Africa (East Africa, Serengeti), Brazil (Campos and Cerrado), Venezuela (Llanos), and northern Australia. They occur in warm climates with distinct wet and dry seasons, with rainfall of roughly 500-1500 mm concentrated in a few months. The long dry season produces water stress that favours grasses over closed-canopy forest. Three factors are generally taken to keep trees in check. First, seasonal rainfall: the prolonged drought limits tree establishment and growth. Second, fire: dry grass burns every year, killing tree seedlings and saplings while grasses regenerate from underground parts. Third, grazing and browsing herbivores (elephants, zebra, wildebeest, antelope) eat or damage young trees and suppress woody growth. Elimination logic: statement 1 (burrowing animals and termites) and statement 5 (soil properties) are not standard primary controls in this context. Option (a) includes 1, (b) includes 5, and (d) includes both 1 and 5. Only (c) contains 2, 3 and 4 and avoids both 1 and 5, so it is correct. Edaphic factors can influence savanna in some places, but the textbook explanation stresses climate, fire and herbivory.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2: Wrong because it includes burrowing animals and termites, which is not a standard control, and omits grazing herbivores and seasonal rainfall.
(b) 4 and 5: Wrong because although seasonal rainfall is valid, soil properties is not the standard factor, and it omits fire and grazing.
(c) 2, 3 and 4: Correct. Fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal rainfall together keep tree growth in check and sustain the grass-dominated savanna.
(d) 1, 3 and 5: Wrong because it includes burrowing animals/termites and soil properties, and omits fire and seasonal rainfall.
keyfact: Savanna trees are held back by fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal (dry-season) rainfall: answer 2, 3 and 4.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs burrowing animals/termites with fire. Termites are social insects that build mounds in tropical savannas and act as ecosystem engineers: they recycle dead plant matter, aerate soil and concentrate nutrients. Fire is a recurrent dry-season disturbance in savannas, set by lightning or humans, that kills woody seedlings and favours grasses. Fire is a key factor, but termites and burrowers are only local modifiers of soil, so the pairing is incomplete and wrong.

Option (b) pairs seasonal rainfall with soil properties. Seasonal rainfall defines savanna climate (Aw in Koppen), with a wet summer and dry winter and about 500-1500 mm annually. Soil properties such as laterite, nutrient-poor, shallow or waterlogged soils influence vegetation locally, giving 'edaphic savannas'. Soil is an influence in some places but is not the general explanation for the absence of forest, and fire and grazing are missing here.

Option (c) combines fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal rainfall, the three classic controls on savanna. Savannas are tropical grasslands of Africa, South America (Llanos, Campos/Cerrado) and Australia, with scattered trees such as acacia, baobab and eucalyptus. They support great herbivore diversity and predators such as lions. Climate, fire and herbivory maintain the open structure. This is the UPSC-official correct answer.

Option (d) combines burrowing animals/termites, grazing herbivores and soil properties. Grazing herbivores are a valid control, as they graze and browse tree seedlings. Burrowers and termites change soil structure and nutrients, and soil type affects plant growth locally. But the combination omits fire and seasonal rainfall, the two major climatic and disturbance factors, and includes two non-standard factors, so it is incorrect.
related: Savanna climate is Koppen Aw: tropical wet and dry.
Cerrado in Brazil is the world's most biodiverse savanna.
Serengeti in Tanzania hosts the Great Wildebeest Migration.
Llanos are the savannas of the Orinoco basin in Venezuela and Colombia.
Veld in South Africa and Pampas in Argentina are temperate grasslands, not tropical savannas.
Savanna is often called a fire climax or disclimax community.
Acacia and baobab are typical savanna trees; elephant grass is typical grass.
Prairies are temperate grasslands of North America; steppes are in Eurasia.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Burrowing animals and termites are not generally cited as the key factors checking forest development in savannas. Termites and burrowers (aardvark, rodents) do modify soil and create termite mounds, which can even host trees, so their effect is local rather than a primary control. Termite mounds in African savannas create nutrient-rich patches where woody plants cluster. They are important ecosystem engineers affecting soil aeration, nutrient cycling and water infiltration, but they do not systematically suppress forest development across extensive savanna areas.

2 — Correct: Fire is a major check on tree growth. Frequent natural or human-set fires in the dry season burn dry grass and kill tree seedlings and saplings, while grasses regrow from protected underground tissues. Fire-adapted trees (such as acacia and baobab) have thick bark or resprouting ability. Fire maintains savanna as a 'fire climax' or disclimax ecosystem. In Africa and Australia, pastoralists and indigenous peoples have long used burning to manage grassland. Fire suppression often leads to woody encroachment and thicker tree cover.

3 — Correct: Grazing and browsing herbivores keep forest development in check by eating seedlings, grazing, trampling and damaging trees. African savannas hold large herds of wildebeest, zebra, giraffe, antelope and elephants. Elephants uproot and break trees, opening woodland into grassland. Browsers feed on shrubs and tree foliage. Together with fire, herbivory maintains the grass-dominated structure. Removal of herbivores through overhunting or replacement by livestock can change tree-grass balance, often leading to bush encroachment.

4 — Correct: Seasonal rainfall is a basic climatic control. Savannas receive rain in one distinct wet season followed by a long dry spell of several months. This seasonality limits deep-rooted trees from forming a closed canopy, while shallow-rooted grasses exploit the wet season quickly. Annual rainfall is usually 500-1500 mm, less than in rainforests, and the drought stress also makes grass dry and flammable, which increases fire. The Koppen Aw climate type represents tropical savanna climate.

5 — Incorrect: Soil properties are not usually cited as the general factor limiting forest development in savannas, though soil does matter locally. Nutrient-poor, shallow, or poorly drained soils (such as laterites, or waterlogged clays) can limit trees in some savannas and influence the distribution of woody cover, which is called edaphic savanna. But the standard explanation in textbooks stresses climate, fire and herbivory. Savanna occurs on diverse soils, so soil is not a universal limiting factor.
summary: The answer is (c) 2, 3 and 4. In savannas, fire, grazing herbivores and seasonal rainfall (a long dry season) check forest development and keep the vegetation as grassland with scattered trees. Burrowing animals/termites and soil properties are not the standard limiting factors in this context.
topic_notes: Savanna is the tropical grassland biome lying between tropical rainforests and hot deserts, roughly 5-20 degrees on both sides of the equator. Climate is Koppen Aw: warm throughout the year (above 18 C), with a wet summer and a long dry winter. Rainfall is about 500-1500 mm. Vegetation is tall grasses (elephant grass up to 3-5 m) with scattered flat-topped trees such as acacia, baobab, and eucalyptus in Australia. Regional names: Llanos (Orinoco basin, Venezuela and Colombia), Campos (Brazil highlands), Cerrado (Brazil, the largest savanna in South America), Pantanal wetland nearby, Sudan savanna and Serengeti (Africa), Downs (Australia), and Veld in southern Africa (temperate grassland, not savanna). Savannas hold the most diverse large mammal fauna, including elephants, giraffes, zebra, wildebeest, rhinos, lions, cheetahs and hyenas. Controls on structure: climate (seasonal drought), fire, herbivory, and to some extent soil (edaphic factors). Fire-adapted plants have thick bark, underground storage organs, and resprouting. The tree-grass balance is a classic ecology topic: savanna is considered a disclimax or fire climax community where human or natural disturbance maintains it. Other grasslands: Prairies (North America, temperate), Pampas (Argentina), Steppes (Eurasia), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia), Canterbury (New Zealand). Indian savanna-like regions include dry deciduous scrub and the Terai grasslands, though India's tropical savanna is mostly secondary and caused by human activity. Threats include overgrazing, agricultural conversion, climate change, woody encroachment and poaching. UPSC may also ask about Cerrado, African savanna national parks (Serengeti, Kruger, Masai Mara), and wildlife migrations such as the Great Wildebeest Migration.

question:
With reference to the water on the planet Earth, consider the following statements :
1. The amount of water in the rivers and lakes is more than the amount of groundwater.
2. The amount of water in polar ice caps and glaciers is more than the amount of groundwater. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Geography
detail: Earth's water is about 97% saline (oceans) and about 2.5-3% fresh. Of the freshwater, roughly 68.7% is locked in glaciers, ice caps and permanent snow, about 30.1% is groundwater, and under 1% is surface water and other freshwater. Within the surface and other freshwater share, permafrost and ground ice are about 69%, lakes about 20% and soil moisture about 3%. Atmospheric water vapour is about 3%, rivers about 0.49% and living organisms (biota) about 0.26%. Lakes and rivers together are only about 0.3% of freshwater (USGS figures), around 0.007% of all water. Groundwater is therefore much larger than rivers and lakes, which makes Statement 1 wrong. Ice is larger than groundwater, which makes Statement 2 correct. The elimination logic is simple. Once you know that surface water is a very small reservoir, Statement 1 fails, which removes (a) and (c). Then only the ice-versus-groundwater comparison decides between (b) and (d). Glaciers and ice caps are the largest freshwater store, so (b) is correct. Antarctica alone holds about 90% of the world's ice.
explanations: Wrong. It says only Statement 1 is correct, but Statement 1 is false because groundwater far exceeds river and lake water.
Correct. Only Statement 2 is true: ice caps and glaciers (about 68.7% of freshwater) exceed groundwater (about 30%), while rivers and lakes are a very small share.
Wrong. Statement 1 is false, so 'both' cannot be right even though Statement 2 is true.
Wrong. Statement 2 is true, so 'neither' fails.
keyfact: Freshwater ranking: glaciers and ice caps (about 69%) > groundwater (about 30%) > surface water (under 1%), with rivers the smallest store.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only would be true only if surface water exceeded groundwater, which it does not. Rivers and lakes are about 0.3% of freshwater. Most accessible freshwater for humans is surface water, but the total volume stored is far smaller than groundwater. Surface water is renewed quickly, which is why it is the most used source despite being a small stock.

Option (b) 2 only is the correct answer. It matches the global freshwater distribution, in which ice is the largest reservoir at about 68.7%, followed by groundwater at about 30%. Ice is mostly inaccessible to humans, which is why groundwater is the biggest accessible store of freshwater. This ordering is a standard fact in USGS and NCERT geography.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong because Statement 1 fails. The true order of freshwater stores is ice and glaciers, then groundwater, then ground ice and permafrost, lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere, rivers and biota. Rivers are among the smallest stores, below even the atmosphere.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because Statement 2 is correct. It would hold only if groundwater were larger than ice, which is false. Note that if saline groundwater is included, groundwater is about 23.4 million km³, still less than the ice volume of about 24 million km³.
related: About 97% of Earth's water is saline ocean water; freshwater is about 2.5-3%.
About 68.7% of freshwater is in glaciers and ice caps; about 30% is groundwater.
Antarctica holds about 90% of the world's ice; Greenland about 8-10%.
Lake Baikal holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater and is the deepest lake.
Rivers hold only about 0.006% of freshwater by stock, though they are the main source of human use.
Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019) is a Central scheme for community-led groundwater management in water-stressed states.
World Water Day is 22 March; World Wetlands Day is 2 February.
India is the world's largest groundwater user.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Rivers and lakes hold far less water than groundwater. Surface freshwater in lakes and rivers is only about 0.3% of freshwater, while groundwater is about 30%. Freshwater lakes hold roughly 91,000 km³, and rivers only about 2,000 km³. Groundwater is estimated at about 10 million km³ or more, including deep and saline aquifers. Major lake reservoirs include the Great Lakes, Baikal (about 20% of surface freshwater) and Tanganyika. Rivers hold a small standing stock but have a very fast turnover of about 2-6 months. Groundwater turnover ranges from decades to thousands of years. India is the largest user of groundwater in the world, drawing about 25% of the global total.

2 — Correct: Glaciers and ice caps hold about 68.7% of freshwater against about 30.1% for groundwater. Ice sheets cover Antarctica (about 90% of the ice) and Greenland (about 8-10%). If Antarctica melted fully, sea level would rise by about 58 m. Greenland's ice would raise it by about 7 m. Himalayan glaciers such as Siachen and Gangotri feed the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra basins, and the region is called the 'Third Pole'. Ice stores are shrinking due to global warming, a topic covered by IPCC reports and by the UNEP and WMO.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Ice caps and glaciers hold about 68-69% of Earth's freshwater, far more than groundwater (about 30%), while rivers and lakes hold only a tiny fraction, much less than groundwater.
topic_notes: Distribution of Earth's water: total water is about 1.386 billion km³. Oceans hold about 96.5%, and saline groundwater and saline lakes make up most of the rest. Freshwater is about 2.5-3.5% of the total, roughly 35 million km³. Within freshwater: glaciers and ice caps about 68.7%, groundwater about 30.1% (fresh groundwater about 30%), surface water and other freshwater about 1.2%. Within that 1.2%: ground ice and permafrost about 69%, lakes about 20-21%, soil moisture about 3%, atmospheric vapour about 3%, wetlands about 2.5-3%, rivers about 0.5% and biota about 0.26%. Only about 0.3% of freshwater is in easily accessible lakes, rivers and swamps. Hydrological cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration. Residence times: atmosphere about 9 days, rivers about 2 weeks to months, lakes years to decades, groundwater from days to thousands of years, glaciers up to tens of thousands of years, oceans about 3,000 years. India's context: about 4% of world freshwater and about 18% of world population. Groundwater is a major irrigation source, and the Central Ground Water Board assesses it. Related schemes are Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019), Jal Shakti Abhiyan and Jal Jeevan Mission (2019). Related international topics are World Water Day (22 March), Ramsar Convention on wetlands (1971), and the cryosphere and sea-level rise.

ocr: Consider the following statements : hy, Moringa (drumstick tree) is a leguminous evergreen tree. Tamarind tree is endemic to South Asia. In India, most of the tamarind is collected as minor forest produce. India exports tamarind and seeds of moringa. Seeds of moringa and tamarind can be used in the production of biofuels. Which of the statements given above are correct? 1, 2, 4 and 5 (a) 3, 4 and 5 (b) 1, 3 and 4 (c) 1, 2, 3 and 5 (a)
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests tropical tree crops that matter for minor forest produce (MFP), trade and bioenergy. Moringa oleifera (drumstick) is native to the sub-Himalayan tracts of north India. It is a fast-growing, drought-resistant tree that is deciduous, and the 'evergreen' claim is the trap. It is a member of the family Moringaceae, not a legume, so 'leguminous' is also wrong. Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is a legume (Fabaceae) native to tropical Africa (Sudan). It was introduced to India in antiquity and is naturalised, so 'endemic to South Asia' is wrong. Endemic means found only in one region. In India most tamarind is collected from forests and village trees, so it is traded as MFP, with Chhattisgarh (Bastar) a major source. India exports tamarind products and moringa seeds, pods and powder. The seed oil of moringa (and tamarind seed kernel) has been studied for biodiesel. Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are both false, so any option containing 1 or 2 is out. Only (b) excludes both.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statements 1 and 2, which are both incorrect: moringa is not a leguminous evergreen, and tamarind is African in origin.
(b) is correct because statements 3, 4 and 5 are true (MFP collection, exports, biofuel potential) and statements 1 and 2 are false.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 5, which is true.
(d) is wrong because it includes statements 1 and 2, which are false, and omits statement 4, which is true.
keyfact: Moringa is a non-legume (Moringaceae), non-evergreen tree; tamarind is a legume native to Africa, collected in India as MFP, with seeds of both usable for biofuel.
option_notes: Option (a) combines statements 1, 2, 4 and 5. It pairs two false claims about moringa's botany and tamarind's origin with two true claims. Moringa (Moringaceae) is not a legume, and tamarind (Fabaceae) is of African origin. Knowing that moringa is native to the sub-Himalayan tract and tamarind is a naturalised exotic lets you reject this option immediately.

Option (b) combines statements 3, 4 and 5 and is the official answer. Tamarind is collected mainly as minor forest produce and is covered by MSP for MFP through TRIFED. India exports tamarind products and moringa seeds and powder. Seeds of both species are potential biofuel feedstocks under the National Policy on Biofuels 2018.

Option (c) combines statements 1, 3 and 4. Statement 1 is false because moringa is not a legume and not a true evergreen. Statements 3 and 4 are true. It leaves out statement 5, though biofuel use of moringa and tamarind seeds is recognised. Moringa belongs to the single-genus family Moringaceae, order Brassicales.

Option (d) combines statements 1, 2, 3 and 5. It wrongly includes the moringa legume-evergreen claim and the tamarind endemism claim. It also omits statement 4 on exports. Endemic species are restricted to one region, whereas tamarind is pantropical today and is native to Africa. This option can be eliminated by spotting either false statement.
related: Moringa belongs to the family Moringaceae, not Fabaceae.
Tamarind is native to tropical Africa and is a legume in the family Fabaceae.
TRIFED is the nodal agency for marketing minor forest produce and tribal products.
The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises community ownership and collection rights over MFP.
Under PESA 1996, gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas have ownership of minor forest produce.
The National Policy on Biofuels 2018 targets 20 percent ethanol blending, now set for 2025-26.
Jatropha and pongamia are common tree-borne non-edible oilseeds used for biodiesel.
APEDA under the Ministry of Commerce promotes exports of agricultural and processed foods.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Moringa is not a leguminous evergreen. It belongs to Moringaceae, not Fabaceae, and is typically deciduous or semi-evergreen. Moringa oleifera is native to the sub-Himalayan region of north-west India. It is called the drumstick tree for its long pods and the horseradish tree for its roots. Leaves, pods and flowers are eaten and are rich in vitamins A and C, calcium and protein. Seeds yield 'ben oil' and are used for water purification. It tolerates drought and poor soils and is widely grown in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. India is the largest producer of moringa.

2 — Incorrect: Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is native to tropical Africa, especially Sudan, and was introduced to India long ago, so it is naturalised and not endemic to South Asia. It is a legume in the family Fabaceae (subfamily Caesalpinioideae). The name comes from Arabic 'tamar hindi', meaning date of India. The pulp is used in cooking, chutneys, sambar and medicine. The seed kernel powder (TKP) is used as a sizing agent in textiles and jute. Major producing states are Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.

3 — Correct: In India most tamarind is collected as minor forest produce (non-timber forest produce), particularly by tribal communities. Chhattisgarh (Bastar), Odisha, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh are important collection areas. Tamarind is among the items covered by the Minimum Support Price for Minor Forest Produce scheme, run by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs since 2013 and expanded in 2018-19. The Forest Rights Act 2006 gives forest-dwelling communities ownership and collection rights over MFP. TRIFED is the nodal agency for marketing MFP. Tamarind is also grown in homesteads and orchards.

4 — Correct: India exports tamarind and moringa seeds and products. Tamarind exports include pulp, concentrate, paste and tamarind kernel powder. Moringa exports include seeds, powder, pods, capsules and oil to the USA, UAE, Europe and others. APEDA, under the Ministry of Commerce, promotes agricultural and processed food exports and includes moringa among its focus products. India is also among the largest tamarind producers and consumers. Domestic consumption is large, so exports form only a share of output.

5 — Correct: Seeds of both moringa and tamarind can be used for biofuel. Moringa seeds contain around 30-40 percent oil that can be turned into biodiesel with good cetane value and oxidative stability. Tamarind seed oil and kernel have also been studied as feedstocks, and tamarind seed is a possible source of bioethanol. India's National Policy on Biofuels (2018) promotes non-edible oilseeds such as jatropha, pongamia (karanj) and other tree-borne oilseeds. It aims at 20 percent ethanol blending by 2030, advanced to 2025-26.
summary: The official answer is (b) 3, 4 and 5. Statement 1 is wrong because moringa is a deciduous (or semi-evergreen) tree, not a true evergreen. Statement 2 is wrong because tamarind is native to tropical Africa, not South Asia, so it is not endemic here.
topic_notes:
Moringa oleifera is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant tree of the family Moringaceae (order Brassicales). It is native to the sub-Himalayan region of India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bangladesh. It is often called a 'miracle tree' because its leaves, pods and seeds are nutritious. It is deciduous or semi-evergreen. Seeds yield ben oil, and the seed cake can purify water through coagulation. India is the largest producer, with Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala leading.

Tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is a Fabaceae tree native to tropical Africa. It spread to South Asia early and is now widely naturalised. It is a long-lived, hardy tree grown in dry regions. Uses include food, beverages, medicine and wood. The seed kernel powder serves as a sizing material in textiles.

Minor forest produce (non-timber forest produce) includes items such as tendu leaves, bamboo, mahua, lac, gums, resins, honey and tamarind. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises community rights to own, collect and sell MFP. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs runs the MSP for MFP scheme, with TRIFED as nodal agency. Van Dhan Vikas Kendras support value addition. The PESA Act 1996 gives gram sabhas ownership of MFP in Scheduled Areas. In 2021 the Government added more items to the MFP MSP list.

Biofuels: the National Policy on Biofuels 2018 classifies fuels as first generation (from sugar, starch and edible oils) and advanced ones, with non-edible oilseeds as feedstocks. India's target is 20 percent ethanol blending by 2025-26. The Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana supports 2G ethanol. Tree-borne oilseeds include jatropha, pongamia, neem and mahua.

Other angles UPSC could ask are the definition of endemism, the families of common crops, GI tags for tamarind or moringa products, APEDA's role in exports, and the distinction between native and naturalised species.

question: The black cotton soil of India has been formed due to the weathering of
subject: Geography
detail: Black cotton soil, also called regur or black soil, is a residual soil derived from the weathering of basalt, the lava of the Deccan Trap fissure eruptions in the Cretaceous-Eocene period (about 66 million years ago). It covers Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, parts of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu, and is concentrated on the Deccan Plateau and the Malwa plateau. Its colour is attributed to titaniferous magnetite and iron, not to humus. It is rich in calcium, magnesium, iron and lime, but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter. Its high clay content (montmorillonite) gives high water retention, swelling when wet and forming deep cracks when dry, which gives a self-ploughing character. It is ideal for cotton, and also suits soybean, sugarcane, jowar, wheat and citrus. Elimination: granite and schist are acidic metamorphic or igneous rocks, and give red and yellow soils. Shale and limestone are sedimentary and give other soils. Brown forest soil is itself a soil, not a parent rock. Only fissure volcanic rock (basalt) fits.
explanations: Incorrect: brown forest soil is a soil type of temperate, humid regions (for example, parts of the Himalaya), not a parent rock, and black soil does not form from it.
Correct: black soil forms from the weathering of basaltic lava from fissure eruptions, i.e. the Deccan Traps.
Incorrect: granite and schist are crystalline and metamorphic rocks whose weathering mainly gives red and yellow soils, as in the Peninsular plateau's eastern and southern parts.
Incorrect: shale and limestone are sedimentary rocks; their weathering gives other soils, such as calcareous or clayey soils, but not regur.
keyfact: Black cotton soil (regur) = weathered basalt from the Deccan Trap fissure eruptions; clayey, moisture-retentive, ideal for cotton.
option_notes: Brown forest soil forms under deciduous and temperate forests with moderate rainfall. It is relatively rich in humus, is slightly acidic to neutral, and is found in hill and mountain regions such as the Himalayan slopes. It is a soil class, not a rock, so it cannot be a parent material in this question.

Fissure volcanic rock means basalt from lava that flowed through long cracks in the crust rather than from a central vent. In India the major example is the Deccan Traps, which cover about 5 lakh sq km of the Deccan Plateau. Their weathering gives regur, the black cotton soil, which is clayey, moisture-retentive and good for cotton.

Granite and schist are igneous and metamorphic rocks of the ancient Peninsular shield. Their weathering gives red soils, which are coloured by iron oxide, are sandy to loamy, and are poor in nitrogen, lime and humus. They occur in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Odisha, Chhota Nagpur and the Eastern Ghats.

Shale and limestone are sedimentary rocks. Shale is a fine-grained clay rock, and limestone is rich in calcium carbonate. Their weathering gives calcareous and clayey soils and karst landscapes, as in the Vindhyan and Cuddapah basins, but not the characteristic black basaltic soil.
related: Black soil is also called regur and is a residual soil.
Its colour is due to titaniferous magnetite and iron compounds.
Deccan Traps are fissure eruptions of the late Cretaceous (about 66 million years ago).
Black soil is best for cotton; it is also good for soybean, sugarcane and jowar.
Red soil colour comes from iron oxide on crystalline rocks.
Laterite soil forms by leaching and suits tea, coffee and cashew.
Alluvial soil covers the largest area in India.
Black soil is self-ploughing because of cracks formed in the dry season.
summary: The answer is (b) fissure volcanic rock. Black cotton soil (regur) forms from weathering of basaltic lava that welled out through fissure eruptions, chiefly the Deccan Traps. Its dark colour and clay-rich, moisture-retentive nature come from this basaltic parent material.
topic_notes: Soils of India are classified by ICAR into major groups: alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid/desert, saline, peaty/marshy and forest/mountain soils. Alluvial soil is the most widespread (about 40% of area) and the most fertile, and is found in the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains. Khadar is new alluvium, while bhangar is old alluvium. Black soil (regur) is formed from Deccan basalt and is found in Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. It is also found along river valleys such as the Godavari and Krishna. It is rich in iron, lime, calcium, magnesium and alumina, and poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter. It is highly retentive of moisture, swells when wet, and has deep cracks when dry. Red soil forms on crystalline rocks, gets its colour from iron oxide, and is deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus and humus. Laterite soil forms by leaching under heavy rainfall and alternating wet and dry conditions, and is found in the Western Ghats, Odisha and Assam. It suits tea, coffee, cashew and rubber. Desert soil is sandy and saline, with low humus. Peaty soil is found in Kerala (Kuttanad) and is rich in organic matter. Forest soils are found in the Himalayas. Key concepts to remember are parent material, residual versus transported soils, soil horizons, and soil conservation methods such as contour ploughing, terracing, shelter belts and strip cropping. Soil Health Card, launched in 2015, and World Soil Day on 5 December are also relevant.

question:
With reference to recent developments regarding ‘Recombinant Vector Vaccines’, consider the following statements :
1. Genetic engineering is applied in the development of these vaccines.
2. Bacteria and viruses are used as vectors. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Recombinant vector vaccines use a harmless, attenuated or non-replicating microbe (the vector) to carry a gene that codes for an antigen of the target pathogen into human cells. The cells then produce the antigen, which triggers an immune response, and the vector itself does not cause the disease. Building one needs recombinant DNA technology: the antigen gene is isolated, cloned and inserted into the vector genome, so statement 1 is correct. Vectors can be viruses (adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, modified vaccinia Ankara, measles virus) or bacteria (Salmonella, Listeria, BCG, Lactobacillus), so statement 2 is correct. Examples: Oxford-AstraZeneca (Covishield, ChAdOx1, chimpanzee adenovirus), Sputnik V (Ad26 and Ad5), Janssen (Ad26.COV2.S) and Ervebo for Ebola (rVSV). Elimination logic: once a student knows that 'recombinant' implies genetic engineering, options (b) and (d) are ruled out. Knowing that adenoviruses are the common vectors rules out (a), because it denies that microbes act as vectors. Do not confuse these with mRNA vaccines (no vector, a lipid nanoparticle delivers the mRNA), inactivated vaccines (Covaxin) or protein subunit vaccines (Novavax, Corbevax).
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong: statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is also correct because genetic engineering is central to making these vaccines.
(c) is correct: both statements hold. Genetic engineering is used to insert the antigen gene, and bacteria and viruses serve as vectors.
(d) is wrong: both statements are factually correct, so denying both is incorrect.
keyfact: Recombinant vector vaccines use genetic engineering to put a pathogen's antigen gene into a harmless virus or bacterium (for example Covishield's adenovirus ChAdOx1).
option_notes: Option (a), 'Statement 1 only', would mean genetic engineering is used but the vectors are neither bacteria nor viruses. In fact, recombinant vector vaccines depend on engineered microbes as carriers. Genetic engineering is the manipulation of an organism's DNA through recombinant DNA techniques such as restriction enzymes, ligases and plasmid vectors. It underpins recombinant protein vaccines (hepatitis B, HPV), vector vaccines and DNA/mRNA vaccines.

Option (b), 'Statement 2 only', would mean viruses and bacteria are vectors but genetic engineering plays no part. This is false, because the vector must be modified to carry a foreign antigen gene. Common viral vectors are adenovirus, MVA, VSV and measles virus. Bacterial vectors are Salmonella, Listeria and BCG. Vectors can be replicating or non-replicating, and are chosen for safety, immunogenicity and capacity to carry genes.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the correct answer. A recombinant vector vaccine is made by genetically engineering a harmless virus or bacterium to carry a gene of the target pathogen. The cells of the recipient then express the antigen and the immune system learns to recognise it. Examples are Covishield/Vaxzevria, Sputnik V, Janssen's Ad26.COV2.S and Ervebo (Ebola). The platform gives strong T-cell and antibody responses and is often easy to store at fridge temperatures.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would deny both the use of genetic engineering and the use of microbial vectors, contradicting the definition of 'recombinant' and 'vector' vaccines. For contrast, vaccines that use no vector include inactivated (Covaxin, polio IPV), live attenuated (MMR, BCG, OPV), protein subunit (Novavax, Corbevax), toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria) and mRNA (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, India's Gemcovac).
related: Covishield uses a chimpanzee adenovirus vector (ChAdOx1) developed by Oxford University and AstraZeneca.
Sputnik V uses two different adenoviruses, Ad26 and Ad5, for the two doses; it was developed by the Gamaleya Institute.
Covaxin is a whole-virion inactivated vaccine, not a vector vaccine.
ZyCoV-D is the world's first plasmid DNA vaccine for humans, from Zydus Cadila.
Corbevax is a recombinant protein subunit vaccine from Biological E.
mRNA vaccines need no vector; lipid nanoparticles deliver the mRNA.
Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) is a vector vaccine for Ebola.
iNCOVACC (BBV154) is India's intranasal adenoviral vector COVID-19 vaccine.
statements: 1 — Correct: Recombinant vector vaccines are made with recombinant DNA technology. The gene for a pathogen antigen, such as the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, is cloned and inserted into the genome of a carrier microbe. Genetic engineering began in the 1970s with restriction enzymes and plasmids (Cohen and Boyer, 1973). The first recombinant vaccine was the hepatitis B vaccine (1986, yeast-derived). Vector vaccines fall in the 'next-generation' category along with DNA and mRNA vaccines. The engineered vector does not cause disease because it is attenuated or replication-deficient, and the expressed antigen primes B and T cell responses. India's Covishield (Serum Institute) uses this platform.

2 — Correct: Both viruses and bacteria serve as vectors. Viral vectors include adenovirus (ChAdOx1, Ad26, Ad5), modified vaccinia Ankara, vesicular stomatitis virus (Ervebo, approved 2019 for Ebola) and measles virus. Bacterial vectors include attenuated Salmonella, Listeria and BCG. Vectors can be replicating or non-replicating. A drawback is pre-existing immunity to the vector, which can blunt the response; this is why Sputnik V uses two different adenoviruses for its two doses. Viral vectors are also used in gene therapy. Non-replicating adenovirus vectors have been used in COVID-19 vaccines worldwide, including Covishield, Sputnik V and Janssen.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Recombinant vector vaccines are made by genetic engineering, in which a gene for a pathogen's antigen is inserted into a harmless carrier (vector), and that vector is usually a modified virus or bacterium.
topic_notes: Vaccine platforms are a recurring UPSC theme, particularly since COVID-19. The main types are: (1) Live attenuated (weakened pathogen): BCG, OPV, MMR, measles, yellow fever. (2) Inactivated or killed: IPV, rabies, hepatitis A and Covaxin (Bharat Biotech, with ICMR and NIV Pune). (3) Subunit, recombinant protein or conjugate vaccines: hepatitis B (yeast-produced HBsAg), HPV, Hib, pneumococcal, Novavax and Corbevax (Biological E, a receptor-binding-domain protein vaccine). (4) Toxoid vaccines: tetanus and diphtheria. (5) Viral vector vaccines: Covishield (ChAdOx1 nCoV-19, Oxford-AstraZeneca, made in India by the Serum Institute), Sputnik V (Gamaleya Institute, Russia; Ad26 first dose and Ad5 second dose), Janssen (J&J, single dose), and Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) for Ebola. India's intranasal vaccine iNCOVACC (BBV154, Bharat Biotech) is also a recombinant adenoviral vector vaccine. (6) Nucleic acid vaccines: mRNA (Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna) and DNA, such as ZyCoV-D (Zydus Cadila), the world's first plasmid DNA vaccine for humans, delivered needle-free. India's Gemcovac-19 (Gennova) is an mRNA vaccine. Advantages of vector vaccines are strong cellular immunity and no need for adjuvants; limitations are pre-existing anti-vector immunity and rare adverse events, such as vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) with adenovirus vectors. Related institutions are CDSCO and DCGI (approval), ICMR, DBT and BIRAC (Mission COVID Suraksha), and the WHO Emergency Use Listing. Future questions could also cover Gavi, CEPI, COVAX, the Universal Immunization Programme and Mission Indradhanush.

question:
In the context of hereditary diseases, consider the following statements : 1, Passing on mitochondrial diseases from parent to child can be prevented by mitochondrial replacement therapy either before or after in vitro fertilization of egg.
2. A child inherits mitochondrial diseases entirely from mother and not from father. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Mitochondria are cell organelles that produce ATP and carry their own small circular DNA (mtDNA, about 16,569 base pairs, 37 genes), separate from nuclear DNA. At fertilization the sperm's mitochondria, found in the midpiece/tail, are generally destroyed or diluted, so the zygote's mitochondria come from the egg. Mitochondrial diseases such as Leigh syndrome, MELAS, MERRF and Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy therefore follow maternal inheritance. Fathers do not pass them on. MRT replaces defective maternal mitochondria with healthy donor mitochondria. In maternal spindle transfer the nuclear DNA is removed from the mother's unfertilized egg and placed in a donor egg whose nucleus has been removed, and this is then fertilized. In pronuclear transfer the pronuclei are moved from the zygote, after IVF, into a donor zygote. The resulting child carries nuclear DNA from both parents and mtDNA from the donor, hence the term 'three-parent baby'. The UK legalised MRT in 2015, and the first such baby was reported in Mexico in 2016. Elimination: statement 1 is correct because MRT is possible both before and after fertilization, and statement 2 is correct because inheritance is maternal. So options (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct. MRT can be done before fertilization (spindle transfer) or after it (pronuclear transfer).
(c) is correct because MRT works at both stages and mtDNA is inherited from the mother alone, so both statements hold.
(d) is wrong because both statements are factually correct.
keyfact: mtDNA is inherited only from the mother, and mitochondrial replacement therapy can be done before fertilization (spindle transfer) or after it (pronuclear transfer).
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only, would hold if maternal inheritance were doubted. It is wrong here because maternal inheritance of mtDNA is well established. Statement 1 is true: MRT includes maternal spindle transfer (before fertilization) and pronuclear transfer (after fertilization). The technique is used to prevent mitochondrial disease and is regulated in the UK by the HFEA.

Option (b), statement 2 only, would deny the two-stage nature of MRT. Statement 2 is true: mtDNA comes from the egg cytoplasm, and sperm mitochondria are degraded after fertilization. Mitochondrial inheritance is called matrilineal or maternal inheritance, which is why mtDNA is used to trace human maternal ancestry, such as 'Mitochondrial Eve'. The option is wrong because it ignores that statement 1 is also correct.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, is the official answer. MRT can be used at either stage of IVF, and mitochondrial disease passes only through the mother. MRT is sometimes called mitochondrial donation. The resulting embryo has nuclear DNA from both parents and donor mtDNA, which gives the 'three-parent baby' label. Ethical concerns include germline modification, because the changes are heritable through female offspring.

Option (d), neither, is wrong because both statements are scientifically accurate. It would be right only if MRT could not prevent disease or if fathers also transmitted mitochondrial DNA. Note that the mitochondrial genome is small, about 37 genes, and codes for components of oxidative phosphorylation, rRNAs and tRNAs. Most mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA.
related: mtDNA is circular and inherited maternally; the Y chromosome passes from father to son.
MRT techniques: maternal spindle transfer (before fertilization) and pronuclear transfer (after fertilization).
The UK legalised mitochondrial donation in 2015; Australia followed with Maeve's Law in 2022.
First 'three-parent baby' via spindle transfer was reported in Mexico in 2016.
CRISPR-Cas9 was developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, who won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel.
He Jiankui produced gene-edited babies in China in 2018, which led to international condemnation.
India regulates ART through the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021.
Heteroplasmy means a cell holds both mutant and normal mtDNA.
statements: 1 — Correct: MRT has two forms, one done on the unfertilized egg (spindle transfer) and one on the fertilized zygote (pronuclear transfer), so it can be applied either before or after IVF. MRT aims to stop mtDNA disease from passing from mother to child. The donor supplies healthy mitochondria, so the child has nuclear DNA from the two parents and mtDNA from the donor, about 0.1% of total DNA. The UK's Human Fertilisation and Embryology (Mitochondrial Donation) Regulations 2015 legalised it, and Newcastle University is the leading centre. A Mexican team led by John Zhang reported a baby born using spindle transfer in 2016. In the US, clinical use is blocked by a congressional rider on FDA funding. Australia legalised it through 'Maeve's Law' in 2022.

2 — Correct: mtDNA is inherited from the mother because the egg contributes the cytoplasm and thousands of mitochondria, while paternal mitochondria in the sperm midpiece are usually eliminated after fertilization by processes such as ubiquitination and mitophagy. Mitochondrial diseases therefore show maternal inheritance: an affected mother can pass the condition to all her children, but an affected father cannot. Examples are Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre syndrome and Leigh syndrome. Heteroplasmy, a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA, explains the variable severity. Rare reports of paternal transmission exist but are exceptional. Some mitochondrial diseases are caused by nuclear gene mutations and follow Mendelian inheritance, but the statement refers to mtDNA-based disease.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT) can be done before fertilization (maternal spindle transfer) or after fertilization (pronuclear transfer), and mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother.
topic_notes: Mitochondria are double-membrane organelles, the 'powerhouses' of the cell. They make ATP by oxidative phosphorylation and have their own circular DNA (16,569 bp; 37 genes: 13 protein-coding, 22 tRNA, 2 rRNA). They are inherited maternally and replicate independently of the nucleus. Heteroplasmy (a mixture of mutant and normal mtDNA) determines symptom severity. Mitochondrial disorders include LHON, MELAS, MERRF, Leigh syndrome and Kearns-Sayre syndrome. They mainly affect high-energy organs such as the brain, muscle, heart and eye. MRT techniques: (1) maternal spindle transfer, done on an unfertilized egg; (2) pronuclear transfer, done on a zygote after fertilization; (3) polar body transfer, which is experimental. The UK became the first country to legalise MRT in 2015. The Newcastle Fertility Centre is licensed, and the first UK births were reported in 2023. In 2016 a team in Mexico reported a baby born after spindle transfer. In the US, a congressional rider bars the FDA from reviewing MRT applications. Australia passed Maeve's Law in 2022. Related genetics for UPSC: gene therapy, CRISPR-Cas9 germline editing (He Jiankui's 2018 case), and the sickle cell and thalassemia gene-therapy approvals, including Casgevy, the first CRISPR therapy, approved in the UK in 2023. Other angles: autosomal dominant, recessive and X-linked inheritance; the Y chromosome passes from father to son; pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD); India's ART (Regulation) Act 2021 and the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021; ICMR guidelines on germline editing; and the Human Genome Project (completed 2003).

question: Bollgard I and Bollgard II technologies are mentioned in the context of
subject: Environment
detail: Bollgard is the trade name of Bt cotton developed by Monsanto and introduced in India through Mahyco (Mahyco Monsanto Biotech). Bollgard I contains a single gene, cry1Ac, which gives protection against American bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera). Bollgard II, approved in India in 2006, has two genes, cry1Ac and cry2Ab, widening protection to include Spodoptera (tobacco caterpillar) and reducing the chance of pest resistance. Bt cotton was approved for commercial cultivation in India in 2002 by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC, now Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Rules of 1989. Cotton remains the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India. The Cry proteins bind to receptors in the insect midgut, forming pores that kill the larva. Elimination: clonal propagation means tissue culture or cuttings, plant growth substances mean hormones such as auxin, and biofertilizers mean Rhizobium, Azotobacter or BGA. None of these has a link to Bollgard. The word 'technology' plus a Monsanto cotton brand points to genetic modification. Pink bollworm resistance to Bollgard II has since emerged in parts of India, and HTBt cotton remains unapproved.
explanations: Incorrect: clonal propagation produces genetically identical plants by vegetative methods or tissue culture. Bollgard involves inserting foreign genes, not cloning.
Correct: Bollgard I (cry1Ac) and Bollgard II (cry1Ac + cry2Ab) are Bt transgenic cotton technologies, so they relate to developing genetically modified crop plants.
Incorrect: plant growth substances such as auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins are hormones. Bollgard is not about producing them.
Incorrect: biofertilizers are microbial inoculants such as Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azolla and mycorrhiza. Bollgard concerns pest resistance in cotton, not nutrient supply.
keyfact: Bollgard I (cry1Ac) and Bollgard II (cry1Ac + cry2Ab) are Bt cotton, GM technologies against bollworms.
option_notes: Clonal propagation is asexual multiplication that gives genetically identical copies (clones). Methods include cuttings, layering, grafting, and micropropagation by tissue culture from meristems or explants. It is used for banana, sugarcane, orchids, potato and teak. It preserves desirable traits and gives disease-free plantlets, but it does not add new genes.

Genetically modified crops carry genes transferred by recombinant DNA technology. In India, Bt cotton (2002) is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation. GM mustard DMH-11 received GEAC environmental release approval in 2022 but is stalled in the Supreme Court. Bt brinjal had a moratorium imposed in 2010. GEAC under MoEFCC is the regulator.

Plant growth substances (phytohormones) are organic compounds that regulate growth in small amounts. They include auxins (IAA), gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene. Auxins promote rooting and cell elongation, gibberellins cause bolting and stem elongation, cytokinins promote cell division, ABA induces dormancy and stomatal closure, and ethylene ripens fruit.

Biofertilizers are living microorganisms that improve soil fertility. Examples are Rhizobium (legumes), Azotobacter and Azospirillum (free-living nitrogen fixers), blue-green algae and Azolla (rice), phosphate-solubilising bacteria and mycorrhiza. In India, the Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana and National Project on Organic Farming promote them. They are cheap and eco-friendly, and they reduce chemical fertilizer use.
related: Bt cotton is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India (approved 2002).
Bollgard II carries cry1Ac and cry2Ab genes; Bollgard I carries only cry1Ac.
GEAC under MoEFCC is the regulator for GM crop approvals in India.
Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010 by the Environment Minister.
GM mustard DMH-11 was cleared by GEAC in 2022; its release is subject to Supreme Court proceedings.
Flavr Savr tomato was the first commercially sold GM food (1994).
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety deals with living modified organisms.
Pink bollworm has developed resistance to Bt cotton in parts of India.
summary: The answer is (b): Bollgard I and Bollgard II are technologies for developing genetically modified (transgenic) cotton. They insert genes from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) so the plant produces proteins toxic to bollworm pests.
topic_notes: Bt cotton is the centrepiece of India's GM crop story. Bacillus thuringiensis is a soil bacterium that produces crystal (Cry) proteins which are toxic to specific insect groups. Cry1Ac targets Lepidoptera such as bollworms. Bollgard I was developed by Monsanto, with Mahyco as the Indian partner, and approved in 2002. Bollgard II, with cry1Ac and cry2Ab, was approved in 2006. Later, unapproved HTBt (herbicide-tolerant, with the cp4-epsps gene) cotton has been a regulatory controversy. India is among the world's largest cotton producers, with Bt varieties covering over 90 percent of the area. Pink bollworm resistance has been seen in Gujarat and Maharashtra. Regulation falls under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the 1989 Rules for hazardous microorganisms and GMOs, with GEAC in MoEFCC as the apex approving body. The Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation sits under DBT. The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms. Other GM topics include Golden Rice (beta-carotene), Flavr Savr tomato (first commercial GM food, 1994), Bt brinjal (moratorium 2010), GM mustard DMH-11 (developed by Delhi University, with the bar, barnase and barstar gene system), and the FSSAI rules on GM food. Related technologies are RNA interference, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants exempted from GM rules in India in 2022), and gene drives. Also remember tissue culture, biofertilizers and growth hormones, as these are the usual distractors.

ocr: In a pressure cooker, the temperature at which the food is cooked depends mainly upon which of the following? 1. Area of the hole in the lid 2. Temperature of the flame 3. Weight of the lid Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (aq) 1,2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. In an open vessel this is atmospheric pressure (about 1 atm, 100°C at sea level), so food cannot be cooked hotter than 100°C. A pressure cooker has a sealed lid with a small vent hole closed by a weight (regulator or whistle). Steam builds up until its pressure can lift the weight, and then the excess steam escapes. At that point the internal pressure is fixed at roughly atmospheric pressure plus the pressure exerted by the weight, which is weight divided by the area of the hole. For a typical cooker this is about 1 atm of gauge pressure, so the total is around 2 atm and the boiling point rises to about 120°C. A heavier lid or weight, or a smaller hole, gives a higher pressure and a higher temperature. A hotter flame only produces steam faster, and the excess is vented, so the temperature stays the same. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong, which rules out (a), (b) and (d). That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2 (flame temperature), which does not control the cooking temperature once the set pressure is reached.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 1. The area of the hole does matter.
Correct: only the area of the hole and the weight of the lid determine the steady steam pressure and therefore the temperature.
Wrong: it includes statement 2. The flame temperature affects only how fast steam is produced.
keyfact: Pressure cooker temperature is set by steam pressure, which depends on the weight of the lid/regulator and the area of the vent, not on the flame.
related: Water boils at 100°C at 1 atm; the boiling point rises with pressure and falls with altitude.
Pressure cooker steam is at about 120°C, which is why food cooks faster.
Latent heat of vaporisation of water is about 2260 J/g (540 cal/g).
Boiling water stays at a constant temperature while it absorbs latent heat.
Impurities such as salt raise the boiling point (elevation) and lower the freezing point (depression).
Pressure on ice lowers its melting point (regelation).
An autoclave sterilises at about 121°C and 15 psi.
Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.
statements: 1 — Correct: The pressure the weight can hold back equals force divided by area, so the area of the vent hole determines the steady steam pressure and therefore the boiling point. A smaller hole means higher pressure and higher temperature. Fact: boiling point rises with pressure (Clausius–Clapeyron relation). At 1 atm water boils at 100°C, and at about 2 atm total pressure it boils at roughly 120°C. This is why food cooks faster in a pressure cooker, and why the pressure-cooker principle is the reverse of water boiling at a lower temperature on mountains.

2 — Incorrect: Once the set pressure is reached, extra heat only converts more water to steam, which escapes through the vent. The pressure and temperature stay constant, so a stronger flame only shortens the time to reach that pressure. Fact: temperature during boiling stays constant while latent heat of vaporisation (about 2260 J/g for water) is absorbed. Heat supplied at the boiling point goes into changing phase rather than raising temperature. This is why it is advised to lower the flame once the whistle starts.

3 — Correct: The weight of the lid or regulator sets the extra pressure required to lift it, so a heavier weight allows a higher internal pressure and a higher cooking temperature. Fact: the same principle applies to safety valves and to autoclaves used for sterilisation (about 121°C at 15 psi gauge). Cookers also have a fusible safety plug or a gasket release that opens if the vent blocks. At high altitude, where atmospheric pressure is lower, water boils below 100°C, so cooking takes longer and pressure cookers help.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. In a pressure cooker the cooking temperature is set by the steam pressure inside, which is regulated by the weight of the lid (or regulator/vent weight) and the area of the vent hole it covers. The flame temperature only changes how quickly the cooker reaches that pressure.
topic_notes: Boiling point and pressure: a liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure. Raising the pressure raises the boiling point and lowering it reduces the boiling point. The relationship is described by the Clausius–Clapeyron equation. Water boils at 100°C at 1 atm (101.3 kPa) at sea level. On Mount Everest, where the pressure is about one third of 1 atm, water boils at roughly 70°C. A pressure cooker works by trapping steam so that the pressure inside is about 2 atm absolute (about 1 atm gauge, or 15 psi), giving about 120°C. The pressure is regulated by a weighted valve (regulator or whistle) over a vent, with a safety valve and a gasket as backups. The pressure from the weight is P = mg/A, so the pressure depends on the mass of the weight and the area of the vent. The flame only controls the rate of heating. Related concepts: latent heat of vaporisation (about 540 cal/g or 2260 J/g for water), latent heat of fusion of ice (about 80 cal/g or 334 J/g), and the effect of dissolved impurities, which raise the boiling point (elevation of boiling point) and lower the freezing point (depression of freezing point). Ice melts at a lower temperature under pressure, which is called regelation and explains ice skating. Other applications: autoclaves for sterilising medical instruments (121°C), industrial boilers, and distillation under reduced pressure (vacuum distillation) to avoid decomposition. Cooking at high altitude takes longer because of the lower boiling point. UPSC often asks about these properties through everyday applications. The topic also links to the gas laws (Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's law: pressure is proportional to temperature at constant volume).

question:
Consider the following :
1. Bacteria
2. Fungi
3. Virus Which of the above can be cultured in artificial/synthetic medium?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Culturing an organism in an artificial or synthetic medium requires that the organism can carry out its own metabolism and reproduction once given nutrients. Bacteria (prokaryotes) and fungi (eukaryotes) both qualify. Bacteria grow on nutrient agar, MacConkey agar, blood agar and similar media. Fungi grow on Sabouraud dextrose agar and potato dextrose agar. Viruses are acellular. They have no ribosomes and no metabolic machinery, and they carry only DNA or RNA in a protein coat (capsid). They can replicate only inside living host cells. Viruses are therefore cultured in living systems: embryonated hen's eggs, primary or continuous cell lines, or live animals. Some bacteria are also obligate intracellular, such as Chlamydia, Rickettsia and Mycobacterium leprae, and cannot be grown on cell-free media either. The question, however, refers to bacteria as a group, and most bacteria can be cultured. The elimination logic is simple: viruses cannot be grown on synthetic media, so any option containing 3 (b, c, d) is wrong. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct. Bacteria and fungi have their own metabolic machinery and grow on artificial media, while viruses do not.
Wrong. It includes viruses (3), which cannot be cultured on synthetic media, and it leaves out bacteria (1), which can.
Wrong. It includes viruses (3) and leaves out fungi (2), which grow readily on media like Sabouraud agar.
Wrong. It includes viruses, which need living host cells. Only bacteria and fungi can be grown on artificial media.
keyfact: Bacteria and fungi grow on artificial media; viruses, being obligate intracellular parasites, need living host cells.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only means bacteria and fungi. Both are cellular organisms that can be grown in pure culture on nutrient agar, Sabouraud agar and similar media. This is the right answer. Koch's postulates rely on pure cultures of bacteria. Fungal cultures are used in industry (yeast fermentation, penicillin from Penicillium) and in diagnosis.

2 and 3 only pairs fungi with viruses. Fungi can be cultured on synthetic media, but viruses cannot because they are obligate intracellular parasites without ribosomes or metabolism. Viruses are grown in embryonated eggs, cell lines or animals. Wrong because it includes viruses and omits bacteria.
