He wrote the Sanskrit farce Mattavilasa Prahasana, satirising Kapalika and Buddhist practices. He is credited with introducing the cave-temple style (Mandagapattu inscription: a temple built without brick, timber, metal or mortar), with sites at Mahendravadi, Mamandur, Dalavanur, Pallavaram and Tiruchirappalli. He was originally a Jain, converted to Shaivism through the saint Appar (Tirunavukkarasar), and was defeated by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas at Pullalur, losing the northern Pallava territory. Elimination: Simhavishnu is known for defeating the Kalabhras and the Cholas. Narasimhavarman I bore the title Mamalla and conquered Vatapi. Simhavarman is an early Pallava name with no link to these titles.
explanations: Correct: Mahendravarman I held the titles Mattavilasa, Vichitrachitta and Gunabhara, along with many others.
Wrong: Simhavishnu (c. 575-600 CE) founded the Pallava line's imperial power and defeated the Kalabhras. He is not associated with these birudas.
Wrong: Narasimhavarman I (c. 630-668 CE) took the title Mamallan ('great wrestler') and Vatapikonda after sacking Vatapi in 642 CE. He founded Mamallapuram.
Wrong: Simhavarman is an early Pallava name (4th-5th century), known from the Prakrit and Sanskrit charters. He is not linked to these titles.
keyfact: Mattavilasa, Vichitrachitta and Gunabhara were titles of the Pallava king Mahendravarman I (c. 600-630 CE), the cave-temple pioneer and author of Mattavilasa Prahasana.
option_notes: Mahendravarman I (c. 600-630 CE) was a Pallava king of Kanchi, a polymath who wrote Mattavilasa Prahasana and possibly Bhagavadajjukiya. He introduced rock-cut cave temples (Mandagapattu), was a patron of music (the Kudumiyanmalai inscription on musical notation) and was converted from Jainism by Appar. He lost the northern territory to Pulakeshin II.

Simhavishnu (c. 575-600 CE) was the father of Mahendravarman I and revived Pallava power after the Kalabhra interregnum. He defeated the Kalabhras, the Cholas, the Pandyas and the Ceylon king, and took the title Avanisimha. Bharavi, the author of Kiratarjuniya, is said to have lived at his court. He was a Vaishnava.

Narasimhavarman I (c. 630-668 CE), also called Mamalla, was the son of Mahendravarman I. He defeated Pulakeshin II and captured Vatapi (642 CE), earning the title Vatapikonda. He founded Mamallapuram and built its monolithic rathas. The Chinese traveller Xuanzang visited Kanchi in his reign, and he sent naval help to the Sri Lankan prince Manavamma.

Simhavarman is the name of several early Pallava kings, such as Simhavarman IV (c. 436 CE), known from the Lokavibhaga, a Jain text, and the Pallava copper-plate charters. These early Pallavas used Prakrit and Sanskrit grants from Andhra and the Kanchi region. The name is distinct from Simhavishnu, who began the Great Pallava line.
related: Mandagapattu inscription calls the temple built without brick, timber, metal or mortar, as Lakshitayatana.
Mahendravarman I wrote Mattavilasa Prahasana, a Sanskrit satire.
Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi in 642 CE and took the title Vatapikonda.
Shore Temple at Mamallapuram was built by Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha.
Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha and Mahendravarman I at Pullalur.
Xuanzang visited Kanchi in Narasimhavarman I's reign.
Mahendravarman I was converted from Jainism to Shaivism by Appar.
Dandin was associated with the court of the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II.
summary: The answer is (a) Mahendravarman I, the Pallava king who ruled c. 600-630 CE. Mattavilasa, Vichitrachitta and Gunabhara were among his many birudas (titles), which reflect his role as a playwright, musician, painter and builder of rock-cut temples.
topic_notes: The Pallavas of Kanchipuram ruled northern Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra from the 6th to the 9th century CE. Their rise followed the Kalabhra interregnum, ended by Simhavishnu (c. 575 CE). Mahendravarman I (600-630) was a polymath who wrote Mattavilasa Prahasana and Bhagavadajjukiya and was patron of music (Kudumiyanmalai and Tirumayam inscriptions). He started cave temples such as Mandagapattu, Mamandur and Pallavaram, and defended Kanchi against Pulakeshin II (battle of Pullalur). Narasimhavarman I Mamalla (630-668) took Vatapi in 642 and built the Mamallapuram rathas. Later kings: Mahendravarman II, Paramesvaravarman I (battle of Peruvalanallur against Vikramaditya I), Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha (built the Shore Temple and Kailasanatha temple at Kanchi), Nandivarman II Pallavamalla (Vaikuntha Perumal temple) and Aparajita, defeated by the Cholas (c. 897). Architecture phases: Mahendra (cave), Mamalla (monolithic rathas), Rajasimha (structural temples), Nandivarman (later structural). Literature: Dandin (Dashakumaracharita) lived at Narasimhavarman II's court. Bhakti saints (Nayanars and Alvars) flourished. Administration: the village assemblies sabha and ur, and the land grants of brahmadeya and devadana. The Pallavas used the Pallava-Grantha script. Their capital Kanchipuram was a centre of learning (Ghatika).

question: Fa-hien (Faxian), the Chinese pilgrim, travelled to India during the reign of
subject: Ancient History
detail: Fa-hien (Faxian) was a Chinese Buddhist monk who travelled overland from Chang'an via Central Asia to India, seeking authentic Vinaya (monastic discipline) texts. He stayed in India roughly 399-414 CE, then returned to China by sea via Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Java. His account, Fo-kuo-ki (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), is a key source for Gupta-era India. He does not name the king, but the chronology matches Chandragupta II Vikramaditya. He visited Mathura, Kannauj, Shravasti, Kapilavastu, Lumbini, Kushinagar, Vaishali, Pataliputra, Varanasi and Sarnath, and Tamralipti. He noted mild administration, no death penalty (fines and mutilation for repeated rebellion), free travel, the low status of Chandalas, who lived outside towns, and the use of cowries as currency. Elimination: Samudragupta (c. 335-375) was earlier, famed for the Allahabad Pillar inscription by Harishena. Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455) founded Nalanda and was later than Fa-hien's stay. Skandagupta (c. 455-467) faced Huna invasions and repaired Sudarshana lake. Hsuan-tsang came in the 7th century under Harsha, and I-tsing in the late 7th century, which are distinct visits often confused with Fa-hien's.
explanations: Incorrect: Samudragupta ruled c. 335-375 CE, before Fa-hien's visit (c. 399-414 CE).
Correct: Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE) was the reigning Gupta emperor during Fa-hien's stay in India.
Incorrect: Kumaragupta I came to the throne c. 415 CE, after Fa-hien had left India.
Incorrect: Skandagupta ruled c. 455-467 CE, decades after Fa-hien's visit.
keyfact: Fa-hien (c. 399-414 CE) visited India under Chandragupta II Vikramaditya and wrote Fo-kuo-ki.
option_notes: Samudragupta (c. 335-375 CE), son of Chandragupta I and Kumaradevi (Licchavi), was the great conqueror. The Allahabad (Prayag) Prashasti, composed by Harishena, records his Dakshinapatha campaign and the policy of 'grahana-moksha-anugraha'. Called the 'Napoleon of India' by V. A. Smith. He issued veena-playing and Ashvamedha coins and was a patron of poetry and music.

Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375-415 CE) was the son of Samudragupta and Dattadevi. He expanded the empire by defeating the Western Kshatrapas (Rudrasimha III), gaining Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra, and made Ujjain a second capital. He married his daughter Prabhavatigupta into the Vakataka family. The Mehrauli iron pillar is associated with him. Navaratnas, including Kalidasa, are linked to his court. He issued silver coins and took the title Vikramaditya.

Kumaragupta I (c. 415-455 CE) was the son of Chandragupta II and Dhruvadevi. He is credited with founding Nalanda Mahavihara and issued many coin types, including peacock types. He performed the Ashvamedha and ruled a largely peaceful empire. Late in his reign, the Pushyamitra tribes troubled the empire. He took the titles Mahendraditya and Shakraditya.

Skandagupta (c. 455-467 CE), son of Kumaragupta I, is called the last great Gupta ruler. He repulsed the first Huna invasion, as recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription. His governor Parnadatta and Chakrapalita repaired the Sudarshana lake at Girnar, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription. His reign saw coin debasement and the start of Gupta decline. He took the title Vikramaditya.
related: Fa-hien's travelogue is Fo-kuo-ki (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms).
Hsuan-tsang visited under Harsha and wrote Si-yu-ki; he studied at Nalanda.
I-tsing visited in the late 7th century and wrote about Nalanda and Srivijaya.
Chandragupta II took the title Vikramaditya and defeated the Shaka Western Kshatrapas.
The Allahabad Pillar inscription by Harishena records Samudragupta's conquests.
Kumaragupta I is credited with founding Nalanda.
Skandagupta's Bhitari inscription records resistance to the Hunas.
The Gupta era began in 319-320 CE.
summary: The answer is (b) Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya). Fa-hien visited India c. 399-414 CE, which falls within Chandragupta II's reign (c. 375-415 CE), and he described the Gupta realm's peace and prosperity in his travel account.
topic_notes: Chinese pilgrims are a standard UPSC topic. Fa-hien (Faxian) came c. 399-414 CE in the time of Chandragupta II and wrote Fo-kuo-ki, in which he describes Madhyadesha as a prosperous land with mild governance. He stayed three years at Pataliputra, studying Sanskrit and copying texts, and mentioned the Ashokan palace there. Hsuan-tsang (Xuanzang) visited c. 630-645 CE under Harsha, studied at Nalanda under Shilabhadra, attended the Kannauj and Prayag assemblies, and wrote Si-yu-ki. His biography was written by Hwui-li. I-tsing came c. 671-695 CE and described Nalanda and Vikramashila, as well as the Srivijaya Buddhist centres. Other foreign accounts include Megasthenes (Indica, Chandragupta Maurya's court), Alberuni (Kitab-ul-Hind, Mahmud of Ghazni), Ibn Battuta (Rihla, Muhammad bin Tughluq), Marco Polo (Pandya and Kakatiya lands), Abdur Razzaq and Nicolo Conti (Vijayanagara), and Fernao Nuniz and Domingo Paes (Vijayanagara). Gupta history essentials: Sri Gupta founded the dynasty; Chandragupta I began the Gupta era in 319-320 CE; Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar; Chandragupta II's conquests and the Meharauli pillar; Kalidasa and Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE); Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa; Kumaragupta I's Nalanda; Skandagupta and the Hunas. Gupta administration used Bhukti (province), Vishaya (district) and Vithi, and the terms Kumaramatya and Sandhivigrahika.

question: Who among the following led a successful military campaign against the kingdom of Srivijaya, the powerful maritime State, which ruled the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and the neighbouring islands?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Rajendra I (r. c. 1014-1044 CE), son of Rajaraja I, took the title Gangaikonda Chola after his northern campaign to the Ganga and founded the capital Gangaikondacholapuram. His naval expedition to Southeast Asia in c. 1025 CE is known from the Tanjavur (Thanjavur) inscription of 1030-31 and the Tiruvalangadu copper plates. They record the capture of Kadaram (Kedah) and its king Sangrama Vijayottungavarman, and the seizure of places such as Pannai, Malaiyur, Ilangasogam (Langkasuka) and Tamralinga. Srivijaya, based at Palembang in Sumatra, controlled the Straits of Malacca and the Malay trade route. Chola motives were probably to secure and protect trade with China, and possibly to curb Srivijaya's control of the straits. Chola-Srivijaya relations had earlier been friendly; Srivijaya's king Maravijayottungavarman built the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam in Rajaraja I's time. Elimination: the Rashtrakutas (Amoghavarsha) were a Deccan power with western-coast interests, the Kakatiyas (Prataparudra) ruled Telangana in the 13th-14th centuries, and the Hoysalas (Vishnuvardhana) ruled the Karnataka plateau in the 12th century. None had a naval tradition or a Southeast Asian campaign.
explanations: Amoghavarsha I (Rashtrakuta, c. 814-878 CE) was a patron of literature and Jainism, and he fought mainly the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Eastern Chalukyas. He had no campaign against Srivijaya, so (a) is wrong.
Prataparudra (Kakatiya, c. 1289-1323) ruled Warangal and faced the Delhi Sultanate. The Kakatiyas had no naval campaigns in Southeast Asia, so (b) is wrong.
Rajendra I Chola launched the c. 1025 CE naval expedition against Srivijaya, taking Kadaram and other ports. This matches the question, so (c) is correct.
Vishnuvardhana (Hoysala, c. 1110-1152) expanded the Hoysala kingdom in Karnataka and was associated with Ramanuja and the Belur temple. He had no overseas campaign, so (d) is wrong.
keyfact: Rajendra I Chola attacked Srivijaya (Kadaram/Kedah) around 1025 CE, the notable Indian naval expedition to Southeast Asia.
option_notes: Amoghavarsha I (c. 814-878 CE) was the greatest Rashtrakuta ruler, with capital at Manyakheta. He wrote the Kannada work Kavirajamarga, patronised Jainism under Jinasena, and is said to have taken the title Nripatunga. Arab traveller Sulaiman called the Rashtrakuta kingdom one of the world's four great empires. He had no overseas conquests.

Prataparudra (Prataparudra II, r. c. 1289-1323) was the last major Kakatiya ruler of Warangal, successor of Rani Rudramadevi. He resisted Delhi Sultanate attacks by Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur and later Ulugh Khan (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), and was defeated in 1323. The Kakatiyas are known for the Ramappa temple (UNESCO site 2021) and tank irrigation.

Rajendra I (r. c. 1014-1044 CE) was the Chola emperor who extended Chola power to the Ganga in the north and, around 1025 CE, to Srivijaya across the sea. He took titles Gangaikonda Chola and Kadaramkondan, and built Gangaikondacholapuram. He also conquered Sri Lanka fully, completing the work begun by Rajaraja I. His reign marked the peak of Chola naval power.

Vishnuvardhana (r. c. 1108-1152) was the Hoysala king who made the dynasty independent of the Western Chalukyas and defeated the Cholas at Talakad. His capital was Dorasamudra (Halebidu) and he is linked with the Vaishnava saint Ramanuja, after whose influence he converted from Jainism. The Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are known for their Vesara architecture.
related: Rajendra I built Gangaikondacholapuram to commemorate his Ganga victory.
Rajendra I's naval expedition to Srivijaya took place around 1025 CE.
Srivijaya's capital was Palembang in Sumatra.
Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam was built by a Srivijaya (Sailendra) king.
Tanjavur inscription of 1030-31 and Tiruvalangadu plates record Rajendra's campaigns.
Kadaram is the Tamil name for Kedah in Malaysia.
Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur.
Yijing visited Srivijaya in the 7th century CE.
summary: The answer is (c) Rajendra I (Chola). Around 1025 CE he sent a naval expedition against Sangrama Vijayottungavarman, the Srivijaya king of Kadaram (Kedah), and raided key Srivijayan ports. This was a rare Indian overseas military campaign, and no other ruler listed took part in anything similar.
topic_notes: Chola-Srivijaya relations form the core of this topic. Srivijaya was a Buddhist thalassocracy centred at Palembang (Sumatra) from the 7th to 13th century, controlling the Malacca and Sunda straits. Chinese pilgrim Yijing (I-tsing) stayed there in the 7th century to study Sanskrit and Buddhism. Under the Sailendra dynasty it was linked with the Borobudur monument in Java. Relations with the Cholas began cordially: King Sri Mara Vijayottungavarman built the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam, and Rajaraja I granted the village Anaimangalam for its upkeep (Leiden copper plates). Under Rajendra I the relations turned hostile, probably because of trade rivalry and Srivijaya's obstruction of Chola merchants travelling to China. The 1025 expedition weakened Srivijaya's dominance and the Chola ruler's mission to China followed in 1033. Later, Kulottunga I also sent embassies to China (1077). Other Chola facts: the Chola navy dominated the Bay of Bengal, called the 'Chola lake'; local self-government is described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I; the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I; Dravidian architecture and Chola bronzes (Nataraja) are important; village assemblies were called Ur, Sabha and Nadu. Other angles UPSC may ask: Indian cultural influence on Southeast Asia (Angkor Wat, Borobudur, Prambanan), Indianised kingdoms such as Funan, Champa, and Majapahit, and Indian Ocean trade guilds like Manigramam and Ayyavole.

question:
With reference to ancient India (600-322 BC), consider the following pairs : Territorial River flowing region in the region
I. Asmaka ‘ Godavari Il. Kamboja : Vipas Ill. Avanti : Mahanadi
IV. Kosala ‘ Sarayu How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests the geography of the Mahajanapadas, the sixteen states of the 6th century BC listed in the Anguttara Nikaya (and the Bhagavati Sutra with variations). Asmaka (Assaka) lay on the Godavari in the Deccan, with its capital at Potana/Podana (Paudanya), and was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas. Kosala, with capitals at Shravasti and Ayodhya (Saketa), lay in the Sarayu (Ghaghara) plain, and the Sarayu flows past Ayodhya. Kamboja belonged to the north-west, in the Hindukush and Pamir region of Rajouri-Hazara, and is associated with Rajapura and Dvaraka. It was not on the Vipas (Beas) in Punjab. Avanti was in the Malwa region, with Ujjain (Ujjayini) in the north and Mahishmati in the south. Its rivers were the Narmada, Shipra and Betwa, not the Mahanadi, which flows through Odisha and Chhattisgarh and is linked to Kalinga. Elimination logic: knowing that Asmaka–Godavari and Kosala–Sarayu are correct, and that Kamboja is north-western and Avanti is central India, gives exactly two correct pairs, so (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong: two pairs are correct, I and IV, so 'only one' undercounts.
(b) is correct: Asmaka–Godavari and Kosala–Sarayu are right, while Kamboja–Vipas and Avanti–Mahanadi are wrong.
(c) is wrong: it would need Kamboja or Avanti to be matched correctly, but Kamboja was in the north-west and Avanti in Malwa.
(d) is wrong: neither Kamboja nor Avanti is associated with the river named.
keyfact: Asmaka = Godavari and Kosala = Sarayu are right; Kamboja is north-western (not Vipas) and Avanti is Malwa (not Mahanadi) – answer (b), only two.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean a single correct pair. It is the result if a student recognises only the Godavari or the Sarayu link, which is a common trap. Both are firmly established in the sources: Asmaka lay in the Godavari basin and Kosala was centred on the Sarayu (Ghaghara).

Only two: this is the official answer. Of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, Asmaka was the one in the south on the Godavari. Kosala under Prasenajit was a rival of Magadha and was ultimately absorbed by it. The other two pairs fail because Kamboja is north-western and Avanti is in Malwa.

Only three: this would require one of the Kamboja or Avanti pairs to be right. Kamboja was a north-western state in the Hindukush region, well known for horses, and Avanti was a Malwa state on the Narmada and Shipra, with Ujjain as capital and Pradyota as its famous king.

All the four: this would mean every river link is right. The traps are the Vipas (Beas), a Punjab river associated with Alexander's farthest point, and the Mahanadi, a major river of Odisha and Chhattisgarh, which have nothing to do with Kamboja or Avanti.
related: Asmaka was the only Mahajanapada south of the Vindhyas, on the Godavari.
Vipas is the ancient name of the Beas, and Vitasta is the Jhelum.
Avanti's capitals were Ujjayini (north) and Mahishmati (south).
Vajji and Malla were gana-sangha (republican) Mahajanapadas.
Kosala's capitals were Shravasti and Ayodhya (Saketa), and its king Prasenajit was a contemporary of the Buddha.
Kamboja and Gandhara were in the north-west and are mentioned in Ashoka's Rock Edict V.
The Anguttara Nikaya lists sixteen Mahajanapadas.
Magadha's first capital was Rajagriha (Girivraja), later Pataliputra.
statements: 1 — Correct: Asmaka lay on the Godavari. Asmaka (Assaka) was the southernmost Mahajanapada, in the Godavari basin between the Godavari and Manjira, in present-day Telangana and Maharashtra. Its capital was Potali/Podana (Paudanya), identified with Bodhan in Telangana. It appears in the Buddhist texts and in Panini's Ashtadhyayi, and was associated with the Ikshvaku line. It is also mentioned in the Mahabharata and the Puranas. Avanti later swallowed or dominated it.

2 — Incorrect: Kamboja was not on the Vipas. Kamboja was a north-western Mahajanapada in the Hindukush and Pamir region, with Rajapura (Rajouri) and Hataka among its centres. It was known for its horses and appears in Ashoka's Rock Edict V along with Gandhara and Yavana. The Vipas (Beas) is a Punjab river, one of the five rivers of the Punjab, and the Greek Alexander turned back at its banks (326 BC). Gandhara lay on the Indus around Taxila and Pushkalavati.

3 — Incorrect: Avanti was not on the Mahanadi. Avanti covered Malwa and Nimar, with Ujjayini (Ujjain) as its northern capital and Mahishmati as its southern one. Its king Pradyota (Chanda Pradyota Mahasena) was a contemporary of the Buddha and Bimbisara. Avanti was one of the four great powers of the age, with Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa, and was annexed by Magadha under Shishunaga. Its rivers include the Shipra, Narmada and Betwa. The Mahanadi was in Kalinga/Odisha territory.

4 — Correct: Kosala lay on the Sarayu. Kosala covered the Awadh region of eastern Uttar Pradesh, with the Sarayu (Ghaghara) river flowing through it. The Sarayu divided it into northern and southern parts. Its capitals were Shravasti (Sahet-Mahet) and Ayodhya (Saketa), and Kushavati was a capital in the south. King Prasenajit was a contemporary of the Buddha, and his son Vidudabha was the last king before Magadha annexed Kosala under Ajatashatru's line.
summary: The answer is (b): only two pairs are correctly matched. Asmaka–Godavari (I) and Kosala–Sarayu (IV) are correct, while Kamboja–Vipas (II) and Avanti–Mahanadi (III) are wrong.
topic_notes: The sixth century BC saw the rise of sixteen Mahajanapadas (Anguttara Nikaya): Anga, Magadha, Kashi, Kosala, Vajji (Vriji), Malla, Chedi, Vatsa (Vamsa), Kuru, Panchala, Machchha (Matsya), Surasena, Assaka (Asmaka), Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja. Most were monarchies, while Vajji and Malla were gana-sanghas (republics). Vajji was a confederacy of eight clans, including the Licchavis, with its capital at Vaishali. Magadha eventually won the contest, with rulers including Bimbisara (Haryanka), Ajatashatru, Shishunaga and the Nandas. Its capitals were Rajagriha (Girivraja) and later Pataliputra. Capitals to remember: Anga – Champa; Kashi – Varanasi; Vatsa – Kaushambi; Kuru – Indraprastha; Panchala – Ahichchhatra and Kampilya; Matsya – Viratanagar; Surasena – Mathura; Chedi – Sothivati; Gandhara – Taxila; Malla – Kushinara and Pava. Kamboja's capital was Rajapura. Avanti was split between Ujjain and Mahishmati. Other angles UPSC could ask: the Alexander invasion of 326 BC (the Battle of the Hydaspes against Porus, on the Jhelum/Vitasta), the Persian conquest of Gandhara under Darius I, the ancient names of rivers (Vitasta – Jhelum, Askini – Chenab, Parushni – Ravi, Vipasa – Beas, Shutudri – Sutlej, Kubha – Kabul, Gomati – Gomal, Drishadvati – Ghaggar), the Buddhist and Jain sources, and the rise of iron use, punch-marked coins and urbanisation (the second urbanisation) in the Ganga plain.

ocr: The first Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, a music training school, was set up in 1901 by Vishnu Digambar Paluskar in (a) Delhi (b) Gwalior (c) Ujjain (ad) Lahore
subject: Ancient History
detail: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (1872-1931) was a Maharashtrian vocalist of the Gwalior gharana tradition, trained under Balkrishnabuwa Ichalkaranjikar. He wanted to lift music's social standing, which had fallen because it was linked with courtesans and court patronage, and to take it to the middle class. In May 1901 he founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore, then in undivided Punjab. It was a school with a structured syllabus, graded examinations, printed textbooks and notation, and public concerts. Students did not need a guru-shishya relationship or hereditary standing. The school moved to Bombay in 1908, and its branches spread across India. He also devised a notation system, published the Sangeet Bal Prakash and other books, and trained disciples such as V.N. Patwardhan, Omkarnath Thakur, B.R. Deodhar and Vinayakrao Patwardhan. Elimination: Delhi was not the original seat, though later associated with music institutions. Gwalior is his gharana's home but not the school's founding place. Ujjain is associated with Kalidasa and ancient culture, not this school. Lahore is the only option linked with the 1901 founding.
explanations: Incorrect. Delhi was not where the school was first set up. Paluskar worked in Punjab and later Bombay, and Delhi is not linked to the 1901 founding.
Incorrect. Gwalior is a famous centre of the Gwalior gharana, to which Paluskar's tradition belonged, but he did not found the first Mahavidyalaya there.
Incorrect. Ujjain is a historic cultural city linked with Kalidasa and Vikramaditya, and has no connection with this school's founding.
Correct. The first Gandharva Mahavidyalaya was established in Lahore in 1901 by Vishnu Digambar Paluskar, and it later shifted to Bombay in 1908.
keyfact: Gandharva Mahavidyalaya was founded by V.D. Paluskar at Lahore in 1901 and moved to Bombay in 1908.
option_notes: Delhi: capital of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire, and capital of British India from 1911. It is home to institutions such as the Sangeet Natak Akademi (founded 1952), the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya (Delhi, founded 1939 by Pt. Vinay Chandra Maudgalya) and the Delhi gharana of tabla and khayal. It is not the site of the 1901 school.

Gwalior: in Madhya Pradesh, it is the cradle of the oldest khayal gharana, the Gwalior gharana. Raja Man Singh Tomar (15th century) patronised dhrupad there, and Tansen was linked with the region. The annual Tansen Samaroh is held at Gwalior (Behat). It was not the school's first location.

Ujjain: ancient Avanti city on the Shipra river in Madhya Pradesh. It is a Mahakaleshwar jyotirlinga site, the seat of Kumbh (Simhastha) mela, and associated with Kalidasa and Vikramaditya. It was a centre of Indian astronomy, with prime meridian traditions. It has no link to Paluskar's 1901 school.

Lahore: historic capital of Punjab, now in Pakistan. It was a major cultural and educational centre under the Mughals, the Sikh Empire and British rule. The Gandharva Mahavidyalaya was founded there in 1901 by V.D. Paluskar. Other institutions there include Punjab University (1882) and the Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens (UNESCO sites).
related: Paluskar founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore in 1901 and moved it to Bombay in 1908.
V.N. Bhatkhande formulated the thaat system of 10 thaats for classifying ragas.
Bhatkhande University in Lucknow began as Marris College of Music in 1926.
The Gwalior gharana is considered the oldest khayal gharana.
Sangeet Natak Akademi was established in 1952 as India's national academy of music, dance and drama.
Paluskar's disciple Omkarnath Thakur became a leading Hindustani vocalist and the first principal of Banaras Hindu University's music college.
The Tansen Samaroh is held annually at Gwalior in Madhya Pradesh.
summary: The answer is (d) Lahore. Vishnu Digambar Paluskar founded the first Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore in 1901 to give Hindustani classical music organised, institutional training open to all, outside the hereditary gharana and court system.
topic_notes: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (1872-1931), born in Kurundwad in Maharashtra, was a pioneer of music education in modern India. He belonged to the Gwalior gharana tradition and was a disciple of Balkrishnabuwa Ichalkaranjikar. He opposed the idea that music was a low-status pursuit tied to courts and courtesans, and he made bhajan and devotional music, including Ram dhun, popular among the middle class. In 1901 he founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore. In 1908 he moved it to Bombay, and in 1931 he died. He introduced standardised syllabi, graded exams, notation, printed textbooks and public concerts. Disciples included Omkarnath Thakur, V.N. Patwardhan, B.R. Deodhar, Narayan Rao Vyas and Shankar Rao Vyas. He also created the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya Mandal, which runs examinations across India. The rival reformer of the period was Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande (1860-1936), who systematised Hindustani music through the thaat system of 10 thaats, wrote Hindustani Sangeet Paddhati, and organised All India Music Conferences from 1916 onward. He helped found the Marris College of Music in Lucknow (1926, now Bhatkhande Sangeet Vishwavidyalaya) and the Madhav Music College in Gwalior. Related institutions include the Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952), the first national academy for performing arts. UPSC may ask about gharanas (Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Jaipur-Atrauli, Patiala), the contributions of Bhatkhande and Paluskar, Tansen, Amir Khusrau, Purandara Dasa, the Carnatic Trinity, and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Fellowships.

question: Ashokan inscriptions suggest that the Pradeshika’, ‘Rajuka’ and ‘Yukta’ were important officers at the
subject: Ancient History
detail: Mauryan administration was layered: the centre (king, Mantriparishad, high officials such as Amatyas and Mahamatras), the province (Prantas, headed by Kumaras or Aryaputras, e.g. Tosali, Ujjain, Suvarnagiri, Taxila), the district and the village. Ashoka's Rock Edict III orders that the Yuktas, Rajukas and Pradeshikas go on anusamyana (tours) every five years, to inspect the work of administration and to teach dhamma. Megasthenes, Arthashastra and the edicts indicate that the Pradeshika was the head of the district, comparable to the Arthashastra's Pradeshta, who supervised collectors and tax officials and was responsible for the revenue and law-and-order of the region. The Rajuka was a revenue/survey and judicial officer with powers of reward and punishment (Pillar Edict IV). The Yukta was a subordinate officer who kept accounts and managed the king's property and records. Elimination: the village was under the Gramika, so (a) is wrong. Provincial governors were royal princes (Kumara/Aryaputra), so (c) is wrong. Central officials were Mahamatras and Amatyas, so (d) is wrong. Hence (b).
explanations: Wrong: village administration was under the Gramika (village headman) and Gopa (accountant of a group of villages), not these three officers.
Correct: Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta were district-level officers who toured the districts and handled revenue, survey, justice and accounts, as in Rock Edict III.
Wrong: provinces (Prantas) were governed by Kumaras or Aryaputras (royal princes) with Mahamatras; the three officers served below that level.
Wrong: central administration comprised the king, Mantriparishad, Amatyas, Mahamatras and heads of departments, not these three officers.
keyfact: Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta were Ashokan district-level officers who toured every five years (Rock Edict III).
option_notes: Village-level administration: the Gramika headed the village; the Arthashastra mentions Gopa (in charge of 5-10 villages) and Sthanika (in charge of a quarter of the district). Villages enjoyed considerable autonomy over local matters, and the village was the base unit of revenue (bhaga, one-sixth of produce) and land records.

District-level administration: the Mauryan empire was divided into districts (ahara or janapada) administered by officers such as Pradeshika (head), Rajuka (revenue, survey, judicial) and Yukta (subordinate accountant). They toured every five years under Ashoka's order and enforced dhamma along with ordinary administration.

Provincial administration: the Mauryan empire had four or five provinces: Uttarapatha (Taxila), Avantirashtra (Ujjain), Prachyapatha (Pataliputra), Kalinga (Tosali) and Dakshinapatha (Suvarnagiri). Governors were Kumaras or Aryaputras (royal princes), assisted by Mahamatras, and answered to the king in Pataliputra.

Central administration: the king was assisted by the Mantriparishad and high officials (Tirthas) such as the Mantri, Purohita, Senapati, Yuvaraja, Samaharta (revenue chief) and Sannidhata (treasurer), with 18 tirthas listed in the Arthashastra. Ashoka added Dhamma-mahamatras, appointed in his 13th regnal year, to promote dhamma and the welfare of subjects.
related: Rock Edict III orders Yuktas, Rajukas and Pradeshikas to tour every five years (anusamyana).
Pillar Edict IV gives Rajukas independence in reward and punishment.
The Arthashastra's Pradeshta is equivalent to the district head, the Pradeshika.
Provinces were governed by Kumaras or Aryaputras (royal princes).
Dhamma-mahamatras were appointed by Ashoka in his 13th regnal year.
The Gramika was the village headman; Sthanika and Gopa were intermediate officers.
Maski edict names Ashoka explicitly; James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837.
Samaharta was the revenue chief and Sannidhata the treasurer of the Mauryan state.
summary: The answer is (b) district-level administration. In Ashokan inscriptions (Rock Edict III and Pillar Edicts), the Pradeshika, Rajuka and Yukta are officers who toured and administered the district (ahara/janapada) level, handling revenue, survey, justice and assessment tours every five years.
topic_notes: Mauryan administration (c. 321-185 BCE) was highly centralised, with sources including Kautilya's Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indica, Ashokan edicts and Greek accounts. At the centre, the king held supreme authority, aided by the Mantriparishad, with 18 tirthas (high officials) and numerous departmental heads (adhyakshas) for areas such as mining, trade, agriculture, ships and the treasury. Samaharta handled revenue collection and Sannidhata the treasury. The empire was divided into provinces (Prantas) under royal princes (Kumara/Aryaputra), with capitals at Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri and Pataliputra. Provinces were divided into districts (ahara/janapada), headed by the Pradeshika, with Rajukas (revenue and justice, with powers of punishment as in Pillar Edict IV) and Yuktas (subordinate accountants). At the village level, the Gramika was the headman. Megasthenes describes Pataliputra's municipal administration through six committees of five members each, and the Nagaraka was the city officer. Ashoka introduced Dhamma-mahamatras (13th regnal year) and Prativedakas (reporters) to ensure access to the king. Spies (Gudhapurushas) formed a large network. Revenue came from bhaga (land tax, one-sixth), bali, and trade taxes; the army had six boards in Megasthenes' account. Ashokan edicts were in Prakrit using Brahmi script, with Kharosthi in the northwest, Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837. Key edicts: Rock Edict XIII (Kalinga War), Rock Edict III (tours by officers), Pillar Edict IV (Rajukas), and Minor Rock Edict I (Maski names Ashoka).

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of the Non-Cooperation Movement :
I. The Congress’ declared the attainment of ‘Swaraj’ by all legitimate and peaceful means to be its objective.
II. It was to be implemented in stages with civil disobedience and nonpayment of taxes for the next stage only if ‘Swaraj’ did not come within a year and the Government resorted to repression. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Modern History
detail: At the Calcutta Special Session (September 1920), presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai, the Congress approved the Non-Cooperation programme in principle, on Gandhi's resolution. The Nagpur Session (December 1920), presided over by C. Vijayaraghavachariar, confirmed it and changed the Congress creed. The goal became the attainment of Swaraj by all legitimate and peaceful means, replacing the earlier aim of self-government by constitutional means. This marked a shift to mass politics, and the Congress also reorganised itself with linguistic provincial committees and a smaller Working Committee. The movement was planned in phases. The first phase involved surrender of titles and honours, boycott of councils, law courts, and government schools and foreign cloth, and promotion of the charkha, khadi and national institutions. Civil disobedience and refusal to pay taxes were reserved for a later stage, to be launched only if Swaraj did not come within a year (Gandhi promised Swaraj within a year) and the government resorted to repression. Bardoli (Gujarat) was chosen for the later tax-refusal campaign, but the Chauri Chaura violence in February 1922 led Gandhi to withdraw the movement. Elimination: both statements match the Nagpur resolution and the staged plan, so (a), (b) and (d) fail.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it rejects Statement II, which is also correct as the movement was phased.
(b) is wrong because it rejects Statement I, which accurately describes the Congress goal adopted in 1920.
(c) is right because both statements accurately reflect the Congress objective and the staged design of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
(d) is wrong because both statements are historically accurate.
keyfact: Nagpur 1920: Congress goal became Swaraj by legitimate and peaceful means; Non-Cooperation was staged, with civil disobedience and tax refusal held for a later phase.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Nagpur Congress (1920) changed the creed to the attainment of Swaraj by all legitimate and peaceful means.
2 — Correct: The movement was staged, with civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes held in reserve for a later phase if Swaraj did not come within a year and the government used repression.
summary: The correct answer is (c): both statements are correct. The Congress, at its Nagpur session in December 1920, adopted the goal of Swaraj by all legitimate and peaceful means, and the Non-Cooperation Movement was designed to proceed in stages, with civil disobedience and non-payment of taxes held back as a later step.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. Austria Il. Bulgaria Ill. Croatia
IV. Serbia
V. Sweden VI. North Macedonia How many of the above are members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization?
subject: Economy
detail: NATO was founded by the North Atlantic Treaty (Washington Treaty) of 4 April 1949, and its collective defence clause is Article 5. Its headquarters are in Brussels. It has 32 members after Finland joined in April 2023 and Sweden in March 2024. Bulgaria joined in 2004 in the 'big bang' eastern enlargement. Croatia joined in 2009 along with Albania. North Macedonia joined in March 2020 as the 30th member, after resolving its name dispute with Greece through the Prespa Agreement. Sweden became the 32nd member on 7 March 2024 after Turkey and Hungary ratified its accession, ending its long policy of non-alignment. Austria has permanent neutrality under its 1955 constitutional law, so it participates only in Partnership for Peace and not as a member. Serbia is militarily neutral, takes part in Partnership for Peace, and has not applied for membership. Elimination logic: Austria and Serbia are out, so the count is 6 minus 2 = 4. That rules out (c) and (d), and (a) undercounts because it misses one of the four actual members.
explanations: (a) Wrong: three undercounts, since Bulgaria, Croatia, Sweden and North Macedonia are all members.
(b) Correct: Bulgaria, Croatia, Sweden and North Macedonia are members, which makes four, while Austria and Serbia are not.
(c) Wrong: five would require counting either Austria or Serbia, and both are non-members.
(d) Wrong: all six would include neutral Austria and Serbia, which are not NATO members.
keyfact: NATO has 32 members; Sweden (2024) and North Macedonia (2020) are recent entrants, while Austria and Serbia stay outside as neutral states.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Austria is permanently neutral and is only a Partnership for Peace partner, not a NATO member.
2 — Correct: Bulgaria joined NATO in 2004.
3 — Correct: Croatia joined NATO in 2009.
4 — Incorrect: Serbia is militarily neutral and is a PfP partner, not a NATO member.
5 — Correct: Sweden became a member in March 2024.
6 — Correct: North Macedonia joined in March 2020.
summary: The answer is (b): only four of the listed countries are NATO members. Bulgaria, Croatia, Sweden and North Macedonia are members, while Austria and Serbia are not, because Austria is constitutionally neutral and Serbia is a non-aligned partner.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. Bolivia Il. Brazil Ill. Colombia
IV. Ecuador
V. Paraguay VI. Venezuela Andes mountains pass through how many of the above countries?
subject: Geography
detail: The Andes are the longest continental mountain range in the world, about 7,000 km long, running north to south along the western edge of South America. They pass through seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. Of the six countries listed, Bolivia (I), Colombia (III), Ecuador (IV) and Venezuela (VI) have Andean territory, which gives four. Venezuela is the one students most often miss: the Cordillera de Mérida, the northeastern spur of the Andes, runs through it, and Pico Bolívar is its highest peak. Brazil (II) has the Guiana Highlands and the Brazilian Highlands but no Andes. Paraguay (V) is a lowland country covering the Gran Chaco and the Paraná plateau region, and it has no Andes. Elimination logic: start from the seven Andean countries, strike out Brazil and Paraguay as eastern interior or Atlantic-side countries, and count the remaining four. Options (a) and (b) undercount, and option (d) wrongly adds Brazil or Paraguay. The highest Andean peak is Aconcagua (6,961 m) in Argentina.
explanations: Wrong: only two undercounts. Four of the listed countries (Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela) have Andean territory.
Wrong: three misses one of the four, most likely Venezuela, whose Mérida Andes spur is easy to forget.
Correct: Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela are Andean. Brazil and Paraguay are not.
Wrong: five would require Brazil or Paraguay to have Andes, and neither does.
keyfact: The Andes span 7 countries (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina); Brazil and Paraguay have none.
option_notes: Only two: not the answer here. For reference, the Andes cross seven countries in total, and only a few (such as Chile and Argentina) are the ones most commonly associated with the range, so students often undercount.

Only three: not the answer here. Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador are often named as the 'central Andes' countries, but Colombia and Venezuela in the north also belong to the Andean system, so counting only three is wrong.

Only four: the correct answer. Bolivia has the Altiplano and the Cordillera Real and its capital La Paz is high in the Andes. Colombia's Andes split into three cordilleras (Occidental, Central, Oriental). Ecuador has the volcanic avenue including Cotopaxi and Chimborazo. Venezuela has the Cordillera de Mérida with Pico Bolívar (about 4,978 m).

Only five: not the answer here. It would need an extra country, and Brazil and Paraguay, the likely candidates, do not have the Andes. Brazil's relief is dominated by the Amazon basin and old plateaus, and Paraguay is divided by the Paraguay River into lowland regions.
related: The Andes pass through seven countries: Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina.
Aconcagua (6,961 m, Argentina) is the highest peak in the Andes and in the Western and Southern Hemispheres.
Chile and Ecuador are the two South American countries that do not share a border with Brazil.
Lake Titicaca on the Peru-Bolivia border is the highest navigable lake in the world.
The 'lithium triangle' comprises Chile, Argentina and Bolivia.
Venezuela's Pico Bolívar in the Cordillera de Mérida is its highest peak.
The Atacama Desert lies in the rain shadow of the Andes in Chile.
summary: The answer is (c) Only four. The Andes run through Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela among the listed countries, while Brazil and Paraguay lie east of the range and have no Andean territory.
topic_notes: The Andes are the world's longest exposed continental mountain chain, about 7,000 km long and up to 200-700 km wide, formed by the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate. This makes them part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with frequent earthquakes and volcanoes. The seven Andean countries are Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. Regions: Northern Andes (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador), Central Andes (Peru, Bolivia, northern Chile and Argentina, with the Altiplano plateau) and Southern Andes (Chile and Argentina, including Patagonia). Highest peak: Aconcagua (6,961 m, Argentina), the highest outside Asia. Ojos del Salado (Chile-Argentina) is the highest active volcano. Cotopaxi in Ecuador is one of the highest active volcanoes, and Chimborazo is the point farthest from Earth's centre. Lake Titicaca (Peru-Bolivia) is the highest navigable lake. The Atacama Desert lies west of the Andes in Chile and is among the driest places. The Amazon rises in the Peruvian Andes. Resources: copper (Chile, Peru), lithium (the 'lithium triangle' of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia), silver and tin. Crops of Andean origin: potato and quinoa. Livestock: llama and alpaca. Civilisation: the Inca empire. Countries that are not Andean: Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana. Chile and Ecuador are the two South American countries that do not border Brazil. Likely future angles: the Andes compared with the Rockies, the Himalayas and the Great Dividing Range, the rain shadow effect on Patagonia, and the Atacama.

question:
Consider the following water bodies :
I. Lake Tanganyika
II. Lake Tonlé Sap Ill. Patos Lagoon Through how many of them does the equator pass?
subject: Geography
detail: The equator (0° latitude) crosses Africa through Gabon, Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Somalia. In South America it crosses Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil. Of the great African lakes, Lake Victoria is the one the equator crosses, just north of its centre near Entebbe and Kampala. Lake Tanganyika extends from about 3°20'S (Bujumbura, Burundi) to about 8°48'S (Zambia), so it is wholly in the southern hemisphere. A student who assumes every East African Rift lake is equatorial would choose it wrongly. Tonlé Sap, Cambodia's great lake, lies at roughly 12.5-13.5°N, well north of the equator, and is known for its reversing flow with the Mekong. Patos Lagoon in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil, lies at about 30-32°S, close to the Uruguay border. Elimination logic: Tonlé Sap is in mainland Southeast Asia and Patos is in subtropical southern Brazil, so both are easily ruled out. Tanganyika is the only tricky one, and its latitudes between about 3°S and 9°S rule it out. So none is crossed.
explanations: Wrong: the equator does not pass through any one of them, because all three lie off the equator. Tanganyika is south of it, Tonlé Sap is north of it and Patos is far south of it.
Wrong: no two of the three are crossed. Tanganyika, Tonlé Sap and Patos are all clear of 0° latitude.
Wrong: this would require all three to straddle 0°, but they are at about 3-9°S, 13°N and 31°S respectively.
Correct: none of the three is crossed by the equator. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: Lake Victoria is the major African lake the equator crosses; Tanganyika (3°-9°S), Tonlé Sap (13°N) and Patos Lagoon (31°S) are not crossed.
option_notes: Only one: this would be right if Lake Victoria were listed, since the equator crosses it. Victoria is Africa's largest lake and the world's second largest freshwater lake by area. It is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania and is the main source of the White Nile. The Nile leaves it at Jinja, Uganda. Its only equatorial rival among the major lakes is Lake Kivu, which is just south of the equator, near 1.7°-2.5°S.

Only two: no pair among these lakes is crossed. The equator in Africa crosses Gabon, Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya and Somalia. It also crosses Lake Victoria, Mount Kenya's vicinity and the Congo basin. In Asia it passes through Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi) and in South America through Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil. It crosses the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans, and São Tomé and Príncipe in the Gulf of Guinea.

All the three: this is impossible because the three lakes lie on different continents, at widely different latitudes. Tanganyika is in the African Rift, Tonlé Sap in Southeast Asia and Patos in South America. The equator is 0° latitude, the longest circle of latitude at about 40,075 km. It divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres, and day and night are about equal there.

None: this is the correct answer. None of the three bodies is crossed by the equator. Tanganyika is in the southern hemisphere, in Africa's Great Rift Valley. Tonlé Sap is in the northern hemisphere, in Cambodia. Patos Lagoon is in the southern hemisphere, in Brazil at about 31°S. All three are therefore on one side or the other of 0° latitude.
related: The equator crosses Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake.
Lake Tanganyika is the world's longest freshwater lake and the second deepest, after Baikal.
Tonlé Sap's flow reverses in the monsoon because of Mekong floodwater.
Patos Lagoon in Brazil is the largest lagoon in South America.
Lake Baikal in Russia is the deepest lake, at about 1,642 m.
Lake Titicaca, shared by Peru and Bolivia, is the highest navigable lake.
Indonesia, Brazil, Ecuador and Kenya are among the countries the equator crosses.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states.
statements: I — Incorrect: Lake Tanganyika lies between about 3°S and 9°S, so the equator does not cross it. It is the world's longest freshwater lake (about 670 km) and the second deepest (about 1,470 m), after Baikal. It is the second largest by volume. It is shared by Tanzania, DR Congo, Burundi and Zambia, and is a Rift Valley lake. It drains through the Lukuga River into the Congo basin. It is famous for its cichlid fish, with many endemic species.

II — Incorrect: Tonlé Sap lies in Cambodia at about 13°N, far north of the equator. It is Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake and is connected to the Mekong by the Tonlé Sap River. The river reverses its flow in the monsoon, around June to October, when Mekong floodwater enters the lake and its area expands several times over. It was designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1997 and supports a major inland fishery. The Angkor temples lie near its northern shore, close to Siem Reap.

III — Incorrect: Patos Lagoon is in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, at about 30-32°S. It is the largest lagoon in South America and one of the largest in the world, about 250 km long. It is separated from the Atlantic by a sandbar and connects to the sea through the Rio Grande channel. Porto Alegre lies near its northern end, and the Guaíba lake flows into it. It is shallow and brackish, with Lagoa Mirim to its south. It supports ports and fisheries.
summary: The answer is (d) None. The equator passes through none of the three water bodies. Lake Tanganyika lies entirely south of the equator, Tonlé Sap is at about 13°N in Cambodia, and Patos Lagoon is at about 31°S in Brazil.
topic_notes: The equator is the 0° parallel, about 40,075 km long. It crosses 13 countries: Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, São Tomé and Príncipe, Gabon, Republic of Congo, DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Somalia, Maldives (marine waters), Indonesia and Kiribati. Of these, Maldives and Kiribati are crossed at sea or in island waters, and the Maldives are in the open Indian Ocean. Among water bodies, the equator crosses Lake Victoria, and it also passes over parts of the Amazon mouth region, the Gulf of Guinea, and the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Lake Kivu lies about 1.5°-2.5°S, and Lake Albert and Lake Edward lie close to the equator. Lake Edward is crossed by the equator. Lake Albert is north of it, near 1.5-2°N. Lake Turkana is at about 3-5°N. Lake Malawi (Nyasa) is at about 9-14°S. Lake Chad is at about 13°N. African Rift Valley lakes include Tanganyika, Malawi, Turkana, Kivu, Albert and Edward. The deepest is Baikal (about 1,642 m), then Tanganyika. Tonlé Sap is notable for its reverse flow. Patos Lagoon is the largest lagoon in South America. Other angles UPSC may ask: Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states, and Tropic of Capricorn passes through Chile, Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil, Namibia, Botswana, South Africa, Madagascar and Australia. Also: which countries share Lake Titicaca (Peru, Bolivia) and Lake Victoria, and which lakes are endorheic, such as the Caspian Sea and Aral Sea.

question:
Consider the following statements about turmeric during the year 2022-23 :
I. India is the largest producer and exporter of turmeric in the world. Il. More than 30 varieties of turmeric are grown in India. Ill. Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are major turmeric producing States in India. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is a rhizomatous spice, and India accounts for roughly 75-80% of world production and a dominant share of global exports, which makes it the leading producer, consumer and exporter. The Spices Board of India and the Ministry of Commerce report that India grows over 30 varieties, such as Lakadong (Meghalaya, high curcumin), Salem, Erode, Alleppey Finger, Rajapuri, Sangli and Duggirala. Major producing States are Telangana (the largest in recent years, with Nizamabad as a key hub), Maharashtra (Sangli, Hingoli), Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu (Erode), with Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Assam also contributing. In 2022-23, turmeric exports were reported at around 1.5 lakh tonnes, worth over 200 million USD. The National Turmeric Board was announced for Telangana (Nizamabad) in 2023 and notified in January 2025. Elimination logic: since statements I, II and III are each factually supported, any option that excludes one of them (a, b, c) must be wrong. Only the option accepting all three, (d), is consistent. In such 'consider the statements' questions, check whether any statement is an obvious extreme claim; here none is.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it omits statement III, which is correct; these four States are major producers.
(b) is wrong because it omits statement I, which is correct; India is the top producer and exporter.
(c) is wrong because it omits statement II, which is correct; India grows over 30 varieties.
(d) is correct because statements I, II and III are all factually accurate.
keyfact: India produces about 75-80% of the world's turmeric, grows 30+ varieties, and the National Turmeric Board is based in Nizamabad, Telangana.
statements: 1 — Correct: India is the largest producer, consumer and exporter of turmeric in the world, with a share of about 75% or more of global output.
2 — Correct: India grows more than 30 varieties, including Lakadong, Salem, Erode, Alleppey and Rajapuri.
3 — Correct: Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are among the major turmeric producing States.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. India is the world's largest producer and exporter of turmeric, grows more than 30 varieties, and its major producing States include Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

question:
Which of the following are the evidences of the phenomenon of continental drift?
I. The belt of ancient rocks from Brazil coast matches with those from Western Africa. Il. The gold deposits of Ghana are derived from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side. Ill. The Gondwana system of sediments from India is known to have its counterparts in six different landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Geography
detail: Continental drift was proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 (published 1915, 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans'). He argued that all continents formed a single supercontinent, Pangaea, which broke up about 200 million years ago into Laurasia and Gondwanaland. His evidences were: (1) Matching coastlines (the Sir Edward Bullard computer fit at 1000 fathom depth); (2) Rock-type similarity, where ancient rock belts of Brazil match those of western Africa; (3) Tillite, glacial deposits of the Gondwana system, found in India, Africa, South America, Australia, Antarctica and the Falkland Islands (the six landmasses); (4) Placer deposits, such as the gold of Ghana, which has no source rocks locally and is believed to come from the Brazil plateau; (5) Distribution of fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris. Since I, II and III each match these standard NCERT evidences, none can be eliminated. Options (a), (b) and (d) each wrongly reject a valid statement. The key is to recall the NCERT list: continental fit, rock similarity, tillite, placer deposits, fossils.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement II, which is also a valid evidence (Ghana gold placer deposits).
Wrong: it leaves out statement III, the Gondwana system sediments found across six southern landmasses.
Correct: statements I, II and III are all standard evidences of continental drift.
Wrong: it leaves out statement I, the match of the Brazil and West Africa ancient rock belts.
keyfact: Evidence for continental drift: coastline fit, matching rock belts, tillite (Gondwana), placer gold (Ghana-Brazil) and fossils.
option_notes: Statements I and III only: this combination would be correct only if the Ghana gold placer link were not an evidence. It is, so this option is incomplete. It includes rock-belt matching and the Gondwana sediments, which are both genuine evidences used by Wegener and in NCERT.

Statements I and II only: it would omit the Gondwana system. The Gondwana sediments are among the strongest evidences, since tillite shows glaciation across India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica. The option is therefore incomplete.

Statements I, II and III: this is the full set. Wegener's evidences include coastline fit, rock similarity, tillite, placer deposits and fossil distribution. This option captures rock belts, placer gold and Gondwana sediments, and is the official answer.

Statements II and III only: it would drop the Brazil-West Africa rock belt match. That match, about 2 billion year old rock belts on both sides of the Atlantic, is a classic piece of evidence, so the option is incomplete.
related: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912.
Pangaea split into Laurasia and Gondwanaland.
Mesosaurus fossils are found in South Africa and Brazil.
Seafloor spreading was proposed by Harry Hess in 1961.
Vine and Matthews explained magnetic striping on ocean floors in 1963.
Plate tectonics was formulated in 1967 by McKenzie, Parker and Morgan.
India's Gondwana coal is found in the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys.
statements: I — Correct: The ancient rock belts of the Brazil coast match those of western Africa, indicating the two were once contiguous. The Brazilian and West African belts are about 2 billion years old and have similar rock ages and structure. Wegener used such geological continuity, along with the jigsaw fit of the South Atlantic coasts, as proof that South America and Africa were joined within Gondwanaland before separating in the Mesozoic.

II — Correct: The gold deposits of Ghana have no local source rocks, so they are regarded as placer deposits derived from the Brazil plateau when Africa and South America lay side by side. Placer deposits are minerals concentrated by water in sediments. NCERT cites this as evidence from the Gulf of Guinea coast, supporting the idea that the two continents shared a drainage and geological history before drifting apart.

III — Correct: The Gondwana system of sediments in India, named after the Gondwana region of central India, contains coal, tillite and plant fossils. Its counterparts occur in India, South Africa, South America, Australia, Antarctica and Madagascar, six southern landmasses. The Gondwana sequence spans late Carboniferous to Jurassic. The tillite shows a widespread glaciation, which is best explained if these landmasses were joined near the South Pole. India's Gondwana beds hold most of its coal.
summary: The answer is (c): all three statements are accepted evidences of continental drift. Matching ancient rock belts across the Atlantic, the Ghana gold placer deposits linked to the Brazil plateau, and the Gondwana sediments found in six southern landmasses all point to continents once joined.
topic_notes: Continental drift theory was put forward by Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, in 1912. He proposed that all continents formed a single landmass, Pangaea, surrounded by the global ocean Panthalassa. About 200 million years ago Pangaea split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south). Drift forces proposed were pole-fleeing force (due to Earth's rotation and equatorial bulge) and tidal force (Moon and Sun). Evidences: continental fit, rock-age similarity, tillite deposits, placer deposits, and fossils such as Mesosaurus (a freshwater reptile in South Africa and Brazil) and Glossopteris flora. Criticism: the forces were too weak to move continents. Later evidences led to new theories. Post-war studies of the ocean floor found mid-oceanic ridges, and Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in 1961. Palaeomagnetism and the magnetic striping on both sides of ridges (Vine and Matthews, 1963) supported it. In 1967 McKenzie, Parker and Morgan formulated plate tectonics, with seven major plates (Pacific, North American, South American, African, Eurasian, Indo-Australian, Antarctic) and several minor plates. Plate boundaries are divergent, convergent and transform. Convection currents in the mantle, as proposed by Arthur Holmes, are the driving mechanism. India moved north after separating from Gondwana, collided with Eurasia and raised the Himalayas, and the Deccan Traps formed as it passed over the Réunion hotspot. Possible next questions: Pangaea's breakup, plate boundaries, Wegener versus Hess, and the Gondwana coalfields.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : The amount of dust particles in the atmosphere is more in subtropical and temperate areas than in equatorial and polar regions.
Statement II : Subtropical and temperate areas have less dry winds. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct [ P.T.O
subject: Geography
detail: This question comes from the NCERT chapter on the composition and structure of the atmosphere. Dust particles (solid particles or aerosols) come from fine soil, smoke-soot, ash, pollen, sea salt, and meteoritic debris. They are concentrated in the lower atmosphere. NCERT states that dust is more abundant in subtropical and temperate regions because of dry winds there, and less abundant in equatorial and polar regions. The subtropical belts (about 20-35 degrees N and S) lie under descending dry air of the high-pressure zones. They contain the major deserts: the Sahara, Arabia, Thar, Australian deserts, and Kalahari. Dry, loose soil and strong winds lift large quantities of dust. Temperate interiors, such as the loess areas, also have dry winds. The equatorial region is humid and rainy, so rain washes dust out. Polar areas have little loose, dry soil because of ice cover. Dust acts as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation, and it causes scattering that produces the colours of sunrise, sunset and the sky. Elimination: Statement I is true, and Statement II contradicts the NCERT reasoning, so only (c) fits.
explanations: Wrong. This option treats Statement II as correct and as the explanation. Statement II is factually wrong, because the dry winds in these areas are more, not less.
Wrong. This option also treats Statement II as correct. Statement II is not correct, so the option fails whether or not it explains Statement I.
Correct. Statement I matches NCERT, and Statement II is false because subtropical and temperate areas have more dry winds, which cause more dust.
Wrong. This option calls Statement I incorrect, but Statement I is correct. It also treats Statement II as correct, which is false.
keyfact: Dust is most abundant in subtropical and temperate areas because dry winds there lift loose soil, and equatorial and polar areas have less dust.
option_notes: Both statements correct with II as the explanation. This is the standard assertion-reason format in UPSC. It would hold only if dry winds were fewer and that fewer winds led to more dust, which makes no physical sense. Dust generation needs dry, loose soil and strong winds. The real explanation is more dry winds in the subtropics and temperate interiors.

Both statements correct but II is not the explanation. This format is used when both statements are true yet unconnected. Here Statement II is factually false, because the dry subtropical belts and desert-bordering temperate areas have more dry winds. So the option is invalid even though the format is common.

Statement I correct and Statement II incorrect. This is the correct answer. Dust is more abundant in subtropical and temperate regions because of dry winds, deserts and loose soils. Equatorial regions are humid and rainy, and polar regions are icy, so both have less dust. Statement II reverses the actual condition.

Statement I incorrect and Statement II correct. This is the reverse of the true position. Statement I is correct, since dust is indeed more in subtropical and temperate areas, and Statement II is wrong, since dry winds are more there. UPSC often uses reversed options like this as distractors.
related: Atmosphere composition by volume: N2 78%, O2 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO2 about 0.04%.
Water vapour decreases from equator to poles and with altitude.
Dust and aerosols act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation.
The Harmattan is a dry, dusty northeasterly wind from the Sahara toward the West African coast.
Loo is a hot, dry summer wind in northwest India and Pakistan.
Foehn and Chinook are warm, dry downslope winds on the leeward side of mountains.
The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere at about 15-35 km.
Troposphere is thickest at the equator (about 18 km) and thinnest at the poles (about 8 km).
statements: 1 — Correct: NCERT says dust is more abundant in subtropical and temperate regions than in equatorial and polar regions. Dust (aerosol) particles come from soil, smoke, ash, pollen, sea salt and meteors. They are concentrated in the lower troposphere. They serve as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour condenses to form clouds and fog, and they scatter light, producing red sunsets and the blue sky. Hot deserts at 20-35 degrees (the Sahara, Thar, Arabia) are major sources. Dust storms such as the Harmattan and Saharan dust travel across oceans. Equatorial rain and polar ice reduce the amount of dust.

2 — Incorrect: Subtropical and temperate areas have more dry winds, not fewer, and this explains the larger dust load. The subtropical high-pressure belts have descending, dry air and many deserts. Examples of dry winds are the Loo in the Indo-Gangetic plain, the Harmattan from the Sahara toward West Africa, the Sirocco and Khamsin from North Africa, and the Foehn and Chinook in temperate mountain regions. The equatorial belt is humid with convectional rain, and polar areas are cold and ice-covered. These conditions mean little dry-wind lifting of dust there.
summary: The answer is (c). Statement I is correct because dust is more abundant over subtropical and temperate latitudes than over equatorial and polar regions. Statement II is incorrect because these areas, especially the subtropical belts, have more dry winds, not fewer, and that dryness is part of why dust is abundant.
topic_notes: Atmospheric composition: Nitrogen is about 78%, oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%, and carbon dioxide about 0.04% by volume. Water vapour varies from 0 to 4% and decreases from the equator toward the poles. Dust, or solid particles, includes smoke, soot, ash, pollen, sea salt and fine soil. It is found mainly in the lower troposphere and is concentrated in subtropical and temperate regions because of dry winds. Dust is much less abundant in equatorial regions, where rain removes it, and in polar regions. Roles of dust and aerosols: they act as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation and cloud formation; they scatter and reflect sunlight, causing the blue sky and the red colours at sunrise and sunset; and they influence visibility, health and climate. Large volcanic eruptions can inject aerosols into the stratosphere and cool the globe, as with Pinatubo in 1991. Ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere at about 15-35 km and absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Layers of the atmosphere are the troposphere (about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator), the stratosphere, the mesosphere, the thermosphere (which holds the ionosphere), and the exosphere. Dry winds and dust events include the Loo, Harmattan, Sirocco, Khamsin, Simoom, and Foehn and Chinook winds. Pressure belts: the subtropical highs lie at about 30 degrees, and the Sahara and other hot deserts lie under them. Likely angles for the future are particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10, the Air Quality Index, dust storms in Rajasthan and the Thar, Saharan dust crossing the Atlantic, and the role of aerosols in cloud seeding and climate change.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Statement I : In January, in the Northern Hemisphere, the isotherms bend equatorward while crossing the landmasses, and poleward while crossing the oceans. Statement II : In January, the air over the oceans is warmer than that over the landmasses in the Northern Hemisphere. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I (b) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I (c) Statement I is correct but
subject: Geography
detail: Isotherms are lines joining places with equal temperature (reduced to sea level). They would run parallel to latitudes if the Earth's surface were uniform, but the unequal heating of land and water deflects them. Water has a high specific heat, mixes by currents and waves, and allows heat to penetrate deeper, so it heats and cools slowly. Land has a low specific heat, is opaque, and heats and cools quickly. In January (Northern Hemisphere winter) the land loses heat rapidly and becomes colder than the sea at the same latitude. Oceans hold the stored heat and are further warmed by warm currents such as the Gulf Stream/North Atlantic Drift and the Kuroshio. Hence warm air over the oceans pushes isotherms poleward, for example over the North Atlantic off Norway, while cold continental interiors such as Siberia and Canada pull isotherms equatorward. In July the pattern reverses. The elimination logic is as follows. Statement II is factually true. It is also the direct cause of the bending in Statement I, so (b) fails. (c) and (d) deny a true statement.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and the warmer ocean air of Statement II is the reason the isotherms bend poleward over oceans and equatorward over land in Statement I.
Wrong. Although both statements are correct, Statement II does explain Statement I, because the land-sea temperature contrast is the cause of the bending.
Wrong. Statement II is correct, since oceans are warmer than land in the Northern Hemisphere in January.
Wrong. Statement I is correct, because the bending of isotherms is exactly as described. Only a reversed description would be wrong, and that applies to July.
keyfact: In January in the Northern Hemisphere, isotherms bend equatorward over cold land and poleward over warm oceans, because water heats and cools more slowly than land.
option_notes: Both statements correct and II explains I is the standard 'reasoning' option in UPSC assertion-type questions. It applies when the second statement states the cause of the first. Here, differential heating and cooling of land and water explains the isotherm pattern. This is the official answer.

Both statements correct but II does not explain I applies when the two statements are true but independent. For example, 'The Equator receives the most insolation' and 'Doldrums are a low-wind belt' would be related but not causal. It is the commonest trap option in this format, but here the link is causal, so it is wrong.

Statement I correct but II incorrect would hold if the isotherm description were true but the oceans were colder than land. In January the opposite holds. In July the Northern Hemisphere oceans are cooler than the land, so Statement II would be wrong in that month. The month matters.

Statement I incorrect but II correct would apply if the isotherm bending were reversed, as in July in the Northern Hemisphere, when isotherms bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans. In January the description in Statement I is accurate, so this option fails.
related: Normal lapse rate is about 6.5°C per 1000 m, also called vertical temperature gradient.
Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature, reduced to sea level.
In July, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans.
Thermal equator lies on average near 5°N and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.
Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift keep north-west European ports ice-free in winter.
Earth's albedo is about 35% of incoming insolation.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are more parallel because of the dominance of oceans.
Verkhoyansk and Oymyakon in Siberia record the greatest annual range of temperature in the Northern Hemisphere.
statements: I — Correct: In January in the Northern Hemisphere, isotherms bend equatorward over the landmasses (cold land) and poleward over the oceans (warm water). Isotherms join places with the same temperature, usually reduced to sea level to remove altitude effects. The bending shows the land-sea contrast. It is most striking in the North Atlantic, where the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry heat towards Norway, and over the cold Siberian and Canadian interiors. In the Southern Hemisphere, which has much more ocean, isotherms are far more parallel to the latitudes. In July the bending reverses: isotherms bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans.

II — Correct: In January the air over Northern Hemisphere oceans is warmer than over the landmasses at the same latitude. Water has a high specific heat, so it warms and cools slowly. Heat penetrates deep into water through mixing, currents and waves, and the stored heat is released slowly in winter. Land is opaque, has a low specific heat and cools quickly, producing intense winter highs such as the Siberian High. Warm ocean currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) add to oceanic warmth. This is why coastal places have a maritime climate with a low annual range and continental interiors have a high annual range, as at Verkhoyansk.
summary: The answer is (a): both statements are correct and Statement II explains Statement I. In January the oceans in the Northern Hemisphere are warmer than the landmasses at the same latitude, so isotherms bend poleward over oceans and equatorward over continents.
topic_notes: Distribution of temperature is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea (continentality), ocean currents, prevailing winds, cloud cover and relief. Isotherms are lines joining places of equal temperature, usually reduced to sea level to remove the altitude effect. They would run east-west if the Earth's surface were uniform. Land-sea contrast makes them bend. In January in the Northern Hemisphere, isotherms bend equatorward over land (cold continents) and poleward over oceans (warm currents). In July, isotherms bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans. The Southern Hemisphere has more ocean, so its isotherms are more regular and parallel, and the deviation is smaller. Water has a high specific heat, is transparent, and mixes by currents, so it warms and cools slowly. Land is opaque, has a low specific heat, and heats and cools quickly. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift keep north-west Europe warm, with ports such as Hammerfest and Murmansk staying ice-free. The Labrador and Oyashio cold currents cool eastern Canada and Japan's north-east. The coldest Northern Hemisphere regions in winter are Siberia (Verkhoyansk, Oymyakon) and Greenland, and the hottest in summer are the subtropical deserts. Annual range of temperature is highest in continental interiors and lowest in the equatorial oceans. Thermal equator is the line joining the highest mean temperature at each longitude. It moves north in July and south in January, and lies north of the geographic equator on average, near 5°N. Temperature inversion, lapse rate (about 6.5°C per km, the normal lapse rate), and heat budget (insolation 100 units, 35 reflected as albedo) are other related angles.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : In the context of effect of water on rocks, chalk is known as a very permeable rock whereas clay is known as quite an impermeable or least permeable rock.
Statement II : Chalk is porous and hence can absorb water. Statement III : Clay is not at all porous. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I Only one of the Statements II and
Ill is correct and that explains Statement I Neither Statement II nor State
subject: Geography
detail: Porosity and permeability are different properties. Porosity is the proportion of void space in a rock, which decides how much water it can hold. Permeability is how easily water flows through those voids, which depends on pore size, connectivity and fractures. Chalk is a soft, fine-grained limestone made of calcite from microscopic marine organisms (coccoliths). It is porous and also jointed, so it absorbs water and lets it percolate. This is why chalk forms good aquifers, for example in the London Basin and the North and South Downs. Clay is made of very fine particles (under 0.002 mm). Its total porosity can be high, often 40-70 percent, but the pores are so small that molecular attraction holds water tightly and blocks flow. So clay is an aquiclude, an impermeable layer. Statement III says clay is 'not at all porous', which is factually wrong, so it cannot explain Statement I. Statement II gives the right reason for chalk's permeability. Elimination: since III is false, options (a) and (b), which need both statements correct, fall. Option (d), which says neither is correct, fails because II is correct. That leaves (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it requires both II and III to be correct. III is false, since clay is porous but its pores are too small and unconnected to transmit water.
