The Mission is linked to India's goals of net zero by 2070 and 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.

Applications: fertilisers (green ammonia), refining, steel (direct reduced iron), heavy transport, shipping and energy storage.

Challenges: high cost, electrolyser supply chains, water needs, storage and transport infrastructure, and low demand.

Other angles UPSC could ask about: electrolyser types, fuel cells, the Hydrogen Council, the Hydrogen Valley Platform under Mission Innovation, Hydrogen Energy missions in other countries, and the Hydrogen Bus pilot projects in India.

question:
Consider the following statements with regard to involvement of private entities in India’s space programme : 48. ila The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) is an autonomous agency formed to facilitate participation of private entities.
2. Agnikul Cosmos launched the world’s first flight using 3D-printed rocket engine. :
3. Skyroot Aerospace has developed liquid fuel for GSLV. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: India opened its space sector to private players in June 2020. IN-SPACe was created as a single-window, autonomous agency within the Department of Space. It authorises private launches and satellites, shares ISRO facilities and expertise, and promotes industry. Its chairman reports to the Space Commission. NSIL, the PSU arm of the Department of Space, handles commercial exploitation of ISRO's products and services. The Indian Space Policy 2023 defines roles: ISRO focuses on R&D, NSIL on commercial work, and IN-SPACe on authorisation. Agnikul Cosmos (IIT Madras incubated, Chennai) launched Agnibaan SORTEd on 30 May 2024 from its own private launchpad at Sriharikota. It was powered by Agnilet, a single-piece, fully 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine, billed as the world's first such launch. Skyroot Aerospace (Hyderabad) launched Vikram-S on 18 Nov 2022, India's first private rocket to reach space. It develops the Vikram series of launch vehicles with its own solid and liquid engines (Kalam, Raman, Dhawan). GSLV is ISRO's vehicle and uses the Vikas liquid stage, so Skyroot did not develop its fuel. Eliminate 3 and you are left with (c).
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, which is correct because Agnibaan used a single-piece 3D-printed engine.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false, since Skyroot did not develop liquid fuel for GSLV.
Right: statements 1 and 2 are correct, and statement 3 is incorrect.
Wrong: it counts statement 3 as correct, but Skyroot builds its own Vikram rockets and engines and is not tied to GSLV fuel.
keyfact: IN-SPACe = autonomous private-space facilitator; Agnikul = single-piece 3D-printed engine flight (2024); Skyroot = Vikram rockets, not GSLV fuel.
option_notes: Option (a) says 1 only. It would be right if IN-SPACe were the only correct item, but Agnikul's 3D-printed engine flight (Agnibaan SORTEd, 30 May 2024) is also accurate. IN-SPACe is the autonomous Department of Space agency, created in 2020, that authorises and promotes private space activity. It is headquartered in Ahmedabad and works alongside ISRO and NSIL under the Indian Space Policy 2023.

Option (b) says 2 and 3 only. It wrongly rejects statement 1 and wrongly accepts statement 3. Statement 2 is accurate: Agnikul's Agnilet engine is a single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine. Skyroot Aerospace, however, builds the Vikram launch vehicle series, and Vikram-S flew on 18 Nov 2022. It is unrelated to GSLV fuel, so this combination fails.

Option (c) says 1 and 2 only. This is the correct answer. IN-SPACe is the autonomous facilitator and authoriser of private space players, and Agnikul's Agnibaan SORTEd (30 May 2024, from the Dhanush launchpad at Sriharikota) used a 3D-printed engine. Skyroot's work is on its own rockets, so statement 3 is excluded.

Option (d) says all three are correct. It fails only because of statement 3. Skyroot Aerospace of Hyderabad developed the Vikram-S sub-orbital rocket and engines such as Raman, Kalam and Dhawan. GSLV is ISRO's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, with a solid, a liquid Vikas and a cryogenic stage, and Skyroot did not develop its fuel.
related: IN-SPACe was announced in June 2020 and is headquartered in Ahmedabad.
NSIL was set up in 2019 as a PSU under the Department of Space.
Vikram-S (Skyroot) was launched on 18 Nov 2022 and was India's first private rocket to reach space.
Agnibaan SORTEd launched on 30 May 2024 from the private launchpad Dhanush at Sriharikota.
Indian Space Policy 2023 defines the roles of ISRO, NSIL and IN-SPACe.
Agnikul is incubated at IIT Madras, and Skyroot is based in Hyderabad.
Up to 100% FDI is allowed in space under the 2024 liberalisation, with limits by segment.
A Rs 1,000 crore VC fund for space startups was announced in 2024.
statements: 1 — Correct: IN-SPACe is the autonomous, single-window nodal agency under the Department of Space for private participation. It was announced in June 2020 as part of space-sector reforms and is headquartered in Ahmedabad. It authorises space activities by non-government entities, lets them use ISRO facilities, and promotes and hand-holds startups. It also acts as a regulator and a promoter. Its board is chaired by a chairperson, and it works alongside ISRO and NSIL. The Indian Space Policy 2023 formalised its role. It also runs schemes such as the seed fund and technology adoption support for space startups.

2 — Correct: Agnikul Cosmos, founded in 2017 by Srinath Ravichandran and Moin SPM, is incubated at IIT Madras. Its Agnibaan SORTEd (Sub-Orbital Technology Demonstrator) flew on 30 May 2024 from India's first private launchpad, Dhanush, at Sriharikota. The single-stage vehicle used the Agnilet semi-cryogenic engine, which is fully 3D printed as one piece. It ran on liquid oxygen and kerosene. The flight was widely described as the first launch of a rocket with a single-piece 3D-printed engine. The company signed a framework agreement with ISRO in 2021.

3 — Incorrect: Skyroot Aerospace, founded in 2018 in Hyderabad by Pawan Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka, builds the Vikram family of launch vehicles. Its Vikram-S became India's first private rocket to reach space (18 Nov 2022, mission Prarambh). It develops in-house engines named Raman, Kalam (solid) and Dhawan (cryogenic, 3D printed). Dhawan-1 uses liquid natural gas and liquid oxygen. It is not a supplier of fuel to ISRO's GSLV, which is an ISRO vehicle with a solid, liquid and cryogenic stage design.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 2 only, so the unofficial key is right. IN-SPACe is an autonomous agency under the Department of Space that authorises and promotes private participation, and Agnikul's Agnibaan SORTEd (May 2022) used a single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine. Statement 3 is wrong because Skyroot builds its own Vikram rockets and engines (Raman, Kalam, Dhawan), not liquid fuel for GSLV.
topic_notes: India's space sector was opened to private players in June 2020 through reforms announced under Atmanirbhar Bharat. The institutional framework has three arms. ISRO focuses on R&D and missions. NSIL (New Space India Limited, created in 2019, a PSU under the Department of Space) handles commercial and demand-driven operations such as PSLV and SSLV production through industry. IN-SPACe is the autonomous single-window agency for authorising, promoting and regulating non-government entities, and it offers access to ISRO facilities. The Indian Space Policy 2023 sets out these roles and allows private participation across the space value chain. FDI in space was liberalised in 2024, with up to 100% allowed (automatic route for some segments such as satellite manufacturing and component making, with limits for launch vehicles). Key startups: Skyroot Aerospace (Vikram-S, 18 Nov 2022, India's first private rocket launched to space; Vikram-1 orbital rocket planned); Agnikul Cosmos (Agnibaan SORTEd, 30 May 2024, 3D-printed engine, own launchpad Dhanush at Sriharikota); Pixxel (hyperspectral imaging satellites); Dhruva Space; Digantara (space situational awareness); Bellatrix. Government support includes a Rs 1,000 crore venture capital fund for space startups, announced in 2024. The sector aims to raise India's share of the global space economy. Other angles UPSC may test include PSLV and SSLV technology transfer, the HAL-L&T consortium that builds PSLV, SSLV technology transfer to HAL, the Space Activities Bill, and the Gaganyaan and Bharatiya Antariksh Station plans.

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to drone swarms is/are correct ? il They use Terahertz band of frequency to communicate with the command centre. 2: Individual drones in the swarm can communicate with other drones in the swarm.
3. GPS Spoofing is a commonly used technique to counter drone swarm attack. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: A drone swarm is a group of unmanned aerial vehicles that operate collectively through decentralised, networked control, often using swarm intelligence inspired by bees or birds. The defining feature is peer-to-peer (mesh or ad hoc) communication: each drone shares position, status and targets with its neighbours, so the swarm can self-organise, redistribute tasks and continue even if some drones are lost. Links to the command centre typically use established radio-frequency bands such as 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz, sometimes cellular or satellite links, and military datalinks. Terahertz communication is still experimental, suffers heavy atmospheric absorption and has short range, so it is not what swarms commonly use; this removes statement 1 and therefore options (a), (c) and (d). Counter-drone (C-UAS) measures include radar and RF detection, jamming of control links, GPS jamming and spoofing to mislead navigation, lasers, high-power microwaves, nets and kinetic interceptors. Since many drones depend on GNSS navigation, spoofing is a commonly cited soft-kill technique. India has fielded systems such as DRDO's anti-drone system with jammers and spoofers. Only statements 2 and 3 survive, giving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes only statement 1, which is false, and omits correct statements 2 and 3.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 are accurate and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it includes false statement 1 and leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
Wrong: it accepts statement 1, but Terahertz is not the common swarm communication band.
keyfact: Swarms coordinate via inter-drone mesh links over ordinary RF bands, and GPS spoofing/jamming is a standard counter-drone tool; Terahertz is not in common use.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Swarms use conventional RF bands (2.4/5.8 GHz, datalinks), not Terahertz, which is experimental and heavily attenuated.
2 — Correct: Inter-drone communication in a mesh or peer-to-peer network is the core feature enabling swarm coordination.
3 — Correct: GPS spoofing, along with jamming, is a recognised soft-kill counter-drone technique against GNSS-dependent drones.
summary: The unofficial key (b) looks doubtful, and I think the correct answer is most likely (b) only if statement 1 is false, which it is, so (b) holds. Statement 1 is wrong because drone swarms use conventional radio/Wi-Fi/mesh links, not Terahertz bands. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: swarm members communicate with each other, and GPS spoofing is a recognised counter-drone technique.

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to GenomeIndia Project is/are correct ?
1. It is a part of the Human Genome Project.
2. The project is funded by _ the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Government of India.
3. Its primary aim is to build a catalogue of genetic diversity of the Indian population. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Science & Tech
detail: GenomeIndia is a national genomics initiative launched by DBT, coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research (CBR), IISc Bengaluru, with about 20 partner institutions. It aims to sequence 10,000 genomes initially, drawn from over 99 distinct population groups across India, to build a reference genome database for the Indian population. In January 2025 the PM released the first phase data of 10,000 genomes, which is stored at the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC), Faridabad, under the Indian Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy framework. The aim is to understand population-specific variants, support precision medicine and diagnosis of genetic and rare diseases, and reduce reliance on Western reference datasets. The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a separate international effort, run from 1990 to 2003 and led by the US and UK with other countries, and India did not take part. Elimination logic: statement 1 is false, which removes (a), (c) and (d). Statements 2 and 3 are both true, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes only statement 1, which is false because GenomeIndia is not part of the Human Genome Project, and it leaves out the true statements 2 and 3.
Correct: statements 2 (DBT funding) and 3 (cataloguing Indian genetic diversity) are true, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which is false, and rejects statement 3, which is true.
Wrong: it includes the false statement 1, so 'all three' cannot hold.
keyfact: GenomeIndia is a DBT-funded national project to catalogue the genetic diversity of Indians, not a part of the Human Genome Project.
option_notes: Statement 1 alone. It would hold only if GenomeIndia were a sub-project of the Human Genome Project, which it is not. The HGP (1990-2003) was an international effort to map all human genes and sequence the roughly 3 billion base pairs. It was funded mainly by the US NIH and DOE and by the UK Wellcome Trust, and its data was released publicly under the Bermuda Principles. India was not a partner.

Statements 2 and 3 only. GenomeIndia is a DBT-funded programme. It is led by the Centre for Brain Research, IISc, and builds a genetic variation catalogue of the Indian population. The first 10,000 genomes were announced in January 2025, and the data is hosted at the IBDC, Faridabad. It supports precision medicine and the diagnosis of rare diseases.

Statements 1 and 2 only. This pairs the DBT funding fact, which is true, with the wrong claim of HGP linkage. DBT is under the Ministry of Science and Technology, was set up in 1986, and is headquartered in New Delhi. It runs BRIC, the Indian Biological Data Centre and the BioE3 policy. It also funded INSACOG for genome surveillance of SARS-CoV-2.

All three statements. This option fails because statement 1 is false. Genome projects related to the HGP include ENCODE, the 1000 Genomes Project, HapMap and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium. Other national projects include UK Biobank, Genome of Europe, Genome Asia 100K, and Saudi and Emirati genome programmes. GenomeIndia is India's counterpart of these.
related: GenomeIndia phase 1 data of 10,000 genomes was released in January 2025.
The Centre for Brain Research at IISc Bengaluru coordinates GenomeIndia.
GenomeIndia data is hosted at the Indian Biological Data Centre, Faridabad.
The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003.
INSACOG was launched in December 2020 to track SARS-CoV-2 variants.
The CSIR IndiGen programme sequenced 1,008 Indian genomes.
The Department of Biotechnology was set up in 1986 under the Ministry of Science and Technology.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: GenomeIndia is an independent Indian initiative, not a component of the Human Genome Project. The HGP was an international public consortium that began in 1990 and declared the sequence essentially complete in April 2003. It was coordinated by the US NIH and the Department of Energy, with major contributions from the UK (Wellcome Trust Sanger), Japan, France, Germany and China. India was not a formal member. It produced the first reference human genome of about 3 billion base pairs, and the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium completed the gaps in 2022.

2 — Correct: The project is funded and driven by the Department of Biotechnology under the Ministry of Science and Technology. DBT approved it in 2020 as a mission-mode project. It is coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research at IISc Bengaluru, with partners including IITs, CSIR labs, NIBMG Kalyani and other universities and research institutes. DBT also supports related efforts such as the Indian Biological Data Centre at Faridabad, the Biotech-KISAN scheme, the BioE3 policy and the Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG).

3 — Correct: The primary aim is to create a catalogue of genetic variation across Indian populations, and eventually a reference genome. Samples were collected from about 99 groups across the country, with 10,000 genomes sequenced in phase 1 using whole genome sequencing and genotyping arrays. India has thousands of endogamous groups, so it harbours unique variants. The catalogue helps in precision medicine, polygenic risk scores and understanding genetic disorders such as thalassemia and sickle cell disease. Data access is through the IBDC under controlled-access rules.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only, so the unofficial expected answer is correct. GenomeIndia is an Indian national project funded by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) to catalogue the genetic diversity of the Indian population. It is not a part of the international Human Genome Project, so statement 1 is wrong.
topic_notes: Genomics is a recurring UPSC theme. The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003, sequenced about 3 billion base pairs, and identified roughly 20,000-25,000 genes. The Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium published a gapless human genome in 2022. India's major genomic efforts include GenomeIndia (DBT), which has 10,000 genomes in phase 1. Its ambition is to scale to a larger number later, and it covers 99 populations. Data is stored at the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC) at Faridabad, and the project is coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research at IISc. The Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG), launched in December 2020, tracks coronavirus variants through a network of sequencing labs. The Genome Sequencing for Public Health Challenge and the Phenome India project at CSIR add to this. CSIR's IGIB ran the 'Indigen' programme, which sequenced 1,008 Indian genomes. The Human Pangenome aims to capture diversity beyond a single reference. Related applications include precision or personalised medicine, pharmacogenomics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 to Doudna and Charpentier), gene therapy for sickle cell disease and the Casgevy approval, and India's own gene therapy trials for haemophilia. Also note the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023), the DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill, and the Biological Diversity Act 2002. UPSC could ask about institutions such as DBT, ICMR, CSIR and NIBMG, and about terms like SNP, whole genome versus exome sequencing, and reference genome.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard 51. to the National Quantum Mission (NQM) is/are correct ? 5 It aims at developing intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits. Its implementation includes setting up of four Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs) in academic and national R&D institutes across India. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The National Quantum Mission (NQM) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19 April 2023 for 2023-24 to 2030-31, with an outlay of about Rs 6,003.65 crore. It is under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), and the Principal Scientific Adviser's office guides it. Its aim is to seed, nurture and scale up scientific and industrial R&D in quantum technology (QT) and make India a leading nation in the field. Its targets are intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits within 8 years on superconducting and photonic platforms, satellite-based secure quantum communication over 2,000 km within India, inter-city quantum key distribution over 2,000 km, and multi-node quantum networks with quantum memories. Sensing and metrology and quantum materials and devices are also covered. Four Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs) are set up in top academic and national R&D institutes, covering quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices. Since both statements match the Mission's design, option (c) is correct, and (a), (b) and (d) fail because each denies at least one true statement.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because statement 2 is also correct: the Mission does include four T-Hubs.
(b) 2 only is wrong because statement 1 is also correct: the 50-1000 physical qubit target is part of the Mission.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is correct, as the qubit target and the four T-Hubs are both features of NQM.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because both statements match the Mission's official design.
keyfact: NQM (approved April 2023, Rs 6,003.65 crore, to 2030-31): 50-1000 physical qubit computers and four T-Hubs, so both statements are correct and the answer is (c).
option_notes: (a) 1 only would be right if the Mission had no T-Hub structure. But NQM does include four hubs, so this is incomplete. The qubit target of 50-1000 physical qubits is correct, as are the satellite communication and sensing goals.
(b) 2 only would be right if the qubit target in statement 1 were misquoted. In fact the official target is 50-1000 physical qubits in 8 years, so this option wrongly excludes a true statement.

(c) Both 1 and 2 is the correct choice. NQM was approved in April 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31. It is run by DST, aims at intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits, and builds four T-Hubs at IISc, IIT Madras, IIT Bombay and IIT Delhi.

(d) Neither 1 nor 2 would be right only if both statements were wrong. Both match official descriptions, so this option is wrong. Students should note that UPSC often tests whether a statement's numbers match the official document.
related: NQM was approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2023 with Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31.
NQM is implemented by the Department of Science and Technology.
Four T-Hubs cover computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices.
NQM targets satellite-based quantum communication over 2,000 km.
A qubit can exist in superposition of 0 and 1, unlike a classical bit.
Quantum key distribution offers theoretically secure key exchange based on quantum mechanics.
Entanglement links qubits so that their states are correlated regardless of distance.
Logical qubits are error-corrected combinations of many physical qubits.
statements: 1 — Correct: NQM targets intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits over 8 years. The Mission's computing goals use superconducting and photonic technologies, with neutral atoms and trapped ions also in the mix. Physical qubits are the actual hardware qubits and are error-prone, unlike logical qubits, which are error-corrected combinations of many physical qubits. The Mission's staged target is 20-50 qubits in 3 years, 50-100 in 5 years and 50-1000 in 8 years. The Mission is run by DST, and the National Quantum Mission has a Mission Director and governance bodies. It places India among the few countries with a dedicated national quantum programme, such as the USA, China, the EU, the UK and Japan.

2 — Correct: NQM sets up four Thematic Hubs in leading academic and national R&D institutes. The hubs cover quantum computing (IISc Bengaluru), quantum communication (IIT Madras with C-DOT), quantum sensing and metrology (IIT Bombay), and quantum materials and devices (IIT Delhi). They work as a hub-and-spoke network linking institutions across India, and they train a skilled workforce, create IP, and support start-ups and industry. The hubs are meant to concentrate expertise while spreading research around the country. NQM also has the broader aim of building a quantum ecosystem, including fabrication facilities, testbeds and international collaboration.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2, so the unofficial key (c) looks wrong. The National Quantum Mission (2023-24 to 2030-31, Rs 6,003.65 crore) targets intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits, which makes statement 1 correct. It sets up four T-Hubs, so statement 2 is also correct, and (c) is the right answer. Correction: on re-verification, (c) is right and the unofficial key stands.
topic_notes: The National Quantum Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19 April 2023 with an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31. It is implemented by the Department of Science and Technology under the Ministry of Science and Technology. Its goal is to build a quantum ecosystem in India and make the country a leader in quantum technologies. Key deliverables include intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits, satellite-based secure quantum communication between ground stations over 2,000 km within India, long-distance communication with other countries, inter-city quantum key distribution over 2,000 km, multi-node quantum networks with quantum memories, magnetometers and atomic clocks with high precision for sensing, and design and synthesis of quantum materials such as superconductors, semiconductor structures and topological materials. Four T-Hubs are being set up: computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices. Concepts to know: qubit, superposition, entanglement, quantum supremacy, quantum key distribution, post-quantum cryptography, logical versus physical qubits, and decoherence. India's other efforts include QpiAI's quantum computer, the DRDO-IIT Delhi quantum communication demonstration, and ISRO's work on free-space quantum communication. Other nations with national quantum strategies include the USA (National Quantum Initiative Act 2018), China, the EU (Quantum Flagship), the UK and Japan. UPSC could ask next about qubit definitions, quantum key distribution, the ministry in charge, the hubs' host institutions, and applications in drug discovery, cryptography and sensing.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard to India’s Deep Ocean Mission is/are correct ? It was launched by the Ministry of i Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Government of India. Matsya-6000 has been designed to carry 3 people for deep sea exploration. Samudrayaan is a project under this mission. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land 2 only (dd) 1,2and3 Mr. X, a senior officer, was overseeing a critical vaccination programme during a pandemic. He found that a private service provider responsible for vaccine distribution was compromising on quality
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021 with a budget of about Rs 4,077 crore over five years. It is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) and supports the Blue Economy vision. Its main components are: development of technologies for deep-sea mining and a manned submersible; ocean climate change advisory services; technological innovations for exploration and conservation of deep-sea biodiversity; deep-ocean survey and exploration; energy and freshwater from the ocean; and an advanced marine biology station. The manned submersible is MATSYA-6000, built by the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai. It is designed to carry 3 persons to a depth of 6,000 m, and its personnel sphere is made of titanium alloy. The manned project is called Samudrayaan. Polymetallic nodules are the main target of the deep-sea mining component, in the Central Indian Ocean Basin, where India holds an exploration licence from the International Seabed Authority. Elimination logic: the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways runs Sagarmala, so statement 1 is wrong. This rules out (a), (c) and (d), because each of them includes statement 1. Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it accepts only statement 1, which is false because the mission is a MoES initiative, and it rejects the true statements 2 and 3.
(b) Right: statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect.
(c) Wrong: it includes the false statement 1 and omits the true statement 3.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which wrongly names the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways as the launching ministry.
keyfact: Deep Ocean Mission (2021) is a MoES programme; Samudrayaan's Matsya-6000 carries 3 people to 6,000 m.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Deep Ocean Mission is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (which handles Sagarmala).
2 — Correct: Matsya-6000, developed by NIOT, is a manned submersible designed to carry 3 people to a depth of 6,000 m.
3 — Correct: Samudrayaan is the manned deep-ocean submersible project under the Deep Ocean Mission.
summary: The correct answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is incorrect. The Deep Ocean Mission was approved in 2021 and is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. Matsya-6000 is a 3-person submersible and Samudrayaan is the manned submersible project under the mission, so the unofficial answer (b) is confirmed.

question: Which one among the following principles of public administration was most strongly demonstrated by Mr. X’s actions ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question depends entirely on a case passage about Mr. X that did not come through the OCR, so any definite answer would be a guess. The four options come from classical administrative theory, and each has a distinct trigger. Esprit de corps is Henri Fayol's 14th principle, 'union is strength'. It means team spirit, harmony and morale within an organisation, and it is shown when Mr. X builds cohesion, avoids dividing his team, or promotes a shared identity. Equity is also a Fayol principle, meaning kindliness combined with justice in treating employees. It is shown by fair, non-discriminatory treatment, especially when a rule is applied with compassion. Accountability means answerability for actions and results to a superior, to the legislature or to the public. It is shown when Mr. X accepts responsibility, explains his decisions, reports honestly, or faces consequences for failure. Delegation means passing authority and tasks to subordinates, and it is shown when Mr. X assigns powers or duties to others. The elimination logic is to ask who is acting and toward whom. Look for internal team bonding (esprit de corps), fair treatment of people (equity), owning outcomes (accountability) or handing over authority (delegation). Please supply the passage for a verified answer.
explanations: (a) Esprit de corps: correct only if the passage shows Mr. X building team unity, morale or cohesion. This cannot be confirmed without the passage.
(b) Equity: correct only if the passage shows fair, kind and non-discriminatory treatment of staff or citizens. This cannot be confirmed without the passage.
(c) Accountability: this is the unofficial key, but it is unverifiable because the passage is missing. It is correct only if Mr. X takes responsibility or answers for his actions and results.
(d) Delegation: correct only if the passage shows Mr. X assigning authority or tasks to subordinates. This cannot be confirmed without the passage.
keyfact: Fayol's principles include equity and esprit de corps; accountability means answerability for results and delegation means passing authority down.
summary: The question as supplied is incomplete: the passage describing Mr. X's actions is missing, so the answer cannot be verified. The unofficial key (c) Accountability cannot be confirmed or rejected, and I am not claiming it is wrong. Below is a framework for choosing among the four options once the passage is available.

ocr: Ina multi-ethnic district where both economic 53 competition and _ historical grievances : frequently led to community tensions, a flashpoint has arisen with a Government decision to allocate land for a waste management facility near a tribal hamlet, sparking protests by the tribal community, which claimed that the land was sacred and critical to their cultural identity. At the same time, urban residents and local industries supported the project, citing severe solid waste challenges and health concerns due to lack of a proper disposal site. The conflict has escalated with road blockades, soci
subject: Environment
detail: This is an ethics and case-study question on conflict resolution, built on the principles of participatory governance, procedural justice and sustainable development. A good resolution process builds trust first, then uses evidence, then reaches a negotiated solution. Recognising the sacredness of the land is the first step because it shows respect and legitimacy. Next, a multi-stakeholder platform brings tribal leaders, experts, municipal bodies and civil society together. An independent ESIA then supplies neutral, transparent evidence and can compare alternative sites. Legal anchors a student should know: Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas), PESA Act 1996 (Gram Sabha consultation before land acquisition and for minor forest produce), Forest Rights Act 2006 (Gram Sabha consent and recognition of cultural and community rights), the LARR Act 2013 (Social Impact Assessment, consent), and the Environment Impact Assessment Notification 2006 (public hearing). The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (replaced in 2026 by the 2026 rules) require sites that follow environmental norms. The elimination logic is simple: any statement that dismisses a minority's sentiments or says 'proceed without delay' is an absolutist, majoritarian stance and fails the test of mediation. Dropping statement 2 leaves 1, 3 and 4, which is option (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 all contribute to resolving the conflict through acknowledgement, dialogue and evidence, and statement 2 does not.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2, which promotes unilateral action and disregards tribal concerns, so it would deepen the conflict.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 1, which is the essential first step of acknowledging cultural concerns.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2, which is a majoritarian and non-consultative stance that contradicts mediation.
keyfact: In conflict resolution, acknowledge concerns, create inclusive dialogue and use transparent evidence (ESIA); never override a community's rights unilaterally.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 3 and 4 only, is the set of the three conflict-resolution statements: acknowledging cultural concerns, setting up multi-stakeholder dialogue, and carrying out an independent, transparent ESIA. It reflects the participatory, rights-based approach recommended in governance and ethics. It is the correct answer to this question, and it excludes the unilateral approach in statement 2.

Option (b), 2, 3 and 4 only, combines statement 2 (proceed immediately because urban health concerns outweigh a small group's sentiments) with the dialogue and ESIA statements. It is internally inconsistent: it asks for dialogue while ignoring the sentiments of one party. It is wrong because statement 2 is a majoritarian, utilitarian shortcut that breaches tribal rights under PESA, FRA and the Fifth Schedule.

Option (c), 1 and 2 only, pairs the correct first step of acknowledgement with the incorrect decision to proceed regardless. It is wrong because it excludes the dialogue platform and the ESIA, which are practical mechanisms for a sustainable outcome, and because statement 2 contradicts statement 1. Acknowledging concerns while pushing ahead without delay would be tokenism.

Option (d), 1, 2, 3 and 4, accepts every statement. It is wrong because statement 2 weakens mediation: it dismisses minority concerns as 'sentiments of a small group' and prioritises speed over consensus. UPSC often uses an 'all of the above' option to test whether students can spot a single flawed statement.
related: PESA Act 1996 makes the Gram Sabha central in Scheduled Areas.
Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises community and cultural rights over forest land.
Niyamgiri (2013): Supreme Court let Gram Sabhas decide on religious and cultural rights over the hills.
LARR Act 2013 requires a Social Impact Assessment for land acquisition.
EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 mandates public hearings for listed projects.
Mediation Act 2023 provides a legal framework for mediation in India.
National Green Tribunal was established in 2010 to handle environmental disputes.
Article 29 protects the distinct culture of minorities.
statements: 1 — Correct: Acknowledging the community's cultural concerns first builds trust and legitimacy, and mediation requires parties to feel heard before technical options are discussed. Background: sacred groves and sites are protected as cultural and community rights under the Forest Rights Act 2006, which recognises community rights over sacred and customary areas. Gram Sabhas have the power to protect cultural identity and heritage. Article 29 protects the distinct culture of any section of citizens, and Article 342 provides for the notification of Scheduled Tribes. Empathy and active listening are core values in Ethics (GS-IV) for dealing with conflict.

2 — Incorrect: It treats the tribal community's concerns as less important and proceeds unilaterally, which would escalate the conflict and violate principles of justice, inclusiveness and tribal rights. Background: the idea that majority interests override minority interests is a utilitarian-majoritarian approach that constitutional morality rejects. PESA 1996 requires Gram Sabha consultation before land acquisition in Scheduled Areas, and the LARR Act 2013 requires consent and Social Impact Assessment in many cases. The Supreme Court in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals, and in Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (Niyamgiri, 2013) upheld the Gram Sabhas' role on religious and cultural rights.

3 — Correct: A multi-stakeholder dialogue platform is a classic mediation and deliberative tool that builds mutual understanding and de-escalates tension. Background: participatory governance and stakeholder consultation are central to public administration. Examples include public hearings under the EIA Notification 2006, Gram Sabhas under PESA, and local ward committees under the 74th Amendment (Article 243S). Inclusion of tribal leaders, experts and municipal representatives reflects the principles of procedural fairness, transparency and collective problem solving that the Second ARC also stressed for citizen-centric administration.

4 — Correct: An independent Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, with findings shared openly, provides neutral evidence, tests alternative sites and reduces mistrust. Background: ESIA combines environmental impact analysis with social effects such as displacement, livelihoods and cultural loss. In India, the EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 requires prior environmental clearance and public consultation for listed projects, and the LARR Act 2013 mandates a Social Impact Assessment. Transparency and evidence-based decision-making are core to good governance and the Right to Information Act 2005.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 3 and 4 only, so the unofficial key is correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are standard conflict-resolution and mediation steps: acknowledge cultural concerns, create a multi-stakeholder dialogue, and run a transparent independent ESIA. Statement 2 is a majoritarian, unilateral approach that would escalate the conflict and conflicts with tribal rights and constitutional ethics.
topic_notes:
This question belongs to the area of ethics, public administration and conflict resolution in development projects. The core tension is between public interest (urban waste management, health) and community rights (tribal cultural identity, sacred land). Good practice follows a sequence: acknowledge, consult, assess with evidence, negotiate, and implement transparently with safeguards and monitoring.

Key legal and institutional framework: the Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) governs administration of Scheduled Areas, with the Governor's power to regulate land transfer and the Tribes Advisory Council. The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The PESA Act 1996 empowers Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas and requires consultation before land acquisition. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights, including cultural and religious ones, and gives Gram Sabhas a role in consent for diversion of forest land. The LARR Act 2013 requires a Social Impact Assessment and consent in certain cases. The EIA Notification 2006 sets out screening, scoping, public hearing and appraisal. The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 set out waste-site, segregation and processing requirements, and the National Green Tribunal (2010) hears environmental disputes.

Ethics concepts: utilitarianism versus rights-based approaches, justice and fairness, empathy, transparency, accountability, constitutional morality and the principle of 'do no harm'. Mediation methods include negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration, and the Mediation Act 2023 provides a statutory framework for mediation in India. Related ideas: free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) from the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. In case studies, police excesses should be investigated independently, and non-violent protest rights come under Article 19(1)(a) and (b) with reasonable restrictions.

question:
What amongst the following should Ms. X do now ? 1; Immediately disclose the information to the project committee and the public
2. Recommend removing the contractor from the shortlist to protect the project’s integrity
3. Propose a ‘limited disclosure’ to an oversight committee, while keeping the information confidential from the public for the time being Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: This is a CSAT decision-making or ethical-judgement item. These items reward responses that are proportionate, lawful, and procedurally fair, and that escalate through proper channels. The usual principles are: (1) report concerns to the competent authority or oversight body rather than act unilaterally; (2) protect the integrity of the process, such as procurement fairness and the avoidance of conflict of interest; (3) follow natural justice, so no one is penalised before the facts are verified and the party is heard; (4) keep sensitive or unverified information confidential, because premature public disclosure can cause reputational harm, prejudice an inquiry, and trigger legal trouble; and (5) keep transparency and accountability, which are met by informing the oversight body. Applying this: immediate public disclosure is hasty and may be unfair or damaging. Recommending removal of the contractor presumes guilt or exercises authority that Ms. X may not have. Limited disclosure to an oversight committee balances transparency and fairness, so 3 alone fits. The elimination logic is that statements 1 and 2 are both extreme, which leaves only the option containing 3 alone. This depends on the missing passage, so check it against the original paper.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes 1 and 2, both of which are hasty or extreme, and it leaves out the measured option 3.
(b) Likely correct: '3 only' (the OCR's '30') reflects a proportionate, process-based response through an oversight body.
(c) Wrong: statement 2 is a premature punitive step, even though 3 is sound.
(d) Wrong: it combines all three, including the public disclosure and the removal recommendation, which are inappropriate at this stage.
keyfact: In ethics case studies, prefer proportionate escalation to the proper oversight body with confidentiality and due process over public exposure or unilateral punishment.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Immediate disclosure to the public is premature and may prejudice the verification of the information, harm reputations unfairly, and bypass due process.
2 — Incorrect: Recommending removal of the contractor presumes guilt before the information is verified and the contractor is heard, so it breaches natural justice.
3 — Correct: Limited, confidential disclosure to an oversight committee uses the proper channel, preserves transparency and accountability, and avoids public harm before facts are established.
summary: Option (b), '3 only', is the likely answer, but the case passage about Ms. X was not included in the OCR text, so I could not fully verify it. Assuming she has sensitive but unproven information about a shortlisted contractor, a measured step is best: a confidential, limited disclosure to an oversight body. It respects due process and the integrity of the project, and avoids both a public leak and a premature punishment. I have no basis to call the unofficial key wrong.

question: X’ was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term ‘law’ as provided under Article 13, 56. Part III of the Constitution of India. explained that the meaning of the term ‘law’ in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. ‘Y pointed out that the term ‘law’ in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which ‘X’ was not convinced. Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below :
options: X’is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom
The view of ‘Y that ‘law’ included custom is not correct
The views of both ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are correct
The view of only ‘Y is correct
subject: Polity
detail: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights void to the extent of the inconsistency. Article 13(3)(a) gives an inclusive definition of 'law': any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law. Because of this width, executive and delegated legislation can be tested against Part III, not just parliamentary statutes. Article 13(3)(b) defines 'laws in force' to include laws passed or made by a legislature or competent authority before the Constitution's commencement and not previously repealed, even if not operative in particular areas. Article 13(2) bars the State from making laws that take away or abridge Fundamental Rights. Article 13(4) was added by the 24th Amendment (1971) and excludes constitutional amendments under Article 368 from 'law'. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) held that amendments may still be struck down if they violate the basic structure. Personal laws are a debated area. Courts have held that uncodified personal laws derived from scriptures are not 'laws in force' (State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali, 1952), though custom and usage are covered by Article 13(3)(a). Elimination: since both speakers state things the Article expressly includes, any option rejecting either is wrong. That leaves (c).
explanations: Incorrect: X is right about ordinances, orders, rules and regulations, but custom is included in 'law', so the claim of non-inclusion is wrong.
Incorrect: Y's view is correct, because Article 13(3)(a) expressly includes custom or usage having the force of law.
Correct: both views match Article 13(3)(a). X lists ordinance, order, rule and regulation, and Y adds custom or usage.
Incorrect: it wrongly treats X as incorrect. X's statement is also supported by Article 13(3)(a), so Y is not the only one who is correct.
keyfact: Article 13(3)(a): 'law' includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law.
summary: The correct answer is (c), not the unofficial (d). Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India. So X (ordinances, orders, rules, regulations) and Y (custom or usage) are both correct.

question:
Consider the following statements with reference to the Constitution of India : 1 There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Constitution of India will be officially called the ‘Constitution of India’.
2. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and _ the Government of India Act, 1935 stand repealed.
3. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that mentions 26" January, 1950 as the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: There are two correct statements that include statement 3
There is only one correct statement
subject: Polity
detail: Part XXII of the Constitution (Articles 392-395) contains the short title, commencement, authoritative Hindi text and repeal provisions. Article 393 says, 'This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.' Article 394 says that Article 394 itself and Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 came into force at once, on 26 November 1949, when the Constitution was adopted. The remaining provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, 'referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution'. Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with the enactments amending or supplementing the latter. The Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949 is excluded from this repeal. Article 394A, inserted in 1987, deals with the authoritative Hindi text. Because all three statements wrongly claim that no Article covers these matters, all three are incorrect. That leaves option (b) as the only one that fits.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it says all three statements are correct, but each denies an Article that exists (393, 395 and 394).
(b) is correct because all three statements are factually wrong, so there is no correct statement.
(c) is wrong because statement 3 is not correct, as Article 394 mentions 26 January 1950, and statement 2 is also incorrect.
(d) is wrong because not even one statement is correct.
keyfact: Art. 393 = short title; Art. 394 = commencement (26 Jan 1950); Art. 395 = repeal of the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 393 states that the Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.
2 — Incorrect: Article 395 expressly repeals the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935.
3 — Incorrect: Article 394 states that the remaining provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, called the commencement of the Constitution.
summary: The answer is (b), so the unofficial key is correct. Each statement denies the existence of an Article that actually exists: Article 393 gives the short title, Article 395 repeals the two Acts, and Article 394 fixes 26 January 1950 as the commencement date. So none of the three statements is correct.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard to the persons with disabilities in India is/are correct ? The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, an Act passed by the Parliament of India in 2018, mandates reservation in education and employment, places a legal duty on Governments to ensure accessibility and non-discrimination. The Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan focuses on achieving universal accessibility for Persons with Disabilities across three key domains — built infrastructure, transport systems and information and communication technology. The National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corp
subject: Economy
detail: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act was enacted in December 2016 and came into force on 19 April 2017. It replaced the PwD Act, 1995, and gives effect to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). It recognises 21 categories of disabilities, provides 4% reservation in government jobs for benchmark disabilities (those of at least 40%), and 5% reservation in higher education. The year 2018 in Statement 1 is therefore a deliberate factual error. The Accessible India Campaign (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan) was launched on 3 December 2015 by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD). It targets universal accessibility in three domains: built environment, transport systems, and ICT/information ecosystem. NDFDC was incorporated in 1997 as a not-for-profit company under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956. It works under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (DEPwD), not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and provides concessional finance to PwDs for self-employment. Elimination: Statements 1 and 3 are both wrong, so every option containing either is out, which leaves only (b), 2 only.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes Statement 1, which gives the wrong year (2018 instead of 2016).
(b) Correct: only Statement 2 is accurate.
(c) Wrong: it includes both Statement 1 (wrong year) and Statement 3 (wrong ministry), and leaves out the correct Statement 2.
(d) Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because of the year, and this option also leaves out the correct Statement 2.
keyfact: RPwD Act = 2016 (in force 2017, 21 disabilities, 4% job reservation); Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan = 2015; NDFDC is under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The RPwD Act was passed in 2016, not 2018. The content about reservation, accessibility and non-discrimination is otherwise accurate.
2 — Correct: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (Accessible India Campaign, 2015) targets built environment, transport systems and ICT ecosystem accessibility.
3 — Incorrect: NDFDC is under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (DEPwD), not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only, so the unofficial key is right. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed in 2016, not 2018, which makes Statement 1 incorrect. NDFDC was set up by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, which makes Statement 3 incorrect. Statement 2 on Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan is correct.

question:
Consider the following statements about the 59. provisions pertaining to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in India : a Provisions regarding the administration of the Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are given in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India. 2: Some tribes of India are entitled to exemption from paying Income Tax on certain incomes.
3. The Constitution of India provides for reservation of seats in Panchayats for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: There are two correct statements, that include statement 2
There are two correct statements, that are statements 1 and 3
There is only one correct statement
subject: Polity
detail: The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) covers the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than the four northeastern states Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It provides for Tribes Advisory Councils and gives the Governor powers to regulate land transfer and to direct that laws apply with modifications. The Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2) and Article 275(1)) covers the Tribal Areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram through Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils. Statement 1 swaps these two schedules. On tax, Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 exempts the income of members of Scheduled Tribes living in specified areas, such as the northeastern states, Ladakh and the Lahaul-Spiti area. Section 10(26AAA) exempts certain income of Sikkimese individuals. So some tribes do enjoy exemption on certain incomes. On Panchayats, Article 243D reserves seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population. Not less than one-third of these reserved seats are for women belonging to SCs and STs, and Article 243D also reserves not less than one-third of all seats for women. Statement 3 is therefore correct. With statements 2 and 3 correct and statement 1 incorrect, option (a) is the answer.
explanations: Correct: exactly two statements (2 and 3) are correct, and they include statement 2.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because it names the Fifth Schedule instead of the Sixth, so 1 and 3 cannot be the correct pair.
Wrong: two statements are correct, not just one.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so not all three are correct.
keyfact: Sixth Schedule governs the Tribal Areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; the Fifth Schedule governs Scheduled Areas in other states.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Tribal Areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are administered under the Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth.
2 — Correct: Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act exempts certain income of Scheduled Tribe members in specified areas.
3 — Correct: Article 243D provides for reservation of seats in Panchayats for SC and ST women, as at least one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs.
summary: The unofficial answer (a) is correct. Statement 1 is wrong, since the administration of Tribal Areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram is governed by the Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so exactly two statements are correct and they include statement 2.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of questions asked by the Members in the 60. Parliament of India : ie Unstarred questions are those to which a Member desires an oral answer in the House.
2. Starred questions are those to which a Member desires a written answer.
3. No supplementary question can be asked on an unstarred question. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: All the three statements are correct
There are two correct statements, that include statement 2
There is only one correct statement
subject: Polity
detail: In Parliament, questions are classified as starred, unstarred, short notice and questions to private members. A starred question (marked with an asterisk) is one to which a Member wants an oral answer in the House. Supplementary questions can follow it, and the Question Hour lasts about an hour, usually the first hour of the sitting. An unstarred question is one to which a Member wants a written answer. The answer is laid on the table of the House, it is not read out, and no supplementary questions arise. In the Lok Sabha, up to 20 starred and 230 unstarred questions are listed per day. A short notice question is on a matter of urgent public importance, needs less than ten days' notice, and is answered orally. A starred question not reached in the hour gets a written answer, which is then treated as unstarred. The question swaps the two definitions in statements 1 and 2, which makes them incorrect, while statement 3 is accurate. Elimination: if 1 and 2 are wrong and 3 is right, exactly one statement is correct, so only (c) fits.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statements 1 and 2 reverse the definitions of unstarred and starred questions, so not all three are correct.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect, and there is only one correct statement, not two.
(c) is correct because only statement 3 is correct.
(d) is wrong because statement 3 is correct, so there is at least one correct statement.
keyfact: Starred = oral answer, supplementaries allowed; Unstarred = written answer, no supplementaries.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Unstarred questions seek a written answer; it is starred questions that seek an oral answer.
2 — Incorrect: Starred questions seek an oral answer; written answers belong to unstarred questions.
3 — Correct: An unstarred question gets a written answer laid on the table, so no supplementary question can be asked on it.
summary: The unofficial key (c) is correct. Only statement 3 is correct: no supplementary question can be asked on an unstarred question, since it receives a written answer. Statements 1 and 2 swap the definitions of starred and unstarred questions.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes of the Parliament of India :
1. Although members of this Committee are elected from both Houses of Parliament, the Chairperson of this Committee is appointed by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
2. Twenty members are elected by the Rajya Sabha and ten members by the Lok Sabha.
3. No Minister, except for the Union Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, is eligible to be a member of this Committee.
4. Members are elected for a fixed term of two years from the date they enter their office. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: There is only one correct statement, that is statement 2
There are two correct statements, that include statement 1
subject: Polity
detail: The Committee on the Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is an ad hoc-turned-standing parliamentary committee, set up in 1968 and constituted afresh every year. It has 30 members: 20 elected by the Lok Sabha and 10 by the Rajya Sabha, through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. Its term is one year. The Chairperson is appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker from among the Lok Sabha members, because it is a Lok Sabha-led committee. A Minister is not eligible to be a member, and a member who becomes a Minister ceases to be a member from the date of appointment. There is no exception for the Social Justice Minister. The Committee examines the reports of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, and it reviews the welfare measures for SCs and STs and the working of constitutional safeguards. Elimination: statement 1 gets the appointing authority wrong. Statement 2 reverses the numbers. Statement 3 invents an exception. Statement 4 gives two years instead of one. All four fail, so (d) holds.
explanations: (a) is wrong because none of the four statements is correct.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 reverses the numbers: it is 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
(c) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect, as the Speaker appoints the Chairperson, and no other statement is correct either.
(d) is correct because all four statements contain factual errors.
keyfact: SC/ST Welfare Committee: 30 members (20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha), one-year term, Chairperson appointed by the Speaker, no Ministers.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the Chairperson is nominated by the Lok Sabha Speaker, not the Rajya Sabha Chairman, and is drawn from the Lok Sabha members.
2 — Incorrect: 20 members come from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha, the reverse of what is stated.
3 — Incorrect: no Minister can be a member, with no exception for the Social Justice Minister.
4 — Incorrect: the term is one year, not two.
summary: The unofficial key (d) is correct: none of the four statements is accurate. The Committee has 30 members, 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha, and its Chairperson is appointed by the Lok Sabha Speaker. Ministers cannot be members at all, and the term is one year.

question:
Consider the following statements about Mission Sudarshan Chakra of India :
1. It aims to enhance India’s air defence, ballistic missile defence and aerial offensive capabilities.
2. This Mission is being designed to enhance rapid, precise, and powerful defence responses, reinforcing India’s strategic autonomy.
3. One of the aims of this Mission is to cover all public places of India by an expanded nationwide security shield by 2035. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Mission Sudarshan Chakra was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his Independence Day speech on 15 August 2025, after Operation Sindoor. It is a mission to build an indigenous, multi-layered national security shield against enemy aerial and missile threats, and the target date is 2035. The shield is meant to neutralise attacks and also to deliver a decisive counter-strike, so it has both a defensive and an offensive element. Its stated components cover air defence, ballistic missile defence and aerial offensive capability, as in statement 1. It draws on indigenous technology, including DRDO systems such as Project Kusha and the S-400 systems, together with AI-enabled surveillance, sensors and command-and-control networks. Statement 2 follows the official language on rapid, precise and powerful response and strategic autonomy. Statement 3 is the one that needs care. Government descriptions speak of protecting strategic and civilian areas, including public places, through an expanded nationwide shield by 2035. A strict reading of 'all public places' could be questioned, but it matches the official framing. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 match the stated aims closely. Statement 3 is the only plausible trap, and it reflects the 2035 target, so option (a) is the best fit.
explanations: (a) is right: all three statements reflect the mission's announced aims, including the 2035 target.
(b) is wrong: it leaves out statement 3, which reflects the 2035 nationwide shield aim.
(c) is wrong: it leaves out statement 1, but the mission does include air defence, ballistic missile defence and offensive capability.
(d) is wrong: statements 2 and 3 are also correct, so 1 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: Mission Sudarshan Chakra: announced 15 Aug 2025, indigenous multi-layered air and missile defence shield with counter-strike capability, target 2035.
statements: 1 — Correct: The mission covers air defence, ballistic missile defence and aerial offensive capability, with a counter-strike element alongside the defensive shield.
2 — Correct: It is designed for rapid, precise and powerful responses and to reinforce strategic autonomy through indigenous systems.
3 — Correct: One aim is an expanded nationwide security shield, covering strategic and civilian sites including public places, by 2035.
summary: The correct answer is most likely (a) 1, 2 and 3, so the unofficial key appears right. Mission Sudarshan Chakra, announced by PM Modi on 15 August 2025, is a national shield against aerial threats that aims to cover critical civilian and strategic sites by 2035. It is meant to give rapid, precise and powerful responses and to strengthen strategic autonomy. I am working from memory of the announcement and government statements, so check the exact wording against the official source.

question:
Consider the following statements about gg, river bridges connecting India with neighbouring countries : Ts “Maitri Setu’, built over Feni river, connects Ramgarh in India with Sabroom in Bangladesh.
2. Jhulaghat suspension bridge connects India with Myanmar.
3. Mechi bridge and its approaches connect Panitanki Bypass in India with Kakarvitta in Nepal. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The question tests border infrastructure linking India with Bangladesh and Nepal. Maitri Setu spans the Feni river, which forms part of the India-Bangladesh boundary in southern Tripura. It was inaugurated in March 2021 and connects Sabroom (Tripura, India) with Ramgarh (Chattogram division, Bangladesh). Its significance is access to Chattogram port, about 80 km from Sabroom. The statement swaps the two places, so it fails. Jhulaghat is on the Kali (Mahakali/Sharda) river at the Pithoragarh (Uttarakhand) border and links Jhulaghat with Baitadi in Nepal. Myanmar is the wrong country, which eliminates statement 2. The Mechi river bridge is on the Mechi river, which forms the India-Nepal boundary in Jhapa district. It links Panitanki (West Bengal, near Siliguri) with Kakarvitta in Nepal, on the East-West Highway route. The Mechi bridge was built with Indian assistance, as part of the Indo-Nepal border infrastructure and cross-border connectivity programme. The elimination logic is simple. Statement 1 has swapped countries, statement 2 has the wrong country, and only statement 3 is accurate. So only (d) works.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which reverses the locations of Sabroom and Ramgarh, and statement 2, which names Myanmar instead of Nepal.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because Jhulaghat connects India with Nepal, so this option fails even though statement 3 is correct.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because Sabroom is in India and Ramgarh is in Bangladesh, and the option also leaves out the correct statement 3.
Correct: only statement 3 is accurate, since the Mechi bridge links Panitanki in India with Kakarvitta in Nepal.
keyfact: Maitri Setu: Sabroom (India) to Ramgarh (Bangladesh) over the Feni; Jhulaghat: India-Nepal on the Kali; Mechi bridge: Panitanki (India) to Kakarvitta (Nepal).
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 together: Maitri Setu is on the Feni river between Sabroom (Tripura) and Ramgarh (Bangladesh), and was inaugurated in 2021. It was built by NHIDCL. It is about 1.9 km long and gives Tripura access to Chattogram port. Jhulaghat, by contrast, is on the India-Nepal border over the Kali river in Pithoragarh, not on the Myanmar frontier. This option is wrong because both statements contain errors.

Statements 2 and 3 together: Jhulaghat is an India-Nepal suspension bridge on the Kali river near Pithoragarh, linked to Baitadi in Nepal. The Mechi bridge links Panitanki (West Bengal) with Kakarvitta (Jhapa, Nepal) over the Mechi river. Only the Mechi statement is correct, so this option fails on statement 2.

Statement 1 only: Maitri Setu spans the Feni river, which separates Tripura from Bangladesh. It connects Sabroom in India with Ramgarh in Bangladesh, and was opened in March 2021 to improve connectivity and trade. The Feni river rises in South Tripura and enters the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh. The statement reverses the countries of the two towns, so this option is wrong.

Statement 3 only: this is the correct option. The Mechi river rises in the Mahabharat range of Nepal and forms part of the eastern India-Nepal boundary. The Mechi bridge connects Panitanki (West Bengal, near Siliguri) with Kakarvitta in Nepal's Jhapa district. It is part of the Mechi Bridge and approaches project and supports trade and movement between eastern Nepal and India, including onward travel to Siliguri.
related: Maitri Setu over the Feni river links Sabroom (Tripura) with Ramgarh (Bangladesh) and gives access to Chattogram port.
Jhulaghat on the Kali river connects Pithoragarh (Uttarakhand) with Baitadi (Nepal).
The Mechi bridge links Panitanki (West Bengal) with Kakarvitta (Nepal).
The Land Ports Authority of India (LPAI) manages Integrated Check Posts, under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Motihari-Amlekhgunj pipeline is South Asia's first cross-border petroleum pipeline (India-Nepal).
The Kaladan Multimodal project links Kolkata to Sittwe port in Myanmar and onward to Mizoram.
Petrapole-Benapole is the largest land port on the India-Bangladesh border.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Maitri Setu connects Sabroom in India with Ramgarh in Bangladesh, not Ramgarh in India with Sabroom in Bangladesh. Maitri Setu is a bridge over the Feni river, which marks the boundary between Tripura (India) and Bangladesh. It was inaugurated virtually by the Indian and Bangladeshi Prime Ministers in March 2021. It was built by the National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd (NHIDCL). It is about 1.9 km long and is linked to the Integrated Check Post at Sabroom. The bridge gives Tripura access to Chattogram port, roughly 80 km away, and supports trade with Bangladesh.

2 — Incorrect: Jhulaghat suspension bridge connects India with Nepal, not Myanmar. It lies over the Kali (Sharda/Mahakali) river, which forms the boundary between Uttarakhand and Nepal. It links Jhulaghat in Pithoragarh district with Baitadi district in Nepal. The Kali river rises near Kalapani and forms part of the boundary under the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli. Jhulaghat is an important trade and people-to-people crossing and also a transit point for the Kailash Mansarovar route. India-Myanmar crossings are different, such as Moreh-Tamu in Manipur and Zokhawthar-Rih in Mizoram.

3 — Correct: the Mechi bridge links Panitanki Bypass in West Bengal with Kakarvitta in Nepal. The Mechi river forms part of the India-Nepal border in the eastern sector, flowing between Darjeeling/Kishanganj in India and Jhapa district in Nepal. The Panitanki-Kakarvitta crossing is among the busiest land routes between the two countries and is linked to Siliguri and Nepal's East-West Highway (Mahendra Highway). India has helped build the bridge and its approaches to improve cross-border trade and connectivity. An Integrated Check Post at Jogbani-Biratnagar and the Panitanki corridor support Nepal's trade, including its access to Kolkata/Haldia.
summary: The answer is (d) 3 only, so the unofficial expected answer is correct. Statement 3 is right: the Mechi bridge links Panitanki in India with Kakarvitta in Nepal. Statement 1 is wrong because Maitri Setu connects Sabroom in India with Ramgarh in Bangladesh, and statement 2 is wrong because Jhulaghat links India with Nepal, not Myanmar.
topic_notes: Cross-border bridges and connectivity projects are a recurring theme in UPSC prelims, linked to the Neighbourhood First policy and the Act East policy. For Bangladesh, Maitri Setu (Feni river, Sabroom-Ramgarh, 2021) gives Tripura access to Chattogram port. Other India-Bangladesh links include the Akhaura-Agartala rail link, the Petrapole-Benapole land port (the biggest land port), Maitree Express, Bandhan Express and Mitali Express, as well as the Kulaura-Shahbazpur and Haldibari-Chilahati rail links. For Nepal, key crossings are Raxaul-Birgunj (with the first Integrated Check Post in Nepal and a rail link), Jogbani-Biratnagar, Sunauli-Bhairahawa, Panitanki-Kakarvitta (Mechi bridge), Banbasa-Mahendranagar and Jhulaghat-Baitadi. The Raxaul-Kathmandu electrified rail line was proposed, and Jaynagar-Kurtha broad gauge rail has been operational. The Motihari-Amlekhgunj petroleum pipeline, South Asia's first cross-border petroleum pipeline, was opened in 2019. For Myanmar, important points are Moreh-Tamu, the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project (Sittwe port, Paletwa, Zorinpui) and the Rih-Zokhawthar crossing. For Bhutan, there are Phuentsholing-Jaigaon and the Gelephu and Samtse rail projects. Rivers matter too: the Feni (India-Bangladesh), the Mechi (India-Nepal), the Kali/Mahakali (India-Nepal) and the Tumsa and Teesta in the Bangladesh context. Bridges and ICPs are developed by NHIDCL and the Land Ports Authority of India (LPAI), under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

question:
Which of the following statements about a Zero First Information Report (Zero FIR) under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 is/are correct ?
1. A Zero FIR can be lodged at a police station, even though the place of commission of a cognizable/non-cognizable offence is outside the territorial jurisdiction of that police station.
2. The Officer-in-Charge of the police station where a Zero FIR has been lodged may, with the permission of the competent authority, initiate a preliminary enquiry. 3: Under Zero FIR, it is obligatory for the informant to furnish information electronically. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Zero FIR is provided for under Section 173 BNSS, 2023 (corresponding to Section 154 CrPC). Under it, information about a cognizable offence can be given orally or electronically to the officer in charge of any police station, irrespective of where the offence occurred. The station registers it, and then transfers it to the police station having jurisdiction. It carries a regular number only after transfer. The Supreme Court in Lalita Kumari (2013) made registration mandatory for cognizable offences. Section 173(3) allows a preliminary enquiry, for offences punishable with 3 years or more but less than 7 years, within 14 days, with the permission of an officer of DSP rank, to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists. This is a general FIR provision, not a Zero FIR feature as such, and it is generally for the police station with jurisdiction. Electronic information is permitted but must be signed within three days by the informant, and is not obligatory. The informant may also give the information orally or in writing. So Statement 3 fails. Statement 1 is broadly correct about the Zero FIR concept (non-cognizable matters are recorded as a daily diary entry under Section 174, but the Zero FIR idea is commonly framed as covering offences outside jurisdiction). Statement 2 is the debatable one: the preliminary enquiry is tied to the general FIR procedure, and the question's phrasing treats it as a Zero FIR power, which is dubious. A reading that accepts 1 alone leads to (c). Note that the official key may differ, so verify against the final UPSC answer key.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 3 is incorrect: furnishing information electronically is optional, not obligatory.
(b) is wrong because it includes Statement 3 and excludes Statement 1, which is correct.
(c) is the likely correct answer: only Statement 1 clearly holds, as the Zero FIR concept is about registration irrespective of jurisdiction.
(d) is probably wrong because it rejects Statement 1, which correctly describes Zero FIR, and accepts Statement 2, which attributes a general FIR provision to Zero FIR.
keyfact: Zero FIR (Section 173 BNSS): register at any police station irrespective of jurisdiction, then transfer; electronic reporting is allowed, not compulsory.
statements: 1 — Correct: A Zero FIR can be registered at any police station regardless of territorial jurisdiction, then transferred to the competent station.

2 — Incorrect: The preliminary enquiry under Section 173(3) is a general provision with DSP-rank permission and conditions on offence type; it is not a power specific to a Zero FIR station, which mainly registers and transfers. This is the most contestable statement.
3 — Incorrect: Electronic information is permitted but not obligatory; oral or written information is equally valid.
summary: The unofficial key (d) looks wrong; I am fairly confident the correct answer is (c) 1 only. Statement 1 is wrong only if 'non-cognizable' is read strictly, but the Zero FIR concept under Section 173 BNSS applies to cognizable offences, so this needs care. Statement 2 is not what the law provides, and Statement 3 is plainly incorrect.
