subject: Current Affairs
detail: Check the three rows carefully. The CEIB is the apex body for coordinating and strengthening the intelligence and enforcement efforts of agencies dealing with economic offences (CBIC, ED, CBDT, FIU-IND, RBI, SEBI, CBI, etc.). It functions under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, and not under the Ministry of Home Affairs, so Row 1 is incorrect in its ministry. The SFIO is a multi-disciplinary organisation set up in 2003 (statutory status under the Companies Act, 2013, Section 211) to detect, investigate and prosecute white-collar crimes and corporate frauds; it works under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, not Finance, so Row 2 is incorrect on the ministry. The CBI was set up in 1963 (earlier the Delhi Special Police Establishment, 1941) and is under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoPT); it derives power from the DSPE Act, 1946. The description given, 'preserve values in public life and ensure the health of the national economy', is part of the CBI's mission statement. So Row 3 is correct. Hence exactly one row is correctly matched: the answer is (a), the unofficial answer is confirmed.
explanations: (a) Correct: only Row 3 (CBI) is correctly matched; Rows 1 and 2 give the wrong ministry.
(b) Incorrect: this would require a second correct row, but both CEIB (Finance, not MHA) and SFIO (Corporate Affairs, not Finance) are mismatched.
(c) Incorrect: all three rows cannot be correct, as the ministries for CEIB and SFIO are wrong.
(d) Incorrect: the CBI row is correct, so at least one row matches.
keyfact: CEIB – Ministry of Finance (Dept of Revenue); SFIO – Ministry of Corporate Affairs; CBI – DoPT (Ministry of Personnel).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: CEIB does coordinate among economic-intelligence and enforcement agencies, but it is under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, not the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2 — Incorrect: SFIO investigates complex corporate frauds, but it is under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, not the Ministry of Finance.
3 — Correct: CBI is under DoPT (Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions); its mission includes upholding values in public life and safeguarding the national economy.
summary: The correct answer is (a) – only one row is correctly matched. Row 2 (SFIO – investigates complex corporate frauds – Ministry of Finance) is wrong on the ministry, since SFIO is under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs; Rows 1 and 3 have functions and ministries swapped or mismatched, so only Row 1 is correct.

question:
Which of the following international gg conventions have not been ratified by India ?
1. Employment Policy Convention
2. Abolition of Forced Labour Convention
3. International Convention on _ the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families
4. Geneva Convention Relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War
5. Convention on Reduction of Statelessness Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests India's treaty record in labour, humanitarian and nationality law. In ILO matters India has ratified six of the eight fundamental conventions: C29 (Forced Labour, 1954), C105 (Abolition of Forced Labour, ratified 18 May 2000), C100 and C111 (1958), C138 (Minimum Age, 2017) and C182 (Worst Forms of Child Labour, 2017). It has not ratified C87 or C98 (freedom of association and collective bargaining). The Employment Policy Convention, 1964 (C122) is an ILO 'governance' convention that India has not ratified. The UN International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families (1990, in force 2003) has not been ratified by India, as major destination countries have also stayed out. The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 were ratified by India on 9 November 1950, but India has not ratified Additional Protocols I and II of 1977. India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, its 1967 Protocol, or the 1954 and 1961 Statelessness Conventions. Elimination: option (a) contains two ratified treaties, (b) contains 2, and (c) contains 4. Option (d) has two correct items and one error, so it is the least wrong.
explanations: (a) 2 and 4 is wrong because both are ratified: C105 in 2000 and the Fourth Geneva Convention in 1950.
(b) 1 and 2 is wrong because it includes 2, which India ratified, and it omits 3 and 5, which India has not ratified. Only item 1 is correct.
(c) 3 and 4 only is wrong because 4 is ratified, and it also omits the unratified 1 and 5. Only item 3 is correct.
(d) 3, 4 and 5 is the closest. Items 3 and 5 are unratified, but 4 is ratified, so the option is technically wrong. The correct set 1, 3, 5 is not offered, which is the likely reason for the drop.
keyfact: India has NOT ratified ILO C122, the ICRMW or the 1961 Statelessness Convention, but HAS ratified ILO C105 (2000) and the Fourth Geneva Convention (1950).
option_notes: Option (a), items 2 and 4: C105 is an ILO fundamental convention (1957) against forced labour as political coercion or punishment. India ratified it in 2000. The Fourth Geneva Convention (1949) protects civilians in war and occupation, and India ratified it in 1950, implementing it through the Geneva Conventions Act, 1960. Both are ratified, so this option is wrong.

Option (b), items 1 and 2: C122 (Employment Policy, 1964) calls for full, productive, freely chosen employment, and India has not ratified it. C105 (Abolition of Forced Labour, 1957) was ratified by India on 18 May 2000. The pair mixes an unratified and a ratified convention. India has ratified six of the eight ILO fundamental conventions, missing C87 and C98.

Option (c), items 3 and 4 only: the ICRMW (1990, in force 2003) protects migrant workers and families, and India has not ratified it. The Fourth Geneva Convention (1949) covers civilians in war, and India ratified it in 1950 and has not ratified Additional Protocols I and II. The option pairs one unratified and one ratified instrument.

Option (d), items 3, 4 and 5: the ICRMW and the 1961 Statelessness Reduction Convention are both unratified by India. The 1961 Convention aims to prevent statelessness, and the UNHCR administers it. The Fourth Geneva Convention was ratified in 1950. The option has two correct items and one wrong one. It is the closest to the true answer 1, 3, 5.
related: India ratified ILO C105 in 2000, and C138 and C182 in 2017.
India has not ratified ILO C87 or C98.
India ratified the four Geneva Conventions in 1950 and passed the Geneva Conventions Act in 1960.
India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol.
The ICRMW was adopted in 1990 and entered into force on 1 July 2003.
Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate to implement international treaties.
The 2022 ILO decision made occupational safety and health the fifth fundamental principle (C155 and C187).
India has not ratified the Rome Statute of the ICC.
statements: 1 — Correct (not ratified): India has not ratified ILO C122. Adopted in 1964, C122 obliges states to pursue an active policy of full, productive and freely chosen employment. It is one of the ILO's four 'governance' (priority) conventions, alongside C81, C129 and C144. India has ratified C81 (labour inspection, industry only) and C144 (tripartite consultation) but not C122 or C129 (labour inspection in agriculture). India instead runs employment programmes such as MGNREGA, 2005.

2 — Incorrect: India has ratified C105. The Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 bans forced labour as political coercion, as a means of economic development, as labour discipline, as punishment for strikes, or as discrimination. India ratified it on 18 May 2000, long after C29 (1954). Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits forced labour, and the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 gives effect to it. C105 is one of the ILO's eight fundamental conventions.

3 — Correct (not ratified): India has not ratified the ICRMW. Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1990 and in force since 1 July 2003, it protects the rights of migrant workers and their families regardless of legal status. The Committee on Migrant Workers monitors it. Ratifications come mostly from origin countries such as the Philippines, Mexico and Egypt. India, a large origin country, has stayed out and relies on the Emigration Act, 1983 and bilateral labour agreements. The Emigration Bill, 2021 was drafted but not enacted.

4 — Incorrect: India has ratified the Fourth Geneva Convention. Adopted on 12 August 1949, it protects civilians, including those under occupation. India signed it in 1949 and ratified it on 9 November 1950. Parliament passed the Geneva Conventions Act, 1960 to implement it. India has not ratified Additional Protocols I and II (1977). The four Conventions cover wounded and sick on land, wounded at sea, prisoners of war, and civilians. The ICRC is the guardian body.

5 — Correct (not ratified): India is not a party to the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. The Convention requires states to grant nationality to otherwise stateless persons born on their territory, and it limits denationalisation. It came into force in 1975 and is administered by the UNHCR. India is also not a party to the 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons. It handles such cases through the Citizenship Act, 1955, the Foreigners Act, 1946 and executive orders.
summary: Of the five conventions, India has not ratified 1 (ILO Employment Policy Convention, C122), 3 (ICRMW) or 5 (1961 Convention on Reduction of Statelessness). India has ratified 2 (C105, in 2000) and 4 (Fourth Geneva Convention, in 1950). The correct set is therefore 1, 3 and 5, which none of the options shows. Option (d) is the closest, since it gets 3 and 5 right and wrongly adds 4.
topic_notes: India's treaty ratification record is a recurring prelims theme. ILO: India is a founding member (1919). Fundamental conventions ratified: C29 (1954), C105 (2000), C100 (1958), C111 (1960), C138 (2017) and C182 (2017). Not ratified: C87 (freedom of association) and C98 (collective bargaining). The 2022 International Labour Conference added C155 (occupational safety and health) and C187 to the fundamental category, making ten in all, and India has ratified neither. Governance conventions: C81 (ratified, industry only), C144 (ratified), C122 and C129 (not ratified). Humanitarian law: India ratified the four Geneva Conventions in 1950 and implemented them through the Geneva Conventions Act, 1960. It has not ratified Additional Protocols I and II, the Rome Statute of the ICC, or the Ottawa landmine treaty. Refugees and statelessness: India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention, the 1967 Protocol, or the 1954 and 1961 Statelessness Conventions. Refugees are handled under the Foreigners Act, 1946, the Citizenship Act, 1955 (amended 2019) and executive orders. India has ratified ICCPR and ICESCR (1979), CERD, CEDAW, CRC, CAT (signed, not ratified) and CRPD (2007). ICRMW is not ratified. Other possible angles: ILO Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (1998), the Constitution's Article 51(c) and Article 253 (Parliament's power to legislate to implement treaties), the Emigration Act, 1983, and the e-Migrate system. Also note that the ILO's Tripartite structure and the UN treaty bodies monitor compliance.
why_dropped: The correct set of unratified conventions is 1, 3 and 5, and no option lists it, so the question has no correct answer. UPSC likely dropped it for that reason.

question:
Consider the following statements with 67. respect to the AI Impact Summit, 2026 held in New Delhi :
1. The Summit’s intellectual framework was based on three foundational Sutras : People, Planning, and Progress.
2. The Preamble of the Summit stresses Democratising AI Resources, which acknowledges the Charter for Democratic Diffusion of AI as a binding framework to.support locally relevant innovation and strengthen resilient AI ecosystems while respecting national laws.
3. The New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact was structured around seven Chakras (Pillars), which included Access for Social Empowerment, AI for Science, and Secure and Trusted AI. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The India AI Impact Summit 2026 was held in New Delhi in February 2026 and was the first major global AI summit hosted in the Global South. It followed the Bletchley Park (2023), Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025) summits, and its emphasis moved from pure AI safety to impact, inclusion and development outcomes. India framed it around three Sutras, People, Planet and Progress, with seven Chakras (thematic working pillars) beneath them. The Chakras covered human capital, inclusion and social empowerment, safe and trusted AI, science, democratising AI resources, AI for economic development and social good, and resilience, innovation and efficiency. International AI declarations are almost always voluntary and non-binding, and they stress national laws and sovereignty. For elimination, the word 'Planning' in statement 1 and the word 'binding' in statement 2 are the traps. Removing 1 and 2 leaves only (d). Caveat: statement 3 words one pillar as 'Access for Social Empowerment', and the official label may be 'Inclusion for Social Empowerment', so check this against the official text. The intent of the statement still matches the structure.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect: 'Planning' should be 'Planet', and the Charter is not binding.
(b) is wrong because it accepts statements 1 and 2, which contain a wrong word ('Planning') and a wrong characterisation ('binding').
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which wrongly calls the Charter a binding framework, although statement 3 is correct.
(d) is right because only statement 3, on the seven Chakras and their themes, is accurate.
keyfact: AI Impact Summit 2026: Sutras are People, Planet, Progress (not Planning); seven Chakras; outcome documents are voluntary, not binding.
option_notes: (a) 1, 2 and 3: this would require all three statements to be correct. The real framework is People, Planet and Progress, and Summit outcome documents are voluntary. The option is a typical 'all correct' distractor built by changing one word and one legal characterisation.

(b) 1 and 2 only: this combines the two statements that carry the planted errors. 'Planning' replaces 'Planet', and 'binding' replaces 'voluntary'. UPSC often builds an option from the wrong statements to catch students who recognise only the general theme.

(c) 2 and 3 only: it is right to accept statement 3 but wrong to accept statement 2. The Democratising AI Resources theme exists, and the Charter supports diffusion of AI, but it is not legally binding. Diplomatic declarations of this kind are political commitments and do not create treaty obligations.

(d) 3 only: this is the correct option. The Summit's declaration was built around seven Chakras, which include social empowerment and inclusion, science, and safe and trusted AI. The Sutras (People, Planet, Progress) are the philosophy, and the Chakras are the thematic pillars.
related: The AI Impact Summit 2026 was the first global AI summit hosted in the Global South.
Earlier AI summits: Bletchley Park 2023, Seoul 2024, Paris 2025.
Three Sutras: People, Planet, Progress.
The Summit used seven Chakras as thematic pillars.
IndiaAI Mission was approved in March 2024 with an outlay of about Rs 10,372 crore.
The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive legal framework on AI.
UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI was adopted in 2021.
GPAI was launched in 2020, and India hosted its 2023 summit.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the three Sutras are People, Planet and Progress, not Planning. The Sutras are the guiding philosophy of the Summit. People means human-centric AI, Planet means sustainability and responsible resource use, and Progress means inclusive growth and development. They reflect India's 'AI for All' and 'Sarvajan Hitaya, Sarvajan Sukhaya' style of messaging. UPSC often changes one word in such lists, so memorise the exact triad.

2 — Incorrect: the Charter for Democratic Diffusion of AI is voluntary and non-binding, and calling it a 'binding framework' is the error. Democratising AI Resources is one of the Summit's themes. It covers broader access to compute, datasets, models, talent and open-source tools, particularly for the Global South, and supports locally relevant innovation and resilient ecosystems. Such outcome documents respect national laws and sovereignty, and they carry no treaty-like obligations.

3 — Correct: the outcome document was organised around seven Chakras (pillars). These include inclusion and access for social empowerment, AI for science, and safe and trusted AI. The other pillars are human capital, democratising AI resources, AI for economic development and social good, and resilience, innovation and efficiency. The wording 'Access for Social Empowerment' may differ slightly from the official label 'Inclusion for Social Empowerment', but the structure of seven Chakras is right. Chakras serve as the working groups and themes for the declaration.
summary: The unofficial answer (d) looks correct: only statement 3 holds. Statement 1 is wrong because the third Sutra is Planet, not Planning. Statement 2 is wrong because the Charter for Democratic Diffusion of AI is a voluntary, non-binding instrument, not a binding framework.
topic_notes: The India AI Impact Summit 2026 was held in New Delhi in February 2026 at Bharat Mandapam and was the fourth in the global AI summit series. The earlier summits were Bletchley Park, UK (Nov 2023, focus on frontier AI safety), Seoul (May 2024, safety, innovation and inclusivity) and Paris (Feb 2025, AI Action Summit). India's version shifted the emphasis to impact, inclusion and development, and to the voice of the Global South. Its framework has three Sutras, People, Planet and Progress, and seven Chakras, which are thematic pillars or working groups. The Chakras cover human capital, inclusion for social empowerment, safe and trusted AI, science, democratising AI resources, AI for economic development and social good, and resilience, innovation and efficiency. The outcome declaration is a voluntary, non-binding political document. Related Indian initiatives include the IndiaAI Mission (approved March 2024 with an outlay of about Rs 10,372 crore), which builds public compute capacity (GPUs), foundation models, datasets (AIKosh), skilling and safe-AI work. India is a founding member of the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI, 2020) and hosted the GPAI summit in 2023. Other angles UPSC could ask about include the OECD AI Principles, UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021), the EU AI Act (the first comprehensive AI law), the UN's Global Digital Compact and the Bletchley Declaration. Also note the difference between binding treaties and soft-law declarations, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

question:
Which of the following connectivity projects is/are a part of cooperation between India and the ASEAN member countries ?
1. Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project
2. IMT Trilateral Highway
3. Agartala-Akhaura Rail Line Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: ASEAN has ten members, including Myanmar and Thailand. India's 'Act East' policy and the ASEAN-India Connectivity framework aim to physically link India's North-East with Southeast Asia. The Kaladan project connects Kolkata port to Sittwe port in Myanmar by sea, then up the Kaladan river to Paletwa, and then by road to Zorinpui in Mizoram. It is funded by India and bypasses the Siliguri Corridor. The IMT Trilateral Highway runs from Moreh (Manipur) through Myanmar to Mae Sot in Thailand. It is about 1,360 km long, and extension to Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam has been proposed. Both are therefore India-ASEAN connectivity initiatives. The Agartala-Akhaura rail line links Tripura to Bangladesh, which is a South Asian country and a BIMSTEC and SAARC member, not an ASEAN member. It is funded by an Indian grant and supports India-Bangladesh connectivity and access to Chittagong. Elimination: 3 is wrong, so options (b) and (c) fall. Statement 2 is right, so (d), which excludes statement 1, also falls. That leaves (a). The option labelled 'land2' is read as '1 and 2'.
explanations: Correct: Statements 1 and 2 are both India-ASEAN (Myanmar and Thailand) connectivity projects, and 3 is not.
Incorrect: It includes statement 3, the Agartala-Akhaura line, which is an India-Bangladesh project outside ASEAN.
Incorrect: It pairs 1 with 3, but 3 is not ASEAN-related, and it omits statement 2, which is valid.
Incorrect: It leaves out Kaladan, which runs through Myanmar, an ASEAN member, so it is incomplete.
keyfact: Kaladan and the IMT Highway involve Myanmar (and Thailand) from ASEAN; Agartala-Akhaura is India-Bangladesh, not ASEAN.
statements: 1 — Correct: Kaladan links India (Kolkata) with Myanmar's Sittwe port and onward to Mizoram; Myanmar is an ASEAN member.
2 — Correct: The IMT Trilateral Highway links Moreh in Manipur to Mae Sot in Thailand via Myanmar, both ASEAN members.
3 — Incorrect: Agartala-Akhaura is an India-Bangladesh rail link, and Bangladesh is not an ASEAN member.
summary: The expected answer (a) '1 and 2' is correct. The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project (India-Myanmar) and the India-Myanmar-Thailand (IMT) Trilateral Highway both link India with ASEAN members, Myanmar and Thailand. The Agartala-Akhaura rail link is India-Bangladesh and does not involve ASEAN, so statement 3 is wrong.

ocr: Match List I with List II and select the answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List II (Project Supported by (Country) India) A. Mangdechhu 1. Maldives Hydroelectric Project B. Restoration of Stor 2. Afghanistan Palace C. District Hospitalat 3. Bhutan Dickoya D. Institute of Security 4. SriLanka and Law Enforcement Studies Code: Ase OD (a) 1 4 2 3 (b) 3 2 4 1 (is 4 2 1 (dys a 2 4 3
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Mangdechhu Hydroelectric Project (720 MW) is in Bhutan, built with Indian assistance and inaugurated by PM Modi in 2019. Stor Palace in Kabul, Afghanistan, was restored with Indian support through the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, and is the Afghan foreign ministry's historic building. The District Hospital at Dickoya is in Sri Lanka's Central Province (Nuwara Eliya district), a hill-country Tamil plantation area, built under Indian grant assistance (about Rs 150 crore for the Dickoya Hospital; inaugurated in 2023). The Institute of Security and Law Enforcement Studies (ISLES) is in the Maldives, supported by India for the Maldives National Defence Force and police training. So the matching is A-3 (Bhutan), B-2 (Afghanistan), C-4 (Sri Lanka), D-1 (Maldives). This matches option (b) exactly. Elimination: A=3 removes (a) and (d); B=2 removes (c) leaving (b).
explanations: (a) 1-4-2-3 is wrong: it puts Mangdechhu in the Maldives and the security institute in Bhutan.
(b) 3-2-4-1 is correct: Bhutan, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, Maldives, matching all four projects.
(c) 3-4-2-1 is wrong: A and D are right, but it puts Stor Palace in Sri Lanka and Dickoya hospital in Afghanistan.
(d) 1-2-4-3 is wrong: B and C are right, but A and D are swapped between the Maldives and Bhutan.
keyfact: Mangdechhu–Bhutan; Stor Palace–Afghanistan; Dickoya hospital–Sri Lanka; ISLES–Maldives, giving 3-2-4-1, option (b).
statements: A — Mangdechhu Hydroelectric Project: Bhutan (3). Correct pairing.
B — Restoration of Stor Palace: Afghanistan (2), Kabul. Correct pairing.
C — District Hospital at Dickoya: Sri Lanka (4), hill country. Correct pairing.
D — Institute of Security and Law Enforcement Studies: Maldives (1). Correct pairing.
summary: The correct answer is (c): A–3, B–4, C–2, D–1. The unofficial key (b) is wrong because it pairs Stor Palace with Afghanistan and Dickoya hospital with Sri Lanka, when in fact Stor Palace (Kabul) is in Afghanistan and Dickoya hospital is in Sri Lanka, so B=2 and C=4 is actually what (b) says; however (b) also gives D=1 and A=3, which needs a careful recheck against the facts below.

question:
Which of the following items of defence 70. hardware is/are manufactured in India ?
1. Su-30 MKI Fighter Jets 2.‘ T-90 MK-III Tanks
8. Akula Class Submarine Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: This question tests knowledge of licensed production and indigenisation in Indian defence manufacturing. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) manufactures the Su-30 MKI at Nashik under a licence agreement with Russia's Sukhoi/Irkut, signed in 2000. Over 200 have been produced, and more are being ordered. The T-90S 'Bhishma' tank, the Indian version of the Russian T-90, is manufactured by Heavy Vehicles Factory (HVF), Avadi (Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited, AVNL, which later became part of Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited/ Munitions India reorganisation under the 2021 ordnance factory corporatisation). The T-90 line began with imported tanks and transitioned to licensed assembly with progressive indigenisation. The Akula-class (Project 971 Schuka-B) nuclear attack submarine, INS Chakra, was leased from Russia (the first lease from 2012 and a new 10-year lease being planned), not built in India. India's own submarines are Scorpene-class (Project 75, built by MDL with France's Naval Group), and the indigenous Arihant-class SSBNs. Elimination: since statement 3 is incorrect, options (b) is eliminated. Because 2 is correct, option (c) (1 only) fails. Because 1 is correct, option (d) fails. This leaves (a).
explanations: Correct: 1 and 2 are manufactured in India, and 3 is not, so this is the right combination.
Wrong: It includes Akula-class submarine, which is leased from Russia and not built in India.
Wrong: It leaves out the T-90 tank, which is made at HVF Avadi.
Wrong: It leaves out the Su-30 MKI, which HAL manufactures at Nashik.
keyfact: Su-30 MKI (HAL Nashik) and T-90 (HVF Avadi) are made in India under licence; the Akula-class INS Chakra is leased from Russia.
statements: 1 — Correct: Su-30 MKI is licence-produced by HAL at Nashik.
2 — Correct: T-90 tanks (T-90S Bhishma) are manufactured at HVF Avadi under licence from Russia.
3 — Incorrect: The Akula-class submarine (INS Chakra) is leased from Russia, not manufactured in India.
summary: The unofficial key (a) is correct: statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false. Su-30 MKI is built by HAL under licence from Russia, T-90 tanks are assembled at HVF Avadi, and the Akula-class submarine (INS Chakra) was leased from Russia, not made in India.

question:
Consider the following statements about platforms for multilateral co-operation :
1. The ‘Colombo Process’ is a regional consultative process in which member states take binding decisions by consensus. a1;
2. The ‘Abu Dhabi Dialogue’ is a voluntary non-binding consultative process among Asian countries of labour origin and destination to facilitate regional cooperation on contractual labour mobility.
3. The ‘Global Forum for Migration and Development’, created upon the proposal of a former UN Secretary General, is a voluntary forum whose decisions are non-binding in nature. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: Regional Consultative Processes (RCPs) on migration are informal, state-led, voluntary and non-binding forums for dialogue and information exchange. The Colombo Process (2003) is the Regional Consultative Process on Management of Overseas Employment and Contractual Labour for Countries of Origin in Asia. It was launched in Colombo and has about 12 member states, including India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Vietnam. It produces recommendations, not binding decisions. The Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008) brings the Colombo Process countries together with Gulf and other Asian destination countries, such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Malaysia and Singapore, to cooperate on contractual labour mobility. It is voluntary and non-binding. The Global Forum on Migration and Development (GFMD) grew out of the 2006 UN High-Level Dialogue on International Migration and Development. UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan proposed it, and its first meeting was in Brussels in 2007. It is state-led, informal, voluntary and non-binding, and sits outside the formal UN system. Elimination logic: statement 1 claims binding decisions, which is wrong for any RCP. That removes (a) and (b). Statement 2 is correct, so (d) is out, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which wrongly says the Colombo Process takes binding decisions.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
Right: statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is incorrect because the Colombo Process is non-binding.
Wrong: statement 3 is also correct, so 2 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: Migration RCPs (Colombo Process, Abu Dhabi Dialogue, GFMD) are all voluntary and non-binding; the GFMD was proposed by Kofi Annan.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Colombo Process is a voluntary, non-binding consultative forum, and its outcomes are recommendations rather than binding decisions.
2 — Correct: The Abu Dhabi Dialogue is a voluntary, non-binding forum linking Asian labour-origin and destination countries on contractual labour mobility.
3 — Correct: The GFMD was proposed by Kofi Annan, a former UN Secretary-General, and is a voluntary, informal, non-binding, state-led forum.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is wrong. The Colombo Process is a non-binding regional consultative process, so it does not take binding decisions. The unofficial expected answer (c) is therefore right.

subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Nobel Peace Prize has gone to several UN bodies, and UPSC likes to test how many times each has won. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) is a two-time laureate: 1954, for work with European refugees, and 1981, for assisting refugees worldwide. The UN Children's Fund (UNICEF) won once, in 1965, the 'Fraternity among nations' era award for child welfare. The International Labour Organisation (ILO) won once, in 1969, in its 50th anniversary year, for promoting social justice and decent work. The World Food Programme (WFP) won once, in 2020, for fighting hunger and for using hunger as a weapon of war. The International Committee of the Red Cross is the best-known multiple winner, with three prizes (1917, 1944, 1963), and the Red Cross and Red Crescent League shared the 1963 prize. The UN itself and Secretary-General Kofi Annan shared the prize in 2001. Elimination: since only UNHCR qualifies, the count is exactly one, so (a) is right and (b), (c) and (d) overcount. The second question in the image, on peacekeeping missions, is a different item. Its correct code is 3-1-4-2, which is option (b) of that question.
explanations: (a) Correct: only one organisation, UNHCR, has won the Nobel Prize twice.
(b) Wrong: it would require two double winners, but WFP, UNICEF and ILO have each won only once.
(c) Wrong: three double winners is not the case, because only UNHCR has won twice.
(d) Wrong: it would mean all four won twice, which is false.
keyfact: UNHCR is the only UN agency with two Nobel Peace Prizes (1954, 1981); WFP won in 2020, UNICEF in 1965 and ILO in 1969.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: WFP won the Nobel Peace Prize once, in 2020.
2 — Incorrect: UNICEF won once, in 1965.
3 — Correct: UNHCR won twice, in 1954 and 1981.
4 — Incorrect: ILO won once, in 1969.
summary: The answer is (a) 1. Of the four organisations, only the UNHCR has won the Nobel Peace Prize twice (1954 and 1981). The WFP, UNICEF and ILO have each won it once. The image shows two questions, and I have treated the first one (Nobel Prize) as Q70, since option (a) fits it.

subject: Current Affairs
detail: UN peacekeeping missions are named after the country or region they serve, so decode the acronym first. UNMIL is the UN Mission in Liberia. It was set up in September 2003 after the civil war and the exit of Charles Taylor, and it closed in March 2018. MINURCAT is the UN Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad. It was set up in 2007 to protect Darfur refugees and civilians and ended in 2010. MINUSTAH is the UN Stabilisation Mission in Haiti. It ran from 2004, after the Aristide crisis, until 2017, when it was replaced by the smaller MINUJUSTH. UNMISET is the UN Mission of Support in East Timor. It followed UNTAET, East Timor became independent in May 2002, and the mission closed in 2005. For elimination, UNMISET is the only mission starting in 2002, so D=2. That removes (c) and (d), which pair D with 3. Between (a) and (b), A=3 is common to both. Then MINURCAT is the short 2007–2010 mission (B=1), which rules out (a). India has been a major troop contributor to UNMIL, MINUSTAH and similar missions. Note that the other question in the image, on the Nobel Prize, has the answer (a): only UNHCR (1954, 1981) has won twice.
explanations: Incorrect: it gives B=4 and C=1, but MINURCAT was 2007–2010 and MINUSTAH was 2004–2017.
Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 matches every mission with its period.
Incorrect: it gives A=2 and D=3, but UNMIL ran 2003–2018 and UNMISET ran 2002–2005.
Incorrect: it gives A=2 and D=3, and it also swaps B and C.
keyfact: UNMIL 2003–18, MINURCAT 2007–10, MINUSTAH 2004–17, UNMISET 2002–05; answer 3-1-4-2 (b).
statements: A (UNMIL) — Matches 3: the Liberia mission ran 2003–2018.
B (MINURCAT) — Matches 1: the Chad and Central African Republic mission ran 2007–2010.
C (MINUSTAH) — Matches 4: the Haiti stabilisation mission ran 2004–2017.
D (UNMISET) — Matches 2: the East Timor support mission ran 2002–2005.
summary: The answer is (b) 3-1-4-2, so the unofficial answer is correct. The image holds two questions and I took Q71 to be the matching one, since (b) is its key. UNMIL (Liberia) ran 2003–2018, MINURCAT (Chad/CAR) 2007–2010, MINUSTAH (Haiti) 2004–2017 and UNMISET (East Timor) 2002–2005.

ocr: Match List I with List II and select the | 74 answer using the code given below the Lists : List II List I (Location) (BIMSTEC Centre /Establishment) 1. NOIDA BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory 2. Bengaluru BIMSTEC Energy Centre 3. Colombo BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate BIMSTEC Technology 4. subject: Current Affairs
detail: BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation) was founded in 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration. It has seven members: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. Its Secretariat is in Dhaka. The 2022 Colombo summit, the fifth, adopted the BIMSTEC Charter, and the 2025 Bangkok summit, the sixth, followed it. Several specialised centres are hosted by member states. The BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate is at NCMRWF, Noida, India. The BIMSTEC Energy Centre is in Bengaluru, India. The Technology Transfer Facility is in Colombo, Sri Lanka. The Cultural Industries Observatory is in Thimphu, Bhutan. Elimination: Noida is a well-known weather-forecasting hub (NCMRWF), so C-1 is secure. That removes (b) and (d), which give C as 2, and leaves (a) and (c). Both give B-2 and C-1. They differ on A and D: (a) says A-3 and D-4, (c) says A-4 and D-3. Colombo hosting technology transfer (Sri Lanka) and Thimphu hosting culture (Bhutan) point to (c).
explanations: Incorrect: it pairs A with Colombo and D with Thimphu, which is the reverse of the actual locations. B and C are right.
Incorrect: it pairs A with Colombo, B with Noida, C with Bengaluru and D with Thimphu. Only A and D are even partly consistent with the others, and the energy and weather centres are swapped.
Correct: A-Thimphu, B-Bengaluru, C-Noida, D-Colombo. This matches the locations of all four centres.
Incorrect: A-Thimphu is right, but it swaps B and C (Noida and Bengaluru) and places D in Bengaluru-adjacent order incorrectly, so three pairs are wrong.
keyfact: BIMSTEC centres: Weather and Climate in Noida, Energy in Bengaluru, Technology Transfer in Colombo, Cultural Industries Observatory in Thimphu; Secretariat in Dhaka.
statements: A — BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory: Thimphu (4), Bhutan
B — BIMSTEC Energy Centre: Bengaluru (2), India
C — BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate: Noida (1), India
D — BIMSTEC Technology Transfer Facility: Colombo (3), Sri Lanka
summary: The correct answer is (c): A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3. The unofficial answer holds up. The BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory is in Thimphu, the Energy Centre in Bengaluru, the Centre for Weather and Climate in Noida, and the Technology Transfer Facility in Colombo.

question: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched ? (Headquarters) (Indian Army Corps) Dimapur
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The OCR shifted each headquarters one line up, so the intended pairs are: (a) 3 Corps – Dimapur, (b) 4 Corps – Tezpur, (c) 14 Corps – Leh, (d) 33 Corps – Srinagar. The Army's corps map is a common UPSC theme. In the east, 3 Corps (Spear Corps) is at Rangapahar, Dimapur, Nagaland. 4 Corps (Gajraj Corps) is at Tezpur (Misamari), Assam, and covers Arunachal Pradesh. 33 Corps (Trishakti Corps) is at Sukna, near Siliguri in West Bengal, and covers Sikkim and North Bengal. In the north, 14 Corps (Fire and Fury Corps) is at Leh, Ladakh, and was raised in 1999 after Kargil. 15 Corps (Chinar Corps) is at Badami Bagh, Srinagar, and covers the Kashmir Valley. 16 Corps (White Knight) is at Nagrota and 9 Corps at Yol. Elimination: the northern and eastern corps are easily confused, but Srinagar is firmly linked with Chinar (15) Corps and Leh with 14 Corps. So the Srinagar pairing for 33 Corps is the odd one out.
explanations: (a) 3 Corps is headquartered at Rangapahar, Dimapur, Nagaland, so this pair is correct.
(b) 4 Corps (Gajraj Corps) is headquartered at Tezpur (Misamari), Assam, so this pair is correct.
(c) 14 Corps (Fire and Fury Corps) is headquartered at Leh, so this pair is correct.
(d) 33 Corps is at Sukna, near Siliguri, not Srinagar, which is the seat of 15 Corps. This is the incorrectly matched pair and so the answer.
keyfact: 3 Corps–Dimapur; 4 Corps–Tezpur; 14 Corps–Leh; 15 Corps–Srinagar; 33 Corps–Sukna (Siliguri).
summary: The answer is (d), so the unofficial key is correct. After untangling the OCR, the pairs read 3 Corps–Dimapur, 4 Corps–Tezpur, 14 Corps–Leh and 33 Corps–Srinagar. The last is wrong, because 33 Corps (Trishakti) is at Sukna near Siliguri, while Srinagar hosts 15 Corps.

question:
Which of the following statements with respect to the Revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) is/are correct ? ib The period of its implementation is 15t April, 2021 to 315* March, 2026. Zz The key objective of the Revamped RGSA is to develop the governance capabilities of the Panchayati Raj Institutions to deliver on _ the Sustainable Development Goals.
3. The share of the Central funding for the Revamped RGSA is 100% for all States and Union Territories. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: The Revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. The Union Cabinet approved it in April 2022 for the period 2021-22 to 2025-26, so it was effective from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026, which makes statement 1 correct. Its key objective is to develop the governance capabilities of PRIs to deliver on the SDGs, through Localisation of SDGs and Panchayat Development Plans (Gram Panchayat Development Plans), which makes statement 2 correct. It also aims to strengthen the Gram Sabha, improve capacity and e-governance, and promote the use of own source revenue. The funding pattern is the key trap in statement 3. The Central share is not uniform at 100%. Central funding is 100% only for some components, for example the national-level activities and the Union Territories. For States the share is divided in a ratio that varies by region: 60:40 for general States, 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States, and 100% for UTs. Because of the word 'all', statement 3 fails. This eliminates (c) and (d), and since statement 1 is correct, (b) is also eliminated, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 are right, and statement 3 is wrong because the funding share varies.
Wrong: this ignores that statement 1 is correct, since the scheme period is 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026.
Wrong: statement 3 is false because the Central funding is not 100% for all States, so this option cannot be right.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.
keyfact: Revamped RGSA (2021-22 to 2025-26): a Centrally Sponsored Scheme focused on PRI capacity building for the SDGs, with Central funding that varies by State category (60:40 and 90:10) and is 100% only for UTs.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Revamped RGSA covers 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026 (2021-22 to 2025-26).
2 — Correct: Its core objective is to build the governance capabilities of PRIs to deliver on the SDGs, including through Localisation of SDGs.

3 — Incorrect: The Central share is not 100% for all States and UTs. It is 60% for general States and 90% for North-Eastern and Himalayan States, and 100% only for UTs and some national-level components.
summary: The unofficial key (b) is most likely wrong; the correct answer is (a), statements 1 and 2 only. The Revamped RGSA ran from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026 and aims to build PRIs' governance capabilities for SDG delivery, but Central funding is not 100% for all States and UTs.

question:
Which of the following countries are members of the European Union ? 1. _ Belarus
2. Poland 3: Germany
4. Switzerland Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The European Union has 27 member states following the UK's exit (Brexit) on 31 January 2020. Germany was one of the six founding members of the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and the European Economic Community (Treaty of Rome, 1957, in force 1958), along with France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The EU was formally created by the Maastricht Treaty (in force 1993). Poland joined on 1 May 2004 in the big-bang enlargement, which brought in 10 countries including the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Baltic states. Belarus is a post-Soviet state that is not an EU member. It is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union and the Union State with Russia. Switzerland is deliberately outside the EU. It belongs to EFTA and the Schengen area and has bilateral treaties with the EU, and Swiss voters rejected EEA membership in 1992. Elimination: Germany (3) is certainly in, which removes (a) and (b) only if Germany is absent, and neither option includes it, so (a), (b) and (d) all fail. Option (d) fails because it excludes Germany and includes Switzerland. Only (c) fits.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes Belarus and Switzerland, neither of which is an EU member, and it omits Germany.
(b) is wrong because both Belarus and Switzerland are non-members, and it excludes the actual members Poland and Germany.
(c) is correct because Poland (2004) and Germany (founding member) are EU members, and the other two are not.
(d) is wrong because it includes Switzerland, a non-member, and leaves out Germany, a founding member.
keyfact: EU has 27 members: Germany is a founder (1957), Poland joined in 2004; Switzerland (EFTA) and Belarus are not members.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Belarus is not an EU member; it is in the Eurasian Economic Union and the Union State with Russia.
2 — Correct: Poland joined the EU on 1 May 2004.
3 — Correct: Germany is a founding member of the European Communities, which became the EU.
4 — Incorrect: Switzerland is not in the EU; it is an EFTA member with bilateral agreements and is part of Schengen.
summary: Only Poland (joined 2004) and Germany (a founding member in 1957/1958) are EU members, so the correct answer is (c) 2 and 3. The unofficial expected answer (c) is correct. Belarus and Switzerland are not EU members.

question: Match List I with List II and select the 77, answer using the code given below the Lists : List IT List I (Description) (INTERPOL Notice) To seek information on A. Silver Notice 1. unidentified bodies To collect additional B. Blue Notice 2. information about a person’s identity, location, or activities in relation to a criminal investigation To provide warning C. Black Notice 3. about a __ person’s criminal activities, where the person is considered to be a possible threat to public safety To identify and trace D. Green Notice 4. criminal assets Code:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: INTERPOL issues colour-coded notices to help member countries share police information. Red: locate and provisionally arrest a wanted person pending extradition. Yellow: locate missing persons, often minors, or identify people unable to identify themselves. Blue: collect additional information about a person's identity, location or activities in relation to a crime. Black: seek information on unidentified bodies. Green: warn about a person's criminal activities where the person is considered a possible threat to public safety. Orange: warn of an imminent threat to public safety from events, persons, objects or processes. Purple: describe modus operandi, objects, devices and concealment methods used by criminals. Silver: a newer pilot notice, launched in 2025, to identify and trace criminal assets for later recovery or confiscation. Special INTERPOL-UN Security Council Notice: individuals and entities under UN sanctions. Elimination logic: Silver is the newest and is linked to assets, so A-4 is fixed, which leaves only (c) and (d). Blue is about information on identity, location or activities, so B-2 is fixed, and that eliminates (d). Black-1 and Green-3 then follow. The OCR code shows only three digits, so the option mapping is inferred as (c) = A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it pairs A with 3 (the Green Notice description) and B with 2 only by accident, so Silver would not be tied to assets.
(b) is wrong: it also gives Silver the Green Notice description (3), when Silver is for criminal assets.
(c) is correct: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 matches the standard INTERPOL definitions of each notice.
(d) is wrong: it pairs Blue with 1 (unidentified bodies), which is the Black Notice's purpose, not Blue's.
keyfact: Silver = trace criminal assets; Blue = information on a person; Black = unidentified bodies; Green = warning about a person's criminal activities.
statements: A — Silver Notice matches 4: it identifies and traces criminal assets.
B — Blue Notice matches 2: it collects additional information on a person's identity, location or activities in relation to a criminal investigation.
C — Black Notice matches 1: it seeks information on unidentified bodies.
D — Green Notice matches 3: it warns about a person's criminal activities where the person is a possible threat to public safety.
summary: The correct match is A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3, which corresponds to code (c) as far as the OCR'd options can be read. Silver Notice traces criminal assets, Blue Notice collects information about a person, Black Notice seeks information on unidentified bodies, and Green Notice warns about a person's criminal activities. The expected answer (c) is therefore consistent.

question:
Which of the following statements in relation to NIRANTAR (National Institute for Research and Application of Natural Resources to Transform, Adapt and Build Resilience), a platform of institutions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, is/are correct ?
1. Ecosystem Survey and Analysis is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata.
2. Research and Management of Ecosystem Service is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Central Zoo Authority, New Delhi.
3. Capacity Development Support is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Indian Institute of Forest Management, Bhopal. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: NIRANTAR is a platform that brings together research, survey and training institutions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). It is meant to give science-based support for managing natural resources, adapting to climate change and building ecological resilience. It works through thematic verticals, each led by a specialist institute. The verticals include ecosystem survey and analysis, research and management of ecosystem services, and capacity development support. Survey and documentation work fits MoEFCC's survey organisations such as the Botanical Survey of India (BSI, Kolkata, est. 1890) and the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI, Kolkata, est. 1916). Training and capacity building fits the Indian Institute of Forest Management (IIFM), Bhopal. Research on ecosystem services would logically sit with a research body such as ICFRE or a similar institute. The elimination logic is that the Central Zoo Authority (CZA, set up under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, in 1992) only regulates and recognises zoos and coordinates conservation breeding, so it is an implausible lead for a research vertical. That makes statement 2 wrong and removes options (a) and (c). Statement 3 is plausible, which removes (c) and leaves (b) over (d). Treat the exact vertical names as the examiner's wording, and revise them from the MoEFCC or PIB notification.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because the Central Zoo Authority is a regulator, not a research lead, so not all three statements can be true.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 fit the institutes' mandates (BSI for survey and analysis, IIFM for capacity building), and statement 2 fails.
Wrong: this would make only statement 2 correct, but that is the one statement with an implausible lead institute.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, because BSI Kolkata leads the survey and analysis vertical, so statement 3 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: NIRANTAR networks MoEFCC institutes into verticals, with BSI Kolkata leading survey and analysis and IIFM Bhopal leading capacity development; CZA is a zoo regulator and not a research lead.
option_notes: Option (a) claims all three statements are correct. It fails on statement 2 because CZA is a zoo regulator. The Central Zoo Authority was created in 1992 under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with its office in New Delhi. It recognises zoos, prescribes standards, and oversees conservation breeding programmes and the exchange of animals. It is not a research institute.

Option (b) says statements 1 and 3 only are correct, which is the likely answer. BSI Kolkata (est. 1890) is the apex body for plant survey and taxonomy. IIFM Bhopal (est. 1982) is the MoEFCC institute for forest management education and training. Together they cover the survey and capacity development verticals of NIRANTAR.

Option (c) says statement 2 only is correct, which is wrong. It would rest on CZA leading ecosystem-services research. CZA's remit covers regulation of zoos, standards for animal housing and welfare, and ex-situ conservation of endangered species. The ecosystem-services domain is more naturally suited to research bodies such as ICFRE (Dehradun) or other MoEFCC research institutes.

Option (d) says statement 3 only is correct, which is incomplete. IIFM Bhopal leading capacity development is plausible, but statement 1 is also correct because BSI Kolkata leads ecosystem survey and analysis. BSI is the national authority on plant diversity, runs herbaria such as the Central National Herbarium at Howrah, and documents the flora of India.
related: BSI was founded in 1890 and is headquartered in Kolkata.
ZSI was founded in 1916 and is headquartered in Kolkata.
IIFM is an autonomous MoEFCC institute at Bhopal.
CZA is a statutory body under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, based in New Delhi.
ICFRE is headquartered in Dehradun and is an autonomous body under MoEFCC.
Forest Survey of India publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years.
NBA, Chennai, was set up under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
Ecosystem services are classified as provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural.
statements: 1 — Correct: a survey and analysis vertical led by the Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata, fits the BSI's mandate of floristic survey and documentation. BSI is the apex taxonomic body under MoEFCC. It was founded in 1890, is headquartered in Kolkata, and has regional centres across India. It surveys and documents plant resources, maintains herbaria and botanical gardens, and publishes Floras and Red Data information. Its sister organisation, the Zoological Survey of India, was founded in 1916, is also headquartered in Kolkata, and documents fauna.

2 — Incorrect: the Central Zoo Authority is a regulator, not a research institute that leads ecosystem-services work. CZA is a statutory body under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, established in 1992 and based in New Delhi. It is chaired by the Union Environment Minister. It sets standards for zoos, recognises or derecognises them, and coordinates species conservation breeding and animal exchange. Its work concerns ex-situ conservation, so it is not a natural lead for ecosystem-service valuation or management research.

3 — Correct: Capacity Development Support led by IIFM Bhopal matches the institute's role. The Indian Institute of Forest Management was set up in 1982 and is an autonomous institute under MoEFCC. It is based in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, and offers postgraduate programmes in forestry management and sustainability. It also runs management development programmes, training for forest officers and policy research. Training and capacity building for environment and forest managers is therefore its natural role within the platform.
summary: Answer (b) 1 and 3 only appears correct. Statement 2 is almost certainly wrong because the Central Zoo Authority is a statutory regulator of zoos, not a research institute that could lead an ecosystem-services vertical. Statements 1 and 3 fit the platform's design: a survey and analysis vertical led by the Botanical Survey of India, and a capacity-building vertical led by IIFM Bhopal. I could not check the official vertical list offline, so confidence is moderate to high rather than absolute.
topic_notes:
NIRANTAR is a MoEFCC-led platform that networks the ministry's research, survey, training and academic institutions so they work together on natural-resource management, climate adaptation and ecological resilience. Instead of institutes working in silos, it organises them into thematic verticals, each with a lead institute. The verticals are ecosystem survey and analysis, research and management of ecosystem services, and capacity development support. Policy and knowledge-support functions may also feature, so check the official list.

Institutes under MoEFCC that UPSC often asks about:
- Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata, est. 1890.
- Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata, est. 1916.
- Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE), Dehradun.
- Indian Institute of Forest Management (IIFM), Bhopal, est. 1982.
- Wildlife Institute of India (WII), Dehradun, est. 1982.
- Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun, which publishes the biennial India State of Forest Report.
- Central Zoo Authority (CZA), New Delhi.
- National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA).
- National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Chennai.
- Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
- Indian Plywood Industries Research and Training Institute (IPIRTI), Bengaluru.
- G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment (GBPNIHE), Almora.
- National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), Chennai.
- Salim Ali Centre for Ornithology and Natural History (SACON), Coimbatore.

Likely angles for future questions are which institute is under which ministry, the statutory basis of each body (CZA under the Wildlife Act; NBA under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002; NTCA under the Wildlife Act), headquarters locations, and the concept of ecosystem services. Ecosystem services fall into provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural categories, as classified by the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment. Related national frameworks include the National Mission for a Green India, the National Action Plan on Climate Change, and the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.

question:
The Chancellor of the Federal Republic of go, Germany visited India in January, 2026. Which of the following is/are not correct in terms of outcomes of this visit ?
1. Signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the All India Institute of Ayurveda and_ the University of Hamburg
2. Signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on Youth Hockey Development between Hockey India and the German Hockey Federation
3. Establishment of a bilateral dialogue mechanism on the Indo-Pacific
4. Opening of an Honorary Consul of Germany in Lucknow Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: Questions of this type are answered from the MEA 'List of Outcomes' released after a bilateral visit. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited India in January 2026, with Gujarat and Bengaluru on his itinerary and talks with PM Modi. Such visits usually produce cooperation on defence, trade (the India-EU FTA context), green hydrogen, skilled-labour mobility, education and research, and sports or cultural exchanges. Indo-Pacific cooperation is normally handled through foreign-policy consultations and joint statements, so a 'dialogue mechanism' mention is plausible. A sports MoU such as the hockey one fits Germany's strength in the sport and the pattern of niche people-to-people outcomes. The two statements that look most like altered details are the Ayurveda MoU partner (the real partner may be a different German university) and the honorary consulate in Lucknow (a city-specific diplomatic opening that is unusual to announce on a Chancellor's visit). The exam logic is to find the outcome that was wrongly attributed or invented. Because this question tests recall of an outcome list, verify against the MEA document before relying on it in a permanent note.
explanations: (a) 2 and 3: wrong under the provisional key, because these two are treated as genuine outcomes.
(b) 1 and 4: matches the unofficial key and is the provisional answer, with the caveat that it is not verified against the MEA list.
(c) 3 and 4: wrong under the key, because statement 3 is treated as a genuine outcome.
(d) 1 only: wrong under the key, because statement 4 is also treated as not an outcome.
keyfact: For 'outcomes of a visit' questions, check the MEA list of outcomes; here the provisional answer is (b), but it needs verification.
statements: 1 — Likely incorrect (unverified): the AIIA–University of Hamburg Ayurveda MoU does not match my recollection of the outcome list; the partner institution or the MoU itself may have been altered.
2 — Likely correct (unverified): a youth hockey development MoU between Hockey India and the German Hockey Federation fits the pattern of sports cooperation outcomes.
3 — Likely correct (unverified): an Indo-Pacific dialogue mechanism fits the strategic-partnership agenda, and the key treats it as a real outcome.
4 — Likely incorrect (unverified): opening an honorary consulate of Germany in Lucknow is not something I can recall as an outcome of the visit.
summary: The unofficial key (b), statements 1 and 4 not correct, is plausible but I could not independently confirm it from the official outcome list of Chancellor Merz's January 2026 visit. I am not confident enough to say it is wrong, so treat (b) as provisional until checked against the MEA outcomes document.

question: Which of the following statements about DHRUV64 is/are correct ? i It is the third chip fabricated under the DIR-V Programme with an overall aim to enable the creation of microprocessors 81. for India. 2: It is India’s first homegrown 1:0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core microprocessor. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: DHRUV64 is a microprocessor developed by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), under MeitY. It is part of the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) Programme, run under the Microprocessor Development Programme. The programme aims to build indigenous processors on the open-source RISC-V instruction set architecture, so that India depends less on imported chips and proprietary architectures such as ARM and x86. The earlier C-DAC VEGA series and IIT Madras's SHAKTI processors belong to the same push towards processor self-reliance. DHRUV64 is described as India's first homegrown 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core microprocessor, and it is aimed at applications such as telecom, automotive, consumer electronics, industrial automation and strategic uses. Because it is a 64-bit design, it can address much more memory than 32-bit designs. For elimination, the two statements are consistent with the DIR-V description, so options (a), (b) and (d) fail unless one statement is a distortion. Neither statement contains the usual UPSC twist, such as a wrong agency, a wrong clock speed or a wrong core count.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it treats statement 2 as incorrect, but the 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core description is accurate.
(b) Wrong: it treats statement 1 as incorrect, but DHRUV64 is placed under the DIR-V Programme as its third chip.
(c) Correct: both statements match the official description of DHRUV64, a C-DAC chip under DIR-V.
(d) Wrong: at least one statement is correct, and in fact both are.
keyfact: DHRUV64 = C-DAC's 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core RISC-V microprocessor, the third chip under the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) Programme.
statements: 1 — Correct: DHRUV64 is reported as the third chip fabricated under the DIR-V Programme, whose aim is to enable indigenous microprocessor creation for India.
2 — Correct: It is India's first indigenous 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core microprocessor, developed by C-DAC.
summary: The expected answer (c) appears correct: both statements are right. DHRUV64 is C-DAC's indigenous 1.0 GHz, 64-bit dual-core RISC-V microprocessor, and it is reported as the third chip fabricated under the Digital India RISC-V (DIR-V) Programme. I am confident about statement 2 but only fairly confident about the 'third chip' count in statement 1, which I am taking from memory of press reports.

ocr: The Bureau of Indian Standard (BIS) recently introduced a national standard to test and assess bomb disposal system. Which of the following statements with regard to this system is/are correct ? 1. The new standard is known as IS 19445 : 2025. 2: It will improve interoperability of equipment across agencies. 3. It was developed by TBRL, DRDO in collaboration with the 30 Central Scientific Research Institute, Russia. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) 1,2and3 (b) 2and 83 only (c) land 2 only (d) lonly *X’, born in the UK, was conferred the Nobel Prize in 2025. He was a professor
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret and John M. Martinis. They were honoured for discovering macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit. Their work used superconducting circuits with Josephson junctions, showing that quantum effects appear in a chip-sized, human-scale system. This underpins superconducting qubits in quantum computing. Clarke was born in Cambridge, UK, and worked at UC Berkeley, so he fits both clues. Elimination: the 2025 Chemistry Nobel went to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs). Robson is British-born but was a professor at the University of Melbourne, Australia, not in America. The 2025 Economics prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for innovation-driven growth. Mokyr was born in the Netherlands and teaches at Northwestern. Devoret shared the Physics prize but was born in France, and he is associated with Yale and UC Santa Barbara. So 'born in the UK' plus 'professor in an American university' leaves only Clarke.
explanations: Incorrect: Michel Devoret shared the 2025 Physics Nobel, but he was born in Paris, France, not the UK.
Incorrect: Richard Robson was born in the UK and won the 2025 Chemistry Nobel for MOFs, but he was a professor at the University of Melbourne, Australia, not in an American university.
Correct: John Clarke was born in the UK, was a professor at UC Berkeley, and shared the 2025 Physics Nobel for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
Incorrect: Joel Mokyr won the 2025 Economics prize. He was born in the Netherlands and is at Northwestern University, USA, so the UK birth clue fails.
keyfact: Nobel Physics 2025: John Clarke (UK-born, UC Berkeley), Michel Devoret and John Martinis, for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits.
summary: The answer is (c) John Clarke, so the unofficial key is correct. I have taken Q80 to be the Nobel Prize 'X' question, since the image shows two questions. Clarke was born in the UK, was a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q81.
ocr: The Bureau of Indian Standard (BIS) recently introduced a national standard to test and assess bomb disposal system. Which of the following statements with regard to this system is/are correct ? 1. The new standard is known as IS 19445 : 2025. 2: It will improve interoperability of equipment across agencies. 3. It was developed by TBRL, DRDO in collaboration with the 30 Central Scientific Research Institute, Russia. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) 1,2and3 (b) 2and 83 only (c) land 2 only (d) lonly *X’, born in the UK, was conferred the Nobel Prize in 2025. He was a professor
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is India's national standards body, set up under the BIS Act, 2016 and working under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. It publishes Indian Standards (IS numbers) through technical committees. These include experts from user agencies, research labs and industry. The new standard for testing and assessing bomb disposal systems is IS 19445:2025. It lays down common test and performance criteria for equipment such as robotic bomb disposal systems. This is expected to give uniform quality benchmarks, support indigenous manufacturing and make equipment interoperable across police, paramilitary and defence agencies. Terminal Ballistics Research Laboratory (TBRL), Chandigarh, is a DRDO lab and is a plausible contributor of technical expertise. Statement 3 adds a collaboration with the '30th Central Scientific Research Institute, Russia', which is a made-up, trap-style detail. The standard was a BIS/domestic technical committee effort with no such Russian partner. Elimination: once statement 3 is rejected, options (a) and (b) fall. Statement 2 is a logical outcome of standardisation, so it is correct and (d) falls. That leaves (c). Note that this reasoning relies on recall of the BIS release, not on a source I checked here.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes statement 3, which wrongly credits a Russian institute.
(b) Wrong: it excludes statement 1, which is correct, and includes statement 3, which is incorrect.
(c) Right: statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect.
(d) Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, and interoperability is a core aim of standardisation.
keyfact: BIS standard IS 19445:2025 sets test and assessment norms for bomb disposal systems. It was issued by BIS, with no Russian co-developer.
statements: 1 — Correct: The new BIS standard is designated IS 19445:2025.
2 — Correct: Common test and assessment criteria improve interoperability and uniform quality of bomb disposal equipment across agencies.
3 — Incorrect: It was issued by BIS through its technical committee, and the collaboration with a Russian '30th Central Scientific Research Institute' is not supported.
summary: Taking the first question on the page (the BIS bomb disposal standard) as Q81, the answer is (c) 1 and 2 only, so the unofficial key holds. Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because the standard was issued by BIS through its technical committee, not co-developed with a Russian institute. The second question on the page (Nobel 2025, John Clarke) also has answer (c).

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to the Grand Slam Tennis Tournaments is/are correct ?
1. The tournaments have a_ shared governance structure establishing the partnership among the four Grand Slam tournaments.
2. They are open for entry to all internationally ranked tennis players above the age of 14.
3. There is a limitation on the number of ‘Wild Cards’ a player may receive to compete in a Grand Slam Tournament. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The four Grand Slams are the Australian Open (January, Melbourne), the French Open (Roland Garros, May-June, clay), Wimbledon (July, grass, the oldest, from 1877) and the US Open (August-September, hard court). They are run by four separate national bodies: Tennis Australia, the Fédération Française de Tennis, the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, and the USTA. Since the 1990s they have coordinated through the Grand Slam Board (earlier the Grand Slam Committee), which handles shared rules, prize-money and anti-doping or integrity matters with the ITF. So statement 1 is correct. Entry is mainly by ATP/WTA ranking, with qualifying draws and wild cards, and the ITF age-eligibility rules set a minimum of about 14 for professional play, which supports statement 2. Wild cards are discretionary invitations by the host organisers, and the limit applies to how many each tournament can issue, roughly eight in each singles main draw. No rule caps how many times a player can receive one, so statement 3 fails. Elimination: rejecting statement 3 removes (b) and (d), leaving (a) and (c). Statement 2 is the deciding one, and it matches the ranking and age-eligibility framework, so (a) is preferred.
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 hold, and statement 3 is the only false one. This is the best fit.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which misstates the wild-card rule as a per-player limit, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.

Wrong: statement 1 is true, but this option ignores statement 2, which reflects the ranking-based entry and minimum-age framework. This is the only rival to (a), and it fails only if statement 2 is read strictly.
Wrong: it includes statement 3. Wild cards are limited per tournament, not per player.
keyfact: The four Slams are coordinated through the Grand Slam Board, and wild cards are limited per tournament, not per player.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only: the combination of the Grand Slam Board governance link and ranking/age-based open entry. It reflects how the four majors (Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, US Open) are separately owned yet coordinated. Entry is by ATP/WTA ranking, qualifying and wild cards under the ITF age-eligibility rules. This is the option selected as the answer.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only: it pairs the open-entry statement with the wild-card cap. The cap, though, applies to tournaments (about eight main-draw wild cards per singles event), not to individual players. It also drops the shared-governance fact. Wild cards are used to give home players, juniors and returning champions a place in the draw. This option is wrong.

Option (c), 1 only: it accepts only the governance statement. The Grand Slam Board is the joint forum of the four majors, formed from the earlier Grand Slam Committee, and it works with the ITF, ATP and WTA. It would be right only if statement 2's age and ranking wording were judged inaccurate, since Slams also admit unranked players via wild cards.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: it takes all three statements as true. Statement 3 is false because wild cards are capped per event, not per player. The Slams give a fixed number of wild cards to host-nation players, juniors and former champions. Players such as Ivanišević (2001) and Clijsters (2009) show that wild-card entrants can go all the way.
related: Wimbledon, the oldest Slam, began in 1877 and is played on grass.
The French Open is the only Slam on clay.
Rod Laver won the calendar Grand Slam twice, in 1962 and 1969.
Novak Djokovic holds the men's record of 24 Slam singles titles.
Rohan Bopanna won the 2024 Australian Open men's doubles, the oldest to do so.
The ITF is the global governing body of tennis and was founded in 1913.
Wild cards are discretionary entries given by the host tournament.
statements: 1 — Correct: the Grand Slam Board is a shared governance body linking the four majors. The Grand Slam Board coordinates the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and US Open. It grew out of the Grand Slam Committee, set up in the late 1980s and 1990s to speak with one voice on rules, prize money, calendar and drug-testing. Each tournament is owned by a different body (Tennis Australia, FFT, AELTC, USTA), yet they cooperate with the ITF, ATP and WTA. The ITF's Rules of Tennis and a common Grand Slam Rulebook keep the four events largely uniform.

2 — Correct (with the caveat that it is loosely worded): entry is by ranking and is open to eligible players at or above the ITF minimum age of about 14. Direct entry into the 128-player singles draw is by ATP/WTA ranking. The rest of the field comes from 16 or 32 qualifiers and wild cards. The ITF Age Eligibility Rule limits how much 14-17 year olds may play on the pro circuit. Players below 18 are restricted in tournaments, and full freedom comes at 18. Teenagers such as Coco Gauff (Wimbledon 2019, aged 15) have entered via qualifying.

3 — Incorrect: the limit is on how many wild cards a tournament may give, not on how many a player may receive. Wild cards are discretionary entries awarded by the host federation, typically to home-country players, rising juniors, or past champions. Each Slam gets about eight in the men's and women's singles main draws, plus some for qualifying. Reciprocal wild-card arrangements exist between the Slams. A player can receive wild cards repeatedly, since there is no personal cap. Famous wild-card finalists or winners include Goran Ivanišević (Wimbledon 2001 champion) and Kim Clijsters, who returned in 2009.
summary: The best answer is (a), 1 and 2 only. The four Slams share governance through the Grand Slam Board, and entry is open to ranked players meeting the ITF minimum age of about 14. Statement 3 is wrong because wild cards are limited per tournament (the organisers allot a fixed number), not per player. I cannot say with certainty that the unofficial key (a) is wrong, so I keep it.
topic_notes: The Grand Slams (Majors) are the four most prestigious tennis events. Australian Open: January, Melbourne Park, hard court. French Open: May-June, Roland Garros, clay. Wimbledon: late June-July, All England Club, grass, and the oldest, begun in 1877. US Open: late August-September, Flushing Meadows, hard court. A calendar Grand Slam means winning all four in one year. Don Budge did it in 1938, Rod Laver in 1962 and 1969, Maureen Connolly in 1953, Margaret Court in 1970 and Steffi Graf in 1988 (the Golden Slam, including Olympic gold). Novak Djokovic holds the record of 24 men's singles Slams, and Margaret Court has 24 in women's singles. Draw size is 128 in singles, with 32 seeds. Matches are best of five sets for men and best of three for women, with final-set tie-breaks now standard at all Slams. Governance: each tournament is owned by a national federation or club and coordinated through the Grand Slam Board, which also works with the ITF (the world governing body, founded 1913, based in London), the ATP (men's tour) and the WTA (women's tour). Entry is by ranking, with qualifying draws and wild cards (discretionary entries decided by the host). Prize money, equal pay (since 2007 at all four Slams), electronic line-calling and anti-doping rules are standardised through shared bodies. India's record: Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi won doubles Slams, Sania Mirza won six Slam titles in doubles and mixed doubles, and Rohan Bopanna became the oldest men's doubles Slam champion at the 2024 Australian Open. UPSC can also ask about the Davis Cup, the Billie Jean King Cup, the ATP Finals, the Olympic tennis format and the Hawk-Eye technology.

question: Which one of the following pairs of semiconductor plants in India and their locations is not correctly matched ?
options: CG Power and Industrial : Gujarat Solutions Pvt. Ltd. in partnership with Renesas Electronics and STARS Microelectronics
Tata Semiconductor : Assam Assembly and Test Pvt. Ltd
HCL-Foxconn Joint : Madhya Venture India Chip Ltd. Pradesh
subject: Science & Tech
detail: India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), under the Digital India Corporation and MeitY, runs the Rs 76,000 crore Programme for Development of Semiconductors and Display Ecosystem approved in December 2021. Projects approved by the Union Cabinet include: Micron's ATMP unit at Sanand, Gujarat; Tata Electronics' fab with PSMC at Dholera, Gujarat; Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test (TSAT) at Jagiroad, Morigaon, Assam; CG Power with Renesas and Stars Microelectronics at Sanand, Gujarat; Kaynes Semicon at Sanand, Gujarat. In 2025 further approvals followed: SiCSem (with Clas-SiC, UK) for silicon carbide compound semiconductors in Odisha (Bhubaneswar), 3D Glass Solutions in Odisha, ASIP Technologies in Andhra Pradesh, and the HCL-Foxconn joint venture at Jewar, Uttar Pradesh. Elimination logic: Gujarat, Assam and Odisha matches are well known, so the odd one out is the Madhya Pradesh match. Remember the state for each project, since such pairs are repeatedly tested.
explanations: Correctly matched: CG Power with Renesas and Stars Microelectronics has an OSAT unit at Sanand, Gujarat.
Correctly matched: Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test Pvt. Ltd is at Jagiroad, Morigaon, Assam.
Not correctly matched: the HCL-Foxconn JV (India Chip Pvt Ltd) is at Jewar, Uttar Pradesh, not Madhya Pradesh. This is the answer.
Correctly matched: SiCSem Pvt. Ltd. is setting up a silicon carbide fab and packaging unit in Odisha.
keyfact: HCL-Foxconn chip unit is at Jewar, Uttar Pradesh, not Madhya Pradesh.
option_notes: CG Power and Industrial Solutions, a Murugappa Group company, partners with Japan's Renesas Electronics and Thailand's Stars Microelectronics. It is setting up an OSAT pilot line at Sanand, Gujarat, approved in February 2024 with an investment of about Rs 7,600 crore. It targets chips for consumer, automotive, industrial and power applications, and it is one of the first approved OSAT projects.

Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test Pvt. Ltd (TSAT) is a Tata Electronics unit at Jagiroad, Morigaon, Assam, approved in February 2024 with investment of about Rs 27,000 crore. It does advanced packaging and assembly (wire bond, flip chip, ISIP) for automotive, EV, consumer electronics and mobile uses. It is a major semiconductor project in the Northeast and is separate from Tata's Dholera fab in Gujarat.
